Series set for epic finale as Aussie batters must stand up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:21:19 UTC
06:21:19 KST

Although doubts have been expressed in the last few days that the Cape Town speed gun is operating with flawless accuracy, late on day four of the third Test there appeared to be some validity to its claim that Mitchell Starc had breached the 150km/h barrier.
Soon after, one couldn't help thinking of that speedometer figure — illegal in a car, faintly alarming in a sporting arena — and wince. One of Starc's typically brutish bouncers had spat up off the Newlands pitch and was rearing towards a Proteas batsman.
In the split second it took him to realise his gloves would soon be in the ball's path, and having prized his wicket all day, Ryan Rickelton got his hands out of the way on the understanding the ball would cannon into his ribs with that horrifying thud only a rare breed of cricketer accepts as his duty. And boy did it thud.
There was a time not long ago when the done thing in such situations was to grit one's teeth and pretend it hadn't happened. Think David Boon's thousand-yard stare, or Justin Langer grinning sans tooth. Not Rickelton.
He was on 92 by that point, hours into a game-turning innings, and knew that if a nasty bruise was blossoming, there was no point in pretending it wasn't so. Up came his shirt and sure enough, the mark was already ranking high on the Brian Close scale.
Rickelton showed it off to Travis Head at short leg, either for confirmation or possibly approval of its nastiness. Head seemed to offer both.
It is one of those unspoken paradoxes of Test cricket: the more two teams respect each other, the more they try to hurt each other, and vice versa. As they had the previous evening, and for the telling first two-thirds of the fourth day, Australia's bowlers had been throwing everything at Rickelton and none of it was working.
In the end, it took a run-out to remove him — moments after he brought up a century that slowly but surely ruined Australia's hopes of a quick kill. Rickelton already has a Test double century to his name.
He is a world champion. But here was the sort of high-stakes, backs-to-the-wall performance that can define a career.
As a result, from 4-140 at the start of the day, South Africa piled on 387 to convincingly rebut suggestions they'd roll over. For the third time in the series, a Test between these two proud cricket nations will go down to the fifth day.
The pressure is now all on Australia, who will need to chase down 288 runs to win and retain the status of world number one, with Kagiso Rabada, Marco Jansen and Simon Harmer licking their lips at the prospect of series-winning wickets.
That Australia's task is so onerous is mostly a result of Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder's 154-run partnership for the sixth wicket, which stretched across 53 overs after Matthew Breetzke's dismissal for a spiky, counterpunching 43 in the morning.
Mulder was no second fiddle. After Rickelton departed for a brave and controlled 101 from 219 deliveries, Mulder carried on with a faltering tail, scattering fielders and clubbing sixes to reach a superb 115 of his own.
The above numbers should not give the impression the Australian attack misfired, per se, nor that Australia lacked intent. Until the last minute of the day, they fielded with great gusto to create pressure and affect run-outs to make up for the lack of help from the pitch.
All day, Nathan Lyon bowled with guile and control, jagging the ball at right angles.
It was just that for almost as long, Rickelton and Mulder defied him with the disciplined application of a solid plan: put your ego to one side, get back and across, don't hit against the spin, concede Lyon's end in the knowledge that the quicks at the other end would not get as much help from the surface.
Of the latter, Starc, in particular, gave everything of himself and more, and as late as the final half-hour of play was literally bowling himself off his feet to try and take South Africa's final wicket.
His nine dismissals for the game on a pitch that has offered him little represented a superhuman endeavour.
Where Australia can be faulted, perhaps, is for squandering the second new ball. South Africa was 5-222 when it arrived and there was no repeat of Starc's first-innings clean-up job.
In a day of thankless toil, skipper Pat Cummins broke his wicket drought but otherwise rarely threatened, only claiming his second when Mulder holed out in the final over of the day.
Again, there were industrial quantities of interpersonal drama, although nothing that crossed the line. Hyped up and a little uncoordinated between the wickets, Breetzke tangled with Lyon and spoiled for battles with every other bowler, including a prolonged one-way conversation with Starc.
Loading Twitter content
After taking the bails to run out Rickelton, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted down the pitch like a terrier in the Crufts dog show to let Mulder know it was his fault.
Of course, Labuschagne and others will need their bats to do the talking on the final day, and there is a sense that Rabada will not miss out twice in one game, even without his muse Steve Smith around to get his blood boiling.
A week ago, one might have asked: who will be Australia's Rickelton and Mulder? But all of a sudden, there are a few more convincing answers.
So, a gripping Test series — worthy in every way of its billing as a de facto world title — will now get its fitting conclusion.

Hypersonic Missile Interceptors for Patriot: USA Allocates $660 Million to Develop PAC-3 Edge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:15:51 UTC
06:15:51 KST

The U.S. Army has signed an agreement with Lockheed Martin to support the development of new missiles for the Patriot systems, the PAC-3 Edge, designed to intercept hypersonic targets as part of the Future Interceptor program.
This was reported by the U.S. Army Public Affairs Office.
The total estimated cost of the project is $1.08 billion, of which $660.4 million is government funding and $423 million will be raised by the company itself as part of a co-funding arrangement.
The Future Interceptor is being developed to counter modern, ever-changing air and missile threats by increasing interception range and altitude, boosting speed, and improving maneuverability.
Under the terms of the agreement, the U.S. Army, in collaboration with Lockheed Martin, will continue to develop prototypes and conduct testing and evaluation to determine whether the system’s performance meets established operational requirements.
Further decisions regarding development and production will be made based on the actual performance of the prototypes, operational requirements, available resources, and relevant procurement procedures.
Lockheed Martin clarified in its press release that these funds will be directed specifically toward the development of the PAC-3 Edge anti-aircraft missiles.
The new interceptor was developed as a further evolution of the PAC-3 MSE anti-aircraft missiles. The missile features a new multi-pulse solid-fuel rocket motor manufactured by Northrop Grumman and an improved guidance system.
One of the key components of the PAC-3 Edge will be a new homing seeker, which is being developed at Lockheed Martin’s Strigo Product Center.
The company notes that it has invested $250 million in this center to implement new homing technologies designed to improve the accuracy and maneuverability of the interceptors.
Testing of the PAC-3 Edge is scheduled to begin in 2027. The interceptor is expected to be ready for deployment by 2031.
The new interceptor missile is intended to integrate with the U.S. Army’s existing and future integrated air and missile defense systems, including the IBCS combat command system, the M903 launcher, containerized launchers, and HIMARS Flex.

UK govt announces new ‘safe and legal’ routes for refugees in India to resettle in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:15:21 UTC
06:15:21 KST

UK announces three new refugee resettlement routes for people in India and six other countries, allowing sponsorship through charities, employers and universities.
TOI correspondent from London: In a bid to dissuade asylum-seekers from arriving in Britain on the backs of lorries or via small boats, the UK home office has announced three new “safe and legal” sponsorship routes for refugees in India and six other countries to come to the UK and claim asylum.The new routes are initially targeted at refugees who have sought protection in India, Bangladesh, Egypt, Kenya, Malaysia, Pakistan and Uganda.To be eligible, the refugees will need to be outside their country of nationality, to have been verified by the UNHCR as meeting the definition of refugee and to have registered with the UNHCR or relevant authorities in one of these seven countries before Oct 1. So, in India’s case, it could be Tibetans, Sri Lankan Tamils, Afghans, Rohingya and others from Myanmar, who could be eligible for these routes, but not Indian nationals residing in India, nor internally displaced people.The refugee sponsorship routes, modelled on a similar programme in Canada, allow sponsors in the UK to identify refugees they wish to sponsor. The new routes are named community sponsorship, which enables UK charities to identify refugees they wish to sponsor; refugee work, which enables UK employers to sponsor and provide refugees jobs; and refugee study, which enables UK universities to sponsor refugees to study in the UK.
Once resettled, the refugees will have an immediate right to work, study and to access welfare benefits in Britain and be placed on a five-year path to permanent resettlement.Sponsors will have to finance and provide their accommodation, the aim being to reduce the amount UK’s govt spends on asylum hotels.Applications to be sponsors for the community and study route have opened and the first arrivals are expected in autumn 2027. Applications under the work route will open in spring 2027.Both Reform UK and the Conservatives vowed to shut the scheme if they come to power. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said until illegal migration is stopped, “we should not be creating new routes into the UK for asylum claimants”.

Tusk-Nawrocki battle escalates as chief judge is ousted from Poland’s top court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:12:50 UTC
06:12:50 KST

Poland’s constitutional court descended into turmoil Friday evening as judges barred from hearing cases moved to oust the institution’s nationalist-linked leadership, sparking accusations of a coup and tense protests.
Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge with the court, ordered its president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy to be suspended for a month and announced she was taking charge. Święczkowski rejected her authority, accusing those involved of a “coup d’état,” while his deputy was turned away at the building’s gates.
The showdown marks an escalation in Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s struggle to undo the judicial overhaul carried out by the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) former government. During its eight years in power, PiS filled the Constitutional Tribunal with its appointees, including Święczkowski and his deputy, placing it at the heart of Poland’s confrontation with Brussels over the rule of law.
Advertisement
Outside the tribunal, protesters clashed with police, who said objects had been thrown at officers and three people detained after climbing over the court’s fence. Police said they had deployed to maintain security following warnings of threats to judges and staff, but had not entered the building.
PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński took part in the protest and tried to force his way into the court building. He accused Tusk of staging a “coup” against the court and turning Poland into a “police state,” and demanded presidential intervention.
President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally and rival of Tusk, interrupted his official trip to Senegal, declaring, “At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland.”
Tusk was defiant. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote on X. “After years of PiS lawlessness, it’s a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
But efforts to change the court’s makeup have met resistance. Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority. They took their oaths in parliament instead, but Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.
Advertisement
Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek blamed the turmoil on Święczkowski, who he accused of turning the institution into his “private fiefdom” and preventing newly elected judges from doing their jobs.
“And now the judges have spoken,” Żurek told POLITICO.
Żurek, who also serves as Poland’s prosecutor general, said he submitted five requests to lift the immunity of Święczkowski and his deputy, backed by 50 volumes of case files. He defended Korwin-Piotrowska’s move as a decision by a legally appointed judge, insisting that the government had nothing to do with it.

Iran reports three tanker mine strikes in Hormuz; U.S. disputes claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:12:25 UTC
06:12:25 KST

Iran reports three tanker mine strikes in Hormuz; U.S. disputes claims
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Friday that three oil tankers, including a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, had struck naval mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, claims disputed by the United States and not independently verified, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
According to the IRGC Navy, the supertanker struck a mine while traveling along a southern shipping route that Tehran considers unauthorized. The resulting explosion reportedly set the vessel ablaze, forcing its abandonment near the entrance to the strait. Iranian authorities described it as the third tanker to suffer an explosion on Friday while attempting to transit routes not approved by Tehran.
Earlier in the day, the IRGC Navy reported that two other tankers had caught fire after allegedly striking mines in the waterway. It claimed the vessels had disabled their navigation and positioning systems and ignored repeated radio warnings before the incidents. Iranian authorities did not identify the ships, their operators or flag states, and provided no information about the crews. The reported mine strikes have not been independently confirmed.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) rejected Iranian claims that commercial vessels were striking naval mines, maintaining that American forces had cleared all internationally recognized primary transit routes through the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military said those routes remained free of sea mines and continued to be used by commercial shipping.
Oman’s Maritime Security Center reported that the Royal Navy of Oman had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged commercial vessel following an attack that caused a fire off the coast of Musandam Governorate. The crew members received medical care following their evacuation. Omani authorities did not identify those responsible for the attack or provide details about the vessel’s condition. It remains unclear whether the incident was connected to any of the tanker fires reported by Iran.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) also reported that a tanker traveling through the Strait of Hormuz was attacked Thursday, approximately 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. A small boat reportedly approached the vessel and attached two explosive devices to its hull, triggering blasts that caused an engine-room fire and temporarily disabled the tanker. UKMTO subsequently reported that the fire had been extinguished, all crew members were safe and the vessel had resumed its journey. No environmental damage was reported.
The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global oil and gas shipments and has faced mounting security threats since the United States and Israel launched military operations against Iran on February 28. Tehran has repeatedly warned that vessels attempting to cross the waterway without its authorization could face attacks, while Washington maintains that internationally recognized shipping routes remain navigable.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that several oil tankers had caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after reportedly striking naval mines three weeks ago.

Bhutan GLOF creates new lake downstream, raises fears of secondary hazards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:11:49 UTC
06:11:49 KST

Bengal spared Bhutan GLOF impact, water of Sankosh recedes
DEHRADUN/KOLKATA/GUWAHATI: A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) originating in Bhutan, which prompted an alert across parts of Assam and West Bengal on Friday, has led to the formation of a new temporary lake downstream, raising concerns about a possible secondary hazard.Bhutan’s National Centre for Hydrology and Meteorology (NCHM) confirmed that the outburst had led to the creation of a new artificial lake at Taktsemakhang, situated at the confluence of Sintaphu Chhu and Lungu Chhu, also known as Gangchen Tag Chhu. The newly formed body of water is being monitored for any potential secondary flood hazard, with NCHM advising residents in the Mochhu and Punatsangchhu river valleys to remain vigilant and avoid riverbanks and low-lying areas.The Oct 29 GLOF originated from Shintaphu glacial lake which, according to International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) estimates, contained 6 to 7 million cubic metres of water, equivalent to approximately 2,400-2,800 Olympic-size swimming pools, before the breach. The volume of water released remains under assessment. India’s Central Water Commission (CWC) subsequently issued a special flood advisory for West Bengal and Assam, warning that water levels in Alipurduar and Dhubri districts could rise sharply as floodwaters moved downstream through the Sankosh river system.
West Bengal had issued a high alert across north Bengal but the GLOF has had little or no impact in the state. On Friday morning, as water from the Bhutan hills came downstream, the Sankosh river rose 1.5 metres from its normal level but began receding soon. By Friday afternoon it appeared the crisis was over and people who had taken refuge in flood centres returned to their homes. No damage was reported. The Alipurduar district administration had opened 18 flood shelters in Kumargramduar block on Thursday night and around 10,000 people living along the banks of the Sankosh in Kumargram tea estate, Kumargram forest village, Pakriguri and Bholka had taken refuge in these shelters along with a couple of thousand from Assam.Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said the state was closely monitoring the possible impact of the glacial lake outburst across all vulnerable revenue circles of Dhubri and Kokrajhar districts. “Our teams … are ready to respond if needed. Residents are requested to stay alert, follow official updates and cooperate with officials,” he said.According to Bhutan’s national daily “Kuensel”, the GLOF sent floodwaters down the Mochhu river, damaging roads, bridges and public infrastructure in Gasa and Punakha. No casualties have been reported. Floodwaters washed away facilities at Gasa Tshachu, damaged sections of the Punakha-Gasa Secondary National Highway and the Gasa-Laya road, and swept away a Bailey bridge in Punakha built in 2022 with Indian support.Ashim Sattar, a glacial hazard expert at IIT Bhubaneswar, told TOI that the formation of temporary lakes downstream is a known risk during such disasters. “During GLOFs, powerful floodwaters erode river valleys and carry large amounts of debris, which can temporarily block river channels and form new lakes. Such lakes generally drain naturally, but they can also become secondary flood hazards if not regularly monitored,” Sattar said.He explained that Shintaphu was a medium-sized glacial lake located close to the Lunana glacial lake complex, a cluster of four lakes, including Thorthormi, considered one of Bhutan’s most hazardous.According to NCHM, the flood crossed Taktsemakhang around 8.27 pm on Thursday. Warning sirens along Mochhu and downstream Punatsangchhu were activated as monitoring stations recorded a sharp rise in river levels. At Yebesa, the water level peaked at 6.7 m at 11 pm before receding to a normal level of 2.84 m around 12.30 am on Friday, a drop of 3.86 m within 90 minutes.Sattar noted that timely activation of the regional early-warning network prevented loss of life.
The incident highlights the growing threat of cascading disasters in the Himalayas, where an initial glacial breach can trigger secondary hazards downstream through valley erosion, sediment deposition and temporary river blockages.Previous assessments by ICIMOD and UNDP identified 47 major potentially dangerous glacial lakes (PDGLs) across the transboundary Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins. Current estimates show that 388 GLOFs have been documented across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, including Karakoram and the central and eastern Himalayas.In 2015, a GLOF in the headwaters of the Mo Chuu river, where Sintaphu lake is located, prompted Bhutanese authorities to work with the SERVIR-Himalaya initiative to assess glacial lake risks in the catchment, according to experts at ICIMOD.

Russian victories, Spanish tragedy, elections without answers: RT stories that shaped the week

Russian victories, Spanish tragedy, elections without answers: RT stories that shaped the week
Russia’s diplomatic victories
Four years of unprecedented sanctions and an active conflict didn’t deter four dozen African nations from sending delegations to Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit this week. Forty-eight out of Africa’s 54 countries were represented at the summit, 22 of them by their heads of state.
More than 60 bilateral and multilateral agreements were signed, including a Russia-Africa Action Plan for 2027-2029, and a joint declaration opposing unilateral sanctions and the unlawful seizure of civilian shipping, pledging deeper counter-terrorism cooperation, and supporting increased African representation on the UN Security Council. RT covered the summit minute-by minute, and broke down Putin’s plan to help bring about the “second awakening” of Africa.
Before he welcomed the African delegations to Moscow, Putin held a rare phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb – a figure repeatedly floated as a potential EU envoy to Russia – and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. Putin later said that Russia welcomes “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations,” and while the call brought the Russia/Ukraine conflict no closer to an end, Russian analyst Sergey Strokan noted that it should serve as a warning to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky that “metal fatigue is setting in across Europe’s political machinery – and that time is running out for the regime in Kiev.”
With the EU nowhere to be seen, and Stubb and Store incurring the wrath of their fellow European leaders for even daring to speak to Putin, the tone in the US could not be more different. There, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov touched down in Atlanta for a meeting of G20 foreign ministers on Friday. Sanctions on Russian diesel exports have been lifted, trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev, and Washington are slated for next month, and Putin has been invited to the G20 leaders’ meeting in Florida in December. However, the most tangible result of Russian-American diplomacy came 5,000 miles away from Washington, in the besieged town of Alyoshki.
The Alyoshki breakthrough
Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region last Friday, with both sides agreeing to suspend all military operations to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for civilian evacuations.
The Kremlin confirmed this week that the ceasefire was coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump, who said she was moved by the plight of Alyoshki’s “elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water.”
Ukraine had accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving the embattled town, but residents who escaped earlier this month told RT that Alyoshki was besieged by Ukrainian forces, who carried out drone attacks on vehicles carrying food, fuel, and medicine.
As Russian forces got to work clearing mines from the roads surrounding Alyoshki, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the humanitarian truce, if successful, “could set a precedent” for other areas. The interactions between Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, who worked together on the ceasefire, certainly seem to confirm that cooperation is possible.
Three elections, fewer answers
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva narrowly defeated right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday, in the first of three major elections this week. After a first-round loss to Bolsonaro, whose father was jailed last year Brazil’s Lula-aligned Supreme Federal Court, Lula won the runoff election by a margin of 51.79% to 48.21%, securing a fourth term in office.
The drama did not end when the votes were counted. Bolsonaro was ordered by the court to surrender his passports the following day, but he instead fled Brazil to the US, with the help of Argentina’s right-wing government. After landing in Florida, Bolsonaro accused Lula of fraud, declared himself “the leader of Brazil,” and pledged to “lead the opposition” from abroad.
US President Donald Trump is a close ally of Bolsonaro, and it remains unclear whether Washington will turn up the diplomatic pressure on Lula in the wake of the election.
Hours after Lula claimed victory in Brazil, former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic lost his bid to extend his party’s decade in power. Serbia’s Student List defeated Vucic’s SNS party by 53.03% to 38.97%, and despite accusing the students of doing the “dirty work” of “various European countries and the American deep state,” Vucic conceded and congratulated his opponents.
Although the Student List entered politics as an outgrowth of youth-led protests, its base is broader than similar pro-Western movements in the region. Student List representative Jovo Bakic told RT that his party will not sever relations with Russia or impose sanctions on Moscow, while representative Radomir Saicic has promised to negotiate long-term gas contracts with Russia.
However, the Student List has not yet chosen a candidate for prime minister, and Vucic has claimed that the party will walk back these promises in the coming months.
In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced voters on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack plunged Israel into a multi-front war. Netnayhu’s opponents – most of whom differ little with the prime minister on matters of war and national security – accused him of corruption, incompetence, and failure to heed forewarnings of October 7. These arguments succeeded in destroying Netanyahu’s right-wing majority, but left neither him nor the opposition bloc in a position to form a government.
Enter the Arabs. Israel’s Arab parties almost doubled their representation in parliament, and are now in a position to play kingmakers – if only Netanyahu’s opponents would work with them. This outcome is highly unlikely, and as RT Middle East correspondent Elizabeth Blade reported, the only certainty is that somebody will be left feeling betrayed.
Spain’s train tragedy
The collision of two high-speed trains near the Spanish city of Toledo on Wednesday was the country’s deadliest railway disaster in more than a decade. At least 69 people were killed and 179 injured when a high-speed Renfe AVE train struck a stationary Iryo train on the Madrid–Seville line.
The crash happened at a time of political crisis in Spain, after weeks of anti-government protests over housing and inflation. While the circumstances are still being investigated, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is already bearing the brunt of public anger, with the right-wing Vox party blaming Sanchez and the left-wing Frente Amplio coalition demanding political accountability.
Fires were set outside the Spanish Transport Ministry in Madrid on Wednesday night, at a protest organized by the far-right Falange and Revuelta groups. “How many more people have to die before we throw these murderers and traitors out of our institutions?” Falange spokesman Federico Campanero said in a speech.

How hard is it to recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:05:07 UTC
06:05:07 KST

How hard is it to recover the $6.3 billion hackers stole from Binance?
After hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange said Friday it is working to recover the assets, a multi-pronged process that experts said involves coordinating with law enforcement and tracking the movement of the stolen funds.
"Binance has begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.
Ari Redbord, a former federal prosecutor and the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company tracking the stolen funds, called the heist the "largest bank robbery in human history."
TRM and other security firms attributed the attack to an elite hacking unit linked with North Korea known as "TraderTraitor." The funds were siphoned from internet-connected wallets on Binance's trading platform, Redbord said. The entire operation took roughly 20 minutes, according to Binance.
"The way a cryptocurrency exchange works is basically just like a bank. People put their funds in the bank, and those funds go onto wallets that are controlled by the exchange," Redbord told CBS News. "What North Korea was able to do was breach the hot wallets where Binance was keeping all of those funds."
As it works to recover the stolen assets, Binance vowed in a social media post to cover the full losses using company funds.
"We will pursue all available avenues to identify those responsible and hold them accountable," Binance said.
How does the recovery process work?
Redbord called the effort to recover Binance customers' funds the "fastest and largest" he's ever seen.
The first step involved blocking the hackers from transferring the funds. Within an hour after the attack, stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether had frozen $2.4 billion of the stolen assets, he said. Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, also froze assets, according to TRM Labs.
Issuers of stablecoins — a type of cryptocurrency pegged to a stable asset, such as the U.S. dollar — can block transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world, speeding the recovery effort. A total of $3 billion in crypto assets have been frozen, the Binance spokesperson told CBS News.
However, roughly $2.4 billion in stolen funds consist of bitcoin and ether — those funds are now "beyond any issuer's reach," according to a blog post from TRM Labs.
Bitcoin and ether "move on public blockchains, and they cannot be frozen," Redbord said. "That is a very, very specific capability that [only certain] stablecoin issuers have."
The best shot at recovering those funds is if the thieves try to convert the crypto to regular currencies, including cash, he added.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
The cyberattackers are now likely laundering the stolen funds to evade detection by law enforcement, according to Redbord.
How long could it take to recoup the funds?
To actually recover the frozen funds, stablecoin issuers will start by moving the assets into a wallet that North Korea cannot access, he said.
"Law enforcement will follow up with what they call a 'seizure warrant,' which basically says we need you to actually physically transfer these funds to a U.S. government account," Redbord told CBS News.
After the funds are seized, government officials will have to pursue a civil forfeiture proceeding in court to recover the crypto assets.
"The government must show that the funds were associated with the activity at issue," Redbord said. "It is the final step before the funds can be taken permanently from the bad actor and given to the government or victims."
Any of the Binance funds that aren't recovered could be used by North Korea to carry out illicit transactions with countries like Russia, Roman Bieda, chief intelligence officer at Recoveris, a Swiss blockchain intelligence company, told CBS News.
"Freezing assets and recovering them are two very different things," he said. "North Korea has a history of using stolen cryptocurrency to circumvent international sanctions and finance its activities."
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
Given the scale of the Binance theft, it's unclear how long it could take for the crypto exchange to recoup the stolen assets. In one case, Bieda said his team worked for a Swiss client in which it took 14 months to recover $10.5 million in stolen crypto.
"The process remains unpredictable," he said in an email, emphasizing the close coordination required between law enforcement, crypto issuers and other stakeholders to track down the funds. Figuring out where the money went is only half the battle, he said.
"Knowing whom to contact and reaching them before the assets move again can make all the difference, and this is really challenging," Bieda said.

Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the tribunal late on Friday amid a heavy police presence, while right-wing politicians addressed the crowd accusing Tusk's government of carrying out a coup against the court.
"At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," Nawrocki said on X/Twitter.
New drama in long-running conflict over court
A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralyzed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognize appointees put forward by the other side.
Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors - the Law and Justice Party - of subverting.
"This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way," he said.
The dispute dates back to 2015, when the nationalist Law and Justice Party sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.
Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.
After Tusk's coalition took office in 2023, it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his election as president in 2025.
Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
Last month, the parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said undermined the government's stated goal of restoring checks and balances.

Swiss supreme court upholds Liberian ex-rebel commander’s 20-year sentence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:00:51 UTC
06:00:51 KST

Swiss supreme court upholds Liberian ex-rebel commander’s 20-year sentence
Alieu Kosiah killed civilians and unarmed soldiers, and ordered lootings and other crimes against humanity.
Switzerland’s supreme court upheld a 20-year jail sentence for former Liberian rebel commander Alieu Kosiah on Friday, but overturned a conviction for crimes against humanity.
In 2021, Switzerland’s Federal Criminal Court found Kosiah, now 51, guilty of multiple atrocities committed during the first of Liberia’s back-to-back civil wars, in which about 250,000 people died between 1989 and 2003.
In 2023, the court’s appeals chamber upheld his 20-year sentence for war crimes and, for the first time in Swiss history, also made a new ruling that Kosiah was guilty of crimes against humanity.
The Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland was asked to review the case, and its verdict, dated September 28, was published on Friday.
The court “rejected the appeal filed by a high-ranking Liberian military official challenging his conviction for violations of the laws of war committed between 1993 and 1995 during the first Liberian civil war”, it said in a statement.
“However, the court has acquitted the individual of the charge of crimes against humanity, based on a strict application of the principle of non-retroactivity.”
Switzerland recognises the principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows it to prosecute individuals suspected of international crimes, regardless of where those crimes were committed.
The court said the offence of crimes against humanity – introduced into Swiss law in 2011 – could not be applied to acts committed before then.
Kosiah’s conviction for violating the law of war was upheld, as was the maximum 20-year custodial sentence imposed.
“The decision makes final the first war crimes conviction ever handed down by a Swiss civilian court, and the first conviction anywhere of a Liberian for war crimes committed during the country’s civil wars,” said the Swiss organisation Civitas Maxima, which works to bring perpetrators of international crimes to justice.
Kosiah settled in Switzerland in the late 1990s and was arrested in 2014.
“Today the survivors of Alieu Kosiah’s crimes have final justice,” said Civitas Maxima director Alain Werner, who represents victims in the case.
“We are, however, deeply disappointed by the acquittal on crimes against humanity. What happened in Lofa between 1993 and 1995 is the very definition of a crime against humanity.”
Like war crimes, crimes against humanity refer to atrocities, including murder, torture and rape. However, instead of isolated or sporadic events, the charge is used for incidents carried out in a widespread or systematic way.
In the 2021 verdict, Kosiah was found guilty of a slew of war crimes committed as commander of the United Liberation Movement of Liberia for Democracy rebel group.
He ordered or participated in the killing of 17 civilians and two unarmed soldiers, as well as rape and the deployment of a child soldier, the court ruled.
He had also ordered looting and repeatedly ordered, or had himself inflicted, cruel and humiliating treatment of civilians and mishandled corpses, according to the verdict.

Dubai Design Week’s 12th edition celebrates bold Middle Eastern design
From an eye-catching exhibition spotlighting geometric forms to installations designed by prominent architects, Dubai Design Week is set to host its 12th edition to honour the Middle East’s vibrant design, craft and culture.
The programme takes place across Dubai Design District (d3), the city’s creative hub, from 3 to 8 November 2026.
The festival’s headline event is Downtown Design, an annual fair that spotlights regional and global design brands, makers and manufacturers.
Dezeen readers can get 50 per cent off their tickets using the code DESIGN50.
Taking place from 4 to 8 November, Downtown Design presents site-specific installations, talks and networking series and exhibitions for furniture, textiles, lighting and kitchen and bathroom products.
This year, British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has added his creative touch to Veuve Clicquot‘s annual lounge at the fair, which will serve as a place to relax, as well as a venue to host talks and parties.
Italian design brand Memphis Milano will also unveil an exhibition that honours the bright colours and geometric forms utilised by the group’s founder Ettore Sottsass in the 1980s, known as the Memphis movement.
Also returning to the 2026 edition is the UAE Designer Exhibition – a platform for emerging talent in the emirate within a B2B and B2C environment, creating a space for future mentorship.
Under the theme Inherited Futures, the exhibition features 30 UAE-based designers’ works, which will focus on materiality, form and technology.
With architect AlZaina Lootah as design collaborator, the exhibition tasks contributors to design products that are producible, durable, high-quality and referential to cultural contexts.
Alongside the fair, Dubai Design Week will also exhibit installations across the district, created by global architecture practices Nikken Sekkei, Sobokuya, Aestudio, Alter, Palm and Palazzo, design firm Dubai Duette Studio, architect Rasha Saffarini, cultural platform Avid Learning Middle East and craft group Dakhnii Diaries.
Programme highlights also include the annual Urban Commission competition, which will showcase the winning proposal by Dubai-based studio Nao Architects.
Titled Three Gardens and a Room, Nao Architects’ installation responds to the competition’s theme Atmospheres, which asked participants to consider “how light, temperature, sound, material and spatial design shape how we feel, move and connect”.
On display for the duration of the design week, the installation by the practice’s founder Reem Nassour reconsiders a garden with four key architectural elements – a roof, mound, hearth and enclosure – in the form of three gardens connected by a central room.
Abwab, Dubai Design Week’s flagship commissioning programme, presents In Other Words, a group exhibition open from 3 to 8 November.
The exhibition presents commissioned works by five selected practices from West, South, Southeast and East Asia, and Africa.
Its overarching theme explores communication beyond speech and writing, addressing symbols and gestures used throughout history.
Other exhibitions curated for the 2026 edition include the Worlds Ahead: 25 Years of Design, Place and Impact in the Middle East exhibition by architecture studio Woods Bagot, and the showcase by Paris’ L’école School of Jewellery Arts, which is supported by jewellery brand Van Cleef and Arpels.
Dubai Design Week’s Marketplace also returns for the latest iteration from 7 to 8 November, serving as a platform for independent makers across the Middle East.
The platform enables artisans to sell their handmade pieces, from fashion and jewellery to homeware and food, and offers a series of live performances and culinary experiences.
The festival is held under the patronage of Her Highness Sheikha Latifa bint Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, chairperson of the Dubai Culture and Arts Authority (Dubai Culture).

Bulgaria's Nikola Tsolov Impresses on Formula 1 Debut in Mexico
Nikola Tsolov recorded the 12th-fastest time in his first official Formula 1 session, delivering a strong performance in the opening free practice ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix.
The Bulgarian, known as the "Bulgarian Lion," set his best lap at 1:19.604 on his third flying lap, using Pirelli soft-compound tires. He finished 0.126 seconds behind his Racing Bulls teammate Arvid Lindblad, who placed 10th.
Tsolov started the session with two runs on medium-compound slick tires, alternating between fast laps and slower ones. His only notable mistake came near the end of the second run, when he locked up his front-left tire under braking for the first corner. Speaking over the team radio, he explained that the car had "bottomed out" at the beginning of the braking zone, briefly lifting the wheel off the ground before it touched the track again and locked up.
He then switched to soft tires and completed three fast laps, with cool-down laps in between. After this first stint on the soft compound, he briefly got out of the car because of a cramp in his right leg. He returned to the track for the closing minutes, again on soft tires, and completed 28 laps in total.
Charles Leclerc topped the session, which featured 10 rookies, with a time of 1:18.128, finishing 0.659 seconds ahead of Andrea Kimi Antonelli. Frederik Vesti was third, 0.733 seconds off the pace, after taking George Russell's place in the second Mercedes for the opening 60-minute practice at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.
Ferrari was the only team not to field a rookie in the first practice session in Mexico. Lewis Hamilton took fourth place, 0.738 seconds behind his teammate. Ayumu Iwasa, driving Max Verstappen's car, finished fifth. The top 10 also featured Pierre Gasly, Fernando Alonso, Oscar Piastri, Oliver Bearman and Lindblad, while Hadjar finished between Bearman and Tsolov.
The Mexico City Grand Prix, the 19th round of the 2026 Formula 1 season, continues tonight at 00:00 Bulgarian time with the second free practice session at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez. All 22 full-time drivers are scheduled to take part.

House Democrats Demand Trump Preserve Grok AI Chats After TIME Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:56:29 UTC
05:56:29 KST

The top Democrats on the House Judiciary and Oversight Committees are demanding that President Donald Trump preserve his conversations with artificial intelligence chatbots as part of an inquiry into whether Elon Musk’s AI system Grok has influenced official White House policy. The demand offers a preview of the intense scrutiny Trump would face in the final years of his presidency if Democrats reclaim the House in next week’s midterm elections.
In a letter to Trump, unveiled Oct. 30, Representatives Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Robert Garcia of California call on the President to preserve “any prompts” submitted to AI chatbots, including Musk’s Grok, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and Anthropic’s Claude, while “carrying out your constitutional, statutory, or other official or ceremonial duties,” along with the responses the chatbots generated. They also request a briefing on the matter by 5 p.m. on Nov. 11. Raskin and Garcia would be in line to chair the Judiciary and Oversight Committees, respectively, if Democrats win the House.
The request stems from a TIME report earlier this month detailing a previously undisclosed December 2025 meeting between Trump and Musk in the Oval Office. According to an official who was present, Trump spent hours asking Grok questions about his presidency and legacy.
At the time, Trump was ordering missile strikes on Venezuelan boats he alleged were smuggling drugs into the United States. He asked Grok how Venezuelans would react if the U.S. captured President Nicolás Maduro. The chatbot responded that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator whose downfall many Venezuelans would likely celebrate, the official said. The following month, Trump ordered a military operation to seize Maduro, and celebrations erupted in the streets of Venezuela. Trump came away convinced that Grok was ingenious, according to officials familiar with his thinking.
The lawmakers cited TIME’s reporting that Trump sought Grok’s “advice on carrying out some of your presidential duties,” including asking it to opine on how Venezuelans would respond to Maduro’s capture. Just “weeks later,” they noted, Trump “ordered the U.S. military, without congressional authorization, to attack Venezuela and capture President Maduro.”
They called the episode “deeply troubling,” arguing that Trump “consulted Grok—but not Congress—on your military deployment to Venezuela, circumventing Congress’s constitutional power to declare war and introducing instead into American foreign policy decision making a technology that is highly manipulable and demonstrably error-prone.” The White House’s use of AI chatbots, they warned, “exposes the United States to acute national security risks” and leaves the country vulnerable to “malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties.”
A Trump Administration official says that the White House “preserves all required records in accordance with the law” but declined to answer specific questions stemming from the letter. A spokesperson for Musk did not respond to requests for comment.
The preservation demand rests on the Presidential Records Act, enacted in the wake of the Watergate scandal, which makes presidential records the property of the public and requires that they be filed separately from personal materials. In 2014, lawmakers passed amendments that extended the law to include electronic records. The principle of preservation, the statute said, applied to the content of the information rather than the medium that holds it, a standard that on its face would seem to reach chatbot exchanges tied to official duties.
But the statute itself does not mention AI, and the most direct federal guidance, from the National Archives, covers agencies under the separate Federal Records Act. That language treats prompts and outputs as likely records only if they are captured and saved in an agency system, a caveat critics say limits its reach for commercial chatbots. In April, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel declared the Act unconstitutional, although the White House has told a court its staff are still preserving materials related to their work. A federal judge ordered the administration in May to preserve presidential records for now.
The dispute comes as Democrats are preparing for the possibility of reclaiming congressional investigative powers after two years in the minority. A Democratic-controlled House could use committee hearings, document requests, and subpoenas to examine how Trump and his advisers have conducted official business, including the extent to which emerging technologies have entered the administration’s decision-making process.
Whether the White House complies with the Democrats’ demand, ignores it, or fights it could offer an early glimpse of the confrontations that await Trump in the final years of his presidency.

30% in 2019, cancer drug margins at 700% now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:56:20 UTC
05:56:20 KST

Anti-cancer drugs show mark-ups of up to 700% despite NPPA's 2019 price curbs, raising questions over one-time price cuts
A look at the mark-up on some of the drugs on which National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) put a trade margin cap of 30% on selling price in Feb 2019 shows that a majority had mark-ups of 100%-700% in the Authority's 2026 list. Citing this data, the All-India Drug Action Network, which works on access to affordable medicines, pointed out the futility of one-time MRP reduction as a policy measure in the absence of a mandate to maintain permanent margin caps along with consistent monitoring.Of the 137 anti-cancer drugs that NPPA listed for reduction of trade margin, 34 are from the 2019 NPPA list of 42 anti-cancer drugs. However, the recent list put out by NPPA, showing steep reduction in MRP, reveals that most drugs from the 2019 list that feature in the 2026 list have breached the 43% mark-up level. This level is equivalent to a 30% trade margin because while the margin is calculated as a percentage of the final MRP, the mark-up is a percentage of the price to the stockist.
Evidence shows 1-time caps give limited relief: Activist group
The mark-up in 2026 prior to the latest order was higher than it was even before the 2019 order and hence the percentage reduction in prices too is much higher in most cases now compared to seven years back. However, in the case of drugs which saw very steep reduction in MRP in 2019, the percentage reduction is lower in 2026.
For example, the MRP of a brand of an anti-cancer drug Pemetrexed fell from Rs 7,000 to Rs 800 in 2019. In the latest MRP reduction, it has fallen from Rs 1,095 to Rs 297, a more modest reduction than in 2019. Many multinationals which reduced the MRP by significant amounts in 2019 have done little or no reduction this time and some originator companies - those that held the patent for the medicine originally - did not slash the MRP by much on either occasion.
Only five brands from the 2019 list had a mark-up of 43% prior to the latest order, another four had mark-ups ranging from 43% to 100%. The mark-up on the remaining 39 ranged from 100% to over 700%."NPPA is calling it trade margin capping, as they did in 2019 also. That's misleading because it is not a cap. It is just a one-time reduction of MRP by restriction of the mark-up," said Malini Aisola of AIDAN adding that this would not be enough to prevent mark-ups rising again as happened after 2019.

Mark Carney: Canada has 'learned we are overdependent on the US'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Mark Carney: Canada has 'learned we are overdependent on the US'
October 30, 2026
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU.
Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump, representing Canada's biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south.
"The lesson we've taken, Canadians as a whole, is we're overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally," Carney said.
What did Carney say about EU talks and closer ties to the bloc?
An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday.
They're discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an "associate membership" — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor.
"Well, I think the advantage of what we're doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that's used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership," he told DW's Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower.
"What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession." Carney said.
What scope for EU-Canada cooperation does Carney see?
Asked if he was looking to create a "new transatlantic bloc without the US," Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada's other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner.
"We're both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in NATO. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States," he said. "But in many cases, there'll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States."
He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), calling it "one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world," and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges.
But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.
Is Canada concerned the talks could alienate the US, or Trump?
Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump's attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents.
"The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They're very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two," he said.
Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was "to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are." He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring "the negotiations back to the core issues."
But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada's other most natural partners around the world.
He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, "the scale of the relationship with the United States" would be "very hard to replace."
Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, "We've been living with this for some time."
"There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had," he said. "Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement."
Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a "positive association" and partnership "to help solve global problems" and address global challenges.
"It's not against somebody. It's for. It's a positive act," he said.
DW's Katharina Kroll conducted the interview in Montreal.

Mark Carney: Canada has 'learned we are overdependent on the US'
October 30, 2026
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU.
Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump, representing Canada's biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south.
"The lesson we've taken, Canadians as a whole, is we're overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally," Carney said.
What did Carney say about EU talks and closer ties to the bloc?
An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday.
They're discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an "associate membership" — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor.
"Well, I think the advantage of what we're doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that's used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership," he told DW's Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower.
"What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession." Carney said.
What scope for EU-Canada cooperation does Carney see?
Asked if he was looking to create a "new transatlantic bloc without the US," Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada's other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner.
"We're both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in NATO. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States," he said. "But in many cases, there'll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States."
He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), calling it "one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world," and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges.
But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.
Is Canada concerned the talks could alienate the US, or Trump?
Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump's attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents.
"The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They're very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two," he said.
Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was "to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are." He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring "the negotiations back to the core issues."
But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada's other most natural partners around the world.
He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, "the scale of the relationship with the United States" would be "very hard to replace."
Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, "We've been living with this for some time."
"There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had," he said. "Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement."
Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a "positive association" and partnership "to help solve global problems" and address global challenges.
"It's not against somebody. It's for. It's a positive act," he said.

Lavrov leaves EU diplomats fuming at G20
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s presence at a G20 meeting in the US has angered European diplomats, with several reportedly threatening to boycott a group photo. Germany’s top diplomat, Johann Wadephul, objected to being photographed alongside Lavrov but ended up in the same frame as him.
Lavrov arrived in Atlanta, Georgia, on Friday for the two-day gathering, which precedes the G20 leaders’ summit scheduled for mid-December in Florida.
US President Donald Trump has expressed hope that Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the summit, although Moscow has yet to decide whether to accept the invitation, according to the Kremlin.
Lavrov’s presence at the ministerial meeting has proved particularly contentious for several European delegations, which have opposed Washington’s decision to invite Russian officials.
“There will be no family photo featuring our European partners together with Mr. Lavrov,” Wadephul told reporters, insisting that “we must avoid sending the wrong visual signals.”
According to several media outlets, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio eventually scrapped the traditional group photo after European foreign ministers reportedly refused to stand alongside Lavrov and threatened to walk out.
However, the German minister was unable to avoid appearing in the same frame as his Russian counterpart.
A photograph of the G20’s first plenary session, published Friday on X by DW correspondent Benjamin Alvarez, showed Wadephul casting a sidelong glance at Lavrov.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul looks over to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, during the first plenary session of the G20 Foreign Ministers's Meeting in Atlanta. pic.twitter.com/Z01xQmpO7A
— Benjamin Alvarez (@BenjAlvarez1) October 30, 2026
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova seized on the image, suggesting in a Telegram post that Western journalists had disregarded the German diplomat’s objections by capturing the two ministers together.
Zakharova also pointed out that Wadephul himself had requested a last-minute meeting with Lavrov on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly just a month earlier.
The encounter was their first since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Lavrov later described the discussion as disappointing, saying his German counterpart had merely repeated Berlin’s familiar anti-Russian positions.
The dispute in Atlanta follows earlier European objections to Washington’s decision to restore Russian participation in G20 gatherings.
When Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended G20 talks in late August, becoming the first Russian finance minister to do so since 2022, Trump defended his administration’s approach.
“We like getting along with everybody. One of the reasons I’m so successful, I get along with everybody,” the US president said at the time.
Lavrov last attended a G20 ministerial meeting in September 2025, on the sidelines of the 80th UN General Assembly in New York. Despite Western efforts to isolate Moscow diplomatically, he has maintained an active international schedule, including official visits to countries across Africa and Asia.
The latest gathering also comes ahead of a fourth round of Washington-mediated trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US, expected next month.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Wednesday that European representatives would be excluded from the talks despite their efforts to secure a seat at the negotiating table.

UN Security Council renews Libya mission, Western Sahara resolution fails after Russian veto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:52:34 UTC
05:52:34 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The UN Security Council on Friday renewed the mandate of its support mission in Libya for another year, then rejected a US-drafted resolution on the Western Sahara region after Russia used its veto.
The Libya resolution, put forward by the UK, passed 13-0, with Russia and Greece abstaining. It extends the mandate of the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) and backs efforts to move the country toward elections, reunify state institutions, and establish a unified executive authority.
The US welcomed the vote, saying Libya is facing a “historic opportunity” and stressing the need for a single government and unified security institutions. Washington also warned that those who deliberately obstruct Libya's political transition could face consequences.
Russia abstained, saying UNSMIL still has an important role to play but cautioning against rushing the political process or imposing solutions from abroad.
Russian Ambassador Vasily Nebenzya said agreements reached through the recent political process still need wider support among Libyan stakeholders.
The council then turned to Western Sahara, where a US-drafted resolution received 11 votes in favor, three abstentions, and one against with Russia's veto.
The resolution sought to reshape the UN's approach to the long-running dispute and advance a political settlement. US Ambassador Mike Waltz argued that repeated efforts to hold a referendum had failed for decades and said maintaining the status quo was no longer acceptable.
He said Washington supports self-determination but believes there are other ways to achieve it, while urging the parties to move toward a lasting political agreement.
Western Sahara remains a key issue in North African diplomacy. Morocco has proposed broad autonomy for the territory under its sovereignty, while the Polisario Front continues to seek a referendum on self-determination, a position supported by Algeria.
The dispute over Western Sahara dates back to 1975, when Spain ended its colonial rule of the territory. It escalated into armed conflict between Morocco and the Polisario Front until a 1991 ceasefire.

UN nature summit approves two key agreements after marathon negotiations
Almost 200 nations approved two agreements on Friday to halt biodiversity loss by 2030, following almost two weeks of negotiations that ran into extra time on the final day.
Nearly 200 nations on Friday adopted hard-fought agreements at a UN biodiversity summit aimed at putting the world back on track in efforts to halt nature's destruction by 2030.
Watch moreRoad to COP30: What are the climate targets?
Delegates cheered as the crucial texts were approved in overtime following two weeks of tense negotiations at the COP17 conference in Armenia's capital Yerevan.
"And that's it. Perfect", said COP17 president Hambardzum Matevosyan to applause as he brought down the gavel on the documents, the final versions of which were not made immediately available to the public.
The world adopted a historic pact in 2022 setting ambitious targets to halt biodiversity loss by 2030.
But ahead of the summit, the UN warned that countries would fail to meet the goal unless they urgently corrected course.
Most of the objectives are falling short, including targets to protect 30 percent of Earth's land and oceans, tackle pollution, and provide poorer countries with greater conservation finance.A draft COP17 text earlier called on countries to "accelerate" efforts to keep the pact alive and stressed "increased action" was needed to tackle the root drivers of nature loss.

Highlighting the disagreements that dogged the talks, the document proposed various options to achieve the 2030 goal. It was not immediately clear which of those options made the cut.
During negotiations, countries wrangled over reforming subsidies and other incentives that encourage activities harmful to nature, such as fossil fuels, intensive agriculture and overfishing.
A separate row revolved around finding new cash sources to fund conservation efforts around the globe – a hot-button issue with public budgets under strain amid an energy crisis and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
To restore degraded ecosystems, save endangered species and conserve forests, wetlands and other vital natural habitats, the world needs an estimated $700 billion more every year than it currently spends.

The European Union led a charge for wealthy emerging economies such as China to join in paying for global conservation efforts – a contentious issue at COP17.
In a sign that a compromise was in the offing, another draft text that circulated earlier Friday invited countries outside the list of developed country donors to voluntarily join the group.
Read moreNations accused of undermining science at UN nature talks
Science under attack
Efforts to refine the lacklustre Cali Fund – a UN mechanism for sharing profits from corporations that use genetic data from plants and other organisms – also proved difficult.
The fund set out to raise $1 billion a year for conservation in developing countries when it launched in early 2025. So far, it has attracted around $10,000.
Nations have also feuded over key scientific reports, with a small handful of countries accused of stonewalling efforts to accept the benchmark findings of a UN-backed biodiversity body.
"The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said.
Around 70 ministers joined the negotiations this week in an effort to nudge things along, while indigenous leaders and civil society activists appealed to nations to act with greater urgency.
At the last biodiversity summit in Colombia in 2024, talks ran overtime as nations haggled over conservation finance and ended without a deal. Negotiations resumed in Rome in 2025 where an agreement was reached.
The COP17 summit was also expected to decide on Friday whether Panama or Ecuador will host the next biodiversity summit in 2028.

Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:52:01 GMT
05:52:01 KST

Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
- Published
Riot police have been deployed at Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
The row pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS).
The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and on Friday defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw in protest.
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff.
Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal mid-air in order to attend to the confrontation in Warsaw. He had been on his way to the Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.
In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.
Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.
The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.
Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.
"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

Ukraine’s government is allocating Hr. 354.6 million ($7.8 million) to repairing shelters in maternity hospitals amid near-daily Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure.
Hr. 294.8 million ($6.5 million), reallocated within the Health Ministry’s budget, will go toward shelter repair at 84 maternity hospitals and wards, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Friday, Oct. 30. Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The aim is to ensure that doctors can continue delivering children and care for mothers and infants even during air raid alerts, Koretskyi said, adding that shelters must be safely accessible to women with limited mobility as well.
At the time of the report, it was not specified which hospitals or cities the funds are intended for.
Reinforcing critical hospital units
The remaining Hr. 59.8 million ($1.3 million) will fund additional protection for facilities with inpatient departments, including intensive care units, operating rooms, neonatal intensive care units and delivery rooms.
The measures include installing gabions, metal roller shutters and impact-resistant film on windows in order to shield patients and staff from possible blast and debris.
The move comes as Ukraine seeks to keep daily life and the economy running as normally as possible despite the war.
New rules for medical facilities
Koretsky’s government had already imposed new rules for hospitals in September, as a response to Russia’s increasingly changing attack tactics.

Life-saving procedures, such as surgery, resuscitation and intensive care, are now to be performed even during a red-level air threat, when patients and medical personnel must otherwise move to shelters immediately.
“Emergency medical services will operate without interruption. Patients with urgent conditions will be admitted regardless of the threat level,” Koretskyi said on Sept. 21.
Under a yellow-level alert, medical facilities will continue operating, but must provide employees, patients and visitors with unrestricted access to shelters.
Around the same time, Russia struck a Kyiv maternity hospital as the capital was targeted with ballistic missiles.

“Each of you deserves to give birth to your child in peace, without sirens or explosions. And every newborn deserves to begin life in peace. We are doing everything to make this happen as soon as possible,” he said.
Only a month later, on Oct. 20, Russian forces struck an operating room in Kyiv’s Strazhesko Institute of Cardiology, injuring a patient. The strike marked the second time Russia targeted the heart center that serves patients nationwide, after a September 2025 strike killed two people there.
Earlier on Friday, Ukraine requested an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council over Russia’s latest wave of missile and drone attacks that left at least 25 civilians dead and 110 wounded nationwide.
Although deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure are prohibited under international law, strikes on civilians across Ukraine continue near-daily, including those on children and medical facilities.
On Thursday, a Russian guided aerial bomb (KAB) strike on Izium killed five employees of a local healthcare institution.

Pentagon Asks NATO Allies to Avoid “Poking” Russia, Reuters Reports
