In another recent meeting, Pentagon officials urged an Estonian delegation to remain “measured” in its public communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter.
The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia did not respond to Reuters requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.

99 Ranch Market to close two California locations
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
99 Ranch Market, one of the country’s largest Asian supermarket chains, will close two of its California stores before the end of the year, putting employees out of work.
Tawa Supermarket Inc., the Buena Park-headquartered parent company of 99 Ranch Market, filed two Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices on Monday.
99 Ranch Market will permanently close its Chino store at 4024 Grand Ave. on Nov. 15, laying off 49 employees. It will also close its Pleasanton store at 4299 Rosewood Drive on Dec. 5, affecting 54 employees.
“This decision will optimize our store network and allocate resources more effectively to better serve our customers,” the company said in an email.
Once a local mecca for Chinese culinary delights, 99 Ranch has become a national pan-Asian behemoth under Jonson and Alice Chen.
“With other 99 Ranch Market locations in the Tri-Valley and Chino/Chino Hills areas already, we remain committed to providing the community with convenient access to the quality products, diverse Pan-Asian food selections, and service our customers have come to expect,” the company said.
Taiwanese immigrant Roger Chen founded 99 Ranch Market in 1984 after noticing a gap in the American supermarket sector. Chen opened the first store in Westminster. The chain now operates more than 60 stores across 11 states. Most of its branches are in California.
The closures come as competition among Asian grocers in California heats up, especially in the Bay Area.
They grew up at the nearly 40-year-old Asian grocery chain in the San Gabriel Valley. Now, siblings Alice and Jonson Chen are overseeing the national expansion of 99 Ranch Market.
Korean American chain H Mart has been expanding in California, with a new location in the East Bay and plans for a 100,000-square-foot, two-level store in Fremont with a food hall and bar.
Jagalchi, a Korean market in Daly City, opened last year with a 75,000-square-foot supermarket with fresh seafood, a bakery, a K-beauty section and sit-down dining.
T&T Supermarket, a Canadian chain, opened a 55,000-square-foot store in San José in June and plans stores in San Francisco and Millbrae.
Other California grocery chains have also had to make major changes to their store footprints.
Grocery Outlet announced in March that it was closing 36 underperforming stores, including six in Southern California.

US appeals court again rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:39:50 UTC
05:39:50 KST

US appeals court again rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots
The 9th Circuit Court calls the petition to remove 20,000 ballots from California’s vote count unconstitutional.
For the second time in less than a week, a United States appeals court has rejected a petition from the administration of President Donald Trump to set aside 20,000 ballots in California over concerns about non-citizen voting.
The decision came down on Friday, with less than four days until the November 3 midterm elections.
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Trump’s request would violate the US Constitution and risk disenfranchising eligible voters.
“The consequence of the United States’s request is not merely ballot segregation, but ultimately both the cancellation of the ballot and the removal of voters from the voting rolls,” the majority wrote in its ruling.
Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez – appointed by Trump and his Democratic predecessor Joe Biden, respectively – formed the majority.
A third judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, issued a dissent, saying the administration’s petition was a “reasonable request”.
The Trump administration has claimed that nearly 20,000 “likely non-citizens” received mail-in ballots to vote in California’s midterm elections on November 3. It sued the state on October 15 to prevent those ballots from being counted.
But the accuracy of the Trump administration’s list has been called into doubt, as have its claims of widespread non-citizen voting.
Election fraud in the US is extremely rare. So is non-citizen voting, despite Trump’s assertion earlier this year that as many as 278,000 foreign nationals across the country were registered to vote.
Like California, states such as Nevada and Washington have also received lists of alleged non-citizen voters, but officials there have found the documents largely inaccurate.
In Nevada, for instance, state authorities issued a statement in September saying the Trump administration had erroneously identified citizens as non-citizens on its list. Not a single name was correct, according to the statement.
California, a Democratic stronghold, will elect 52 members of the House of Representatives, one of Congress’s two chambers, on November 3.
The state has long been Trump’s target for criticism, with the president accusing its Democratic leadership of “cheating” in elections.
But California officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, have countered that the Trump administration is seeking to meddle in the state’s elections to sow voter distrust and undermine the results.
“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters,” Newsom said in a news release after the October 15 lawsuit.
Non-citizen voting in federal elections is against the law in all 50 US states, including California.
The Constitution’s Elections Clause also grants states exclusive authority to administer elections, though it does allow for Congress to pass regulations concerning voting procedures.
The Trump administration initially sent California its list of 20,000 “likely non-citizens” on October 12, barely three weeks before the midterm election.
California officials refused the administration’s demand to set aside the 20,000 ballots, requesting proof that the names on the list were indeed foreign nationals. According to the California government, no such evidence has been provided.
The Trump administration last week charged 28 foreign nationals in California with election-related infractions, but some of the accused told the Los Angeles Times they had never registered to vote.
The newspaper’s reporting suggested some of the non-citizen defendants shared the same name as eligible voters.
As the October 15 lawsuit navigated the court system earlier this month, the Trump administration sought an emergency ruling from the 9th Circuit Court to suspend the 20,000 ballots.
But the appeals court rejected the petition on Monday, saying the Trump administration had not given lower courts adequate time to weigh the matter.
A lower court ultimately ruled against the Trump administration on Wednesday, and the administration again appealed to the 9th Circuit Court.
In its majority decision, the appeals court framed the Trump administration’s lawsuit as an attempt to violate the Constitution’s Elections Clause.
“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the majority wrote.
The majority also wrote that it had “major concerns” that granting the Trump administration’s request would “harm the public interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire tabulation process in jeopardy”.

Amber Infrastructure Plans 10-15 Year Exits as 2 Ukraine Funds Hunt ‘Ready-to-Build’ Projects

As Amber Infrastructure’s Managing Director and Ukraine Lead Dominykas Tuckus sat down for our interview, opposite an enormous panoramic window overlooking Kyiv’s city center, a “yellow” air raid warning sounded, meaning that drones were flying somewhere above Kyiv.
We were able to continue.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Amber Infrastructure is among those foreign investors that aren’t waiting for the war to end – they’re willing to risk investing in the country while the war is still going on.
The London-based company partnered with the country’s largest investment firm, Dragon Capital, to announce Amber Dragon Ukraine Infrastructure Fund I, with a first close of €207 million ($231.8 million) on May 27.
Amber Dragon Ukraine Infrastructure Fund I is backed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) up to €60 million ($67.2 million), the European Investment Bank up to €50 million ($56 million) and the International Finance Corporation up to €40 million ($45 million). The fund’s target size is €350 million ($390.4 million), the EBRD wrote.
Amber Infrastructure’s Dominykas Tuckus (second from left) and EBRD First Vice President Greg Guyett (third from left) pose with other participants at the signing ceremony for Amber Dragon Ukraine Infrastructure Fund I during the Ukraine Recovery Conference 2025 (URC2025). (Photo provided to Kyiv Post by the EBRD press service)
80% of Ukrainians Back Refinery Strikes Despite Risks of US Aid Cut
The second vehicle, the European Flagship Fund for the Reconstruction of Ukraine, announced about €260 million ($291 million) in commitments on June 25, but this is not its final size. “The EU Flagship Fund size is less defined because it has not yet reached the first close… We have a possibility to attract private capital on top of that [amount],” Tuckus told Kyiv Post.
The EIB, German KfW, Italian Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP), Polish Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego (BGK), and French Proparco signed the first commitments, along with Amber Infrastructure and Dragon Capital, according to the press release. The fund is backed by the European Commission initiative and was announced during the Ukraine Recovery Conference 2025 (URC2025). The British International Investment also announced its commitment of £13 million ($17.4 million) to the fund in its press release.
The two funds co-invest in the same assets, with Amber acting as a single manager, Tuckus told Kyiv Post on the sidelines of the Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF).
That said, Amber still says Ukraine has always been “on the radar,” but its donors “never had this mandate to look at Ukraine,” Tuckus said.
“We have a mandate to look at and manage transactions that are located in the EU part of Central and Eastern Europe… everything from Bulgaria, Romania, then Hungary, then Western Balkans also, like Slovenia, Croatia, Czech Republic, etc., all the way to the north”, he said.
The investment company is a part of Boyd Watterson Global Asset Management Group LLC. Founded in 2009, Amber Infrastructure has made almost 200 investments in 22 countries so far, according to its website. Assets under management stand at about £14 billion ($16.9-19.3 billion) as of Dec. 31, 2025, the website says. The countries of operation include the UK, the US, New Zealand, and Germany. Amber’s other funds include the Three Seas Initiative Investment Fund (3SIIF), a dedicated commercial fund targeting critical infrastructure investment in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE).
“We are operating in countries next to Ukraine, and we never had a mandate to invest in Ukraine. And this is when we started looking at Ukraine more seriously. And this is how we met Dragon Capital,” he added.
The company was looking for a partner on the ground, and Dragon Capital was the candidate. Led by Tomash Fiala, the fund is the country’s largest B2B real estate owner but lacks enough expertise in energy and infrastructure. Amber decided to bring in its experience in these investments, Tuckus said. “What is useful is that they have worked with real assets,” he explained.
Tuckus said Amber aims to invest on the infrastructure side into “real assets” that generate forecastable cash flows – he referred to them as “passive assets that benefit the economy”. Amber wants to use the same strategy as with the 3SIIFs fund in Ukraine, targeting energy, transport, and digital infrastructure.
But the focus is on smaller, ready-to-build projects that are fully permitted, have undergone full technical due diligence, and can enter construction early. “I think it would be difficult to rely on regulation only to generate sufficient returns on our investments,” he added. During the panel discussion at KIEF, Tuckus also said the fund sees a lack of “bankable” projects, and potential candidates don’t spend time preparing the documentation and due diligence.
Still, Amber targets energy, transport and logistics, digital infrastructure, and critical reconstruction infrastructure, with an exit strategy in 10 to 15 years.
“In the fund, like the Infrastructure Fund for Ukraine, there is a very clear starting period, you know, where we have an investment period, and then we have a holding period, and then we have an exit,” Tuckus said.
“Whatever we do now, all the investments that we will execute in the next few years, during the investment period, we’ll need to exit to pay back the investors their invested capital plus their returns,” he added.
But despite having already raised billions of euros, Amber announced only one transaction when the interview was published. “There are [an additional] two projects identified already a while ago, and we are now just simply in preparatory works on those,” Tuckus said.
The first announced investment is the distributed energy project Power One, led by ex-Ukrenergo CEO Volodymyr Kudrytskiy, who claimed that it also hired 50 other colleagues from Ukrenergo in the project, saying this during one of KIEF’s panel discussions.
Volodymyr Kudrytskiy, who leads the distributed energy project Power One and is a former CEO of Ukrenergo, speaks during a panel discussion at the Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) in Kyiv. (Photo provided to Kyiv Post by the KIEF press service)
Power One (Power 1 LLC) is installing 36.8 megawatts (MW) of gas-piston units and 31.5 MW of energy storage systems in the Zakarpattia region. Power One’s decentralized generation facilities will be located across several sites, each with a capacity of up to 10 MW, the project’s website says.
Tuckus did not disclose the size of Amber’s investment in the project. The EBRD provided a €22.3 million ($25 million) loan, against a total project cost of €41.8 million ($46.8 million), according to the project’s profile on the website.
Amber’s chair believes the investment projects will be found because Ukraine has “a huge gap” for better electricity, mobile, and internet connections. “The strikes have widened it,” he said. War-risk insurance is a must for the projects, but he feels okay with the current menu of commercial products available in the market to cover war risk. Investing in distributed assets rather than large centralized objects is another risk mitigation strategy for the fund, he said.
“Ukraine is a bit more advanced in digital infrastructure, at least in mobile connection. But at the same time, if I ride a train from Poland to Kyiv, there are only a few spots where I can have a proper connection,” Tuckus told Kyiv Post.
But Ukraine is a risky market in the full-scale war – Amber could have lived without it. Is the fund okay with the risky environment?
“The risk is a relative thing,” Tuckus said. “I come from Lithuania, from a market which was, a long time ago, seen as super risky. Then the risk profile went down substantially. Whoever was involved in any kind of business before this happened made a lot of money. So it’s just a matter of entering the market at the right time,” Tuckus told Kyiv Post.
He believes that, at some point, Ukraine will be perceived as less risky as well.

A Democratic Wave In the Midterms Could Change How Companies Talk About Climate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:39:41 UTC
05:39:41 KST

For the last year, I’ve been asking corporate executives how they might expect anticipated Democratic victories in the midterm elections to shape the future of the U.S. climate and energy agenda. I was surprised how often they gave the same answer: investigations.
Democratic control of congressional committees would give Democrats new subpoena power and new dedicated staff to conduct investigations. Companies may be compelled to turn over documents, and CEOs could be called to testify before Congress about how they have approached a range of issues.
Corporate executives have largely worried about staying on the right side of President Trump over the last few years. But a Democratic Congress would introduce a competing political pressure—and potentially change how companies talk about climate and energy.
Climate may not be a top priority on its own for Democratic politicians in 2026, but it will come up in Washington for two key reasons. The first is rising fuel and power costs. Democrats in Congress will want to probe how companies have responded to current energy market conditions triggered in part by rapid growth in demand for AI and the war in Iran, and whether their actions have raised costs. You can expect those questions to take a pro-clean energy bent. And then there is the corruption discussion, which has emerged as a key theme in Democratic midterm campaigning. Democrats will want to probe any company or industry that is perceived to be close with the administration, including the oil and gas industry.
In September, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat from New York, and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, released a report that gives a hint at the expected line of argument. It highlights donations from oil and gas executives and links them to the Trump Administration’s regulatory rollback. And, to conclude, it suggests that those decisions have contributed to higher prices for consumers.
For understandable reasons, analyses of how the election might shape the future of energy and climate tend to focus on policy outcomes. And there are many areas to follow closely. The results will shape efforts to pass a permitting reform bill in the time between the election and when new members of Congress take office in January. And members will debate funding levels for clean energy programs that survived cuts under Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill last year. We will also see the seeds of bigger discussions about how the U.S. might rethink its approach to climate change if Democrats regain the White House, too.
But the bigger story may indeed be the zeitgeist shift that a big Democratic wave would portend. Investigations and congressional testimony will force companies to answer questions in the public sphere that they have largely been able to elide recently. What is the role of clean energy in the power system? How might clean energy affect competitiveness? And how are you approaching risks related to climate change?
In this new environment, incentives change. A utility CEO might emphasize the role of renewables in bringing down costs. A bank might underscore how it’s financing clean energy technologies. And an oil-and-gas CEO might focus on how they’re cutting methane emissions. In general, executives decline to speak on the record about how they are preparing, but in background conversations the story is clear. Companies are lawyering up. Public relations firms are crafting modulated messages to address concerns. And CEOs are reaching out to Democratic members of Congress to plead their case.
For the last several years, many businesses have either tip-toed around Trump or openly embraced him, out of fear that doing otherwise would harm the bottom line. A new Congress with Democrats in charge would remind the corporate world that Trump is not the only force to be feared. And, perhaps, it would give CEOs cover to embrace a grounded climate agenda.

A Supply Chain Attack Put Malicious Anthropic Claude Extensions on Thousands of Devices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:38:46 UTC
05:38:46 KST

The AI software-development platform Cursor, which is owned by SpaceX, had a malicious Anthropic Claude Code extension for Windows, macOS, and Linux live in its integrated development environment extension marketplace for roughly 11 hours on Thursday. The company says the rogue extension was downloaded by “at most 5,000 users.” Cursor briefly shut down the extension marketplace while it investigated the situation, which the company says did not impact any other extensions.
The tainted extension was designed with a backdoor to give attackers access to victim devices—the type of implant that malicious hackers often use as a stepping stone to deeper control inside a target network. Cursor published remediation steps on Thursday for the roughly 5,000 affected targets. A saving grace of the situation, though, was a flaw in the malware's design that blocked it from fully establishing itself on the vast majority of targets.
“Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first researchers to spot the malicious extension after detecting it on a customer's Mac.
What is still unclear is how the malicious extension made its way into the Cursor marketplace at all. Some researchers initially speculated that it came from a compromised Anthropic system. But Cursor said in its Thursday security alert that “these malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic.”
Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, posted on X on Friday: “We’re working with Cursor on this incident, but it wasn’t a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension, which we didn’t build or publish. The versions on our official channels are not affected and this only impacts Cursor users.”
David Dworken, who works on security at Anthropic, posted on X shortly after, explaining that “this did not involve a compromise of any Anthropic systems … We were not involved with building, publishing, or hosting this.”
Cursor did not return WIRED's request for comment about how the malicious upload happened and whether it was the result of a breach at Cursor.

The Atlanta talks are the last ministerial meeting of the US G20 presidency before leaders meet in Miami on December 14 and 15.

Polish president cuts short foreign trip as constitutional crisis escalates in Warsaw
Editor's note: This developing story has been updated with the Polish president's return to Warsaw, a planned meeting of Constitutional Tribunal judges, new requests to lift judicial immunity, and the sudden resignation of Poland's ambassador to China.
Latest developments — Oct. 30
- President returns: Karol Nawrocki has returned to Warsaw after cutting short his trip to Senegal amid an escalating Constitutional Tribunal dispute.
- Judges' meeting announced: Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge elected to the Constitutional Tribunal - but whose appointment remains contested, has called a general assembly of judges for Nov. 3.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki returned to Warsaw after cutting short a trip to Senegal on Oct. 30, amid an escalating dispute over the leadership of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal.
"At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning,” Nawrocki wrote on X.
The confrontation follows a longstanding dispute over judicial appointments between pro-European Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and Poland's conservative opposition, which is aligned with President Nawrocki.
The latest escalation followed the reported suspension of the tribunal's president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and deputy president, Bartłomiej Sochański, according to Reuters.
Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who was elected to the Constitutional Tribunal by Poland's parliament, issued the suspension orders.
However, the tribunal's existing leadership does not recognize her appointment as a judge and disputes her authority make such decisions, and suspend its officials. They accused those responsible of attempting a coup, and said their web site had been unlawfully taken over.
The dispute escalated further when Prosecutor General Waldemar Żurek announced five requests to lift judicial immunity.
Four requests concern Święczkowski and one concerns Sochański. Żurek said the requests were accompanied by 50 volumes of case files. The requests do not constitute criminal charges.
Protesters gathered outside of the court, where some threw objects at police officers stationed and breached a perimeter fence, with three people detained.
The confrontation escalated when a protester cut through a chain securing a gate to the Constitutional Tribunal, allowing its disputed president, Bogdan Święczkowski, to enter the grounds.
Święczkowski said the gate had been opened on his instructions, according to Polish Radio.
He confronted police officers and demanded entry to the building, but was prevented from entering.
Former deputy Foreign Minister Arkadiusz Mularczyk accused the government of attempting a coup, alleging that legally appointed judges were being prevented from entering the court.
"Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of lawlessness, it is a difficult process, sometimes painful and requires decisive action. There is no other way," Tusk wrote on X on Oct. 30.
In another dramatic turn of events, the political crisis also prompted the resignation of Poland's ambassador to China, Jakub Kumoch, who announced on Oct. 30 that he had submitted his resignation and requested recall.
"In light of events in the country, I have concluded that it is no longer possible for me to continue serving as ambassador of the Republic of Poland," Kumoch wrote on X.
Kumoch previously served as the Polish ambassador to Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Turkey, was Secretary of State in the Chancellery of President Andrzej Duda, and was also head of the International Policy Bureau.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski responded that he acknowledged the "unprofessional" end to Kumoch's mission, adding that the diplomat no longer represented Poland.
Marcin Przydacz, head of the Polish president's International Policy Bureau, linked Kumoch's sudden decision to the Constitutional Tribunal crisis, accusing Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government of unlawfully intervening in the court.

‘We won't transport weapons’: Dockworkers at over 100 ports strike over Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:34:25 UTC
05:34:25 KST

Dockworkers in several European countries and on other continents went on strike Friday, with one of their main demands being an end to weapons shipments to Israel through their ports. 
Dockworkers' unions in France, Italy, Spain, Greece, Turkey and Morocco issued a joint call opposing arms shipments and demanding an end to what they described as "the militarization of ports." They also called for an end to the war in Gaza.
The joint statement also declared: "Ports must not be used to transport weapons, ammunition, military equipment or troops. Dockworkers do not work for war!" According to the unions, more than 100 ports in several countries joined the protest, and the actions could disrupt maritime traffic in Europe, the Mediterranean region and North America. During the demonstrations, workers also raised demands concerning social rights, but the main focus was stopping the movement of weapons through ports. Palestinian flags could be seen in some of the photographs circulated from the protests.
In Greece, dockworkers' unions declared a strike at Piraeus, the country's largest port. Giorgos Gogos, president of the local dockworkers' union, said: "We do not want to take part in any war, anywhere in the world. We do not want our ports to serve as transit hubs for military equipment intended to kill people."
In Turkey, protesters gathered outside Haydarpasa port in Istanbul, carrying a banner reading: "No to war, no to armament!" In Italy, demonstrations were planned at major ports, including Genoa, Trieste and Gioia Tauro.
Meanwhile, the French dockworkers' union called a one-day strike at major ports, including Le Havre, Marseille, Dunkirk and Rouen. The union said it opposed what it described as "the militarization of port facilities." Earlier this month, pro-Palestinian workers at an airport in France attempted to prevent a shipment intended for Israeli defense company Elbit from being flown out.
Despite the large number of ports involved in Friday's protests, experts estimated that the impact on maritime operations would be limited. Marcus Baker, global head of marine, cargo and logistics at insurance and risk advisory firm Marsh, told the Associated Press that the one-day strike was unlikely to significantly disrupt global trade, although it could affect perishable goods and time-sensitive shipments. 
He said Friday's strike and similar actions would further complicate supply chains already under pressure from tensions in the Middle East, climate-related events such as El Niño storms, restrictions affecting the Rhine River and Panama Canal, and changes in tariffs imposed by various countries.
Since the beginning of the Swords of Iron war, several countries have imposed restrictions on the transit of weapons bound for Israel through their territory. Spain, for example, announced an official policy barring ships carrying weapons for Israel from docking at its ports. 
The first measure of this kind was implemented in 2024, when Madrid refused to allow the Marianne Danica, a vessel arriving from India carrying dozens of tons of explosives, to dock at the port of Cartagena. Other vessels were subsequently denied permission to dock, including ships from the United States suspected of transporting weapons to Israel.
In March, U.S. President Donald Trump said France had barred American aircraft carrying supplies for Israel from passing through its territory, against the backdrop of French opposition to Israeli military operations in Gaza and Lebanon.

Satellite Images Confirm Destruction of Two Su-34s by Neptune Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:27:36 UTC
05:27:36 KST

Satellite images have confirmed the destruction of two Su-34 bombers as a result of a strike by Neptune cruise missiles on the Russian military airfield Marinovka in the Volgograd region.
The satellite images were published by the monitoring channel AviVector.
The strike on the deployment site of the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment took place on the night of October 29. After the strike, satellites detected a fire at the aircraft parking area.
Judging by the published images, the Su-34 was completely destroyed. In addition, one of the aircraft hangars near the impact site was damaged as a result of the missile’s warhead exploding and the subsequent fire.
As noted by the OSINT community CyberBoroshno, low-resolution satellite imagery from October 28 shows that the Su-34 was already at the site of the subsequent strike, meaning this was its usual parking spot.
According to a statement by the Navy, the strike was carried out using Long Neptune ground-launched long-range cruise missiles.
According to estimates, this is the farthest publicly known use of this variant of the Neptune missiles. The likely distance the missile had to travel is over 600 km.
Compared to the original R-360 missile, the Long Neptune features a longer fuselage with a larger diameter, a modified nose section, enlarged control surfaces, and the new designation R-360L.
The stated flight range of the missile for the Long Neptune system is up to 1,000 km; the missile is 6 m long, has a fuselage diameter of 500 mm, and a warhead weight of 260 kg.
It is also claimed to be capable of flying over complex terrain, following a route without satellite navigation, and targeting ground targets.
The Long Neptune has been equipped with a new launch system mounted on a Tatra chassis, featuring two large square-section transport-launch containers — likely due to incompatibility with the old launch system resulting from the increased dimensions.
It was a strike by these missiles on Borisoglebsk airfield on October 15 that enabled the Defense Forces to destroy at least four Su-34 bombers and damage two more.

Turkish basketball team Anadolu Efes handed EuroLeague leaders Panathinaikos their second defeat of the season Friday, securing an 83-68 home victory in Round 9 of the competition.
Efes controlled much of the game before holding off a fourth-quarter comeback attempt by the Greek visitors, who saw their lowest-scoring performance of the season.
Efes made a strong offensive start, taking a 17-9 lead midway through the opening quarter before Panathinaikos tightened their defense to narrow the deficit to 21-18.
The hosts regained control in the second quarter, stretching their advantage to 12 points at 39-27 before heading into halftime with a 45-37 lead.

The hosts kept control in the closing minutes to seal an 83-68 victory.
Colin Malcolm and Bruno Fernando led Efes with 15 points each, while Cameron Payne added 14, including nine in the final quarter.
Dario Saric racked up a double-double with 11 points and 12 rebounds.

US approves potential $2.1B sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
That is according to the State Department's Bureau of Political-Military Affairs, Ukrinform reports.
The funds for the purchase will be provided by Ukraine's partners and allies.

US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:24:51 UTC
05:24:51 KST

Breadcrumb
US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
The US State Department said on Friday it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion.
Ukraine will pay for the defensive interceptor missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through the US JUMPSTART programme, along with national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.
Delayed missile deliveries added to Ukraine's tensions with the US after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelensky for Ukraine's unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
The Ukrainian leader has repeatedly called on the US, which supplies missiles purchased by NATO allies under a programme known as PURL, to speed up deliveries ahead of winter.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.
In July, the US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.
Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030 and increase jobs at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50%, to about 1,850 from 1,200. Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck earlier this year at the centre of efforts to increase missile output.

Polish president aborts Africa trip as power struggle erupts at Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:22:33 UTC
05:22:33 KST

Jo Harper
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Polish President Karol Nawrocki aborted a flight to Senegal and returned to Warsaw on Friday as a major power struggle erupted over control of the country’s Constitutional Tribunal.
Warsaw police said officers had been sent to the tribunal after receiving information about possible threats to judges and staff and a risk of public disorder. Police said they had not entered the court building and denied claims that officers had stormed it. Three people were detained after allegedly climbing over the fence surrounding the tribunal, while police said objects had also been thrown at officers.
Orders appeared on the tribunal’s website on Friday temporarily removing its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice president, Bartlomiej Sochanski, from their duties. But the tribunal’s official account on X later rejected the decision as illegal, saying that both remained in office and describing the attempt to remove them as a “coup.”
The confrontation prompted Nawrocki to abort an official visit to Senegal while his plane was over southern Spain. “In such a moment the president must be in Poland. I am interrupting the flight to Senegal. I am returning,” Nawrocki wrote on X.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the process later on Friday evening. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of PiS lawlessness, it is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he wrote on X, referring to the former ruling Law and Justice (PiS) party.
Tusk’s government and Nawrocki, who is allied with the conservative PiS, now in opposition, have been locked in a dispute over Poland’s courts and judicial appointments.
PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski and other opposition politicians arrived outside the court and accused the government of trying to seize control of the institution. Kaczynski described the events as a “coup against the Constitutional Tribunal” and called on Nawrocki to intervene.
At the center of the dispute is Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who said she had ordered Swieczkowski and Sochanski to stop carrying out their duties.
She told public broadcaster TVP Info that seven judges were inside the building and that no police officers had entered it. 
Deeper dispute over judges at top court
The conflict reflects a deeper dispute over who can legally sit on the tribunal.
Parliament elected Korwin-Piotrowska and several other judges earlier this year, but Nawrocki refused to formally receive the oaths of some of them.
His office argues they therefore never legally took office. The judges and the governing coalition reject that interpretation.
Friday’s crisis also came as Justice Minister and Prosecutor General Waldemar Zurek sought to lift the judicial immunity of Swieczkowski and Sochanski.
Zurek said he had filed five applications with the tribunal, four concerning Swieczkowski and one concerning Sochanski. “These are serious criminal cases,” he told reporters.
The Constitutional Tribunal has been at the center of Poland’s long-running dispute over the rule of law.
The PiS reshaped the court after coming to power in 2015, drawing criticism from opposition parties and European institutions over judicial independence.
Since taking office in late 2023, Tusk’s coalition has argued that the court must be rebuilt to restore constitutional order.
The PiS and Nawrocki accuse the government of using the rule-of-law campaign to remove political opponents from key state institutions.
Nawrocki was expected back in Warsaw on Friday evening as the standoff continued.

Carney Sets Target for E.U. 'Associate' Membership Amid U.S.-Canada Trade Standoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:19:51 UTC
05:19:51 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday laid out his vision for Canada becoming an “associate” member of the European Union as he moves to reduce Canada’s reliance on the U.S. amid a trade standoff with Washington.
Closing out a two-day E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal, Carney told reporters: “Today, the European Union and Canada are launching the ‘Alliance for the Future,’ a new partnership of nations that will leverage our strategic capabilities and a variable geometry of like-minded nations to address common issues.” He noted that the alliance will focus on “increasing our collective sovereignty and resilience in areas such as AI, energy, critical minerals, quantum, and beyond.”
In parallel, Carney continued, the E.U. and Canada are working toward “the deepest possible partnership, short of accession, because of our geography, with Canada becoming the European Union's first ‘associate’ member. In the coming months, we will determine the full substance, scale, and scope of this new form of membership." Carney said he plans to attend a meeting of European leaders in June to conclude negotiations on the proposed relationship.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen announced her plan for the first-of-its-kind membership to mixed responses last month. While both von der Leyen and Carney referred to an “associate” membership throughout the summit, the term notably does not appear in the final statement of the E.U.-Canada summit. Instead, the joint statement pledges to "work to define by the 2027 Canada-E.U. summit the concept of an ever-closer association of Canada to the E.U., short of full membership itself."
Carney’s forging of international ties comes after talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed in August, leading to a trade standoff. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect last month, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. The White House has since lifted tariffs on some Canadian goods. Trump, meanwhile, has repeated his threats to annex Canada and make it the “51st state.” That, on top of domestic separatist movements in some Canadian provinces, has placed added strain on Carney to maintain his “Canada Strong” strategy and establish trade and security ties away from the U.S.
In Montreal, von der Leyen said the broader E.U.-Canada alliance would go beyond Canada’s potential associate membership, allowing for ambitious economic opportunities. Carney added that the partnership would hopefully provide opportunities for young Canadians to live, travel, and study in Europe.
“Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the E.U. because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” von der Leyen said in a speech Thursday. “This is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union.”
Still, there has been reported pushback and uncertainty from some European officials.
Matthias Luttenberg, the German ambassador to Canada, acknowledged there are worries about the potential new “associate” member label.
“If you come up with a new concept in the European Union, and you propose something, be it the Commission or somebody else, then of course it takes some time to reflect for all 27 member states,” Luttenberg told CTV on Tuesday, admitting “we have been a little surprised by the announcement, which doesn’t mean that we cannot agree on it.”
Paula Pinho, the European Commission’s chief spokesperson, told TIME Friday that "following the discussions at the summit this week, we will continue to work with the European Parliament, member states, and the Canadians to achieve our common objectives."
She added: "We have worked intensely with all our Member States on this and the basis for associate membership is clear in the summit text. We regret that we did not yet have complete unity from member states on the initial wording but we have a strong basis agreed and we are now working to flesh out the details of what this ambition looks like and how it will work.”
Carney, meanwhile, told reporters Thursday: “This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter. What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our [Europe and Canada’s] sovereignty.”
He continued: “Why does sovereignty matter in a dangerous and divided world? It allows us to withstand shocks. It means that we’re not held up by some country—or some technology company that wants to dictate how we’re going to live our lives.”
Earlier this year, Carney discussed a “rupture in the world order” and suggested that the U.S.-led international order was breaking down—his warning came against the backdrop of Trump threatening economic pressure to yield desired results.
When von der Leyen first invited Canada to work toward becoming an “associate” member last month, in what she described as an “urgent” reimagining of partnerships, Trump again threatened economic pressure. He called the proposal “laughable” and threatened to “put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things” if such an idea were to go ahead.
But experts say Carney’s burgeoning international relationships—with the E.U., China, and elsewhere—have proven to be a strong move for the Canadian leader, despite threats from Washington.
“People believe in [Carney], as there are other trade partners that Canada can build something with, even if there is no substitute for the U.S.,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor of political science at Dalhousie University, acknowledging the integration of the Canadian and U.S. economies. The U.S. accounted for 72.5% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025, according to the country’s annual trade report, making it Canada's largest trading partner by a wide margin.
Confidence in Carney among the public was seemingly reflected last week, as over 75% of Albertans voted against a future referendum on independence, opting instead to remain part of Canada.
What is the status of the U.S.-Canada trade talks?
Officials from both Ottawa and Washington have pointed toward some progress in talks over the past week, yet the path to a trade deal remains unclear.
“We will have [a deal] when it suits Canadians,” Carney told reporters Wednesday, downplaying any suggestion of a trade deal being reached before the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3. “If those deals present themselves, we will pursue them, but we're not at that position right now.”
Carney had previously indicated on Monday that trade talks with the Trump Administration had picked up, but said any progress was down to Washington moving closer to Canada’s demands.
“To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the U.S. is coming closer to our position,” Carney told reporters.
Trump, however, has painted a markedly different picture. Addressing the crowd at a South Carolina rally on Thursday, he said that Canada “is learning their lesson” amid the trade conflict, and remarked how Ottawa has been “treating [the U.S.] extremely nicely lately.”
At a rally last weekend, Trump insisted the trade dispute would be “settled pretty soon,” but did not offer specific details.
A spokesperson for Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s Internal Trade Minister, told TIME Tuesday that “Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities” and said Ottawa is ready to “work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship.”
A White House official told TIME Wednesday that U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer “have had discussions with their Canadian counterpart in recent days.”
Reuters, citing two U.S. and four Canadian sources, reported this week that negotiators across both sides are working on a deal to ease U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and autos.
TIME has reached out to the White House and Carney's office for comment.
According to a report published by the Royal Bank of Canada in August, "auto trade between Canada and the U.S. is $100 billion." After talks collapsed in August, Trump threatened to raise U.S. tariffs on all cars, trucks, and automotive parts from Canada to 50% starting Jan. 1, 2027. Honda executive Jennifer Thomas warned Tuesday that should a hike like this come into effect, it “really would be catastrophic for the entire industry.”
For any deal to progress, Carney will need to secure protections regarding the vital industry, experts tell TIME.
“The Prime Minister is not going to be able to get a deal that Premiers will accept if there's still these major tariffs on major industries,” says Turnbull.

20:19:37 UTC
05:19:37 KST

Every day, Tahani Fayez, a 52-year-old mother from Gaza, searches her phone for photos and videos of her son. Manar was 22 when he left the family’s tent in Gaza’s al-Mawasi in November 2024 and never returned.
It’s a ritual she cannot skip, she said, crying as a photo of her son filled her phone screen. Manar used to ask her to take pictures of him, so that his mother could feel his presence even when he was far away.
Fayez still has her son’s clothes, shoes, and other belongings, which she kept not just as keepsakes but in the hope that he will one day return home. She laid them out carefully, kissing his things and telling the story behind each item: the blue trousers and shirt he wore for the last Eid al-Adha he celebrated, the black tracksuit he lounged in at home. Even the socks had a story.
Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023. According to the Gaza Health Ministry, over 1,400 were killed after the October 2025 ceasefire.
21,500 people have been officially reported missing, according to Omar Nofal, head of the government committee for the missing and a judge on Gaza’s Supreme Sharia Court. Most have since been confirmed dead, including 8,000 who remain buried under the rubble, but the fate of 6,000 people is still unknown: no one knows where they are, what happened to them, and whether they are dead or alive. These figures cover only the cases that were registered, Nofal said. Thousands more have never been reported.
‘I can’t bear to imagine the answers‘
Fayez said she hasn’t felt a single moment of peace since Manar went missing.
One of four brothers, Manar had a neurological condition and needed more care than the others. As a boy, he would leave his mother notes in a notebook and on scraps of paper, apologizing for tiring her out, raising his voice, and coming home late, always telling her that she was the dearest person in the world to him. When she reached for them, her hands were shaking. She described them instead.
“My whole life has been turned upside down,” she told Mondoweiss. “Imagine, I know nothing about my son, and no one will answer our question: what happened to him, and where is he now?”
“Was he killed? Was he taken prisoner? What happened? How did he spend his last moments? Was he wounded and left bleeding? Was he hungry, thirsty, cold? I can’t bear to imagine the answers,” she said.
All she wants to know is where he is: whether he is in Israeli detention, or whether he has died, so she can bury him, grieve for him, and visit his grave when she misses him.
“A grave, I don’t want more than that. Or tell me my son is a prisoner, or wounded, or where he is now.”
Fayez sobbed as she spoke, while her husband, 58-year-old Mohammed, tried to calm her with verses from the Qur’an.
Since Manar’s disappearance, the family has looked at more than 70 bodies in the hope that one would be his, Mohammed said.
At one point, they believed they had found him, until Fayez knelt to look closer. The body was in trainers and socks, but Manar had been wearing slippers when he went missing. His hair was coarse, not soft like the hair on the body before them.
Mohammed said they have searched everywhere: hospitals, police stations, burial sites. He contacted the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and gave them a description of what his son was wearing on the day he disappeared, hoping for information about his whereabouts. He hasn’t heard back since.
“Our homes were destroyed, we were displaced from the first days of the war, and we lost loved ones. But what happened to my son is the most painful,” he said. “We don’t know if he’s dead or still alive. And worse, there is no Palestinian, international or Israeli body that will give us a clear answer.”
“I, like other families of the missing, am lost,” he said. “We have no information, the occupation refuses to give us any, and we have no way of settling our son’s fate. If he’s dead, I’ll pray for him and I want his remains. If he’s been detained, let them tell us.”
‘By every means available‘
“We have received no information from the Israeli side about the living or the dead, except what it announces about Gaza’s prisoners,” said Omar Nofal.
Confirming a death does not always mean a body has been found, Nofal said. Some were incinerated in Israeli strikes, and their families confirmed they were inside when the building was hit.
Israel has handed over 800 sets of remains, he said, but families have identified only 120 from photographs. The rest were buried in numbered graves. DNA samples have been taken from only 400 people because of the war, and Israel will not allow them to leave Gaza for testing.
The committee has met with the ICRC more than 20 times, he said, but the organization said it has no power to force Israel to reveal the identities of the bodies it has returned or holds, or information about detainees.
Gaza also has no heavy machinery to clear rubble and recover bodies, and some of the dead bodies are still in bombed buildings behind Israel’s “Yellow Line,” where Palestinians are barred from going. “Our resources are non-existent,” Nofal said. “But our national, humanitarian, and legal responsibility drives us to carry this out by every means available.”
Nofal stressed that these numbers count only what has been registered. There are thousands of missing people who have never been registered, he said, for many reasons: entire families were killed with no one left to report them, relatives are outside Gaza, or a child is the only survivor.
“For the thousands on our lists, we have no information at all. That is our biggest challenge,” he said.
Searching for signs
Like the Fayez family, Ahmed al-Astal, 56, has been searching for his son Saeed since February 22, 2024.
Saeed, then 15, left his displaced family’s tent in al-Mawasi to try to return to their home in northern Khan Younis, in an area where the Israeli army was operating.
He never returned.
Relatives and friends have searched relentlessly for Saeed: digging up graves, looking through bodies and destroyed homes, checking hospitals, and contacting every organization that might help.
“Nothing. We found nothing,” al-Astal said. “I wished I could find his body, or his remains, or even scraps of the clothes he was wearing, so we could put our doubts to rest and know for certain that he was dead. At least we would have some peace, and he would have a grave, as my wife dreams.”
The day after Saeed went missing, his sister’s fiancé went looking for him and was shot and killed by the Israeli army, al-Astal recounted.
“We were able to bring back my daughter’s fiancé’s body and bury him,” he said.
Al-Astal contacted HaMoked, an Israeli human rights organization, and the Palestinian rights group Al-Dameer. Both told him that the Israeli army had refuted Saeed’s imprisonment.
“But the Red Cross and other rights organizations tell me that’s not necessarily accurate,” al-Astal said. “There are large numbers of people the Israeli army hasn’t disclosed, even though their families witnessed the moment they were arrested.”
Al-Astal said he still hopes for some news of his son, so that he, along with his wife and siz children, can find some relief.
Without a body or proof of death, the government committee for the missing cannot issue a death certificate for Saeed.
A deliberate policy
Dr. Hussein Hammad, a human rights activist in Gaza, said Gaza’s missing fall into three groups: those under the rubble, those who have been detained and forcibly disappeared by the Israeli army, and those who vanished or fled under fire.
Any figures for the missing are estimates, he said, because there is no central system to accurately count them amid continued war, displacement and Israel’s destruction of records. UN experts have also warned that the figures for Gaza’s missing and forcibly disappeared are hugely underreported. Israel has ignored legal inquiries and appeals from rights organizations and refused to deal with the ICRC for almost the entire war. The ICRC said it resumed visits to places of detention in Gaza in the first half of 2026, but not to those inside Israel.
Hammad said Israel deliberately keeps the fate of the missing shrouded in ambiguity, as a tool of psychological warfare and collective punishment.
“There are certainly dozens, if not hundreds, of detainees held by the occupation whose families know nothing about them, and who have not been visited by a lawyer to this day,” Hammad said.
He alleged that Israel has repeatedly handed over bodies and body parts with no identifying information, medical records or forensic evidence. In his view, that is a flagrant breach of international law and a way of evading accountability for how these people died, deaths he said often show signs of torture or extrajudicial execution. Hammad said Israel is legally responsible for the fate of everyone it detained or killed under the Fourth Geneva Convention, which obliges an occupying power to protect civilians, provide accurate information about detainees and respect the dead.
International bodies, such as UN agencies, have shown “severe shortcomings and bureaucratic slowness,” Hammad said, and have limited themselves to “timid documentation and statements of concern” without putting any real pressure on Israel.
In the meantime, Palestinians have built their own institutions to discover the fate of their missing, such as the Palestinian Center for Missing and Forcibly Disappeared Persons and the Palestinian Foundation for the Missing. Despite their limited resources, Hammad said they are a “lifeline” for preserving the rights of the missing, and could provide crucial evidence to hold Israel legally accountable.
He called for an independent international commission dedicated to Gaza’s missing and forcibly disappeared, firm diplomatic and legal pressure to open Israel’s prisons and camps to the ICRC without restrictions, and urgent funding for a national DNA bank and forensic laboratories.
“Systematic enforced disappearance is not incidental,” Hammad said. “It is a political and military decision designed to multiply the families’ suffering and terrorize the whole of society.”

Chaos erupts at Poland’s top court amid ‘coup’ claims (VIDEOS): Live updates
The longstanding struggle between Poland’s right-wing president and centrist government over control of the country’s top court dramatically escalated on Friday night as riot police surrounded the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw.
Police were deployed as an announcement appeared on the court’s website stating that its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice-president, Bartlomiej Sochanski, had been suspended from their duties. Their profiles were reportedly removed from the website.
Shortly afterward, the tribunal’s official X account claimed that its website had been subjected to an “unlawful takeover” and insisted that both officials remained in their posts. “All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” the account stated.
Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who ordered the suspensions, also assumed the role of acting head of the tribunal, citing her seniority as a judge. However, the court’s existing leadership disputes her authority and maintains that Swieczkowski remains its president.
Protesters gathered outside the court building, denouncing what they described as an attack on the tribunal by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Trump’s bluff meets Iran’s resolve : Limits of American power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:17:09 UTC
05:17:09 KST

Trump’s bluff meets Iran’s resolve : Limits of American power
Goa, India – Donald Trump has been bluffing for far too long. He threatens, he warns, he issues ultimatums, and then he expects the world to believe that he has everything under control. But there comes a point when even the loudest threats begin to lose their effect. Iran may well be that point for Trump. He seems to have underestimated a country whose political instincts, historical memory and civilisational confidence cannot be understood through the narrow lens of American power.
Trump appears to believe that if he raises his voice, threatens military action and keeps the world guessing, Iran will eventually surrender. That might work with some governments. It is unlikely to work with Iran. The Iranian leadership has survived decades of sanctions, isolation, political pressure and military threats. It has learned to live with adversity, and it has developed its own ways of responding to pressure. One may disagree with Iran's government, its policies or its political system, but to dismiss its capacity to think, plan and respond would be a serious mistake.
This is where Trump seems to have got it wrong. He is accustomed to dealing with politics as though it were a business negotiation in which the other party must eventually accept his terms.
But international politics does not work like a real estate deal. Countries have their own histories, their own interests and their own understanding of what they can and cannot concede. Iran is not going to abandon its strategic interests simply because the American President demands it.
The gap between Trump's threats and reality
For months, the world has watched the familiar performance. Trump makes a dramatic announcement, the threat of military action hangs over the region, and then everyone waits to see what happens next. His supporters may interpret this as strength. But there is a difference between strength and the ability to keep making threats without securing a political outcome. At some stage, the threats themselves become a problem. If you repeatedly promise decisive action and the other side refuses to bend, you must either escalate or find a way out. Neither option necessarily makes you look strong.
Iran understands this dilemma. It does not have to respond to every American statement with an equally dramatic announcement. It can wait, calculate and choose its moment. It can also make the costs of escalation sufficiently high to force Washington to think twice. The point is not that Iran is invulnerable or that it can dictate every outcome. It is that the United States cannot assume that its military superiority automatically translates into political victory.
History has repeatedly demonstrated this distinction. A powerful military can destroy targets, damage infrastructure and inflict enormous suffering. But can it compel a country to accept the political future designed for it by a foreign power? That is a different question altogether. The United States has learned this lesson in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan, often at an enormous cost. Yet American presidents continue to behave as though the application of sufficient force will eventually produce the desired political result.
Trump appears determined not to learn from these experiences.
Iran is more than a military challenge: it has a long historical memory
One does not have to romanticise Iran to recognise the depth of its historical consciousness. Persian civilisation stretches back thousands of years. Its political culture has developed through periods of empire, foreign intervention, revolution and war. Modern Iran has also experienced the overthrow of its elected prime minister in the 1953 coup, the restoration and support of the
Shah by the United States, and the revolution of 1979 that transformed the country's political order. The Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s left a deep mark on the national psyche.
These experiences matter. They have helped shape the Iranian leadership's suspicion of American intentions and its determination to resist what it sees as attempts to dictate the country's future. Washington may regard its demands as reasonable or necessary. Tehran may see the same demands as another attempt to impose American will on Iran.
That difference in perception cannot be wished away.
Trump may believe that Iran will eventually calculate that resistance is too costly. But Iranian leaders must also calculate the political cost of surrendering under American pressure. They have to consider not only the immediate military situation but also their standing at home, their credibility with regional partners and the message that capitulation would send to other countries. A government that believes it is fighting for its sovereignty will not necessarily make the choices Washington expects.
This is why the language of ultimatums is so dangerous. It leaves little room for compromise without humiliation. And when leaders begin to see compromise as humiliation, even a sensible settlement can become difficult to achieve.
There is another issue that deserves attention: the reports and speculation surrounding Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
Uncertainty surrounding the Iranian leadership has prompted reports about Khamenei’s condition, attracting considerable attention because of his central position in Iran’s political system.
However, Iran’s leadership and institutions cannot be understood simply through speculation about one individual.
Khamenei occupies the country's highest political and religious office, and his influence over its strategic direction has been considerable. But Iran also has a wider political and security establishment, including the presidency, the cabinet, the parliament and powerful security institutions. Their roles and relationships matter when assessing how the country might respond to a crisis.
The assumption that removing one individual would bring Iran to its knees is questionable. Washington would be making a serious miscalculation if it assumed that eliminating Iran’s supreme leader would force the country into submission.
Such an act could escalate the conflict, provoke retaliation and undermine prospects for a negotiated settlement. The consequences would extend beyond Iran, potentially drawing the wider region into a much broader confrontation.
The unanswered question of Trump's endgame
This is the question that needs to be asked more often. Military threats are one thing. Having a clear idea of what comes afterwards is quite another. If the objective is to weaken Iran's military capabilities, what happens next? If the objective is to force political concessions, what concessions are actually achievable? If the aim is regime change, what makes Washington believe that the result would be a stable, friendly government rather than prolonged instability and a more dangerous regional conflict?
These are not academic questions. They concern the lives of millions of people.
Iran is situated in one of the world's most sensitive regions. Any major conflict could affect neighbouring countries, international energy markets, shipping routes and the wider global economy. The consequences would not be limited to Washington and Tehran. Countries that have little influence over the confrontation could find themselves paying a heavy price through rising fuel costs, disrupted trade and regional insecurity.
The Strait of Hormuz is particularly important in this regard. A serious disruption to shipping through this narrow waterway could have consequences for global oil supplies and the economies that depend on them. Iran knows the strategic significance of its geography. Washington knows it too. That is precisely why military escalation cannot be treated as a cost-free exercise in presidential toughness.
Trump may be confident that American military power gives him the upper hand. In conventional terms, the United States possesses formidable advantages. But Iran does not need to match America weapon for weapon to make a conflict costly. It can use its regional relationships, asymmetric capabilities and geographical position to complicate American calculations. Even a militarily superior power must consider what it will have to endure in order to achieve its objectives.
That is the reality behind the bravado.
Ultimately, the question is not whether Trump can sound more threatening than Iran. It is whether he can achieve what he claims to want without plunging the region into a wider war. If his strategy is built on the assumption that Iran will eventually submit, he may discover that the bluff has become a trap of his own making.
The world does not need another war born of presidential arrogance and strategic miscalculation. It needs diplomacy grounded in realism, respect for sovereignty and an honest recognition that American power, however formidable, has limits. Trump may believe that Iran will eventually blink. But if he mistakes Iran’s refusal to surrender for an invitation to escalate, the consequences could extend far beyond Tehran and Washington. The ultimate test of American power will not be how much destruction it can inflict, but whether it possesses the wisdom to know when to stop.

A jewel of the Romanovs: Historic 197.80-carat sapphire heads to auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:16:39 UTC
05:16:39 KST

A jewel of the Romanovs: Historic 197.80-carat sapphire heads to auction
A 197.80-carat sapphire once worn by Russian Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna is heading to auction at Sotheby’s in a Cartier diamond bracelet, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Known as the Romanov sapphire, the cushion-shaped gemstone was part of the Russian crown jewels before passing into private ownership after the Russian Revolution, according to Sotheby’s catalog.
Maria Feodorovna wore the sapphire at the 1903 Winter Palace Ball, placing it and a second, larger sapphire on the front panel of her skirt. Both were in diamond settings by Fabergé. Members of the imperial court attended in elaborate 17th-century Muscovite costumes adorned with jewels.
The exact date the sapphire entered the imperial collection is unknown. Sotheby’s says its unusual faceting suggests a Mughal-era origin. Gemological reports identify Sri Lanka, formerly known as Ceylon, as the stone’s geographical origin and indicate no evidence of heat treatment.
Despite its imperial provenance, the sapphire was placed in a category of gemstones considered to have no historical or artistic significance beyond their intrinsic value when Soviet authorities divided the crown jewels for retention or sale, according to Sotheby’s. It was subsequently sold anonymously.
Socialite and singer Ganna Walska purchased the sapphire from Cartier in 1927, when it was the central pendant of a long necklace.
Walska had the jewel redesigned several times. In 1929, she paired the sapphire with a carved Mughal emerald weighing 256.60 carats in another long necklace. By the time the sapphire appeared at Sotheby’s Parke Bernet in New York in 1971, it was the centerpiece of a shorter sapphire bead necklace.
The stone returned to auction at Sotheby’s Geneva in 1992, set in a necklace of emerald and sapphire beads.
In 2015, nearly nine decades after selling the sapphire to Walska, Cartier created its current setting: a geometric diamond bracelet inspired by the Art Deco style popular at the time of her purchase. The design connects the gemstone’s imperial history with Cartier’s own jewelry-making heritage.
The bracelet also has an interchangeable engraved rock crystal centerpiece decorated with triangular diamonds. It was exhibited in Tokyo in 2019 as part of “The Crystallisation of Time.”
The lot includes gemological reports, Cartier documentation and a French edition of the Fersman catalog, which documented the Russian crown jewels between 1924 and 1926.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Fabergé’s “Winter Egg,” created in 1913 as a gift from Emperor Nicholas II to his mother, Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna, had sold at Christie’s in London.

Ukrainians trapped in Russia-held city evacuate during local ceasefire

Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during U.S.-brokered ceasefire
Kyiv - Ukrainian and Russian humanitarian delegations began evacuating residents from Russian-occupied Oleshky on Friday, with plans to move the evacuees through Russia and Belarus before arriving back in Ukraine on Saturday.
Oleshky, a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war, has seen one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict. Russian strikes on the surrounding area have prevented food, water, and medicine from reaching the city for months. Last week, first lady Melania Trump brokered a temporary ceasefire in Oleshky from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1 to allow humanitarian aid to enter, and for some residents to evacuate the area. Pope Leo also pressed for a truce.
On Friday morning, Ukrainian and Russian humanitarian delegations reached the city and began administering aid and preparing for evacuations.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to leave safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay can stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support," Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who led the Ukrainian delegation, said.
The convoy included 25 buses, and some ambulances arrived to deliver food and medicine. Local authorities say about 2,000 people remain in Oleshky.
The localized ceasefire comes after President Trump increased pressure on Kyiv to stop striking Russian energy targets ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next week, with some Ukrainian officials doubting Russian motives.
"Because these negotiations were led by the U.S. and Melania Trump, it seems to me that the Russians have agreed to this ceasefire to show that they are a reliable partner for these negotiations and other future peace negotiations with Ukraine," Vadym Ivchenko, a Ukrainian parliament member on its Defense, Intelligence, and National Security Committee, told CBS News.
But on social media platforms, Ukrainians expressed skepticism about the local ceasefire, and what it could mean for Ukraine's broader Kherson region, in the midst of its own humanitarian crisis.
"Under the pretext of evacuating people from Oleshky, they are moving their troops forward. This poses a direct threat to the city of Kherson and the Right Bank," Ukrainian journalist Nastia Nagorna wrote on Facebook. "This risk escalates if such humanitarian missions become a 'monthly' occurrence—or take on any other form of 'regularity.' It would allow Russian forces, under the guise of delivering humanitarian aid, to amass a significant concentration of troops and resources."
Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire. On Thursday afternoon, a Russian strike on a passenger train station in Ukraine's eastern city of Dnipro killed at least 14 people. Overnight into Friday, Russia launched an attack on Kyiv's energy grid, leaving hundreds of thousands without power, while Kyiv struck a Russian oil refinery for the first time in two weeks.
