Influenza vaccination in Ukraine is delayed — the Ministry of Health cited the reasons
Kyiv • UNN
The supply of influenza vaccines is delayed due to the switch to trivalent vaccines and production difficulties. The Ministry of Health expects them in November 2026.
As of the end of October, the supply of influenza vaccines to Ukrainian pharmacies has been delayed due to the global transition to trivalent vaccines following WHO recommendations. At the same time, the Ministry of Health assured that as of October 30 there was no shortage of other vaccines. This was stated in the Ministry of Health's response to a request from UNN.
Details
The Ministry of Health reported that as of October 30, influenza vaccination in the 2026–2027 epidemic season had not yet begun.
According to information from manufacturers' representatives, the start of vaccine deliveries to Ukraine's retail network is expected in November 2026. The delivery timelines were affected by the transition from quadrivalent to trivalent vaccines in accordance with updated recommendations from the World Health Organization, the later availability of materials and reagents for quality control, as well as production difficulties involving certain vaccines
At the same time, the ministry noted that similar changes to delivery schedules are also being observed in a number of other European countries. Measures are currently being taken to facilitate the fastest possible arrival of vaccines in Ukraine.
The agency also assured that as of October 30, stocks of other vaccines included in the mandatory vaccination schedule were sufficient. Vaccination is carried out according to age.
The ministry said that during the same period last year — by the 43rd week of 2025 — 6,123 people had been vaccinated against influenza. During 2025, 20,000 doses of influenza vaccine were supplied through humanitarian aid programs. This figure covers the entire year of 2025 and does not reflect the total volume of supplies through all channels for the comparable period in question.
In addition, the Ministry of Health said that supplies of medical immunobiological products for preventive vaccinations included in the Schedule are funded from the State Budget of Ukraine, while vaccinations based on epidemic indications are funded from local budgets and other sources not prohibited by law.
Influenza vaccinations are recommended. At the same time, the Schedule provides for their administration based on health status and epidemic indications. Vaccinations based on health status are mandatory as part of the medical care of patients with the diseases and conditions specified in the Schedule. Currently, centralized procurement of seasonal influenza vaccines using funds from the State Budget of Ukraine is not carried out. Vaccines are supplied to the Ukrainian market on a commercial basis and may be purchased by citizens themselves, using funds from local budgets and other sources not prohibited by law. Local executive authorities and local self-government bodies, within their powers, may provide for the purchase of influenza vaccines and vaccination of designated target groups under the relevant local programs. The volumes and timelines of commercial vaccine supplies to Ukraine, including additional batches, are determined by importers in accordance with market demand, orders from pharmacy chains and healthcare facilities, and manufacturers' capabilities. Vaccines are distributed among regions by suppliers in accordance with the orders received
The ministry also said that influenza vaccination is primarily recommended for people at increased risk of severe disease and complications: young children starting at six months of age, older people, pregnant women, women planning to become pregnant during the epidemic season, patients with chronic diseases, as well as healthcare workers and other people at increased occupational risk of infection.

IN BRIEF: How humanitarian mission in Alyoshki went
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

03:59:26 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Some residents of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region travelled freely towards Russia, while the others travelled to Ukraine, said Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova.
TASS has compiled the key facts about the humanitarian mission.
Lantratova's statements
- Lantratova said that Alyoshki residents thanked all parties for carrying out the humanitarian mission: "It's very important that people waited, they thank both sides."
- According to her, some of the residents travelled "absolutely unhindered" towards Russia, the others to Ukraine: "People gathered, families with children, the elderly, and buses were organized."
- She said that the residents took their pets with them.
- Humanitarian aid was provided to those who were unable to leave the town due to various circumstances.
- Lantratova said that everything was going on normally: "Both offices of the ombudspersons are monitoring the situation."
- She noted the contribution of the First Lady of the United States Melania Trump to the organization of the humanitarian mission: "This is very important to us, and we thank the First Lady for helping people, for saving lives."
Statements by the Ukrainian ombudsman
- Ukraine’s Ombudsman Dmitry Lubinets declared full observance of the silence regime in the Kherson direction and the absence of any violations from the moment of its establishment: "We came to Alyoshki as safely as was possible in the current conditions. The silence regime is fully respected. I emphasize that there have been no violations since the establishment of the silence regime."
- He said that residents of the city who did not have time to submit an evacuation request can still leave the town: " "There are already cases when people who did not sign up came - they were also given the opportunity: ‘Please, come in if you want to leave Alyoshki’."
Lubinets highly appreciated the work of Lantratova's team in Alyoshki, noting high professionalism of the staff: "Yana Valeryevna's staff, together with my staff, have worked out a very systematic approach. And today we are really here, on the ground, seeing how everything works. This is why I rate the organization of the work as very professional, for which I am especially grateful to Yana Valeryevna."
Preparation of the humanitarian corridor
- On the evening of October 29, the Russian military completed the clearance of routes for the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- The Dnepr battlegroup neutralized the roads adjacent to the town from unexploded ordnance, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- Two people, including a field engineer, were killed while demining to ensure the safe passage of a humanitarian mission, Lantratova said.
- According to the ministry, field engineer of the 98th Guards Airborne Division, Sergeant Andrey Vedernikov was killed.
- Earlier, the Defense Ministry said that Ukraine was remotely mining access roads with drones to prevent the evacuation of civilians and block the delivery of food, medicines and socially important goods to the town.
On conducting a humanitarian operation
- The humanitarian mission in Alyoshki is taking place in full compliance with the agreements between Russia and Ukraine, Melania Trump said.
- In the town, Lantratova and Lubinets coordinated the implementation of the agreements reached with the assistance of the First Lady of the United States.
- The Alyoshki residents who decided to leave the settlement could do so before 2:00 p.m. Moscow time (11:00 a.m. GMT).
- The distribution of humanitarian aid was scheduled for after 2:30 p.m. Moscow time (11:30 a.m. GMT)..
- All security measures were taken.
- According to Lantratova, several dozen tons of humanitarian aid were distributed to the residents of Alyoshki - food, hygiene products, fuel for generators and other necessary things. The list of what is needed was compiled at the request of the residents.
- She noted that it is important for those who decided to stay in the settlement.
- Lantratova said that the ombudspersons of Russia and Ukraine are considering regular delivery of humanitarian aid to Alyoshki.
- Chairman of the Russian Red Cross Pavel Savchuk said that the RCC provided humanitarian aid to the people in Alyoshki. The cargo was delivered by the office of Russia’s ombudsman as part of a humanitarian mission.
Evacuation of the people
- A humanitarian aid convoy was sent to the central district hospital.
- It consisted of 25 buses, Lantratova said.
- Special buses for bedridden people with 30 seats and nine ambulances were also prepared.
- A separate bus was also organized for people with pets.
- On the afternoon of October 30, Lantratova said that all those who expressed the desire to leave Alyoshki were placed on the evacuation buses.
- According to her, people traveled to both Russia and Ukraine.
- On October 26, Lantratova called Kiev's statements about the forced removal of children from Alyoshki unacceptable.
- The ombudswoman called on Ukraine to give the residents of Alyoshki the opportunity to make an informed decision, let them live in peace and order their military to stop the daily shelling of the town and mining roads.
The work of journalists
- According to Lantratova, more than 50 journalists from different countries arrived in the Kherson Region to cover the operation.
- As the ombudswoman noted, all of them will be able to personally communicate with the residents of Alyoshki.
- The humanitarian mission in the city was documented, among others, by Newsmax journalists.
- Melania Trump said they act as neutral observers, will independently film and document the progress of the mission.
- One of the American journalists from the mission, John Chay, said that he was in touch with the first lady of the United States.
Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he considers the presence of Russian, not foreign, journalists to be the key to covering the humanitarian mission.
Coordination of the humanitarian operation in Alyoshki
- According to Lantratova, the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki has been prepared since May.
- As previously reported by Russia’s Chief of the General Staff, Army General Valery Gerasimov, Russian troops will introduce a ceasefire regime in the Kherson direction from 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27 for the humanitarian operation.
- Ukraine’s General Staff also said it was complying with the ceasefire from 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27.
- Lantratova later said that the temporary ceasefire in the Kherson direction would last until 10:59 p.m. Moscow time (7:59 p.m. GMT) on November 1.
- Since the beginning of the silence regime, she has been reporting daily on its observance by both sides.
Reaction to the announcement of the ceasefire
- Lantratova thanked Melania Trump and all the participants of the negotiating group for their cooperation in organizing a humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed the agreement, his official representative Stephane Dujarric said in a statement.
- White House Communications Director Steven Cheung called the agreements an important step towards resolving the Ukrainian conflict.
The situation in Alyoshki
- On September 21, Peskov called the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki critical.
- It was impossible to bring food or medicines to the town due to shelling and drone attacks from Kiev.
- On September 1, a determined attempt was made to break the blockade of Alyosha to deliver humanitarian aid to the people, but Ukrainian militants fired at a convoy of vehicles and almost completely destroyed the cargo, said Rodion Miroshnik, Ambassador-at-large of the Russian Foreign Ministry for crimes of the Kiev regime.
- A little more than 1,000 people remain in Alyoshki, he informed.
- Miroshnik noted that the situation has worsened in the last four to five months.
- Residents of nearby settlements on the left bank of the Dnepr River tried to deliver food to Alyoshki, but Ukraine prevented this, evacuated resident Svetlana Popova told TASS.
- According to her, the civilian population of the city did not receive humanitarian aid from Ukraine, all reports about this are lies.

“Shto mi e milo i drago” by Dobri Hristov: A benchmark of Bulgarian Choral Music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:57:47 UTC
03:57:47 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
Article
Highlights of Bulgarian musical culture
“Shto mi e milo i drago” by Dobri Hristov: A benchmark of Bulgarian Choral Music
Friday 30 October 2026 20:00
Friday, 30 October 2026, 20:00
Dobri Hristov (1875 – 1941)
PHOTO Archives State Agency
Font size
Dobri Hristov, one of the great creative figures of the first generation of Bulgarian composers, holds an exceptional place in the country’s cultural history. His work as an outstanding conductor, inspiring teacher, perceptive scholar and active leader of leading musical institutions helped lay the foundations of professional music in Bulgaria. His contribution to the collection and study of Bulgarian folklore is immense, as is his role in creating classical examples of choral and solo song and in shaping the aesthetic and creative principles of the country’s second generation of composers. Among his pupils were such eminent figures as Pancho Vladigerov, Veselin Stoyanov, Philip Koutev and Marin Goleminov.
Hristov’s choral output, which brought together authentic Bulgarian folk music and Orthodox Church Slavonic chant with the principles of classical harmony, made a fundamental contribution to Bulgaria’s classical music. Drawing on folk songs from different regions of the country, he composed dozens of works for mixed, male and children’s choirs. Many of the texts in these vivid miniatures retain their original dialect features, allowing Hristov to blur, to a considerable extent, the boundary between his own artistic creation and the folk tradition.
Although he began his musical journey as a self-taught, albeit exceptionally gifted, musician in his native city Varna, Hristov composed two choral suites, Lilyana, the Beautiful Maiden and The Girls of Zheravna, before he had even turned 20. He submitted them to a competition for a scholarship to study abroad. His rejection by the selection committee was regarded as an affront by the people of Varna, who raised funds to send the young musician to the Prague Conservatory, where he studied under Antonín Dvořák.
His three years in Prague broadened Hristov’s understanding of the standards and values underpinning national musical art.
The cover of the collection "Madeconian Songs" from 1923
PHOTO Archive
After returning to Bulgaria in 1903, Dobri Hristov began arranging folk songs from the region of Macedonia, which he considered particularly well suited to artistic treatment using the techniques of classical harmony.
Most of these arrangements, written for male choir, were published in 1923 in the collection Macedonian Songs. Among the best-loved and most frequently performed is Shto mi e milo i drago (“How Dear and Precious It Is to Me”), in which a young man sings of his longing to own a shop in the town of Struga, sit outside it and watch the beautiful young women on their way to fetch water from the local springs.
In recent decades, this folk song from the Struga region, a picturesque town in present-day North Macedonia on the northern shore of Lake Ohrid, has become particularly popular in the interpretation of the celebrated Bulgarian folk singer Kostadin Gugov. Bulgarian choirs also favour and frequently perform the arrangement by Petko Staynov, a distinguished composer of the country’s second generation. Yet it was the great master Dobri Hristov who created the first choral arrangement. His version, scored exclusively for male voices, has been performed by numerous ensembles.
Mihail Milkov (1923 – 2003)
PHOTO archives.bnr.bg
One of the most remarkable interpretations dates from the early 1990s and features the male singers of the Bulgarian National Radio Mixed Choir under the baton of conductor Mihail Milkov (1923–2003).
A leading authority on Bulgarian choral performance, Mihail Milkov founded the BNR Mixed Choir in 1952 and led it for more than four decades, leaving the Radio archives a legacy of over 500 recordings. The choir’s landmark international tours and its collaborations with some of the world’s greatest conductors, including Herbert von Karajan, Claudio Abbado and Riccardo Muti, remain particularly noteworthy.
The performance of the song Shto mi e milo i drago conducted by Mihail Milkov is striking for its expressive power, the richness and beauty of its vocal timbres, and its remarkably balanced, cohesive ensemble sound.
You can find more installments in Radio Bulgaria's running series "Highlights of Bulgarian Musical Culture" HERE.
Photos: Archives State Agency, archives.bnr.bg, archive
Editor: Elena Karkalanova
English version: R. Petkova

Five children among seven dead in eastern Syria floods
Oct 30 - Seven people, including five children, have died and seven others were injured after torrential rains triggered flash floods in eastern Syria, authorities said on Friday.
Four people remain missing and rescue teams are continuing to search flooded areas, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said in a statement on X.
The five children drowned in pools of water formed by the floods, while another person died in a traffic accident, Saleh said, without providing details of the seventh death.
Flooding has hit the eastern provinces of Raqqa, Deir al-Zor and Hasakah, as well as parts of Aleppo, damaging infrastructure, cutting off roads and forcing families to leave their homes.
Syria's civil defence teams have carried out more than 550 emergency operations since the storms began, rescuing 60 people trapped by floodwater and responding to more than 900 distress calls, Saleh said.
Emergency crews evacuated more than 350 students from two schools and helped 375 families leave camps in Raqqa province. Teams also responded to flooding at camps in rural Aleppo and Idlib, and pumped water from around 250 homes and public buildings.
In Deir al-Zor, the floods damaged roads and telecommunications infrastructure, disrupting transport and communications, state news agency SANA reported. Heavy rainfall also caused seven culverts to collapse, cutting off access to several areas.
Authorities suspended classes in Raqqa, Hasakah and Deir al-Zor on Thursday, while forecasters warned unsettled weather could continue into Saturday. REUTERS

Pakistan army ‘cautiously optimistic’ about US-Iran mediation efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:55:36 UTC

Pakistan army ‘cautiously optimistic’ about US-Iran mediation efforts
Pakistan’s military spokesman warns of ‘powerful spoilers and detractors’ who still believe the conflict serves them.
Pakistan’s army is “cautiously optimistic” about mediation efforts between Iran and the United States as regional countries seek to revive a ceasefire in the eight-month-old war.
Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, spokesman for Pakistan’s military, suggested on Friday that there were positive signs in attempts to de-escalate the conflict. His comments to the Reuters news agency were the first since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief mediator, has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday, alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
He also warned that there are parties seeking to obstruct mediation between the US and Iran.
There are still “powerful spoilers and detractors” who believe conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan’s armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed in Tehran or whether the US had backed the trip.
His comments on Friday came as Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran in another apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the June ceasefire that collapsed months later.
Mecca defence pact
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Pakistan’s Munir in Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. “We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict,” he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group has been reignited by the Iran conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.

‘Deepest possible partnership’: Canada and EU announce new alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:54:51 UTC
03:54:51 KST

Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.
Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.
“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.
As they concluded their two-day summit, Canada agreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.
While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.
Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.
Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.
Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.
“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.
Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.
In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.
“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.
“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.
The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.
“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.
European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.
Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever between European Union and a non-European country”.
Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.
“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.
He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.

Putin’s African ties: Military cooperation, “history” wars, and sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:50:50 UTC
03:50:50 KST

Russia and a range of African countries have adopted declarations on political and economic cooperation following the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow. In the outcome documents, the parties agreed to counter the “rewriting of history,” the blocking of sovereign assets, and the politicization of international justice while working to foster cooperation in security, space, mineral extraction, and AI. Vladimir Putin said that Russia already has agreements on military and military-technical cooperation with 45 African nations. The Insider has compiled the main statements and agreements of the two-day summit.
The third Russia–Africa summit took place in Moscow on Oct. 28–29, with delegations from 48 of the continent’s 54 countries in attendance. Two dozen states were represented by high-level officials, with sessions co-chaired by Putin and Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who currently heads the African Union.
As a result of the gathering, the parties adopted three main documents: the final declaration of the summit, a declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of AI, and the action plan of the Russia–Africa partnership forum for 2027–2029. In addition, more than 60 official agreements were signed at the summit and at the parallel economic and humanitarian forum, Russian presidential adviser Anton Kobyakov announced via Telegram.
Countering sanctions, “rewriting of history,” and colonial legacies
A significant part of the final declaration is devoted to international politics. Russia and the African states in attendance agreed to oppose the blocking and seizure of sovereign assets, as well as to resist outside political and economic pressure. The parties intend to coordinate their positions when it comes to sanctions against African countries.
The summit participants also agreed to counter attempts at “rewriting and falsifying history.” These and other provisions are included in the final declaration, which consists of 101 points.
Another area will be assessing the damage “inflicted on African states during the colonial period.” Russian scientists are already developing a methodology for such assessment jointly with African colleagues. Preliminary results should be presented in 2027, and a special research laboratory is expected to open in Uganda in November 2026.
In his speech on Oct. 28, Vladimir Putin accused Western countries of trying to preserve Africa’s economic dependence and impose new debt obligations on it. The Russian president claimed that Moscow is ready to transfer technology and foster production on the continent.
African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf stressed in his speech that African states are interested in developing local industry and gaining access to international capital. He also called for reforming the U.N. Security Council by expanding African representation.
Military cooperation and fight against terrorism
Putin stated that Russia has intergovernmental agreements on military and military-technical cooperation in effect with 45 African states, noting that Moscow trains African servicemen and law enforcement officers at Russian educational institutions.
In the final statements, the parties reaffirmed their intention to expand cooperation in the fight against terrorism and extremism, counter the use of new technologies by terrorist organizations, and develop joint security mechanisms.
Special attention was paid to the Sahel states: Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. Commenting on the statement of Assimi Goïta, the head of Mali’s military government, Putin stressed the global importance of resolving the situation in the Sahel.
Russia’s military presence in the region has expanded in recent years. After the Wagner Group wound down its activities following the death of founder Yevgeny Prigozhin in August 2023, Russia's state-run Africa Corps stepped in to take over the role in several African states. Russian military units currently operate in Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, and the Central African Republic.
Two days ahead of the summit, African branches of Amnesty International appealed to its participants with a call to demand that Moscow stop the deceptive and coercive recruitment of citizens of African states to take part in the war against Ukraine. Human rights activists claim that Russia recruits foreigners under the guise of employment and then sends them to the front.
AI, space, and control over technology
The summit participants devoted a separate declaration to cooperation in AI — to promote equal and fair access to safe AI technologies, the development of joint educational programs, and capacity-building efforts. Satellite communications and the use of space were discussed separately.
According to Putin, approximately 40,000 students from African countries are studying in Russia, and Moscow is expanding training programs for foreign civil servants, including in the digitalization of public administration. Putin also characterized Russia as being one of three countries with full digital sovereignty — a claim The Insider has examined in its Antifake section.
Precious metals, nuclear power plants, and trade
The economic part of the summit focused on energy, transportation, agriculture, and the mining and processing of minerals.
Russia’s Rusal and the state-owned Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation agreed to create two joint ventures in Ghana. The companies plan to develop the Nyinahini deposit with annual output of up to 5 million metric tons of bauxite and build an alumina refinery with a capacity of 1.2 million metric tons per year, with Rusal receiving controlling stakes in both ventures. Reuters notes that the company is seeking to reduce its dependence on external suppliers of raw materials after losing part of its supplies from Ukraine and Australia in 2022.
Ghana’s President John Dramani Mahama also announced the start of negotiations with Rosatom on building the country’s first nuclear power plant.
According to Putin, Russia’s trade with African countries reached $27 billion in 2025, and since 2023 Moscow has opened eight new embassies on the continent. In the near future, Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo intend to open diplomatic missions of their own in the Russian capital.
Putin also said that in the first nine months of 2026, Russia had supplied African countries with 13 million tons of agricultural products. Deliveries of mineral fertilizers, he said, exceeded 2.2 million tons this year, compared with 1.5 million tons for all of last year.
Trade with Africa remains significantly below the level promised by Putin
Despite claims of successful cooperation, Russia’s trade with Africa has not yet reached the level that Putin promised at the first summit in 2019. As Chatham House notes, the Russian leader set a goal of bringing trade turnover to $40 billion; however, in 2025, it totaled only $27 billion. For comparison, also according to data cited by Chatham House, China’s trade with African countries reached $348 billion in 2025, and the European Union’s was about $395 billion.
At the same time, Russia continues to expand its political and military presence on the continent. Earlier, The Insider described how Moscow uses cooperation with African governments to gain access to natural resources and strengthen its influence in international organizations.
Six days before the current summit, The Insider identified a GRU officer who in April 2025 infiltrated the diplomatic residence of the African Union in Ethiopia. He turned out to be Alexander Dubikov, who worked undercover as an assistant to the Russian military attaché and is linked to hackers from the Sandworm group. The incident occurred at a compound used by the current chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, who also took part in the Moscow summit.
Dialogue with Europe, possible war, and situation in the Baltic Sea
At the press conference following the summit, Putin took questions about relations with Europe. Commenting on his Oct. 27 phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Putin said the European leaders themselves initiated the call, stressing that they were acting in their national capacity, not on behalf of the European Union. Despite being critical of his counterparts, Putin called the conversation the right step and supported attempts to restore dialogue with European countries.
Nevertheless, Putin said that Russia is ready for war with Europe, even if it does not seek one. He criticized statements by European politicians about the need to prepare for a possible military conflict by 2030 and expressed confidence that Russia cannot be dealt a strategic defeat. “If it goes too far, there will be no winner at all,” he commented, adding that Russia remembers the lessons of the First and Second World Wars and is doing everything it can to prevent reliving them.
Finally, Putin touched on the situation in the Baltic Sea, which he had discussed with the leaders of Finland and Norway. According to Putin, his Nordic interlocutors had invoked the need to comply with international maritime law. Putin supported their position but warned that a situation similar to what is happening in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz could develop in the Baltic. Russia, according to him, does not want such a development but is ready to respond to any challenge.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA) will strengthen its diplomatic missions abroad with 46 additional positions to improve consular services; competitions to fill these positions will be announced shortly, the ministry's head, Andriy Sybiha, has said.

Information on the conditions for participation, requirements for candidates, and the procedure for conducting the selection processes will be published on the MFA official websites.
Sybiha drew attention to complaints and appeals from Ukrainians regarding difficulties in scheduling appointments and accessing consular services. "Since 2022, the number of Ukrainians abroad has risen sharply, while the consular service's staffing capacity has not kept pace. The decision to create 46 additional positions is, in particular, our response to citizens' criticism and requests," the minister said.

Serhiy Prytula’s Foundation has, for the first time, delivered 45 Black Betty loitering munitions — a new, cost-effective variant of the RAM-2X — to the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
The foundation told Militarnyi that the drone is designed for high-precision strikes against enemy logistics.
They were part of a batch of reconnaissance and strike assets with a total value of UAH 69.8 million, which was distributed to seven units as part of the “Shchelypy” fundraising campaign.
In total, the military received 45 Black Betty systems, 14 Shark-M systems, and nine systems equipped with RAM-2X loitering munitions.
The equipment was received by the 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade, the 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the 65th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the Intelligence Command Center, the 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Systems Forces, the 98th Special Operations Reconnaissance Center, as well as units of the Security Service of Ukraine.
Black Betty is a new, cost-reduced variant of the RAM-2X developed by Ukrspecsystems.
It is designed for mass production and intended for high-precision strikes against enemy logistics, particularly moving targets.
The Shark-M and loitering munitions operate in tandem. The Shark-M can remain airborne for up to seven hours, cover a distance of up to 180 km, and relay signals to operational-tactical-level kamikaze drones. The first drone detects the target, and the second strikes it.
In September, it was reported that RAM-2X strike drones had already hit over 450 targets.
The RAM-2X loitering munition operates at the operational-tactical level and has a range of up to 180 km. The drone is designed to strike enemy targets and can remain airborne for over two hours.
The drone is equipped with a warhead containing a 2.7- or 3.5-kg strike core and supports the integration of artificial intelligence systems. The system is characterized by a high degree of automation and a variety of communication channels.
The drone can operate via multiple radio frequency bands as well as through a Starlink terminal.

Russia-Ukraine humanitarian truce: What is happening in Alyoshki?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:47:05 UTC
03:47:05 KST

Russia-Ukraine humanitarian truce: What is happening in Alyoshki?
Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian teams have begun delivering aid and evacuating civilians from the frontline town of Alyoshki under a temporary ceasefire brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump.
Residents of the town in Russia’s Kherson Region have faced months of severe shortages, with Ukrainian drone attacks and mines disrupting supply routes, according to Russian officials and evacuees interviewed by RT.
An RT correspondent is on the ground covering the mission, which has brought representatives from both sides together to assist civilians. Here is how the agreement came about, what is happening on the ground and what residents have said about conditions in the town.
Where is Alyoshki?
Alyoshki lies on the left bank of the Dnieper River, opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson. It has been under Russian control since 2022 and is part of Russia’s Kherson Region, which Ukraine continues to claim.
The nearby Antonovsky Bridge, once a key crossing between the two cities, was put out of action in 2022. The river has since formed part of the front line separating Russian and Ukrainian forces.
The humanitarian mission is using land routes into Alyoshki, which Russian military engineers have been clearing of mines and unexploded ordnance.
Why was a humanitarian ceasefire needed?
Russian authorities estimated that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians remained in Alyoshki before the operation, including elderly residents and children. Food, medicine, drinking water and fuel have been scarce, while damaged utilities have deprived residents of basic services.
Kherson Governor Vladimir Saldo has accused Ukrainian forces of attacking supply vehicles and remotely mining access roads. Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods.”
Ukraine, meanwhile, has accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving. However, evacuees interviewed by RT blamed Ukrainian attacks for making both aid deliveries and evacuation attempts dangerous.
What have residents told RT?
“There’s nothing to eat. No medicine. Drones are constantly hovering above you,” one evacuee said. He described residents being unable to step outside without encountering drones and recalled three supply vehicles being destroyed in succession in the spring, leaving people to survive on vegetables grown in their gardens.
Others recounted receiving food, water and fuel from Russian soldiers and volunteers.
One woman said her husband was killed by a mine while collecting potatoes. She described how Russian troops guided her to safety using drones and a radio during a five-hour journey to a hospital.
Another resident, whose husband was killed in a Ukrainian attack, described houses being “blown away” during bombardments. Another evacuee noted that the people of Alyoshki were treated by Ukraine as “scum” and “traitors.”
Who negotiated the agreement?
The humanitarian crisis was raised during an October 9 telephone conversation between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. The two leaders agreed to establish direct contact between Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova and Melania Trump’s office.
Subsequent negotiations secured a temporary pause in fighting around Alyoshki, with the US first lady and Pope Leo XIV helping advance the initiative.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has credited Melania Trump with coordinating the effort, linking her involvement to earlier work reuniting children separated from their families during the conflict.
Is the EU involved?
The EU has played no role in negotiating or carrying out the mission. The operation has instead relied on direct Russian-Ukrainian coordination, US mediation and logistical support from Belarus.
Who is leading the humanitarian teams?
Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, have coordinated the practical arrangements and are taking part in the mission.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has also participated in contacts and public announcements related to the operation.
Belarus has provided logistical assistance, with delegations from both countries traveling through the Belarusian city of Gomel before proceeding toward Alyoshki.
How long does the ceasefire last?
The truce took effect at 4am Moscow time on October 27 and is due to expire at 10:59pm on November 1. It covers the humanitarian mission and the routes used to bring in supplies and evacuate residents.
On Friday, Melania Trump said the ceasefire had held for 80 hours, allowing Russian and Ukrainian teams to deliver aid and prepare civilian evacuations.
Lantratova confirmed that both sides were honoring their commitments, reporting no violations.
What is happening on the ground?
Aid distribution and the boarding of evacuation buses were underway on Friday, according to Lantratova.
The humanitarian convoy includes 25 buses and vehicles carrying food, medicine, drinking water, hygiene supplies and fuel for generators.
Residents are free to stay or leave, with evacuation options available for those wishing to travel deeper into Russia or to Ukrainian-held territory.
Those remaining in Alyoshki are receiving essential supplies, Lantratova said. Some have chosen not to leave because they want to remain in their homes or care for relatives.
More than 50 journalists from several countries have arrived to cover the mission, according to Lantratova. They include an RT correspondent and four Newsmax reporters whom Melania Trump identified as observers documenting the operation.
What did securing the routes involve?
Military engineers had to clear mines and unexploded ordnance before humanitarian vehicles could enter Alyoshki.
The Russian Defense Ministry released footage of remotely operated mine-clearing equipment and said many of the explosives discovered along the routes had been dropped by Ukrainian drones.
The operation has already claimed a life. The ministry confirmed that Sergeant Andrey Vedernikov of the 98th Guards Airborne Division was killed on October 28 while clearing a road leading into the town.
According to the ministry, he was fatally wounded by a drone-laid explosive device equipped with a proximity sensor.
Could the operation be repeated?
Although the agreement applies only to Alyoshki, Peskov has suggested it could serve as a model for future humanitarian missions.
He said a successful truce “could set a precedent,” opening the way for similar ceasefires in other areas of the conflict zone.

Costa Rica's Grynspan extends lead in informal UN chief poll, sources say
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 30 - An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Friday showed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan extended her lead as frontrunner in the race to become the 10th UN secretary-general, two people close to the process said.
Grynspan got 11 votes in favor and 4 against on the 15-member council, marking her strongest showing in seven closed-door ballots conducted in recent months to replace Antonio Guterres as he finishes his second five-year term this year.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body's declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
Securing the council's recommendation requires at least 9 positive votes and no "discourage" votes from the five permanent members - France, Britain, the US, Russia and China. Friday's ballot was not coded in a way that would allow decyphering of how the "P5" voted.
Friday also marked the first poll since United Arab Emirates diplomat Lana Nusseibeh entered the race, but the Middle Eastern contender and former ambassador to the UN received 7 votes in favor, 6 against and 2 marked as "no opinion." REUTERS

Ukraine's largest fixed-line telecommunications operator, Ukrtelecom, increased revenue by almost 13% in January-September 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, to UAH 4.3 billion, while EBITDA rose 46% year over year to more than UAH 1.3 billion, according to a company press release published Thursday.
"Throughout the third quarter of 2026, Ukrtelecom continued to ensure the stable operation of telecommunications infrastructure and uninterrupted services for our subscribers throughout Ukraine," Ukrtelecom CEO Yuriy Kurmaz said in the press release.
Revenue from optical internet services increased by 12% over the nine-month period compared with the same period last year. As of the end of September, 85% of the company's business-to-consumer (B2C) subscribers and 93% of its business-to-business (B2B) subscribers were using its optical internet services.
Among other indicators, the EBITDA margin for the reporting period stood at 30.5%, up 7 percentage points from last year.
The company added that it had laid more than 3,400 kilometers of fiber-optic lines in the first nine months of this year, bringing the total length of its optical network to 96,300 kilometers.
According to the press release, nearly 1,500 medical facilities and 2,038 educational institutions were connected to the fixed-line operator's optical network as of the end of the third quarter of this year.
In addition, since the beginning of this year, the company's specialists have extended optical internet connections to 82 medical facilities and 143 educational institutions.
Ukrtelecom separately reported that revenue from commercial property rentals totaled almost UAH 495 million in January-September 2026.
The company said it had paid nearly UAH 1.3 billion in taxes and fees to budgets at all levels during the first nine months of 2026.
The company also recalled that the virtual mobile operator U Mobile began operating in Ukraine in September this year. It is a trademark for mobile communications services provided by Trimob LLC, whose sole founder is Ukrtelecom.
The virtual mobile operator offers a range of Semerka tariff plans, which provide opportunities for messaging through apps, watching video content and working.
As reported, Ukrtelecom increased its total revenue by 12.6% in January-June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, to UAH 2.78 billion, while EBITDA rose by 50% to more than UAH 810 million.

As Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent newspapers, is forced to close after 33 years, three former staffers look back on its legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:41:49 UTC
03:41:49 KST

As Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent newspapers, is forced to close after 33 years, three former staffers look back on its legacy
Novaya Gazeta has announced that it is closing. For more than 30 years, it covered Russia’s biggest events and told stories about Russians that readers couldn’t find anywhere else. Many outstanding journalists worked at Novaya. Some were killed for telling the truth. Meduza asked former Novaya Gazeta journalists Ekaterina Glikman, Elena Kostyuchenko, and Nadya Yurova to reflect on three decades of work by one of the country’s most important independent publications, which they were all part of.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Ekaterina Glikman
Special correspondent and deputy editorial director at Novaya Gazeta from 2002 to 2022. Now deputy editor in chief of Novaya Gazeta Europe
My last years of high school coincided with Novaya Gazeta’s best years. I couldn’t get enough of it. Maybe that’s just my impression, but 1997 and 1998 were brilliant years. Above all, because of its star lineup of journalists. Novaya Gazeta was always a paper built around individual writers: Everyone had a very distinctive style, and the articles were fairly opinionated.
That’s not how people write now — everything has to be uniform, polished, and objective. There’s probably something to that; times have changed. But I miss that journalism, where the writer’s voice came through. You could start reading an article halfway through, without looking at the byline, and know who wrote it. Every writer was recognizable. I loved them all.
For my very first university internship, in 1998, I ran straight to Novaya — without arranging anything beforehand. I wanted to be like all those journalists, starting with [investigations editor Yuri] Shchekochikhin. I’m not sure Novaya deliberately recruited young people, but there were lots of kids like me.
Ekaterina Glikman on Yuri Shchekochikhin
I remember Novaya’s old website — it was terribly dated. There were two buttons in the menu linking to memorial pages: “Politkovskaya” and “Shchekochikhin.” For years afterward, I’d click on them to read their articles, until the old website was replaced. Shchekochikhin’s memorial site had an archive of his articles, people’s memories of him, and his prose.
For the first anniversary of his death, we put together a book of memories — a white cover with his signature on it. It was later reissued and expanded. We asked everyone who knew and loved him to write a short chapter. Those chapters were then posted on the memorial site.
Unfortunately, I don’t have any of it with me: I couldn’t take anything with me when the war began, and I can’t travel to Russia anymore. I’d like to reread it now — but I have neither the book nor the website. My whole library is still in Russia.
I joined Novaya in 2002, working in Yuri Shchekochikhin’s investigations department. Before that, I’d worked at the newspaper Segodnya, which was shut down [in 2001]. Salaries at Novaya were terribly low. You couldn’t survive on them. I really wanted to work there, but once you were no longer a student and had to pay rent, it was impossible. I’d stand at the newsstand at the journalism school, looking at the national newspapers — and I didn’t want to work for any of them. There was nowhere to go except Novaya. I had to resign myself to living in poverty but doing what I loved.
I think Shchekochikhin initially screened out most of my story ideas [for my safety]. Of course, that made me absolutely furious. But given how young I was then [Glikman was under 30 at the time], it’s understandable. My favorite kind of work was investigative reporting in the field: from Kuzbass, for example, about miners who’d died, or from Kamchatka, about a man wrongly sentenced to life in prison.
From 2004 to 2006, the last two years of Politkovskaya’s life, I was deputy to editorial director Sergei Sokolov. He handed some of his work over to me. That meant Politkovskaya’s articles, Chechnya — all the hardest stuff.
Novaya had like-minded colleagues at other outlets who reported on realities that made ordinary people uncomfortable. But some outlets were shut down, like Segodnya, and many others willingly turned to sensationalism to rake in cash. Novaya had to pick up the slack for everyone. There were so many stories that nobody but us would write that we could barely cram them into our poor little newspaper.
Everyone disliked us for that — except our loyal readers, who refused to give up access to information. Mainstream readers saw us as a fringe newspaper obsessed with misery. They preferred the sensationalist press, where they could find entertainment and gossip and hide from unpleasant information.
Of course, there are people now who read using a VPN. There aren’t that many of them, but it’s still worth it: This group will play an important role when change comes. But we’ve lost the mass audience. And that audience has lost more than objective information — it’s lost an understanding of the world.
To me, the scariest thing about propaganda isn’t the lies; it’s what gets left out. They don’t actually lie that much. Mostly, they leave things out. And we may even underestimate the effect. When refugees from the Belgorod region fled the shelling for neighboring regions, people there mistook them for Ukrainian refugees — they simply didn’t know the Belgorod region was being shelled.
Novaya was a very influential newspaper. Ministers were removed after our stories came out — remember what happened to [Yevgeny] Adamov. All the top officials read our investigations.
If you look through the print editions, you can barely find an issue without a piece by Politkovskaya. Because if someone had been abducted in Chechnya, the story had to be published as quickly as possible: If the person hadn’t been killed yet, there was a pretty good chance that publishing it in Novaya Gazeta could save them.
Here’s another example. It was 2003, the year Shchekochikhin was murdered. One of the investigations he did let me pursue was about the fishing mafia in the Far East (in fact, it wasn’t a mafia at all — it was the state). We planned a major series of investigations and published only a brief preview, not even the first installment. And after that tiny introduction, I was immediately invited to see the fisheries minister at the State Fisheries Committee, as it was called then. If we had no influence, why would the minister bother inviting a journalist in for a conversation?
On the other hand, many journalists felt disappointed, frustrated, and depressed. You write story after story about outrageous injustices, and nothing changes. Years go by, and suddenly you catch yourself describing the same situation you wrote about two years ago: a different region, a different official’s name, the same schemes. Sometimes even the region is the same — there was one governor, and now there’s another. A lot of people hit a wall with their work; some quit.
Journalism is an alarm that starts flashing and screeching when there’s smoke. Without it, one disaster follows another, until there’s no way out.
It’s very natural not to want to worry about other people’s problems. Why spoil a lovely moment by reading that a missile hit an apartment building in Ukraine today? Looking away isn’t a Russian trait — it’s a perfectly healthy reaction people have all over the world.
Real journalism gets in the way of that comfortable life. A thorn in your side. An irritant. But without it, we won’t have the very comfort we love so much.
Now I find myself wondering: Could we really do all that? When everything has been wiped out, censorship is total, and journalism and free speech have been destroyed, you keep thinking: Wow, back then we could actually write things, go places, talk to people.
Federal troops are killing people in one of the country’s regions [Chechnya]. Abducting civilians, carrying out “mop-up operations.” And Novaya Gazeta journalist Anna Politkovskaya goes to those villages to talk to the residents, and we publish it: who was abducted, who was killed, who was tortured, how they were tortured, where the body was found, and what condition it was in. In 2026, it’s hard to imagine that was ever possible.
Yes, journalists in Russia are threatened, beaten — even killed. But until 2022, we were publishing stories from inside the country about war crimes committed by our own country’s army.
Around the world, journalism is increasingly done at a desk rather than out in the field. But I hope reporting in the field survives. It’s the heart of real journalism — nothing can replace it. But the skills are disappearing, and there’s no one to learn from.
Because of the war and emigration, I suddenly found myself one of the few people in the [Novaya Gazeta Europe] newsroom who’d known Politkovskaya personally. All your life in Moscow, you were one of the younger ones, surrounded by so many people whose memories went back further — and suddenly people like me were the oldest.
I remember Shchekochikhin; I remember Politkovskaya. When she was killed, I was on the team putting that issue together. I was in the thick of so many events — I just never thought that was valuable. And then you suddenly realize you’re carrying all these memories, and you need to tell people how it happened.
Elena Kostyuchenko
Correspondent at Novaya Gazeta from 2005 to 2022
I remember exactly how I first found out about Novaya Gazeta.
I was 14, waiting to see the dentist, and I was really scared. It was going to be a long wait. There were some fashion magazines lying around, but I couldn’t look at them — I actually felt sick. I went outside. There was a newsstand nearby, and I decided to buy something. I noticed a newspaper I’d never seen before, because, as I later learned, Novaya Gazeta sold out very quickly.
I bought it, sat down on a bench in a little park, and opened it to an article. It was Anna Politkovskaya’s piece about a “mop-up operation” in the village of Mesker-Yurt, where Russian soldiers had killed 36 people, if I’m remembering correctly. And one of the local residents had been crucified. I was deeply shaken — I don’t even really remember the dentist’s appointment, because in my head I was still back there.
Afterward, I went to the library and asked for back issues of Novaya Gazeta. I sat there and read them all, one after another. And the more I read, the worse I felt, because I realized I knew absolutely nothing about my country, even though I’d thought I was a pretty well-informed girl, that I’d read a lot and seen a lot. And here were people writing things that didn’t fit my picture of the world at all — a picture that included, for example, “our boys,” “our valiant troops” in Chechnya protecting local people from terrorists.
After Politkovskaya’s articles, I didn’t believe that anymore. At first I was angry at Novaya Gazeta and at Politkovskaya personally. The way she writes, you can’t ignore it anymore, can’t push it out of your head — it stays with you.
Then I realized that this was what journalism was actually about. It has to bring people back to reality, even when they really don’t want to come back. That was when I decided I wanted to work at Novaya Gazeta and started thinking about how to get there.
I lived in Yaroslavl, and my family was dirt-poor. I needed to move to Moscow. The best idea I could come up with was to get into a university with a dorm. The only university I knew in Moscow was Moscow State University, so I applied there, and they accepted me. I’m still very grateful to Moscow State — it’s a wonderful place to grow up.
And here’s how I got into Novaya Gazeta. Russian media outlets usually hired people who’d made a name for themselves, who had experience and qualifications. Novaya Gazeta took us in when we were practically babies and helped us grow into journalists. My plan was to stand outside the newsroom door — like, “Take me on for anything, I’ll mop floors, make coffee, whatever you want.”
But I got lucky. I was writing poetry then, and I was shortlisted for a poetry competition whose judges included Oleg Khlebnikov, who worked on the paper’s culture desk. Oleg noticed me, this girl staring at him, found out from his colleagues that I was studying journalism, and came over: “Your writing’s quite good! You probably have an internship coming up. Would you like to do it at Novaya Gazeta?”
The first person I saw when I came to the newsroom was Politkovskaya. I didn’t recognize her, because Novaya Gazeta was in black and white then. So Oleg and I are walking along, and this incredibly beautiful woman comes flying down the hallway toward us. I ask Oleg, “Who’s that?” And he says, “Oh, that’s Politkovskaya.”
Oleg worked out pretty quickly that I wasn’t especially interested in writing about culture and sent me to the reporting team. That decision shaped my whole life. Nugzar Mikeladze — one of Novaya’s founders — taught an incredible number of reporters everything we know. Not just about journalism, but about being human.
When I joined Novaya Gazeta, I didn’t even know how to turn on a computer! And Nugzar sent me straight out into the field — to Khodorkovsky’s trial. Naturally, I had no idea who Khodorkovsky was or where the trial would be.
To me, one of the most important stories Novaya Gazeta covered was the shelling of parliament in 1993. That was a turning point: I think that was when Russia chose an undemocratic path. Putin won the election in part because people didn’t believe in democracy. Unlike many other supposedly “democratic” publications, Novaya Gazeta — which had only just been founded — didn’t support the shelling.
I also think everything Politkovskaya did was extremely important. Take her reporting on the Nord-Ost hostage crisis. That piece is special to me because it never lost sight of the human beings involved. Despite what was happening, Politkovskaya saw the terrorists as people.
That’s probably the most important thing she taught me and a whole generation of journalists — there’s no virtue in dehumanizing people. Even with an assault rifle pointed at them, journalists have a duty to see the person behind the gun. Such a simple rule. And such a difficult one.
Another hugely important story Novaya Gazeta covered, and a turning point for Russia, was Beslan. Lena Milashina flew there in place of Politkovskaya, who had been poisoned on the plane. Milashina was the first journalist to report that there weren’t 354 hostages, as the authorities were saying, but more than a thousand.
Novaya Gazeta investigated Beslan like no other newsroom. It found grenade launchers on the roof of a building near the school. It carried out a huge investigation whose findings were confirmed by the European Court of Human Rights. I’m talking about the fact that the assault wasn’t intended to save the hostages. I think that was when Putin stopped playing at democracy. Because why bother? You can literally blast a school full of hostages, children, with flamethrowers, tanks, and small arms on live television, and nothing will happen to you.
Novaya Gazeta published many other important stories — about the extermination of gay men in Chechnya, about events in the Donbas.
Why is it important to preserve this whole archive? On the wall of the journalism school in New York where I studied [after Moscow State], it said that journalism is the “rough draft of history.” Journalism is a way to understand what happened, what people thought, what the journalists themselves thought, what perspective they brought to it all.
The shorter the pieces and the smaller the events that prompted them, the more important it is to preserve them. Major events and investigations that make a lot of waves will be archived. But the small details of everyday life probably won’t be.
Novaya Gazeta’s archive is a chronicle of our fuckups as well as Putin’s. At Novaya Gazeta, we also wrote about how lots of small, individual choices lead to catastrophic consequences. I wouldn’t want my pieces “Internat” (“The Institution”), “Trassa” (“The Highway”), or any part of “Nam zdes zhit” (“We Have to Live Here”), about Kushchevka, to disappear.
Novaya Gazeta was founded by a group of journalists — and that same group owned it. We had no owner other than the staff. That meant we could elect the editor in chief, the editorial committee, and the editorial board. You listened to your bosses because you’d voted for them. And if you’d made the wrong choice, you could change it two years later. That made for much healthier relationships among the staff and a healthier approach to work in general. There was no authority you obeyed just because it was authority.
It was my home, my family, and the most important thing in my life.
Nadya Yurova
Podcast producer at Novaya Gazeta from 2020 to 2022. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, she moved to Latvia and continued working at Novaya Gazeta Europe as a YouTube and podcast host
I never particularly dreamed of becoming a journalist. After high school, I applied to drama school, but I hadn’t really dreamed of an acting career either. I spent two years at the Shchepkin drama school in Moscow and left — it was awful, and I decided I’d had enough.
The only option left that wouldn’t mean retaking entrance exams was journalism. I enrolled at the Higher School of Economics.
In my second or third year, I hosted a student talk show [“V tochku!” (“Right on Target!”)]. It was cool, a pretty big production. But in 2018, [Putin’s press secretary Dmitry] Peskov came on the show, and there was a scandal. They started censoring us and telling us who to invite and who not to invite. I really, really didn’t like that, and I started getting disillusioned.
I needed to earn money, so I started working at a coffee shop while I studied. Around the same time, I met Kirill Martynov — he taught us a course called “Media in the Post-Truth Era.”
Martynov noticed me because I worked really hard and always spoke up in his classes. At that point, I had pretty much no idea what my career was going to look like.
When COVID started, before the strictest restrictions came in, I was working at a small cafe that was part of a chain. Everyone wanted to support small businesses then, and Martynov came to my coffee shop. I remember taking off my apron, stepping outside for a smoke, and he goes, “Nadezhda, would you like to work at Novaya Gazeta?”
I had that feeling again that none of this was real, but I didn’t let it show and said with a straight face, “Well, maybe. Doing what?” He said, “What are you interested in?” I said I loved podcasts. He said, “We’re looking for someone for podcasts, actually. Come meet everyone.”
I’d been ready to give up and stay a barista for the rest of my life. Novaya Gazeta came out of nowhere. I’d grown up reading Politkovskaya; this was everything I could have dreamed of, but I had this feeling that it wasn’t real — like, “Is this possible?”
I suggested starting with the most straightforward thing — a news podcast. A Novaya Gazeta writer would write a piece, we’d invite them into the studio, and we’d talk about the article. I did the interviews.
During COVID, we recorded from home. I didn’t have a microphone, so I spoke into my iPhone’s voice recorder under a blanket. Interviewing someone for 30 minutes under a blanket is a bit tricky, but it was worth it.
It felt like fate handed me those first podcast episodes. The very first was with Elena Milashina, the second with Lena Kostyuchenko. It was freaking amazing: Here I was, a young employee who didn’t understand a thing, suddenly getting to know people across the whole newspaper.
A lot of young people joined the paper around the same time I did. We started doing YouTube, podcasts, TikTok — it was madness, and the best time of my career. This was the great Novaya Gazeta, with all these towering figures looking so serious. And we were just a bunch of goofballs and screwups. We sat on the floor during editorial meetings and rode skateboards down the newsroom hallways. They let us do all of it.
[Dmitry] Muratov told me that, in a way, we’d breathed new life into the newspaper.
Then February 24 came. During the first weeks of the war, we were in the newsroom around the clock, putting on daily livestreams with a team of four. We were shouting as loud as we could.
At the end of March 2022, Novaya Gazeta suspended publication. That was a huge blow. It felt like that was it — I no longer had the work that had kept me afloat.
Before I joined the paper, of course, I knew nobody could have written about Chechnya the way Novaya did. Nobody else had that enormous legacy handed down by Politkovskaya and Milashina. The newspaper had always been built around its writers’ individual voices. But only gradually did I come to understand just how great a newspaper I worked for.
Lena Kostyuchenko looks like a beautiful, delicate little flower, but then she goes and spends two weeks living in a residential institution for people with psychiatric and neurological disabilities. Right after Lena returned from the institution, she came onto my podcast [to talk about her piece “The Institution”]. It was as if you could still smell the horror on her — it chilled you to the bone. She was one of the first to say publicly that these institutions are a Gulag — and, in a way, to articulate that idea for the public. I remember not being able to believe I was part of all this.
There’s one project I’m very proud of. I’d dreamed of making a narrative podcast, and Kostyuchenko went to Taimyr to investigate the fuel spill in Norilsk. Around the same time, she also went on assignment to visit the Nganasans, an indigenous people of northern Russia.
When the oil spill happened, it polluted the river where they fished, and the fish disappeared. Lena went to talk to them, partly just to understand how they lived. I gave her a recorder to take along and asked her to record everything that happened to her. Lena brought me dozens of hours of material. That [the podcast “Poka ne vypal sneg” (“Before the Snow Falls”)] was the most interesting work I’ve ever done in my life.
That was also when I realized just how expendable people are to the authorities. This [what’s happening to the Nganasans] mirrors what’s happening across the country, including in the war.
I think that as long as I keep telling people what’s happening in Russia, as long as I keep the idea [of Novaya Gazeta] alive, it won’t be so easy to erase us and shut us up. In the newsroom, people are always talking about [Novaya Gazeta’s] legacy, remembering the journalists who were murdered.
From beginning to end, Novaya Gazeta was a thorn in the authorities’ side. In a country where nothing is allowed, there was one newspaper that caused them trouble — so much trouble that people were killed over it.
Novaya Gazeta is a memory, a record, and a chronicle of the Russian authorities’ fuckups.
On November 5, RIMA and Kronika will open the Novaya Gazeta archive. All 3,373 issues of the Moscow edition from 1993 to 2022, special editions, and much more will be freely available. Some of this material was previously inaccessible. It includes, for example, articles the newspaper was forced to remove on orders from the Prosecutor General’s Office and the media regulator Roskomnadzor. Among them are Elena Kostyuchenko’s reporting from occupied Kherson and the full versions of four issues from February to March 2022 whose contents are hidden on the newspaper’s website. For the first time, Novaya’s entire print archive will be available in one place. Researchers will also be able to request datasets containing the archive’s metadata from RIMA.

Isro’s GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission successful: Next-generation navigation satellite placed in orbit; NavIC constellation gets a boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:40:00 UTC
03:40:00 KST

It was the 20th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle. (Photo by C Suresh Kumar)
SRIHARIKOTA: India's regional satellite navigation system, NavIC, which was facing a shortage of operational satellites, got a boost with the successful launch of NVS-03 on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday by Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro).GSLV-F18 carrying 2,250kg next-generation navigation satellite -- NVS-03 -- lifted off from the second launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) in Sriharikota at 11.51pm on Friday, as scheduled. It was the 20th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV). Around 18 minutes later, NVS-03 satellite was placed in a geosynchronous transfer orbit (GTO) of 37,023km apogee and 170km perigee."The rocket has successfully and precisely placed the satellite into its intended elliptical orbit. It achieved a 170km perigee and 38,080km apogee. This is the 5th mission from Sriharikota this year. GSLV has carried 34 tonnes of spacecraft to space so far. We achieved this mission with a turnaround time of just 56 days after the GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission in September. With this launch, we have restored NavIC constellation operation as we need a minimum of four satellites to perform positioning, navigation and timing services," said Isro chairman V Narayanan.
He said, “The satellite is healthy, and the solar panel has been deployed. Already three pyro walls are operated, and we have lifted. Every system is totally healthy, and we are going to continue the operation and place the satellite in the intended circular orbit.”NVS-03 is the third satellite in Isro's next-generation navigation satellite system, designed to ensure continuity of services under the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS), operationally known as NavIC. The satellite carries an indigenously developed atomic clock along with procured atomic clocks. It also carries the L1 frequency signal in addition to the existing L5 and S-band signals.NavIC is India's independent regional satellite navigation system, designed to provide positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) services across the country and an area extending approximately 1,500km beyond the Indian landmass. The additional L1 signal, alongside the existing signals, is expected to improve compatibility with other satellite navigation systems and widen the potential use of NavIC in civilian applications.The NVS-03 mission is part of Isro's plan to deploy five second-generation navigation satellites -- NVS-01 to NVS-05 -- to augment the existing NavIC constellation and improve continuity and reliability of navigation services.The launch assumes significance as NavIC was unable to provide standalone positioning services because of a shortage of operational satellites. In a written reply to the Lok Sabha on July 29, Union minister of state for space Jitendra Singh said the constellation had only three satellites providing positioning, navigation and timing services, against the minimum four required for basic positioning services. While its timing service remains functional, the addition of NVS-03, once commissioned, could help restore standalone positioning capability."Since NavIC is being used in a multi-constellation environment for most of the use cases, there is no vulnerability for the users. The next NavIC satellite, NVS-03, is ready for launch and two more satellites, NVS-04 and NVS-05, are in an advanced stage of realisation," the minister had said then.The setback to the constellation followed the failure of NVS-02, launched on Jan 29, 2025, to complete its orbit-raising manoeuvres. An Isro review committee found that an electrical signal had failed to reach a pyro valve in the satellite's oxidiser line, preventing the propulsion system from firing and the satellite from reaching its intended orbit. The failure prompted Isro to undertake corrective measures for subsequent missions.
The first satellite in the second-generation series, NVS-01, was launched aboard the GSLV-F12 on May 29, 2023. It was also the first satellite in the series to carry an indigenous atomic clock.The Isro chief said five more launches are planned this financial year. “We are moving closer to Gaganyaan G1 uncrewed flight,” he added.

EU, Canada forge strategic alliance as Trump’s policies strain transatlantic ties
