Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:06:00 UTC
03:06:00 KST

Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya
October 30, 2026
This year, almost 20,000 people have already tried to make the perilous crossing from Libya in north Africa to the Greek island of Crete.
The route, which runs from the east coast of Libya to Greece, has become an increasingly significant corridor for irregular migration into Europe, Greek daily Kathimerini recently reported.
On Oct. 20 alone, Greek authorities registered 710 people in 14 boats. Hundreds more arrived the next day.
Many of the boats depart from areas around Tobruk, a port city on Libya's eastern Mediterranean coast. According to Kathimerini, migrants pay as much as $4,000 (€3,600) for the crossing, which takes around a day and a half.
This particular route is becoming more popular in part because of crackdowns on alternative passages.
After eastern Libyan armed forces acted against people smugglers heading for Italy in 2023, the smuggling networks changed their methods, using smaller boats and sailing them towards Crete instead.
Fuelling the conflict economy
According to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a think tank based in Switzerland, other groups have since entered the people smuggling business too, including those who previously mostly moved goods, vehicles or drugs.
Human trafficking in Libya is closely connected with what is known as the "conflict economy."
This sees armed actors gaining economic resources and political influence by controlling informal markets and transport routes. It also sees local power brokers using measures against smuggling to obtain financial or political support for themselves.
"Conflict and subsequent instability in Libya have created a fertile environment for migrant smuggling and TIP [trafficking in persons] activities to develop, in turn leading to the growth of smuggling in other locations along an established route," researchers at British think tank Chatham House wrote, after looking in depth at three different transit hubs across Libya. "This has led to an increase in the number of migrants entering Libya and the expansion of Libya's conflict economy."
"It remains the case that an entire business has developed around smuggling routes, regardless of whether that [smuggling] involves weapons, goods, people or drugs," Hager Ali, a researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, told DW.
If there are already contacts, transportation and security arrangements in place, then these can also be used for illegal activities like people trafficking, Ali said. Since 2014, Libya has been split into two. In the west, a United Nations-backed administration is based in Tripol; and in the east, in Tobruk, the second Libyan leadership is backed by former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar.
Haftar has managed to consolidate control over various armed militias, ruling with an iron fist. His sons also hold important positions. However, there are no proven links between the Haftars' networks and people smugglers on that coast.
But, as Ali explained, even the appearance of having some influence over these sectors can confer political influence.
"The more apparent control one has over this market, the greater one's influence," Ali told DW.
Those Libyans who can influence, or even prevent, departures are demonstrating their importance to other actors. For example, high profile operations against the smuggling networks can serve as a sign of political legitimacy. "They present themselves as somebody who can restore order and curb migration," Ali noted.
There's also increasing geopolitical competition in the eastern Mediterranean. In late October, the Tobruk government signed a maritime agreement with Turkey, a deal that Turkey had actually originally concluded with Libya's other government in Tripoli.
Turkey previously fought Haftar-sponsored militias during the Libyan civil war, and this deal represents rapprochement between the two. It is also a way for Turkey to get what it wants in a rivalrous situation in this maritime area — Greece rejects the agreement, saying that it infringes on Greek economic rights around islands like Crete and Rhodes.
A direct link between the new agreement and rising numbers of irregular migrants in Crete is not clear. However, Ali suggested that it wouldn't be inconceivable that irregular migrants could be used as leverage in these kinds of geopolitical conflicts.
European cooperation
The European Union has been cooperating with Libyans to prevent irregular migrants from getting to Europe — despite the Libyan actors' links to armed groups and their disputed political legitimacy.
There's an obvious contradiction in that, argued Andreas Dittmann, a retired professor from Giessen University and expert on human geography and development. Such cooperation between the EU and Libyans can serve as a control on irregular migration but it also adds to the Libyans' local power.
"If those in charge in eastern Libya are actually able to influence the scale and timing of such [migrant] movements, they're demonstrating their own strategic importance to European governments," Dittmann told DW.
A report by the United Nations' International Organization for Migration, or IOM, illustrated how precarious the situation is for many migrants.
According to the report, which is based on data from May and June this year, around 950,000 migrants and refugees were registered as living in Libya. Many have only limited access to healthcare and tend not to have residence or work permits, all of which increases their dependence on informal markets as well as the risk of exploitation.
This story was originally published in German.

2026-10-30
18:04:24 UTC
03:04:24 KST

Six women who have been “haunted” by their encounters with Russell Brand came forward to give evidence against him with nothing to gain and no appetite for fame, a court has heard.
The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said the women, who do not know one another, had not been compelled to make police complaints by the “magic force” of media reporting on Brand’s alleged misconduct.
In her closing speech, she told jurors at Southwark crown court that the women had “vivid recollections” and had “bravely” come forward to the tell “the truth” after realising they were not alone.
Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Karmy-Jones denied that a 2023 Dispatches documentary about Brand had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.
She said the complainants had described a similar pattern of behaviour, saying: “Six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not looked out for some form of publicity, who have not taken part in a documentary, not made claims for compensation.
“There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago.”
She said the women described how Brand’s “demeanour changed” before he assaulted them. “Listen to their accounts,” the prosecutor told the jury. “Many said he was nice and then it was like there was a personality change. A pivot. His eyes changed, he snapped from charming to frightening and nasty.
“He didn’t listen when they said no, he didn’t stop, he didn’t care, he kept pulling, pushing, tugging, thrusting. In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim.”
She said the women had given the court “specific details” about Brand’s conduct. “What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago.
“The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years,” she said.
The prosecutor also accused Brand of using “gaslighting” to “good effect” by asking some of his accusers for their telephone numbers or emails after the alleged assaults.
She said women were a “disposable commodity” to Brand and later added: “He was a defendant who was rampant in his desire to have sexual contact whenever her wished, whenever he pleased.”
Karmy-Jones described the account of the youngest witness, a fan then in her early 20s who accused the TV personality of anally raping her at his London townhouse after meeting her at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.
He cared only about his “birthright orgasm” and ignored her pleas for him to stop, the prosecutor said, adding that she was “just another number to add to his 5,000 notches which he was marking up”.
The court heard Brand had a “flavour of disdain” towards the allegations, which the prosecution suggested was “a reflection” of his “whole approach to the female species at that time”.
“Women as a whole were disposable, they didn’t matter to him. He didn’t even need to know their names. They were just a means to an end.
“As he said in a 2017 interview, they were the amusements in what he described as his playground of orgasms,” Karmy-Jones continued.
Earlier on Friday the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, gave legal directions to the jury in which he pointed out that they would have “rival arguments” to consider.
Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
His barrister, Ian Winter KC, is due to deliver his closing speech on Monday.

Vote for UAE candidate for UN chief will endorse genocide

Vote for UAE candidate for UN chief will endorse genocide
TEHRAN - A vote for Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE's candidate for the post of UN secretary general, will mark an endorsement of genocide, mass atrocities and war, a former UN Security Council says.
Dino Mahtani, writing an article in Middle East Eye published on Oct. 29, says “evidence of the UAE's support for genocidal forces” by RSF militia in Sudan has piled up for years, yet Abu Dhabi denies it all while “cultivating a polished international reputation.”
Rights groups also say Nusseibeh has spent the last three years denying her country's role in the genocide in Sudan, deeming her “too dangerous” to the international order.
"We cannot afford to have the UN led by somebody who is a genocide denier, and indeed somebody who heads a government that has been aiding and abetting genocide, that is basically criminally complicit in that genocide, and she's a lead person in covering that up," Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, said on a joint virtual panel on Oct. 27 that called for Nusseibeh's disqualification.
Mahtani, also a former acting director of the Africa program at the International Crisis Group, writes that Anthropic established in September with "high confidence" that the UAE was behind an influence operation “targeting UN experts and critics of its role in Sudan.”
The following is the text of his article titled “The UAE Deals in the Darkest of Politics - its representative should be nowhere near the UN”:
A bid by the United Arab Emirates to install one of its top diplomats as secretary general of the United Nations, even as the country stands accused of supporting a genocidal paramilitary force in Sudan, has polarized opinion and left many wondering about the future of the world body’s moral authority.
The bid of Lana Nusseibeh, who is a switched-on, worldly diplomat, was pushed by UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, autocrat and sponsor of warlords, paramilitaries and mercenaries across the Middle East and Africa, and reflects the rapacious politics of our times.
Evidence of the UAE's support for genocidal forces in Sudan has piled up for years including in the form of UN investigations, yet the Persian Gulf Arab state denies it all while cultivating a polished international reputation.
In September, Anthropic established with "high confidence" that the UAE was behind an influence operation targeting UN experts and critics of its role in Sudan. Given the killings and disinformation and her role in denying them, placing Nusseibeh at the head of a world body already struggling to stay relevant and stem a deluge of wars would all but seal the coffin on its moral authority.
Until October, the race to succeed Antonio Guterres was dominated by centrist or left-leaning Latin American candidates. But US President Donald Trump, who has called the UN prone to "a far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats", rejected them all.
That opened the door for Bin Zayed, whom Trump calls a "warrior", to advance Nusseibeh’s bid. The monarch has committed $1.4 trillion of investment to the US, including in artificial intelligence. Bin Zayed is in contact with Trump on containing Iran, and is the Middle East's staunchest ally of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose separate genocide has decimated Gaza, where the UAE is helping Israel's redevelopment plans.
Of Palestinian descent herself and with an academic history in Israeli studies, she has secured the backing of her nomination by the Palestinian Authority, which is partially dependent on Israel for its revenues.
Denials and disinformation
Nusseibeh says that as the UN's first female leader she will act "with the interests of the United Nations only in view".
Many are skeptical.
The women-led Centre for International Policy, a US think tank, says her career will continue to owe itself to an "authoritarian regime that serves as a haven for global kleptocracy and corruption".
As UAE ambassador to the UN, then minister and foreign-policy envoy, Nusseibeh has led her government's categorical denials of UN and media reports that it supported Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, whom even the Trump administration has confirmed as committing genocide. The denials persist as UN investigators keep reporting the UAE's role to the Security Council.
Questioned at the UN this week about whether she would continue to reject the findings of UN investigations on the UAE’s support to the Rapid Support Forces, she sidestepped the question saying the allegations were something for the UAE to answer directly, as she has now taken a leave of absence from her ministry to focus on her candidacy.
Instead, she insisted, vaguely, that resolving Sudan’s conflict would be a "litmus test" for the success and credibility of any UN secretary general.
As a Security Council investigator, I saw first-hand how the UAE mission to the UN under Nusseibeh’s ambassadorship behaved when faced with overwhelming evidence of UAE complicity in sanctions-busting.
During 2013 and 2014, just after she took up her post, I documented over 160 shipments of charcoal shipped from Somalia to the UAE, in violation of a UN resolution linking the trade to the financing networks of the Al-Qaeda affiliated group al-Shabab.
During meetings with her team, I was always struck by how her office routinely dismissed the evidence at hand. My investigations culminated in the identification of a site in the UAE desert where I was able to find and photograph multiple warehouses stuffed with Somali charcoal, in flagrant violation of international law.
In 2022, long after I had left the UN but when Nusseibeh was still ambassador, I passed through the UAE in transit only to be detained on arrival, questioned for several hours and then expelled.
My own investigations, including enquiries made via a UAE-based lawyer, established that my detention was connected to the work I had previously done in the UAE and was provoked by renewed UN investigations on Somali charcoal. However, Nusseibeh’s office flatly denied her government’s involvement.
Regional supremacy
Back to today, the UAE is still not shy of intimidation tactics.
A UN report drafted this year and detailing the UAE's deployment of Colombian mercenaries in support of the RSF as they committed atrocities during last year's siege of the Darfuri city of El Fasher has been blocked for months, after the UAE's ally Bahrain, a non-permanent council member, requested a stay in proceedings.
In August, the UAE's UN ambassador demanded UN investigators to "immediately remedy the serious defects" in the report.
Controlling the Sudan narrative is vital to how the UAE shapes perceptions of its role in wars across the Red Sea region. It has backed a warlord controlling eastern Libya, supported pro-Israel secessionists in Yemen, and armed an Ethiopian regime now fighting several factions, including one in northern Tigray, where hundreds of thousands have been killed or starved since 2020.
These conflicts run parallel to the UAE's multi-billion-dollar port developments on the Red Sea's vital waterways, such as Berbera in the breakaway region of Somaliland, now recognized as independent by Israel.
The projects are partly designed to encircle and outflank Saudi Arabia, with which the UAE is locked in a contest for regional supremacy. They also cement its role as an indispensable hub of global capitalism; by some estimates its trading systems touch a third of humanity.
The cost of influence
The UAE has used its vast wealth to buy influence with the permanent Security Council members who could have vetoed Nusseibeh. It has committed billions of pounds to the UK, whose government now tiptoes around the UAE's role in Sudan and in the Manchester City football club scandal.
It has pledged billions of euros to France, while hosting a French military base and a branch of the Louvre in Abu Dhabi.
China's reticence about a candidate so heavily backed by Trump and so close to Israel may be tempered by Beijing's view of the UAE as its most important Middle Eastern strategic partner.
Some 60 percent of Chinese trade is re-exported through UAE ports to more than 400 cities. Beijing is still committed to a Latin American candidate, but may yet be swayed.
The UAE has also tightened ties with Russia, taking large volumes of Russian oil and refined products via intermediaries since Western sanctions were applied on Moscow.
Bin Zayed also recently mediated Trump's diesel supply deal with Putin, a trade Trump needs to lower fuel prices and soothe voters before US mid-term elections.
With all five Security Council permanent members so tied to and dependent on the UAE, it will be no surprise if they eventually wave Nusseibeh through. Her ascension may thus smooth the superpowers' collusive politics. But don't expect her to act in the interest of the victims of wars, mass atrocities and genocides.

====================================================================================================

Twice as many plants and animals sold in wildlife trade as previously thought, says report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:19 UTC
03:00:19 KST

The number of plant and animal species in use or sold in the wildlife trade is more than twice as high as previously thought, researchers have discovered.
A study, published in Science Advances, warns that there are huge gaps in global assessments of how wildlife is traded, and that past estimates have failed to keep up with changes such as the boom in the online exotic pet trade, where sellers offering to post spider eggs across the world or sneak reptiles on to planes are just a click away.
“The dimensions of trade have changed. Without monitoring it in a representative way, we cannot manage it,” said Alice Hughes, a professor at the University of Melbourne and lead author of the study. “At the moment, we are completely underestimating what modern trade looks like – for the pet trade and for the ornamental trade, we are not capturing it. And it poses a major risk to species.”
The study comes as the US-based nonprofit, the Center for Biological Diversity, filed a petition asking the US Fish and Wildlife Service to list the Javan slit-faced bat under the Endangered Species Act, warning that consumers are buying the bat for decor, placing it at risk of extinction. Taxidermy bats are sought after, particularly by US consumers, who are looking for gothic or spooky decorations for Halloween or Christmas gifts, the centre said.
The wildlife trade study identified 107,356 species that are either in use or traded globally – far higher than a previous estimate of about 50,000, which was made by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES).
The study draws on more comprehensive datasets, as well as newer research papers that have tracked species sold online for decoration. It shows flaws in our understanding of what species are at risk; for example, the number of butterfly species found to be traded is greater than the IPBES’ entire estimate for all traded terrestrial invertebrates.
Molly Brown, programme officer for wildlife use and trade at the International Union for Conservation of Nature and a co-author of the paper, said the findings were a reality check. “The number of species that we are talking about is still an underestimate, and that’s really clear in the paper, because we cannot access and we do not have the type of monitoring data that we really need,” she said.
Discussions about the wildlife trade often focus on criminal activities, such as illegal smuggling of ivory or pangolin scales. However, the wildlife trade encompasses sectors such as fisheries and the timber trade as well as fashion and the sale of species as ornaments. This includes activities that may be sustainable, as well as trade that is driving species to extinction.
Even assessing the value of the legal trade compared with the illegal trade is challenging. The under-regulation of wildlife trade has created loopholes that allow species, including sought-after exotic pets, to be “laundered into legality”, researchers said.
Four years ago, nearly 200 countries agreed to ensure that trade of wild species was “sustainable, safe and legal”, as part of a landmark set of targets aimed at ending the destruction of nature. Efforts to meet these targets are hampered by a lack of data about what is being sold and where it originated.
The main data point for measuring progress on a globally agreed wildlife trade target refers only to fish stocks, which would account for at most 3% of all traded species, said Hughes.
Experts say there needs to be more systematic data collection and sharing. Globally, fisheries are monitored by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, while the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites) monitors and regulates international trade in about 40,000 species to protect them from over exploitation.
However, researchers said that this excludes large numbers of potentially vulnerable species, warning the Cites system is too slow moving to keep up with new trends in threats to wildlife. Most countries lack any systematic data outside Cites, the study says. “Sometimes, it is years before things get listed and that means that they can be virtually extinct in the wild by that point,” said Hughes.
Species that are newly described are often rare and have a small range, meaning they are especially valuable to trade, and can be quickly wiped out.
Chris Shepherd, a conservation advocate at the Centre for Biological Diversity, who was not involved in the study, added that he had observed the wildlife trade for decades and that new species were continually appearing.
“The demand for wildlife, especially live wildlife traded for pets, is growing fast, as is the number of species involved,” he said. “This trade is pushing an ever-growing list of species towards extinction, and as such, putting in place mechanisms to better monitor this trade are essential.”

====================================================================================================

Low-fat diets do not prevent dementia deaths in older women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:17 UTC
03:00:17 KST

Adopting a diet low in fat and high in fruits, vegetables, and grains does not lower the risk of dying from dementia for most postmenopausal women. While earlier research hinted at potential cognitive benefits, a secondary look at a large clinical trial revealed that these dietary modifications did not prevent dementia related deaths over a twenty year period. The findings were published in the journal Menopause.
Dementia and cognitive impairment represent major health risks associated with aging. Women make up more than two thirds of people over the age of sixty five living with Alzheimer’s disease in the United States. Researchers want to understand whether modifying everyday habits like eating patterns can protect brain health and delay the onset of severe cognitive decline.
In the past, observational studies have linked diets lower in fat to better cognitive health. An observational study is one where researchers simply track people’s behaviors over time without asking them to change their habits. However, these studies can only show associations, rather than proving that a specific diet directly prevents cognitive decline. To find stronger evidence, scientists rely on randomized clinical trials, where participants are randomly assigned to follow a specific intervention or act as a control group.
A major project called the Women’s Health Initiative previously conducted one such trial. This large study tracked the health of tens of thousands of postmenopausal women, meaning women who had permanently stopped having menstrual periods. In previous reports from a subset of this trial, researchers noticed that women assigned to a low fat diet had lower rates of possible cognitive impairment, based on scores from a test of global cognitive functioning, compared to those eating their usual diet.
Based on those initial results, researchers wanted to test if this dietary pattern also translated to a lower risk of eventually dying from dementia. Rowan T. Chlebowski, a researcher at The Lundquist Institute in Torrance, California, led a team of investigators to examine this question. They looked at the long term survival data of the original trial participants. The goal was to see if the dietary intervention provided lasting protection against fatal neurodegenerative conditions.
The researchers analyzed data from a large randomized clinical trial that originally enrolled 48,835 postmenopausal women in the United States. The participants ranged in age from fifty to seventy nine years old. When they joined the study between 1993 and 1998, all of the women consumed diets where at least thirty two percent of their daily calories came from fat. Cognitive function was not a strict requirement for joining the study, but all participants had to be functionally independent.
The research team randomly assigned the women into two groups. Forty percent of the participants joined a dietary intervention group. Nutritionists guided this group to reduce their fat intake to twenty percent of their daily calories while increasing their consumption of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. The remaining sixty percent of the women served as a comparison group.
The women in the comparison group received standard health materials but did not receive ongoing counseling from study nutritionists. The intensive dietary intervention lasted for a median of eight and a half years. During this time, women in the intervention group successfully reduced their fat intake and increased their consumption of plant based foods. The differences in fat intake between the two groups remained measurable for up to thirteen years.
To determine how this dietary shift affected dementia mortality, the researchers tracked the participants for a median of twenty years. They verified causes of death using medical records, death certificates, and the National Death Index, which is a centralized database of death record information in the United States. They looked specifically at deaths caused by Alzheimer’s disease and non-Alzheimer’s forms of dementia.
The results showed that the dietary intervention did not prevent deaths from dementia. Out of the original study population, 1,386 women eventually died from dementia related causes. The rates of dementia mortality were almost identical between the group that ate a low fat diet and the group that consumed their usual diet. The difference between the two groups was not statistically significant.
The researchers also looked at specific types of dementia to see if the diet had a targeted effect. They found that the low fat eating pattern did not change the rate of death from Alzheimer’s disease. It also did not change the rate of death from other types of dementia, such as vascular dementia or Lewy body dementia. The overall impact on severe cognitive decline resulting in death was effectively zero.
The research team did perform analyses on specific subgroups of women based on their age at the start of the study. In one of these subgroup analyses, they noticed a trend toward lower dementia mortality for younger women, particularly those in their fifties and sixties when the trial began. The researchers noted a gradual decrease in dementia deaths for these younger age brackets compared to older participants. However, this trend did not extend to women who were seventy or older when they altered their diets.
The researchers noted that the low fat diet did produce other measurable health benefits during the trial. The intervention positively influenced body weight, physical activity levels, and the risk of developing diabetes and high blood pressure. Medical professionals widely consider these factors to be potential contributors to dementia risk. Because the diet improved these health markers but failed to reduce dementia mortality, the study suggests that improving cardiovascular health in later life may not be enough to reverse existing neurodegenerative processes.
While the study tracked thousands of participants over two decades, readers should consider a few important caveats. The researchers evaluated dementia mortality, which means they only counted cases where dementia was recorded as a cause of death. They did not measure dementia incidence, which is the number of people who developed the condition but perhaps died of something else. This distinction means the diet might still influence the onset of mild cognitive issues without necessarily changing the ultimate cause of death.
Determining the exact cause of death in older adults can also be imprecise. As people age, they often develop multiple overlapping health conditions, making it difficult for doctors to pinpoint a single fatal disease on a death certificate. This inherent ambiguity in medical records could obscure subtle benefits of the dietary intervention. The reliance on death certificates is a standard practice in long term studies, but it is an imperfect measure of cognitive health.
The positive trend observed in women under the age of seventy also requires cautious interpretation. Because the researchers analyzed many different subgroups, this single positive finding could simply be a result of statistical chance. Alternatively, it might suggest that lifestyle changes need to start much earlier in life to effectively protect the brain. Future clinical trials will need to test dietary interventions specifically in younger age groups to confirm if early changes offer true protection against dementia.
The study, “Low-fat dietary pattern and dementia mortality: a secondary analysis of the Women’s Health Initiative dietary modification randomized clinical trial with long-term follow-up,” was authored by Rowan T. Chlebowski, Stephen Rapp, Aaron K. Aragaki, JoAnn E. Manson, Kathy Pan, Marian L. Neuhouser, Karen C. Johnson, Linda G. Snetselaar, Victor W. Henderson, Lihong Qi, Kathleen M. Hayden, Laura D. Baker, Orena Garcia, Margaret D. Pichardo, Jean Wactawski-Wende, and Ross L. Prentice.

Politics is an image game, and the government needs to find better visuals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Politics is an image game, and the government needs to find better visuals
Politics at its most visceral is visual, which is why governments and oppositions spend so much time crafting the perfect image. Burnishing and beavering away to dispel the dismal, disguise the dishonest and nudge the narrative.
When it gets really fun is when the unexpected happens. Like a purposeful set-up that backfires, embarrassing the participants. Awks, as the kids might say.
There have been many examples over the years, but there was something in the air this week that rekindled memories of a 2015 photograph of then-prime minister Tony Abbott and his treasurer, Joe Hockey.
Taken in the prime minister's office on the eve of that year's budget, the photograph captured the two men side-by-side. Abbott leans to his left and puts a pastoral hand on Hockey's bare forearm.
Hockey looks miserable. Forlorn. Like a man beaten. Which it turned out he was. As was Abbott.
The photo was taken 12 months after what was regarded at the time as one of the least popular budgets in history: the notorious 2014 edition with all its broken-promise spending cuts.
A year later, still in its first term but with an eye on the coming election in 2016, the Coalition released its second budget at a time of deep poll trouble.
Hemmed in by the Senate and a popular backlash against the cuts, a politically battered and bruised Hockey was forced to shelve his ambitions for big reform that began when he declared an end to the "age of entitlement".
Instead, his second budget was a plodding affair full of cash handouts that spent almost every dollar saved. It was panned by the economic commentariat as a do-little effort that left the country drifting sideways.
Having Abbott sit with Hockey was intended to demonstrate unity and resolve. Instead, it produced snickering.
Four months later, almost to the day, both men were out of their jobs, rolled by Malcolm Turnbull who cited the fact Abbott had lost 30 straight NewsPolls to Labor.
What's the relevance of this?
Towards the end of Question Time on Wednesday — a day of bleak news on the economy, with rising inflation and interest rate worries — the prime minister got a question from the opposition about when he plans to replace Jim Chalmers with cabinet secretary Andrew Charlton.
The question was a political shit stir, designed to highlight the bad blood between the prime minister and treasurer.
Albanese used his answer to pump up the treasurer, who has made no secret in recent weeks of his frustration at being seen as the locus of blame for everything wrong with the government.
"This treasurer produced back-to-back surpluses," the prime minister began, before laying it on thick.
"This treasurer returned 75 per cent of revenue upgrades to the bottom line. He's one of only nine treasurers of finance ministers around the world to have a AAA credit rating from all of the agencies."
As he sat listening, Chalmers had the air of a man who wasn't entirely over the moon about the praise. How helpful it was, given tensions in the air, is debatable.
It certainly reminded those who saw it of the pressure Chalmers is under, which is looking more and more like an uncontrolled pile-on.
Going through some things
The risk when prime ministers have to defend their treasurers in a performative manner is that it sets tongues wagging.
Why now? What's the goal? Who is he trying to convince?
"If Jim could have flipped Albanese the bird in the middle of it, he would have," said one Labor observer.
A cynical interpretation is that the prime minister was also reminding the public that it's the treasurer who owns the government's economic story.
Which — as Donald Trump once said of an ill-fated US ambassador to Ukraine — is "going to go through some things".
Next week will almost certainly be brutal for the government, given the likelihood of another Reserve Bank rate hike on Tuesday, the fifth this year.
The prime minister will be in the Caribbean for a Commonwealth Heads Of Government Meeting (CHOGM), leaving Chalmers to face the music.
Like a rogue wave bouncing off a seawall, a story then appeared on Friday in the Sydney Morning Herald citing "government sources", suggesting Chalmers is a victim rather than villain of the government's deteriorating economic story.
The Herald quoted people saying that Chalmers' push for spending discipline was obstructed by the prime minister's razor gang in the lead-up to the May budget. And that his heroic fiscal rectitude was undermined by the prime minister's inner cabal of spendy left-faction ministers, led by Katy Gallagher, Mark Butler, Penny Wong and Tim Ayres.
This columnist has heard similar tales.
Alarmingly for the government more broadly, it hints at a shift in the underlying ecosystem of the government. It is far from irretrievable or terminal — and old hands speak of the current tensions as nothing compared to the Gillard-Rudd years. But the change is noticeable.
People are getting jittery, looking sideways. The easy confidence of key figures in the government is dwindling.
Loading
The souring reality
This week — like workers returning to the office on a Monday to discover the fridge stopped working over the weekend — drove home the sense that things that used to be certain have gone off.
Next to the soured milk sits the slightly whiffy items of the government's thus-far successful operating model — like the notion that cabinet stability is an unquestionable virtue. The government is in its fifth year, and many ministers have been in their portfolios since 2019.
As this columnist noted in February, some of Labor's frontbench is starting to look tired.
Nearly eight months on and that hasn't changed. Too many are carrying baggage. Punters have tired of them. Their lines resonate a little less each day.
One view is that it's also strange that Labor is not making opportunities for its next generation of leaders. The backbench is full of talent, some of whom are reduced to nodding for the Question Time camera.
Another souring reality is that Labor can no longer blame the previous government for all of today's problems, even if that were true.
Finally, on the war against Iran, it's not clear voters are as forgiving of the consequences as they were in March, April and May, when the government scrambled to secure fuel supplies. Back then, voters blamed Donald Trump.
Today's mood — as reflected in the polls, social media comments and political observers — suggests voters are blaming the government for rising transport costs.
It might be time for some better visuals.
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

Students use 'rage bait' and AI bots to sway fictional election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

University students attempt to manipulate fictional election in 'Kingstonia' using AI bots
Computer engineering student Kaira Dumasia has an unusual university assignment — using AI bots to interfere in an election.
"I am really going to try to rage bait everybody," she said.
Fortunately for democracy, the election — and the voters she hopes to influence — are not real.
Kaira is part of a competition led by researchers at the University of New South Wales, which pits teams against one another to manipulate social media to win a simulated vote.
They're allowed to build AI bots to post, like, share and reply on a made-up social media platform. Points are awarded for grabbing attention, changing voters' views and spotting rival teams' bots.
The aim is to help students understand how AI can conduct in-authentic behaviour online by experimenting with controlling it themselves.
UNSW computer science senior lecturer, Hammond Pearce, said it helped students recognise the signs of manipulation, and functioned as a Petri dish for academics hoping to study AI electoral interference.
"We're trying to expose that tech… to students in a safe environment so they can learn both what the attackers are doing by doing it themselves and also what the defenders need to do in order to try and catch that kind of attack," he said.
A vote on dolphin flu
This year, the competition is set in Kingstonia, a fictional island nation that is having a referendum on whether proof of vaccination against dolphin flu should be required to enter public spaces.
Teams campaign for their chosen side on a platform called Legit Social. The AI-powered citizens read posts, interact and change their views over the month-long competition.
Kaira's strategy has been inspired by real life. Her plan is to make people angry enough to comment, boosting her posts and earning more points.
"I see a lot of it is rage bait content, engagement bait content,"
she said.
But there is a countervailing force: rival teams can report posts they suspect have been sent by other bots, and not simulated citizens.
Correctly identifying this AI bot activity also earns points for a team.
Dr Pearce said they built Legit Social specifically for the competition to have a safe place to practise their manipulation and detection skills under the watchful eyes of the organisers.
Beyond the game
The fictional vote is taking place in the lead-up to the US midterm elections and shortly after Australia's election watchdog warned about AI's role in amplifying existing election integrity threats.
Earlier this month, Australian Electoral Commissioner Jeff Pope told parliament's joint committee inquiry into AI that includes misinformation, influence operations and foreign interference, as well as physical security risks through harassment and impacts on social cohesion.
Researchers also use the game to study how participants build AI bot networks and identify other bot activity.
A preliminary academic paper published online about last year's competition examined the techniques used by competitors to win.
It found some participants turned to high-volume posting because the scoring rewarded engagement.
Kaira, who was a moderator in last year's competition, said the competition helped her recognise more AI-generated, bot-like posts.
She also recognises how easily attention-grabbing content can work on her.
"Yes, my strategy does come from a lot of posts that I see on social media. And I often find myself falling to rage bait and then I'm like, whoa, take a step back."

How a 'kickstart' gift helped a Victorian man escape homelessness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

'Kickstart' gift helps Victorian man escape homelessness
By the time he met Dorothy Maafu, Jake Dell'Aquila had been sleeping in a tent on a Melbourne beach for months.
Every evening, he would unpack his things and settle in with his German shepherd dog on the Rosebud foreshore.
Every morning, he would pack them up again.
He had been unhoused for more than a year.
Loading...
"I'd tried everything," he told Mornings with Raf Epstein on 774 ABC Melbourne this week.
"I'd tried all the resources. I'd tried the Salvation Army. I'd tried everything and nothing had worked.
"I was so desperate for help and there [was] no help through … any of these programs because I've got a dog, [and] there's the housing crisis."
It was on those cold mornings that Ms Maafu, a nearby resident, started to see him as she walked her own dog.
The pair started talking. After a while, the polite chat turned into an invitation to come visit Dorothy's home for some meals and a shower.
"I wanted to understand what it was that drove him to the streets," she said.
"From my own experience, homelessness isn't always about someone needing a roof over their head for one night.
"It's about giving people stability, dignity, and a chance to just get their lives back on track."
'Just one person can make a difference'
For Mr Dell'Aquila, the path to that Rosebud beach involved cutting off his family and friends, escaping dysfunction and abuse.
"I seemed to be doing circles and things had not been working out the best for me," he said.
"At times it was very hard. But I never gave up."
Sometime after those first few shared meals and moments of connection, Ms Maafu took a further step.
She purchased a second-hand caravan, and booked Mr Dell'Aquila into caravan parks for the next six months.
"I haven't been able to solve everything, but knowing he has shelter rather than a broken tent means a lot to me," she said.
"It was a tough road for both of us in just getting him stable.
"But I would do it all over again for another Mr Dell'Aquila on the street because it just breaks my heart to see these people, the situations they get into.
"My friends and family couldn't believe what I did. But if I don't do it, who else is going to do it?
"Just one person can make a difference in someone's life."
The stability meant Mr Dell'Aquila has been able to find work, and to find a spot in a safe rental property.
Ms Maafu, he said, would remain a lifelong friend.
"Everyone just needs a little bit of a helping hand," he said.
"I wasn't being approached by anyone the way Dorothy approached me, and it was so moving and so powerful and so life-changing what she's done.
"I may not be in the situation I'm in now with my own house and stability and paying bills if it wasn't for that little kickstart that Dorothy helped me with."
Homelessness 'rapidly' increasing across Australia
The Mornington Peninsula Shire, where Ms Maafu and Mr Dell'Aquila were located at the time, had the highest number of people sleeping rough out of any Victorian local government area as of mid-2025.
In June last year, there were 110 people in the area recorded as homeless, with the majority of them sleeping rough "in tents, cars, and on foreshore reserves".
Almost 1,000 people in the area sought homelessness services in the 2024-25 financial year.
There were 2,624 applicants waiting for public housing in March 2025.
A report by the Mornington Peninsula Shire at that time blamed a lack of appropriate affordable housing.
"Homelessness is rapidly increasing, and is likely to worsen without action,"
the report said.
According to Homelessness Australia, there were 122,494 people experiencing homelessness nationwide on Census night in 2021.
Just 6.2 per cent of them would be sleeping rough, with the rest experiencing "hidden" homelessness: staying in crisis accommodation, insecure housing, or couch surfing.
Almost 289,000 people were being assisted by specialist homelessness services in 2024-2025, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW).
A further 370,000 requests for assistance either went unanswered or were turned away in the same time period, with services stretched to breaking point.

Yemeni army claims 336 Houthis neutralized in &#8216;Dawn of Yemen&#8217; operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:58:30 UTC
02:58:30 KST

Yemen’s armed forces said they had neutralized around 336 Houthi fighters and commanders during ongoing military operations under the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, Anadolu reports.
On US social media company X, military spokesman Col. Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said government forces had carried out 1,087 strikes in recent hours using warplanes, drones, field artillery, and rocket launchers.
He said the strikes targeted Houthi command and control centers, troop concentrations, reinforcements, firing positions, fortifications, and supply routes.
In the southwestern province of Taiz, government forces and allied Popular Resistance fighters continued raids and counterattacks on strategically important Houthi positions, he added.
Al-Nuzaili said warplanes also carried out concentrated strikes on Houthi troop concentrations, reinforcements, and military positions in the province.
In the provinces of Al-Jawf, Marib and Al-Bayda, as well as southern and southwestern fronts, reconnaissance operations were followed by targeted strikes aimed at preventing infiltration attempts and disrupting Houthi reinforcements, he said.
The operations resulted in the neutralization of approximately 336 Houthi commanders and fighters, while 112 military vehicles, pieces of equipment, supply assets and heavy weapons were destroyed or damaged, according to the spokesman.
READ: Over 135,000 displaced in Yemen’s Taiz province in 2 months: Minister
He said the armed forces would continue targeting Houthi military capabilities while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The military operations come amid renewed fighting between Yemen’s internationally recognized government and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital Sanaa since late 2014.
The Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Fighting has intensified in recent weeks under the government forces’ “Dawn of Yemen” operation, with both sides reporting attacks across several provinces.
The escalation has also extended into Saudi Arabia, where the Saudi-led coalition has reported intercepting Houthi missiles targeting several regions.
On Friday, the coalition announced the interception and destruction of a Houthi cruise missile launched toward western Saudi Arabia.
A day earlier, coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said air defenses had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the capital, Riyadh.
The Houthis have also claimed attacks against Saudi oil facilities, airports and military installations amid the ongoing escalation.

'Global South bears burden': At G20 meet, Jaishankar flags attacks on ships &amp; Indian seafarers in Hormuz

17:58:29 UTC
02:58:29 KST

NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Friday raised concerns over repeated attacks on civilian shipping and seafarers at the G20 foreign affairs ministers' meeting, stressing the urgent need to safeguard freedom of navigation.In a post on X, Jaishankar said the Global South was disproportionately bearing the consequences of attacks in the Middle East, which were threatening the availability and cost of fuel, food and fertilisers."Global South is disproportionately bearing the consequences of attacks on civilian shipping and seafarers, jeopardising the availability and cost of fuel, food and fertilizers," Jaishankar said.He stressed the need to protect freedom of navigation and end attacks in accordance with international law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)."Urgent need to preserve the freedom of navigation and ensure cessation of attacks within the framework of international law, especially UNCLOS. India and Liberia have launched a joint initiative to safeguard seafarers," he added.Jaishankar also flagged concerns over restrictions on industrialisation, saying the right to industrialise was being undermined by market flooding, the weaponisation of supply chains, restricted market access and market distortions.
"Right to industrialize is being denied through the flooding of markets, weaponizing supply chains, constricting market access and encouraging market distortions. This must cease," he said."Tactical calculations should not lead to overlooking the dangers of terrorism. It is a high-risk activity which has come back to bite even the practitioners," he added.
This comes as a Panama-flagged oil tanker MT LOUISE 1 carrying 27 Indian seafarers was targeted with limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz, marking the first known successful use of the explosives against a vessel in the area since the US-Iran war began in February.Union minister for ports, shipping and waterways Sarbananda Sonowal said on Friday that all 29 Indian seafarers aboard two tankers targeted in separate attacks on October 29 and 30 were safe, with no injuries reported.In a post on X, Sonowal said, "On October 29, Liberia-flagged VLCC MT ARZANAH, carrying 2 Indian nationals, and on Oct 30, Panama-flagged crude oil tanker MT LOUISE 1, carrying 27 Indian seafarers, were targeted in projectile attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.""All 29 Indian seafarers across both vessels are completely safe with no injuries,"he said.

The Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal England | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:56:11 UTC
02:56:11 KST

Following Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringing declaration of long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action.
Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolution roadmap unveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal.From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue. That figure will potentially rise to 100% by the end of the decade, while a new overnight visitors levy will add another local income stream.
These are structural changes that will transform the relationship between local government and a notoriously overly centralised state. They have so far failed to generate anything like the coverage that accompanied the Conservatives’ levelling-up programme, which degenerated into a tawdry pork barrel exercise for “red wall” Tory MPs. But it is on this municipal terrain that Mr Burnham’s aspiration to rebalance the country, reduce regional inequality and “roll back” the 80s will be played out.
Replacing government grants with guaranteed income streams will give strategic authorities more certainty over future revenue – against which they will be able to borrow – and the ability to plan flexibly according to locally set priorities. The devil will be in details to be announced in next year’s spending review, in particular regarding mechanisms to ensure poorer areas with a smaller tax base do not lose out. But the roadmap is a first move towards restoring proper agency to local authorities struggling to cope with the disastrous twin legacy of deindustrialisation and austerity.
Further steps will need to be taken if, as the prime minister intends, local government is to drive “good growth” that improves general living standards and prospects throughout communities. As the Local Government Association pointed out, cash-strapped councils on the frontline face a £7bn funding gap by 2028-29, and are in a perennial struggle merely to meet their statutory obligations on social care. Strategic authorities need to be given the capacity to gradually reassume control of priorities in sectors such as care, housing and the utilities. That will take time and investment at scale in forms of community provision that can offer an alternative to a model in which services have been outsourced and profits offshored.
Devolution will not of itself reduce inequalities or restore a degraded public realm. But this week’s budget measures began the necessary process of rewiring British politics. Mr Burnham’s core conviction is that radical devolution can redistribute power to those who know their own community best, and allow councils to rebalance the relationship between the public and the private sector. After decades in which the latter has profited hugely from calling nearly all the shots, that is very much the right direction of travel. The starting gun has been fired in a process that can lead to a genuine renaissance of municipal England.

Trade, sovereignty and reform: key Russia-Africa Summit 2026 takeaways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:55:51 UTC
02:55:51 KST

Trade, sovereignty and reform: key Russia-Africa Summit 2026 takeaways
Russia and African countries have agreed to deepen economic cooperation, strengthen political coordination, and push for reforms of global institutions, Russian President Vladimir Putin and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye said in a joint press statement on Thursday.
Speaking at the conclusion of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, the two leaders outlined the results of the October 28–29 gathering, which brought together senior delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 led by heads of state.
The gathering resulted in the adoption of three documents: the Declaration of the 3rd Russia-Africa Summit, the Declaration of Cooperation in the Civilian Application of Artificial Intelligence Technologies, and the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum Action Plan for 2027–2029.
Turning political solidarity into economic cooperation
Ndayishimiye said African countries are seeking to diversify their international partnerships and strengthen their sovereignty, with Russia playing a role in accelerating economic development and regional integration.
Speaking about the summit’s three-year action plan, he said that the leaders “outlined priorities, financing mechanisms, implementation schedules and areas of responsibility, and set dates by which expect to see results.”
The African Union chair called for greater Russian investment to help African countries create added value locally. He also stressed that African youth expected tangible results, including more scholarships, reliable energy supplies, and digital solutions.
Expanding trade and financial independence
Putin said Russia-Africa trade currently stood at $27 billion but remained well below its potential, and called to double it.
The Russian president noted national currencies, including the ruble, now accounted for 85% of settlements in commercial transactions between Russia and African countries.
Reducing technological dependence
Ndayishimiye called for reducing Africa’s technological dependence. He stressed the summit had adopted a separate declaration on artificial intelligence, advocating equitable international cooperation with a central role for the United Nations.
Putin said Russia and African countries had signed agreements aimed at introducing Russian digital solutions, including AI-based technologies, in African economies and public administration.
Africa must choose its own partners
Asked whether Africa risked becoming an arena for competition between major powers, Putin rejected the suggestion that Moscow viewed African countries as objects of geopolitical rivalry.
“We have not pursued any colonial policies. It is the opposite: we helped them to liberate themselves from the neo-colonial yoke,” he stated.
Ndayishimiye similarly stressed that African nations were no longer in a position where outside powers could determine their partnerships.
Reforming global institutions
Putin backed permanent African representation on the UN Security Council. “I am absolutely convinced that Africa must be represented there on a permanent basis, including in the Security Council,” he said.
Ndayishimiye reaffirmed Africa’s position on UN reform, while calling for greater representation in global financial institutions and closer cooperation with BRICS.
Strengthening security and humanitarian cooperation
Putin said Russia would continue consultations with parties involved in African conflicts and expressed hope that Moscow’s diplomatic efforts could help prevent further escalation.
He also pledged to expand cooperation in healthcare and education, including medicine supplies, mobile laboratories, and training for African students.
Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for African countries has been extended through 2029, Putin said, adding that African partners supported expanding Russian university branches and educational centers on the continent.
Moscow Declaration sets out common political positions
The 101-point declaration, adopted in Moscow on October 29, is divided into five sections covering political and legal cooperation, security, economic ties, humanitarian cooperation, and environmental protection and climate issues. Here are its key points.
- Maritime security: Oppose the unjustified detention, seizure or arrest of civilian vessels, including African-flagged ships, in violation of international law. The document warns that such actions against commercial vessels turn maritime trade into “a tool of economic and political pressure.”
- Sanctions: Oppose unilateral coercive measures that violate international law, including measures imposed outside the UN Security Council, and strengthen coordination to reduce their impact on trade, energy, healthcare and food security.
- Sovereign assets: Oppose the freezing and attempted confiscation of sovereign assets, as well as political and economic coercion against sovereign states.
- Colonial reparations: Pursue legal mechanisms to assess and compensate for damage inflicted on African countries during the colonial era, alongside efforts to complete the continent’s decolonization.
- International justice: Counter the politicization and misuse of international criminal justice mechanisms, including their use to exert neocolonial pressure on African states, and strengthen cooperation to ensure the independence and impartiality of international courts.
- UN reform: Work toward reforming the Security Council to increase African representation, taking into account the continent’s common position under the Ezulwini Consensus and the 2005 Sirte Declaration.
- Counterterrorism: Strengthen cooperation against terrorist groups’ use of drones, encrypted platforms, and digital finance, while also addressing terrorist financing, organized crime, and maritime piracy.
- Arms control: Oppose the politicization of international arms control, disarmament, and nuclear nonproliferation mechanisms, and support compliance with existing treaties governing nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons.
- IMF and World Bank: Push for reforms to give African countries greater representation in the leadership of both institutions and more influence over decision-making.
- G20: Call for South Africa’s full and active participation in the group to be restored as soon as possible, while strengthening the voice of African countries and the wider Global South.
- Cultural heritage: Support the return of cultural objects and historical artifacts removed from African countries during colonial rule, alongside efforts to protect cultural heritage from illicit trafficking.
- Space cooperation: Expand cooperation in peaceful space exploration, satellite communications, Earth observation, and joint research, including spacecraft technologies and equipment.
- Trade and infrastructure: Expand cooperation in precious metals, strengthen industrial value chains, and develop maritime, river, road, rail, and aviation infrastructure. Remove trade barriers, increase African exports of value-added products and establish reliable financial settlement mechanisms to support trade and investment.
- Energy cooperation: Expand cooperation across oil and gas, nuclear, hydropower, hydrogen, and renewable energy to strengthen energy security and improve access to electricity.
- Education and healthcare: Expand academic exchanges, Russian-language education and joint research, while strengthening healthcare systems through medical training, laboratory development, and epidemic preparedness.
- Media cooperation: Strengthen ties between Russian and African media through the opening of representative offices, journalist training, information exchanges, and joint media projects.
- Climate policy: Oppose discriminatory protectionist measures introduced under the pretext of combating climate change, while expanding cooperation on climate adaptation and environmental projects that take national priorities into account.
- Sovereignty: Counter neocolonial practices that undermine states’ independence, restrict their decision-making, or facilitate the exploitation of natural resources, while upholding countries’ right to determine their own development paths.
- Conflict resolution: Support African-led efforts to resolve and prevent conflicts on the continent, guided by the principle of “African solutions to African problems.”

French economy stalls as budget deadlock fuels concerns over public finances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:55:18 UTC
02:55:18 KST

France has recorded no growth since the start of the year and GDP fell 0.1% between July and September. The government is urging political forces to adopt the 2027 budget, as the country's ability to reassure markets is in doubt. Analysis.
A setback. French gross domestic product fell by 0.1 % in the third quarter, the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee) announced (source in French) on Friday, after stagnating in the second quarter and a 0.2% decline in the first.
It is another blow for the government, with Frances borrowing costs having climbed above 5% on the financial markets last week and the social climate still highly volatile, on the eve of a new nationwide day of mobilisation against the high cost of living and in support of young peoples demands.
While household consumption is accelerating (+0.4 %), the fall in output is one of the main drivers of the contraction in French GDP. It is particularly sharp in transport equipment (-3.5%), dragged down by aerospace (-4.5 %) and automotive (-1.5 %). Activity is also declining in the agri-food sector (-1.5%), which is suffering from the impact of poor summer harvests.
This drop effectively leaves the eurozones second-largest economy on the brink of recession. At the same time, inflation has picked up again, reaching 3.4% year on year in October, compared with 3.1% in September. According to Insee, this is its highest level since January 2024.
The poor figures do not come as a surprise to experts, given the particularly unfavourable macroeconomic environment. "France is highly likely to experience a technical recession over the coming quarters", says Jérémie Peloso, chief strategist for Europe at BCA Research, speaking to Euronews.
"This scenario was already conceivable before the recent budgetary turmoil and the rout on the bond market", he adds.
"We will hit the wall"
The government has been shaken by the news and is stressing the need to secure adoption of the 2027 budget on time, in a parliament where it has no majority.
Speaking on Franceinfo, Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure described the French economy as "at a standstill". He also warned that the country "will hit the wall" if the "recovery" budget is not adopted.
If parliamentary talks fail, the government is not ruling out using article 49.3 of the Constitution, which allows a bill to be passed without a vote, unless a motion of no confidence is carried. Another possibility is to resort to ordinances, a procedure that has never been used to pass a budget since the creation of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
"The main risk to the French economy is not the absence of a budget"
According to Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University and author of the blog "La finance au cœur de nos vies" (source in French), adopting a budget is not "decisive" in itself, as it would not, "through any kind of leverage effect, miraculously revive activity in the short term".
"On the contrary, a fiscal adjustment plan generally tends to weigh on growth in the immediate future". The researcher points out that the issue is not just getting the governments bill through, but giving investors medium and long-term visibility over the trajectory of Frances public finances.
France is borrowing at increasingly high cost on the markets. "Each rise in interest rates gradually feeds through into the state budget, reduces future room for manoeuvre and ultimately weighs on private investment", Jérôme Mathis reminds us. Budget uncertainty can also become a drag on activity, he warns. "Companies postpone some investments, households defer some spending and the markets demand a higher risk premium".
As of Friday, the yield on 10-year French government bonds stands at 4.9%, 0.17 percentage points below the peak reached on 22 October. The Franco-German spread, which measures the gap between the two countries borrowing rates, is hovering at around 1.55 percentage points.
"Yesterdays ECB meeting, which was relatively free of surprises, certainly contributed to this easing, even though its president, Christine Lagarde, refused to comment on the French situation", notes a strategy paper written by Jérémie Peloso for BCA clients and seen by Euronews.
"The main risk to the French economy is not the absence of a budget. It is the absence of visibility over the trajectory of public finances", insists Jérôme Mathis. In this context, "the main economic cost of the current deadlock lies less in the content of the measures that would not be voted than in the prolongation of uncertainty".
Ordinances: what signal?
As for a possible adoption of the budget by ordinance, the professor does not see it as "an obvious economic solution". In his view, investors do attach importance to the speed of political decisions, but also to their "legitimacy" and their "durability". A budget adopted by ordinance may reduce uncertainty in the short term, but is not enough to restore long-term fiscal credibility, he warns.
"Markets generally prefer a contested decision to a prolonged lack of decision. But if a budget adopted by ordinance is seen as fragile, liable to be overturned after the presidential election or indicative of a lasting inability of the political system to build majorities, the positive impact on confidence could be limited", explains Jérôme Mathis.
In his view, this is precisely what distinguishes the current situation from "more classic" budget crises: markets are not questioning Frances technical ability to raise taxes or repay its debt. "They are more doubtful about its ability to slow their increase".
"As long as this question remains, pressure on interest rates is likely to persist, whatever institutional vehicle is chosen to pass the budget", he concludes.

This drop effectively leaves the eurozones second-largest economy on the brink of recession. At the same time, inflation has picked up again, reaching 3.4% year on year in October, compared with 3.1% in September. According to Insee, this is its highest level since January 2024.
The poor figures do not come as a surprise to experts, given the particularly unfavourable macroeconomic environment. "France is highly likely to experience a technical recession over the coming quarters", says Jérémie Peloso, chief strategist for Europe at BCA Research, speaking to Euronews.
"This scenario was already conceivable before the recent budgetary turmoil and the rout on the bond market", he adds.
"We will hit the wall"
The government has been shaken by the news and is stressing the need to secure adoption of the 2027 budget on time, in a parliament where it has no majority.
Speaking on Franceinfo, Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure described the French economy as "at a standstill". He also warned that the country "will hit the wall" if the "recovery" budget is not adopted.
If parliamentary talks fail, the government is not ruling out using article 49.3 of the Constitution, which allows a bill to be passed without a vote, unless a motion of no confidence is carried. Another possibility is to resort to ordinances, a procedure that has never been used to pass a budget since the creation of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
"The main risk to the French economy is not the absence of a budget"
According to Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University and author of the blog "La finance au cœur de nos vies" (source in French), adopting a budget is not "decisive" in itself, as it would not, "through any kind of leverage effect, miraculously revive activity in the short term".
"On the contrary, a fiscal adjustment plan generally tends to weigh on growth in the immediate future". The researcher points out that the issue is not just getting the governments bill through, but giving investors medium and long-term visibility over the trajectory of Frances public finances.
France is borrowing at increasingly high cost on the markets. "Each rise in interest rates gradually feeds through into the state budget, reduces future room for manoeuvre and ultimately weighs on private investment", Jérôme Mathis reminds us. Budget uncertainty can also become a drag on activity, he warns. "Companies postpone some investments, households defer some spending and the markets demand a higher risk premium".
As of Friday, the yield on 10-year French government bonds stands at 4.9%, 0.17 percentage points below the peak reached on 22 October. The Franco-German spread, which measures the gap between the two countries borrowing rates, is hovering at around 1.55 percentage points.
"Yesterdays ECB meeting, which was relatively free of surprises, certainly contributed to this easing, even though its president, Christine Lagarde, refused to comment on the French situation", notes a strategy paper written by Jérémie Peloso for BCA clients and seen by Euronews.
"The main risk to the French economy is not the absence of a budget. It is the absence of visibility over the trajectory of public finances", insists Jérôme Mathis. In this context, "the main economic cost of the current deadlock lies less in the content of the measures that would not be voted than in the prolongation of uncertainty".
Ordinances: what signal?
As for a possible adoption of the budget by ordinance, the professor does not see it as "an obvious economic solution". In his view, investors do attach importance to the speed of political decisions, but also to their "legitimacy" and their "durability". A budget adopted by ordinance may reduce uncertainty in the short term, but is not enough to restore long-term fiscal credibility, he warns.
"Markets generally prefer a contested decision to a prolonged lack of decision. But if a budget adopted by ordinance is seen as fragile, liable to be overturned after the presidential election or indicative of a lasting inability of the political system to build majorities, the positive impact on confidence could be limited", explains Jérôme Mathis.
In his view, this is precisely what distinguishes the current situation from "more classic" budget crises: markets are not questioning Frances technical ability to raise taxes or repay its debt. "They are more doubtful about its ability to slow their increase".
"As long as this question remains, pressure on interest rates is likely to persist, whatever institutional vehicle is chosen to pass the budget", he concludes.

Local devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:53:51 UTC
02:53:51 KST

Scotland and Wales’s first ministers have told Andy Burnham that decisions on local devolution rest solely with their parliaments, in response to the prime minister’s push to extend English-style regional powers across the UK.
After Burnham held discussions in Glasgow with John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth about localised employment and reindustrialisation powers, Downing Street characterised the talks as constructive.
However, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, caused friction before the summit by criticising Swinney’s government for hoarding powers it acquired from Westminster rather than devolving them further.
Streeting told BBC Scotland: “One of the critiques we have … is that for the Scottish government, devolution is often about transferring power, responsibility, resources from Westminster to Holyrood and the challenge Andy Burnham is setting out is: ‘What about devolving more power also from Holyrood to local government across Scotland?’”
Northern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, had also been due at the talks, but did not attend after a political row between Sinn Féin and the DUP. Burnham said it was “disappointing” she was not there.
The prime minister said he hoped to have all four UK nations moving at the same pace on devolution, particularly on efforts outlined in Wednesday’s budget to give mayors in England more powers over tax revenues.
“There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind,” Burnham said. “I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also, crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.”
Ap Iorwerth said he had pushed Burnham on his wish to have more powers for his government.
He added: “I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd.”
Swinney’s comments after the summit took a similar line, saying he would “work constructively and collaboratively” in devolving more powers to his government, while adding that Burnham had assured him “that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour”.
Despite the emollient tone, tensions remain. Shortly before the summit, ap Iorwerth said Burnham’s first budget, which the Welsh government said amounted to a real-terms funding cut for the country, showed the prime minister was “not serious about Wales”.
Plaid Cymru, which won May’s Senedd elections, putting nationalists in office in all three of the UK’s Celtic nations for the first time, has already formally asked Burnham to give Wales the same devolved powers as Scotland.
The SNP-led government is frequently irritated by comments such as those by Streeting, characterised by one Scottish official as “lecturing us on devolution”.
Separately, Lee Waters, who was a minister in the Labour-led Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until the elections in May, told the Guardian that Burnham, who was the Greater Manchester mayor before becoming prime minister, should not try to impose an English-style mayoral model on Wales, as “we are not comparing like with like”.
He said: “The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas.
“Transposing an English mayoral worldview on to a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.
“Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government.”
