Kremlin rules out pause in fighting ahead of Ukraine trilateral talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:53:45 UTC
02:53:45 KST

The Kremlin has ruled out suspending military operations ahead of planned trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine, saying Moscow opposes a ceasefire that would give Kiev a "respite."
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said preparations for the talks, scheduled for November in Abu Dhabi, did not entail a pause in fighting.
"We have stated repeatedly that we are opposed to a ceasefire that would provide a respite for the Ukrainians," Peskov said, according to Russia’s state-run TASS news agency.
Asked whether European countries would participate, Peskov said their involvement could become necessary later, but no substantive discussions had taken place.
"At some stage, yes, the involvement of Europeans will be required, but so far no one has discussed this in any concrete terms," he said.
Peskov also said Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries would not jeopardise the planned negotiations.
Moscow did not intend to raise the issue at the Abu Dhabi meeting, he added, describing it as a matter for Washington and Kiev to discuss.
EU ready to participate
Meanwhile, the European Union said on Friday it was ready to participate in negotiations to end the war.
"We are prepared, and we have been preparing for a long time, and we are just looking forward to the moment where indeed Russia will be ready to engage in real discussions and in real terms to put an end to this war," European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho told reporters in Brussels.
Her remarks followed recent phone calls between the leaders of Finland and Norway and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which have renewed attention on diplomatic efforts to end the war, which began in February 2022.
Intensifying strikes
Moscow and Kiev have intensified strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centres, ports and energy infrastructure. Both deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, saying their attacks are aimed at military targets or facilities supporting military operations.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Ukraine had informally suspended attacks on Russian oil refineries amid mounting pressure from US President Donald Trump and uncertainty over continued US support for Kiev.
The unofficial pause reportedly began early last week and was expected to last until after the US midterm elections, potentially extending further into November. Ukraine has not officially announced a halt.

At the same time, the publication reported that Vance, with Trump’s approval sent a letter to Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran Mohsen Rezaei with a proposal of a meeting between representatives of the United States and Iran, adding he could lead the US negotiating team. Tasnim news agency said that Iran had received the letter, but had not yet responded to it.

US woman who survived botched execution says she’s in constant pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:51:44 UTC
02:51:44 KST

US woman who survived botched execution says she’s in constant pain
- Christa Pike said she is in “constant pain” after surviving a botched execution in Tennessee, and still struggles to speak.
- Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital on 30 September, was taken to hospital in critical condition, and later returned to prison.
- Her lawyers want Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison, while he has suspended executions pending an independent investigation.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Convicted murderer Christa Pike said on Oct 30 that she is in constant pain, a month after surviving a botched execution attempt in the US state of Tennessee.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike said, in a statement released by her lawyers.
“My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts,” she said.
“I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”
Pike, 50, was given two doses of the drug pentobarbital at a state prison on Sept 30 – a usually fatal dose that nevertheless failed to kill her.
She was transported to hospital in critical condition and returned to prison after receiving medical treatment.
Pike is the only inmate to ever survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre.
Pike was sentenced to death in Tennessee after she and her boyfriend beat and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp. Pike was 18 at the time of the murder.
In her statement, Pike said she is recovering “but healing is not the same as being okay.”
“I don’t know why I survived that night,” she said. “I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time.”
Since the botched execution, Pike’s lawyers have repeatedly called on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison.
Lee, a Republican, has suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation.
Asked by reporters this week about Pike’s fate, Lee said: “I suspect her sentence will be the same as it was before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
There have been 32 executions in the United States this year, all by lethal injection.
The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others – California, Oregon and Pennsylvania – have moratoriums in place. AFP

Pakistan military ‘cautiously optimistic’ on Iran-US mediation
RAWALPINDI, Pakistan, Oct 30 - Pakistan’s military is “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between Iran and the United States, its spokesman said on Friday in his first interview since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir — Pakistan's chief mediator in its efforts to de-escalate the now eight-month-old Iran war — has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.
PACT DOES NOT BAR NEW MEMBERS
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
There were still "powerful spoilers and detractors," who believed conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan's armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed or whether the United States had backed the trip.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Munir in Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Security Council on Friday adopted a resolution to extend the mandate of the UN Verification Mission in Colombia for another year, until Oct. 31, 2027.
Resolution 2833 decides that the mission's mandate will be focused on its primary function only: the reincorporation of former combatants of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and personal and collective security guarantees.
The Colombian government and the FARC struck a peace deal in August 2016 after four years of negotiations in Havana, Cuba. The mandate of the mission was later expanded to include monitoring the implementation of the 2016 peace agreement's comprehensive rural reform and ethnic chapters. Friday's resolution retained only the primary tasks of the mission. ■

Ethiopia's bike-sharing service grows popular
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:46:39 CST
02:46:39 KST

Bicycles of Addis Bike are seen at a docking station in Addis Ababa, capital of Ethiopia, Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Michael Tewelde/Xinhua)
ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Sitting in his office in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, Yeabsera Yismashewa monitors bicycles being rolled out along the city's newly constructed bike lanes.
Yismashewa works as chief technical officer for Addis Bike, the country's first station-to-station bike-sharing operator. Launched in August 2024 with a fleet of 20 mechanical bikes, Addis Bike has now deployed 100 bikes, offering service along selected routes and designated bike lanes in the city.
"We have seen a growing number of people using the bike-sharing service in the city," Yismashewa said, adding that the public's awareness of and interest in using the service is surprisingly improving.
Yismashewa attributes the launch of the new transport service to government-led expansion of the infrastructure network for non-motorized vehicles, prompting demand for the biking service.
"We recognized that many daily journeys in the city cover relatively short distances, yet people often spend considerable time and money to reach their destinations. We want to offer an alternative transportation service that combines convenience, technology, and environmental friendliness," he told Xinhua in a recent interview.
The service mainly addresses transportation challenges faced by government employees, who may find it difficult to get a taxi or bus while going to the office during morning hours, said Yismashewa.
Since the fleet's launch in 2024, Addis Bike has reported over 35,311 sign-ups and 51,720 trips, with an average ride lasting 30 minutes. Riders are charged per minute, with a 30-minute ride costing 95 Ethiopian birr (about 0.6 U.S. dollars).
However, established travel habits, low public awareness, and insufficient parking and docking stations remain a challenge to the business, said the company.
Eyoas Girma is one of the many students who often use the bike-sharing service to commute between home and school.
"These days, it is very difficult to get a taxi during morning hours. I prefer to ride the bike to school," Girma said, noting that he finds the service more "flexible and economical."
Addis Bike's operating model incorporates digital fleet management, including Global Positioning System tracking and a smart-lock system, to help trace the bikes on the road, determine their status, and take appropriate follow-up action in case of misuse.
Other residents share similar sentiments. "I am happy the bike-sharing service is launched in Ethiopia. I have been enjoying the service since six months ago," Etsub Getahun said. "I ride the bikes to keep me strong and fit."
Since 2020, the government of Ethiopia, through the Addis Ababa City Administration, has been building bicycle lanes and pedestrian walkways as part of its corridor development project, aiming to slash greenhouse emissions and promote green mobility.
Accordingly, the government banned imports of petrol and diesel vehicles in 2024, while reducing taxes on electric vehicles (EVs), a policy that helped increase the adoption of EVs nationwide. The transition also aims to ensure energy sovereignty by saving foreign currency spent on fuel imports. ■

A man rides a bicycle of Addis Bike in Addis Ababa, capital of Ethiopia, Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Michael Tewelde/Xinhua)

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The UN Security Council on Friday renewed the authorization of an EU-led stabilization force in Bosnia and Herzegovina for another 12 months.
The 15-member council unanimously adopted Resolution 2834, which re-authorizes European Union Force Althea (EUFOR ALTHEA) and the NATO presence in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a further period of 12 months, starting from the date of the adoption of the resolution.
EUFOR ALTHEA, a successor to a NATO-led stabilization force, has a mission to ensure continued compliance with the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, which put an end to the 1992-1995 Bosnian War.
The resolution authorizes UN member states to take all necessary measures, upon request, in defense of EUFOR ALTHEA or the NATO presence respectively, and to assist both organizations in carrying out their missions.
It recognizes the right of both EUFOR ALTHEA and the NATO presence to take all necessary measures to defend themselves from attack or threat of attack. ■

Feature: Stones, craft and commerce -- reviving Aleppo's ancient souks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:46:05 CST
02:46:05 KST

This aerial drone photo taken on July 20, 2026 shows the historic markets and surrounding buildings in the Old City of Aleppo, northern Syria. (Photo by Monsef Memari/Xinhua)
by Hummam Sheikh Ali
ALEPPO, Syria, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Abdul Qader al-Qusaib, who owns a roastery in Aleppo's Old City, remembers a time when the souks bustled with merchants and customers, and the sounds of trade filled the narrow passageways.
The hustle and bustle came to an abrupt end when fighting engulfed the historic marketplace in northern Syria. Shops were damaged or shuttered, commercial activity ground to a halt, and merchants lost not only their workplaces but also the livelihoods they had built over the years.
When restoration began, al-Qusaib closely followed the work and witnessed the changes firsthand.
Initially, some shopkeepers were reluctant to reopen while nearby markets remained damaged and customer numbers were low.
Gradually, the situation began to change. As more sections were restored, merchants reopened their shops, customers returned and the once-disconnected markets began functioning again. Al-Qusaib eventually reopened his own shop.
Al-Qusaib's return reflects a broader revival taking place across the historic marketplace.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1986, Aleppo's historic souks had long been a vibrant trading hub along the Silk Road. Once the largest covered market in the world, the 13-km labyrinth through the old city was devastated during some of the fiercest fighting of Syria's civil war.
A massive fire in 2012 swept through large sections of the souks, destroying hundreds of shops and damaging centuries-old structures. Shelling and fighting between 2012 and 2016 further devastated the area, forcing traders to abandon shops passed down for generations.
In 2017, restoration projects began reconnecting parts of the marketplace after the fighting subsided. Rehabilitation has been completed in several markets, including Souk al-Hibal, while work has continued in other sections of the old city.
Yet those involved in the recovery say preserving the markets requires more than reconstructing their historic appearance.
Firas Qasmo, involved in the old city's rehabilitation efforts, stressed the importance of bringing economic activity back alongside physical restoration, including supporting traditional trades and creating opportunities for younger generations.
For Osama Rostom, who runs a handicrafts and art shop in Souk al-Hibal, this means bringing life back to the souks and repairing their historic structures.
Having witnessed the market's destruction and rehabilitation, Rostom remembers how wartime damage left parts of the historic commercial district empty and disrupted trades associated with its specialized souks for generations.
Rostom reopened his shop in 2023 and gradually saw other businesses follow. As more shopkeepers returned, visitors began walking through the restored lanes again, bringing activity back to streets that had once stood largely deserted.
For Rostom, the recovery means more than just revenue.
He said that Aleppo's traditional markets are not simply collections of historic buildings. Their identity is closely connected to the crafts, skills and commercial practices passed down through generations.
Therefore, the reopening of neighboring souks has become an important part of his own business's recovery, drawing more visitors into the wider commercial district and improving the prospects of merchants who have already returned, he added.
In the old city, physical reconstruction and economic recovery are closely linked: restored streets allow shops to reopen, returning merchants help attract customers, and growing commercial activity encourages more shopkeepers to return.
"We hope everything will come back, but little by little, as the rest of the markets are restored," al-Qusaib said. ■
Workers conduct restoration work inside one of the historic markets in the Old City of Aleppo, northern Syria, July 20, 2026. (Photo by Monsef Memari/Xinhua)
A worker conducts restoration work inside one of the historic markets in the Old City of Aleppo, northern Syria, July 20, 2026. (Photo by Monsef Memari/Xinhua)

====================================================================================================

How cuts under Colombia’s de la Espriella threaten a key human rights court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:43:21 UTC
02:43:21 KST

Bogota, Colombia – Angela Cordon was only a teenager when her father and uncle disappeared.
They were among a string of farmers and merchants to go missing in the southwestern department of Huila in Colombia.
First came her uncle Reynaldo Cordon Herrera's kidnapping. A grocer by trade, he had been travelling by truck on January 22, 2003, when he went missing.
The next month, Guillermo Cordon Herrera — Angela's father — set out to discover what happened to his brother, tracing his whereabouts through rural Colombia.
Guillermo called home one night with news: He had made contact with the rebel fighters he believed to be responsible for his brother's abduction.
It was the last time his family would ever hear from him. His body was never found, nor was his brother's.
Angela's father and uncle are among the more than 450,664 people killed as part of Colombia's six-decade-long internal armed conflict.
In the 23 years since their disappearance, Angela and her family have sought any information they could find about their loved ones' last days. "I have dedicated my life to this search," she told Al Jazeera.
She credits one institution in particular with helping her find answers: Colombia's Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), a transitional justice court.
Set up in 2016 as part of a peace deal between the government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country's largest rebel group at the time, the court handles the prosecution and investigation of crimes committed during the conflict.
But victims, their loved ones and even some former fighters fear that budget cuts could gut JEP, leaving the court unable to fulfil its mission.
This month, the administration of right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella announced it would enact a 2027 budget with dramatic reductions for government bodies like JEP.
The total cuts to JEP were valued at around 181 billion Colombian pesos, or roughly $57m.
On Wednesday, a Senate committee also advanced a bill to eliminate JEP altogether by March 2028, with a proposal to transfer its functions to the general court system.
Angela, however, credits JEP with offering closure that the criminal justice system was never able to provide. She worries that slashing the court's funding — much less shuttering it entirely — could derail its work.
Through JEP, Angela learned about her father and uncle's time in captivity, as well as the site of their execution. JEP has also worked with former FARC members to try to locate their remains.
"Fewer resources mean fewer missions to the field to find answers, less humanitarian personnel," Angela said, bracing for the cuts.
"It probably means that we will never be able to return to the site."
A 'duty to manage spending'
De la Espriella has framed the budget reduction as necessary to combat Colombia's rising public debt, which exceeds $370bn.
"It is my duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the government's limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone," de la Espriella wrote in a September statement, defending his decision to trim JEP's funding.
He estimated that its payroll budget alone was north of 404 billion pesos, or $127m, in 2026.
Critics, however, have questioned whether austerity is the motive for the downsizing.
At around 634 trillion pesos or $200bn, de la Espriella's 2027 budget increases spending overall.
Passed by presidential decree, the budget is considered the largest spending package in the history of the country.
But de la Espriella has targeted JEP for reasons beyond its cost. He has repeatedly criticised JEP as slow and ineffective, failing to deliver on its promises of justice.
He has also slammed the court's investigations as biased against military members — and too lenient on rebels.
In an interview with the radio show Recap Blu, he accused JEP of "persecuting the heroes of the homeland" while "washing the hands of the guerrillas who committed crimes against humanity".
'Disastrous for victims'
But many victims' rights advocates dispute that assessment.
Ana Maria Rodriguez, a lawyer who represents victims of Colombia's conflict, described the accusation of bias as "patently false".
She pointed out that JEP has convicted some of the top leadership in the FARC, the rebel group that disarmed as part of the 2016 peace deal.
“It hasn’t been perfect or complete,” Rodriguez said of the JEP's work. "But the peace process here has become a model studied by other countries around the world. We have to keep this process functional.”
She believes that cuts to the court's budget will lead to fewer convictions, furthering impunity rather than preventing it.
“Many of the [perpetrators] have never faced any justice mechanisms outside of the JEP,” Rodriguez said.
In its effort to close unsolved cases, the court has offered leniency to soldiers, rebels and other fighters in exchange for cooperation with ongoing investigations.
Those cases typically result in rehabilitation work instead of a prison sentence, with defendants asked to engage in community service.
Those kinds of sentences have fuelled some of the criticism against JEP. But Rodriguez feels such trade-offs are necessary to offer resolution to victims' families.
After all, more than 100,000 people have been reported missing in Colombia's conflict. Their fate remains unknown.
“It isn’t clear how cases will be able to proceed without witness cooperation programmes," Rodriguez said.
She predicted that shrinking JEP's funding will be "absolutely disastrous for victims".
A fear of jeopardising investigations
Ahead of the anticipated cuts to JEP this month, more than 20 Colombian Congress members signed an open letter to the International Criminal Court (ICC), asking for help.
The ICC shares a similar mandate as JEP, as both are charged with investigating and prosecuting war crimes.
The international court was also supportive of the 2016 peace deal that gave rise to JEP's creation.
"We are concerned that [the budget's] approval will jeopardise investigations, trials and the execution of sentences for crimes under the court's jurisdiction," the lawmakers wrote to the ICC, in a request for support.
Alberto Yepes, a spokesman for the Colombia-Europe-United States Coordination Group, a human rights coalition, is among those rallying against the JEP cuts.
He sees a connection between the attacks on JEP and de la Espriella's heavy-handed approach to law enforcement.
De la Espriella, he explained, has modelled his security platform on hardline programmes in countries like El Salvador and Ecuador, where police and soldiers have been granted expanded powers.
Yepes believes that, by weakening JEP, the president may seek to prevent the future prosecution of military leaders in cases involving state crimes.
"These policies accompany aggressive new security measures, and combined, I think it seems very clear that this government is seeking impunity for the military," Yepes said.
In addition to reducing JEP's funding, de la Espriella's government is reportedly weighing a 116-page "counterterrorism" bill that would increase penalties for certain offences, criminalise some forms of protest, and make it more difficult to suspend military operations.
In Yepes's view, the ultimate goal is to shield law enforcement from accountability.
"De la Espriella is making decisions for a minority of the people that will benefit from these policies," he said.

The recent Israeli elections brought the terrifying views of Israeli youth into full view. Videos of young Israelis calling for the mass slaughter of Palestinians or expressing their desire for the new Israeli government to go even further to the right than it already has have been making waves online, and while it’s no surprise that these soundbites go viral on social media, it is important to understand just how pervasive these views are. It is not just one or two fanatics who were taken out of context online. It is a whole new generation of Israeli youth who, in the wake of October 7 and the genocide in Gaza, are fully embracing fascism.
This is not typical internationally, where younger generations are often less nationalist-conservative than older ones. A poll from this year, conducted by Israeli Channel 12, shows that among 18- to 21-year-olds who hadn’t voted in the 2022 elections, the share identifying as right-wing rose to 75%, up from 68% in the older population. This segment, consisting of about half a million potential new voters, formed in their teens by genocide, is simply more genocidal than ever, and this obviously played a part in the elections this week.
With votes in Israel now fully counted, it is clear that the Israeli public still voted overwhelmingly right. Netanyahu’s Likud leads with 27 seats (the big opposition party Yashar, headed by ret. general Gadi Eisenkot, mastermind of the murderous ‘Dahiya Doctrine’, comes in second with 21). Although Netanyahu’s current government bloc hasn’t got a majority (it has 53 and one needs a 61 majority), the opposition bloc still contains right-wing parties like Yashar, as well as Avigdor Lieberman’s further-right Yisrael Beitenu (7), Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s Together (12), and even The Democrats led by ret. general Yair Golan (8) don’t want to talk about two states anymore. The left that is not Zionist is represented by the Palestinian-representative Joint List, with a surprising 11 seats (the conservative Palestinian Ra’am got 8) – but the Jewish Zionist bloc by and large refuses to touch them. So the ‘opposition bloc’ without the Palestinian parties has 48 seats, and while the Democrats have started considering cooperation, it is contentious. Zionist racism is the overall frame of this picture.
Perhaps one of the best ways to understand the views of this new generation of Israeli voters, and how Israeli “liberal” Zionists are trying to distance themselves from the current reality — in a futile attempt to restore a fictional version of the liberal Israeli “democracy” they cherish — is with a popular video series that veteran TV host and comedian Lior Schleien made this year.
The series followed Schleien, a proud “liberal Zionist,” as he toured schools across the country, engaging in debates with Israeli youth on topics related to the “conflict” with the Palestinians, Middle East geopolitics, and other national and religious issues.
Brace yourselves: the views of the Israeli youth, and Schleien’s misguided attempts to sway them to more “liberal” views, reveal a grim picture of the state of the Israeli political landscape, and how the genocidal apartheid state is only getting more genocidal.
Confronting extremism…to a point
In his tours of schools around the country, Schleien confronts explicitly genocidal youths and films his encounters. In one video, which has since been removed by request of the student’s parents, one student tells him, “Every Arab in the world should die, whether he is good or not good… I have no problem killing fifty Arabs and dying – Arabs, terrorists, I don’t care which.”
Schleien asks whether there is a difference between a terrorist and an Arab – the student answers “no, every Arab should be in the grave, that’s it”.
That’s clearly way too far for Schleien – he asks whether such a thing is “possible,” that is, to kill every Arab.
So Schleien seeks dialogue with this ‘extremist’ youth, because as he told Haaretz in an interview, “Israel is still a democracy, and there’s only one way to change things in a democracy, and that’s by persuading people to see things your way.”
In another encounter, Schleien argues with a right-wing settler-student that she and her peers are “not human shields,” in response to her claim that Israeli settlements are strategic. Instead, he argues for ethnic “separation.” So he proposes pragmatic solutions, based on the Zionist apartheid logic, that speak to the fears of these upcoming voters:
“If Israel annexes the West Bank and grants all the Palestinians citizenship and the right to vote, they would soon have a majority in the Knesset, and you all would lose this Jewish state that is so important to you. And if you prefer to deny them citizenship and the right to vote, then prepare yourselves for Israel to be boycotted by most of the world.”
In another video with the “Hilltop Youth“, Schleien tries to persuade them not to “bother Palestinians, or beat them up, or rob them”, since that will “not convince 3 million people to get up and leave their home, even if their life sucks” (in the West Bank). “It won’t happen,” he emphasizes, “I’m not telling you it’s not moral, or not legal – it’s not gonna happen.” Schleien is countered by a teenager who says that “here in Judea and Samaria” (biblical names for the West Bank, which Schleien also uses), “we have deterrence. Every Arab here experiences deterrence by a Jew; when he sees a Jew, he fears that Jew more than in Tel Aviv or any other place, and I think that in general, deterrence is our victory.”
Schleien’s argument about “ain’t gonna happen” doesn’t seem to harmonize with the witnessed experience of ethnic cleansing, and also genocide. These youths see what their state is doing. “Bothering Palestinians” is an understatement, and it’s not just the “Hilltop Youth” doing it; it’s the state.
The liberal Zionist fight against the right and the left
The increasingly extremist views of Israeli youth are no doubt disturbing. However, as an Israeli myself, who has been documenting this racist and genocidal society and its views for a long time, what stood out to me more than the views of the youth was the attempts of Schleien to push back against them in pursuit of his vision for an Israel that does not, and has never existed.
In the context of the elections, Israel’s supposedly liberal Zionist opposition to Netanyahu is struggling to make itself relevant. Although no Zionist party advocates the elusive ‘two-state solution,’ there are those who still struggle to portray it as liberal – perhaps mostly for the sake of their own self-view.
Schleien is one of the main representatives of this effort. He seeks to fight Netanyahu, while simultaneously fighting the growing isolation of Israel through boycotts, divestment, and sanctions (BDS).
Schleien’s series is not just about confronting the right-wing views of Israeli youth. Simultaneously, he also charges American liberals, and particularly Jews, with being too extreme on Israel – chiding them for supposedly doing the same thing Netanyahu is doing to the liberal Zionists, just from the left (by, for example, boycotting Israeli academia).
Schleien thus seeks to position himself in the middle of all that – precisely as a proud ‘liberal Zionist’.
“Because of the catastrophic mistakes of this government we elected – and I’m obviously using the royal ‘we’ here – we are in danger of losing this beloved country of ours,” he says, cited by Haaretz. “We elected a government that is dismantling this country and will continue to do so if it remains in power. So, before our haters ‘free Palestine from the river to the sea,’ we Israelis need to free Israel from this government that is pushing us to the brink.”
Schleien’s portrayal of this as a fight between the Zionist left and the Zionist right is betrayed by a reality wherein both are fighting a similar fight against Palestinians. As the former head of the Kibbutz Movement, Nir Meir, said in his interview to Haaretz in 2024, the right-wing settlers are “correct”, in that this “is the way to seize and hold land, and their claim that, any place we Israelis leave, the Arabs will come in our place, is correct”. Meir also noted that the settlers “learned from us how to settle and seize land”. And Meir is correct about this being a cardinal Zionist view. The supposedly leftist kibbutzniks, who have had a major inciting role in the genocide of Gaza, are arguing with the right-wing settlers about location and speed, not principle.
So Schleien has taken up a balancing act.
Zionist gaslighting
Lior Schleien is thus seeking to advocate for the ‘good Zionism.’ His is open to dialogue with the extremists, much in the nature of the late author Amos Oz, who was also a major propagandist for Zionism. While calling the settlers ‘zealots,’ Oz also mocked Palestinians for their ‘illness’ in seeking their right to return, opining that one needed a “big stick” to deal with them.
Schleien professes to be apolitical, as it were. “I’m not a campaigner, and I don’t tell them which party to support,” he tells Haaretz. “All I tell them is that they need to formulate their political positions based on facts rather than fallacies, that they need to think critically, and I present a non-apologetic liberal democratic worldview.”
But that worldview is limited by Zionism, in which apartheid is central. So he seeks to make an ultra-nationalist ideology relevant in liberal thinking, portraying himself as the moderate in debating the extremists – both for the personal image, but also for the international one. Yet it is doubtful whether Schleien will be able to convince the world that Israel can heal itself from within, and that external pressures must be fended off for that to happen. Many have just stopped consuming that ‘liberal-Zionist’ gaslighting.
It is not yet clear how the recent elections will end up in terms of government. The unwillingness to involve Palestinians in governance may result in another forever-elections cycle like the one experienced in 2019-2022, with five elections taking place within less than four years. But any result will be a manifestation of Israel’s increasingly explicit right-wing turn, and the youth indicate that this tide is only growing.
Some, like Schleien, seek hope through internal Zionist discussions. But those of us who know better know that Zionism’s settler-colonialist vein is ultra-nationalist, so it’s natural for it to go that way. If one wants a more serious solution to this problem, then this will require outside pressure. Any other talk is just naiveté or hypocrisy. Schleien seeks to stem precisely that pressure, which is why his effort amounts to window-dressing at best.

Drone strikes on Ethiopia displacement camp kill at least 15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:42:09 UTC
02:42:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Drone strikes on Ethiopia displacement camp kill at least 15, sources say
At least 15 people, several of them children, died in a series of drone strikes that hit a camp for displaced civilians in Ethiopia's Amhara region, two sources involved in a rescue operation said on Friday.
It was not clear why the camp was targeted or who was behind the attack, but the strikes highlight continuing clashes in the area despite a lull in the heavy fighting that erupted last month between an alliance of rebels from northern Tigray region and the government in Addis Ababa.
"There were around five explosions. Then ... we started collecting bodies," a community representative involved in the burials told Reuters, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.
The representative said they helped bury 13 people at the camp, which is known as Jari 2 and is home to more than 1,700 people who fled previous violence.
Two of the injured later died at a hospital in Hayk, a town 17 km (10 miles) away.
A spokesperson for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A local official said they were aware of the incident and were helping get medical treatment to 36 people who had been injured.
A man who lost a family member described seeing a drone circling overhead on Wednesday and then returning on Thursday.
“Then finally it hit the camp … three times,” the relative told Reuters. “Their body parts were scattered everywhere. We collected and buried pieces of their body parts.”
A resident of Hayk who was helping provide shelter to survivors also said 15 people had been killed. "Those from the camp are now sheltering in a school," the resident said.
The dead included five children, according to the two sources involved in the rescue.
The relative of one of the victims said they had seen at least 10 injured children under the aged of five receiving treatment.
All three sources said there had been no fighting in the area when the strike took place, but members of the Amhara Fano National Movement, which is part of the rebel alliance spearheaded by fighters from Tigray, had been nearby.
Government troops have driven back the rebel alliance since their offensive was launched on 23 September.
They retook the capital of Tigray region earlier this month and advanced towards the border with Eritrea, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebellion by sending troops over the border.
Eritrea denies the accusation and says Addis Ababa's allegations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a "declaration of war".
Given the web of interconnected conflicts in the Horn of Africa, with neighbouring countries and powers further afield backing their respective proxies, experts have warned that war in Ethiopia could trigger a broader conflict in the region.

Activist exposes event promoting clinics in illegal settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:41:00 UTC
02:41:00 KST

Breadcrumb
UK activist exposes event 'promoting clinics in illegal Israeli settlements'
When medical student Jane, whose name has been changed for anonymity, heard there was a medical event to help Jewish doctors across the UK move to Israel, she decided to look further into whether they were promoting illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The event, hosted by MedEx, took place in Camden on 25 October and was mainly organised by Israeli government officials. MedEx is also part of a series of organisations that help Jews from around the world make 'Aliyah' to Israel -- a term used to describe their migration to the country and granting of Israeli citizenship.
"I wanted to see if it was still happening and also be able to report it and prevent its normalisation as much as possible," Jane, a member of Jewish Anti-Zionist Action, told The New Arab.
Recalling the Great Israeli Real Estate event in June, where activists exposed the promotion of homes in illegal settlements, Jane wanted to see if it was still happening, as nothing concrete has come from the UK Charity Commission.
"That was my main motivation, to sort of prevent as much as I could."
The event encouraged conversation with clinics and recruiters and began the Israeli licensing process, while also promoting tax benefits should they decide to make the move.
"It's just the banality of people just happy to be there and be like, 'great, we're going to get to move to the homeland', and it's acting like there's not a massive, massive price being paid by a lot of people for it, like there's nothing happening under the surface," Jane said.
After witnessing heavy police presence on the way to the centre and going through three rounds of security checks, including being asked about what synagogue she attends, Jane was welcomed to the event.
The student received a promotional pack of materials from medical companies with clinics in the occupied West Bank, including Shivat Zion, which a report by Declassified said was helping people move to illegal Israeli settlements and actively promoting it within the UK.
Jane was also handed a leaflet by Terem, an organisation promoting medical jobs in settlements, Ma'ale Adumim, Beitar Illit, and Modiin Illit in the occupied West Bank and Katzrin in the occupied Syrian Golan Heights – settlements which are all considered illegal under international law.
Open positions in the settlements included general and urgent care physicians, paediatricians and medical directors.
While Jane was surprised clinics that roles in the occupied territories were still being promoted, she was also shocked by the apparent lack of secrecy.
"It was so easy, there was nothing difficult about getting that information at all," Jane said. "There was nothing under the table about it. It was all just out there in the open."
Growing up Jewish in the UK, the activist says she was raised with very strong values around justice as part of her Jewish beliefs, which led her to oppose Israel's occupation of the Palestinian territories.
"In a lot of ways, being so pro-Palestine because I was always taught that if you see something wrong, you do something about it, that's the Jewish way."
The UK government has imposed sanctions on illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, though Jane says a much more conscious effort is needed to stop events in the UK where these settlements are promoted.
"These events really normalise illegal settlements, especially during this time of increased settler violence with no repercussions and in the current climate, that's just totally unacceptable because of the amount of death and injury we've been seeing done to Palestinians and their allies," Jane said.

Kazakh folk song AQERKE performed flamenco-style at Dimash Qudaibergen fan event
A traditional pre-party for fans of Dimash Qudaibergen took place Thursday in Madrid ahead of the artist’s concert as part of his DIMENSIONS World Tour, Qazinform News Agency cited DimashNews.
The event brought together fans of the Kazakh singer who had travelled to the Spanish capital from around the world. The organisers prepared a vibrant cultural programme celebrating Kazakh national traditions, Spanish performing arts, and the music of Dimash Qudaibergen.
One of the evening’s most remarkable highlights was a performance by El Boti, a flamenco dance school from Seville. The dancers presented a flamenco interpretation of the traditional Kazakh folk song AQERKE, bringing together the distinctive melodies of Kazakh music with the expressive movements and passion of Spanish dance.
The evening’s distinguished guests included Danat Mussayev, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Kazakhstan to Spain, representatives of the Kazakh Embassy, members of Dimash’s family and team, representatives of the Kazakh diaspora, the Otandastar Foundation, and figures from the arts and cultural community.
The programme opened with a performance by young dombra players Alinur and Alikhan Amangeldy, who performed the traditional Kazakh instrumental pieces Balbrauyn and Er-Turan. The celebration of Kazakh heritage continued with a fashion show featuring a collection by Kazakh designer Tarbiya Aidymbayeva.
Performances by the Naz State Dance Theatre were another highlight of the evening. The dancers presented a selection of traditional Kazakh dances, including Shashu, Qalyndyq Bii, Aqqu, Sherniyaz, and Samgau.
The musical programme featured performances by Spanish artist Jonhy Calleja and singers Zhanel Ali, Viryam Amor Ondas, and Rachel Rustria. They performed a selection of well-known songs, including pieces from Dimash Qudaibergen’s repertoire such as Unforgettable Day, Tau Ishinde, Ave Maria, SOS, and others.
Fans also prepared a special dance performance to Living for the Game. The programme concluded with the presentation of commemorative gifts, after which the celebration continued with dancing to Dimash’s songs.
Today, October 30, Dimash Qudaibergen will perform his first-ever solo concert in Madrid, continuing the European leg of his DIMENSIONS World Tour following performances in Kraków and Düsseldorf.
Earlier, Dimash performed at a concert hosted by the Organization of Turkic States in Türkiye.

Elusive lynx spotted in Kazakhstan's Ertis Ormany Nature Reserve
                  22:05, 30 October 2026
                
A rare sighting of a lynx has been captured on camera by staff at the Ertis Ormany Nature Reserve in Kazakhstan, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the reserve, around 70 lynxes live in its forests, but sightings of these elusive predators in the wild are extremely rare.
"Agile and remarkably elusive, the lynx is one of the forest's most mysterious predators. It moves almost silently through the trees and rarely allows itself to be seen by humans. Its keen hearing, powerful paws, and camouflaged coat help it remain virtually undetectable in its natural habitat," the reserve said.
Previously, Qazinform reported that a rare ermine had been spotted in Kazakhstan's Kaindy Gorge.

This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:39:47 UTC
02:39:47 KST

This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat
Astronomers also have their eyes on objects near Neptune that may be solar system building blocks
The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.
Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.
Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.
“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”
A possible dwarf planet hid in historical data
Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.
Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.
The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.
“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”
When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”
Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.
Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.
“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”
So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.
By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.
Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”
Icy objects could offer clues to solar system beginnings
A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.
Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.
“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.
The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.
Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.
“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”
“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”
Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.
“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week, and they keep getting bigger and brighter. These discoveries will be hindered by that.”
But even with the satellites, Lawler anticipates many more cool discoveries from Rubin.
“Just finding a dwarf planet so quickly, maybe we’ll find something even bigger,” she says. “There could be something the size of Mars out there. And then we’d have the whole planet debate all over again. It would be fun.”

Ukraine, France sign 10-year roadmap for cooperation on veterans' affairs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:37:53 EET
02:37:53 KST

Ukraine and France have signed a 10-year roadmap for cooperation in the field of veterans' policy for 2026-2035, according to the Ministry of Veterans Affairs of Ukraine.
According to the report, the agreement was signed by Ukraine's Minister for Veterans Affairs Vitaliy Kim and Minister Delegate for Veterans Affairs of the French Republic Alice Rufo.
It is noted that cooperation between our countries will focus on four key areas.
Specifically, the rights and status of male and female veterans: a comparison of the French "combatant's card" (which is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year) with the Ukrainian system of automatic granting of combatant status, the Unified State Register of War Veterans, and the electronic ID card; protecting the rights of families of the fallen and implementing the French model of joint governance with the participation of veterans' organizations.
In turn, Ukraine will share its experience with digitalization through Diia and its own support system.
"Physical and Mental Health: Joint university programs for Ukrainian medical professionals and psychologists, internships at military hospitals in France and the Hôtel des Invalides. Training in evidence-based therapy methods (particularly for veterans who have become psychologists themselves), annual seminars on rehabilitation, sharing of experience with hotlines, and expert support for long-term and family recovery centers," the ministry said.
The third area of cooperation will be rehabilitation and reintegration. Specifically, this includes drawing on the expertise of the French Military Sports Academy in Fontainebleau and a sports-based rehabilitation program; implementing the French ATHOS program in Ukraine for veterans with PTSD, including a visit by its team to Ukraine; assistance with employment; support for state-run veteran centers; and inviting wounded French military personnel to the Veterans Games.
"Preserving Memory: Consultations on the maintenance of military cemeteries and the development of visitor centers at the National Military Memorial Cemetery. Creating an illustrated guide for Ukrainian communities on memorials, providing methodological support for local projects, sharing experience in conducting official ceremonies, and involving veterans in remembrance policies," the agency said, describing another area of cooperation.

HIMARS Just Learned to Hit Moving Targets—Bad News for Russian Guns and Air Defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:37:10 UTC
02:37:10 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
HIMARS Just Learned to Hit Moving Targets—Bad News for Russian Guns and Air Defenses
Lockheed Martin and the US Army have demonstrated a new way for HIMARS-launched GMLRS rockets to strike moving targets by updating their coordinates while the missile is already in flight—a capability that could make it much harder for mobile artillery and air-defense systems to escape after being detected.
The test was conducted at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, according to Defense Express on October 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During the demonstration, a GMLRS rocket launched from an M142 HIMARS was redirected in flight using updated target coordinates transmitted through Lockheed Martin’s Strigo datalink and a Remote Interceptor Guidance-360, or RIG-360, targeting device.
The rocket successfully struck a moving target. What makes the test particularly notable is how the capability was achieved.
Weapons designed to hit moving targets usually require a dedicated seeker capable of finding and tracking the target during the final phase of flight. In this case, however, Lockheed Martin used radio-transmitted targeting updates rather than making major modifications to the GMLRS itself.
That could offer a comparatively inexpensive way to expand the missile’s capabilities without installing a specialized seeker on every rocket.
Lockheed Martin said the equipment was integrated using company funding and could potentially be paired with other precision weapons as well, including Extended Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile, or PrSM.
PrSM Increment 2 is already being developed with a multimode seeker intended to provide a moving-target capability, particularly against ships. The GMLRS demonstration takes a different approach by continuously updating the target’s location through the RIG-360 system rather than relying on an onboard seeker.
For battlefield targets, that distinction could be significant.
Mobile artillery, air-defense systems, command vehicles, and other high-value equipment often depend on “shoot-and-scoot” tactics—firing or operating briefly before rapidly relocating to avoid counterstrikes.
A GMLRS rocket capable of receiving fresh coordinates after launch could reduce the effectiveness of that tactic, provided friendly sensors can continue tracking the target and transmit updated position data to the missile.
Defense Express notes that Lockheed Martin and the Army have not disclosed exactly what type of moving target was used during the test. The location offers one clue: White Sands is dominated by desert terrain and lacks large permanent bodies of water, making a ground vehicle or another mobile land target more likely than a ship.
For Ukraine, the development is particularly relevant because HIMARS is already routinely used to hunt Russian artillery, ammunition sites, command posts, and other high-value targets.
Ukrainian forces have previously combined US-made HIMARS with systems such as French CAESAR self-propelled howitzers to destroy Russian artillery and field ammunition depots in sectors including Pokrovsk.
Earlier, the 45th Artillery Brigade of the 11th Army Corps destroyed a Russian 9A316 transporter erector launcher and radar element from the Buk air defense system using an M142 HIMARS rocket system.

Report reveals campaign promoting racist, Islamophobic, anti-Qatar views
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:34:27 UTC
02:34:27 KST

Report reveals campaign promoting racist, Islamophobic, anti-Qatar views
Investigation finds that years-long operation sought to portray Qatar as driving force behind mass migration to Europe.
A years-long, paid-for influence operation promoting racist, Islamophobic and anti-Qatar views has been uncovered by two academics, with the evidence suggesting the campaign was intended to serve Israeli interests.
The investigation, which took three years, was published on Thursday. It detailed an operation that likely cost more than $11m and was carried out across 30 countries, including in Europe, the United States and Lebanon.
As part of the campaign, several million internet users were exposed to advertisements on sites like YouTube, TikTok and Facebook that pushed an agenda, according to the report titled Manufacturing the “Great Replacement”.
Marc Owen Jones, a professor at Northwestern University’s Doha campus, and independent researcher Sohan Dsouza, the academics who published the report, called it “perhaps one of the biggest digital influence and disinformation operations ever documented”.
Their report uncovered at least 533 million exposures of social media advertisements promoting anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, racist and anti-Qatar views between October 2023 and October 2026. It added that the advertisements were launched ahead of elections in some of the target countries.
One example, also reported by French newspaper Le Monde, looked at how the campaign had targeted France and found that “a historical analysis of the ads pushed by the campaign’s backers suggests that they repeatedly sought to align with national electoral calendars”, the newspaper said.
“Buying in France ran through the months before the June 2024 European Parliament elections, and UK buying stopped on 17 May 2024, days before the general election was called,” the researchers said.
“Its sustained promotion of anti-Muslim and anti-migrant narratives raises concerns about attempts to shape the political environment ahead of these votes, beyond the formal election campaign period,” they added.
Additionally, the report warned that “the campaign remains active in countries approaching major elections, including France and Italy in 2027”.
Qatar targeted
France accounted for about a third of the total number of advertisement placements, the highest share among the countries targeted, the report said. Meanwhile, the advertisements recorded the largest number of exposures in the United Kingdom, at 154 million. The US came second, with 100 million.
“In Europe, the ads use the structure of the Great Replacement conspiracy theory, that white people are being replaced by immigrants,” Jones said.
“Qatar takes the role that anti-Semitic versions give to George Soros: a hidden power directing Muslim immigration to ‘Islamise’ Europe,” he noted, referring to the Jewish billionaire philanthropist and frequent target of anti-Semitic conspiracy theories.
Separately, one of the campaigns that appeared on TikTok promoted regime change in Iran to audiences in Europe. The ads first began running on February 24, four days before the US and Israel launched their war on the country, the investigation found.
According to the report, the evidence suggests with “moderate to high confidence” that the influence operation was launched from within Israel and sought to portray Qatar as the driving force behind mass migration meant to allegedly “Islamise” Europe.
The researchers said metadata shows that video editors working on the campaign did so in the Israeli time zone. It also reveals that they used machines with Hebrew drive and folder names.
Qatar has been the focus of Israeli-linked campaigns before. Last month, the Israeli newspaper Haaretz found that a group of Israeli influence experts and political advisers had worked on a secret campaign targeting Doha in the weeks after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks.
Israeli politicians have also lashed out at Qatar several times in recent years, with former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett calling for the country to be declared an enemy state.
Most recently, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party accused Doha, without evidence, of interfering in Israeli elections held on Tuesday. The Qatari Foreign Ministry has denounced the allegations as a “disinformation campaign”.

Israel lost the elections: An open letter to President Isaac Herzog - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:31:16 UTC
02:31:16 KST

Dear President Isaac Herzog,
Israel has voted. The ballots have been cast, the people have spoken, yet the country appears to have emerged from one of its most consequential elections without a clear winner.
Likud may be the largest party. The opposition may claim a mandate for change. Arab parties may wield considerable influence over the next government’s formation. But beyond the arithmetic of Knesset seats lies a more disturbing conclusion.
Israel lost the elections.
Not because democracy failed. Israelis exercised their democratic rights and demonstrated that the democratic spirit remains alive.
Israel lost because the election resolved little of the conflict dividing the nation. Millions awakened convinced that their country’s future remained at stake, regardless of who eventually forms a coalition.
Mr. President, this presents perhaps the most consequential opportunity of your presidency.
When democracy becomes existential
Democracy was never intended to guarantee that everyone wins. It was designed to ensure that losing an election does not mean losing one’s country. I trust that you have heard the conversations of those who claimed that if the outcome was not to their liking, they would plan on leaving Israel.
A healthy democracy requires more than majority rule. It requires confidence that institutions will endure, political opponents remain legitimate, and another election offers another opportunity to change direction.
Yet Israel has increasingly transformed electoral competition into an existential struggle. For too many, victory by the opposing bloc is portrayed not as an undesirable outcome but as a national catastrophe.
That is dangerous for any democracy, particularly one confronting Israel’s security challenges.
We remain engaged across military, diplomatic, economic, and cognitive fronts. Iran and its proxies remain threats.
Efforts to delegitimize the Jewish state continue internationally. The approaching American midterm elections introduce further uncertainty about Washington’s political direction and Israel’s strategic environment.
At home, increased electoral participation among Arab citizens and the potential parliamentary influence of anti-Zionist parties intensify debates over the state’s future character.
Only in the last few hours, before this column was submitted for printing, has it come to light that there is sufficient evidence for the chairman of the Central Elections Committee, Judge Noam Sohlberg, to call for the immediate investigation of the surprisingly massive voter turnout of the Arab Israelis, which was allegedly financed by foreign entities and funneled via Arab organized crime members to Arab Israeli voters.
While this disturbing news might actually invalidate the election results, there is now a need to also investigate, even through the use of polygraph testing, whether any Arab Israeli party leaders were aware of this horrific crime.
Mr. President, my unusual request for polygraph testing of Arab Israeli party leadership is further strengthened by MK Ahmad Tibi’s reported visit to Qatar two days before the elections.
The truth is that the terrible division in the Israeli electorate was an issue before and after this discovery.
Therefore, the opportunity for the Israeli president to find new pathways toward resolving the counterproductive electoral stalemate is, in my humble opinion, unchanged by this disturbing attack on our democracy.
Israel cannot afford political paralysis while its adversaries exploit national weakness. But neither can it afford to mistake another appeal for unity for a solution.
Unity is not the answer
Mr. President, I suggest a different objective.
Not unity. Interoperability.
Unity implies ideological reconciliation that may be impossible in the foreseeable future. Israeli society is divided across political, religious, cultural, and philosophical lines. Democracy should not demand uniformity.
Interoperability means that independent, even competing, groups can function within a common system while preserving their convictions and identities.
We do not all have to row in the same direction. But we must understand that we are all in the same boat.
History demonstrates that cooperation is possible. During the Yom Kippur War, Israelis confronted a common threat despite their differences. After October 7, 2023, citizens across the political and religious spectrum mobilized to defend the country, assist soldiers, and support displaced families.
These experiences did not erase disagreement. They demonstrated that cooperation does not require agreement.
The challenge is to institutionalize that understanding before another emergency forces it upon us.
A remarkable historical parallel
Mr. President, history has placed you in a position reminiscent of one confronted during your father’s presidency.
In 1984, president Chaim Herzog witnessed an election that left neither major political bloc able to govern independently. Israel faced the consequences of war in Lebanon, severe economic distress, and bitter political division.
What followed was an extraordinary accommodation: Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Shamir, representing opposing political traditions, agreed to share power through a rotating premiership.
They did not embrace each other’s ideologies. They found a mechanism through which their movements could function together.
That was interoperability before we had a name for it.
Forty-two years later, another President Herzog faces a divided electorate amid extraordinary challenges. History does not demand that you reproduce the 1984 solution. It reminds us that deadlock need not become paralysis.
Your father’s presidency witnessed a political accommodation transcending electoral arithmetic. Yours could establish a precedent for confidence in the constitutional process itself.
The presidency’s defining test
Your immediate responsibility is constitutionally straightforward but politically extraordinary: deciding which Knesset member receives the mandate to form a government.
The law does not require you to choose the leader of the largest party. Following consultations with parliamentary factions, you must assign the mandate to a consenting member of the Knesset.
That discretion places you in an almost impossible position. Whichever candidate you choose, millions may question not merely your judgment but your impartiality. The problem is not necessarily a lack of good intentions. It is a shortage of public trust.
You have already experienced the consequences of irreconcilable expectations.
The controversy over possible clemency for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu placed your office under intense domestic and international pressure. US President Donald Trump publicly urged you to act; others demanded the opposite.
Whatever one’s position on clemency, the episode exposed the difficulty of navigating a deeply divisive national question through presidential authority alone.
The decision now before you could be even more consequential. Do not repeat that experience.
An eminent council for national confidence
There is another way.
Before assigning the mandate, establish a small, temporary council of eminent advisers: two individuals of exceptional national standing acceptable to Netanyahu’s bloc, and two similarly respected figures acceptable to Gadi Eisenkot and the principal opposition parties.
They should not be party operatives or political negotiators, but individuals whose integrity, judgment, and service command respect beyond their affiliations.
They would not select the next prime minister. That constitutional responsibility remains yours. Instead, they would examine competing possibilities, advise on a fair process, and help demonstrate that your decision follows balanced deliberation.
The council must supplement, never replace, the legally required consultations with parliamentary factions. Its role and the principles guiding its work should be explained publicly.
There is a relevant precedent. In the 1990s, an independent committee of eminent persons chaired by former Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker examined dormant Swiss bank accounts linked to Holocaust victims.
Its composition brought together interests divided by profound distrust, establishing a credible investigative process.
The circumstances differed, but the lesson applies: when trust is scarce, respected individuals and credible procedures can help bridge competing interests.
That is interoperability in practice.
The opportunity of a presidency
Israel’s presidency possesses limited executive power but extraordinary symbolic potential. Your greatest contribution may not be the identity of the next prime minister or the survival of the next coalition.
It may be establishing a precedent for public confidence when elections produce uncertainty rather than resolution.
This advisory council would advise the President only during the formal seven-day consultation window, ensuring no appearance of circumventing the statutory faction consultations mandated by the Basic Law.
The council would be a first step toward identifying the minimum common commitments that allow our democracy to survive political disagreement.
Not ideological unity. Not artificial reconciliation. Not abandoning convictions. Rather, accepting that no election should become a referendum on whether the state itself can survive its result.
A government will eventually be formed, or Israel may vote again. Either way, the nation will remain divided.
Mr. President, history rarely offers leaders the opportunity to define their legacy through a single institutional decision. This may be such a moment.
Israel does not need you to make everyone agree. It needs you to help ensure that Israelis can continue to live, compete, and govern together even when they do not.
We are all in the same boat. And its survival must remain more important than who holds the oars.
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn

Sudan civilians face drone strikes and arbitrary arrests: UN

Breadcrumb
Sudan: El Obeid's civilians face RSF drone strikes and arbitrary arrests by army, UN warns
Civilians in the Sudanese city of El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, are facing the threat of drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and an increase in arbitrary arrests by Sudanese army-affiliated forces amid escalating violence in the war-torn country, UN-appointed investigators have warned this week.
In its latest report, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan said that, more than three years after the conflict broke out in April 2023, the war was becoming increasingly widespread and dangerous for civilians.
The latest warnings also highlight deteriorating humanitarian conditions in El Obeid, which had already been identified as being at risk of famine, alongside other parts of Sudan.
"Thousands have been arrested by SAF security cells, detained and tortured in unofficial locations and in El Obeid Central Prison, kept under appalling conditions,” said Mona Rishmawi, an expert member of the UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan.
“These practices must stop immediately.”
Roughly 30% of hospitals in El Obeid are currently functioning following RSF drone attacks, according to the UN report.
It added that the strikes had continued to kill and injure civilians in the city, while also targeting homes, schools, displacement sites, and electricity and water systems.
The report cited a drone attack on a market in Abyei earlier this month, reportedly carried out by forces aligned with the military government, which killed at least 80 people.
The UN also said it would investigate reports of Egyptian airstrikes on goldmining sites near the Sudan-Egypt border, which reportedly killed at least 72 miners.
The UN further highlighted an increase in detentions, with approximately 2,000 people reportedly being held at El Obeid Central Prison.
The report cited a former detainee who said people were being confined in a cell measuring roughly 2.5 metres by 2 metres.
UN investigators have warned that security actors affiliated with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have increased surveillance and are "targeted people engaged in humanitarian, human rights and peace work".
The latest findings come a year after the brutal RSF takeover of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, where more than 10,000 people were reportedly massacred by the paramilitary group over two days after it seized the city in October 2025, following an 18-month siege.
A reported surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas since June has prompted the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of the atrocities in El Fasher.
Joy Ngozi Ezeilo, another expert member of the UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan, has renewed calls to extend the UN arms embargo to cover the whole of Sudan, as it is currently limited to Darfur.
"Sovereignty should not shield mass atrocity crimes, period," Ezeilo said.
"One year after the devastation of El Fasher, civilians in other parts of Sudan continue to pay the price of a conflict that is becoming increasingly destructive and difficult to escape."
She added: "In El Obeid, attacks on electricity networks, water facilities, hospitals, schools and displacement sites demonstrate how damage to critical civilian infrastructure can reverberate through entire communities long after an attack has occurred."
“The passage of time should not diminish attention to what has happened in El Fasher. On the contrary, it should remind us of the cost of impunity.”
Now in its fourth year, Sudan's war began in April 2023, when fighting broke out in Khartoum between the RSF and the Sudanese military before spreading across the country.
The conflict has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, although other aid groups argue that the true death toll is likely to be higher.

На заводе боеприпасов в испанской Гранаде произошёл взрыв. Пострадали несколько работников
Предприятие принадлежит чешской группе CSG и поставляет боеприпасы Украине
На территории завода боеприпасов Fábrica de Municiones de Granada (FMG) на окраине испанской Гранады утром 30 октября произошёл мощный взрыв. Троих работников с лёгкими повреждениями слуха доставили в больницу, сообщила служба экстренной помощи Андалусии 112.
Позднее профсоюз UGT сообщил о пяти пострадавших: по его данным, ещё двое работников получили лёгкие ожоги. Владеющая предприятием чешская оборонная группа CSG привела другую оценку — два человека с лёгкими травмами слуха.
Чтобы не пропустить новые тексты «Вёрстки», подписывайтесь на наш телеграм-канал
Что известно о взрыве
Первый из более чем 30 звонков о сильном взрыве поступил в экстренные службы в 8:57 по местному времени. На место прибыли полиция, пожарные, медики и специалисты по взрывчатке. Повреждений расположенных рядом жилых домов не обнаружили.
По словам представителя CSG Андрея Чиртека, компания задействовала процедуры реагирования на чрезвычайные ситуации, включая эвакуацию сотрудников. Причины происшествия устанавливаются.
Компания и профсоюз описали разные обстоятельства происшествия
CSG заявила, что взрыв произошёл в зоне демилитаризации — на участке для уничтожения старых, повреждённых или непригодных боеприпасов. Он расположен на безопасном расстоянии от производственных объектов и гражданской недвижимости.
По данным компании, производственные мощности не повреждены. CSG не ожидает долгосрочного влияния инцидента на выпуск продукции и сотрудничает с властями при выяснении причин взрыва.
Представитель UGT, в свою очередь, сообщил, что взрыв мог произойти во время проверки качества одного из снарядов. По его словам, участок был огорожен, а сотрудники находились на безопасном расстоянии.
Чтобы не пропустить новые тексты «Вёрстки», подписывайтесь на наш телеграм-канал
Завод поставляет боеприпасы Украине
FMG входит в словацкую MSM Group, принадлежащую чешской CSG. Группа приобрела испанское предприятие у американского владельца в 2020 году — это была её первая инвестиция в Западной Европе.
Завод выпускает танковые и артиллерийские боеприпасы, включая снаряды калибра 155 мм, а также компоненты ракет. После начала полномасштабного российского вторжения он стал одним из поставщиков боеприпасов и ракетных компонентов для Украины, пишет ABC. На фоне войны предприятие значительно расширило производство, хотя прежде обсуждалась возможность его закрытия.
CSG — один из крупных европейских производителей артиллерийских боеприпасов. Помимо Испании и Чехии, группа располагает производственными предприятиями в США, Великобритании, Италии, Германии, Словакии, Сербии и Индии.
Ранее «Вёрстка» рассказывала о пожаре и взрывах на складе боеприпасов компании EMCO под болгарской Трявной. По предварительным данным, огонь перекинулся на склад с автоцистерны. Пострадавших не было. EMCO поставляет Украине вооружения, включая артиллерийские боеприпасы советских стандартов.
