Kosiniak-Kamysz: Poland transfers two MiG-29s to Ukraine after they reach end of their service life
This was announced on Friday during a briefing at the 12th UAV Base in the town of Mirosławiec by Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
According to the Polish official, these two MiG-29s are being decommissioned because they have reached the end of their service life and would therefore no longer be suitable for the Polish military.
“I see all this lamenting and various Russian propaganda being spread by certain political circles. Don’t mourn equipment that will either go to an army defending itself against an aggressor or end up as scrap. If there’s such a choice, then the choice is obvious. Instead, the Polish Army will have unmanned systems,” Kosiniak-Kamysz noted.
He also emphasized that Ukraine has the most experience “among the nations on the side of good” in using drones, and Poland should draw on this experience.
Commenting on the fate of the remaining Polish MiG-29s, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the possibility of selling some of these aircraft is being considered. According to him, Bulgaria has expressed interest in this. This issue was the main topic of discussions with the Bulgarian prime minister and defense minister during their visit to Warsaw in September.
Kosiniak-Kamysz also announced that the first MQ-9B SkyGuardian drone will be delivered to the 12th Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Base in January of next year.
In a comment to Ukrinform, Polish expert and former Polish Minister of National Defense Janusz Onyszkiewicz expressed the view that if an agreement with Sofia cannot be reached, Warsaw may revisit the issue of transferring the remaining MiGs to Ukraine.
On October 29, Poland announced that it would soon transfer two more MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine as part of a new military aid package worth approximately 50 million euros. The package will also include ammunition and air defense systems.

Hezbollah chief declares US-brokered framework agreement 'effectively nonexistent'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:27:56 UTC
02:27:56 KST

Hezbollah chief declares US-brokered framework agreement 'effectively nonexistent'
TEHRAN — Hezbollah Secretary General Sheikh Naim Qassem said in a speech on October 28 that the resistance will keep its weapons for as long as Israel occupies Lebanese land.
There is "no room for discussion" on disarmament while the occupation and aggression continue, he said, declaring the U.S.-brokered framework agreement signed in June "effectively nonexistent."
Addressing the "sacrificing and honorable" people of Lebanon, Sheikh Qassem placed the resistance on legal ground. It acts, he said, under a legitimate right that the Taif Agreement and the constitution protect.
His demand was concrete: an Israeli pullout under the November 27, 2024 ceasefire and UN Security Council Resolution 1701, with the Lebanese army deployed south of the Litani River.
Israel has delivered neither. After the November ceasefire, it kept troops at five positions it deems strategic and went on striking Lebanon almost daily.
Sheikh Qassem sees a pattern older than any of this. He said the resistance exists because of an occupation backed by the world's tyrants, America first among them.
Israel's wars, launched on flimsy pretexts, serve the "Greater Israel" agenda, he said, adding accords such as Madrid and Oslo were stops on the way to the next war.
Without American and Western backing, Israel could neither hold its gains nor expand, and the same backing sustains the genocide in Gaza and the West Bank. Israel quit south Lebanon in 2000 under fire, with no agreement to sign.
A framework with no withdrawal date
Sheikh Qassem said the June 26 text of the framework agreement has no legitimacy because it contradicts the constitution, Taif, the president's inaugural speech and the government's own policy statement.
It gives the enemy what is not his, surrenders sources of Lebanon's strength and feeds on strife, he lamented.
The terms help his case. A "phased" Israeli withdrawal is tied to Hezbollah's verified disarmament, and no date is set. The resistance is supposed to disarm first, and Israel is supposed to leave when it decides it is satisfied.
Four months on, President Joseph Aoun told a visiting German minister Thursday that a ceasefire, Israeli withdrawal, border demarcation and the release of prisoners had still not materialized, a week after trilateral talks at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa.
War Minister Israel Katz said on October 14 that Israeli forces remain in "security zones" in Lebanon and Syria.
Sheikh Qassem wants an end to American tutelage over parts of the Lebanese state. "Tutelage is like occupation," he said, adding, “Both violate sovereignty."
Lebanon's Health Ministry counts 4,389 people killed and 12,424 wounded between March 2 and October 12.
A so-called ceasefire took effect on April 17 and has not stopped the drones. On October 12, Israeli aircraft hit Kfar Tibnit and Tallousah while artillery shelled Beit Lif, Majdal Zoun and Yater.
Even Aoun has said Israel has demolished homes, bulldozed lands and kept farmers out of their fields.
Iran, America and Israel's election
Sheikh Qassem said Hezbollah follows the diplomatic moves between Iran and the U.S. closely.
The Iran-U.S. memorandum in June earned its keep as soon as it was announced, he said, by lowering Israeli aggression on Lebanon.
Iran has placed an end to that aggression and an Israeli withdrawal at the top of its priorities, "a great sacrifice we appreciate" from "the icon of the free people of the world," the Hezbollah chief said.
On Washington, Sheikh Qassem said "tyrannical America" is in no better shape. Iran buried the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Sayyed Ali Khamenei, his family and many commanders, yet frustrated the American and Israeli aim of toppling the government and disintegrating the country, the resistance leader pointed out.
He credited the Iranian people and the leadership of Ayatollah Sayyed Mojtaba Khamenei.
The U.S., by contrast, is mired in erratic decisions and a severe economic crisis, has lost its global standing and is preparing to leave the region, Naim Qassem noted.
Israel's election earned no kinder review. Results from the October 27 vote left Netanyahu's bloc with 53 seats, eight short of a majority, which Sheikh Qassem called "one of the expressions of defeat."
"We do not concern ourselves with who governs the usurping Israeli entity," he said. "But it must know it cannot continue its occupation, and it must leave our land."
Unity, with conditions
At home, Sheikh Qassem renewed Hezbollah's "promise and commitment" pledge to provide shelter, repairs and reconstruction, and to press the state to do its part with help from friendly countries.
He affirmed the bond with the Amal Movement and allied forces, support for the army, rejection of sedition and readiness for dialogue within the constitution. He attached a condition: "actions from others" that prove they mean it.
"The cost of resistance is heavy," he said, "but surrender and concession leave nothing." He closed with the Quranic verse: "Allah will surely support those who support Him."

All seven finalists for the 2027 Car of the Year turned out to be electric cars
Kyiv • UNN
BMW, Cupra, Hyundai, Kia, Renault, Volkswagen and Volvo will compete for the 2027 Car of the Year title. The winner will be announced on January 8.
Today, October 30, leading automotive industry experts announced the seven finalists for the 2027 "Car of the Year" award, which will compete to take the European crown from the Mercedes-Benz CLA, reports UNN.
Electric vehicles are taking over the world
The jury members selected seven cars that will compete for this year's "The Car of the Year" award. They are: the BMW iX3, Cupra Raval, Hyundai Ioniq 3, Kia EV2, Renault Twingo, Volkswagen ID.Polo and Volvo EX60.
The seven finalist models will attempt to impress with their technologies, engineering solutions, dynamic characteristics, equipment and value for money.
The choice for the European automotive industry will not be easy. After electric vehicles won for two years in a row, last year the Mercedes-Benz CLA returned the premium brand to the throne (with both electric and internal combustion engines).
This year has become a historic milestone. All seven cars competing in this final are 100% electric vehicles, in line with the general trend in the European market, which is developing rapidly in this area. The fuel crisis caused by the war in Iran contributed to the growing number of electric vehicle users. This is the first time in the 63-year history of this European award that all finalist models have been electric vehicles.
The first of a new era - BMW iX3 50 xDrive
The spacious exterior and interior of the new BMW iX3 clearly highlight the brand's unmistakable design features and, combined with a modern interior and BMW's characteristic driver-focused approach, create maximum comfort.
With a range of up to 805 km and charging power of 400 kW, the BMW iX3 50 xDrive sets new standards in the fully electric SUV segment. The innovative BMW Panoramic iDrive takes intuitive control and driver orientation to a new level.
Thanks to BMW Heart of Joy and optimized driver assistance systems, a new level of driving pleasure is achieved.
The BMW Panoramic iDrive display and control system combines four central control elements for a unique user experience. Interact intuitively by touch or voice using the intelligent BMW Personal Assistant.
A comprehensive set of sensors, cameras and radar systems continuously monitors the surroundings of the BMW iX3. These technologies detect obstacles and other road users, providing accurate data for the driver assistance systems.
The BMW iX3 is the first car in which powertrain and driving dynamics control have been combined in a single unit - BMW Heart of Joy. The central computer, together with BMW Dynamic Performance Control software, coordinates all relevant processes in a matter of seconds, delivering exceptional dynamics and precision that inspire confidence. The revolutionary Soft Stop function ensures a smooth and safe drive - right through to a complete stop.

Inspired by El Raval - Cupra Raval
In 2026, Cupra, a subsidiary of Seat, presented the pre-production version of its new electric city car – the Cupra Raval. The model demonstrates the brand's further step toward electrification and opens up the Electric Urban Car Family, which Cupra is developing and implementing in cooperation with the Volkswagen Group. The pre-production test drive in Martorell made it possible to assess the model's initial characteristics, dynamics and design concept.

It was precisely this spirit of urban freedom and individuality that became the foundation for the model’s design concept. A New Level of Electric Vehicle Technology - Hyundai IONIQ 3
In April, Hyundai Motor Europe unveiled the IONIQ 3 - a fully electric compact hatchback created to make mobility more intuitive and comfortable for the everyday needs of Europeans.
The IONIQ 3 combines bold design inspired by Hyundai’s "Art of Steel" philosophy, technologies that are simple and convenient to use, and a spacious, comfortable interior. Fulfilling the mission of the IONIQ lineup to lead in advanced electrification, the model was created using a design approach that combines simplicity, precision, and the authenticity of materials.

Its low front end transitions into a distinctive roofline that runs evenly above the front and rear rows of seats before gently descending and integrating organically with the rear spoiler. This geometry maximizes interior space, providing noticeable headroom and enhanced comfort for rear-seat passengers.
The new "Aero Hatch" concept provides a unique balance between aerodynamic efficiency and cabin space, with an expected drag coefficient of 0.263 - one of the best in its class.
Hyundai’s "Art of Steel" design language creates expressive, crisp surfaces complemented by the signature pixel light design and four central dots that reference the letter "H" in Morse code.
Two battery options with a projected WLTP range of 344 km (Standard Range), while the Long Range version is aimed at delivering one of the best figures in its class - up to 496 km.
Fast DC charging from 10% to 80% in approximately 29 minutes, as well as support for AC charging at up to 22 kW.
The cabin offers upper-segment levels of space thanks to its flat floor and the "Furnished Space" interior concept, providing full comfort for five passengers and convenient seating for three adults in the rear row.

The smallest electric crossover with an unusual design - Kia EV2
The Kia EV2 has become the brand’s sixth model based on a purpose-developed electric platform and, as with its older siblings, its styling is, to put it mildly, bold.
Amid a sea of luxury crossovers, the Kia EV2 has boxy proportions and is offered with a GT-Line trim that adds a slightly sportier style from day one. The rear lights, pressed into the lower corners of the body, are an eccentric touch reminiscent of the Chrysler PT Cruiser. Up front, the split vertical headlights look as though they were taken straight from a concept car, helping the electric subcompact stand out immediately in a crowded segment.
Although some exterior details create the impression that the EV2 has come from the future, the interior is not entirely science fiction.
Developed on the E-GMP platform that underpins many Hyundai and Kia electric vehicles, the EV2 is offered with two battery options. The base 42.2 kWh unit provides a WLTP range of up to 317 kilometers, while the larger 61 kWh battery increases this figure to 448 kilometers on a single charge.
The standard-range model produces 144 horsepower, allowing it to accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 8.6 seconds, while the extended-range model sacrifices 10 horsepower and needs 9.5 seconds to reach the same mark. Both versions are electronically limited to 159 km/h. Fast DC charging from 10 to 80 percent takes 29 minutes with the smaller battery and 30 minutes with the larger one.
The return of an icon and a revolution in its segment — Renault Twingo E-Tech Electric
Launched in 1992, the Renault Twingo radically changed the A-segment with its bold new concept for a city car. Fun, bright and modular, the Twingo invited customers to “invent a life that suits it.” At the time, the market offered a wide choice of city cars, and their number grew every year. Today, this segment accounts for less than 5% of the European market.
Contrary to popular belief, the current size of the A-segment does not reflect low demand: drivers across Europe are still looking for compact, affordable cars designed for urban life or as a second car for the family. The problem lies in the limited supply. Faced with the difficulties of combining competitiveness, regulatory compliance and modern customer expectations, most manufacturers have simply abandoned this segment.
Since 1992, the Twingo has established itself as an iconic city car. It was a huge success: more than 4.1 million units sold in 25 countries, winning over several generations thanks to its innovative one-box design, spacious and modular interior, and cheerful character.
The Twingo E-Tech electric was created to achieve three main goals:
-  to make electric mobility more affordable and sustainable: with an
entry price of less than €20,000 (excluding subsidies), the Twingo E-Tech
electric is an affordable and more environmentally friendly solution for European families; 
-  to reduce the vehicle development period to two years:
for the first time in Renault’s history, this achievement became part of a pilot project that
provides valuable experience for the company’s future initiatives; 
-  to maintain a competitive production base in Europe:
assembling the model in Novo Mesto (Slovenia) became possible thanks to optimized
industrial organization and a local supply chain. 
The car is equipped with a 60 kW (82 hp) motor producing 175 N·m of torque, allowing it to accelerate to 130 km/h and deliver a range of up to 263 km.
Much more than just a city car — Volkswagen ID.Polo
The ID. Polo brings Volkswagen’s bestseller into the electric vehicle era. For decades, the Polo has been part of people’s everyday lives. With the ID. Polo, we are making electric mobility accessible to many more people: thanks to its clean and timeless design, intuitive operation, high quality and upper-segment technologies. A true Volkswagen, as our customers expect from us, said Volkswagen AG Board Member Thomas Schäfer during the car’s premiere.
The new Volkswagen ID. Polo features a minimalist design with slim front headlights connected by an LED strip. It is the first production model to fully embody Volkswagen’s new Pure Positive design language.
A narrow light cluster is located at the rear. The new model also features a compact rear diffuser.
The Volkswagen ID. Polo is the second of four entry-level electric vehicles from Volkswagen AG that will use the new MEB+ platform. Volkswagen said that, compared with the internal-combustion-engine model, the new car makes significantly better use of interior space. For example, the rear luggage compartment has a capacity of 441 liters, compared with 351 liters in the Polo. With the rear seats folded, luggage capacity increases to 1,240 liters.
The Volkswagen ID. Polo is available only with a single electric motor on the front axle, producing 116, 135 or 211 hp (85–155 kW). The base versions will be equipped with a lithium iron phosphate battery with a capacity of 37 kWh, while the most powerful version gets a nickel-manganese-cobalt battery with a capacity of 52 kWh. The range will be between 329 and 454 km.
Scandinavian character — Volvo EX60
In January, Volvo Cars officially unveiled the fully electric mid-size EX60 SUV, which is set to be a turning point for the brand and the entire mass-market electric vehicle segment. The five-seat family crossover was designed as a comprehensive response to electric vehicle buyers’ main concerns, combining a long range, ultra-fast charging, a high level of safety and a competitive price.
One of the Volvo EX60’s main advantages is its range of up to 810 kilometers on a single charge in the all-wheel-drive version. This is the best figure in its class, allowing the model not only to outperform other electric Volvos but also to establish a new benchmark for competitors. Even a short stop during a journey is no longer a problem, as the EX60 can add up to 340 kilometers of range in just ten minutes at a 400 kW fast-charging station.
The car is available with several powertrain options. The top-end P12 AWD version offers the longest range and 680 hp, while the P10 AWD and rear-wheel-drive P6 provide a balance between travel range and affordability, producing 510 and 380 "horsepower" and offering ranges of 550 and 560 kilometers, respectively.
In addition, the top-spec EX60 can accelerate to 100 km/h in just 3.8 seconds. All versions come with a 10-year battery warranty, underscoring Volvo’s confidence in its own technologies.
Choosing the winner
Until December 31, jury members will be able to cast their votes by distributing 25 points among the finalists, and must determine the winner in each round of voting, awarding it no more than 10 points. The award will be presented (and announced) on January 8 at the Brussels Motor Show — the same venue where the last three award ceremonies were held.

Source: Lubinets on X (Twitter)
Quote: "I personally continue to coordinate the humanitarian mission. At this stage, those who wished to leave Oleshky have had the opportunity to do so and are now on their way to Ukraine. Humanitarian aid has been delivered. The convoys have split up, and I am now heading back to Ukraine."

Quote: "Our work continues in accordance with the agreements reached with Russia's Human Rights Commissioner, Yana Lantratova, with the support and coordination of US First Lady Melania Trump."
Previously: Under an agreement reached by the Russian and Ukrainian sides, the evacuation route for residents of Oleshky will pass through Russia and Belarus before reaching Ukraine.
Lubinets' office explained why the evacuation is taking place via this specific route.
Background:
- Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced that 527 residents of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast will be returning to Ukraine. He later apologised and clarified that the numbers are still changing and that official information will be available only once the evacuation is over.
- Lubinets announced the start of the ceasefire in the Oleshky area from 03:00 Kyiv time on 27 October. Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed that the ceasefire has been introduced.
- On 23 October, the White House announced that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine in the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky, where a humanitarian disaster is currently unfolding.
- The ceasefire is scheduled to remain in effect until 22:59 on 1 November.

From Yamal to Western Siberia: Ukraine is preparing strikes on the most remote corners of the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy said that Ukrainian long-range strikes can already reach targets from Yamal to Western Siberia. Ukraine is scaling up these capabilities.
Ukraine is working to make its missiles and drones even longer-range and to strike remote areas of Russia in response to attacks by the Russian Armed Forces on Ukrainian cities. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported this on October 30 following a briefing on the results of deep strikes in September–October, UNN reports.
According to him, targets along the line from Yamal to Western Siberia are currently within reach of Ukraine’s long-range strikes.
Details
Ukrainian forces continue to carry out long-range strikes against facilities on the territory of Russia in response to the occupiers’ attacks on Ukrainian cities and communities.
There is always a completely justified response to every Russian strike on our cities and communities. As of today, Russian facilities along the line from Yamal to Western Siberia are within reach of our deep strikes, and we are working to ensure that our drones and missiles can reach even more remote Russian territories
The President noted that, based on the results of the briefing, key areas for the further use of Ukrainian long-range weapons had been identified. In particular, they plan to scale up the units carrying out long-range strikes. This concerns the development of the capabilities of the Security Service of Ukraine, including the "Alpha" Special Operations Center, intelligence structures, and other components of the Defense Forces.
The head of state emphasized that the development of long-range weapons is an important element of ensuring national security both during the full-scale war and after its end.

Taiz governor says city 'didn’t choose war' as supplies dwindle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:21:41 UTC
02:21:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Taiz governor says city 'didn’t choose this war' as supplies dwindle, rubbish fills streets
The governor of Yemen's Taiz province has urged the international community to help reopen supply routes to its besieged capital, Taiz, as litter piles up on streets and essential supplies dwindle.
Speaking to the Sanaa Centre, a Yemeni think tank, on Thursday, Nabil Shamsan described a dire situation, with remaining food and water supplies being distributed at minimum levels, and pregnant women unable to access healthcare facilities.
"Civilians must not be made to pay the price for the [Houthis] militia's recklessness in their failed attempt to storm the city," he said from his office in Taiz, adding, "Their basic needs must not be used as a means of applying pressure or achieving military gains."
Since the war in Yemen reignited in early September with fighting on the Red Sea Coast, Taiz has been one of the focal fronts of the renewed escalation, with the Houthis closing an encirclement of the city in early October.
According to Shamsan, the encirclement placed six of the province's districts, housing two million of Taiz's 4.47 million people, under Houthi control.
The gains, which cut the main supply corridor to the southern city of Aden, have affected access to water, food and fuel, much of which was imported from outside the city's boundaries.
Only 500 cubic metres of the 5,000 cubic metres of water Taiz received per day before the latest escalation is available to those residing in the city. The city is estimated to need 35,000 cubic meters under normal circumstances.
Shamsan said that there is also a deficit of 2,314 tonnes of wheat per day in relation to the city's needs, leading to famine and around 275,000 children suffering from malnutrition.
According to the UN's World Food Programme, the city is experiencing high levels of food insecurity, with 10 out of 16 districts classified at emergency level, or the equivalent of IPC Level 4 of food insecurity.
In addition to food insecurity, the governor added that services were also breaking down, with the city's 12 hospitals and 18 health centres seeing a deterioration of service provision. Cancer patients and pregnant women are unable to obtain treatment, while surrounding districts have seen 120 health centres close and 66 partially close.
The situation has become so dire that some 15 ambulances and 22 intensive care beds have been looted, Shamsan said, with rubbish being dumped on Taiz’s streets as the city lost access to dumps, leading to a spread of disease.
"We call on the United Nations, the Security Council, influential countries and international organisations to take practical action to ensure that roads are open, and that water tankers and supplies can pass without conditions or obstacles," Shamsan said.
"Taiz did not choose this war, nor is it seeking special privileges. It is asking only for its people's right to live in safety, to have access to water, food and medicine, to move freely, and to manage their own affairs within a state that protects everyone."
Accusations of child soldiers as war continues
The governor also accused the Houthis of violations against civilians in the areas newly under their control, including the forcible conscription of child soldiers who have been sent to fight in the northern province of Saada.
He also said that the Houthis were entrenching themselves in civil institutions in newly-controlled areas.
"They have become the people in control and the decision-makers. They decide what can and cannot be done."
"They have taken up residence inside mosques and schools. They have taken control of water projects and everything else. They have left nothing in the districts untouched."
He added that, as part of increasing their mechanisms of control, Houthis have forced tribal leaders to fill out forms that declare they are now supportive of the Houthis.
Taiz is known for having been a bastion of opposition to the Houthis since the war began, as well as being central to the 2011 revolution that toppled longtime president Ali Abdullah Saleh.
"This is not simply a military war; it is a war aimed at changing identity. Taiz will never accept that," Shamsan said.
The New Arab was unable to verify the claims made by the governor.
Taiz has been a frontline city since the war erupted in 2014 when Houthis took over the capital of Yemen, Sanaa, having been placed under a complete siege in 2015, and later a partial siege.
According to the governor, the Houthis have mobilised 60,000 fighters in their campaign to take over the city, which has seen residential buildings shelled and ongoing fighting in the areas of Saber, al-Mawadem, Mashra'a and Hadnan.
The Houthi offensive on Taiz, though managing to encircle the city, has slowed following an uptick in Saudi airstrikes aimed at supporting government forces in the pocket.
Those airstrikes have also killed Yemeni civilians, with the Houthi health ministry reporting that Saudi airstrikes killed at least 13 people in Taiz on Thursday.
Shamsan said that some 271 people have been killed and 1,129 injured in fighting around Taiz since the start of the Houthi offensive.
Alongside the death toll, which the World Health Organisation records as 1,677 killed and 7,395 wounded, hundreds of thousands have been displaced, mostly from Taiz province.

====================================================================================================

‘Paleo lighting’ can fix your brain’s clock after daylight savings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:16:00 UTC
02:16:00 KST

At 2 A.M. on November 1, the clocks will fall back, and for one weekend out of the year, the whole country will think about light and time. Most people will spend the extra hour asleep and the following week complaining that it’s nearly dark at 5 P.M. Regardless of how you feel about the time change, for the next four months the sun will rise in the sky closer to the time you do. That alignment is the best thing that could happen to your body clock—and your sleep—all year.
Of course, you can try to buy your way into a better night’s sleep right now: mouth tape, tablets of magnesium glycinate, blackout curtains, a wearable sensor that grades your sleep, a mattress that maintains a chill 62-degree-Fahrenheit temperature. The stack of such approaches can run into the thousands of dollars and has a name on social media—“sleep maxxing.” It’s the wellness market’s latest way of turning a basic human function into a product line.
But the two things that will do the most for your sleep cost nothing. That is because nobody has figured out how to package them.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
I’m talking about light: bright days, dark nights. Think of it as a return to nature. Call it Paleo lighting.
I shamelessly borrowed the term from the “Paleo diet,” which sold the premise that human physiology took shape under conditions that no longer exist and that the mismatch costs us something. We built an industry around what goes into our mouths. We left the eyes alone. Our ancestors could not dim the day, postpone the night, or order light at midnight. That is not an argument for candlelight or for unplugging the grid. It is the same dietary logic aimed at the organ that sets our internal clock.
This clock sits at the base of the brain, about 40,000 nerve cells in a structure called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus, and it generally runs slightly long. Shut a person in a laboratory with no windows and no clocks, and typically the body settles into a day of roughly 24 hours and 12 minutes.
Light early in the morning is what pulls the clock back in line with the sun. Bright light at night does the opposite, telling it the day isn’t finished. And the clock in your head is not the only clock you own. Your liver, pancreas and immune cells all run on their own daily schedules, taking their cues from that cluster of cells in the hypothalamus linked to the sun. When the SCN loses alignment with the sun, these rhythms drift apart and optimal functioning may be lost.
The disruption to our circadian rhythms comes at a physiological price. Light at the wrong hour can suppress melatonin, the hormone that tells your body it is night. And from there, the effects may spread to digestion, heart rate and the timing of metabolic and immune programs evolved to run on a 24-hour schedule. How far that reach extends is still being mapped. The clearest view comes from animals, for which you can hold everything else steady and change only the light.
In my laboratory, we have kept mice at night with lights set to five lux, roughly the brightness of a night-light in a kid’s bedroom. They gained more weight than mice sleeping in genuine darkness. They were not sleep-deprived; the night-light just disrupted their clock-gene rhythms, subsequently shifting their food intake to the wrong part of the day. In the case of nocturnal mice, they shifted their food intake from night to daytime. Because they generally sleep during the day, light at night can scramble their circadian timing without touching their sleep or rest time. Related work found the same dim night worsened weight gain, glucose control and inflammation in animals on a high-fat diet. Sleep, metabolism and immunity seem to act as gears in a clock: if there’s one misalignment, the whole system is disrupted.
The obvious objection is fair: these are mice, they are nocturnal, they live in cages, and nobody has ever asked one how it slept. What happens when you run the experiment on people?
Researchers at Northwestern University put healthy young adults to bed for a single night in a room lit to 100 lux—dimmer than a well-lit kitchen, brighter than a night-light—and measured them in the morning. Their heart rates ran higher through the night. And by breakfast, they were measurably worse at handling sugar, assessed by increasing insulin resistance, than another group that slept in the dark.
That was one night in a laboratory, with 20 participants. “What happens over years in ordinary bedrooms?” is the harder question, and the best answer we have comes from 43,722 women, none of them shift workers, who were tracked for about five years. Those who slept with a television or a light on in the room were 17 percent more likely to gain 11 pounds or more and 33 percent more likely to develop obesity over that time, after researchers accounted for diet, exercise and sleep duration. Night-shift workers, who experience the extreme case of circadian rhythm disruption, carry higher rates of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, mood disorders and several cancers—though people who live that far out of phase with the sun differ from non-shift workers in many ways besides light.
The prescription costs almost nothing. Within an hour of waking, get outside for 10 to 30 minutes in whatever the sky is offering—an overcast morning outdoors still runs to thousands of lux; a well-lit kitchen only manages a few hundred. Sit near a window if you have one. In one small study, office workers with windows got far more daytime light than colleagues without them and slept the better part of an hour longer at night. When indoors in the evening, dim the lights and use warm light bulbs rather than overhead and blue lighting.
Then deal with the bedroom, which is the part everyone skips. Stand in yours tonight with the lights off and count what still glows: the router, the smoke detector, the charger, the standby light on the television, the sliver where the curtains refuse to meet.
Nobody is ever going to sell you a dark night. You will have to make it on your own.

Trump’s falling popularity hangs over a midterm vote shaped by Iran war, inflation
TEHRAN — Donald Trump is not on the ballot, yet the election is about little else. On November 3, roughly 210 million registered voters will decide all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships.
Their verdict on the war on Iran, inflation and the campaign his party has run will determine how much power Trump keeps for the last two years of his term.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on October 26 put Trump’s approval at 32 percent, one point above the record low set a week earlier. Registered voters preferred Democrats on the congressional ballot, 47 percent to 36 percent. Counting undecided voters who lean toward a party, the gap is 50 to 41.
History offers Republicans little comfort. Since 1946, the president’s party has lost an average of 26.5 House seats in midterms. No president has entered midterm election so unpopular since Harry Truman, and Trump sits nearly 10 points below where he stood in 2018, when Republicans still held onto several Senate seats in friendly territory.
Democrats need a net gain of three seats for the House. The Senate is a steeper climb. Republicans hold 53 seats, Democrats and their two independent allies hold 47, and a 50-50 split would still favor Republicans because Vice President JD Vance breaks ties. Democrats need four seats, and many of the contests lie in states Trump won comfortably two years ago.
The price problem
Prices are the one issue Trump promised to fix. In 2024 he vowed to “rapidly bring down costs.” Since then, they have outrun wages, and households feel it in gasoline, groceries, insurance premiums, rent, mortgages and credit-card balances.
The White House answers with “growth” figures. Output rose at a 3.4 percent annual rate over the summer, and consumer spending climbed 3.8 percent in the third quarter. Voters are unmoved.
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett has called worries about affordability a “myth,” and Trump has called the issue a “hoax.” At a rally in Lubbock, he insisted prices had fallen while signs in the crowd demanded “LOWER PRICES.”
Gasoline costs more than $1 a gallon above its level on the day Trump returned to office, according to AAA. Tariffs, tax cuts that pushed the federal debt past $40 trillion, and cuts to food and health benefits have added to the strain.
The war on Iran added more. The blockade and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz lifted oil prices and, with them, the cost of farming, trucking, heating and shipping. About 73 percent of Americans say they are extremely or very concerned about fuel prices driven by the war.
The Iran war quagmire
Nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose U.S. involvement in the war on Iran, and the aggressive campaign has split both parties. The fighting has hardened into an open-ended confrontation with no political settlement in sight.
At least 21 U.S. service members have died and more than 800 have been wounded. Iranian missiles and drones have damaged American bases, including Al Udeid in Qatar. Even so, the Pentagon blocked Senator Chris Murphy from visiting the base on a fact-finding trip.
“War” Secretary Pete Hegseth, who helped lead the campaign, has run the department with secrecy, purges of senior officers and open hostility toward Congress.
Democrats are preparing to answer in kind. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has promised to “run Pete Hegseth out of town” if his party wins the House.
A Politico poll found 63 percent of Democratic midterm voters support impeaching him, and Republican Representative Thomas Massie has already filed eight articles accusing Hegseth of plotting an illegal war and obstructing oversight.
Conviction in the Senate is unlikely. Hearings would still put the legal and human cost of a war Trump never asked Congress to authorize on the public record.
Campaigning on fear
Candidates who cannot run on prices or the war have found another subject. In Michigan, Trump and his allies have turned the Senate race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed into a sustained attack on Muslims.
Trump has mocked El-Sayed’s name, called him a “jihadist” and suggested he should pass through a metal detector before entering the Capitol. Republican nominee Mike Rogers has baselessly tied him to Hamas, Hezbollah, Iran and the Muslim Brotherhood.
The rhetoric has gone mainstream within the GOP. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claimed “Arabs do not produce literature or science and do not win Nobel Prizes.” Senator Ted Cruz called El-Sayed a “jihadist leprechaun.”
Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud says his city receives daily threats, and Muslim advocates describe a climate worse than the weeks after September 11.
Ohio supplied a different kind of ugliness. Vivek Ramaswamy promoted an advertisement featuring the estranged birth mother of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, using her childhood abuse and homelessness to suggest instability.
Republican Governor Mike DeWine asked for it to come down. Trump and Vance defended it. Campaigning in the Midwest, Barack Obama called the approach “cruelty” and “indecency.”
Billionaires bankrolling
Money is meant to do the work persuasion cannot. Elon Musk has given more than $445 million to federal political committees this cycle, the largest disclosed donation total in modern midterm history.
He put $77 million into America PAC in the first half of October and $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund in September, aimed at the Senate seats Republicans must hold.
He has company. Public Citizen reports that 515 donors giving at least $1 million have supplied $4.2 billion to super PACs in 2026, with Musk alone responsible for about 10 percent. Trump-aligned committees and Republican congressional super PACs raised $2.1 billion through the third quarter, against $1.3 billion for Democratic groups.
Spending on that scale reads as an attempt to buy protection, taken out on an unpopular president, an unpopular war and a message built on scapegoats.
After November comes the fight over inheritance. Who will carry a failing GOP?

Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:13:48 UTC
02:13:48 KST

People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.
The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.
The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.
The localised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region allowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.
While Ukrainian territory lies just 3 miles (5km) from Oleshky, evacuees will need to travel to the southern Russian city of Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.
Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to Anapa.
“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he said.
Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post: “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky.” Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.
While earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled in the convoy.
Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.
Asked if she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a woman who identified herself as “Anna” was shown on video saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”
Oleshky’s population has declined to about 2,000 since the star of the war, according to authorities and volunteers, and many of those who stayed have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.
Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.
“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in a report broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”
Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.
“They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press. “They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added.
The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides.
On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement.
Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023.
“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.
“I’ve been told that it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”
He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for such a significant duration.”

Bukele secures Trump’s green light for Salvadoran troop deployment to Haiti: reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:13:26 UTC
02:13:26 KST

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele secured US President Donald Trump’s approval before proceeding with a major military deployment to Haiti, where up to 2,000 Salvadoran troops are expected to help combat powerful armed gangs, Axios reported on Friday.
Bukele called Trump on Tuesday to ensure Washington would not oppose the operation, which has received approval from the Haitian government, according to the report.
“Do what you have to do,” Trump reportedly told Bukele, while also expressing sympathy over four Salvadoran military personnel who went missing following an ambush in Haiti.
The Salvadoran leader had previously proposed that his country take charge of efforts to pacify Haiti, effectively acting as a US-backed force.
However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly opposed the proposal, preferring to keep Washington at a distance.
US declines requests for military equipment
According to Axios, Bukele also asked Washington to provide military equipment, including drones and transport aircraft, but the requests were rejected.
Colombia could potentially act as an unofficial channel for supplying equipment, allowing the operation to move forward without direct US involvement, the report said.
El Salvador announced on Wednesday that it would send up to 2,000 troops to Haiti, with the possibility of increasing the deployment.
Bukele defended the mission in a post on X on Thursday, saying his country was not seeking financial gain from the operation.
“We didn't come to Haiti to make money, because no one is paying us to do it. We came to Haiti to fight against the wicked,” he wrote.
Haiti grapples with escalating gang violence
Haiti has struggled for years to contain heavily armed gangs, which control large areas of the country and have undermined security, displaced communities and disrupted access to essential services.
More than 5,700 people have been killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, according to the figures cited in the report.
The proposed Salvadoran deployment comes as Haitian authorities seek international support to restore security and strengthen efforts against armed groups.
The operation would mark a significant expansion of El Salvador's role in international security efforts beyond its borders.

Italian Ambassador Luca Franchetti Pardo visited Kielce today with the aim of strengthening ties between this city and the region and Sistema Italia. The dialogue with Italian companies and Polish stakeholders linked to Italy provided an opportunity to explore their activities and prospects for collaboration in greater depth. The potential of Expo Kielce as a meeting point for Italian and Polish companies was also highlighted.

Oleshky: No access to basic needs, ceasefire offers limited opportunity for humanitarian assistance
Issued on:

Catherine Viette is pleased to welcome Jens Schumacher, Field Coordinator in Mykolaiv and Kherson with Solidarity International. Just a few kilometers separate the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson from Russian-occupied Oleshky. For civilians caught between military occupation, disrupted essential services and uncertain evacuation arrangements, geographical proximity offers little guarantee of access to life-saving assistance. Schumacher examines the humanitarian implications of a temporary ceasefire around Oleshky, where approximately 2,000 civilians were reported to remain. Although the cessation of attacks has created a limited opportunity for humanitarian operations, the geographical scope of the agreement, the prospects for evacuation and the possibility of sustained humanitarian access remain uncertain.

This budget fails to live up to Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric | Letters

Aditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget (Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October). It was a drop in the ocean of what is needed to bring about the scale of change this country needs and, importantly, was promised by Andy Burnham.
As the affordability crisis rages on, people may feel some relief at the small cost of living measures announced for households and businesses. But when we’ve been told we’ll get a wholesale reset and an end to neoliberalism, 4p off the price of gherkins and a temporary tiny bank tax isn’t going to cut it.
So, what’s the solution? The government must fairly tax the vast fortunes of the richest people and corporations, left mostly untouched. Recouping the massive wealth and profits siphoned off to shady tax havens each year, equalising how the tax system treats income from wealth and work, and building HMRC’s capacity to properly measure and collect tax from the very richest would raise tens of billions to help pay for targeted, meaningful cost of living support and Burnham’s ambitious plans to fix the housing crisis, fund social care and devolve power and wealth to every region.
Reforming capital gains tax – a proposal supported by members of his own party – would make things fairer and raise around £19.7bn a year, enough to build 90,000 new council homes (the number needed each year to end the housing crisis) and train 128,000 new NHS nurses.
This government cannot survive much longer on vibes alone, and Labour is already on its last chance. Burnham must use his 10-year plan and spending review to lay out a proper roadmap to genuinely improve lives and transform the country, otherwise he risks being remembered for gherkins, which isn’t much better than Liz Truss’s lettuce.

Saudi Arabia suspends travel, entry from Kenya over Ebola concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:10:54 UTC
02:10:54 KST

Saudi Arabia on Friday announced additional precautionary measures against the Ebola virus, including suspending travel to and entry from Kenya, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
The measures, introduced following an assessment of the epidemiological situation by health authorities, include suspending travel by Saudi citizens to Kenya and halting the issuance of all types of visas to travelers from the East African country.
The kingdom will also prohibit entry to travelers arriving from Kenya, including those traveling through third countries who have stayed in Kenya or other Ebola-affected countries during the 21 days preceding their arrival.
The restrictions are part of preventive measures introduced in 2019 and strengthened this May for travelers arriving from countries facing Ebola outbreak risks, SPA reported.
This June, Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and entry from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan.
The kingdom also strengthened preventive measures for arrivals from countries neighboring Ebola-affected areas, including screening at entry points, epidemiological investigations, and early health response mechanisms.
The Saudi Public Health Authority, known as Weqaya, said the country’s public health situation remains reassuring and under continuous monitoring.
It added that authorities are closely following epidemiological developments regionally and internationally and coordinating with relevant agencies to implement preventive measures as necessary.
Ebola is a severe viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of infected people. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.

This is a wonderful campaign by Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow to ban the use of school uniform in pornography (We’re teenage girls fighting to ban the use of school uniform in porn. Why have you left it up to us?, 23 October).
Perhaps it could be followed by another to ban school uniforms altogether. The reasons for having them are specious and outdated. There is an idea that it makes class differences invisible. As someone who wore a visibly secondhand and well-worn uniform at school and was the butt of much teasing, I know it does no such thing.
There is another idea that they are worn as a badge of honour and indicate pride in being part of a community. On the contrary, some children have to wear home clothes on the way to and from school to avoid being bullied on the bus or the street because of their uniform.
Most schools in Europe do not make uniform a part of school life – they should be banned. This would also undermine the pornography industry’s fixation with school uniforms, thus killing two birds with one stone.

As a not-so-little feminist and former schoolgirl decades ago, it struck me how we just took it for granted that we would be catcalled in our uniforms. Pedestrianisation won’t save Oxford Street | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:10:19 UTC
02:10:19 KST

The real causes of the problems seen in Oxford Street (The long read, 22 October) are high rents, the chaotic system of business rates and the replacement of many smaller footprints with larger ones; these are the main factors that have made the street less viable. The large flagship shops depend on being surrounded by good-quality small businesses to attract customers.
Much of what the mayor of London is doing here is a de facto part-privatisation – stopping up a very important public highway for a large number of users of “unwelcome” modes of transport, to benefit private landowners.
Rather than buses being a main culprit here, it is much more likely that the gradual downgrading of bus services along Oxford Street has contributed significantly to its decline.
The strategic mistake of routing Crossrail along Oxford Street – long after this plan lost its part-justification (dating from when it was conceived decades ago) of stimulating the West End – has caused the dangerously high footfall levels that have become a main motivation for pedestrianisation.
The Crossrail route should have been changed to connect Heathrow and Stratford through centres in south London, but we have to live with it now. There is a natural limit to how much footfall is beneficial for urban centres, and disadvantaging everyone who doesn’t want to get there by underground railway isn’t going to change this.
The factors at play that have weakened Oxford Street are not unique to it, and none of them will be affected by these actions from the mayor of London, who is largely powerless to address them without central government taking corrective action.
 
Oliver Schick
 
London
 I like to see Sadiq Khan contributing to the Guardian, but on this occasion I have to quibble with his description of Oxford Street as “our nation’s high street” (We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too, 26 October). I live on the border of Wales, and whether a street in London is pedestrianised or not is entirely irrelevant to me. It’s not my high street and never will be.
 
Iain Nelson
 
Selattyn, Shropshire
 Credit where credit is due. Contrary to accusations at the time that businesses had suffered, footfall on Oxford Street actually increased by 13.5% as visitors were drawn to the utopia that was Extinction Rebellion’s blockade in April 2019 – a harbinger, in microcosm, of what a greener, less polluted world might look like.
 
Tom Hardy

Pope Leo XIV Votes in US Elections: First Time for a Pontiff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:10:15 UTC
02:10:15 KST

Pope Leo XIV, who has repeatedly clashed with US President Donald Trump over immigration and the war in Iran, has cast his ballot in the US midterm elections by mail – officially becoming the first pontiff to do so.
Describing the vote as an expression of his belief in “the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” the pontiff submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago, according to Vatican News on Friday, Oct. 30.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I have no fear of the Trump administration or speaking out loudly of the message of the Gospel,” the pontiff said during his papal flight to Algeria earlier in April.
Before becoming pope, Robert Francis Prevost had voted in every election for which he was eligible, including those during his years living in Peru. Friday’s vote continues that long-standing practice, the Vatican said.
The vote comes two weeks after the first American pope personally intervened over Russian-occupied Oleshky. In two separate telephone discussions, he urged Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky to agree to a humanitarian ceasefire for the town.
The evacuation of Oleshky’s residents began earlier on Friday, marking the first humanitarian operation of such scale since Russian forces occupied it in February, 2022.
Long-standing disputes with Trump
Since being elected pope in May 2025, the pontiff has repeatedly found himself at odds with the Trump administration, particularly over immigration enforcement, the US-Israeli war with Iran and Venezuela.
Dnipro Station Hit Again as Russian Strikes Spark Fire
He has been a long-standing, outspoken critic of mass deportations and family separations, and has even warned against the risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI).
Tensions with Trump, however, peaked in April, when the pontiff called for peace following strikes on Iran. “I don’t think he’s doing a very good job,” Trump said about Pope Leo XIV at the time, BBC reported, adding that he is “not a big fan” of him.
Trump also drew criticism for sharing an AI-generated image of himself as Jesus, which he later deleted, the CST reported.
A registered Illinois voter
The pope remains registered to vote at an address in New Lenox, Kim Fladhammer, Will County’s clerk office chief of staff, told the Chicago Sun-Times.
According to county records, Prevost voted in Democratic primaries in 2008 and 2010 and in Republican primaries in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
He also voted in general elections of 2012, 2014, 2018 and 2024, but did not vote in this year’s March primary.
The elections will be held on Tuesday, Nov. 3, to elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats and governors in 36 states.
The 71-year-old pope, who grew up in the Chicago suburb of Dolton, returned to the Vatican on Oct. 18 following surgery to remove part of his right lung due to cancer.
He has since gradually resumed his public duties, and the Vatican confirmed he is planning to travel to Peru, Argentina and Uruguay in early November.
Diesel deal ahead of the vote
The elections come as Trump faces severe pressure over record-high diesel prices, for which he has previously blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries instead of US-Israeli war on Iran.
On Oct. 9, Trump struck an abrupt diesel deal with Putin, after which the US Treasury authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
During the same time, a Ukrainian delegation was in Miami holding negotiations with Trump’s administration, hoping to reach a breakthrough in Russia’s war.
The following day, Trump blamed Zelensky for high fuel prices again, criticizing Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries and saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The deal has drawn criticism from both Washington and Kyiv, as well as from European leaders.
Meanwhile, the Russian Direct Investment Fund, which helped arrange the diesel shipments, is now seeking the removal of US sanctions against it, The New York Times reported.

Re Emily Bratt’s suggestion that schoolchildren should help with “caring” for their school, when I was at Dartington Hall – a progressive co-educational boarding school – in the 1960s we did what was called “useful work” before classes. It involved us in the processes of running the school. Among other things, I tidied the library, thus learning the Dewey classification system; was printer’s devil to the bookbinder, Eric McNally, producing play programmes and the school prospectus; spent two terms in my O-level year setting up chemistry lab equipment for A-level classes; and was filing clerk for the careers advice department.
Responsibility was a key word at Dartington, it being well understood that freedom is not free – it comes at a price – and that consideration for others and support for the community are essential.

The Greatest Is a Biographical Drama That Understands Why Muhammad Ali Became a Legend

“What do you think it is about Cassius that makes him able to do things that other men find impossible?” Malcolm X (Michael Ealy) asks Muhammad Ali’s stalwart trainer, Angelo Dundee (Giovanni Ribisi), in Prime Video’s stylistically conventional yet unusually insightful The Greatest. “What spark inside him makes him so different from other people?”
These questions fuel the series, streaming in full on Nov. 4, which finds in the relative newcomer Jaalen Best an ideal young Cassius Clay, a bold boxing phenom on a quest to become the heavyweight champion of the world—and a spiritual journey that will change both his faith and his name. There are reasons to be skeptical of this show. It counts his widow, Lonnie Ali, among its executive producers. (Michael B. Jordan, who played the Ali-esque title character in the Creed movies, is another.) Such projects can default to hagiography. And Ali has already been portrayed many times on screen. But creator Ben Watkins (Cross) doesn’t dodge the tougher aspects of his subject’s life. What justifies this retelling is not only the care he and Best take in recounting what Ali achieved, but also conveying what made him capable of greatness.
The Greatest is bookended by career highlights: the 1960 Rome Olympics, where Ali won gold at 18, and his first heavyweight championship in 1964. That fight, against Sonny Liston, must be his most extensively documented moment. Michael Mann opened his 2001 biopic Ali, starring Will Smith, with an immersive restaging of the match. Regina King’s 2020 film One Night in Miami imagines its afterparty, a meeting of the minds between Eli Goree’s Ali, Malcolm X, Jim Brown, and Sam Cooke. In ending where these predecessors begin, the series traces how the upstart Cassius Clay crafted Muhammad Ali, the legend.
Best’s Ali reads as a significantly younger man than the versions in Mann’s and King’s movies. Instead of detracting from his astonishing self-possession, Cassius’ fresh face makes those qualities seem more remarkable. Upon his return from Italy, where he enjoyed a relative reprieve from anti-Black racism, to his segregated hometown of Louisville, Ky., he is again a teenager in his parents’ humble household. He has a mutually adoring bond with his mother, Odessa (Dana Gourrier, excellent), a domestic servant who wants nothing fancier than to give her children a better life. His father, Cash (Omari Hardwick), had dreams of becoming a great artist but settled for painting signs and drowning his disappointment in alcohol and women. Cassius’ younger brother Rudy (Kai Parham) is also a boxer. But any rivalry is outweighed by Rudy’s sincere wish to help a sibling he recognizes as a generational talent.
An 18-year-old rocketing to the top of a lucrative sport is sure to meet many people eager to buy stock in his future. Especially if he is Black and working-class, he’ll be treated as though he owes them something. As he prepares to go pro, Cassius is swarmed by this type. “I knew you had the skill,” one tells the gold medalist. “Wasn’t sure you had the work ethic.” The prejudice underlying this comment would be obvious even if we didn’t see Cassius exhaust himself in training sessions. But he knows he deserves respect, and he refuses to work with anyone, Black or white, who tries to humble him. This can look like arrogance, but it’s also an accurate self-assessment. As Angelo puts it: “You don’t teach Michelangelo how to paint.”
How does a person as systemically disadvantaged as Cassius come to believe so fervently in himself? Watkins offers three compelling explanations, all implied through his behavior rather than overstated via exposition. One is the strength of his will—his innate ability to tune out skeptics and distractions. Another is his mother and brother’s unwavering love, which counteracts the hatred he experiences. Finally, in rare instances when his poise wavers, he can fall back on the rhyming, boasting showmanship he gleans from the flamboyant pro wrestling heel Gorgeous George (WWE alum Chris Jericho, in an apt cameo).
Cassius’ singular personality is thrown into relief by Sonny (Amin Joseph), who is depicted as his antithesis in life as in the ring. An ex-con and abuse survivor, he has internalized every monstrous caricature of Black manhood Cassius actively resists. Even as the champ, with the love and guidance of a canny wife (Erica Tazel), he’s poisoned by self-hatred. Ultimately, he behaves like the beast a racist press makes him out to be. Watkins lets us sit in discomfort, watching Cassius use the same stereotypes (“big, ugly bear”) to taunt Sonny.
The Greatest rarely deviates from the bio-drama template, with its archetypal hero’s journey. But the approach suits this story of a man figuring out who he is and what he values through a noble quest. It’s when the show tries to loosen up, as in boxing montages scored to energetic hip-hop that feel like Gatorade ads, that it rings false. It occasionally struggles to balance complex truths. On the Nation of Islam, it makes clear-eyed distinctions between Malcolm X, framed as a true mentor to Cassius, and the tactics of polarizing Nation leader Elijah Muhammad (Hill Harper). Yet in illustrating why Cassius chooses the Nation’s militance over turn-the-other-cheek Christianity, hurting his mother in the process, it minimizes the Black church’s centrality to the civil rights struggle.
Even so, as it distinguishes Malcolm from Elijah, Odessa from Cash, Angelo from a legion of white guys with dollar-sign eyes, and most of all Cassius from Sonny, The Greatest builds a strong case for integrity as the key ingredient of greatness. A hero of Ali’s magnitude doesn’t just embody that virtue. He demands it from the people who surround him.

Breadcrumb
Pope Leo makes history with US midterm vote
Pope Leo XIV, the Catholic Church's first US-born pontiff, has voted in the United States midterm elections, the first known time a pope has voted in a political election.
The head of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, who has clashed with US President Donald Trump, submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago, the Vatican said Friday.
The Chicago-born pontiff "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so" and believes in "the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," it said.
A rift earlier this year between US President Donald Trump and the pope sparked global headlines.
Leo and Trump repeatedly clashed over papal criticism of the harsh crackdown on immigration in the United States and of the war on Iran, with Trump calling the pontiff "weak" on crime and "terrible" on foreign policy.
The pope said he was "not afraid" of Trump.
In April, after Trump's threat to destroy Iran, Leo called on everyone to do their part for peace, urging them to "contact the authorities - political leaders, congressmen - to ask them, to tell them, to work for peace and to reject war and violence."
The crucial US midterm elections are scheduled to be held on 3 November.
In September, Leo urged the faithful to shake off "all passivity and indifference" toward current events.
"We cannot remain as unengaged spectators; rather, we must listen with our hearts, allow ourselves to be challenged, and become involved," he said during the weekly general audience in St Peter's Square.
Robert Francis Prevost, as he was known before his papal election, voted in Democratic primaries in 2008 and 2010 and in three Republican primaries in the years that followed, according to the New York Times, citing state and local records.
In primary elections in Illinois, voters may choose any party's ballot at the polls, and Prevost varied in his selection, it said.
Prevost spent nearly two decades as a missionary in Peru and has both US and Peruvian citizenship.
"The Holy Father has also confirmed that, during his years of residence in Peru he exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so," the Vatican said.

Am I too old to have best friends?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:02:37 UTC
02:02:37 KST

Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at best friends.
I flew to America last week.
I packed a travel bag full of books, articles, and intellectual fodder to gorge myself on. Which was either aspirational or hopelessly naive, depending on how you look at it. I spent the entire flight messaging people, staring absently at clouds, and watching Deadpool & Wolverine.
I was flying to America to meet some friends. Now, I might still be jet-lagged and deliriously sleep-deprived, but I hope you will forgive me a moment of sentimentality. Because I would say that these friends have very quickly become some of my best friends. If I had my way, I’d see them every week. But in the meantime, I’ll have to settle for the occasional transatlantic jaunt.
I’m limping my way into middle age. I’ve more salt than pepper in my beard, and my forehead is a crinkly mesh. I’m too old to have “best friends.” You have best friends when you’re ten years old. You swap notes, play video games, and giggle over sexual innuendos. As it happens, I still do all those things. So, what does a best friend look like to me?
Well, of course there’s no one simple thing. I trust these friends totally. I think each of them embodies certain characteristics I want to develop in myself. I love them and have told them so. But one thing I want to examine today is something overlooked but oh so important. It’s overlooked because we often take it for granted: You have to enjoy being around your best friends.
So, this week we look at the philosophy of best friends.
Go well,
Jonny
We were sitting around a table, playing the guitar.
I’m not especially good at the guitar. I can shuffle my way around something that sounds a bit like the twelve-bar blues, but my friend is one of those people who can hold a coherent conversation while absently plucking something straight out of a recording studio. I was shuffling, he was riffing, his wife was singing. It sounded okay, but, more importantly, it felt good.
There’s an ancient need in all humans to both make music and participate with one another. Chanting, drumming, dancing, and playing the blues are primal. Music is nice in itself, of course, but playing music with someone is a different kind of nice.
Because there are sounds and songs you can never play on your own. There are things in life you need others for. In philosophy, an “emergent property” is something that emerges only when you put various parts together. A traffic jam made up of cars. Birds swooping in hundred-winged union. And the music you get from “jamming” or “just playing” is a kind of emergent property. Join a choir, join a band, sing around the campfire after a few too many beers. You’ll feel it.
The best kinds of friendships are emergent properties. Yes, there’s a form of therapy that involves “making friends with yourself,” but friendship is usually seen as an interaction between different people. You are who you are, I am who I am, and we’ll whip up a jazzy infusion. This is what some psychologists call an “ecosystemic” relationship — where all members not only take a place within the whole but are conscious of being part of the whole.
The opposite of an ecosystemic friendship is an “egosystemic” one. This is where everyone fixates on themselves. They stay in their own heads, obsessed with their own thoughts, and see “listening” only as a necessary pause before they can talk about what they want. An egosystemic friend is like a guitarist who changes tune in the middle of a song. It’s the chorister who refuses to read the sheet. It’s the drum soloist who won’t stop drumming. An egosystemic table is really just a collection of discrete individuals who happen to be near each other. I wouldn’t be so categorical as to say these aren’t friendships. I follow Aristotle on this and think there are a few kinds of friendships — some better, some worse. And ecosystemic friendships are the best kind.
One good way to identify an ecosystemic friendship is by listening to what it sounds like. Because when you’re sitting around the table with your best friends, the conversation often flows. It adapts to what one person says and picks up the same rhythm. You listen, and you reply. You offer a bit of yourself, and you nudge the conversation somewhere else. Another friend picks up that nudge and joins in. It could be funny, sentimental, or philosophical, but the point is that the conversation plays with the swinging joy of a jazz band lost in the jam. Hi-hats tapping, trumpets blaring, and the bass thumping. On and on in a sweaty, joyous euphoria.
Best friendships are ecosystemic, and they are rare because they require two things:
First, a basic degree of empathy and other-regardingness. Ecosystemic friendships need you to attend to another person. They take your partner’s step and dance with it. Second, they require that far more elusive je ne sais quoi we often call “being on the same wavelength.” When one person finishes a thought, someone else knows where to take it. It’s not quite finishing each other’s sentences, but it’s the feeling of union that explains why best friendships often feel so relaxed. So familiar. Because for the briefest of moments around a table, your thoughts are dancing together.
Of course, this goes beyond just nattering around a table for a few hours with a guitar, and an ecosystemic relationship will look different to each of us. It might be a breathless, cackling back-and-forth in the pub. It might be a slower, contemplative unearthing of the soul. It might be years or decades of mutual support. “They’ve always been there for me.” But in each case, best friends reach beyond the self-concerned parameters of their own minds to engage with someone else.
In an ecosystemic relationship, all members care for each other, and each feels cared for. This is why the members of an ecosystemic group work hard to nurture the friendship itself. The ecosystemic friendship is treated as a thing — an identifiable emergent property.
“I like jamming; let’s keep doing it. I love not only you, but this relationship. I will protect it.”
As I touch on in this week’s Mini Philosophy column, this je ne sais quoi factor of clicking with someone isn’t necessarily common. We need to meet a lot of people, try a lot of things, and accept that not all friends are meant to last forever. Not all friends have to be best friends. But if you are lucky enough to find them as you’re limping into middle age, it’s important to pause and appreciate them. Invest, nurture, protect. And book another flight to America as soon as you can.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.
