Protests, riots and the paradox of tolerance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:57 UTC
01:46:57 KST

On Sept. 21, a teacher shortage at a high school on the outskirts of Paris sparked student protests meant to express long-standing frustration over a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and outdated facilities. The protests gained further traction through social media and resonated with a wider audience. The French government’s heavy-handed response only intensified the conflict, while mutual accusations between politicians added fuel to the fire. Civic groups and other organizations joined the movement, and the protests spread nationwide.
However, some demonstrations turned into violent riots, with fires being set and causing collateral damage to innocent people and property. Among the losses was the 19th-century town hall in Limoges, whose clock tower, spire and roof collapsed in flames at the hands of masked protesters. In an interview with Reuters, one Limoges resident lamented, “It broke my heart. I saw Notre-Dame all over again, except this time it was our town.” Inspired by this example, students and other members of the public took to the streets in Milan, Italy, and other cities across Europe under the slogan, “Let’s do it like in France.”
In June 2023, Nahel Merzouk — a French 17-year-old of Algerian descent — was shot and killed after refusing to comply with a police traffic stop, sparking protests across France over the use of excessive force by law enforcement. Merzouk’s mother initially organized a peaceful protest in the place where her son died, but demonstrations in several cities soon spiraled out of control, resulting in arson and looting. Merzouk’s grandmother soon called for an end to the violence, accusing rioters of using his death as a pretext for damaging property and causing disorder.
In July, I visited several parts of France and spoke with police officers. One thing I observed is the way the media sometimes sensationalized — or even misrepresented — events. For example, videos that circulated online purportedly showing the Alcazar Library in Marseille being burned down were actually depicting a fire at the Central Post Office in Manila that had occurred months earlier. It is true that the library’s windows and doors had been the targets of Molotov cocktails, but the fires were quickly extinguished before they could spread inside the building.
Today, social media algorithms act as filters, creating echo chambers that reinforce pre-existing views. Generative artificial intelligence can conjure up almost any sensational scenario. Dramatic scenes — such as clashes between police and protesters or fires consuming buildings — are highly attention-grabbing. They might even draw more people into the fray, blurring the lines between peaceful protesters, opportunistic rioters and radical groups.
In poor countries, people struggle to meet even their most basic needs. In authoritarian states, public demonstrations often face severe repression. How should those of us living in a free and prosperous society view the unrest in France?
Austrian-British philosopher Karl Popper argued that the driving force of progress lies in identifying and correcting errors. When applied to society, this means that allowing for criticism and dissent offers a more effective way to address problems. Popper’s concept of the “open society” posed a serious challenge to totalitarianism. Yet, he also took an objective view of the global landscape and proposed the “paradox of tolerance” — the idea that tolerance without limit would ultimately lead to the extinction of tolerance itself. Therefore, we must defend a tolerant society against attacks by the intolerant. This is a lesson we should all take to heart.
Lin Ji-shing is a university professor.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Vatican celebrates popemobile at exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:57 UTC
01:46:57 KST

The Vatican is opening a celebration of the popemobile, the now-iconic vehicle that for nearly a century has let popes get close to the faithful at home and abroad.
The Vatican Museums on Wednesday unveiled a preview of the exhibition commemorating “A Century of the Popemobile,” featuring eight Mercedes-Benz versions of the car that popes have used since 1930. It officially opened to the public on Thursday.
Separately, Pope Leo XIV — a big car lover — met with top Mercedes-Benz executives and thanked them for their partnership with the Holy See.
Photo: AP
In his remarks, the Chicago-born pope said that the advances in automotive technology had accompanied the advances and evolutions of papal travel.
“Over the decades, the popemobile has evolved from a means of transportation into an instrument of encounter, enabling the pontiff to draw closer to the faithful during pastoral visits and public celebrations,” Leo said. “In this way, your work has helped facilitate the church’s mission of reaching out to people and bringing a message of faith, of hope and of charity to the world.”
The oldest car on display in the Vatican Museums exhibit was given to Pope Pius XI on May 23, 1930. The Mercedes-Benz Nurburg 460 featured a luxurious armchair upholstered in silk brocade and finishes of fine wood and metal.
It “was specifically built, designed and prepared for papal use, so much so that just by comparing it, you can see how it transitions from the serial to the unique,” said Sandro Barbagallo, curator of the Historical Collections Department at the Vatican Museums.
“From this point, it is clear how all the cars were then made, precisely to allow the pope to be seen, but to be seen and to see in total safety and, I would even say, comfort,” he said.
Later versions of the popemobile on view reflected the changing needs of a pope on the road, most importantly his need to engage with the faithful and — more recently — bless babies that were brought to him.
In 1960, Pope John XXIII was presented with the 300 d Landaulet, with a detail that foreshadowed change: The removable rear side windows allowed the future saint to reach out to those he met along the way.
In 1980, for St John Paul II’s visit to Germany, Mercedes-Benz developed the 230 G, which featured another major innovation: a tall, transparent dome at the rear, providing safety, but also guaranteeing a clear view for the millions of faithful gathered to see him.
In his remarks to the Mercedes-Benz executives, Leo recalled the electric popemobile they presented to Pope Francis in keeping with the Argentine pope’s ecological priorities.
“In this spirit, I encourage you to continue placing technological innovation at the service of human dignity, care for creation and the common good,” he said.

Delta says Q4 revenue to rise from last quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:55 UTC
01:46:55 KST

Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) on Thursday said that revenue this quarter would increase from the previous quarter’s NT$197.06 billion (US$6.07 billion), driven by rising demand for its power and thermal management products amid robust investment in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Order momentum for this quarter remains high and is expected to extend into next year, supported by robust demand for AI data center-related products, Delta chairman Ping Cheng (鄭平) told an earnings conference.
Despite component shortages, power constraints, labor shortfalls and project delays, long-term AI data center demand and growth remain intact, Cheng said.
Photo: CNA
“I think no matter what [short-term] problems it faces, the trend remains unchanged,” Cheng said, adding that Delta remains optimistic about its long-term business outlook.
Data center and AI-related products accounted for about 50 percent of the company’s revenue of NT$539.7 billion in the first three quarters of this year, he said.
Capital expenditure among the world’s four major cloud service providers is expected to top US$1 trillion next year, driving global data center investment to US$1.5 trillion, Delta vice president Lanford Liu (劉亮甫) said.
Power electronics products accounted for 54 percent of Delta’s revenue last quarter, followed by infrastructure products at 33 percent, automation devices at 8 percent and mobility applications at 5 percent, the company said.
Delta reported net profit of NT$23.5 billion last quarter, down 6.5 percent quarter-on-quarter, but up 26.3 percent year-on-year.
The earnings results were the strongest for the third quarter in the company’s history.
Third-quarter earnings per share dropped to NT$9.04 from NT$9.68 the previous quarter, but were up from NT$7.16 a year earlier.
Gross margin fell to 34.08 percent last quarter from 35.64 percent the previous quarter and 34.87 percent a year earlier as component shortages and delays in customers’ data center construction plans pushed up inventory costs, Delta said.
Gross margin is expected to be no lower than last quarter, Cheng said.
Material costs have risen about 2 percent since the beginning of this year, Cheng said.
Delta is considering price hikes this quarter or next quarter due to higher material costs, he said.
Delta booked inventory write-down provisions equivalent to about 1.7 percent of revenue last quarter, mainly due to customer order adjustments, chief financial officer Yu Po-wen (余博文) said.
In its thermal solutions business, liquid-cooling products accounted for 13 percent of Delta’s revenue, or about NT$25 billion, last quarter and are expected to remain at a similar percentage for the rest of this year, Yu said.
Separately, Delta’s Singapore subsidiary on Wednesday approved a planned US$120 million capital injection into its wholly owned Malaysian subsidiary.
Delta plans to build a large production base in Malaysia and aims over about five years to expand its capacity to a scale comparable with its Thailand operations, Cheng said.

New rail opens vistas in Tainan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:55 UTC
01:46:55 KST

Tainan’s urban railway undergrounding project, which has been in the works for 16 years, reached a major milestone this month. The Railway Bureau of the Ministry of Transportation and Communications held a farewell event for the above-ground station on Oct. 17, and the first section of its underground successor opened for business the following day. The railway line that has long cut through central Tainan is set to fade from the city’s landscape.
Across the project’s full span of 8.23km, traffic barriers including level crossings, overpasses, underpasses and bridges are to be removed, reconnecting the eastern and western sides of the city.
However, the most important policy questions are yet to come. This includes how the freed up land is to be used, how the plans to turn the former railway corridor into a greenway are designed, how neighborhoods are reconnected, and how the new railway station is integrated with bus, walking and cycling links and the future metro system. Together, these factors would determine the long-term value of this major public infrastructure project for residents.
Current plans for the greenway envision cycle paths, pedestrian spaces and green areas. Done right, this corridor could reconnect residential neighborhoods, schools, shopping districts and public facilities that were previously separated by the railway. Design priorities should include continuous pedestrian routes, shade, nighttime lighting, accessible facilities, cycling routes and safe crossings at intersections. It should not be divided up into fragmented parking areas. Given Tainan’s hot summers, the choice of plants, tree canopy coverage and the provision of rest spots would also prove critical.
The city government could publish design plans for each section, construction schedules and records of public consultation, allowing local residents to understand the planned changes in advance. After significant levels of public investment, the space that is given back should be genuinely walkable and offer people a place in which to slow down; only then would the benefits of the underground railway be borne out in residents’ daily commutes, walks and shopping trips.
Tainan has long been dependent on cars and scooters for transportation. If people still have to drive themselves to get to the new underground stations, the benefits of the railway investment could be limited. The city government should review bus stop locations, transfer distances, taxi ranks, YouBike stations, bicycle parking and pedestrian crossings to ensure easy access to railway stations.
As Linsen (林森) and South Tainan (南台南) stations begin operating, and plans for the Tainan Metro network advance, Taiwan Railways could also become a key component of the city’s north-south public transport network. A unified transfer plan and passenger information system should be established now, with ticketing data being used to identify passenger routes and transfer needs. The value of major rail infrastructure increases with the degree of integration with surrounding transport networks; roads and bus services near the stations should be adjusted in tandem with the undergrounding project.
The government has tended to evaluate major infrastructure projects primarily in terms of construction progress, budget execution and opening dates. After the railway opens, more meaningful indicators would include travel time reductions, whether public transport use increases and conditions for pedestrians and cyclists improve, how the project affects local shopping districts and residents’ daily lives and public utilization of the completed greenway. The city government could publish these figures regularly over the next five to 10 years, allowing residents to see the tangible changes brought about by the underground railway.
The railway’s move underground gives Tainan a rare opportunity to reconfigure its public spaces. If transport, green space, cultural preservation, flood control, public transport and urban renewal can be planned together, the project’s legacy could extend far beyond an underground railway line. A truly successful effort to reconnect the city should allow residents on either side of the former railway corridor to coexist within the same urban space.
Roger Lo is a freelancer and Tainan resident.

Crypto platform Binance confirms US$6.3bn hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:53 UTC
01:46:53 KST

Cryptocurrency platform Binance yesterday said it was working to resolve a “complex attack” that affected about US$6.3 billion in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist.
The company — the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes — said investigations had “uncovered additional points of breach,” contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance wrote on X.
Photo: Reuters
Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said that it had “high confidence” the attack was orchestrated by a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists,” TRM said.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group — which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
Binance confirmed on its X account for Latin America that “the total estimated impact is around US$6.3 billion.”
That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: US$1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform.
That heist was attributed at the time to TraderTraitor.
Binance said the US$6.3 billion figure “may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.”
About US$3 billion in affected assets had been frozen, it said.
Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that “user funds are completely safe,” but also saying it would “cover all losses.”
At about 9am GMT yesterday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been “temporarily suspended.”
“Deposits remain unaffected,” it said.
The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer,” allowing the unauthorized party to access a “service container” and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
“We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.
However, it later said that “subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach.”
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether — a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT — said his firm froze about US$1.6 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.”
Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than US$800 million in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both “stablecoins,” or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.
The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

VP details drone development strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:51 UTC
01:46:51 KST

Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) yesterday detailed the government’s uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) development strategy at the formal opening of the new Global UAV Academy (GUAVA) in Taipei.
The value of Taiwan’s drone exports in the first half of this year already exceeded the total for last year, she told a forum hosted by GUAVA and Taiwan Defense Industry Development Association.
Deputy Minister of National Defense Hsu Szu-chien (徐斯儉), former Czech Chamber of Deputies president Marketa Pekarova Adamova and representatives from the US, Japan, Ukraine and Poland were among the serving and retired officials who attended the event.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
For Taiwan to become the top Asian exporter of drones to fellow democracies, the government must first establish “three pillars” to build a national UAV industry, Hsiao said.
First, the nation must forge fully non-Chinese supply chains to eliminate risks from built-in backdoor exploits and dependence on authoritarian regimes, Hsiao said.
Mircoprocessors, flight control systems, electro-optical sensors and batteries must meet the highest standards for cybersecurity and operational integrity before supply chains can be deemed trustworthy, she said.
Second, edge artificial intelligence must be developed and integrated into truly autonomous platforms capable of unassisted decisionmaking, sensor fusion and navigating under GPS jamming, she said.
Third, Taiwan must cement international partnerships to allow joint research and development, technology transfers and collaborative manufacturing, she added.
This part of the strategy leverages Taiwan’s advantage in researching and developing systems, original equipment manufacturing and production at scale, Hsiao said.
In June, Taiwan reached an agreement with Palau to transfer four multipurpose patrol and rescue training drones, she said.
GUAVA and Palau Community College also launched a collaboration to train drone pilots to bolster the latter’s maritime law enforcement capabilities, she added.
President William Lai (賴清德) has elevated uncrewed system technologies development to the nation’s highest strategic priority given their value to national defense and the economy, she said.
Although a latecomer to the global drone industry, Taiwan’s technical leadership in semiconductors, precision engineering and advanced manufacturing have allowed the nation to rapidly catch up, she said.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs established a drone diplomacy task force in October last year, drawing on its experience with “chip diplomacy” to push Taiwanese drones onto the global stage, Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said.

‘Silicon shield,’ ‘Made with Taiwan’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:43 UTC
01:46:43 KST

Taiwan’s semiconductor industry gives other countries powerful reasons to prevent a conflict in the Taiwan Strait. It also gives them reasons to reduce their dependence on Taiwan. As production spreads, Taiwan needs a “silicon shield” that can adapt: one that keeps it central to the networks behind advanced technology while turning technological partnerships into durable political support.
This tension framed a podcast conversation with sociologist Wu Jieh-min (吳介民) for the NTNU International Taiwan Studies Center, in collaboration with the International Journal of Taiwan Studies. Wu, a distinguished research fellow at Academia Sinica, examines Taiwan’s technological position in Global Taiwan, published by Cambridge University Press this year.
The “silicon shield” rests on the idea that disrupting Taiwanese chip production would damage industries worldwide, encouraging other governments to deter aggression. Yet the same risk drives investment in alternative production. Taiwan must remain an indispensable partner without assuming that economic importance guarantees protection.
A shift from “Made in Taiwan” to “Made with Taiwan” captures the challenge: Taiwan must continue contributing essential knowledge, research and capabilities as production becomes more geographically dispersed.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC) achievement illustrates why. A fabrication plant operates within a network of suppliers, engineers, research institutions and accumulated relationships. TSMC earned customers’ trust by manufacturing their chips without competing against their designs, and helped coordinate design tools and manufacturing expertise. A new factory cannot instantly reproduce that system.
Overseas expansion can deepen partnerships and create opportunities for upgrading. Its consequences depend on where research and engineering capabilities develop, how knowledge circulates, and how overseas operations connect to Taiwan’s industrial base.
Staying central requires more than protecting an existing advantage. Taiwan needs sustained investment in research and skills, international collaboration among universities, suppliers and firms, and the capacity to move into emerging technologies. Joint research, engineer exchanges and training can build these connections.
The value of the “silicon shield” changes as other countries adapt. Wu raises a difficult possibility: If China becomes less dependent on Taiwanese supplies, the economic damage of disruption could fall increasingly unevenly.
This is an argument about changing incentives, not a prediction that Beijing would choose war. Taiwan cannot rely indefinitely on the same distribution of economic costs to discourage aggression. The “silicon shield” must adapt to changing geopolitical, industrial and technological conditions.
At last year’s artificial intelligence and Taiwan studies forum, Wu proposed a “silicon shield 2.0” focused on Taiwan’s participation in supply chain governance and cooperation with democratic partners. “Made with Taiwan” gives that approach a practical direction: cultivate research partnerships and shared capabilities that remain valuable as production locations change.
Partners encouraging Taiwan to diversify production should explain how their policies bolster Taiwan’s resilience. An investment might deepen customer relationships without securing a diplomatic commitment. Supply chain security for importing countries cannot be assumed to provide security for Taiwan.
Taiwan’s right to determine its future should not depend on its market share. International interests in regional stability predate advanced semiconductors. Chips add to those interests; Taiwan’s democracy and its people deserve support even as production networks change.
Security arguments must account for semiconductor growth’s domestic costs. Wu examines demands on workers, land, water and electricity. High salaries coexist with intensive working practices, while expansion can provoke disputes over land acquisition and access to resources.
Calling the industry essential to national survival can make disputes harder to resolve fairly. Residents and workers might find their concerns subordinated to strategic urgency. Public pride in TSMC does not imply consent to every decision made in its name.
Consultation, environmental accountability and fair working conditions help sustain public support. Governments and companies must explain who benefits and who bears the burdens.
Before approving expansion, policymakers should ask how demand for power and water would affect other users, whether environmental assessments allow meaningful challenge and whether workers can raise concerns.
Taiwanese have shown that economic integration is subject to democratic judgement. The 2014 Sunflower Movement connected concerns about closer cross-Strait ties with demands for scrutiny and accountability. Wu’s analysis shows how campaigns for social reform and resistance to China’s encroachment have converged. Civil society remains divided, but its ability to challenge decisions gives Taiwan resources beyond corporate investment and formal diplomacy.
Wu’s public-opinion research also distinguishes support for the cross-Strait “status quo” from confidence that it would endure. Many respondents preferred present stability while expecting a different long-term outcome. Economic interdependence has not settled Taiwan’s security.
A credible strategy would assess semiconductor cooperation by Taiwan’s capacity to innovate, the support its partners provide and the legitimacy of decisions at home. “Made with Taiwan” should mean continued investment in research and talent, reciprocal partnerships and accountability over the costs of growth.
Taiwan’s technological success offers an opportunity to shape a changing global industry. A sustainable “silicon shield” depends on learning and adaptation, alongside political commitments that factories alone cannot supply. Its ultimate measure is whether Taiwanese gain greater freedom to decide their future.
Ming-yeh T. Rawnsley is a research associate at SOAS University of London’s Center for Taiwan Studies.

Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Why is North Korea fortifying its border with South Korea?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:41 UTC
01:46:41 KST

Last week North Korea hit the headlines with a vow to fire up its loudspeaker systems to blare propaganda into the South, but the latest dispute comes against a backdrop of militarization of the border by Kim Jong-un that has been years in the making.
Since April 2024, North Korea has been working on building a permanent fortified border through the demilitarized zone (DMZ) that divides the two sides, work that has led to a mine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers and plunged ties to new lows.
Here’s a brief guide to what is being built, what Pyongyang says it’s for, and why even deciding where the border is has become such a fraught issue.
Photo: Reuters
WHAT IS NORTH KOREA BUILDING AT THE BORDER?
The 250km border is already fortified but not in the way many might traditionally think. It is more of a buffer than a barrier at the moment, in the form of a 4km-wide demilitarized zone (DMZ) which runs across the Korean peninsula.
Since 2024, the North is thought to have laid about 960,000 mines in the DMZ, close to half of all the mines thought to be in an area that is already one of the most heavily mined places on earth.
Photo: AFP
North Korea has also been constructing a continuous physical barrier on its side of the zone, along the full length of the line. It is made up of wire fencing, alongside minefields, tactical roads, and anti-tank barriers laid on ground stripped of vegetation. South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff say the ground-clearing is nearly finished while the construction work is 40-60 percent complete, and expect it to be finished by the second half of 2028.
Under the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, the DMZ was to be cleared of military forces and equipment.
WHY IS KIN JONG-UN DOING THIS?
Photo: AP
Kim Jong-un has abandoned the once-cherished goal of reunification. As recently as 2018, the leaders of the two sides met at the border, and their athletes marched together at the Winter Olympics. But in December 2023, Kim redefined the South as a separate, hostile state, and the construction began a few months later.
Experts in Seoul read Kim’s U-turn as removing the contradiction that lay in threatening nuclear war on people who the North had once called compatriot. When engagement with Seoul collapsed and Moscow emerged as a patron, Pyongyang was left free to press for recognition as a nuclear state.
They also say the construction achieves several goals: stopping North Koreans leaving, slowing any South Korean advance in the event of a return to warfare and turning the frontier into something that works as an international border.
Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, has said the work will eliminate the danger of a conflict at the border. However, analysts argue the opposite: that the new artillery and missile units being installed make an accidental clash more likely to escalate.
WHY ARE TENSIONS RISING?
On Sept. 21, three South Korean soldiers were wounded by a landmine blast while clearing a path inside the DMZ. One soldier lost his foot.
South Korea’s military concluded the blast was caused by a North Korean mine placed south of the border, and Seoul has demanded an apology. Pyongyang denied any responsibility for the incident and called it a “self-staged farce.”
South Korea says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the border during the work to fortify their side of the line, leading to warning shots that Pyongyang says are provocations by “armed rogues.”
Kim Yo-jong has since issued about 10 statements in less than a month criticizing the South, a frequency Seoul’s unification ministry called unusual. She recently said the North’s propaganda loudspeakers would be ready to blast across the border within days.
DOES ANYONE KNOW WHERE THE BORDER RUNS?
No. The armistice drew the military demarcation line (MDL) on maps at a scale of 1:50,000, where a line just a millimeter wide covers about 50 meters of ground. A total of 1,292 numbered markers were then planted to fix it in place, but only about 200 are still identifiable.
So each side has reconstructed it following its own methodology. Seoul works from mapping aligned with the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, while the US-led UN Command (UNC), which oversees the armistice, uses its own survey from a decade ago. North Korea is believed to simply connect the markers it can still see. South Korea’s defense ministry has found that its line and the UNC’s disagree at about 60 percent of the points they have compared, by tens of meters in places. It is unclear how differently the two Koreas read the line.
North Korean troops reportedly crossed the border about 50 times in August and September this year alone, compared with 17 instances in 2025.
IS ANYTHING BEING DONE TO RESOLVE BORDER ISSUE?
Seoul is trying. It has proposed talks to confirm jointly where the MDL runs, restore military communication channels severed in 2023 and agree how to avoid accidental clashes. It is the second such offer in a year. Pyongyang ignored the first.
South Korea’s defense ministry calls the work an armistice violation and has demanded that it stop. The UNC, on the other hand, has said that construction and fortification do not automatically constitute violations, and that each case has to be judged on its facts.
Much attention is being paid to increasing security ties between Taiwan and the Philippines, and rightfully so. The stakes are potentially existential, as explored in “ Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines need to face the common threat from Beijing” (Sept. 12, page 12). Getting less attention is that across the board the relationship is growing stronger, and both sides appear to be planning to put more of their eggs in each other’s baskets. Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) in August last year confirmed plans to open a second Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) representative

CWA forecaster Chang Cheng-chuan (張承傳) said that the first wave strengthened yesterday and would last through tomorrow, although the effects of this weaker wave would not be very noticeable.
Today, the winds are to gradually shift easterly, bringing more moisture to windward areas, Chang said.
Photo: CNA
Localized brief showers are expected along Keelung’s north coast, the greater Taipei area, the eastern half of the country and the Hengchun Peninsula (恆春半島), while areas south of Taoyuan would see mostly cloudy to sunny skies, he said.
Tomorrow, the wind is to shift to a southerly direction, reducing moisture and bringing mostly cloudy to clear weather nationwide, with only isolated showers in the east and on the Hengchun Peninsula, he added.
The second wave of northeasterly winds are to strengthen on Monday and Tuesday, bringing increased rainfall to areas north of Taoyuan and the eastern half of the country, Chang said.
The monsoon would weaken on Wednesday, limiting brief showers to Keelung’s north coast and the east, before a third wave strengthens on Thursday and Friday, bringing renewed localized rain to areas north of Taoyuan and the east, he said.
Lows across Taiwan are to range from 20°C to 23°C over the coming week, Chang said.
Early this morning, areas north of central Taiwan and the northeast were forecast to be slightly cooler, with lows dipping to 19°C in some areas, Chang said.
Highs would reach 26°C to 27°C in the north and northeast, 31°C in central and southern Taiwan, and 28°C to 29°C in Hualien and Taitung counties, he said.
Daytime temperatures in the north and northeast would rebound significantly tomorrow, with highs nationwide reaching 28°C to 32°C, he added.
Meanwhile, Severe Typhoon In-fa is projected to veer north over the waters south of Japan, maintaining a distance of at least 2,000km from Taiwan, Chang said.
The storm is to begin its initial northward turn today before taking a sharper turn to the northeast on Wednesday, he added.
Although In-fa would not directly affect Taiwan, the public should watch out for long coastal waves along Keelung’s north coast, the eastern seaboard and the Hengchun Peninsula for a full week starting tomorrow, he said.

“We are likely to see a K-shaped divergence next year, with AI data center-related business continuing to grow, while other businesses would follow a different trajectory,” Hon Hai chairman Young Liu (劉揚偉) said on the sidelines of the Hon Hai Technology Day conference in Taipei.
Hon Hai’s revenue last year rose 18.13 percent year-on-year to about NT$8.1 trillion (US$249.4 billion), company data showed.
Photo: Chiang Ying-ying, AP
Recent concerns over an AI industry bubble might be overstated, as market demand remains clear, Liu said, adding that concern about financial risks at major AI companies was an overly negative view.
Supply-chain demand far exceeds capacity, making the situation difficult to describe simply as a “shortage,” he said.
Liu met with OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman.
The two discussed potential cooperation.
Liu declined to disclose details.
As AI data center demand continues to grow, Hon Hai plans to add more capacity to its six factory buildings in Houston, Texas, Liu said.
Hon Hai is not moving away from China, Liu said, adding that it remains a major market for its customers.
Regarding a proposed Taiwanese industrial park in Texas, with an investment of up to US$4 billion, Liu said that as the local AI manufacturing supply chain is incomplete, Taiwanese suppliers of key components have to build capacity there.
Hon Hai hopes the project could develop into what Liu described as a “third-generation science park,” following Hsinchu as the first generation and Tainan as the second.
Such a park should go beyond hosting individual manufacturers or assembly sites and instead form a complete industrial ecosystem, supported by suppliers of molds, forming and processing services, cables, connectors and printed circuit boards, Liu said.
The company yesterday showcased an Nvidia Corp DSX POD, a modular data center developed with Teco Electric & Machinery Co (東元電機) based on Nvidia’s DSX POD reference design that allows partners to preintegrate Nvidia Vera Rubin rack-scale AI infrastructure and complete critical validation before shipment.

The US-China tech cold war is moving undersea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:38 UTC
01:46:38 KST

When Australian Minister for Defence Richard Marles described the seabed as a battlefield at a regional defense gathering in Singapore earlier this year, he was preaching to the converted. The security of undersea cables — which carry more than 95 percent of data flows and trillions of dollars of daily financial transactions — was already top of mind for the senior military brass, geopolitical analysts and government ministers in the room.
A new project by Australia, the UK and the US was quickly announced to develop underwater drone technology to protect cables by next year, while Singapore launched a 17-country framework covering Southeast Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Oceania to explore defense cooperation on critical infrastructure.
However, while nations are racing to defend existing networks, the companies building Southeast Asia’s digital architecture face a different challenge: avoiding maritime bottlenecks and the risk posed by China’s expanding sea presence. The Strait of Malacca, the narrow passage between Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, is particularly vulnerable due to the sheer concentration of cables traversing the corridor.
Illustration: Kevin Sheu
Already considered the Indo-Pacific region’s most critical chokepoint — it handles about 21 percent of global maritime trade by value — the Strait is increasingly being bypassed by major private subsea cable projects. Google’s TalayLink, for instance, would connect Australia and Thailand via the Indian Ocean following a route west of the Sunda Strait that avoids the congested corridor.
However, concentration is not the only risk. Nowhere is the geopolitical contest over cable routes more evident than in the South China Sea, where China is using regulation and maritime enforcement to control who can build and repair cable infrastructure across the contested waters. Beijing is effectively trying to redraw the undersea cable map, while the US and its partners are finding new ways to push back.
Google and Meta Platforms Inc’s Echo cable — which links the US to Singapore via Guam and Indonesia — shows how tech companies are redesigning Asia-Pacific networks to reduce their exposure to China. These giants have decided that avoiding Beijing is worth the added costs and the risk of laying cables in less suitable terrain.
Of course, it is tempting to dismiss this as yet more collateral damage from the US-China competition, but it will have long-lasting consequences. The routes chosen for this eye-wateringly expensive critical infrastructure will impact the region for decades to come, cementing ties between nations and increasingly isolating others.
Samuel Bashfield, a research fellow at Melbourne-based La Trobe University and the author of two books including one on submarine cables, has written that installers are increasingly wary of working in the South China Sea, with many avoiding the area altogether.
Beyond deploying Chinese Coast Guard ships to harass repair crews or prevent them from accessing the cable grounds, Beijing has effectively locked out non-Chinese subsea fiber projects through onerous permitting requirements, he said. These delays have forced some new projects to reroute entirely, hugging coastlines and plowing cables into shallow seabeds, a less-than-ideal solution for network resilience, Bashfield said.
The US$700 million Asia Connect Cable System, led by start-up Inligo Networks, for example, would skirt the South China Sea by running through Indonesia and the Philippines. The Pacific Light Cable Network, linking the US to Taiwan and the Philippines, underwent a similar transformation after its planned Hong Kong connection was abandoned following US intervention.
The US has devoted considerable effort to convince Southeast Asian and Pacific nations to shun Chinese vendors in favor of US, Japanese or European alternatives. Both superpowers fear that foreign involvement in cable infrastructure could enable intelligence gathering or sabotage. Washington regards Chinese technology as a security risk, while Beijing has raised similar concerns about US and Japanese equipment.
Amid mounting US scrutiny, Huawei Technologies Co agreed in 2019 to sell its 51 percent stake in Huawei Marine Networks to China’s Hengtong Optic-Electric, which also acquired its British partner’s interest. The cable-building business was subsequently renamed HMN Technologies Co, but its ownership and technological origins mean the US and allies such as Japan and Australia want to reduce its use across Asia.
They have clocked up some recent successes: In August, Australia announced that every Pacific Islands Forum member was connected to the global undersea cable network for the first time. That was a significant achievement, but it does not mean that Chinese companies have been excluded from the Pacific altogether.
The next battleground is data centers. Countries financing submarine cables would also need to help build the infrastructure needed to store and process data locally, or risk Chinese suppliers filling that gap.
Much of that work would fall to Japan, which plays a critical role as a manufacturer and a connectivity hub between North America and Asia. NEC Corp alone is one of the world’s largest subsea cable builders. Tokyo needs to utilize groupings such as the Quad grouping of the US, Japan, India and Australia, as well as the ASEAN to bolster systems in the Indo-Pacific region and expand cable-laying capacity to help reduce China’s dominance.
ASEAN leaders are due to gather in Manila next month, where a Quad leaders’ meeting is also planned. Undersea cable security should be high on their agenda.
However, there is an irony in efforts to curb Beijing’s influence over critical cable routes: Much of that power is instead concentrating in the hands of a small group of US technology giants. What could possibly go wrong?

Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

The Ministry of Agriculture yesterday touted the success of Taiwanese pineapple exports to New Zealand and Australia, while setting its sights on the US market by the end of next year.
Deputy Minister of Agriculture Hu Jong-i (胡忠一) made the remarks in an exclusive interview yesterday with the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the sister paper of the Taipei Times).
Following China’s ban on Taiwanese fruit exports on grounds that Taipei called politically motivated, Taiwan has been exploring foreign markets outside of China, with Japan being the largest, he said.
Photo: Chen Kuan-pei, Taipei Times
Last year, a ministry delegation visited Australia and New Zealand to investigate local conditions and found that local cold chains need at least two weeks to transport Taiwanese pineapples from customs to consumer shelves, Hu said.
The ministry’s experts selected the “mango pineapple” cultivar for export to the Commonwealth countries, as the cultivar’s sweetness is enhanced by weeks of storage at 13°C, the temperature of local cold chains, he said.
Surveys conducted by local retailers showed that more than 90 percent of local consumers have a positive opinion of Taiwanese pineapples, he said.
The ministry’s experience in Australia and New Zealand could be beneficial to Taiwan’s bid to export to the US market, which could happen next year, Hsu said.
Taiwan’s favorite pineapple, the Golden Diamond, or Tainung 17, is unsuited for export, as its flavor and presentation fade relatively quickly, while mango pineapple keeps well, has an edible core, and is sweet, he said.
The nation cultivates mango pineapples on 50 hectares, a number the ministry aims to boost to 1,000 hectares over the next few years, Hsu said.
The ministry has successfully negotiated with Japanese importers to lengthen the average contract to five years from the current 18 months, which imposes daunting initial investment costs on small farmers, he said.
Farmind, Japan’s largest fruit and vegetable importer, has already agreed to the arrangement, which could serve as a model with Taiwan’s future international customers, Hsu said.

Central bank members show concern about inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:36 UTC
01:46:36 KST

Central bank board members expressed concern about rising inflation, but differed on whether to raise interest rates, with two directors favoring a hike — including one who called for monetary policy normalization — while the majority supported holding rates steady, minutes of the bank’s meeting last month showed.
Directors said that import and producer prices were potential sources of further consumer inflation, while the government’s measures to stabilize energy prices had helped shield consumers from higher oil costs.
One director said that Taiwan should begin normalizing monetary policy, saying a rate increase would not necessarily be intended to curb inflation or slow economic activity, but to move borrowing costs toward a more neutral level after a prolonged period of exceptionally low rates.
Photo: CNA
Other directors favored keeping rates unchanged, saying that inflation in Taiwan is more moderate than in the US, the eurozone and South Korea, where price increases had exceeded 3 percent.
The central bank had tightened financial conditions without raising its benchmark rate since March 2024, using higher reserve requirements, stricter property lending rules and open-market operations, they said.
Keeping rates unchanged while the US Federal Reserve raised its policy rate could widen the interest-rate gap between the two economies, putting further downward pressure on the New Taiwan dollar and pushing up import costs, one director said.
The director cited rising producer prices for domestically produced goods sold locally and increases in import prices as threats to the consumer price outlook.
However, other directors said that higher rates could deepen disparities in access to credit.
Technology companies benefiting from strong artificial intelligence-related demand and profitability are generally less sensitive to borrowing costs than traditional manufacturers, they said.
With financing demand from the information and communications technology sector already contributing to tight liquidity, higher rates could make it more difficult for small and medium-sized enterprises, micro-businesses and traditional manufacturers to secure funding, they said.
Directors also highlighted the uneven recovery in domestic demand.
Despite surging exports, private consumption has remained comparatively subdued, limiting the extent to which rapid economic growth has translated into broader inflationary pressure.
Higher import prices for electronic components have also largely been reflected in export prices, while energy-price stabilization measures have helped contain the pass-through of oil costs to consumers.
Separately, one director urged the central bank to closely monitor banks’ growing lending to securities firms amid rapid stock trading, warning that a sharp market correction could expose lenders to greater risks.
All of the board members agreed that policy decisions should take into account inflation trends, domestic financial conditions and monetary policy moves by major overseas central banks.

Chip designer MediaTek Inc (聯發科) yesterday said it has secured a second customer for its customized artificial intelligence (AI) accelerator for data centers, while volume production of a second-generation chip for an existing customer is on track for early 2028, potentially easing market concerns about possible delays.
This is a new customer and, crucially, not from China, MediaTek said.
The remarks were meant to dismiss speculation that ByteDance Ltd (字節跳動), the parent company of TikTok, was the second customer for MediaTek’s new customized AI application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) business.
Photo: CNA
“It is on track, on schedule. We understand there is some noise about the tape-out schedule,” MediaTek chief executive officer Rick Tsai (蔡力行) told investors during an earnings call.
The company’s second AI chip is a powerful XPU using multi-die architecture, he said.
A few dies have already been taped out, while another, larger and more complex die is on schedule to tape out in the coming weeks, he said.
Overall, MediaTek expects to ramp up volume production of the AI accelerator in the first quarter of 2028, he said.
Addressing investor concerns over the adoption of Intel Corp’s advanced packaging technology, called EMIB-T, Tsai said that Intel’s packaging process is “our absolute priority.”
“We are working very closely with our IDM [integrated device manufacturer] partner, with a primary focus on yield improvements,” he said.
MediaTek is using Intel’s EMIB-T advanced packaging for the second-generation project, while continuing to work with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電).
However, MediaTek is not dependent on a single supplier, Tsai said.
“It is critical to make clear that TSMC remains our most important partner,” he said, adding that the company must adapt to changing customer requirements amid a rapidly growing AI market.
MediaTek said that its first AI ASIC program is progressing smoothly, with initial shipments commencing last month.
The chip is projected to generate US$2.5 billion in revenue this quarter, it said.
MediaTek said it anticipates revenue from the program next year to be at the high end of its target at about US$16 billion, capturing roughly 20 percent of the total AI ASIC market.
“This confidence is underpinned by our solid supply outlook. We are working closely with our supply chain partners for additional capacity to meet the strong customer demand,” Tsai said.
MediaTek has not named its existing customer, widely reported to be Google, with MediaTek designing a tensor processing unit — an AI ASIC — for it.
MediaTek said that it is working with its customer on a third-generation AI ASIC project and is in discussions to finalize the details.
The chip designer yesterday said it expects robust revenue growth this quarter of 25 to 32 percent sequentially to between NT$210.1 billion and NT$221.8 billion (US$6.47 billion and US$6.83 billion).
On an annual basis, that would be growth of 40 to 48 percent, it said.
Based on the revenue guidance for this quarter, MediaTek expects full-year revenue growth in US dollar terms would exceed its previous target of high-single-digit percentage growth.
Gross margin is expected to be 43.5 to 46.5 percent this quarter, compared with 46.3 percent last quarter, MediaTek said.
Operating profit margin from this quarter through next year is expected to show a marked improvement, it said.
The firm expects operating margin of at least 20 percent next year, as production of AI ASIC scales, MediaTek chief financial officer David Ku (顧大為) told investors.
Net profit last quarter expanded 14.6 percent sequentially to NT$28.2 billion from NT$24.61 billion in the second quarter, MediaTek said.
That represented annual growth of 10.8 percent from NT$25.45 billion.
Earnings per share rose to NT$17.5 last quarter from NT$15.28 in the second quarter and NT$15.84 in the third quarter last year.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

Have you ever struggled with a problem for hours, only to suddenly think of a solution while taking a shower? This common experience is sometimes called the “shower effect.” Researchers have found that people often come up with fresh ideas during simple activities such as showering, taking a walk, or washing dishes. __1__ As a result, the mind is able to wander more freely.
In 2022, Zachary Irving and his research team at the University of Virginia studied the connection between creativity and mind-wandering. __2__ If an activity is too demanding, the mind will be completely absorbed in it, leaving little room for new thoughts. However, if it is too boring, the mind may lose focus and drift toward distractions such as phones. Activities like showering provide a balance between focus and relaxation, which supports creative thinking.
__3__ Convergent thinking focuses on finding the most logical answer and is commonly used in tests. Divergent thinking, on the other hand, involves exploring many possibilities and connecting unrelated ideas. Experts believe that the shower effect is closely related to divergent thinking because the brain becomes more open to unexpected connections during moments of relaxation.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
The shower itself may also help create the right mental environment. __4__ In this situation, people become less aware of their surroundings, allowing insights to emerge more easily. Similar effects may happen while walking, gardening or doing everyday activities.
Sometimes, the best ideas appear not when people are thinking the hardest, but when the mind is relaxed and free to wander. So, the next time you get stuck on a problem, try taking a shower.
你是否曾為了一個問題苦思好幾個小時，卻在洗澡時突然想到解決方法？這種常見的經驗有時被稱為「淋浴效應」。研究人員發現，人們常會在洗澡、散步或洗碗等簡單活動中想到新的點子。雖然這些事情仍需要一些注意力，但並沒有困難到足以完全占據大腦。因此，思緒便能更自由地漫遊。
2022年，扎卡里．歐文與他在維吉尼亞大學的研究團隊探討了創造力與心智漫遊之間的關聯。他們的研究指出，人們在具有適度投入感的活動中，往往能產生更有創意的想法。如果一項活動太過費神，思緒就會完全投入其中，幾乎沒有空間產生新的想法。然而，如果活動太過無聊，心智又可能失去焦點，轉而被手機等干擾事物吸引。像洗澡這類活動則能在專注與放鬆之間取得平衡，有助於促進創意思考。
心理學家透過兩種不同的思考方式來解釋創造力。聚斂性思考著重於找出最合乎邏輯的答案，常用於考試中。另一方面，擴散性思考則涉及探索許多可能性，並將不相關的想法連結起來。專家認為，淋浴效應與擴散性思考密切相關，因為在放鬆的時刻，大腦會變得更容易接受意想不到的連結。
淋浴本身也可能有助於營造適合思考的心理環境。白噪音、溫熱的水流以及與外界隔離的狀態，都能減少外在干擾。在這種情況下，人們變得比較不會注意到周圍環境，使洞見更容易浮現。類似的效果也可能在走路、進行園藝，或從事日常活動時發生。
有時候，最好的點子並不是在人們最努力思考時出現，而是在思緒放鬆、自由漫遊時浮現。所以，下次當你被問題卡住時，不妨去洗個澡吧！
What Did You Learn?
(A) Psychologists explain creativity through two different styles of thinking.
(B) Experts believe that people use two kinds of thinking when taking risks.
(C) The white noise, warm water and physical isolation can reduce outside distractions.
(D) Although these tasks require some attention, they are not difficult enough to fully occupy the brain.
(E) Their studies suggested that people produced more creative ideas during moderately engaging activities.
答案：1. D 2. E 3. A 4. C
Words in Use
1. emerge vi. 浮現，出現
Clara’s confidence slowly emerged after weeks of practice.
克萊拉練習數週後，信心慢慢浮現。
2. wander vi. 漫遊
During the lecture, Hannah’s mind began to wander toward her vacation plans.
上課時，漢娜的思緒開始飄向她的假期計畫。
3. creativity n. 創意，創造力
Art activities can encourage creativity in young children.
藝術活動能激發小孩子的創造力。
4. demanding a. 費力的
Taking care of two young children can be physically demanding.
照顧兩個年幼孩子可能很耗體力。
5. drift vi. 漂移
Their conversation drifted from school life to travel plans.
他們的話題從校園生活慢慢轉到旅遊計畫。
Practical Phrases

The Memphis Grizzlies, fueled by a triple-double from teenager Cameron Boozer, on Thursday topped the Portland Trail Blazers 124-103 in a battle of NBA unbeatens, with Portland guard Ja Morant injured while playing his first game against his former team.
Boozer, taken third in June’s NBA draft, scored 18 points with 12 rebounds and 12 assists for the Grizzlies.
The game in Portland was billed as Morant’s reunion with the Grizzlies, the team who drafted him second overall in 2019. He earned Rookie of the Year honors in 2020 and emerged as a star in his seven-year tenure in Memphis.
Photo: AP
He also had a pair of lengthy suspensions and, after multiple injuries limited him to 20 games last season, he was traded in June.
Morant finished with 14 points, two rebounds and three assists before exiting in the fourth quarter with a hamstring injury.
Meanwhile, Boozer stole the show, becoming at 19 years, 103 days the second-youngest player in NBA history to post a triple-double, after Josh Giddey in 2022 (19 years, 84 days).
Photo: AFP
“It’s nice,” Boozer said. “I’m going to keep going. Season just started, we’ve got 77 more [games] — so a lot more to come.”
Isaiah Stewart added 18 points off the bench, with eight players scoring in double figures for the Grizzlies, who improved to 5-0. They and the 5-0 Houston Rockets are the only remaining unbeaten teams.
The New Orleans Pelicans, fueled by a 22-point, 13-assist double-double from Jeremiah Fears, bagged their first win of the season with a 132-120 victory over the Sacramento Kings.
Fears, 20, added eight rebounds, four blocked shots, and two steals, while Zion Williamson scored 22 points for the Pels, who had seven players score in double figures to improve to 1-4.
“We’re not off to a great start, but we’re changing this thing around for sure,” Fears said.
Sacramento’s Darius Acuff Jr, the seventh overall pick in the draft, continued his strong rookie season with 34 points and 14 assists — topping his previous career-high of 33 points set last week against Portland.
De’Andre Hunter and Precious Achiuwa added 24 points each for the Kings, but Sacramento fell to 0-5. They are one of two remaining winless teams along with the 0-4 Brooklyn Nets.
The Hawks got a much-needed win in Atlanta, Georgia, taking charge with a 43-point third quarter and holding on for a 114-111 victory over the Cleveland Cavaliers.
Onyeka Okongwu scored 29 points and grabbed 12 rebounds, Nickeil Alexander-Walker scored 25 points and Aaron Wiggins added 20 points off the bench for the Hawks, who had lost three straight and grabbed their first home win of the fledgling season.
James Harden scored 24 points for the Cavs, who led by as many as 15 in the first half.
Donovan Mitchell added 22, including a driving layup that pulled Cleveland within 112-111 with 20.6 seconds remaining. Alexander-Walker made a pair of free throws, and Mitchell missed a pair of potential game-tying three-pointers in the waning seconds.

Apple to lower App Store commission rate to 26% today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) yesterday said it had accepted Apple’s commitment to lower its standard App Store commission rate in Taiwan from 30 percent to 26 percent, effective today, to address competition concerns.
The FTC said it had been investigating whether Apple’s restrictions on app developers, including those related to the so-called “Apple tax,” breached the Fair Trade Act (公平交易法).
Apple tax refers to the commission Apple charges developers for paid apps and in-app purchases made through its App Store.
Photo: AFP
Some critics said Apple requiring developers to use its in-app payment system limits their ability to choose alternative payment methods, and can increase costs for businesses and consumers.
During the investigation, Apple proposed lowering the standard commission rate for paid apps and in-app purchases on its Taiwan App Store from 30 percent to 26 percent under Article 28 of the Fair Trade Act, which allows an investigation to be suspended subject to a company’s commitments.
“Apple is making changes to the Taiwan storefront of the App Store, following discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission,” the company said in a statement on Thursday.
The new rate, which Apple said would also apply in markets such as Japan and Brazil, is to take effect automatically for developers in Taiwan, the FTC said, adding that they would not need to apply or take additional steps to qualify for the lower rate.
The commission said it would monitor Apple’s compliance and could resume its investigation if the company fails to fulfill its commitment, if the facts underlying the decision changes significantly, or if the decision was based on incomplete or inaccurate information.
The FTC said it would continue to investigate any other potentially anti-competitive or unfair practices by Apple on a case-by-case basis.

Beijing denies spying on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:30 UTC
01:46:30 KST

Beijing yesterday dismissed as “groundless speculation” a report that said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) was the target of a Chinese spy plot.
The article by the New York Times, published on Thursday, said that US intelligence officials concluded that a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data center company had been funneling information to Beijing.
“The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China,” Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun (郭嘉昆) told a regular briefing.
Photo: Reuters
China is in a race for tech dominance with the US, which restricts the export to China of the most cutting-edge silicon chips, designed by industry leader Nvidia and used to train and run artificial intelligence (AI) models.
The data center firm Megaspeed was under scrutiny for possibly steering Nvidia AI chips to China, the report said, citing unnamed sources briefed on the matter.
However, the executive Alice Huang — also known as Huang Le (黃樂), and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Jensen Huang — developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the New York Times said.
That could have given her insights into US President Donald Trump’s thinking around AI, an issue likely to arise during talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) next month.
Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about a year ago and chose not to act on the information, the report said.
Nvidia is the world’s most valuable firm thanks to the global drive to build data centers packed with specialist computer chips and other hardware that runs AI systems.
An Nvidia spokesperson yesterday said that Megaspeed was like any other regional customer and “Jensen’s interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected.”
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security,” they said.
The spokesperson added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China “were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”
AFP attempted to contact Megaspeed for comment, but when calling the phone number listed on its Web site, the person who answered said they were unfamiliar with the company and that the number was a residential line.

Antonelli struck with illness ahead of race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:30 UTC
01:46:30 KST

The biggest weekend in Kimi Antonelli’s motor racing life so far began in silence on Thursday when he was excused from media duties at the Mexico City Grand Prix due to a viral illness.
Instead of attending news conferences and talking to reporters at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, the 20-year-old Italian was left to rest and recover ahead of his expected confirmation as Formula One’s youngest champion and first Italian in 73 years.
A spokesperson for his Mercedes team said that Antonelli was feeling under the weather with a viral illness and was excused from the media day by ruling body the International Automobile Federation (FIA) “as a precaution to give him the chance to rest.”
Photo: Reuters
“We expect him to be back tomorrow,” the team said.
The precocious runaway leader of the drivers’ title race would normally have faced a heavy schedule ahead of such a potentially momentous race. He is 123 points clear of nearest rival and Mercedes teammate George Russell and 124 ahead of Ferrari’s seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton.
He can clinch the title, even if Russell wins, by finishing ninth or better and will be champion if either one of his two title rivals fails to win — even if he finishes pointless or does not take part.
Antonelli was not the only driver to go down with illness ahead of the high-altitude second race of a Transamerican triple-header of consecutive races in Texas, Mexico and Brazil as Cadillac’s Valtteri Bottas was also unwell and declared to be absent.
In a statement, the American team said that it had “taken the decision to allow him a day of rest, to support his recovery.”
If Antonelli is too ill to race, his seat is likely to go to Mercedes reserve driver Frederik Vesti, who would make his Formula One racing debut after taking part in six free practice sessions for the team.
Mercedes team chief Toto Wolff called for a cool, calm and collected approach as they bid for part one of a first Formula One double title success.
“The championships are moving closer, but our mindset does not change,” Wolff said, adding that concentration and discipline are essential to success.
“Thinking about the outcome won’t help us achieve it,” he said. “We will stay disciplined, take each session as it comes and concentrate on doing all the fundamentals well.”
Meanwhile, Hamilton said he wants to make sure Ferrari secure second spot in the constructors’ championship.
With five races remaining on the schedule, Hamilton is behind both Mercedes drivers in the championship with 241 points — just one point behind Russell.
For the seven-time world champion, the personal achievement of overhauling Russell is less important than Ferrari’s push to hold its place behind series-leading Mercedes.
Second place “is not something I focus on. Winning the championship is the only thing I care about,” Hamilton said.

EDITORIAL: Elder abuse in a super-aged society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:26 UTC
01:46:26 KST

Discussions about the implications of Taiwan’s demographic structure primarily focus on economic factors — from the shrinking workforce and under-enrolled schools to a financially strained healthcare system. However, less attention has been paid to costs that are more difficult to quantify.
The latest data from the Ministry of Health and Welfare revealed that the number of reported cases of elder abuse in Taiwan rose to 26,684 last year from 20,182 in 2022 — a 32 percent increase in just three years.
The figure might seem reasonable considering that the proportion of people aged 65 or older is growing, with Taiwan officially becoming a super-aged society last year. However, a bit of math dispels that reasoning. In the same three-year period, Taiwan’s elderly population grew by about 15 percent, meaning that reported cases of elder abuse rose at a disproportionately faster rate.
Before considering how to address this issue, it is important to understand what elder abuse entails: inflicting physical, emotional, psychological and financial harm on older people, as well as neglect. Age, gender, health, finances, family dynamics and culture can all affect risk.
Aside from the obvious physical and psychological harm caused to victims of elder abuse, more severe cases can lead to reduced quality of life or even death. A lack of data makes it particularly difficult to address, especially for countries with a higher proportion of elderly people such as Taiwan.
Government efforts to raise awareness and promote the 113 domestic violence hotline, alongside population growth, likely explain some of the increase.
However, elder abuse is underreported worldwide, and many cases in Taiwan are likely still going unnoticed, partially due to the cultural and family pressures that can discourage people from seeking help. Research suggests that elder abuse is most often reported by third parties rather than victims themselves.
More than 85 percent of reported cases involved the victim’s descendants or spouse. Older people might be reluctant to report family members due to embarrassment, shame or fear that their abusive family member would stop supporting them.
Many working children in Taiwan also financially support their elderly parents, and sometimes even act as their primary caregivers. The overwhelming pressure as a result of these compound responsibilities can lead to resentment and might give rise to conflict or abuse.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare has also said that financial abuse can coincide with psychological and physical violence, particularly if adult children depend on their parents’ money.
However, one issue with relying on third-party reporting to address the issue is that it requires that a third party can detect signs of abuse in the first place. Physical injuries might be visible, but emotional abuse, financial control and neglect are harder to identify. Older people who are socially isolated, have dementia or depend on their abusers for daily care can be especially difficult to reach.
The rise in reported cases suggests that government awareness campaigns have been successful to some extent. However, greater emphasis must be placed on identifying and addressing the underlying causes of abuse.
Financial insecurity, gender inequality, the demands of long-term caregiving and unresolved family conflicts can all create conditions in which abuse is more likely to occur. Expanding access to long-term care services and counseling, respite care and practical caregiver training would help families manage the demands of care before they become crises. At the same time, it is essential to fundamentally challenge the cultural stigmas surrounding family conflict that discourage people from seeking help.
It is equally important that elderly people be given more opportunities to participate in community activities and maintain social connections, making it easier for others to notice when something is wrong. Local governments, community organizations and neighborhood networks should cooperate to ensure that elderly residents are not socially isolated.
The authorities should continue to publicize the 113 hotline, promote awareness of the signs of abuse and make clear that neighbors, friends, relatives and caregivers can report suspected abuse even when victims cannot. Local agencies must ensure reports receive timely follow-up and elderly people have access to social workers and legal assistance.
As Taiwan’s population continues to age, the demands on families and the systems meant to support them will only become heavier, as will these risk factors. Addressing elder abuse requires a collective effort, with families, communities and government agencies all playing a role in protecting the vulnerable.

Lawmakers on Thursday disagreed with a government-proposed measure to stop alimony payments to recipients who have remarried, a rift that could delay Cabinet-backed Civil Code reforms.
Ministry of Justice officials and legislators butted heads over the right to alimony at a hearing on the proposed changes to laws governing marriage and divorce at the Legislative Yuan’s Judiciary and Organic Laws and Statutes Committee.
Deputy Minister of Justice Huang Mou-hsin (黃謀信) told lawmakers that divorcees who remarry should not need continued financial support from their former spouse.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
The Cabinet’s draft act does not make financial hardship the sole metric for alimony eligibility, he said in response to criticism from Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Fan Yun (范雲).
The draft act’s reference to hardship was meant to ensure divorcees in urgent financial need would receive alimony; it does not bar divorcees in other circumstances from access to such payments, Huang said.
Fan said the ministry should remove references to financial hardship altogether, as the standard could prevent people who were not poor, but otherwise deserving, from receiving alimony.
The ministry should reconsider the proposal to terminate the right to alimony upon the recipient’s remarriage, she said.
Remarriage would not make up for the career opportunities and income divorcees lost due to their previous marriage, which spousal support payments were intended to compensate, Fan said.
Lawyer Chien Jung-tsung (簡榮宗) told the hearing that the bill conflated subsistence support and financial losses incurred from the division of labor within a marriage, which are separate causes for awarding alimony.
The draft act stipulates that people who intermittently cohabited for three years out of a five-year period should be deemed to have entered a spousal relationship with potential for alimony payments upon the relationship’s break up.
Lawmakers and lawyers present at the hearing agreed with the proposal.
Juvenile and Family Department Director-General Lien Yu-chun (連育群) voiced objections, saying that cumulative cohabitation would be difficult to prove in court.
Allowing litigants to present and dispute the length of a discontinuous relationship would significantly increase the time the court needs to render a ruling for lawsuits, which would be detrimental to judicial efficiency, he said.
