Himalayan Communities Are Relying on Centuries-Old Water Solutions In the Face of Climate Change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:55:56 UTC
00:55:56 KST

The word Laya describes the natural rhythm that has carried the people of the Himalayas through monsoons and drought for centuries. Across the peaks and glaciers, the populated mid-hills and the foothills, communities have harmonized their calendars to the pulsing of water.
Where annual rain falls in just four months, these master engineers funnel rooftop rainwater through handmade bamboo piping into gravel pits to recharge underground wells, maintaining them at the annual festivals. They adapt to the climate by unearthing ancient subterranean medieval stone spout networks for drinking, washing, and bathing.
But there’s another Sanskrit word used in Hindi called Pralaya, passed down through oral tradition like Himalayan myth. It means the melting away of places that no longer exist.
“Recent flooding in Nepal was a pralaya,” says hydrometeorologist and environmental scientist Ngamindra Dahal, chairperson of the Nepal Water Conservation Foundation (NWCF) and executive board member of the South Asian Meteorological Association. “We’ve never witnessed anything like it.”
Himalayans have fallen out of sync with nature at no fault of their own. As earth’s largest swath of ice outside the poles thaws from the unprecedented rapid global warming, high- and mid-mountain villages across eight countries of the Hindu Kush and Himalayan mountain regions have entered a new world of extremes: too little and too much water.
The Himalayas are losing glacier mass 65% faster than a decade ago. The impacts will be felt by 2 billion Asians across 12 major downstream river basins by 2050. And by 2100, it’s projected that 80% of glacier mass will be lost. The reality of dangerous cloudburst floods and water scarcity is, however, already being felt.
On Aug. 26, a 55 million-ton, 93-m.p.h. ice-rock avalanche triggered by a glacier collapse in Nepal near the Tibet border killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands more still missing. Meanwhile, the Nepali government will drain four massive glacial lakes to reduce the danger of yet another catastrophic flood.
The vulnerable, historically low-polluting country has been waiting for a response to its request for compensation from high-emitting nations for the damage created in part by this climate disaster. And on Oct. 22, Nepal became the first country approved for a provisional payout from the U.N.’s Loss and Damage Fund, securing over $21.6 million for recovery from the catastrophic floods. Meanwhile, with deepening uncertainty about the planet’s most basic natural resource, Himalayan people forge on charting their own solutions to save their homes by reviving ancient water systems, building artificial glaciers, and uncovering hidden flood risks.
“The Himalaya is often described as Asia's water tower, but that metaphor is dangerously passive if it makes the mountains sound like a stable reservoir. What the laya-to-pralaya concept clarifies is that the Himalaya is a living, dynamic system—and that climate change is compressing geological time,” says Dahal. “What once happened across generations may now happen within one.”
Reviving Lifelines
For centuries, perennial springs, or mool, have dictated how Himalayan communities live their lives. But that trusted relationship is breaking down. Still, resilient Nepali communities are adapting to the shifting environment of melting snow and ice and unpredictable monsoon rain by reclaiming historic infrastructure.
To combat water shortages often from erratic rainfall shifts disrupted by climate change, they’re reviving an ancient network of underground terracotta canals that channel water to sunken stone spouts, some chiseled as early as the 6th century. Known as hiti or dhara, these water systems connect to ponds that absorb monsoon rain, recharging the groundwater table to keep spouts flowing during dry season. In places like the Kathmandu Valley, local governments are actively restoring and rerouting this massive ancient spring network, originally engineered by the Licchavi and Malla dynasties and now threatened by climate change and rapid urbanization.
Through the NWCF and an intergovernmental organization protecting mountain environments and cultures called the International Center for Integrated Mountain Development, Dahal is replenishing water supplies by taking inventory of more recent drying springs to gauge a new baseline of water availability.
"A community may have adequate water in its landscape but lack the investment to bring it to households,” says Dahal. “Conversely, a community may have taps everywhere but an increasingly unreliable source.”
He’s teaching local communities how to revive and reroute their drying life sources based on changing water movement underground, by tracking seasonal flow rates, water quality, and geographic elevations. Once new water patterns are mapped, Dahal helps communities design localized water-sharing agreements and storage, and adapt household rainwater harvesting systems—in a grass-roots water governance model aligned with the Nepal government adaptation plan. “When a pipe breaks, you repair the pipe; when a tank collapses, you rebuild the tank,” says Dahal. “But when the spring itself stops flowing, repairing the infrastructure solves nothing.”
Hidden Risk
Up in Nepal’s Limi Valley, families are confronting a different kind of uncertainty. Tashi Lhazom recalls being 13, studying at a Kathmandu boarding school, when she received a phone call from her remote high-alpine village. On the other line her mother simply said, “You better study hard because you have nothing to eat here anymore.”
An avalanche had struck her 1,000 year-old ancestral valley—just two years after a massive glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), a sudden violent release of water from a melting glacial lake—and had taken with hundreds of the yaks that were her nomadic herding family’s generational livelihood. This went against everything Limi Valley indigenous villagers had known about trusting the mountain Gods.
“My people believed the Gods were angry with them for being greedy. That was their cultural rationalization,” explains Lhazom, now 26. When what villagers assumed was another catastrophic GLOF washed away bridges and a hydropower plant in the Limi Valley in May 2025, Lhazom was ready to do something about it.
“I couldn’t let the community blame itself for something it was not responsible when I knew it was those emitting greenhouse gases who were partially to blame,” says Lhazom, one of the first from Limi Valley to earn a college degree and now an activist among a wave of Gen Zs fighting climate destruction in Nepal.
She tracked down climate scientists and politicians, urging them to investigate the cause of the flood, until a field team finally agreed to come. After Lhazom directed them around closed flooded roads to local water sources, they trekked upstream, reaching glacial terrain at 17,000 ft. to learn the truth: It wasn’t a GLOF this time.
Instead, thawing permafrost—the ice that acts as glue to bind mountain rock—was without warning, draining trapped small “thermokarst” lakes, releasing massive volumes of underground water down the slope. As a result of their investigation, that 2025 Limi Valley flood was reclassified as Nepal’s first-ever recorded thermokarst lake flood.
After sharing drone footage, photos, and satellite images with the scientists who proved the flood mechanism, Lhazom became co-author of a September 2025 comment paper in the Communications Earth and Environment Journal alerting the world to this overlooked risk.
It led to an acknowledgement and warning in a July 2026 scientific paper about the increased risk of thermokarst lake floods due to climate change—not just in the Himalayas, but across Peru, China, and other high-alpine mountain environments. And from it, a newly defined dangerous hazard category, called Small Alpine Lake Outbursts (SALOs), emerged.
“Limi is fortunate enough to know they are in danger, but there are hundreds of ‘Limi Valleys’ across the Himalaya. There are still villages whose mountains have not been studied. They don't know if they are living in danger or not,” says Lhazom, whose 2024 film documenting the Limi Valley flooding, No Monastery No Village, was screened at Banff.
But most importantly to Lhazom, she was able to convince her Indigenous people of the Limi Valley that the flooding was not their fault. Since finally putting them on the map, Lhazom has been working to help secure government funds to resettle the remaining families away from danger on nearby ancestral land.
As Nepal’s politicians scramble after this year’s floods to reform the legal framework for disaster relocation, Lhazom is traveling high in the mountains to deliver relief for the victims among 33,000 now in need of permanent resettlement after being banned from rebuilding their homes along the permanently destabilized high-risk mountainside.
“The frozen water banks we know are melting, and that means flooding that can sweep an entire village away within a fraction of a second. Our water sources are getting thinner and fewer and that is a grave concern,” says Lhazom. “But what’s most heartbreaking for these mountain people is knowing they can never go home.”
Generational families have no choice but to accept the erasure of their ancient Indigenous settlements. “The mountain is more than land. It is our identity, our history. The water spirits we worship inspired our folk songs and Indigenous wisdom, and polluting means you are being disrespectful to the water spirits,” says Lhazom. “It’ll be a challenge to convince the people to live in safer places, but I don't want them to be in a place that could kill them.”
Growing Artificial Glaciers
Northwest of Lhazom’s home, in Ladakh, India, where –40°winds whip through a remote desert on an 11,500-ft. shelf in the shadow of the Himalaya’s highest northern peaks, the people rely on a single water source: melting glacial ice, now covered in soot from vehicles carrying adventure tourists acclimating in its capital of Leh.
The region’s unbearably beautiful and dry glacial-dependent settlements could become the next Himalayan ghost villages—joining the 2,000 already abandoned from drying glaciers, water scarcity, drought, and unpredictable monsoons in places like Spiti and the Uttarakhand, India, and the Upper Mustang of Nepal.
But here in the “Third Pole,” climate activist and mechanical engineer Sonam Wangchuk is blending modern technology with his traditional knowledge. In 2015, inspired by stories of his ancestors moving “parent” glaciers into a cave to make “baby” glaciers—based on the early work of “the Iceman of India”—Wangchuk developed the science to revive the ancient cultural practice of grafting glaciers. He grew new ice to reverse water scarcity in Ladakh.
He ran a mile a mile-long pipe from a glacier spring down a steep slope; at the bottom in the shade the water shot straight into the air and, in the dead of winter, froze. Over a month, the ice grew into a multistory conical artificial glacier fountain he called an ice stupa after the sacred Buddhist dome-shaped shrines. Rather than wasting down the mountain, his invention preserves a critical water supply for an extra month through June when farmers need it most for planting.
Word of Wangchuk’s ice storage traveled, and he built ice stupas in numerous Himalayan villages facing water scarcity, even allowing a community from Ladakh’s abandoned village of Kulum to return home.
Beneath this elegant solution lurked a critical flaw. The pipes feeding the stupas were freezing. But working with longtime colleague Surya Balasubramanian, who earned his PhD in Switzerland in ice reservoir behavior, Wangchuk last year brought the ice stupas back to life through automation. By integrating solar-powered, computer-controlled sensor networks and motorized valves, the water flow could be turned off remotely to prevent the pipes from icing, ensuring 80% of the incoming spring water is frozen and stored.
“We innovated a method to either spray water from fountains or drain the pipes using valves controlled by weather and pipeline sensors,” says Balasubramania, who in 2023 independently launched Acres of Ice to scale the ice stupas.
Today, they’ve built or supported 160 ice stupas across Ladakh, Nepal, Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan, Chile, and Pakistan, each standing up to 12 stories and capable of storing 3.2 million gallons.
But the fight may never be over for Wangchuk, who knows the temporary nature of his adaptation strategy won’t outlive the glaciers. He is now testing a new application: sourcing water for his stupa from a dangerous glacial lake to help prevent it from collapsing and sending a massive GLOF wave down the mountain—and using natural refrigeration to refreeze the lakes.
With the growing threat of climate-induced glacier collapse, intensifying monsoons, and prolonged dry spells, the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region is nearing a tipping point. As global temperatures rise, the people who have learned to adapt to harsh conditions for centuries have little control over the destabilization of their ancestral homes. Still, they look to nature for a way forward through simple innovation to make every drop of water count. The question is: Will it be enough?
“There’s very little that can be done at this point to protect against glaciers in vulnerable places in the Himalayas, so these communities suffer and pay the price for what the rest of the world does,” says Wangchuk. “The recent avalanche in Nepal is an alarm bell for the rest of the world to mend our ways on this planet.”

15:55:52 UTC
00:55:52 KST

US-Russia cooperation in Arctic: Why energy-hungry economies have big hopes
Speaking at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow on October 27, President Vladimir Putin warned that excluding Russia from global gas markets would raise costs for consumers. He also revealed discussions with potential American partners for exploring cooperation in Arctic gas development. This is happening even as restrictions on Russian energy projects remain in place.
Putin’s remarks come amid continued disruption to LNG supplies. QatarEnergy has extended the suspension of certain deliveries into December, while India’s LNG import bill rose 23% to $8.5 billion during April-September, despite volumes increasing by just 4.4%.
For import-dependent economies such as India, the question is whether prospective Arctic cooperation could eventually expand supply options, or whether sanctions, pricing and transportation constraints will keep that possibility beyond commercial reach.
Arctic gas cooperation meets commercial reality
Russia’s interest in Arctic cooperation extends beyond developing its vast gas reserves. Following Putin’s October 27 remarks, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak clarified that discussions with Washington concerned potential joint development of gas fields and LNG liquefaction facilities, including opportunities involving Russian infrastructure.
One possible example has already surfaced. Russia’s Novatek has acknowledged agreements to provide technology for the proposed $25 billion Polar Train LNG project in Alaska. The venture aims to use Russian liquefaction infrastructure for American gas exports, although its implementation remains subject to regulatory approvals.
Russia and the US compete for LNG buyers, yet Arctic development could give their energy companies reasons to work together. Russia could find opportunities to deploy its Arctic expertise and attract investment, while American developers could benefit from technology and infrastructure suited to challenging northern conditions.
Yet commercial interest alone cannot overcome the obstacles facing Arctic LNG development. Washington sanctioned Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project in November 2023, subsequently extending restrictions to companies and vessels involved in supplying equipment and transporting LNG from the project.
In September, the Novatek-led Arctic LNG 2 project sought approximately $1 billion in damages from South Korea’s Hanwha Ocean in an arbitration dispute over cancelled contracts for specialized ice-class LNG carriers, highlighting the shipping complications facing Russian Arctic gas development.
The regulatory environment remains equally complicated. On October 16, President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act, but the decision did not automatically remove restrictions imposed separately on Russian LNG projects.
Beyond regulatory approvals, Arctic operations depend on a limited fleet of specialized carriers capable of navigating ice-covered waters. Seasonal conditions further restrict their deployment, making transportation capacity a critical consideration for new projects.
India’s LNG security faces an Arctic test
India’s response to recent LNG disruptions offers an indication of how importing economies may approach future supply arrangements. According to Kpler data for the month of October, the US, Oman and Nigeria accounted for 68% of India’s LNG imports between March and September, against 25% a year earlier. Qatar’s share fell sharply before shipments began recovering this month.
India’s changing LNG suppliers expose a distinction between diversifying sources and reducing exposure to international prices. With more than a third of its LNG reportedly sourced through spot purchases, Indian buyers remain exposed to price fluctuations even when physical supplies are available. Adding Russian Arctic LNG to India’s supplier portfolio would not necessarily change that exposure unless the contracts offered a different pricing structure or greater protection against international price swings.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects India’s LNG requirements could reach 64 billion cubic metres annually by 2030, with the gap between contracted supplies and projected demand widening after 2028.
That gap could influence how Indian importers negotiate their next generation of LNG contracts. Long-term agreements offer greater supply certainty, while shorter commitments provide flexibility when demand or prices change. The balance between them will become increasingly important as India seeks to expand natural gas consumption.
Transport economics add another dimension. Analysis by Reuters in May estimated that shipping LNG from Russia’s Yamal project to India’s Kochi terminal via the Northern Sea Route could cost approximately $3.80 per million British thermal units (MMBtu), compared with $2.60-$2.70 through the Suez Canal using transshipment facilities at Murmansk.
In August, the Indian authorities announced plans for a joint Russia–India pilot voyage along the Northern Sea Route in 2027, alongside a bilateral cooperation agreement that is being negotiated. In September, Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov confirmed these plans, stating in the future, Russian-Indian shipments along the NSR could reach 5 million tons annually.
The proposed voyage could help establish whether the NSR offers practical advantages for India-bound cargoes. For LNG, however, that assessment would require more than a successful transit, including evidence of year-round operating reliability and the costs of deploying specialised vessels.
Asia’s LNG market confronts a new supply equation
China offers an early indication of how Arctic LNG is entering Asian markets despite Western restrictions. According to S&P Global Energy, Chinese imports of Russian LNG increased nearly 25% during January-July 2026, supported partly by discounted Arctic LNG 2 cargoes. Reuters reported in June that Beijing was preparing a second receiving terminal for the sanctioned project’s shipments.
Meanwhile, Kpler estimates cited by Reuters on October 22 suggest Asian LNG arrivals could reach 23.31 million tonnes in October, their highest level in three months despite elevated prices.
Yet stronger imports do not necessarily signal sustained demand growth. The IEA reported that Asian spot LNG prices averaged $17.50/MMBtu in the second quarter, up 45% year-on-year, and projected a 0.5% decline in regional gas consumption during 2026 as higher prices encouraged fuel switching and reduced industrial demand.
China’s experience contrasts with that of other Asian importers. On October 1, Britain exempted certain Russian LNG shipments to Japan and South Korea from its sanctions restrictions until March 2028, but only for Sakhalin-2 supplies under existing contracts. India, meanwhile, declined an offer of sanctioned Russian LNG in May, according to Reuters, while remaining open to permitted cargoes. These differences show how sanctions compliance and contractual commitments can shape Asian buyers’ access to Russian gas, regardless of the availability of additional supplies.
Prospective US-Russia cooperation could bring additional Arctic gas into international trade, but new production alone would not redraw global LNG supply patterns. For India and other importing economies, the larger question is whether future projects can offer access on terms that improve their existing procurement choices. The Arctic’s next commercial breakthrough may depend as much on reaching buyers as on producing gas.

"The Ukrainian delegation, along with the evacuated residents of Oleshky, set off for Anapa. From there, they will fly to Belarus and then travel home by bus," said Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia.
A convoy of 25 buses and several ambulances arrived in the war-torn city earlier on Friday, bringing food and medicine and helping residents who wished to leave.
“At this moment, the humanitarian operation is underway in Oleshky,” Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an post online. Budanov is not part of the Ukrainian delegation in the city.
Officials from Ukraine and Russia have worked together on the rare humanitarian mission, offering a brief moment of cooperation amid the ongoing war.
"We are completing our humanitarian mission in Oleshky," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said in a video on Telegram, adding that a "convoy with those who are going to the territory of the Russian Federation is heading to the territory of the Russian Federation".
Around 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, according to local authorities and volunteers.
The local ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region is expected to remain in place until Sunday evening.
“Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will have the opportunity to do so safely,” Russia and Ukraine said in separate, identical statements. “Those who choose to stay may remain and will receive all the humanitarian support they need.”
Although Ukrainian-controlled territory is just a few kilometres across the Dnipro River from Oleshky, evacuees will have to travel hundreds of kilometres through Russia and Belarus before entering northern Ukraine, according to Ukrainian public television. The exact evacuation route has not been disclosed.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said on X that he will "personally continue to coordinate the humanitarian mission."
Despite the local ceasefire, fighting on Friday continued in other areas. Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed to have intercepted more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine reported Russian strikes involving ballistic missiles, other missiles and dozens of drones.

EU to fast-track €45 billion for Ukraine amid acute financial crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:54:54 UTC
00:54:54 KST

In 2027, the EU will provide Ukraine with €32 billion in military aid and €13 billion in budget support. But more funds will be needed as Russia escalates.
The European Union intends to accelerate the disbursement of its €90 billion support loan to Ukraine as the country faces a financial crunch amid Russia's all-out escalation and blockade in the Black Sea.
The loan is split evenly: €45 billion for 2026, with payments underway, and €45 billion for 2027. Initially, the credit was meant to last until the end of next year, but the brutality of the war has upended the calculation.
As a result, Brussels will concentrate funds in the first half of 2027 to avoid a cut-off of assistance that could have catastrophic consequences on the ground.
The second €45 billion envelope will allocate €31.7 billion for the military and €13.3 billion for the budget, according to a strategy published on Friday by the European Commission.
The €31.7 billion will be paid out gradually as Kyiv submits new contracts for weapons. The submissions can begin this year to ensure timely deliveries in 2027.
The €13.3 billion will be conditional on reforms, some of which relate to Ukraine's accession process. EU leaders have urged the country to keep the legislative pace on track.
A €3.7 billion payment has already been delayed.
"We are providing Ukraine with much-needed predictability and helping maintain essential public services," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"Together with our allies, we must also do everything in our power to mount pressure on Russia to stop its barbaric war of aggression."
Ahead of the announcement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked Brussels to speed up disbursements.
"The sooner we start receiving the corresponding tranches for our drone production, air defence procurement, budget support and other vital expenditures, the better our position in 2027 will be," he said.
In the meantime, the Commission is searching for ways to fill the €70 billion shortfall that Ukraine faces next year, which will require fresh funding on top of the existing loan.
Commission officials insist the bloc will cover no more than two-thirds of the gap, roughly €46 billion, with the remainder to be handled by other allies. Joint debt has quickly emerged as the frontrunnerto plug the hole.
An internal document seen by Euronews identifies three main reasons for the deficit.
First, the prolongation of the war, now well into its fifth year. When Brussels designed the €90 billion loan, it did so under the assumption the conflict would end sometime in 2026. The premise, which raised eyebrows last year, has now come apart.
Second, the intensification of Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure and the blockade of the Black Sea, which are "weakening economic activity and Ukraine's capacity to raise domestic revenues", further compounding its reliance on global donors.
Third, the decrease in assistance from non-EU allies. The document says that if all NATO allies deliver on their pledges made at the summit in July, the gap in military aid will be reduced by up to €13 billion next year.
Ukraine's financial needs, the document adds, will be "largely determined" by the ability to resist Russia's airstrikes, which need costly US-made Patriot interceptors.
Kyiv has accused Washington of delaying Patriots that have been paid for with European money. The impasse has been linked with US President Donald Trump's insistence that Ukraine cease attacks on Russia's oil refineries, claiming they raise global fuel prices.
On Friday, a Ukranian drone attack was reported at the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Russia's Samara region.

New Jersey Governor Weighs Blocking Russian Diesel Shipment From State Port
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill stated that she is considering blocking a shipment of Russian diesel from arriving at a port in the state, KYW Newsradio reported on October 29.
The Trump administration announced a deal with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, for Russia to supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel to US and global markets. UNITED24 Media reported that the arrangement included an initial shipment of more than 300,000 tonnes, with larger deliveries expected to follow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a statement to KYW Newsradio, Sherrill commented on US President Donald Trump’s fuel agreement with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, arguing that it has failed to reduce energy costs for American consumers.
“Donald Trump isn’t doing anything to bring down gas prices, diesel prices, or costs,” Sherrill stated. “Instead, he is lining Vladimir Putin’s pockets at the expense of American consumers and our democratic ally Ukraine.”
The diesel volumes involved are unlikely to materially lower US fuel prices. UNITED24 Media calculated that the initial 300,000-tonne shipment would cover less than two hours of global diesel demand, while analysts described the expected effect on prices as marginal.
Sherrill stated that her administration is examining possible steps to prevent the shipment from entering New Jersey.
“Make no mistake: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin is corrupt and illegal, and I am evaluating options to stop it from arriving at a port in New Jersey,” she told KYW Newsradio.
The shipment is also facing pressure from Congress. Dockworkers launch global strike against Israeli and US military shipments (VIDEOS)
Dockworkers across five continents have launched a coordinated anti-war strike, targeting Israeli arms shipments, US military cargo, and the growing militarization of civilian ports.
Organizers say more than 25 unions are mobilizing across 113 ports in 22 countries and regions on Friday in an unprecedented international action. The campaign includes 24-hour strikes, shorter walkouts, blockades, and solidarity rallies.
Major European ports joining the action include Genoa, Marseille, Le Havre, Hamburg, Valencia, Barcelona, and Piraeus. Beyond Europe, protests are planned at Tangier Med in Morocco, Nhava Sheva and Chennai in India, and Oakland and San Francisco in the US, with further actions across Türkiye, Cyprus, Sweden, Denmark, Ireland, Portugal, Brazil, Mexico, and Australia.
France’s CGT Ports et Docks has called 24-hour strikes across 24 ports, while Italy’s USB has declared a nationwide general strike, with protests in more than 40 cities. Unions in Germany, Greece, Spain, India, and the US are also taking part.
Dockworkers at the port of Piraeus, Greece, walked off the job as part of a global day of action, with protesters in more than 100 ports worldwide striking against the arms trade with Israel.

Dockworkers at Piraeus, Greece’s largest port, were among the first to join the action, with a three-hour stoppage scheduled from 08:00 to 11:00 GMT. Other Greek maritime unions announced 24-hour strikes affecting seven ports, threatening ferry services to the country’s islands.

Videos of demonstrations and gatherings at other ports have emerged online, although the full extent of the disruption to shipping operations remains unclear as actions are taking place at different times.
What do the dockworkers want?
The unions demand a halt to weapons, ammunition, military equipment, and troop shipments through commercial ports, targeting both Israeli and US military supply chains. They also oppose turning civilian ports into military hubs and diverting public funds into rearmament while workers face stagnant wages, job insecurity, and worsening conditions.

It says it identified 3,400 shipments of US military cargo through 67 ports in 42 countries over ten months. Is it the first strike of this kind?
Dockworkers have challenged military shipments for years, though resistance was largely scattered and localized. Since 2019, workers in Italy, Greece, Morocco, and France have staged sporadic blockades and stoppages, targeting arms shipments to Israel, US bases, and other conflict zones.
The movement gained momentum in late 2025 after Israel intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla, a 40-plus-vessel convoy attempting to deliver aid to blockaded Gaza. Hundreds of activists were detained, sparking strikes and port blockades across Europe. UK Defence Secretary warns Putin may yet turn on NATO
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:52:39 GMT
00:52:39 KST

Britain has to invest and has to be ready because President Putin is waging a war in Europe while saying he has no interest in one, the Defence Secretary has said, describing investment in capability, in the defence industrial base and in alliances as the things that make war less likely, according to remarks made to reporters in Glasgow.
Wes Streeting was speaking at BAE Systems Scotstoun, where a new offsets policy was announced. Asked by this publication what his warning that Britain has around a thousand days to be ready to fight and win a war means for the armed forces and for the public, and what sacrifices the public are being asked to make to get there, he said: “Well, we’re investing in our capability, we’re investing in our defence industrial base, and we’re investing in our alliances. Those things make us stronger, and the stronger we are, the stronger our deterrence, and the less likely we are to find ourselves at war.
“We don’t seek confrontation with Russia. We have no quarrel with the Russian people. But what we can’t avoid is the hard reality that at the same time that President Putin says he’s not interested in war in Europe, he’s currently waging one, and he gave the Ukrainians those assurances that he had no plans to invade only weeks before the Russian invasion took place.
“So in that climate, we have to invest. We have to be ready. And in terms of what we’re asking of the country, as the Chancellor’s Budget showed this week, we are asking people to make that contribution right across government, and so defence is our number one duty, our number one priority, and that’s why it’s my responsibility to make sure that every penny that goes in is well spent, and that every bit of value we can extract for jobs and growth here in Scotland and right across the United Kingdom is realised. That’s my commitment.”
The contribution he describes falls across government and therefore on departmental budgets, and his answer turned on deterrence, which holds that a force strong enough to make an attack unprofitable is a force that never has to fight.
He was speaking after the announcement of a new offsets policy, under which overseas companies winning British defence contracts worth more than £50 million can be required to put benefits back into the country worth up to the full value of the contract, through jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers or transfers of technology. A central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor each arrangement, and the policy applies to a select number of procurements from April 2027. Ministers consulted industry on the approach earlier this year.
Asked what role Scotland will play in the Defence Investment Plan, John Healey, who moved from defence to the Treasury and delivered Wednesday’s Budget as Chancellor, said: “Defence is our number one priority. We also announced today the defence secretary and policy, where people have seen this is a government that will direct our defence investment first and foremost in British jobs and British businesses. But there will be things that we need to buy from abroad and from allies.
“So Norwegians, for instance, are part procuring some of this portion behind us, and they will require us because they have a policy that we’re now introducing for the first time ever in Britain, which we call an offset policy. We will buy some of the things the Norwegians produce that we can’t here.
“Now, in future, when Britain places contracts abroad, we’ll make sure that those we place those contracts with invest in Britain as well, jobs, business support, innovation, so that we can make sure that every pound of British taxpayers’ money works twice.”
Norway ordered five Type 26 frigates from Britain in a £10 billion deal supporting 2,000 jobs on the Clyde, and Oslo has run an industrial cooperation requirement of its own for decades, obliging foreign suppliers of significant equipment to place work with Norwegian firms. More than £35.2 billion has been spent with overseas industry since 2016, eleven per cent of direct departmental expenditure with industry and commerce, while 85 per cent already goes to British firms.
Streeting also attacked the Scottish National Party’s position on nuclear weapons, responding to the First Minister’s claim that the government is leaving Scotland short of defence. He said: “We’ve got HMS Prince of Wales currently out on a major exercise now, so I think it’s very visible proof that what the First Minister said is both irresponsible and unfounded. I don’t think the SNP should be playing party politics with national defence and security.
“In terms of the risk of leaving the UK with insufficient defence, one of the biggest risks facing that security is the SNP’s position on unilateral nuclear disarmament. It is by far and away the most important deterrent that we have, and it’s not just the UK’s deterrent, it’s NATO’s deterrent. So any time the SNP says that a separate Scotland can be a NATO member, they have to first explain how their white flag policy on unilateral nuclear disarmament would work under a nuclear alliance.”
The party voted narrowly in 2012 to drop its opposition to NATO membership while keeping its opposition to nuclear weapons, a position that would require an independent Scotland to join an alliance whose strategic concept describes nuclear weapons as the supreme guarantee of allied security, while removing the British deterrent from Faslane and Coulport. New members are admitted by unanimous agreement of the existing ones.
Asked whether Scotland is a target for Russia, Streeting said: “The people of Scotland and people right across the United Kingdom can draw comfort and security in the knowledge that we have some extraordinary capability at our disposal. Across our armed forces, as well as our special forces, and the protection of the NATO alliance, and that principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.
“I don’t think that Putin would be foolish enough to seek a direct war with NATO today. What I can’t be certain of is that at some point in the future he might not try, and that’s NATO’s threat assessment, and that’s why we are building our capability, building our defence industry, including here in Scotland, and building our alliances so that we are strong and therefore able to deter any potential Russian threat.”
He added that governments across the United Kingdom and local councils should play their part in national resilience, work led by the Cabinet Office through the Home Defence Programme, whose public awareness campaign launched on 22 October.
Healey rejected the Scottish government’s claim that its budget is being cut by £650 million in real terms, telling reporters: “No, they’re wrong. The Scottish budget is bigger than it’s been before.”
The Budget set a target date of 2030 for defence spending to reach three per cent of gross domestic product, with the route to the NATO commitment of three and a half per cent by 2035 left to next year’s Spending Review, and the Defence Investment Plan is backed by £298 billion over four years. The Scottish defence economy is worth £2.5 billion and directly supports 12,200 jobs, including 300 roles in Edinburgh on a £453 million Typhoon radar contract.

Russia Gets Another Green Light in International Sports as Hockey Teams Are Cleared to Return
Alexander Ovechkin of Russia celebrates after he scores his team's opening goal during the IIHF World Championship at Ericsson Globe on May 17, 2012 in Stockholm, Sweden. (Source: Getty Images)
Russia’s national ice hockey team is set to return to international competitions in the 2026/27 season following a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev announced, according to Russian outlet Vedomosti on October 30.
Degtyarev said the ruling requires the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) to allow Russian teams to participate in relevant international tournaments during the upcoming season.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the minister, the CAS decision is final and cannot be appealed, effectively ending the legal dispute over Russia’s participation in international ice hockey competitions.
The IIHF also acknowledged the ruling, stating on its official website that it would comply with the court’s decision and urgently assess the measures necessary to facilitate the return of Russian national teams.
Russian ice hockey teams have been excluded from IIHF-sanctioned competitions since February 2022, following Russia’s launch of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. During the suspension, the federation repeatedly reviewed the possibility of reinstating Russian teams but ultimately maintained the restrictions.
According to Vedomosti, ice hockey has now become the second major team sport after volleyball in which restrictions on Russian participation have been lifted.
The earlier decision to readmit Russian athletes to international volleyball competitions drew criticism from Polish Volleyball Federation President Sebastian Świderski, who argued that allowing them to return was premature while Russia’s war against Ukraine continued.
“I probably learned about the IOC's decision from social media. We did not receive any official information. I was convinced it was fake news. I later confirmed the information through informal sources,” Świderski said in an interview with Sport.pl on July 9.
He also questioned the justification for reinstating Russian athletes, describing the decision as “strange” and stressing that “nothing has changed on our eastern border.”
“I invite the gentlemen who made this decision to visit Ukraine so they can see what everyday life looks like there. I wonder how they would behave if Russia attacked their own country, and whether they would make such decisions so quickly under those circumstances,” he added.
Why it matters
The gradual reinstatement of Russian athletes in international sports has sparked debate since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine with Belarusian support. Although Russian and Belarusian competitors were initially barred from international tournaments, several sports federations began relaxing restrictions in early 2023 despite the ongoing war.
The controversy also reflects concerns about Russia’s use of sports as a propaganda tool to legitimize its policies, as reported by Ukraїner. Some Russian athletes have participated in state-sponsored events, publicly endorsed or defended the invasion of Ukraine, and even held military ranks, raising questions about the relationship between Russian sports and the Kremlin’s war effort.
Meanwhile, Russia’s invasion has had severe consequences for Ukraine’s sporting community. According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Youth and Sports, at least 19 Ukrainian athletes remained in Russian captivity as of June 2026, while another 13 were reported missing.
An additional 23 athletes had been released and returned to Ukraine. Ukrainian human rights organizations have urged the international community to increase pressure on Russia to secure the release of those still detained.

Seven Tankers Transporting Russian Diesel Are Heading to USA: Some Are Subject to Sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:50:50 UTC
00:50:50 KST

Seven tankers carrying approximately 288,000 metric tons of Russian diesel fuel are heading to the U.S. Three of them are subject to international sanctions and belong to Russia’s shadow fleet.
This was reported by Greenpeace Ukraine, which tracked the ships’ routes.
The tankers in question are the Taurus, PVT Azura, Agioi Fanendes, Talisman, Leruo, Iblea, and Primorye. Three of them—Talisman, Leruo, and Primorye—are on the sanctions lists of several countries, with the first having been subject to U.S. restrictions since January 2025…
The vessels are currently crossing the Atlantic Ocean, and the first shipments are expected to arrive in early November. To monitor the situation, Greenpeace Ukraine has created an interactive map that shows the tankers’ locations, their cargoes, and their declared ports of destination based on data from the MarineTraffic vessel tracking service and the Kpler analytics platform.
Representatives of the Donald Trump administration are trying to convince American companies to accept Russian diesel. According to The Washington Sun, potential buyers are being offered significant discounts, but they fear legal and reputational consequences.
Some of the fuel was loaded onto ships without prior agreements with customers. The cargo owners have been looking for buyers for several weeks now, but American importers are in no hurry to agree to the shipments.
In particular, the Agioi Fanendes is carrying about 40,000 metric tons of diesel and was originally scheduled to arrive at the Port of New York and New Jersey on November 7. Subsequently, its destination was changed in the tracking system to for orders, meaning there is no specified next port of call.
U.S. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, in his post on social media platform X, called on shipowners to turn back tankers carrying Russian diesel. He sent letters to the owners of Agioi Fanendes and PVT Azura, warning them of potential liability for violating U.S. sanctions laws.
The shipments are taking place following the Trump administration’s decision to temporarily allow the import of Russian diesel. The U.S. Department of the Treasury issued General License No. 135, which authorizes such transactions through April 7, 2027. Meanwhile, Greenpeace has raised concerns about a possible violation of European Union and British sanctions.
The agreements between Washington and Moscow call for an initial shipment of 300,000 metric tons of fuel, another 500,000 metric tons in November, and an additional 1 million metric tons at a later date. Meanwhile, Vladimir Putin’s decree of September 28 restricted access to information regarding Russian energy exports, including routes, counterparties, and transportation infrastructure.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported on U.S. plans to allow some tankers from Russia’s shadow fleet to resume legal operations. The report discussed the possible lifting of restrictions following a change in the vessels’ ownership and their use to transport oil not subject to sanctions.

Ukrainian draft officers charged with torture and kidnapping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:50:20 UTC
00:50:20 KST

Ukrainian draft officers charged with torture and kidnapping
Five Ukrainian military recruitment officials have been arrested on suspicion of abducting and torturing men to force them into military service, the State Bureau of Investigation (DBR) has announced.
According to investigators, the officials rounded up men on the streets of a small town in western Ukraine’s Chernovtsy Region and forcibly took them to a recruitment center, where they were beaten, threatened, and subjected to further abuse.
One victim was allegedly shot in the leg and forced to extract the bullet himself after officers denied him medical care.
In another case, recruitment officers allegedly stalked and abducted a war veteran over a personal dispute.
Investigators also uncovered a bribery scheme in which recruitment officials allegedly extorted over $6,000 in exchange for a detainee’s release.
The five suspects face various charges, including torture, kidnapping, unlawful detention, and bribery. The most serious offenses carry up to 12 years in prison. Investigators are searching for additional victims.
Kiev has struggled with manpower shortages due to heavy battlefield losses in the conflict with Russia, widespread draft evasion, and desertion. The government has tightened mobilization laws and resorted to heavy-handed enforcement to replenish its depleted military ranks.
Earlier this month, the DBR charged a draft officer in Lviv with beating a handcuffed recruit to death. The suspect received a non-custodial sentence for bribery just weeks earlier. In April, investigators referred another case to court involving a conscript who died after being beaten and subjected to electric shocks while being transported. His commanding officer also faced charges for failing to intervene.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner, Dmitry Lubinets, has accused military recruitment officers of routinely violating citizens’ constitutional rights. Earlier this month, he said the authorities opened 39 criminal investigations over alleged abuses in just one month, but no court verdicts were issued in cases of illegal detention and forced transportation to recruitment centers.
Attempts to attract volunteers have also largely failed to gain traction. Kiev’s latest recruitment drive, launched in June, attracted just 8,600 people despite higher pay and shorter service terms, Ukrainskaya Pravda reported this week. The figure includes troops already in service, leaving the actual number of new recruits unclear.

British premier calls for coordinated devolution across UK after summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:49:17 UTC
00:49:17 KST

Aysu Bicer
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called for coordinated devolution across all parts of the UK, warning that no nation should be left behind as England moves ahead with plans to transfer more powers to regional authorities.
Speaking to journalists after this morning's devolution summit, Burnham expressed disappointment over the absence of Northern Ireland's First Minister and Deputy First Minister, saying discussions with Stormont would continue.
"Well, obviously, it's disappointing that the first minister and deputy first minister of Northern Ireland weren't here," he said.
"There was some representation, but we will continue the discussions too with Stormont about how do we take forward the same ideas, the same arrangements to get power down into all parts of the UK."
The summit comes amid growing political tensions, with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland currently led by first ministers from nationalist parties that support independence from the UK.
 
'It's really important that we all move at the same pace together'
Burnham said the devolution agenda was progressing quickly in England, pointing to further measures announced in the budget aimed at expanding regional devolution.
"I don't want to see Scotland left behind. I don't want to see Wales left behind, but also crucially, I don't want to see Northern Ireland left behind," he said.
He stressed the importance of all parts of the UK progressing together, adding: "So it's really important that we all move at the same pace together. And I won’t allow anything to delay that. Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."
On the possibility of additional powers for devolved governments, Burnham said discussions at the summit focused on reindustrialization and employment support.
He said one area under consideration was the devolution of innovation funding to the regional level, with Scotland and Wales expected to determine how the arrangements would work in their respective countries.
"It's about creating those structures at a regional level, and that's a matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," he said.
Burnham added that the UK and devolved governments could work jointly to support regional structures and advance reindustrialization through greater devolution of innovation funding.
The second area of discussion focused on employment support, particularly measures aimed at young people.
"There are too many young people out of work here in Scotland, in Wales, and in England too," Burnham said.
He called for employment support to be localized as much as possible to help young people return to work, describing the issue as a significant challenge facing the UK.
Burnham said further discussions following the meeting of the National Economic Council would examine arrangements for transferring additional employment support powers to Scotland and Wales, with a particular focus on young people.

Vice President Karin addresses internal policy meeting
Vice President of Kazakhstan Erlan Karin chaired a national meeting on domestic policy at Akorda, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the Akorda press service, the meeting brought together heads of presidential administration departments, cabinet members, deputy regional governors, and heads of domestic policy departments.
In his speech, the Vice President elaborated on the constitutional values that shape the nation's ideological agenda.
"Our Constitution establishes not only the legal foundation of the state, but also the value framework of society," Erla Karin said. "For perhaps the first time in our history, the country's ideology has gained a clear structure and substantive content. Therefore, our priority is to explain and promote constitutional values."
Vice President Karin emphasized the need to advance and embed progressive constitutional principles across society.
"The Head of State's policy aims to ensure Kazakhstan's continued progress. Our country is on a path of change. Modernization extends to all spheres of public life. Therefore, it is vital to cultivate constructive values of hard work, education, science, and progress in society. At the same time, we must firmly rebuff any attempts to promote archaism, ignorance, or radicalism. We see how society itself now reacts strongly to various manifestations of extreme and uncivil behavior that occasionally surface in the public sphere. This indicates a shift in civic culture and the system of values, proving that the President's progressive reforms command widespread support across society and have become irreversible," Erlan Karin stated.
He noted that implementing presidential directives and initiatives effectively remains a key domestic policy priority.
"In his State-of-the-Nation Address, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev ordered formulating a comprehensive plan for reforming the public administration system," Karin stressed. "We need to build a public administration model tailored to a new economy driven by digitalization and artificial intelligence. Efforts must therefore be expedited to improve the mechanisms of a service-oriented governance model, particularly information platforms for citizen feedback. Integrating all contact centers of central government agencies and regions under a single digital platform is an essential objective."

Explainer-Why is the evacuation of Oleshky by Russia and Ukraine happening now?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:48:48 CET
00:48:48 KST

By Andrew Osborn
MOSCOW, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Residents of the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine began evacuating on Friday as part of a joint relief operation by the two sides, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.
Many questions have been asked about the humanitarian operation and its wider significance under a deal that US first lady Melania Trump was involved in brokering, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo.
WHAT DO RUSSIA AND UKRAINE WANT FROM THE OPERATION?
Besides the safe evacuation of many of Oleshky’s residents, Moscow and Kyiv are trying to use the operation to show US President Donald Trump they are serious about his efforts to secure an overall peace settlement.
Neither side wants to be blamed by Trump for something going wrong in Oleshky, an event that could burnish his self-professed credentials as a peacemaker before US midterm legislative elections.
But the two sides remain far apart on potential terms for ending the conflict in Ukraine, and there appears to be no immediate prospect of it ending.
Both sides want to keep Trump engaged in the peace process, even if it is moving slowly, as even if Trump’s Republican Party performs badly in the midterms, he will be president for two more years and able to influence what is happening in Ukraine.
Moscow hopes Trump can pressure Kyiv into agreeing a deal that meets many of its conditions, such as full Russian control of Ukraine’s Donbas region and a bar on Ukraine joining NATO.
Kyiv wants to ensure US intelligence sharing continues, along with full access to Elon Musk’s battlefield communications system Starshield, and that European-bought US military hardware, including Patriot interceptor missiles, continues to flow.
HOW ARE THE SIDES TRYING TO INFLUENCE TRUMP’S VIEW OF THE OPERATION?
Moscow and Kyiv, keen to court the US president, have lavishly praised Melania Trump’s role in making the operation happen.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has publicly recognised her importance in bringing about the ceasefire and aid operation, and Dmitry Peskov, his spokesman, cited her proven experience in reuniting children affected by the Ukraine conflict with their families as one of the reasons why Moscow agreed to the Oleshky operation. Special Envoy Kirill Dmitriev has repeatedly taken to X to highlight her role in what is happening.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets has paid tribute to Melania Trump too, saying Kyiv wanted to extend its “special thanks” to someone who was “personally devoting her time and attention to the humanitarian mission and assistance to civilians in Oleshky”.
Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky with what state media said was about 50 journalists, including four US journalists from Newsmax, an outlet whose founder has said it is supportive of Trump and his policies.
Russian state TV has shown humanitarian aid boxes destined for Oleshky decorated with Russia’s flag being loaded by people wearing T-shirts saying “Putin’s Team - The People’s Front.”
DOES THE HUMANITARIAN MISSION MEET INTERNATIONAL STANDARDS?
The International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva said on Friday its teams had not been asked to provide support, but stood ready to help within its mandate if requested.
Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, said the UN had not received any request to help but officials were closely monitoring the situation.
He said the question of why the UN had not been invited to observe was one for Ukraine as Oleshky is in territory internationally recognised as Ukrainian.
“What we do know is that we have advocated for and will continue to advocate that all international rules, laws, and practices are upheld during this evacuation,” Laerke said.
The fact that human rights commissioners from Ukraine and Russia were involved inspired some confidence, he added.
COULD OLESHKY BE A MODEL FOR SIMILAR LOCAL CEASEFIRES?
Kremlin statements suggest the operation could be a one-off — at least for now. Asked if the operation meant Russia and Ukraine could find other areas where they could cooperate, Peskov said it was a specific and isolated case that, for now, did not have wider implications for the peace process.
The ceasefire, which was extended to the wider Kherson region, expires on Sunday. There has been no easing of fighting in the other three Ukrainian regions Russia says it has incorporated as its own.
After holding talks with US negotiators, Putin this month agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine next month.
But Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, unhappy about attempted Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow, has hinted at a possible rethink if the attacks continue, while Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian oil refineries after a pause.
There has also been no let-up in Russian airstrikes on infrastructure targets across Ukraine.
(Reporting by Reuters in Moscow and Kyiv, Additional reporting by Olivia Le Poidevin in Geneva, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

Independent commemorations mark Day of Remembrance for victims of Soviet repression across Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:48:25 UTC
00:48:25 KST

On Oct. 29, Russians and foreign diplomats laid flowers at the Solovetsky Stone on Moscow’s Lubyanka Square ahead of the Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Political Repression. Members of Russia’s OMON riot police force were stationed near the monument, according to witnesses. Those who came to pay tribute included diplomats from Sweden, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Germany, Lithuania, and France, as well as Jan Rachinsky — a Kremlin-designated “foreign agent” who formerly served as the chairman of Memorial’s board. This year marks the first commemoration since Russia’s Supreme Court declared Memorial an “extremist” organization in April and outlawed its activities.
On Oct. 25, police detained a woman who had come to lay flowers at the Solovetsky Stone. According to the legal rights project Slovo Zashchite (lit. “Word to the Defense”), she was taken to the Kitai-Gorod police station, where officers threatened to charge her with disobeying police. The official reason for her detention was not disclosed.
State Duma MP Andrei Lugovoi, best known for his role in the 2006 death-by-polonium of Russian intelligence defector Alexander Litvinenko, also came to the memorial on the morning of Oct. 29. According to the Telegram channel Ostorozhno Novosti, he had hoped to encounter the U.S. or British ambassador and present a figurine of an Indian sepoy — a reference to India’s colonial past and the soldiers who served in the British imperial army. However, he did not manage to meet any of the diplomats.
Where commemorations were held in Russia
Public events honoring victims of political repression were planned in several Russian cities. In the Irkutsk Region, activists organized a reading of victims’ names at a memorial in Pivovarikha. Organizers invited residents to submit the names of relatives who suffered at the hands of Soviet repression even if their descendants could not attend the ceremony themselves.
In Kirov, the regional branch of the liberal Yabloko party received approval from city authorities for an Oct. 30 rally at the Solovetsky Stone on Morozovskaya Street.
A similar event was authorized in Veliky Novgorod, where participants planned to gather near the entrance to the 30 Years of October Park, to read the names of victims, and to express support for today’s political prisoners.
In St. Petersburg, a ceremony took place on the morning of Oct. 30, drawing several dozen attendees, including Yabloko members, city officials, lawmakers, ordinary residents, and representatives of foreign diplomatic missions. The event proceeded peacefully, with participants laying flowers and wreaths at the Solovetsky Stone. An additional ceremony and reading of names was scheduled later that day at the Levashovo Memorial Cemetery, a site of mass graves containing victims of Stalinist terror.
Commemorative events were also announced in the city of Kopeysk in the Chelyabinsk Region, where a rally was scheduled for Oct. 30 at the monument to victims of repression, and in Tolyatti in the Samara Region, where city authorities planned a flower-laying ceremony in the city’s Central District Park.
Yabloko also organized a separate 11-hour reading marathon titled “People, Do Not Kill Each Other!” on Oct. 30, bringing together participants from dozens of Russian regions. In Moscow, people could join the readings at the party’s headquarters.
The international “Returning the Names” initiative on Oct. 29 also brought together participants in more than 100 cities around the world. Readings were held both in person and remotely, with organizers running an hourslong online broadcast. In 2025, the event took place in 150 cities.
How authorities restricted the commemorations
The first “Returning the Names” ceremony was held in Moscow on Oct. 29, 2007, at the initiative of Memorial. Participants gathered at the Solovetsky Stone and took turns reading the names, occupations, and execution dates of victims of Stalinist terror.
One of the event’s creators was Elena Zhemkova, executive director of International Memorial. She said organizers had initially hoped to read all 40,000 known names of Moscow residents who had been executed. However, doing so would have required continuous readings around the clock for several weeks.
The mass gathering took place annually until 2020, when it was canceled due to the coronavirus pandemic. However, even after the epidemiological situation eased in subsequent years, Moscow authorities continued citing public health restrictions when refusing authorization for the gathering. In October 2024, Russia’s communications regulator Roskomnadzor blocked the Returning the Names website. Organizers nevertheless continued the readings in other formats, including online.
What happened to Memorial’s members
In December 2021, Russian courts ordered the liquidation of International Memorial and the Memorial Human Rights Center. In 2022, Memorial became one of the recipients of the Nobel Peace Prize, with Jan Rachinsky accepting the award in Oslo.
On April 9, 2026, after a case that was heard behind closed doors, Russia’s Supreme Court designated the International Memorial movement as “extremist” and banned its activities across the country. That same day, the Memorial Human Rights Defense Center announced that it was ending all activities inside Russia.
By then, many of the organization’s employees and leaders had already emigrated. Elena Zhemkova left Russia in 2023 and continues her human rights work in Germany. Russian authorities placed her on the “foreign agents” register in June 2025. Rachinsky and other Memorial representatives, including historian Irina Shcherbakova, have received the same designation.
In February 2026, Russian authorities also declared two Memorial organizations abroad “undesirable”: the International Memorial Association in Switzerland and Zukunft Memorial in Germany. Under Russian law, the designation effectively bans the named group from conducting any activities in Russia and can create legal liability for anyone working with the “undesirable organization.”
Yury Dmitriev, a researcher of Soviet repression and former head of Memorial’s branch in Karelia, continues to serve a 15-year prison sentence. Dmitriev helped discover mass graves of victims of Stalin-era executions at Sandarmokh in Karelia. In September 2026, he was hospitalized in a prison medical facility.

Israel demolishes gunmen’s homes in West Bank operation that has displaced thousands
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:48:23 CET
00:48:23 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Israel demolished on Friday the homes of the assailants who killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron last week, part of an ongoing operation that has forcibly displaced over 3,000 Palestinians.
After the October 23 attack, in which both gunmen were killed, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the Israeli military to launch a in areas near the checkpoint, triggering protests by Palestinian residents.
Palestinian officials have accused Netanyahu of using the operation to drum up support ahead of a general election in Israel on Tuesday. Israel’s government says its operation is a response to the attack on its soldiers.
In a statement announcing the demolitions, Israel’s military said it would “continue to operate proactively and offensively” to thwart attacks in the West Bank and “protect residents in the area”.
The homes demolished on Friday had been occupied by the wives and children of the gunmen before the military forced Palestinians to leave the area over the past week, according to local residents.
The military has also demolished other homes as well as shops, roads, and factories in Hebron since the attack, according to local officials, though the exact scale of the demolitions is unclear.
It has closed most entrances to the city, severely curtailing freedom of movement for Palestinians, including people in need of medical attention.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said this week that the displacement of residents raised “grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force” and that “threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing.”
Netanyahu’s government has presided over a rapid expansion of settlements, deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this.
Under Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition there has also been a surge of militant settler violence against Palestinians.
In Kafr Malik near Ramallah on Friday, Reuters witnesses documented militant Israeli settlers shoving Palestinians and preventing farmers from harvesting their olives, while the Israeli military was present.
The Israeli military said it had responded to reports from Israeli settlers that Palestinians were throwing stones at them, and had arrested two Palestinians.
It did not address the reports of Israeli settlers attacking Palestinians. A Reuters witness present during the incident did not observe the Palestinians throwing stones.
Attacks have surged during the Palestinian olive harvest, which starts at the end of September and ends in November. The Israeli rights group Yesh Din reported at least 135 physical attacks on the olive harvest as of October 23.

By Katharine Jackson
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pope Leo XIV cast a ballot by mail in the US midterm elections, the Vatican press office said on Friday, a historic first for the American-born pontiff.
“In keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago,” the Vatican said. “The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes.”
The Vatican did not say which candidates Leo had voted for.
Leo, 71, was born in Chicago and is the first American-born pope. He registered to vote in Illinois under his birth name Robert Francis Prevost and requested a ballot on October 3, the Chicago Sun-Times reported on Thursday, citing the Will County Clerk’s office.
President Donald Trump’s sagging popularity is hurting his fellow Republicans’ chances of holding onto their majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 election, with the public unhappy about the high cost of living and the Iran war.
Trump repeatedly criticized Leo early in the new pope’s tenure, calling him “weak” and “terrible” on crime.
The pope said in March that God rejects the prayers of those who start wars and have “hands full of blood.” In April, he termed Trump’s threat to destroy the Iranian civilization as unacceptable and previously declined to join the US president’s so-called “Board of Peace” initiative for Gaza.
Leo has also urged a “deep reflection” on the way migrants are treated in the US.
Voters in the solidly Democratic state of Illinois will select a successor for retiring US Senator Dick Durbin and choose whether to re-elect Governor JB Pritzker.
Leo was elected to lead the 1.4-billion-member Church by the world’s cardinals in May 2025.
The pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on October 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Doctors say he will not need further therapy.
He is set to travel to South America next week.

Swiss October weather warmer and drier than average

Unknown Publisher

00:47:51 KST

Swiss October weather warmer and drier than average
The average temperature in Switzerland in October was eight degrees Celcius, which was 1.4 degrees above the reference period from 1991 to 2020.
But the tempertaures were some distance off record highs, said the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology (MeteoSwiss).
Average October temperatures are so far ranked 11th warmest since records began in 1864. The warmest October on record was in 2022, with an average temperature of 10.4 degrees.
October 2026 saw below-average rainfall until shortly before the end of the month. There was more rain in the Jura region as far as Basel, but cantons Graubünden, Valais, the southern side of the Alps and the Engadin recorded precipitation deficits, some of which were considerable.
In terms of sunshine duration, many regions of Switzerland failed to match the 1991–2020 average in October. Only Ticino and the centre of the country recorded more hours of sunshine by comparison.
Autumn colours earlier
Following the record-breaking heat and drought during the summer half-year of 2026, vegetation reacted differently in October to cooler temperatures and scattered rainfall.
Drought stress had already led to colour change and leaf fall in some regions by late summer, but the ‘true’ autumnal colour change set in later than usual.
The premature leaf colour change was observed among beech trees, hornbeams, lime trees, horse chestnuts, birches and fruit trees by about three to four weeks.
The partial recovery in early October resembled a ‘second spring’ in some places. For example, a second flush of leaves and flowering was observed regionally on some apple and pear trees. Spring-flowering plants such as daisies and knapweed also produced a second flush of flowers.

Locatelli in Tokyo: ‘Disability: Inclusion Is a Reality; Invest in Talent’
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:35 CET
00:47:35 KST

Not a conference, not a declaration of principle. A gala dinner served, cooked, and hosted by people with disabilities who had traveled from Italy. This is the message that Alessandra Locatelli, Minister for People with Disabilities, wanted to send from Tokyo, where, together with Ambassador Mario Vattani, she hosted an event at the Diplomatic Residence that combined celebration with a concrete demonstration. The occasion marks the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Italy and Japan. “We wanted to organize this evening because it sends a strong signal of our commitment to concrete action when we talk about workplace inclusion and dignity in the lives of people with disabilities,” the minister explained to ANSA. “Very often, we focus only on limitations; we want to demonstrate that there are talents and skills in which we can and must invest.” Twelve organizations were involved, with ten working in the kitchen and serving tables—supported by chefs Alessandro Circiello and Fabrizio Facchini—and two bands providing entertainment. This is not a mere showcase, but proof that “people with disabilities are not simply beneficiaries of inclusion policies, but active participants in professional, social, and cultural life.” On the international front, Locatelli strengthened an ongoing dialogue with the signing in Tokyo of the Solfagnano Charter, the final document of the first G7 summit dedicated to Inclusion and Disability, initiated by Italy in 2024. “Many countries were delighted to host the exhibition” that illustrates the Charter’s eight priorities, she said, “but challenges remain in placing the issue on the international agenda.” The exhibition tour concludes in Tokyo and will be on display at the Italian Cultural Institute from October 28 to November 4. As for the Italian reform, the minister does not shy away from acknowledging the challenges. “There is still so much to be done. The reform must be implemented: two years of pilot testing are not enough.” The issue is cultural rather than regulatory: “We are changing an approach to care that has been in place for fifty years. Even for those working in the services sector, it’s extremely difficult to change their perspective.” Alongside the “Life Project,” Locatelli cites service innovation, the caregiver law approved by the Chamber of Deputies and now before the Senate, and workplace inclusion, “which is also fundamental from an economic standpoint for the country.” Education is another source of Italian pride: “We’ve had an inclusion law since the 1970s, and many countries—from England to Germany—ask me how we do it.” The answer, he concluded, is an insight: bringing children together not only for their educational journey, “but for a shared journey of growth, respect, dignity, and relationships.”

Hackers drain millions from Polymarket accounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:46:33 UTC
00:46:33 KST

Hackers drain millions from Polymarket accounts
Hackers have swiped at least $2.6 million in user funds from predictive market platform Polymarket that allows people to wager on real-world events, including elections and military action. The company was forced to briefly pause trading on its international exchange, promising to reimburse all affected users.
In an X post on Thursday, a Polymarket-related account said that the company had “identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform.”
“We have temporarily halted trading,” the statement read, adding that the breach occurred after “one of our 3rd party providers was compromised.”
The hack only affected Polymarket’s flagship platform, although Polymarket US, which operates independently as a federally regulated financial exchange, was spared.
Several media outlets, including the Wall Street Journal, reported that the third-party provider that Polymarket referred to was DebugBear - a UK-based performance-monitoring platform.
DebugBear wrote on X on Thursday afternoon that it was “aware of a security incident,” advising clients using its RUM product to “remove the embed code from your website.”
According to Business Today, citing blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps, as many as 700 Polymarket accounts were affected, with users reporting unauthorized withdrawals and sudden balance liquidations.
The breach coincided with a major cyberattack at Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, that saw intruders steal an estimated $6.3 billion.
As for Polymarket, it suffered another breach as recently as June, with hackers getting their hands on more than $2 million.
In recent years, Polymarket, along with its major rival, Kalshi, have been at the center of multiple scandals, involving insider trading by American officials and military personnel, with several US states also accusing them of sidestepping gambling laws.
Last week, the Associated Press reported that US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had issued a directive specifically warning service members against using classified material to bet on prediction markets.
Earlier this year, US Army Green Beret Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke was arrested and charged with illegally profiting from advance knowledge of the January operation to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
Prosecutors alleged that the defendant had placed more than $32,500 in Polymarket bets, mostly on January 2, hours before the US attack on Caracas. Van Dyke allegedly raked in $400,000 by betting on Maduro’s removal from power.
The man pleaded not guilty.
Newly created Polymarket accounts also placed suspiciously timed bets shortly before US President Donald Trump announced an April US-Iran ceasefire, generating hundreds of thousands of dollars in profits. The White House subsequently warned staff against trading on confidential information.
In late August, Trump’s long-time teleprompter operator, Gabriel Perez, was ordered to pay $65,000 to settle a case related to his “unlawful” prediction-market trading about the president’s speeches.
The White House aide was also required to give up $107,000 in ill-gotten profits from his wagers on Kalshi, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said at the time.

Census 2027: Population enumeration from Jan 25-Feb 28 2027; poll-bound, snow-bound areas excluded
Unknown
