The enumeration will not be conducted in poll bound or in the snow-bound areas. (Photo: IANS)
NEW DELHI: Population enumeration for the 2027 Census will be conducted across most of India from January 25 to February 28, 2027, with poll-bound states and snow-bound regions excluded from the schedule, the government announced on Friday.According to a notification issued by Mritunjay Kumar Narayan, Registrar General of India and Census Commissioner, the reference date for the census will be midnight on March 1, 2027, PTI reported.The enumeration will not be conducted during this period in Manipur, Goa, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand and Ladakh, or in the snow-bound, non-synchronous areas of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir.The schedule for Manipur will be announced separately. A revisional round will be held from March 1 to March 5, 2027.The government will also offer a self-enumeration option from January 10 to January 24, ahead of the house-to-house population count.Assembly elections are due in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Goa and Manipur early next year.Census 2027: Two phasesThe 2027 Census, the eighth since Independence, will be conducted in two phases: house listing and housing census, followed by population enumeration.The decennial exercise was originally scheduled for 2021 but was postponed due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Union Cabinet has approved Rs 11,718 crore for conducting the census.The Registrar General of India had announced last month that house-listing operations for Census 2027 in Manipur had been deferred.The census is a nationwide exercise to collect, compile and analyse information about the population and its demographic, social and economic characteristics.
The data provides the government with a detailed picture of the country's population and living conditions.The government has said that information collected during the census will remain confidential and be used only for statistical purposes.India's last census was conducted in 2011, when the country's population stood at 1.21 billion, including 62.32 crore males and 58.75 crore females. The country had 24.95 crore households at the time.

The Key Climate Issues to Watch In The Midterm Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:45:17 UTC
00:45:17 KST

With the midterms approaching, the climate crisis doesn’t seem to be top of mind for most voters. In a recent poll, voters told Gallup that, among 11 issues, the economy, health care, and the war in Iran are the top of their concerns when it comes to this election season.
That doesn’t mean climate isn’t on the ballot. The midterms come as the U.S. has faced a slew of climate rollbacks under the first two years of the Trump Administration, including withdrawing from the Paris Agreement, rolling back the landmark endangerment finding, and leasing public lands for oil and gas drilling. With Democrats being significantly more likely to view climate action as a priority, many in the climate movement are hopeful that if the Democrats take back some leadership in Congress, as it could prove essential in helping to prevent further rollbacks.
“A new government could stop the bleeding,” says Malcolm Araos, assistant professor at the Wagner School of Public Service at New York University, whose work focuses on the politics of climate policy. “A new Congress, or new Senate can't reverse [many of the climate rollbacks], but they could investigate why [they were] repealed, and they could stop things like that from happening in the future.”
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives will be determined on Tuesday, Nov. 3, while 35 Senate seats are up for election. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the Senate.
Why local elections matter these midterms
With a low likelihood of federal climate policy under Trump, regardless of the outcome of the midterms, state races are where most environmental advocates are looking. That’s because state-level elections still leave open the potential for local climate action—especially if Democrats can manage a “trifecta” and win the governor’s mansion and a majority in both chambers, says Geoffrey Henderson, assistant professor of environmental policy and planning at the University of Michigan. “We've seen in recent history that when we have Democratic trifectas at the state level, that lends itself to an opportunity to pass pretty transformative climate policies,” he says. “It's often underrated how important state level races are, because there are states like Michigan that are not currently Democratic trifectas, but that could shift back in that direction…and that can really unlock major policy change.”
Since President Trump took office, several states, including California, Virginia, and Colorado have pushed forward climate policies despite federal rollbacks.
Climate ballot measures to watch in the midterm elections
A number of climate measures are also on the ballot in several states. In Colorado, Amendment 82 will have voters deciding on the constitutional right to buy and sell natural gas—a measure that critics say, if passed, could challenge climate policies in the state by promoting fossil fuel reliance.
On the other hand, in Michigan, a ballot measure hopes to limit utilities from influencing political campaigns. (Michigan utility companies have previously lobbied against community solar expansion.) Voters in Eugene, Ore., meanwhile, will be asked to decide whether to tax large corporate retailers to fund climate resilience projects. (The measure is modeled after a similar program passed in neighboring Portland in 2018.)
These all serve as bellwether cases, says Henderson. “These ballot measures are in some ways testing theories of how each side is going to approach state level climate policy.”
How could the Iran war and data center concerns in the midterms impact climate policy?
Two issues of concern for voters—the war in Iran and data center construction—could also prove an opportunity for climate-friendly policies like renewable energy investments. “These moments of crisis when energy is really really expensive [can] lead to these switches to renewable energy,” says Araos. As the war laid bare the precarity of fossil fuels, many communities around the world began turning to renewable energy for greater energy security.
Voters in 10 states, including California, Kansas, and Ohio, will decide whether to curb data center development in local communities, a fight that’s been resonating with climate advocates. “Data centers have drawn a grassroots bipartisan opposition, and climate groups are very much aligned with that opposition because data centers are major energy users, and in many cases they're major water users,” says Henderson. “I think it is really a climate issue as well as local land use issue, an issue of costs and water availability, and there's an opportunity here for climate advocates to to be a part of a broader coalition.”

Musk pouring more than $445 million into 2026 US elections: Report
Unknown

00:43:53 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Billionaire Elon Musk has contributed more than $445 million to federal political committees during the 2026 US election cycle, making him the largest disclosed individual political donor in modern American history, CNN reported Friday.
The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive's contributions have significantly boosted Republican fundraising efforts ahead of the November midterm elections, placing him among the party's biggest financial backers, the report said.
More than $216 million of Musk's donations went to America PAC, his political action committee, while another $168 million was directed to the Senate Leadership Fund, a major Republican super PAC.
Other recipients include the Congressional Leadership Fund, which received $30 million, and several smaller Republican-aligned political groups.
Musk's total contributions have more than doubled the nearly $177 million donated by Democratic billionaire George Soros to outside groups during the 2022 midterm election cycle.
Brendan Glavin, who oversees research at the nonprofit OpenSecrets, said Musk's financial involvement could have a decisive impact on the midterm elections.
"One person is completely dominating and changing the landscape of how Republicans are able to spend money and defend themselves," he said.
Musk's America PAC has been active in more than 40 House and Senate races, according to federal campaign disclosures.
Musk’s spending has also been heavily concentrated in Texas, where Republican-aligned groups have used substantial funding to support political campaigns and target Democratic candidates, and also where several of the billionaire’s businesses are headquartered or incorporated.

Эвакуированных жителей Алёшек отправили в Украину через Анапу и Беларусь

15:42:27 UTC
00:42:27 KST

Эвакуированных жителей Алёшек отправили в Украину через Анапу и Беларусь
В оккупированном городе началась гуманитарная миссия. Для выезда подготовили 25 автобусов на 750 мест
Украинская делегация и эвакуированные жители подконтрольных России Алёшек Херсонской области (украинское название Олешки) направились в Анапу. Оттуда желающих выехать на подконтрольную Киеву территорию доставят через Беларусь, а затем в Украину, сообщил глава парламентской фракции «Слуга народа» Верховной рады Украины Давид Арахамия.
По согласованному плану, из Анапы жители должны вылететь военно-транспортным самолётом Минобороны России в белорусский Гомель, а затем продолжить путь в Украину. Перелёт запланирован на 31 октября. Офис украинского омбудсмена подтвердил маршрут эвакуации.
Чтобы не пропустить новые тексты «Вёрстки», подписывайтесь на наш телеграм-канал
Как проходит эвакуация
Утром 30 октября в Алёшки прибыли участники гуманитарной миссии, которую координируют уполномоченная по правам человека в России Яна Лантратова и уполномоченный Верховной рады Украины по правам человека Дмитрий Лубинец. Режим тишины продолжает действовать.
Для выезда подготовили 25 автобусов на 750 мест, а также транспорт для лежачих больных и животных. Операцию сопровождают девять машин скорой помощи и более 50 медработников. Подтверждённого числа вывезенных жителей пока нет.
По словам Лантратовой, желающих покинуть город разделили на две группы — направляющихся в Россию и в Украину. Обе группы сначала планируют доставить в Анапу. Выбравшие Россию затем отправятся в Москву, а желающие вернуться в Украину — в Гомель в сопровождении Лубинца и украинских журналистов. Остающимся в городе обещают гуманитарную помощь.
При разминировании дороги погибли два человека
Перед прибытием делегаций подъезды к Алёшкам разминировали. Лантратова сообщила, что во время этих работ погибли два человека, в том числе российский сапёр.
Локальное прекращение огня действует с 27 октября до позднего вечера 1 ноября. Соглашение о гуманитарной операции российская и украинская стороны подписали 23 октября при посредничестве первой леди США Мелании Трамп, рассказывала «Вёрстка». Договорённости предусматривают доставку помощи и добровольный выезд жителей.
Миссию освещают иностранные журналисты
Вместе с участниками операции в Алёшки прибыли журналисты из разных стран. Среди них — представители американского телеканала Newsmax, участие которых ранее анонсировала Мелания Трамп. Их задача — сопровождать и документировать миссию.
Операцию также показывают российские телеканалы. «Россия 24» выпустила сюжет с участием Лантратовой и Лубинца. Корреспондент заявил, что режим тишины «в целом соблюдается», при этом возложил ответственность за удары по городу исключительно на ВСУ.
Чтобы не пропустить новые тексты «Вёрстки», подписывайтесь на наш телеграм-канал
Положение в городе
По оценке украинских властей, перед началом операции в Алёшках оставались около двух тысяч человек. Город расположен на левом берегу Днепра напротив Херсона и находится под российской оккупацией с начала полномасштабного вторжения.
Жители испытывают нехватку продовольствия, лекарств и медицинской помощи. В городе нет газа и стабильного электроснабжения, затруднён доступ к воде. Заминированные дороги и угроза ударов осложняли доставку необходимых товаров и самостоятельный выезд.
Ранее «Вёрстка» писала о подготовке гуманитарной миссии для Алёшек. Для безопасного проезда гуманитарных колонн зону прекращения огня расширили за пределы города, сообщала Мелания Трамп.

Fire affected a Russian Su-57 fifth-generation multirole fighter at the Akhtubinsk military airfield in Russia’s Astrakhan Region, according to the Ukrainian OSINT project Absoliutno Nadiine Dzherelo (lit. “Absolutely Reliable Source”), which analyzed satellite imagery. The project said the incident occurred Oct. 29 “as a result of an abnormal situation during engine startup,” adding that this was the fourth case in which an Su-57 had been lost or damaged since the beginning of 2026. As of Oct. 30, Russian authorities had not publicly confirmed the reported loss, and no independent Russian source had verified that the aircraft was destroyed.
According to Absoliutno Nadiine Dzherelo:
“On Oct. 29, 2026, at Akhtubinsk airfield, a Russian Su-57 fifth-generation multirole fighter caught fire — and burned completely — as a result of an abnormal situation during engine startup.
This is already the fourth Su-57 [to have been damaged or destroyed] in 2026: two were hit in the spring at Shagol airfield, and another was shot down by ‘friendly’ fire on July 23 in the Moscow Region. Considering that production is at most four aircraft per year, the quota has already been met.”
Satellite images published by the project show apparent burn marks at a parking spot used by an Su-57.
Another Ukrainian OSINT project, Oko Hora ✙ News and Analytics, reported that Russian aviation losses in October 2026 totaled 11 fighter aircraft and one helicopter. Two additional Su-34 fighter-bombers were partially damaged, according to the project.
As The Insider reported earlier this year, on July 23 an Su-57 crashed near the village of Lutsino in the Moscow region during a training flight. Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed the loss of the aircraft at the time. Before that, several Su-57s were reported damaged at Shagol airfield in the Chelyabinsk Region, about 1,700 kilometer (1,050 miles) from the border with Ukraine.
The Su-57 is Russia’s newest multirole fighter and is classified by Moscow as a fifth-generation combat aircraft. It made its first flight in 2010 and is considered the most advanced fighter in service with the Russian Aerospace Forces. According to open-source data, Russia had about 30 Su-57s in service at the beginning of 2025.
Akhtubinsk is also home to the Russian military’s 929th State Flight Test Center, one of the country’s main facilities for testing and evaluating military aircraft. Ukraine has previously succeeded in damaging Su-57s. In June 2024, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency reported a strike on the Akhtubinsk airfield that damaged at least one Su-57. Pro-war Russian military Telegram channels also acknowledged damage to an aircraft at the time.

Swiss defence contractor wants fresh start after fraud probe

Swiss defence contractor wants fresh start after fraud probe
Swiss defence contractor RUAG wants to turn the page on a dark chapter following a spate of serious irregularities dating back to 2002.
“The complexity of these projects made the work demanding. However, this investment was a deliberate choice to prepare for our future, and it has borne fruit,” said Jürg Rötheli, chair of Ruag MRO. “We have ensured transparency, learnt the necessary lessons and laid foundations for a fresh start with peace of mind.”
Rötheli acknowledged that some aspects have not yet been fully resolved or require further action. He said that the next steps are already being planned, with a focus on transparency.
The affair came to light in 2025 when the Swiss Federal Audit Office scrutinised the management and governance of Ruag MRO. The findings of fraud and poor stock management were damning.
More
Audit slams Swiss military contractor for suspected fraud
RUAG had already launched an investigation in 2023 after identifying irregularities and unresolved issues. That investigation has now been completed. Investigations carried out by the law firm Niederer Kraft Frey have shed further light on other irregularities and potential offences.
There is therefore a suspicion that a former employee may have unlawfully transmitted sensitive technical drawings to private email addresses and to third parties in Germany.
There are also indications that a South African subsidiary of Nitrochemie (now in liquidation), in which RUAG holds a minority stake, may have been used to facilitate transactions that would not have been authorised from Switzerland or Germany.
Furthermore, the investigation indicates that, as part of the demerger of the RUAG Group, a stake was sold to an acquiring company in which a former RUAG employee had, in a personal capacity and without the required declaration, acquired a minority stake.
Further suspicions relate to possible falsification of original manufacturers’ certificates, as well as the alleged granting of benefits constituting a criminal offence.
Determined to take action
Comprehensive measures have been taken and are being continuously expanded. As part of a reorganisation, the Corporate Services unit was established and the compliance framework was strengthened.
Targeted improvements have been made, in particular, to export controls, the management of relationships with intermediaries in international business, and internal processes.
In addition to these structural improvements, Ruag has taken legal action. In Switzerland, criminal complaints alleging dishonest management, forgery of documents, breach of trade or business secrets and other offences have been filed and supplemented on several occasions, the defence contractor states.
At the same time, RUAG has brought civil claims totalling approximately €51 million against ten individuals. Criminal and civil proceedings remain pending.

Swiss foreign minister talks political ties on rare visit to North Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:37:03 UTC
00:37:03 KST

Swiss foreign minister talks political ties on rare visit to North Korea
Switzerland formally reopens diplomatic office in North Korea after its closure in 2020.
Switzerland has formally reopened its diplomatic office in North Korea as Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis held talks in Pyongyang about normalising political relations between the two countries.
On Friday Cassis wrapped up a two-day visit to North Korea – the first by a Swiss government minister in more than two decades – in which he discussed “regularising political relations and reestablishing a political dialogue”, he wrote on X.
Cassis, who is also Switzerland’s vice president, met Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui and Jo Yong Won, a secretary of the Central Committee of the ruling Korean Workers’ Party.
“We also exchanged views on security on the Korean Peninsula and broader Eurasian security challenges,” he added on X.
After the formal reopening of the Swiss diplomatic office on Thursday, Cassis posted that he was “pleased” to mark a “new chapter” in his country’s presence in Pyongyang, hailing the office as a “concrete step towards strengthening direct dialogue” with North Korea.
The office, operational since October 19, will not have an ambassador. It reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing, which handles diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea. The office had closed in March 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“This office will help to strengthen direct contacts with the authorities of the DPRK [Democratic People’s Republic of Korea] and support political dialogue with them,” the Swiss Foreign Ministry said.
North Korea’s state news agency KCNA confirmed Cassis’s arrival in the country on Thursday but gave no details on the purpose of the visit. It had not been known beforehand whether he would meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and there has been no report of a meeting.
Bern said it intended to maintain its commitment to the region amid heightened tensions and limited international contact with North Korea, having been one of the few Western countries to keep up a dialogue with Pyongyang.
The last Swiss Federal Council member to visit was then-Foreign Minister Micheline Calmy-Rey, in 2003.
Cassis crossed into South Korea on Friday for the final leg of his regional trip.
According to the Swiss foreign ministry, his talks in Seoul will focus on security on the peninsula, prospects for easing regional tensions and bilateral ties.
Switzerland’s involvement on the Korean Peninsula dates back more than 70 years, including its role on the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission.
Also in South Korea, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz invoked his country’s reunification during a visit to the inter-Korean border. “Let us hope that Korea, too, will one day have the chance to regain its national unity,” he said.

PHOTO Council of Ministers
Font size
Bulgaria has been removed from the “grey list” of countries subject to increased monitoring for money laundering, a decision that restores the country’s international standing and opens up new opportunities for the Bulgarian economy, businesses and citizens. Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced this in a statement to the Bulgarian public after being informed by Justice Minister Nayden Nikolov of the decision taken earlier today at a plenary meeting of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) in Paris.
The government press service said that securing Bulgaria’s removal from the “grey list” had been set as a key priority in the government’s programme.
Bulgaria received an official warning in 2021 and was placed on the list in 2023 because of strategic deficiencies in its efforts to combat money laundering and corruption over a ten-year period.
Removal from the “grey list” is expected to put an end to the serious difficulties encountered when conducting financial transactions with foreign countries.

После удара по Новокуйбышевску Кремль заявил, что Украина «ослушалась» Дональда Трампа
В Самарской области два человека погибли при ликвидации последствий атаки беспилотников 30 октября. Об этом сообщил губернатор региона Вячеслав Федорищев.
По его словам, есть также пострадавшие, которым оказывают медицинскую помощь. Их число и состояние губернатор не уточнил. Он не назвал ни населённый пункт, ни предприятие, где погибли люди.
Ранее Astra и украинские мониторинговые каналы Exilenova+ и Supernova+ сообщили об атаке на Новокуйбышевский нефтеперерабатывающий завод. На опубликованных фотографиях и видео над предприятием видны несколько столбов густого дыма.

Что известно об атаке и пожаре
Федорищев назвал число атаковавших область беспилотников рекордным для региона. Он заявил, что ПВО и мобильные огневые группы уничтожили десятки дронов. Поначалу губернатор сообщал об отсутствии погибших, позднее объявил о двух жертвах.
Федорищев также призвал жителей обращаться за медицинской помощью при ухудшении самочувствия из-за дыма и запаха гари.
По данным Astra, жители Новокуйбышевска жаловались, что не слышали сигнала воздушной тревоги, а сообщение губернатора появилось почти через два часа после начала атаки. OSINT-аналитик издания определил место пожара как территорию Новокуйбышевского НПЗ. Власти попадание именно по заводу не подтвердили. Масштаб повреждений и влияние пожара на производство пока неизвестны.
Завод выпускает в том числе реактивное топливо
Новокуйбышевский НПЗ входит в Самарскую группу предприятий «Роснефти». Его производственная мощность составляет около 8,8 млн тонн нефти в год. Завод выпускает автомобильный бензин, дизельное и реактивное топливо.
Предприятие неоднократно подвергалось атакам. По данным Astra, в апреле 2026 года после удара там приостанавливали работу обеих установок первичной переработки нефти — АВТ-11 и АВТ‑9.

Помощник Владимира Путина также связал действия Киева с европейской поддержкой, заявив, что без неё Украина вряд ли решилась бы на подобные атаки. Доказательств участия европейских стран в подготовке конкретного удара он не привёл.
Ушаков напомнил, что Москва планирует трёхсторонние переговоры с Украиной при посредничестве США, и назвал их имеющими «решающее значение».

Trump reverses course, reinstates cancelled campaign rallies

Trump reverses course, reinstates cancelled campaign rallies
The decision marks a sharp reversal after the US president said he didn’t feel like he had to hold the events.
A day after announcing he would cancel a pair of campaign rallies, United States President Donald Trump has reversed course, opting to put those events back on the calendar.
A source close to the Trump administration told Al Jazeera on Friday that Trump will be headlining, in person, the previously cancelled rallies in Kansas and Iowa ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.
“Rallies are BACK ON!” the source said. “No one works harder, fights harder, or loves the American people more than President Donald J. Trump!”
Previously, Trump was due to travel to Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday. But now both rallies will take place on Sunday.
The source said the events were rearranged to include more tele-rallies, which allow Trump to attend virtually.
Republican officials have also not ruled out that an additional campaign event could be added to the president’s schedule before the midterm election.
The decision marks a sharp reversal after Trump told reporters on Thursday, “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas.”
“We are going to have a strong Tuesday night,” Trump said of the midterms.
Iowa and Kansas are states that are normally friendly to the president’s Republican Party. Not since 1932, for instance, has Kansas elected a Democrat to a full term in the Senate.
But according to early polling data, voters in both states have trended more towards Democratic Senate candidates this campaign cycle.
In Kansas, for instance, Republican Senator Roger Marshall is in an increasingly competitive race with his Democratic challenger, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton.
A poll from Emerson College on Friday found Hamilton in the lead, with 49 percent support compared with Marshall’s 45 percent.
Analysts have warned that Republican candidates could feel backlash at the polls over issues like the cost of living, with fuel prices higher than normal due to the US-Israel war on Iran.
Prior to Friday’s reversal, Marshall defended Trump’s decision to cancel his Kansas rally.
“They think that I’m doing so well in the polls that he’s probably got better places to spend his time,” Marshall said Thursday.
Democrats, however, were quick to accuse Trump of abandoning Republican candidates with less than four days remaining until the vote.
David Axelrod, who served as a senior adviser to former President Barack Obama, described the cancellation as a “strategic retreat” in a post on social media.
The Republican National Committee argued the virtual appearances would be more efficient, allowing Trump to reach more voters.
Trump is expected to speak at a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday to help boost two of the state’s Republican candidates: US Senate nominee Ashley Moody and gubernatorial hopeful Byron Donalds.

Police in the Polish city of Świdnica, located in the Lower Silesian Voivodeship, have detained a Russian citizen, according to a report by local outlet RMF24. Officers became suspicious of the 55-year-old Russian national after seeing him photograph passing trains and railway infrastructure. Investigators said his devices contained “hundreds of thousands” of images of other transport facilities — both in Poland and in other countries. He has been accused of spying on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.
The man was detained during a police operation securing a soccer match in Świdnica. He was sitting in a Volkswagen parked near a railroad crossing when officers approached. Police said he backed up and drove away, then was found near another railway site. He was standing beside the car and appeared visibly nervous when he saw the officers again, before trying to get back inside.
Police said they found professional photography equipment, mobile phones, laptops, external hard drives, and several identity documents in his possession.
The Russian citizen was ordered to be held in pretrial detention for three months. Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland’s coordinator for intelligence and security services, said the detention and arrest of a Russian citizen engaged in such activity was unusual:
“The fact that a Russian citizen was detained is rather exceptional. All such activities have always been accompanied by prior reconnaissance and information gathering. This is evidence that Russia plans, prepares, and carries out hybrid sabotage operations.”

Israeli election: 'Netanyahu did not win, he lost dramatically,' former PM Barak says

Issued on: Modified:
In an interview with FRANCE 24, former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "did not win" this week's election in Israel but "lost dramatically", and that his rival Gadi Eisenkot should ally with Arab parties. Barak also suggested that claims of Qatari funding for an Arab party aimed to distract from an ongoing corruption scandal, and warned that Netanyahu was ready to strike Iran to stay in power.
Speaking to FRANCE 24 from Tel Aviv, former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak said that, counting the Arab parties, Benjamin Netanyahu's opponents won 67 seats, against 53 for his right-wing and far-right coalition.
"Netanyahu did not win. He lost dramatically," Barak said.
Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and his allies have ruled out a coalition with Arab parties, but Barak believes they "can change their mind", as Netanyahu would no doubt do in their place.
"If Netanyahu had a similar problem, he would immediately invite Mansour Abbas" (leader of the Arab party Raam) and "give him the role of a minister of interior," Barak said.
Read moreNetanyahu piles pressure on Arab parties with claims of foreign funding to 'steal' election
Netanyahu's camp says the election was rigged, citing alleged Qatari funding of an Arab party, which Doha denies. Barak suggested the claim aimed to divert attention from "Qatargate", the investigation into alleged ties between two of Netanyahu's close aides and Qatar.
"The real suspect should be Netanyahu's own closest aides and government," he said.
Finally, Barak warned that Netanyahu was "ready" to strike Iran, possibly after the US midterm elections, in order to "remain in power until the next (Israeli) election".
"It has nothing to do with the national interest of Israel," he said, dismissing Netanyahu's claims that Iran was "planning something" as "fake news".

Palestinians forcibly displaced by Israeli army rally in Hebron, demand return home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:34:02 UTC
00:34:02 KST

Dozens of Palestinians forcibly displaced by the Israeli army rallied Friday in the southern occupied West Bank city of Hebron, demanding to return to their homes as Israeli raids and closures continued for an eighth consecutive day, Anadolu reports.
The protesters, including women, children and elderly people from displaced families, gathered near Al-Jalda Square, which remains closed off by Israeli forces, an Anadolu correspondent reported.
They called for an end to the military closure and forced displacement and demanded access to their homes in the Al-Jalda and Ein Deir Baha areas.
Israeli forces continue to seal off the two areas while raiding and damaging Palestinian homes.
The military campaign began last Friday following an attack by two Palestinians that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others. The Israeli army later killed the two Palestinians.
Since then, Israeli forces have imposed closures on Hebron and surrounding villages and seized Palestinian homes in Al-Jalda and Ein Deir Baha, converting them into military posts.
The raids have included incursions into residential neighborhoods, closures of city entrances and orders forcing Palestinian families from their homes.
During the first days of the campaign, homes, commercial properties and infrastructure were also demolished or damaged, while Israeli flags were raised over some homes seized for military use.
Hebron Municipality said Tuesday that 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families had been displaced by the continuing Israeli campaign.
The Palestinian Prisoner Society said Israeli forces arrested 110 Palestinians across Hebron governorate between Friday and Wednesday.
Military closures have also disrupted in-person education at 66 schools, affecting 2,872 students.
Of those, 2,198 students are living under direct closure, while another 674 are from forcibly displaced families and have been unable to reach their schools.
The displaced families are demanding that Israeli forces lift the closures and allow them to return to their homes and resume their daily lives.

Saudi Arabia suspends travel, entry from Kenya over Ebola concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:33:03 UTC
00:33:03 KST

Şahin Demir
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Saudi Arabia on Friday announced additional precautionary measures against the Ebola virus, including suspending travel to and entry from Kenya, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
The measures, introduced following an assessment of the epidemiological situation by health authorities, include suspending travel by Saudi citizens to Kenya and halting the issuance of all types of visas to travelers from the East African country.
The kingdom will also prohibit entry to travelers arriving from Kenya, including those traveling through third countries who have stayed in Kenya or other Ebola-affected countries during the 21 days preceding their arrival.
The restrictions are part of preventive measures introduced in 2019 and strengthened this May for travelers arriving from countries facing Ebola outbreak risks, SPA reported.
This June, Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and entry from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan.
The kingdom also strengthened preventive measures for arrivals from countries neighboring Ebola-affected areas, including screening at entry points, epidemiological investigations, and early health response mechanisms.
The Saudi Public Health Authority, known as Weqaya, said the country’s public health situation remains reassuring and under continuous monitoring.
It added that authorities are closely following epidemiological developments regionally and internationally and coordinating with relevant agencies to implement preventive measures as necessary.
Ebola is a severe viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of infected people. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.

RT SIGNS AGREEMENTS WITH A DOZEN AFRICAN COUNTRIES AT RUSSIA-AFRICA MEDIA FORUM CO-ORGANIZED BY RT IN MOSCOW
Published 30 Oct, 2026 15:32 | Updated 30 Oct, 2026 16:35
MOSCOW, OCTOBER 30, 2026 — RT has signed agreements and memoranda with twelve African media organizations and ministries during the “Russia-Africa” media forum, which took place in Moscow over October 26-29 as part of the “Russia–Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.”
RT, which broadcasts in Africa in English, French, and Arabic, signed a memorandum of understanding with the Ministry of Communications and Media of the Central African Republic (CAR), represented by Minister Evariste Ngamana.
Additionally, RT signed a cooperation memorandum with one of Nigeria’s leading television channels, TVC News. This agreement envisions deepening the partnership through the exchange of content and experiences, as well as joint coverage of significant international events. Further agreements were also established with the state broadcasting corporations of Ghana, Tanzania, Namibia, and Zimbabwe, as well as with the Ethiopian FANA Media Corporation and the Ethiopian News Agency.
Furthermore, the RT Arabic channel signed a cooperation memorandum with LANA, one of the oldest state news agencies in Libya; Sudan National Television, among the oldest television broadcasters in the Arab world and Africa; Mauritanian Sahara Media Group; and the Mauritanian broadcasting company.
The “Russia-Africa” media forum, organized by RT in collaboration with the Sputnik and TASS news agencies, gathered over 200 participants from 46 African countries, including political figures and leading experts from the regional media community.
The global RT television news network includes news channels in English, Arabic, Spanish, German, Serbian, and French, as well as the RTD documentary channel in Russian and English. RT also operates online portals in ten languages and the global multimedia agency RUPTLY, which supplies exclusive content to broadcasters worldwide. RT is available 24/7 to more than 950 million viewers in over 100 countries.
Africa is one of the key regions for RT’s operations. The channel is expanding its partnership network with new media corporations and enhancing cooperation with existing partners. Currently, RT has eight bureaus across Africa. Additionally, RT conducts training programs for African journalists and co-hosted the African Media Awards ceremony in Ethiopia in 2025, which is the largest media event of the year for the continent.

Israel demolishes gunmen's homes in West Bank operation that has displaced thousands
JERUSALEM, Oct 30 - Israel demolished on Friday the homes of the assailants who killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron last week, part of an ongoing operation that has forcibly displaced over 3,000 Palestinians.
After the October 23 attack, in which both gunmen were killed, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the Israeli military to launch a in areas near the checkpoint, triggering protests by Palestinian residents.
Palestinian officials have accused Netanyahu of using the operation to drum up support ahead of a general election in Israel on Tuesday. Israel's government says its operation is a response to the attack on its soldiers.
In a statement announcing the demolitions, Israel's military said it would "continue to operate proactively and offensively" to thwart attacks in the West Bank and "protect residents in the area".
The homes demolished on Friday had been occupied by the wives and children of the gunmen before the military forced Palestinians to leave the area over the past week, according to local residents.
The military has also demolished other homes as well as shops, roads, and factories in Hebron since the attack, according to local officials, though the exact scale of the demolitions is unclear.
It has closed most entrances to the city, severely curtailing freedom of movement for Palestinians, including people in need of medical attention.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said this week that the displacement of residents raised "grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force" and that "threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid expansion of settlements, deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this.
Under Netanyahu's right-wing coalition there has also been a surge of militant settler violence against Palestinians.
In Kafr Malik near Ramallah on Friday, Reuters witnesses documented militant Israeli settlers shoving Palestinians and preventing farmers from harvesting their olives, while the Israeli military was present.
The Israeli military said it had responded to reports from Israeli settlers that Palestinians were throwing stones at them, and had arrested two Palestinians.
It did not address the reports of Israeli settlers attacking Palestinians. A Reuters witness present during the incident did not observe the Palestinians throwing stones.
Attacks have surged during the Palestinian olive harvest, which starts at the end of September and ends in November. The Israeli rights group Yesh Din reported at least 135 physical attacks on the olive harvest as of October 23. REUTERS

Is Running a Marathon Good for Your Heart?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:30:27 UTC
00:30:27 KST

Every so often, after a marathon, headlines will pop up about a marathon runner collapsing and dying during or shortly after the race. It’s rare, but it happens: A 2025 study found records of 176 cardiac arrests during long-distance running events in the U.S. out of about 29 million people who finished the races.
Deaths like these raise the question of whether such an intense physical feat as a marathon can possibly be dangerous, or at least unhealthy, for the heart. We asked scientists who study marathoners about long-distance races and heart health, plus what runners can do to keep themselves safe.
Is all that running actually good for you?
Experts are pretty unequivocal: Yes. “Exercise is good for the heart,” says David Oxborough, professor of echocardiography and cardiovascular physiology at Liverpool John Moores University in the U.K. “We know that regular moderate-intensity exercise improves your cardiovascular risk, it reduces mortality, and it has real positive benefits.”
Of course, training for a marathon—which can take months or years of steady increases in endurance—is different from the act of running the race itself, says Daniel Muniz, senior lecturer in exercise physiology at the University of Hertfordshire in the U.K. “Running a marathon is a big physiological stress. You're going to hurt after…and if you look at markers in your physiology, everything is going to be all over the place.” Markers of muscle damage and heart damage are elevated, at least for a little while. (Oxborough, who has studied some of these elevated markers, says that they come back down swiftly and don’t seem to be linked to long-term damage.)
But the consistent training that running a marathon requires carries positive effects for physical and mental health, Muniz continues. “The benefits far outweigh the negatives. I think that's very fair to say.”
Why do people die running marathons, then?
Dying during a marathon is extremely uncommon, says Oxborough. What’s more, it doesn’t seem random. People who die during endurance running events tend to fall into two categories, often identified after the fact: either younger people who have undiagnosed genetic heart problems, or middle-aged men who have heart disease without any symptoms.
“If you've got underlying disease, then there is a risk of sudden cardiac death. If you're under the age of 35, that is usually caused by an inherited cardiac disease, such as cardiomyopathy. As you go over 35, the main cause is more acquired disease, like coronary artery disease,” he says.
How can you find out if your heart is healthy enough for a marathon? And should you?
“You should, absolutely,” says Oxborough. “We do pre-participation cardiac screening for young people in competitive sport. We have charities in the U.K. It's now becoming much more accepted in the U.S., and it wasn't before. This is a simple 12-lead ECG and a questionnaire to young people.”
That’s enough to start the process of figuring out whether people might have an inherited disease, the experts say. If they do, it doesn’t mean they have to stop training. It just might shape how they decide to train and manage their risk.
What about older people?
The problem with coronary artery disease is that many people have no symptoms in the early stages.
If you’re thinking of running a marathon and you’re over 35 or 40, here’s what Oxborough recommends: “Go speak to your GP. Have a 12-lead ECG done. Have your blood done. Make sure your cholesterol levels are normal. Have your blood pressure taken, and if any of them show any sign that they may be a higher risk, then we recommend an exercise stress test. And if you're very lucky, if you're able to access it, a CT coronary angiogram,” he says. These are tests that will help establish your baseline and what is likely to be happening in your arteries before you really ramp up training.
Not all of these are required, but “a baseline test of risk is really important, and that you can do at your GP,” he says.
Can anyone run a marathon?
In principle, yes. “I am of the opinion that most people with training should be able to run a marathon. The important bit there is: with appropriate training for a number of months or or perhaps a year,” says Muniz.
This is not a physical challenge where you can go out and achieve it tomorrow without practice. “But if you start training and you start running for 20 minutes, or run and walk, and then transition to run for 20 minutes, 30 minutes, 40 minutes, and then you do that for a number of months, I think most people should be able to eventually run a marathon,” he says.

Lithuanian police connect Starlink arson attacks in three EU countries to the same group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:30:23 UTC
00:30:23 KST

Lithuanian law enforcement authorities have linked arson attacks targeting Starlink satellite equipment in Lithuania, Bulgaria, and Poland. Investigators believe the same two men carried out the attacks in Lithuania and Bulgaria, while the perpetrators in Poland were connected to them, Lithuanian police said on Oct. 29. Authorities suspect the detainees of participating in an organized terrorist group and are investigating possible links to Russia.
The suspects are two men in their early 20s who live in Germany. One holds German and Turkish citizenship, while the other holds German and Serbian citizenship. They arrived in Lithuania shortly before the arson attack, which took place overnight into Oct. 18, and left the country afterward. According to local broadcaster LRT, Lithuanian police deputy chief Saulius Briginas said the suspects had no ties to Lithuania and traveled there specifically to carry out the attack.
Both men were detained in Duisburg, Germany, on Oct. 23 under European arrest warrants issued by Bulgaria in connection with an earlier arson attack on Starlink equipment near Sofia. Bulgarian news agency BTA previously reported that the suspects are 19-year-olds Zeka Islam and Tirpan Beytulla. Bulgarian authorities accuse them of setting fire to the Plana satellite communications station on Oct. 9. Three antennas were completely destroyed and five others were damaged.
Different perpetrators carried out the Sept. 23 attack in Poland, but Lithuanian police say they were connected to the suspects in the incidents in Lithuania and Bulgaria. At least four people have been detained in Poland in connection with the arson investigation.
On Oct. 27, Lithuanian prosecutors formally named Islam and Beytulla as suspects in a case involving the creation of and participation in a terrorist group, entering the country for terrorist purposes, and carrying out a terrorist attack that could have caused serious consequences. Prosecutor Nerijus Puškorius said creating or participating in a terrorist group alone carries a prison sentence of five to 15 years. A decision on whether the two men will be extradited to Lithuania has not yet been made.
During the attack in Vilnius, a fire broke out on the grounds of the Delska data center, but it was quickly extinguished by a security guard. The Starlink equipment was not damaged and service was not interrupted. The Insider previously reported that U.S. company SpaceX rents premises from the Lithuanian operator and that infrastructure at the site supports nine satellite antennas whose communications are used in part by Ukraine.
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius had previously described the attack as being part of Russia’s hybrid warfare operations, and investigators have also said they are examining possible ties between the suspects and Russia. Briginas said the series of attacks may have been intended to disrupt European Starlink infrastructure in a way that could affect communications in Ukraine. The investigation is continuing, however, and authorities have not yet established the ultimate motive of the attack.
As was previously reported by Der Spiegel, suspects detained in connection with the Starlink arson in Poland have been linked to the Turkish criminal group Daltons. According to the German outlet, the group’s suspected leader, Beratcan Gökdemir, was detained in Russia in 2024 but was later released by Russian authorities and placed under their protection. On Oct. 28, 85 suspected members of the Daltons gang were reportedly detained in Turkey.

Russia’s Justice Ministry adds Russian opposition platform at PACE and independent publisher Vidim Books to its ‘undesirable’ organizations registry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russia’s Justice Ministry adds Russian opposition platform at PACE and independent publisher Vidim Books to its ‘undesirable’ organizations registry
Russia’s Justice Ministry has added the independent publishing house Vidim Books and the Platform for Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces at the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe to its registry of “undesirable” organizations.
In total, the ministry added 11 organizations to the registry. According to the document, Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office declared most of them “undesirable” on October 20, though the move was not made public at the time.
Russia’s law on “undesirable” organizations has been in effect since 2015. Since then, the Prosecutor General’s Office has granted that status to any foreign or international nongovernmental organization whose activities it deems a threat to “the foundations of the constitutional order, Russia’s defense capability, or its security.” Participation in and cooperation with undesirable organizations carries liability up to and including criminal prosecution.
The Prosecutor General’s Office regularly uses that status to target independent media outlets as well as associations of opposition figures and activists critical of the Russian authorities.

'Deeply hurt': Convicted murderer Christa Pike speaks out after botched execution
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike said she remains in constant pain after surviving a botched lethal injection in September, in her first public statement since the failed execution. She expressed gratitude for those who saved her life while urging compassion for her victim's family.
Christa Pike said she is in constant pain since surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month but thankful for the love and support she has received.
Pike issued her first public statement through her legal team on Friday. She said she went into the execution chamber prepared to die in peace and woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed.
Read moreChrista Pike 'angry and confused' after surviving Tennessee execution attempt
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said.
Pike, 50, said she had not contemplated a life beyond her execution date.
"I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured,” Pike said.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on September 30 for her 1995 stabbing of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.

Pike said she is thankful for the medical workers who saved her life and the people who showed her kindness.
“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.
Pike’s attorneys have urged Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to reduce Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment. Lee told reporters this week that, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
Lee called for an investigation into what happened during the failed execution and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled this year.

Pike was hospitalised in the immediate aftermath of the failed execution and then moved back to prison at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center.

Mossad joins Israeli election interference probe, with Qatar and Turkey under scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:29:02 UTC
00:29:02 KST

Israel's Mossad intelligence agency is set to join an investigation into allegations that Qatar attempted to influence the country's parliamentary election through the use of tens of millions of shekels, after the Shin Bet domestic security agency requested its assistance.
The Mossad will help examine aspects of the case that fall within its jurisdiction, particularly whether foreign governments were involved in the suspected influence operations. The Shin Bet had obtained intelligence about the possibility of illegal money transfers even before the election, as part of its responsibility for identifying and preventing threats to national security.
The investigation centers on suspected efforts to influence voters rather than allegations of ballot tampering or irregularities in vote counting. Qatar and Turkey, the two countries at the center of the inquiry, have both denied any involvement.
Qatar's Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al-Ansari rejected the accusations Thursday, saying: "We reject the allegations made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media, who have launched yet another disinformation campaign aimed at dragging Qatar into Israel's political disputes following this week's elections.
"They accuse us of buying Netanyahu, the left, and now the Arab vote. If all these accusations were to be believed, Qatar would apparently own all of Israel."
Turkey also rejected any suggestion that it had interfered in the Israeli election. "The allegations circulating in certain media outlets and on social media are completely baseless," Ankara said. "These accusations are part of a deliberate and blatant disinformation campaign aimed at manipulating the public."
The controversy began with a letter sent by Central Elections Committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg to Shin Bet director David Zini, calling for an investigation into suspected foreign interference. "The integrity of elections is at the heart of democracy," Sohlberg wrote.
Although he emphasized that he could not personally assess the substance of the allegations, the judge said the possibility of foreign involvement made a thorough investigation essential.
"Given that these suspicions concern foreign actors, there is an obligation to investigate them thoroughly in order to safeguard the integrity of Knesset elections and prevent illegal activity intended to undermine the democratic system and engage in subversion," he wrote.
The letter prompted Yesh Atid lawmaker Vladimir Beliak to demand that the presidium of the Central Elections Committee be convened and presented with the evidence underlying Sohlberg's decision to instruct the Shin Bet to investigate.
Dean Livne, the committee's acting director general, responded on Sohlberg's behalf, emphasizing that the allegations under investigation did not mean the election itself had been compromised.
"The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of voting at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for claims of systematic violations of election integrity," Livne said.
He added that statements made by the Israel Police commissioner and the Shin Bet director on Election Day and afterward reinforced that assessment.

Switzerland to receive first Patriot missile parts mid-2027
Swiss defence minister Martin Pfister says that the first components of the United States Patriot missile defence system would arrive in 2027.
He received confirmation of this from the US Ambassador to Switzerland.

The minister was “surprised”, but is delighted with this good news. This gives Switzerland the prospect of expanding its surface-to-air defence capabilities.

‘Life in the old dog’: Germany’s economy grows more than expected

‘Life in the old dog’: Germany’s economy grows more than expected
- Germany’s economy grew 0.2% in the third quarter, beating forecasts. Analysts said it shows “life in the old dog yet” and points to a possible recovery.
- Spending on defence and infrastructure helped growth, while exports and investment weakened. Germany also outperformed France, but trailed the euro zone’s 0.4% rise.
- Inflation fell to 2.8% in October and core inflation to 2.1%. Experts warned of “growing price risks” as gas and oil prices have risen again.
AI generated
FRANKFURT – Germany’s quarterly growth beat forecasts and inflation slowed sharply as energy price pressures fuelled by the Iran war eased, boosting hopes on Oct 30 of a sustained recovery for Europe’s biggest economy.
The official data will come as a relief for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose popularity ratings have been in the doldrums as his plans to revive the manufacturing powerhouse have moved only slowly.
The economy is seeking to get back on its feet after several years of stagnation, hit hard by China’s shift from a key market to a fierce industrial competitor, surging energy costs and deep-rooted structural problems.
Hailing third-quarter growth of 0.2%, which was above analyst estimates, ING economist Carsten Brzeski said Germany is on track for its best growth performance since 2022.
“Some would say there’s life in the old dog yet.”
In the July-September period, the economy was supported by rising public and private spending, though exports weakened noticeably from “the very dynamic trend” seen in the first half of 2026 and investment also declined, statistics office Destatis said.
Germany eclipsed France’s economy, which shrank 0.1% in the quarter at a time when worries were already growing about the dire state of the country’s public finances.
But it was behind the 21-country euro zone as a whole which expanded by a better-than-forecast 0.4%.
‘Growing risks’
Germany’s public spending blitz on defence and infrastructure, unleashed by Merz after he won elections in 2025, is providing a major boost to the economy this year.
The economy has also withstood the fallout from the US war on Iran and higher energy prices better than many had feared.
While higher power prices have weighed on some sectors, others – such as chemicals – benefited as business was redirected from some of their global rivals who were harder hit by supply chain woes.
Still, the GDP expansion was slightly weaker than in the first two quarters of the year.
Some manufacturers, particularly in sectors like petroleum products, were hit by transport problems due to lower water levels on key rivers, particularly the Rhine, during the summer’s drought and heatwaves.
Inflation in October slowed to 2.8% – from 3.3% in the previous month – following the government’s introduction of fuel subsidies to help motorists hit by higher costs triggered by the US war on Iran.
Still the fall was bigger than expected, and economists noted that pressures were easing across the board. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, dipped to 2.1% from 2.4% in September.
But Stephanie Schoenwald, an economist with German public lender KfW, warned there were “growing price risks” ahead.
“Gas and oil prices have risen significantly again in recent weeks – driven by ongoing conflicts and lower stock levels,” she said. AFP

Slovakia reopens criminal case over fighter jet, air defense systems donation to Ukraine

Slovakia reopens criminal case over donation of fighter jets, air defense systems to Ukraine
Slovakia's Prosecutor General Maros Zilinka said on Oct. 30 that he had reopened a criminal case against former Prime Minister Eduard Heger and former Defense Minister Jaroslav Nad over their decision to donate Slovakia's fleet of MiG-29 fighter jets and Soviet-era KUB air defense systems to Ukraine in spring 2023.
Slovakia's caretaker government, headed by Heger, approved the donation of 13 MiG-29 fighter jets and part of the country's KUB air defense systems to Ukraine in March 2023. All 13 jets had been delivered by April that year, making Slovakia the first country to send fighter aircraft to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Prime Minister Robert Fico — widely seen as sympathetic to Moscow — has long criticized Western military aid to Ukraine and the defense assistance provided by the previous Slovak government. In June 2024, his administration filed a criminal complaint against Heger and Nad over the jet transfer.

and it may appear in our Letters section.
The defense ministry accused the two of sabotage, abuse of power, and mismanagement of public property — allegations both Heger and Nad have denied. Current Defense Minister Robert Kalinak also accused his predecessor of "treason."
The investigation had been closed by Bratislava regional prosecutor Rastislav Remeta in February. On Nov. 10, 2025, the Bratislava prosecutor's office said Slovakia's transfer of military aid to Ukraine did not constitute a criminal offense.
Zilinka said on Oct. 30 that the previous investigation had been "closed prematurely," prompting him to reopen the case.
"During the preparatory proceedings, the facts were not established to the extent necessary to make a decision," Zilinka said.
Zilinka reassigned prosecutorial supervision of the case from Bratislava to a regional prosecutor in Trencin to ensure that sufficient evidence is gathered.
The MiG-29 is a fourth-generation fighter jet designed in the Soviet Union, meant to establish air superiority and provide front-line air defense. Both Ukrainian and Russian forces use the fighter jet in their air forces.
The KUB, also known as the 2K12 Kub or SA-6 Gainful, is a Soviet-era, medium-range surface-to-air missile system designed to intercept aircraft and other aerial targets. It uses radar-guided missiles and was developed to protect ground forces and military facilities from air attacks.
The system is mobile and typically consists of radar-equipped vehicles and missile launchers, allowing it to provide air defense cover for troops and strategic sites.

‘Need a Plan B’: Yemenis in Aden prepare for another war as missiles fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:26:00 UTC
00:26:00 KST

‘Need a Plan B’: Yemenis in Aden prepare for another war as missiles fall
As Houthi missiles strike Aden, residents stockpile food and prepare escape plans, fearing a return to all-out war.
For Mohammed Abdul Malik, the powerful explosions that have hit Yemen’s southern city of Aden repeatedly over the past month are an ominous warning of darker days ahead.
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed attacks against several locations in Aden, including the international airport, military camps, the city’s port, and the presidential palace – which serves as a base for Yemen’s government.
Fearing that the city could once again descend into widespread violence, Abdul Malik has begun taking precautions. He has stockpiled food and prepared his car for a long journey if he needs to leave.
“I’ll tell you about myself and my close friends: We’ve started buying and stockpiling basic provisions, like sugar and other staples,” Abdul Malik told Al Jazeera.
If the security situation deteriorates further and state institutions collapse, his Plan B is to flee Aden with his family and seek refuge in Shabwa, to the northeast, or Hadramout, to the east.
“We’ve mapped out an exit route from the city. I’ve prepared my car, checked it over, and set aside an emergency supply of fuel. I’m ready to pack up my family and head out at a moment’s notice,” he said.
Daily life disrupted
After four years of relative calm, Yemen’s war has reignited in recent months, particularly since early September, when the Houthis launched a major offensive to seize government-held areas in the west of the country from the Saudi-backed, pro-government National Resistance Forces (NRF).
Within a week, the Iran-backed armed group – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – had seized districts in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces, including the port city of Mocha, a stronghold of the NRF, and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.
A government counteroffensive launched in early October has made limited gains along the Red Sea coast, but at the same time the Houthis have tightened their siege of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, after capturing a vital road linking it to Aden.
Aden had remained relatively peaceful despite the fierce fighting elsewhere, and had become a refuge for thousands of people displaced by the conflict.
The wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks this month has shattered that calm, and has raised fears that the Houthis may be seeking to capture Aden.
Accounts from friends who fled Taiz, where fighting and the siege have driven up prices and disrupted supplies, have deepened his concerns about what could happen to his city.
“Prices in Taiz have already doubled, and the same could easily happen in Aden. If the [Aden] port were to be struck, prices would skyrocket,” he said.
“At work, my colleagues and I talk about what we should buy, what food we ought to store, what our contingency plan is, and where we would go if we had to leave,” he added.
Abdul Malik described how the Houthi attacks have disrupted daily life in Aden, with some families limiting their movements – especially at night.
“When the [first missile] explosion occurred, one of my colleagues went to the school to pick up her son and found the students frightened and gathered together in one place. We go to work and take our children to school, but there is a sense of anxiety and tension,” he told Al Jazeera.
Airport attacks
Aden international airport, currently Yemen’s busiest airport, has borne the brunt of the Houthi missile and drone attacks, which have repeatedly disrupted air travel, forcing airlines to cancel or delay flights and divert others to airports elsewhere in Yemen or abroad.
For residents living near the airport, the repeated strikes and explosions have taken a psychological toll on families, prompting some to consider moving to safer areas inside and outside Aden. Ahmed Awadh, a resident of Aden’s Khor Maksar district, near the airport, said the attacks have left children struggling with fear and anxiety.
“An explosion jolts the children awake in terror, leaving them unable to sleep for the rest of the night. Even the sound of an ordinary airplane now strikes fear into my family,” Awadh told Al Jazeera.
He said the attacks have disrupted schools and businesses, prompting families to rush home and some parents to keep their children away from school. Some families have sent vulnerable relatives, including children and elderly people, to neighbouring Lahj and Abyan provinces or other districts of Aden. Others have rented homes further away from the airport.
Awadh, who lives with 10 other family members, said they have taken precautions by keeping children away from windows during attacks. He and his neighbours have also created a WhatsApp group to check on one another after each explosion.
“The [Aden] airport, which serves the civilian population, as well as other civilian infrastructure and residential areas, must not be targeted,” Awadh said.
Aden remains vulnerable
Aden, Yemen’s second-most important city after the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, suffered extensive destruction in early 2015 during fierce fighting between the Houthis and their opponents, as well as air strikes by the Saudi-led coalition.
Even after the Houthis were driven out, the city continued to experience sporadic clashes between rival anti-Houthi factions, which sometimes turned their weapons on each other.
Adeeb al-Shatri, a professor of journalism at Aden and Hadramout universities, said the latest wave of Houthi missile attacks had compounded the suffering of a city already plagued by lawlessness and insecurity.
He questioned why Yemen’s internationally recognised government had left Aden, its temporary capital and seat of government, vulnerable to Houthi attacks without adequate air defences to intercept missiles and drones.
“Aden is currently the capital, housing both major and minor state institutions. Therefore, the legitimate government must protect it,” al-Shatri told Al Jazeera.
The Yemeni military has claimed to have air defence forces in Aden, with reports of drone interceptions before they reached civilian areas.
Yemen’s Information Minister, Moammar al-Eryani, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on criticism that air defence systems have been inadequate in protecting Aden.
Al-Shatri argued that only a small proportion of Aden’s wealthier residents could afford to stockpile food and other essential supplies in preparation for an emergency. Most residents, he said, were already struggling to feed their families.
“In Europe and other stable Arab countries, people stockpile food during crises, but in Aden, people need three times their current salaries just to live a simple life,” he said.
Al-Shatri also challenged the notion that Houthi attacks had brought businesses and education in Aden to a complete standstill.
“People’s movement in the city returned to normal just an hour after the explosion because they have to keep moving to earn money and secure their daily bread,” he said. “If work were to stop, it would lead to a financial crisis, and they would be unable to provide food for themselves.”

Russia Designates Opposition Delegation at PACE as ‘Undesirable’

Russia’s Justice Ministry has added the Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces at the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) to its list of “undesirable” organizations, a move that renders affiliation with the anti-war group illegal.
The delegation of Russian exiles was set up in January after years of lobbying efforts by leading opposition figures like former businessman Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
Several members of the anti-war group, including dissident Vladimir Kara-Murza and Pussy Riot co-founder Nadya Tolokonnikova, already face criminal prosecution in Russia.
Under Russian law, individuals affiliated with an “undesirable” entity can face up to four years in prison. Organizing the work of an “undesirable” group carries a maximum sentence of six years in prison.
Neither the Prosecutor General’s Office, which ruled to designate the Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces as “undesirable” on Oct. 21, nor the Justice Ministry, which approved the designation on Thursday, have officially commented on the decision.
Besides the PACE delegation, the Justice Ministry blacklisted another 11 foreign entities on Thursday, including Vidim Books, a publishing house founded in Slovakia in 2023 to print books that are censored or banned inside Russia.
Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe and PACE in March 2022, shortly after launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It had been a member for 26 years.
Introduced in 2015, Russia’s “undesirable” designation has been used to hinder the work of independent media outlets, civil society groups and the political opposition. Hundreds of entities have since been added to the registry, including The Moscow Times.

Queen Ursula comes to Canada with velvet handcuffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Queen Ursula comes to Canada with velvet handcuffs
I’m trying to spend a few weeks back in Canada for some peace and quiet from the usual European drama. Just my luck that Queen Ursula would follow me here, circus and all.
She hadn’t even landed in Montreal for the EU-Canada Summit, and already everyone around me was saying that Canada’s “associate membership” had been canceled. They’d heard that countries like France and Germany objected to the idea, even as Von der Leyen was saddling up her broom for a trip across the Atlantic.
Someone even asked me if that meant that we’re now kicked out of Eurovision. I had to explain that the title never existed in the first place. EU treaties refer only to association agreements. It’s just the usual sort of branding that von der Leyen, the unelected EU chief executive, likes to roll out, much like her endless riffs about unity, as though dissent weren’t an actual virtue in a functioning democracy.
Or like the way she talks a good game about sticking it to Russia while simultaneously celebrating the €977 million spent this winter alone on gas purchases for Ukraine – much of which comes from Russia via Hungary and Slovakia. The EU writes cheques to Kiev. Kiev pays Hungary and Slovakia, who then pay Moscow.
Those middlemen exist mainly so that Queen Ursula can maintain a certain public image while engaging in more practical considerations behind the scenes, albeit at considerably greater expense to the European taxpayer.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney got a taste of the spectacle when Ursula’s marketing campaign became the focus of the event. He was forced to acknowledge that he honestly didn’t give a damn what they called this new cooperation, so long as it was good for Canadians. Meanwhile, other EU leaders, like German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had started referring to it instead as an “alliance for the future.”
But von der Leyen had already landed in Canada and continued promoting the “associate membership” label, smiling as Carney, sitting beside her, subsequently echoed the term.
Of course, all that the mental midgets are going to take away from this whole event is the intrigue over whether or not Canada is joining the EU. Spoiler alert: it isn’t. And never will. It’s not even legally possible. But this idiotic intrigue is distracting from the details of what lurks underneath, which could amount to a whole lot of iron-fisting through velvet gloves.
Turns out someone had already leaked a draft statement on these future relations to Politico, dated September 22, 2026. Cut out the diplomatic fluff and here’s what you’re left with.
Both sides are clearly looking for new markets as they diversify trade away from the US. Great. But it seems rather stupid for the EU to be begging Canada for its natural resources – gas, metals and minerals – while simultaneously slapping on carbon tariffs that get downloaded onto European citizens and companies. What’s the point of trying to bring prices down by increasing supply if you’re just going to top up the cost anyway.
You jokers also killed off your own nuclear industries, only to realize (a bit late) that perhaps it was preferable to having to resort to coal, before subsequently reviving it as the future of clean energy. So maybe you’re not exactly the best people to be doing commie-style central planning.
Technology is already advancing in favor of the environment, with those improvements increasingly built into the conditions for funding and financing. Just let it breathe already. Not every industry needs a Brussels bureaucrat hovering over it.
It also sounds like they’ve roped Canada into their scheme to skim Russian cash from its Western-held assets to pimp themselves out under the pretext of Ukraine’s defence and their own, then just hope that Russia’s ultimately cool with that so they don’t have to stick their own taxpayers either the final bill.
Perhaps the most troubling part is the Orwellian digital cooperation section of the agreement, which aims to “advance cooperation on artificial intelligence security and sovereignty, trusted data flows and digital governance and to align emerging AI and digital regulatory frameworks through associated country status for Canada.”
Does this mean Canadians get to have Queen Ursula block their bank accounts now, too, since we’ll all be connected and harmonized inside one giant digital panopticon? Or worse, some AI bot? It’s hardly reassuring that Carney’s government has just appealed the federal court decision condemning his predecessor Justin Trudeau’s government for unconstitutionally invoking the Emergencies Act, which allowed it to block the bank accounts of Covid-era anti-mandate Freedom Convoy participants without a court order – all for the crime of honking too loudly. Nor is it reassuring that Canada and the EU have already signed an agreement on digital “trust services” involving things like government-controlled digital identity wallets.
One honk too many, one wrong opinion on some social media platform linked to the online ID system that they’re all ushering in – ostensibly under the pretext of adults needing to prove that they aren’t children requiring protection from online pedos – and there goes your whole life with the flip of a switch. It’s not like Queen Ursula’s European Commission isn’t already doing that with sanctions and asset freezes, in the absence of due process, for those whose views it qualifies as “propaganda.”
And if this is what they mean by an alliance for the future, then Canadians – the average citizens of this country – need full and open debate over the fine print before anyone signs us up.

Up to 10,000 Turbojet Engines Per Year: PBS Group Invests $100 Million in U.S. Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

The Czech company PBS Group plans to invest an additional $100 million in expanding the production of small turbojet engines in the United States.
The funds will be directed toward expanding the production capacity of the PBS Aerospace plant in Roswell, Georgia, according to Armádní noviny.
By 2028, the company expects to reach an annual production volume of up to 10,000 engines, which will nearly double its current output.
This volume will correspond to the production of approximately 40 power units per working day.
In parallel with its U.S. operations, the PBS Group is expanding its capacity in the Czech Republic. In Velká Bíteš, the company is investing approximately €40 million in the creation of a new aviation technology division.
The expansion of the plant in Georgia extends beyond the assembly lines. The facility’s floor space has already been increased by 930 m², two new test chambers have been built to double engine testing capacity, and preparations are underway to launch a second production shift.
It is worth noting that the company’s initial plans called for reaching an annual production capacity of 20,000 engines as early as 2026–2027. PBS Group has not yet specified whether these figures remain relevant for later stages.
The U.S. facility is mass-producing the TJ40 and TJ80 turbojet engines, which are being actively integrated into various drones and missile systems.
Among the company’s key customers is the American firm Zone 5 Technologies, which develops and manufactures the Rusty Dagger and White Spike missiles. PBS has signed a long-term contract with the company to supply turbojet engines.
Additional opportunities for cooperation arose after Zone 5 Technologies became part of the Norwegian defense group Kongsberg Gruppen earlier this year.
In addition, the Ukrainian company Airlogix and the Czech company PBS Velká Bíteš signed a memorandum on organizing licensed production of small turbine engines in Ukraine.
The process will begin with engine assembly and the establishment of a certified service center, followed by the expansion of manufacturing operations.
