Swiss components also found in new Russian weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Swiss components also found in new Russian weapons
Ukraine has now named 11 Swiss companies whose components have been found in Russian drones and missiles.
What new discoveries have the Ukrainian authorities made?
The Ukrainian military intelligence service, HUR, regularly publishes details of electronic components found in the wreckage of Russian weapon systems in a publicly accessible database. Findings from spring, September and October of this year show that Swiss components continue to be used in new or upgraded Russian drones, missiles and cruise missiles. Ukraine has identified components from 11 Swiss companies. Swiss components have also been found in North Korean ballistic missiles fired at Ukraine.
How important are these parts for Russian weapon systems?
Very important, says Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s adviser on international sanctions, speaking to Swiss public broadcaster SRF. According to Vlasiuk, 95% of Russian drones and missiles contain parts from Swiss companies. The electronic components supplied by Swiss firms are mass-produced industrial goods. They are used as microcontrollers in the control systems of missiles and drones, in the processing of satellite navigation data, as voltage converters, as sensors or as memory chips.
These components are not military equipment, nor are they dual-use items
And yet these electronic components are of military use. Countries are still struggling to define these goods in a uniform manner, as they have hitherto regarded them as civilian products. With changes in the nature of warfare – for example, the widespread use of low-cost drones – these mass-produced goods are becoming strategically significant. Together with the G7 countries, the EU has placed these goods on a joint sanctions list. Switzerland has adopted this sanctions list. As a result, Swiss companies are also no longer permitted to sell them to Russia.
What is Switzerland being accused of?
Switzerland is not doing enough to prevent shipments to Russia. This is the criticism levelled by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to the Ukrainian president. He is calling on the Swiss government to involve the law enforcement authorities and to strengthen the export control bodies. He is dissatisfied with Switzerland’s responses to date. Sanctions regimes have evolved, as has Russia’s ability to circumvent them, he says, adding that Switzerland cannot simply stick to the logic that there are no production facilities in Switzerland and that it does not export to Russia. That is not enough.
More
Swiss Army combines horses and high-tech drones
What does the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) say?
SECO is aware of the issue regarding the components, the State Secretariat stated in response to an enquiry. It explains that, in most cases, the goods are not produced in Switzerland. Consequently, no exports take place. The export of these goods from Switzerland – including indirectly – to Russia is prohibited. Swiss companies are obliged to comply with certain due diligence requirements. This includes, in the case of exports or sales to third countries, contractually prohibiting the re-export of these goods to Russia. The effective and comprehensive enforcement of sanctions against Russia is a priority for the government, SECO writes.
What is required of companies?
They should take a closer look. Particularly when selecting their distribution partners and intermediaries, says Vladyslav Vlasiuk. He cites the example of the Dutch company NXP. A few years ago, this company attracted even more negative attention than the Swiss firms. By 2026, NXP electronic components were almost entirely absent from Russian weapons.
The Ukrainian government lists 11 manufacturers based in Switzerland, two of which belong to the same group. We have asked the four companies with the most entries in the Ukrainian database for their comments:
STMicroelectronics: The company is headquartered in Plan-les-Ouates (canton Geneva). It emphasises that the use of its products for purposes other than those for which they are intended is neither authorised nor tolerated. The company has a comprehensive global compliance programme that includes training, procedures and guidelines for all sales channels. Since the end of February 2022, STMicroelectronics has taken measures to implement all sanctions packages and export control measures imposed by the EU, the US and other partner countries against Russia and Belarus. The company says it no longer conducts any business in Russia.
u-blox: In its statement, the Thalwil (canton Zurich)-based company condemns Russia’s attack on Ukraine in the strongest possible terms. Upon the outbreak of war, the company suspended all cooperation and deliveries to Russia and Belarus; sales to countries in the Eurasian Economic Union were subsequently halted as well. Since 2021, u-blox has also been working with the organisation Conflict Armament Research (CAR) to investigate how its own components ended up in drones used in the war in Ukraine. On the basis of this collaboration, it says several companies involved have been identified and blacklisted.
Traco Power: The company, based in Baar (canton Zug), points out that its products are electronic components for civilian industrial applications which are not listed in any dual-use regulation and are not intended for military purposes. Until the sanctions came into force, the company had supplied the Russian market exclusively via closely monitored authorised distribution partners. With immediate effect from February 28, 2022, Traco Power says it ceased all deliveries and business relations with Russia – including those via third countries. Any of the company’s components that may be found could therefore under no circumstances have originated from deliveries made after the sanctions came into force. The company says it conscientiously and strictly complies with all applicable regulations, embargoes and sanctions.
TE Connectivity (Schaffner / Axicom): TE Connectivity states that it complies with all export controls and sanctions applicable worldwide and has therefore fully complied with all sanctions imposed following the Russian invasion. Since these came into force in March 2022, the company has not supplied any products to Russia from any of its sites. TE Connectivity says it is committed to a business policy that excludes both direct and indirect deliveries to Russia or other sanctioned countries. These guidelines are communicated to its distribution partners, who are also expected to comply strictly with them.
So why are Swiss components still finding their way into Russia?
There are many indications pointing to China. Research and investigations by thinktanks, NGOs and the media show that intermediaries and distribution partners from China are supplying the goods to Russia. Some Swiss companies have their products manufactured in China.

‘I Won’t Hold Back’: Estonian PM Refuses to Soften Criticism of Putin

Unknown Publisher

23:59:20 KST

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said on Friday, Oct. 30, that he would not soften his criticism of Russian President Vladimir Putin after a report that Pentagon officials had urged Baltic allies to tone down their rhetoric about Russia.
Speaking to Delfi, Michal said Estonia would maintain its position and continue speaking openly about the Russian threat.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I won’t hold back. Putin is a dictator who kills women and children,” he said.
Michal added that Putin would continue doing so until he was forced to change course.
Appeasing dictators brings humiliation without preserving freedom, Michal argued. Estonia and its Baltic neighbors would continue warning about the threat posed by Russia, he said.
Michal said he had not personally received a US request to moderate his language. The issue did not arise when he last met President Donald Trump in Ankara during the summer, he added.
He noted that domestic critics accused his government of being insufficiently assertive, even as reports suggested the US wanted greater restraint.
Pentagon reportedly urges restraint
Reuters reported that Pentagon officials had privately asked several NATO allies, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to tone down their rhetoric about Russia.
Four people familiar with the discussions told Reuters the requests were made during bilateral meetings in recent weeks. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby was among the officials involved.
Zelensky Ready to Discuss Territory With Putin, Sybiha Says
One source said Colby advised a Baltic official against “poking” Russia and cited descriptions of Moscow as cornered and increasingly desperate.
Michal had called Putin a rat in a corner in September, linking Russia’s difficulties in Ukraine to suspected sabotage in Europe. Reuters could not establish whether Colby was referring specifically to those remarks.
The sources described the conversations as cordial. The Pentagon declined to discuss private exchanges between allies, and NATO also declined to comment.
The reported appeals to Baltic governments come as Washington reviews its military presence in Europe and presses European allies to take greater responsibility for their defense.
Estonia backs continued pressure on Russia
At an October summit in Brussels, Michal backed Ukrainian refinery strikes despite US pressure on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil production.
“The faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens the better,” Michal said at the time.
His comments came as European leaders discussed additional financial support for Ukraine and relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated following Trump’s diesel agreement with Russia.
On July 7, President Volodymyr Zelensky and Michal signed a Drone Deal agreement on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara. Zelensky thanked Estonia for its military and humanitarian assistance, as well as its diplomatic support for Ukraine’s EU and NATO ambitions.
Allies debate how to describe the threat
Some believe emphasizing it risks amplifying the fear Moscow seeks to spread; others argue that frank warnings help explain the need for greater defense spending and continued support for Ukraine.
Western intelligence officials have warned of an expanding Russian sabotage campaign in Europe. Moscow denies conducting such a campaign.
Michal said a clear assessment of the threat was essential to preparedness and warned that Ukraine faced a difficult winter.

Russia’s Sevmash Shipyard presents nuclear sub building innovative solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:59:05 UTC
23:59:05 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. A representative of the Sevmash Shipyard, a subsidiary of the United Shipbuilding Corporation (USC), has presented an innovative solution for the construction of modern nuclear submarines at an international research and practical conference in Nizhny Novgorod, the shipyard’s press service reported.
The new solution will save an estimated 81 million rubles ($1.004 mln), it said.
"Sevmash Shipyard representative Igor Kalemintsev demonstrated an innovative development for the construction of fourth-generation nuclear submarines with an economic savings of over 81 million rubles at the international workshop titled ‘Modern Technologies in Shipbuilding and Aviation Education, Science, and Production.’ The event is taking place in Nizhny Novgorod from October 28-30," the press service said.
It specified that Kalemintsev, head of a department at the Sevmash Design Bureau, presented modern technologies for installing equipment and structures using polymer materials. The development includes a unique method for securing mechanisms to the foundation, protected by a Russian patent. He demonstrated practical solutions aimed at improving the efficiency of equipment installation, introducing modern materials, and optimizing production processes in the construction of fourth-generation missile-carrying submarines.
The press service emphasized that the practical application of this design and technological solution has already been confirmed by its successful use in the construction of Yasen-M and Borei-A class nuclear submarines at the shipyard. The technology has been approved by the USC’s Malakhit and Rubin design bureaus, as well as by the Defense Ministry’s Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Technology Center.
"This development significantly reduces the labor required for installation work and ensures the reliability of the structures. The innovative solutions implemented can also be applied to the construction of other vessels in the domestic shipbuilding industry. The assembly unit, which involves securing mechanisms to the foundation using flowable plastic, has been registered as an invention by the Federal Service for Intellectual Property and has been granted a patent. Labor savings per order range from 800 to 2,200 standard hours," the company stated.
Sevmash added that, due to the reduction in the labor intensity of installation work, the total economic benefit from using these components and technology in the construction of nuclear submarines exceeds 81 million rubles.

The Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force were accused of using pellet guns to disperse the protesters and stop their march.Pradhan resigned on July 25, bringing the protests to an end.

Russia has accumulated sufficient winter-grade diesel stocks — Novak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:58:16 UTC
23:58:16 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Russia is accumulating sufficient volumes of winter-grade diesel fuel within its system, with all processes tracking the production schedules of domestic refineries, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
"It is sufficient. It is naturally in line with the enterprises' production programs," Novak said, when asked about the accumulation of winter-grade diesel and its production adjustments.
Winter-grade diesel differs from summer fuel due to its lower pour point and improved filterability, allowing for its use in low temperatures without losing fluidity or clogging fuel filters. With the onset of cold weather, production shifts toward winter-grade fuels, and reserves are built up within the system to ensure an uninterrupted supply for transport, municipal machinery, and industrial enterprises throughout the heating season.

Russia’s Starlink Rival, Rassvet, Draws Ukrainian Sanctions Against Its Developers

Unknown Publisher

23:56:58 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Starlink Rival, Rassvet, Draws Ukrainian Sanctions Against Its Developers
Ukraine has imposed new sanctions on Russian companies and individuals involved in developing the Rassvet satellite communications system, which Moscow intends to use in its war against Ukraine, as well as dozens of vessels operating as part of Russia’s shadow fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the corresponding decrees, according to Ukraine’s Presidential Office on October 30.
The sanctions targeting the Rassvet project cover 10 companies and 19 Russian nationals associated with their activities.
“The Russian Federation seeks to establish a satellite system similar to the Starlink network that would enable it to command troops and target and control attack drones, including ‘shaheds,’ and missiles in real time. The deployment of this system could help Russia not only maintain continuous real-time control of its weapons in Ukraine but also pose threats to other countries,” the statement read.
The sanctioned entities include Bureau 1440, the main developer of the Rassvet project, and its affiliate Labs 1440, which produces spacecraft solar panels. The list also includes FAB Rassvet, a manufacturer of communications satellites and terminals, and Belarus-based Aerospace Instruments, which develops aerospace components.
Other sanctioned companies are 5S Group, which supplies industrial equipment and computers to Russia, including technology used in work for Bureau 1440, and Aquamash Production Association, a manufacturer of precision metal parts.
Also on the list are El-Optics, a supplier of optical and telecommunications equipment, Elesar Group, which imports foreign electronic components, and Small Spacecraft, a developer of satellite communications technology.
Russia’s efforts to develop its own satellite communications network come amid restrictions on its access to Starlink services used in military operations.
In early February, Starlink CEO Elon Musk disabled terminals that were not registered on Ukraine’s approved “whitelists,” following a request from former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Following the restrictions, Ukraine’s General Staff reported a significant decline in Russian assault operations, with 56 attacks recorded on February 5, down from approximately 80 to 110 on previous days.
The latest measures follow findings published by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR), which identified 49 companies in Russia and Belarus in developing Rassvet, Moscow’s planned alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network.
On October 28, HUR released the findings through its War&Sanctions portal, reporting that 23 of the identified organizations, including Russia’s state space corporation Roscosmos, remain outside international sanctions.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the project involves companies specializing in technology, microelectronics, aerospace manufacturing, and scientific research, alongside organizations affiliated with Russia’s Defense Ministry.

Another Russian Su-57 Goes Up in Flames—Fourth Loss or Damage Case of 2026
A Russian Su-57 multirole fighter reportedly caught fire and burned at the Akhtubinsk airfield in Russia’s Astrakhan region on October 29. Marking what could be the fourth known Su-57 loss or damage incident this year, Militarnyi reported on October 30.
The report cited the Telegram channel “Absolutely Reliable Source,” which published satellite imagery of the airfield.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to preliminary information, the fighter caught fire after an abnormal incident during engine startup.
If confirmed, the Akhtubinsk fire would add another aircraft to an unusually costly year for Russia’s small Su-57 fleet.
On April 25, Ukrainian drones struck two Su-57 fighters at the Shagol airfield in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region.

Serial production of the Su-57 is carried out at the Komsomolsk-on-Amur aircraft plant in Russia’s Far East.

Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to cast ballot in US election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:56:27 UTC
23:56:27 KST

Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to cast ballot in US election
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 - Pope Leo XIV cast a ballot by mail in the US midterm elections, the Vatican press office said on Friday, a historic first for the American-born pontiff.
"In keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago," the Vatican said. "The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes."
The Vatican did not say which candidates Leo had voted for.
Leo, 71, was born in Chicago and is the first American-born pope. He registered to vote in Illinois under his birth name Robert Francis Prevost and requested a ballot on October 3, the Chicago Sun-Times reported on Thursday, citing the Will County Clerk's office.
President Donald Trump's sagging popularity is hurting his fellow Republicans' chances of holding onto their majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 election, with the public unhappy about the high cost of living and the Iran war.
Trump repeatedly criticized Leo early in the new pope's tenure, calling him "weak" and "terrible" on crime.
The pope said in March that God rejects the prayers of those who start wars and have "hands full of blood." In April, he termed Trump's threat to destroy the Iranian civilization as unacceptable and previously declined to join the US president's so-called "Board of Peace" initiative for Gaza.
Leo has also urged a "deep reflection" on the way migrants are treated in the US.
Voters in the solidly Democratic state of Illinois will select a successor for retiring US Senator Dick Durbin and choose whether to re-elect Governor JB Pritzker.
Leo was elected to lead the 1.4-billion-member Church by the world's cardinals in May 2025.

G20 foreign ministers' meeting kicks off in US amid global tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:56:26 UTC
23:56:26 KST

Diyar Guldogan
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
A G20 foreign ministers’ meeting kicked off in the US on Friday, bringing together top diplomats from the world’s leading economies for two days of discussions of pressing global economic challenges, geopolitical tensions, and international security issues.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the gathering in the Southern city of Atlanta, Georgia, where the main focus will be on economic growth, energy and food security, freedom of navigation, and the resilience of global supply chains.
The meeting comes against the backdrop of ongoing international conflicts, including the war in Ukraine and tensions involving Iran, which continue to raise concerns about regional stability and their impact on the global economy.
The meeting began directly with Rubio's opening remarks, without a family photo ceremony.
The absence of the traditional photo came after several European officials indicated they would not appear alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the gathering, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul was asked whether he would participate in a group photo with Lavrov.
“I assume there will be no family photograph at all,” he said, adding that European partners would not appear in a picture alongside the Russian foreign minister. “There is no normality with Russia,” Wadephul said.
Addressing the opening session, Rubio urged G20 members to work together to tackle interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, warning of growing threats to global energy and food supplies, international trade, and freedom of navigation.
Rubio described the current period as a “moment of choosing,” saying the challenges facing the US also have implications for the rest of the world.
'Series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises'
“We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, many of which pose severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order,” said Rubio.
He identified disruptions to global energy and food supplies, supply chains, trade, and freedom of navigation as major challenges requiring a coordinated response.
Rubio called on G20 partners to strengthen economic resilience, safeguard markets, and protect the economies that depend on them.
He also stressed the role of foreign ministers and political leaders in coordinating responses to emerging crises and protecting shared interests.
“By translating our shared interests into practical cooperation and real action, we can reinforce global stability and, more importantly, deliver meaningful results for our citizens,” he said.
Rubio said the assembled officials faced a busy two-day agenda, with the opening plenary session focusing on freedom of navigation and food security.
Issues Turkish foreign minister expected to address
Participants include Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Lavrov.
Fidan is set to address the situation in the Gaza Strip, tensions between the US and Iran, and the importance of safeguarding strategic maritime routes. He is also expected to underline Türkiye’s diplomatic efforts to promote regional security and stability.
Lavrov, who is leading the Russian delegation, is expected to call for greater economic cooperation and equal dialogue among G20 members. Moscow has also criticized Washington’s decision to exclude South Africa from the G20 process, calling for its membership rights to be restored.
US President Donald Trump earlier announced that South Africa would not receive an invitation to the 2026 summit. The decision followed Washington’s boycott of the Johannesburg summit and stemmed from Trump’s claims of persecution of white farmers in South Africa.
The Group of Twenty (G20) is an international forum bringing together the world's major advanced and emerging economies to discuss and coordinate global economic policies and address key international challenges.
Established in 1999 in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis, its membership now consists of 19 countries and the European Union and the African Union, which joined in 2023.

Two Airmen supporting the U.S. conflict against Iran died this month in “non-hostile” incidents, according to the official count recently updated by the Pentagon.
The Pentagon has not publicly identified the two Airmen nor said where their deaths occurred, but both were assigned to U.S. Central Command, U.S. officials said. Listing a death as “non-hostile” means the cause was something other than direct military action.
One of the deaths was described as the result of “illness/injury.” That Airman died in the United States after being medically evacuated due to an illness, U.S. officials said. The other death’s cause is listed as “pending,” according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS. The Airman died in the Middle East and the cause is under investigation, the officials said.
The deceased service members, both men, were mid-to-senior enlisted personnel, between the E-5 and E-9 paygrades. Statistics indicate one was 31-35 years old and the other was older than that, according to the database, which is current as of Oct. 29.
At least 23 U.S. service members have died during the conflict with Iran. Fifteen of those occurred during Operation Epic Fury, the initial strike campaign against Iran that the Trump administration says lasted until early May. Eight more have died during operations that followed. The Pentagon has used “Overseas Operations” to refer to its ongoing military pressure campaign and blockade of Iran.
Iranian missile and drone attacks attacks have killed U.S. personnel at Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia, and Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan. Some deaths have also been caused by accidents. Six Airmen were killed in a mid-air collision between two KC-135 Stratotankers over Western Iraq on March 12, when one of the tankers crashed, killing its crew.
At least 865 service members have been wounded in action since hostilities kicked off on Feb. 28. The vast majority are attributed to “hostile” acts, including 64 Airmen.
A shaky ceasefire is now in place between the U.S. and Iran, and the U.S. has maintained a blockade of the country since early April.
The Trump administration is weighing its next move and the Wall Street Journal reported Oct. 28 that President Donald Trump met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, and U.S. Central Command’s Adm. Brad Cooper U.S. Central Command boss Adm. Brad Cooper on military options beyond the blockade. Trump later hinted at future action, saying during a mid-term campaign event, “We may do another little Epic Fury.”

Europe facing gas price shock – Gazprom chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:55:52 UTC
23:55:52 KST

Europe facing gas price shock – Gazprom chief
European gas prices could more than double as depleted reserves threaten winter supplies, Gazprom CEO Aleksey Miller has warned.
Wholesale prices have already reached their highest level in nearly four years, briefly exceeding €97 ($108) per megawatt-hour on Monday. December gas futures climbed another 3.1% on Friday to around $1,164 per thousand cubic meters, according to London’s Intercontinental Exchange.
Miller pointed to unusually low gas reserves across the EU, noting that Germany, the bloc’s largest consumer, has filled just 61.6% of its underground storage capacity.
”Given the series of historic record lows Europeans have set in filling underground gas storage facilities [...] we can expect gas prices in Europe to peak at $2,500 per thousand cubic meters in the event of a cold winter,” he said.
Norwegian energy giant Equinor has echoed concerns over another price shock. CEO Anders Opedal said on Wednesday that European gas reserves were at their lowest seasonal level since 2011, leaving the bloc exposed to further price spikes as it competes with Asian buyers for liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The US-Israeli war on Iran has further strained supplies, disrupting shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which previously handled around a fifth of global LNG trade. Deliveries remain roughly 80% below pre-conflict levels.
EU gas storage facilities were 74.62% full as of October 25, well below seasonal averages, with some member states already drawing on reserves as temperatures fall.
Germany has been particularly hard hit. Gas tariffs for new household customers have jumped 55% this year, according to comparison website Verivox. High energy costs have forced some European fertilizer, chemical, and steel producers to cut output, Reuters reported.
In September, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen warned that the bloc faced its worst energy crisis since 2022, when wholesale gas prices exceeded €300 per megawatt-hour.
Despite mounting supply concerns, Brussels is pressing ahead with plans to eliminate Russian gas imports. Long-term LNG deliveries are set to be banned from January 2027, with remaining pipeline supplies scheduled to end later that year.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned the EU’s energy policy as “suicidal.” Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev argued last week that restoring economic cooperation with Russia “will be inevitable.”

Cambridge, MA city council votes to divest from firms 'complicit in Gaza genocide'
The city council in Cambridge, Massachusetts, voted 5-4 on Wednesday in favour of divesting public funds from companies complicit in Israel's genocide in Gaza.
"Our retirement funds should not be invested in companies that profit off of killing people," Cambridge City Councilor Ayah Al-Zubi, who voted in favour of divestment, told NBC Boston.
The vote will impact the council's public investments, including for pensions. The vote will impact at least $24 million of investments, according to campaign group Cambridge for Palestine.
The firms targeted by the new policy include Palantir Technologies Inc., Elbit Systems, Lockheed Martin, GE Aerospace, and Boeing.
"Our wins are one small step in the much larger international struggle for Palestinian liberation," Cambridge for Palestine said in statement after the vote.
The policy order stated that "Israel is committing genocide in Gaza", and said Israel's treatment of Palestinians "amounts to apartheid" — positions held by UN experts and leading rights groups.
Orphan Black and She-Hulk: Attorney at Law star Tatiana Maslany celebrated the news with an Instagram post captioned "Hell yes @cambridgema4palestine !!!!!!!!!!"
However, the council voted down a boycott of companies complicit in the genocide for city contracts. Vice Mayor Burhan Azeem, who voted in favour of divestment, was the deciding vote against the boycott.
Cambridge follows three other Massachusetts councils -- Medford, Northampton and Easthampton -- in divesting from complicit companies. Neighbouring Somerville City Council is set to vote on similar action in November.
Cambridge, part of the Greater Boston area, is home to two of the world's top universities, Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
Last year, Harvard University faced a legal battle with US President Donald Trump after the president cut funding for the Ivy League institution and blocked visas for international students.
The president claimed the university is an "antisemitic, far left institution", following pro-Palestine protests on campus.
In July 2025, a Boston judge blocked Trump's attempts to bar foreign students from studying at Harvard.

Strikes on camp in Ethiopia kill at least 15, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:54:40 CET
23:54:40 KST

NAIROBI, Oct 30 (Reuters) - At least 15 people, several of them children, died in a series of drone strikes that hit a camp for displaced civilians in Ethiopia’s Amhara region, two sources involved in a rescue operation said on Friday.
It was not clear why the camp was targeted or who was behind the attack, but the strikes highlight continuing clashes in the area despite a lull in the heavy fighting that erupted last month between an alliance of rebels from northern Tigray region and the government in Addis Ababa.
“There were around five explosions. Then … we started collecting bodies,” a community representative involved in the burials told Reuters, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.
The representative said they helped bury 13 people at the camp, which is known as Jari 2 and is home to more than 1,700 people who fled previous violence.
Two of the injured later died at a hospital in Hayk, a town 17 km (10 miles) away.
A spokesperson for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A local official said they were aware of the incident and were helping get medical treatment to 36 people who had been injured.
A man who lost a family member described seeing a drone circling overhead on Wednesday and then returning on Thursday.
“Then finally it hit the camp … three times,” the relative told Reuters. “Their body parts were scattered everywhere. We collected and buried pieces of their body parts.”
NO FIGHTING IN THE AREA WHEN CAMP HIT
A resident of Hayk who was helping provide shelter to survivors also said 15 people had been killed. “Those from the camp are now sheltering in a school,” the resident said.
The dead included five children, according to the two sources involved in the rescue.
The relative of one of the victims said they had seen at least 10 injured children under the aged of five receiving treatment.
All three sources said there had been no fighting in the area when the strike took place, but members of the Amhara Fano National Movement, which is part of the rebel alliance spearheaded by fighters from Tigray, had been nearby.
Government troops have driven back the rebel alliance since their offensive was launched on September 23.
They retook the capital of Tigray region earlier this month and advanced towards the border with Eritrea, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebellion by sending troops over the border.
Eritrea denies the accusation and says Addis Ababa’s allegations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a “declaration of war”.
Given the web of interconnected conflicts in the Horn of Africa, with neighbouring countries and powers further afield backing their respective proxies, experts have warned that war in Ethiopia could trigger a broader conflict in the region.
(Reporting by Nairobi Newsroom; Writing by David Lewis; Editing by David Holmes and Ros Russell)

By Valentini Anagnostopoulou
ATHENS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Dockworkers went on strike across Europe and beyond on Friday, disrupting shipping and ferries as they protested against the use of their ports for arms shipments and the number of seafarers killed in wars from the Gulf to the Black Sea.
Strikers across 113 ports in 22 countries also called for pay rises, better working conditions and the right to have doctors on board vessels crossing war zones.
“We will not work for their wars, and we will not become food for their cannons,” Apostolos Kypraios, head of the Greek union of merchant marine engineers, told Reuters during a rally at the Greek port of Piraeus.
‘SEAFARERS HAVE SUFFERED MANY CASUALTIES’
“We have felt it first hand, and our families have felt it too, living with the anxiety of whether a colleague will get back home,” he added.
More than 25 unions have now backed the strike originally called in Italy, France, Greece, Spain’s Basque Country, Turkey and Morocco.
On Friday, it covered major shipping hubs in Piraeus, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras and Genoa, as well as Morocco’s Tangier Med and India’s Nhava Sheva.
“Seafarers have suffered many casualties — numbering in the hundreds — including both the dead and the severely injured,” the Greek seafarers’ union PENEN said in a statement.
It said there had been 28 attacks on vessels in the Gulf in the first 21 days of October, a record since the start of the Iran war.
It said there had been 570 attacks confirmed in the Black Sea so far this year, leaving 40 seafarers dead and hundreds wounded.
A series of strikes in the western Black Sea has raised concerns about the widening scope of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Cargo operations were disrupted in Piraeus and ferry services to Greek islands were suspended, as about 3,000 dockworkers and seafarers joined the walkout.
Representatives of India’s WTWFI union said about 15 Indian seafarers had died as a result of the Iran war, with many more stranded at sea as waterways were blocked.
A group of dockworkers and other activists, called ‘No Harbour for Genocide’ and campaigning to stop military cargo from reaching Israeli ports, said on Friday the protest would halt some 52,000 containers and snarl cargo worth $2.8 billion.
Reuters was not able to independently verify the impact.
In May 2026, dockworkers’ unions from over 35 European countries published the so-called Istanbul Declaration demanding that port facilities not be used to transport weapons destined for war zones.
Dockworkers said they were also worried about the rising cost of essential goods and energy, stemming from the ongoing conflicts.
“We can’t even afford to fill the car with fuel to get to the supermarket,” George Gogos, head of the Piraeus port dockworkers’ union, said.
(Reporting by Valentini Anagnostopoulou in Athens, Sybille de La Hamaide in Paris; Writing by Angeliki Koutantou; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

GENEVA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - The top Swiss court on Friday confirmed a guilty verdict against a Liberian warlord, upholding his 20 year sentence in the country’s first ever war crimes trial.
Alieu Kosiah, who fought in the 1990s against then-president Charles Taylor’s army during Liberia’s brutal civil war, was originally sentenced to 20 years in prison in June 2021 for rape, murder and cannibalism.

“This is a landmark decision, made possible by the courage of these victims, who have written a page of legal history,” said Alain Werner, Director of Civitas Maxima, an NGO representing victims in this case.
However, the court reversed a parallel conviction for crimes against humanity on the grounds that the law on this crime introduced in 2011 cannot be applied retroactively.

An IOPC spokesperson said: “Following a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, we have decided an independent investigation is required into its failure to pass on allegations of serious offending, contained in a letter it received in 2019, to relevant overseas authorities at the time.”
The Met had announced on Thursday its voluntary referral to the IOPC about the handling of the 2019 letter. It also referred whether its decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duchess of Sussex could have been a breach of data rules because it contained sensitive information. The IOPC has decided it will not investigate that.

The Met has said it did not investigate because the allegations related to potential unlawful activity overseas. A North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor, or Lazarus Group, may be behind the theft of more than $6 billion from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange, according to analytics firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis, the BBC reported.
The independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo notes that the group may have ties to Russia. A UN Security Council panel of experts said in a report published in March 2024 that Lazarus Group is “very active in the Russian Federation” and retains access to Russian systems. In 2025, cybersecurity researchers found that Lazarus had routed internet traffic through servers in the Russian village of Khasan, on the border with North Korea.
A preliminary review by Binance found that the attackers gained access to its system by hacking the laptop of one of its engineers. The exchange also discovered “additional points of breach.”
Binance announced that about half of the stolen funds have been frozen, but a significant portion remains in the hackers’ hands. The exchange has pledged to reimburse customers for their losses and has set aside $6.34 billion of its own funds for that purpose, and it announced that it has already begun returning the assets.
Experts consider the Binance attack the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The previous record belonged to the Bybit exchange hack in February 2025, when hackers stole about $1.5 billion. TraderTraitor was also blamed for the Bybit hack.

Bulgaria signs agreement to join NATO air defence initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:49:39 UTC
23:49:39 KST

Friday 30 October 2026 16:14
Friday, 30 October 2026, 16:14
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Bulgarian Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov signed an agreement on Friday enabling Bulgaria to join a NATO initiative to develop defences against low-flying air threats, including drones and cruise missiles.
The initiative provides a framework for allies to jointly acquire, develop and deploy air defence capabilities. It aims to improve protection against threats flying below 150 metres, including glide bombs, by developing systems to detect, identify, track and counter them.
NATO said the project was established in February 2025, with the initial participants signing a memorandum of understanding in July 2026. Bulgaria’s participation would improve interoperability and bring cost savings and operational benefits, the alliance said.
The accession document will be submitted to Bulgaria’s parliament for ratification.

Putin open to phone call with Zelensky, Ukraine suspects a Kremlin trap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:47:37 UTC
23:47:37 KST

The Kremlin is seeking to avoid a face-to-face meeting between President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin by proposing they speak by phone instead, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
The apparent move comes as Kyiv insists the two leaders should meet in person to address the most pressing issues in negotiations, including Russia's territorial demands and security guarantees. Such a meeting would be their first since 2019.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Oct. 30 that Putin was "open to dialogue with everyone." Asked whether the Russian leader would speak with Zelensky by phone, Peskov added that "no one has called yet."
The comments came as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi, which Kyiv sees as a possible starting point for a meeting between the countries' leaders.
Ukrainian officials privately suspect Moscow is trying to arrange a phone call that they believe would achieve little while avoiding the prospect of a face-to-face meeting.
"They've already tried to do this over the phone," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
read also
Meeting or a call?
Kyiv has long pushed for a direct meeting between Zelensky and Putin.
The two leaders last met in person in Paris in December 2019 during the Normandy Format talks mediated by France and Germany. They have not held direct talks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine has made several attempts to arrange a meeting since then.
Zelensky invited Putin to Istanbul for talks on May 16, 2025, proposing a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump to advance peace efforts. Putin declined to attend and instead sent a delegation led by a low-level presidential aide, Vladimir Medinsky.
After meeting Putin in Alaska in August 2025, the U.S. president said he was working to arrange a meeting between the Russian and Ukrainian leaders.
Trump later said Putin was reluctant to meet Zelensky because "he doesn't like him."
Now, every time the Ukrainian side raises the idea of a meeting at the level of leaders, the Kremlin challenges the Ukrainian president to come to Moscow for it. Zelensky has called for Putin to meet him in a neutral location.
Kyiv continues to argue that only direct talks between the leaders can produce meaningful decisions on the most difficult issues. Ukrainian officials say the Russian representatives sent to negotiations do not have the authority to make such decisions.
"Territorial issues can only be discussed by the leaders of the countries at war, and only at their level," Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 27. "No one else has the authority to do so."
Territory remains one of the main obstacles to an agreement.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the parts of Ukrainian Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts that Russian forces have failed to capture. The strategically important regions in eastern Ukraine remain central to the negotiations.
Ukraine, by contrast, has called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
Several people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent that Washington supports the idea of a leaders' meeting and that Trump could help arrange one.
The G20 summit in Miami in December could serve as a possible venue, the people said. Under this scenario, if Putin accepts Trump's invitation to attend, Zelensky could also travel there to meet the Russian leader.
Kyiv warns against sidestepping direct talks
As Ukraine pushes for a meeting, its officials believe Moscow is trying to undermine the effort by offering alternatives that would not require Putin to meet Zelensky.
One senior Ukrainian official questioned whether a phone call could resolve the issues at stake without U.S. involvement.
"Well, what do we want? To reach a final decision on key issues and security guarantees," the official told the Kyiv Independent. "Is it possible to do this over the phone — and only over the phone — without the U.S.? No."
"We need a trilateral format with the U.S., plus some involvement from the Europeans... But they're like, 'Well, just go to Moscow,' or call us, but what good will a phone call do?"
Ukrainian officials fear that Moscow's insistence on a phone call could give it another reason to walk away from negotiations without making meaningful commitments. They argue a meeting with third parties would better address the disputes.
Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. plan to hold talks in Abu Dhabi in November, focusing on steps to de-escalate the war. Moscow has signaled readiness to resume negotiations with Kyiv after a pause of more than eight months.
Zelensky said the planned technical talks should seek concrete progress on de-escalation, including an energy and maritime ceasefire, prisoner exchanges, and discussions about a possible trilateral meeting between the leaders.
"We hope for a result regarding energy and at sea, an exchange of prisoners, and a discussion of the possible format for a trilateral meeting at the leaders' level."
Kyiv does not expect working-level negotiations alone to end the war.
Ukrainian officials say Putin must take part in the process himself if the talks are to produce actual decisions.
"Putin needs to come out of his bunker and take part in the trilateral talks," the senior Ukrainian official said. "And personally confirm that he is ending the war."

Denmark set for unusually mild but cloudy weekend with rain on Sunday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:46:18 UTC
23:46:18 KST

Denmark can expect a relatively calm autumn weekend, with temperatures reaching 14 degrees Celsius, occasional sunshine and rain arriving on Sunday.
According to Erik Hansen, a meteorologist at the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI), temperatures will remain around five degrees above the seasonal average.
“It’s unusually mild,” Hansen said, forecasting temperatures between 11 and 14 degrees on Friday, accompanied by light to moderate westerly and northwesterly winds.
Friday will begin with widespread clouds, haze and fog, although some areas could see the skies clear as the day progresses.
Northeastern Denmark, particularly Bornholm, is expected to enjoy the most sunshine, while the rest of the country may see only brief sunny spells.
Saturday will remain largely dry but cloudy, with patches of morning fog and haze across the country.
Temperatures will hover around 12 degrees, with light to moderate winds blowing from the north.
Sunday will also begin cloudy but mostly dry before a weak cold front brings rain into northwestern Denmark during the day.
The rain will gradually spread eastward through the afternoon and evening, eventually reaching much of the country.
“That is to say, we get a dry start in most of the country, but then this rain spreads from the northwestern part of the country to the entire country,” Hansen said.
The unsettled conditions are expected to continue overnight into Monday, with further rainfall possible in southeastern Denmark on Monday morning.
Despite the cloud cover and approaching rain, the weekend will remain relatively mild for late October, with little wind and no significant weather disturbances expected.

Man arrested over suspected drug smuggling on first Copenhagen-Ilulissat flight
A 54-year-old man was arrested Thursday after police discovered suspected illegal drugs in his luggage during the inauguration of Ilulissat’s new international airport in Greenland.
Greenland Police confirmed to Ritzau, Denmark’s news agency, that the man had attempted to bring approximately half a kilogram of hashish into the country.
The arrest took place shortly after the arrival of the first direct flight from Copenhagen to Ilulissat, which marked the airport’s official opening.
The Air Greenland flight was scheduled to land at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. in Denmark.
According to Greenlandic news outlet Sermitsiaq, police received a report about the incident at 12:15 p.m., while the inauguration was underway.
The man was arrested at 12:30 p.m. on suspicion of distributing illegal drugs but was subsequently released.
“The man was not brought before a judge, but the case is still being investigated with a view to a later judicial decision,” Greenland Police said in a written statement.
Police declined to say whether any other incidents occurred during the airport’s opening celebrations.
The new airport allows Ilulissat, a town in western Greenland, to receive larger aircraft and direct international flights.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen to Ilulissat had to transfer through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct connection reduces the journey to four hours and 40 minutes.
Air Greenland plans to operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday under its regular schedule.
Additional flights will be available during peak travel periods, including the Christmas and New Year holidays.
The airport’s opening marks a change in how travelers can reach Ilulissat from Denmark and other international destinations.
Nearly two million Danes register organ donation preferences as numbers surge
Nearly four in ten people aged over 15 in Denmark have registered their organ donation preferences, following a sharp increase over the past two years.
According to figures from the Danish Center for Organ Donation, 1,941,790 people had recorded their decision by the end of September, up from 1,404,297 in September 2024.
The increase follows changes to Denmark’s organ donation rules, under which all adults aged 18 and older are automatically registered as potential donors. However, individuals must confirm their registration on sundhed.dk to become active donors.
Helle Haubro Andersen, head of the Danish Center for Organ Donation, said direct communication encourages people to make a decision.
Following the rule changes, residents received notifications through e-Boks, Denmark’s digital mailbox service.
Most of those who responded granted full or partial consent, Andersen said.
Among people who have registered their preferences, 66 percent consented to donating all eligible organs, while 16 percent granted partial consent. Another 14 percent declined donation.
Residents can also indicate that they remain undecided.
Andersen explained that deceased organ donors generally must have suffered a severe brain injury, such as a major stroke or brain hemorrhage.
There is no upper age limit for donation. Denmark’s oldest organ donor was 92 in 2019, although kidneys and livers are generally more suitable for donation at advanced ages.
The figures come amid criticism of Rigshospitalet, which has rejected donor livers for children and adults because of capacity shortages.
Andersen declined to comment on the hospital’s situation but noted that organ transplants have increased nationally.
Last year, 455 patients received organ transplants, compared with 433 in 2024, 430 in 2023 and 338 in 2022.
Danish court rules citizenship denial to woman with disability was not discrimination
A Palestinian woman who was denied Danish citizenship because she could not meet the country’s self-support requirement has lost her discrimination case against the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Denmark’s Eastern High Court ruled Friday that the decision did not constitute unlawful indirect discrimination based on her disability, according to a statement published on the court’s website.
The woman arrived in Denmark in 1999 and was involved in a traffic accident 10 years later.
Following the accident, her reduced ability to work led to her being approved for a flexjob, a Danish employment arrangement for people with permanently reduced working capacity.
She subsequently received unemployment benefits for a period, preventing her from meeting the financial self-sufficiency requirement for Danish citizenship.
Her citizenship application was rejected in February 2023.
The woman and her lawyer argued that the refusal amounted to indirect discrimination and violated international conventions protecting people with disabilities and human rights.
However, the High Court rejected those arguments and ruled in favor of the ministry.
Her lawyer, Petra Alexandra Fokdal, argued that the rules create difficulties for people in flexjobs who become unemployed.
“Once you are referred to a flexjob, you cannot be in an unemployment fund. And if the employer no longer needs you, you receive unemployment benefits, but this makes it impossible to meet the requirement of self-support,” Fokdal said.
Because of its wider legal significance, the case was transferred directly from the district court to the High Court.
Fokdal said she intends to appeal the ruling to Denmark’s Supreme Court.
Parcels arriving from outside the EU to Denmark and other EU countries will face a new fee
Cheap goods from Chinese online shops are arriving in EU in huge numbers, raising concerns about product safety.
In 2025 alone, Danish customs registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Therefore, the European Union will introduce a permanent handling fee of 2 euros per line item in parcels arriving from outside the bloc starting Sunday, November 1, the Danish Customs Agency said Friday.
The fee, equivalent to about 15 Danish kroner, will apply regardless of a parcel’s total value. It will be added to the temporary customs duty introduced this summer on parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Items with the same commodity code count as one line item. Three cotton T-shirts, for example, would incur a handling fee of 2 euros. A cotton T-shirt and a pair of denim jeans would count as two line items, bringing the fee to 4 euros.
The existing customs duty is 3 euros per line item in parcels with a total value below 150 euros.
Christian Lützen, director of the Danish Customs Agency, said the number of low-value parcels sent to consumers from outside the EU had fallen since the customs duty took effect.
“With the handling fee, we are stepping up efforts even further to, among other things, strengthen member states’ opportunities to inspect the contents of parcels,” he said in the press release.
“There are still problems with many of the goods in relation to consumer safety, and as an authority at the border, we must take that seriously.”
When the customs duty was introduced this summer, Lützen said the agency had previously seen a sharp increase in goods arriving from Chinese online shops. He called it “a major problem across EU countries” and said the duty should help make shopping with Danish businesses more attractive.
In 2025, the agency registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros. A count showed that more than 90% of parcels entering Denmark contained Chinese goods.
Shein and Temu were among the 10 online shops most used by Danish consumers in the latest survey by Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, a business organization.
The two platforms sell products ranging from clothing to kitchen equipment and have faced criticism over poor quality and illegal chemicals in their products.

Denmark’s pension sector recorded a negative return of 62 billion kroner in September, according to figures from the country’s central bank, Nationalbanken.
Stock market swings and rising interest rates weighed on both share and bond holdings during the month.
Mads Moberg Reumert, chief economist at pension provider Danica, urged savers to stick to their pension strategy and chosen risk level despite the losses.
“It is not the first time we experience a month or two where things go the wrong way, and it probably will not be the last time either.”
“But if we look over the past six months, Danish pension savers have overall received a return of 314 billion kroner. And after all, it is the long-term return that is ultimately interesting for pension savings,” he said.
Danica reported a customer return of 16.5% from April through the end of October, according to its own figures. That corresponds to 165,000 kroner for every million kroner invested and exceeds what would normally be expected over a full year.
Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension provider Sampension, also described 2026 as “a good year for pension savers” so far.
“Because despite global unrest, war in the Middle East, and rising energy prices, the Danes have generally received really good returns on their pension savings in the first nine months of the year – not least as a result of the tailwind in the stock markets,” she said.

Denmark introduces new GP payment system to improve care for patients with greater needs
Patients in Denmark will be able to book different types of appointments with their general practitioners under a new four-year agreement aimed at improving access to medical care.
The agreement, announced Thursday, was negotiated between Praktiserende Lægers Organisation (PLO), the Danish organization representing general practitioners, and Regionernes Lønnings- og Takstnævn (RLTN), the regional body responsible for negotiating doctors’ pay and fees.
One of the main changes is a new payment system that takes patients’ medical needs into account.
Currently, clinics receive the same payment per patient regardless of whether patients are generally healthy or require extensive treatment.
Under the agreement, clinics treating patients with greater medical needs will receive higher payments.
The change is intended to improve financial conditions for practices in areas with fewer doctors, where patients with the greatest treatment needs are often found.
The agreement also introduces four appointment categories: short, regular, long and complex consultations.
These will allow doctors to address several medical concerns during a single appointment when necessary.
General practitioners will also receive separate payments for continuing education, helping them expand their skills and potentially reduce referrals to other medical services.
“It is a milestone that we now have an agreement on terms and frameworks for general practice that extends four years into the future,” PLO chairman Jørgen Skadborg said.
He added that the agreement would provide stability, allowing doctors to focus on patients and developing their clinics.
The agreement takes effect at the start of the new year, with 4.5 billion DKK allocated to general practice over four years.
By 2030, annual funding is expected to be 1.7 billion DKK higher than today.

Denmark, Greenland and Faroe Islands to jointly lead Nordic Council in 2027
Lars-Christian Brask, a member of Denmark’s parliament for Liberal Alliance, has been elected president of the Nordic Council, which brings together parliamentarians from the Nordic countries.
Brask was elected Thursday during the council’s session in Helsinki, Finland, according to a statement from Folketinget, Denmark’s parliament.
Denmark will take over the rotating presidency from Finland in 2027, sharing leadership responsibilities with Greenland and the Faroe Islands for the first time.
Brask has chaired Denmark’s delegation to the Nordic Council since 2023. He said the presidency involves leading parliamentary cooperation between the Nordic countries.
“Just like in the Folketing, we can make proposals that are voted through and then go to the Council of Ministers, which then has to implement them,” Brask told Ritzau, Denmark’s news agency.
Greenland and the Faroe Islands will share the vice presidency. Justus Hansen of Greenland’s Demokraatit party will serve during the first six months, followed by Sunnvá Dahl Høgfeldt of the Faroese Sambandsflokkurin party.
According to Folketinget, the presidency will prioritize removing barriers between Nordic countries to improve regional cooperation and competitiveness.
Children, young people, civil society, culture and understanding of Nordic languages will also feature in its agenda.
Brask said Denmark intends to focus on practical outcomes rather than formalities.
“There will be fewer ceremonial speeches and more focus on delivering concrete results,” he said.
The Nordic Council has 87 parliamentarians, with its presidency rotating annually among five Nordic countries.
Denmark last held the presidency in 2021, when Bertel Haarder of Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, served as president.
Arctic sea ice survives summer with less melting than expected despite record-low winter
Arctic sea ice has retained more of its coverage than expected this summer, thanks to unusually cool weather conditions, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI).
In a statement Thursday, DMI reported that Arctic sea ice reached a record-low winter extent earlier this year but experienced relatively limited melting during the summer months.
A large low-pressure system over the Arctic helped keep temperatures cooler, slowing the melting process and allowing more ice to survive.
Gorm Dybkjær, a climate researcher at DMI, said the development was surprising but cautioned against interpreting it as a reversal of climate change.
“It is remarkable that the sea ice in the Arctic has retained so much of its winter ice after the winter’s record-low extent. But that does not mean that climate change has released its grip on the ice,” he said.
In September, when Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum, its extent ranked as the 16th-lowest since records began in 1978.
Despite this year’s relatively favorable conditions, scientists continue to observe a long-term decline in the thickness and volume of Arctic sea ice.
Since 2007, the Arctic’s total sea ice volume has fallen by an estimated 20 percent or more.
Dybkjær warned that thinner ice is increasingly vulnerable to changing weather and ocean conditions, which could trigger sudden, substantial losses.
Researchers also monitor sea ice because of its role in regulating Earth’s temperature through the albedo effect.
This refers to how much incoming sunlight is reflected into space.
Ice and clouds reflect substantial amounts of solar radiation, while darker ocean surfaces absorb more energy, contributing to warming.

Copenhagen Police will introduce a stop-and-search zone around Parken on Sunday, 8 November, when FC Copenhagen face Brøndby IF in a match classified as high risk.

Within the zone, police can stop and search people without suspecting them of a criminal offence. The measure is intended to prevent unrest surrounding the derby.

“We will also be present in large numbers so that we can intervene if there should be signs of unrest brewing,” he said.

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Grades in written Danish have fallen across Denmark’s upper secondary education programs, according to the latest exam results released by the Education Ministry on Thursday.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.
Direct flights from Copenhagen to Ilulissat cleared as Greenland airport opens
Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.

Five Danish municipalities agree to take additional Ukrainian refugees
Five municipalities in Jutland have volunteered to accommodate more Ukrainian refugees than their allocated share, offering some relief to municipalities facing pressure elsewhere in Denmark.
Haderslev, Horsens, Skive, Struer and Viborg will receive a combined 133 additional refugees, according to the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Viborg will take the largest share, with 65 additional arrivals, while Skive will accommodate 18.
Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov, from the Social Democrats, welcomed the decision, noting that Copenhagen and municipalities in its western suburbs are particularly stretched.
“It is a shared task to ensure that the Ukrainians who come to Denmark also gain a proper foothold in our local communities,” Bødskov said.
The announcement comes as the government seeks to restrict residence permits for displaced Ukrainians arriving from 14 areas it considers less affected by the war.
Parliament has already passed legislation excluding Ukrainian men aged 23 to 60 from obtaining residence under a special law, aiming to prevent them from avoiding military mobilization.
Several Jutland municipalities previously offered to accept additional refugees, citing available accommodation and demand for workers.
However, only Skive proceeded among the five municipalities that initially expressed interest.
Brønderslev requested additional funding, which Bødskov rejected, saying municipalities willing to help must operate under existing financial arrangements.
More than 47,000 Ukrainian refugees currently live in Denmark, compared with the 100,000 arrivals authorities prepared for in 2022.
Despite the lower number, Bødskov said pressure on municipalities justified tighter admission rules.
He acknowledged the difficulties involved while emphasizing Denmark’s continued military, civilian and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine.
Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”
