UK probes Meta over 'exploitative' new terms for media as global pushback mounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:43:02 UTC
23:43:02 KST

Britain's competition watchdog has opened an investigation into whether Meta was imposing "exploitative" new terms allowing it to use media content for its own products, including AI, without giving publishers adequate choice.
The UK's competition watchdog has launched an investigation into whether Meta is imposing "exploitative" new terms that allow it to use publishers' content for its own products, including AI, without giving media organisations adequate choice.
The probe will examine whether the "terms and conditions" from the US technology giant "unfairly harm news publishers and other content businesses", the Competition and Markets Authority said in a statement.
The CMA said the new terms, which the Facebook and Instagram parent had planned to introduce on November 20 before putting it on hold, could amount to an abuse of its dominant position in the market.
The watchdog will determine whether "Meta is abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers".
Meta's new terms could allow it to access and use content from news publishers' websites to develop and provide its own products, including its AI features.
A Meta spokesperson said "we've already committed not to change our terms without consulting publishers and other stakeholders".
"We welcome the opportunity to explain our approach to the CMA," they added.
Thousands of UK businesses rely on Meta to reach customers and audiences, meaning an unfair imposition of the new terms could breach competition law.
"We've heard concerns from news publishers and other businesses and are acting swiftly to investigate whether Meta's proposed changes may breach competition law," said CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell.
European pushback
The British governments effort follow hot on the heels of action taking place across Europe and around the world against Meta's proposed new rules and its practices in general in using media content.
Since May this year, more than 340 local and national news sites including the Guardian, the New York Times and USA Today have blocked internet archive crawler bots to prevent them from collecting data for training AI models.
A Norwegian court this week temporarily banned Meta from enforcing the new user terms after ten media outlets argued it would threaten their rights to their content.
And in France, the country's appeals court rejected on Thursday an attempt by Meta to overturn an order to negotiate in good faith with French media over rights payments for information used on its social networks.
In two rulings, the Paris Appeals Court found that Meta's conduct had caused "serious and immediate harm to the press sector" in France, affirming the position of the country's anti-monopoly body.
The regulatory authority in July ordered the parent company of Facebook and Instagram to "negotiate in good faith" with French media on neighbouring rights payments — a form of copyright payments for use of information on social media platforms.
It said Meta's conduct could be considered "abuse of a dominant position".
Two associations of media groups had complained to the Competition Authority following a lack of progress in talks to renew deals of neighbouring rights payments.
The regulator noted that Meta was continuing to use the content of the media groups but not making payments to them since their deals lapsed.
The Paris Appeals Court found that Meta had in the negotiations with publishers provided only fragmentary, opaque and unverifiable data about its use of media content.
The DVP association of publishers, of which AFP is a member, called the rulings a "major development" and urged Meta to fully meet its obligations to media.
A Meta spokesman said "we are disappointed with the Paris Appeals Court ruling" and was considering what steps to take.
Meta is in the midst of another battle with media over new user terms and conditions that force professional users to give it the right to collect content -- including content behind a paywall -- and use it for AI training among other things.
The company is also facing mounting global pushback against its platform designs and features, especially amid claims of harms against children and teenagers, and is back in court in the US later this month alongside Snap.

The exiled news outlet Astra said it used those online videos to identify the targeted industrial facility in Samara as the Rosneft-owned Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery, which Ukraine has attacked multiple times in recent years.
Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed that Ukrainian drones targeted three oil refineries and one gas chemical complex overnight, saying at least one suffered “minor damage.” He did identify the facilities by name.
The attacks come after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine earlier this month, which neither side said they had agreed to beforehand. That apparent pause in strikes collapsed immediately as the Russian army continued its attacks against Ukraine's power grid.
The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Ukraine’s military had temporarily paused attacks on Russian oil refineries under pressure from the United States, where high domestic fuel costs are a major issue for voters ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly told journalists that “our guys tried to be a little more careful during these days,” but added that they were not explicitly told to avoid hitting Russian refineries.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 1,043 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Thursday night and Friday morning.

Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies.

In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service.

About 10,000 protesters, mainly pupils, students and their parents, are expected at the Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, with another smaller gathering planned in the early evening in the Mitte district.

In France, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day, adding that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the sidelines of the new wave of protests.
Nuñez said late on Thursday that radical groups had called on social media for violent Halloween gatherings and that the biggest threat to public order would probably come after mainstream cost-of-living demonstrations had officially ended.
“We are seeing many calls from the labour movement, the radicalised far left and certain radicalised gilets jaunes [yellow vests], urging people to attend rallies on public streets starting at 8pm in many cities across France,” he said.
The calls were “accompanied by various messages which are quite radical”, Nuñez added, including some demanding “revolution”. He said authorities would “tolerate zero excesses” and promised an “extremely firm” security response.
Measures introduced last weekend to protect shops would be reinforced, Nuñez said, and while peaceful demonstrations would be authorised, most would not be permitted “in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.
It is unclear what will happen in Paris. Two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. Both sets of organisers are challenging the decision to exclude them from the centre.
The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October.
Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide strike called for 5 November.
Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.

EU to impose €2 fee on all packages entering the bloc as of 1 November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:41:25 UTC
23:41:25 KST

A €3 fee also came into force in July, leading to a 60% drop in small parcel imports over three months. The new rules aim to counter imports from Chinese platforms, whose low prices threaten European retailers.
The European Union will start charging a €2 handling fee on all packages entering the EU market as of Sunday, as cheap imports from China continue to surge.
A €3 duty already came into force in July on small parcels worth less than €150. However, that fee is temporary and will remain in place until 2028, when a new IT customs system becomes operational.
The new measures were deemed necessary as the EU faces a dramatic increase in low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Temu, Shein and AliExpress.
The new €2 fee, which comes into force on 1 November, will apply to all packages, regardless of their value, and will cover customs handling costs. It comes in addition to the €3 duty.
“The logic for the duty is the level playing field: all goods entering the EU should pay the due and justified amount of duty,” an EU official said. The official added: “The logic of the fee is to cover the costs of control, as e-commerce represents a disproportionate cost for our customs authority.”
The new fee will be paid by platforms, sellers or carriers and collected by the 27 EU member states. Of the money collected, 75% will go into the EU budget, while the remaining 25% will be retained by EU countries.
The €3 duty introduced in July has already had an impact on import volumes: Between July and September, the number of small parcels entering the bloc dropped by 60%, according to the European Commission. However, 5 million parcels still enter the EU market every day, the EU executive also said.
In 2024, 91% of those shipments came from China, posing fierce competition for European retailers.
Infringements of EU rules on products are also an issue, as the Commission proposed in September a legislation cracking down on imports of illegal products, particularly those sold through online marketplaces, by ensuring that an economic operator in the EU is always legally responsible for non-compliance.
In May, the Commission also fined Temu €200 million for shortcomings related to dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers. Brussels is also investigating Shein over illegal products, including child-like sex dolls.

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has expressed hope that Israel's elections could create an opportunity to renew peace talks. His surprising comments were reported by the AFP and circulated in regional media, such as Arab News in Saudi Arabia.
“For many years now, we have been extending a hand to the Israeli side in order to achieve peace with them, so that Israel and Palestine may live in security, stability, and peace,” Abbas said during a meeting with Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides in Nicosia, according to Arab News.
The interesting comments indicate that Abbas hopes Cyprus can play a role. Cyprus has grown increasingly close to Israel over the last decades. This is part of a wider East Mediterranean shift alongside Greece. Cyprus and Israel have new defense deals as well. Cyprus has also had good ties with the Arab states. “We hope that, immediately after a new Israeli government is formed, we will be able to engage in dialogue together,” Abbas added.
Arab News indicated that the comments illustrate how the Palestinian leadership is watching developments in Israel. However, the question is whether a new Israeli coalition would be willing or able to make significant changes in policy.
The Israeli-Palestinian peace process has been largely frozen for decades. The last major US-backed negotiations, led by Secretary of State John Kerry, collapsed in 2014. Since then, the political and security environment has changed dramatically. Both Abbas and Israel’s prime minister have been in charge for the last two decades.
Far-right calls for dismantling of PA
Jerusalem has shown no interest in working with the PA. In fact, many voices on the far-right have suggested dismantling the Palestinian Authority. After the attack near Hebron earlier this month, many of the officials who came to the site suggested it was an example of why the PA should be weakened.
The Palestinian Authority continues to exercise limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank, while Hamas's October 7, 2023, attack and the subsequent war in Gaza have transformed Israeli attitudes toward Palestinian security and governance. There have been increasing tensions and clashes in the West Bank. It’s not clear how this trend could be reversed. Nevertheless, Israeli security forces tend to work well with their Palestinian Authority counterparts on security issues. This reflects how the politicians may say one thing, but the reality on the ground is different.
Even if Israel’s prime minister is replaced, a new Israeli government would inherit these challenges. The PA has not had elections since 2006, fearing a Hamas victory. In Israel, the parties that are favorable to Gadi Eisenkot might adopt a different diplomatic tone toward Ramallah. However, they would face pushback to do much more than that.
The composition of any coalition would also matter. Parties that agree on replacing Israel’s current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have very different positions regarding the Palestinians, settlements, and negotiations. The White House would likely want to see progress in Gaza with the Board of Peace. This could mean enabling Palestinian technocrats to help people in Gaza be free of Hamas.
There is also the question of whether the Palestinian leadership is positioned to negotiate a comprehensive agreement.
Abbas has led the Palestinian Authority for more than two decades. His presidency has faced questions about legitimacy, particularly because Palestinian national elections have not been held since 2006. The division between Fatah, which dominates the Palestinian Authority, and Hamas remains another major obstacle.
Any negotiations would need to address who represents Palestinians in Gaza, how the territory would be governed, and whether Palestinian security institutions could prevent renewed attacks on Israel. The Board of Peace has a technocratic team that has been largely prevented from entering Gaza by Israel. The Board was waiting for the elections. There is supposed to be an international force for Gaza, called the ISF. A new logistics center was even built for it.
These questions cannot be resolved simply by having a different Israeli prime minister. Abbas may see an opportunity to reestablish the Palestinian Authority as a diplomatic partner, particularly as international attention turns toward Gaza's reconstruction and future governance. However, renewed dialogue is not the same as a real peace process.
The United States will also play a central role in determining whether talks resume. The Trump administration has focused on regional diplomacy, the Board of Peace initiative for Gaza, and broader efforts to reshape Middle Eastern relationships. However, the US is juggling a potential new Iran conflict and also working on helping Israel with issues in Gaza and with Lebanon and Syria. The Trump administration can only do so much.
Countries such as Egypt, Jordan, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have their own interests in the Palestinian issue. Jordan is particularly concerned about developments in the West Bank, while Egypt has played a central role in Gaza diplomacy. Saudi Arabia has linked normalization with Israel to progress on the Palestinian question.
A new Israeli government could therefore create change in regional diplomacy, especially if Washington sees an opening to connect Israeli-Palestinian discussions with normalization and reconstruction initiatives.
There are several levels of potential progress. The most immediate would be renewed contacts between Israeli and Palestinian officials, improved economic cooperation, and measures to reduce tensions in the West Bank. Symbolic dialogue and positive statements can mean a lot. A more ambitious initiative could involve negotiations and enabling people in Gaza to leave the Hamas zone of control where 2 million are still trapped.
Chances for major Israeli-Palestinian talks low
The chances for major talks with the Palestinians seem low. Abbas is aging, and it is not clear who will replace him. He has postponed elections until next year. The post-October 7 Israel is not ready to take any risks on security.
Abbas's comments suggest that Ramallah wants to keep the possibility of negotiations alive. Whether this leads anywhere will depend on the next Israeli government's priorities, the Palestinian leadership's ability to make commitments, and Washington's willingness to invest in a renewed process. The most likely initial breakthrough may be the resumption of dialogue. The chances for this appear slim. It is not clear how Israel’s parties will come to a new coalition agreement.
The meeting in Cyprus matters. Cyprus is trusted by both sides. The Palestinian news agency WAFA said “President Mahmoud Abbas met with Arab ambassadors accredited to the Republic of Cyprus in the capital, Nicosia, on Thursday. President Abbas briefed the ambassadors on the situation in Palestine and the latest developments in the region.” It added that “The President arrived in Cyprus on Wednesday for an official visit at the invitation of Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides. The two leaders met on Thursday to discuss ways to strengthen bilateral relations between their countries and peoples and exchange views on the latest developments in Palestine and the region.” It did not mention the possibility of more peace discussions with Israel.

Clashes involving French jihadists in Syria's Idlib province highlight the continuing challenges facing Damascus as it seeks to consolidate control over the country and address the legacy of Syria's civil war. The challenge for Syria is that after the civil war ended with the fall of the Assad regime, there were still a number of extremists in Syria who did not want to lay down their arms. These are primarily foreign fighters who arrived in Syria after the civil war began in 2012. They came to fight the Assad regime, but many were also involved in global Jihadist activities and other types of extremism.
Most of these fighters refuse to go home. They are also not easily integrated into the new Syrian security forces. The camp of “French jihadists,” as it is known in media accounts, is only one example. It is in Idlib, which was the heartland of the rebel group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), until HTS toppled the Assad regime in 2024.
According to The New Region, a “French jihadist” was killed and a civilian injured on Wednesday when Syrian security forces confronted armed members of a group based at a camp housing French foreign fighters near Harem, close to the Turkish border.
“An internal security patrol observed an armed group leaving the French camp and heading toward the Harem area in Idlib,” the provincial internal security command told Syrian state broadcaster al-Ikhbariya, according to The New Region. Authorities said the fighters violated an agreement prohibiting them from leaving the camp while armed.
However, Kurdish media outlet Rudaw reported a slightly different account of the incident, citing Rami Abdulrahman, director of the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR). He said masked gunmen opened fire on a vehicle carrying a French commander known as Abu Ayman al-Faransi and several other people on the road between the camp and Harem.
The identity of the attackers has not been independently established.
Syrian authorities struggle to handle foreign jihadists
Rudaw also cited testimony from a French fighter who accused Syrian security authorities of staging an ambush and confiscating surveillance equipment to conceal evidence. These allegations have not been independently verified.
The camp, according to the accounts, is associated with Firqat al-Ghuraba, also known as the Strangers Division or Muhajirun, a group led by Omar Omsen, also known as Omar Diaby, a French jihadist of Senegalese origin. The Jamestown Foundation once noted he had been called the “Spielberg of French Islamism.” It said that in France, an “unassimilated Muslim community” had Islamist “produced scores of jihadists from the Nice region.” Le Monde in France said “Syrian authorities struggle with foreign jihadists…Clashes between Syrian authorities and French jihadists entrenched in the Harem camp demonstrate the challenges the new [government].”

The group accused Syrian authorities of imposing restrictions on its movement and access to food supplies.

The group also accused Damascus of acting on instructions from France, an allegation for which no evidence was provided.

Tensions between the camp and Syrian authorities are not new. In October 2025, security forces surrounded the compound following allegations that fighters linked to Omsen had kidnapped an 11-year-old girl. The confrontation led to clashes and an agreement intended to regulate the group's activities.
The latest incident illustrates the difficulties facing President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government in dealing with foreign jihadists who established themselves in Syria during the civil war.
The foreign fighters have kept their arms and operate as their own unit and seek to run their own small area. Attempts to restrict their activities have led to clashes.
Rudaw also reported that a leader of Hurras al-Din, an al-Qaeda-linked organization, was killed in a separate airstrike earlier in the week. The group of French jihadists attributed that strike to the United States, although the account did not establish independent confirmation of responsibility.
The incidents demonstrate that the toxic legacy of foreign jihadist networks remains a significant challenge for Syria's new authorities. Damascus is attempting to rebuild international relations and demonstrate that it can control armed groups operating on its territory. However, the presence of foreign fighters, some wanted by European governments, continues to complicate those efforts.
The story is not only unfolding in Syria. In Iran the government recently sentenced a number of French ISIS members to long prison terms. This illustrates how the foreign extremist threat affected both countries.

Yuli Edelstein: Israel's election results show why a national unity government is needed - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:40:26 UTC
23:40:26 KST

The Knesset elections are over. Perhaps their most significant outcome was the exceptionally high turnout – something Israel has not seen for many decades.
Most democratic countries without compulsory voting laws can only dream of such levels of public participation on election day. Tens of thousands of Israeli citizens living abroad returned to the country in the run-up to the vote to cast their ballots for one political camp or another.
After an election, the losing side usually says: “If only all our supporters had turned out to vote, the result would have been different.” This time, no party or bloc can fall back on that excuse. The election results clearly reflect the reality on the ground and accurately capture the mood of the Israeli public.
It is equally clear that neither the parties in the current coalition nor the opposition bloc can, on their own, claim to represent a majority of the Israeli people.
We saw this during the political crisis of 2019-2022, when five Knesset elections were held over the course of three and a half years. The results of the October 27 election further confirmed this.
Before the election, both the coalition and the opposition promised their supporters a crushing victory over their rivals. I believe that most of those making such promises understood even then that this was impossible: neither side could win 61 seats in the Knesset on its own and thereby secure the ability to form a government independently.
Of course, the country can be taken to a second, third, or even twentieth consecutive election. The same slogans can be repeated, and the supposedly irreconcilable differences between the blocs – differences said to make it impossible for them to serve in the same government – can be invoked again and again.
Will Israel accept the obvious, or continue the cycle of elections
But, as the familiar saying goes, “Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results.” The only question is whether we will acknowledge this now or go to the polls several more times before accepting the obvious.
Moreover, even if, in some future round of elections, one bloc were somehow to win a majority or manage to form a minority government with outside support, that would not offer a genuine solution.
Such a government would inevitably be held hostage by marginal, anti-Zionist and anti-state forces: either Itamar Ben-Gvir and the haredim (ultra-Orthodox), or the Democrats and the Arab parties.
What Israel needs is a government of national unity. I have been saying this for a long time. It is the central principle of the platform of Achdut (Unity), the party that Gilad Erdan and I founded. We did not take part in this election, but its results have vindicated our position.
Negotiations to form a national unity government will not be easy. Nor will such a government be – or should it be – a gathering of people who agree on everything. Even with my extensive experience, I would not presume to predict what its final composition might look like or which political forces would join it.
But I am convinced that the familiar “80/80” formula holds true: 80% of Israelis agree with one another on 80% of the issues that matter most to our country.
Israel has a stable Zionist Jewish majority. That gives all responsible political forces a basis on which to come together and work jointly, overcoming the disagreements that will inevitably arise.
What issues do I have in mind when I speak of a broad national consensus? First and foremost, security. We all understand that this is an objective challenge that must be addressed regardless of who is in power.
As Hamas demonstrated on October 7, our enemies do not care which party any of us votes for. The same is true of Iran, which dreams of wiping out the despised “Zionist entity” in its entirety, Left and Right alike.
Israel's economic and cost-of-living crisis
It is equally clear that Israel must tackle its long-accumulated economic problems, curb rising prices and address the ever-increasing cost of living. None of this can wait while rival blocs spend months and years fighting one another for the coveted parliamentary majority.
Israel finds itself in a difficult international position. It is no secret that many forces – even in countries we have traditionally regarded as allies – are pushing to isolate us and calling for boycotts and sanctions.
Engagement with the outside world is also far more effective when you can be confident that the government behind you is not a fragile administration riven by internal conflict, but a united government representing the majority of the country’s citizens.
Finally, I cannot overlook the need for a new, fair conscription law, which I fought hard to advance when I chaired the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee.
This issue is long overdue for resolution. It is eating away at Israeli society from within and holds the key to addressing many of our security and economic challenges.
Unfortunately, my efforts to pass such a law failed to win support. The Zionist members of the current coalition were unwilling to stand up to their coalition partners in defense of their principles, while the opposition saw the bill as a battering ram with which to destabilize and bring down the government.
We must break with the prevailing political paradigm and abandon entrenched stereotypes. The logic of confrontation must give way to the logic of solidarity. That requires a change in dominant patterns of political behavior – and in political language itself.
Rather than dwelling on disagreements, often over narrow or secondary issues, we must look for common ground, even when doing so is difficult. Politicians must stop telling voters: “We will not sit with these people, we will not join a government with those people, and we will never vote alongside the others.”
Such declarations only deepen the divisions and fuel confrontation within Israeli society. Genuine responsibility and true leadership mean promising voters that you will seek partners across the political spectrum among all those who belong to that “80/80” majority – and then keeping that promise.
The era of campaign slogans and petty infighting must come to an end. It is time to seek bold, unconventional solutions – solutions shaped not by narrow party interests, but by the interests of the nation as a whole.
The writer served as speaker of the Knesset and as a minister in several Israeli governments.

Looking back at Patrick Stewart's Israeli movie, 'Hunting Elephants'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:40:17 UTC
23:40:17 KST

Although Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British actor who passed away on Thursday, was best known for his roles in the Star Trek and the X-Men movie franchises and his theatrical career, he also had an Israeli movie on his long list of credits: Reshef Levi’s 2013 Hunting Elephants.
The movie, which was the opening-night film of the Jerusalem Film Festival, was a caper comedy set in Jerusalem that featured Stewart alongside an all-star cast of Israeli actors. Stewart played the great-uncle of a young boy (Gil Blank) who spends time with his grandfather (Sasson Gabbai) and his grandfather’s friend (Moni Moshonov) at their assisted-living facility, who are former bank robbers. After the sudden death of his father, a bank guard (Zvika Hadar), the bank refuses to pay out the father’s pension over a technicality. Stewart comes to Israel to help the grandfather and his buddy rob the bank to get the money that is due to the boy’s family.
The movie explains Stewart's connection to the family by saying that the boy’s grandmother, who is now comatose, is British. In my review when the movie when it was first released, I praised Stewart as the best thing about Hunting Elephants: “[Stewart] injects the film with life and flamboyance. His role is a series of comic bits, one of the best of which is a flashback to him in England performing in a Star Wars-themed version of Hamlet… He plays a lord and failed actor who is broke and has even sold his title to pay the bills. Between the two old Israelis’ criminal background, Stewart’s talent for making an impression and deceiving people, and the boy’s knowledge of the bank’s security system, which his father was kind enough to explain to him in detail just before he died, it’s the perfect set-up for a caper movie.” One of the highlights of the movie was a music-hall performance by Stewart at the old people’s home.
'Every other character in the film, but Michael, my character, speaks Hebrew'
In a press conference to promote the movie in Tel Aviv before filming started, Stewart said, “This movie is unlike anything else I’ve ever done, because every other character in the film, but Michael, my character, speaks Hebrew.” It turned out that he was a last-minute substitute for John Cleese, who was originally cast in the role but became ill before filming started. Stewart said he had visited Israel for the first time a year before making the movie, as a tourist, before performing in a stage production of The Merchant of Venice, a role which he had played five times. “In all the decades that had gone by, the one place I should have visited, to give this role verisimilitude, was Israel,” he said. On the earlier visit, he had had spent “four extraordinary days” in Israel and had not wanted to leave.
A few months later, he said, “I open a package and there is a script of an Israeli film and it’s set in Jerusalem. I couldn’t have been happier. And then I read the script and found out it was very funny and it had some very distinguished actors in it. So, I am delighted to be back, not as a tourist but as part of an Israeli film production.”
'If you’re outdoors and everybody is running and you’re standing still, pay attention'
In a reflection of how things have changed in the 14 years since Stewart made the movie, he spoke at the press conference of being a lifelong Labor Party Member who was always engaged in politics, and said that he thought that solving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict would be his priority if he were a world leader. But he emphasized that he believed that the best way to figure out how to do that was to spend time in the region and said he looked forward to having a “clearer mind about the issues” after spending a month filming in Israel.
But some things never seem to change, and he said, “Two Jewish friends of mine said: ‘One piece of advice. If you’re outdoors and everybody is running and you’re standing still, pay attention.’”

Israel's opposition must break its promise, rely on Arab parties to oust Netanyahu - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:40:13 UTC
23:40:13 KST

As in previous elections, the opposition can only point to a majority in the Knesset when the seats won by Arab parties are included in the electoral count. This was the case with the parliamentary camps that backed Yitzhak Rabin in 1992, Ehud Barak in 1999, and Yair Lapid in 2021.
The precise circumstances of those earlier governments differed, but the underlying principle was the same: Arab citizens vote in Israeli elections, their representatives sit in the Knesset, their seats count toward the parliamentary balance, and they do not approve of the Likud and its racist, ultra-nationalist fellow travelers.
However, there is one spectacular complication. Leading opposition politicians promised during the campaign that they would not form a government dependent on Arab parties. Having (pathetically) accepted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s contention that such dependence would somehow taint a government, they may now find themselves unable to take office without violating their solemn commitments.
It’s understandable, up to a point. Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, and other opposition leaders reassured right-wing voters that replacing Netanyahu would not mean relying on parties with positions on the Palestinian conflict and Israel’s national identity that many of those voters find objectionable. It is hard to dismiss this as meaningless campaign rhetoric.
Which campaign promises will the opposition break?
But the opposition also made a far more consequential promise, one that constituted the very essence of its campaign: to replace Netanyahu and reverse the direction in which his government has taken Israel.
If the only parliamentary route to do so requires Arab support, the two commitments cannot both be honored. The question is whether fidelity to a tactical electoral pledge should outweigh the broader responsibility that opposition leaders themselves placed at the center of the election.
The practical circumstances make the dilemma especially unusual. Arab political leaders have indicated that they are prepared to support an alternative minority government from outside the coalition, without demanding cabinet positions.
Their support would not be unconditional, but their concerns are very reasonable: representatives of the Joint List have raised demands regarding crime in Arab communities and the Palestinian question.
Whether breaking the promise can be justified raises a question philosophers and statesmen have debated for centuries. Promises underpin political legitimacy, yet circumstances can make honoring them more damaging than breaking them. The question is whether fidelity to one’s word outweighs responsibility for its consequences.
Niccolò Machiavelli argued in The Prince that rulers cannot always honor commitments when circumstances change and doing so threatens their interests. The German sociologist Max Weber offered a more ethically serious framework in Politics as a Vocation, contrasting an ethic of conviction with an ethic of responsibility. The former emphasizes fidelity to principle; the latter demands accountability for foreseeable consequences.
Edmund Burke approached the question differently. In his famous 1774 address to the electors of Bristol, he argued that representatives owe voters judgment, not blind obedience. A politician who clings to an earlier position despite recognizing its harm may be sacrificing the very judgment voters elected him to exercise.
History provides examples in which the tension involved matters considerably more serious than an abandoned tax pledge or an inconvenient coalition agreement.
Abraham Lincoln entered office in 1861 explicitly assuring the Southern states that he had no intention of interfering with slavery where it already existed. Yet in 1863, he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in areas then in rebellion to be free.
Possibility of Netanyahu remaining prime minister
This brings us to the disastrous possibility that honoring their promise leaves the opposition clearing the way for Netanyahu to stay in power. The man who was in charge on October 7, who risks lives every day by blocking an inquiry meant to prevent a similar disaster, who is undermining Israeli democracy and enabling the outrages of the haredim to continue, who is on trial for corruption, and who is dedicated to sowing divisions, will get away with it and continue causing the nation his destructive harm.
There is also a rather delicious irony in any notion of honesty and the main quality in any context featuring the prime minister. Netanyahu’s political career has featured repeated lies, distortions, betrayals, and prevarications.
This is a person who promised that Itamar Ben-Gvir would never be a cabinet minister; who promised (in a court affidavit!) to recuse himself from interfering with the courts; who enthusiastically backed term limits; who called on prime minister Ehud Olmert to resign over a mere police investigation (while he himself is actually on trial); and who broke his promise to rotate the premiership with Benny Gantz.
Hilariously, he is also the man who, having lost the election in 2021, negotiated with Mansour Abbas to bring the Arab party Ra’am in a government based on a completely new political alignment. It was only the veto by Bezalel Smotrich that blew up that machination – and yet today he dares argue that Ra’am (led by an Arab who has emphatically accepted Israel as the Jewish state) is beyond the pale.
Arab citizens constitute roughly one-fifth of Israel’s population, vote under the same electoral laws as Jewish citizens, and elect representatives to the same parliament.
Their parties hold positions on the Palestinian conflict and national identity that many Jewish Israelis oppose, and those disagreements would create genuine difficulties for a government dependent on their support. But they must be embraced if this country is to have any sort of future. They will never sing “Hatikva” with great gusto, but they have not caused damage and have been remarkably loyal citizens.
Boycotting them is not just stupid politics for the opposition; it is devastating to the future of Israel as a functional country.
Besides, Netanyahu has long relied on ultra-Orthodox parties whose demands concerning military service, education, and public spending have profound consequences for Israel’s security, economy, and social cohesion. Some of those parties are non-Zionist, yet their seats are treated as an entirely normal component of the parliamentary arithmetic.
The opposition should stop overthinking, get out of its own way, thank the Arabs for their support, and get on with saving the country.
The writer is the former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press, the former chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem, and publisher of danperry.substack.com.

Houthis continue to engage in ‘fierce battles’ in mountains near Aden, Taiz - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:40:04 UTC
23:40:04 KST

The Houthis continue to attack Saudi Arabia and are also continuing to engage in “fierce battles” in Yemen. This is an important issue because any talks with Iran, which appear to be happening, will take the Houthis into account. Arab News in Saudi Arabia said on October 30 that the “Saudi-led coalition said on Friday it intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region a drone fired by Yemen’s Houthis.”
According to the Saudis, “a drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region.” The report noted that “the Iran-backed militia has for weeks targeted airports, energy infrastructure and cities across the Kingdom with drones and missiles.”
Now, Al-Ain media in the UAE also says that “dozens of government forces and Houthis were killed and wounded on Friday in fierce battles in Al-Maqatra district of Lahj, following a large-scale attack by the militias.”
Sources in Yemen told Al-Ain News that the Houthi militias launched a large-scale ground attack on government forces’ positions in Al-Maqatirah district, the northern gateway to Lahj, in an attempt to make progress on the ground and control key mountain ranges in the area.
This is an area in southern Yemen where the Houthis are fighting a tough and complex war against the Yemeni government and also other factions aligned with the government. Some of these factions were linked to the Southern Transitional Council, which had been backed by the UAE.
The UAE has excellent sources in this area.
“The sources confirmed that the Houthi militias aim, through the attack, to control the ‘Al-Muqatara Tunnel’ area and the strategically important Al-Muqatara mountain fortress, as well as to reach the Al-Rubu’ market located in the Heijah Al-Abd valley, where the main road linking Taiz and Aden is located.” The sources explained that the battles extended to the Haifan front, where the militias are trying to reach Mount An’an, which overlooks large areas between Haifan and Al-Maqatirah.
Events in Yemen could affect Iran, UAE, Qatar, US
This area appears to be only around 40 to 50 miles from Aden. This means the battles in these mountains, amid palm trees and scrub brush and steep terrain, could determine the next moves in Yemen. What happens here, could also matter in Tehran, Doha, Riyadh and Washington.
Let’s recall why the Houthis matters. The Iran-backed Houthis have emerged as one of the most important armed terrorist armies in the Middle East, using Yemen as a base to threaten Saudi Arabia, Israel and international shipping. The movement, also known as Ansar Allah, emerged from northern Yemen's Zaydi Shi'ite community and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
In early 2015, Houthi forces advanced south toward Aden, forcing Yemen's internationally recognized government to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in March 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition seeking to restore the government and prevent the Houthis from consolidating control over Yemen.
The war devastated the country but failed to defeat the Houthis. Iran's support helped the movement develop an increasingly sophisticated arsenal of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. These weapons enabled the Houthis to strike Saudi Arabia and eventually target Israel.
Following the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, the Houthis began launching missiles and drones toward Israel and attacking commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Israel, the United States and Britain subsequently carried out strikes against Houthi targets. The Houthis resumed attacks on Israel during the 2026 conflict involving Iran.
Yemen's war escalated again in July 2026, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi targets and shipping. In September, Houthi forces advanced along the Red Sea coast, capturing Mocha and reaching the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait. The strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a vital route for international trade and energy shipments.
Fighting has also intensified around Taiz, where the Houthis have sought to threaten the road linking the city to Aden, the internationally recognized government's main base.
The renewed conflict illustrates how Yemen's civil war has become intertwined with the wider regional confrontation involving Iran, Saudi Arabia and Israel. Control of territory around Bab al-Mandab gives the Houthis additional leverage over regional security and international commerce.
Al-Ain says that as the battles in the mountains have continued, “warplanes launched a series of raids on Houthi positions and gatherings to repel the militia's attack on Al-Maqatirah district in Lahj governorate.” Al-Ain concludes that “by attacking Al-Maqatirah, the Houthi militias are trying to reach Tur Al-Bahah district in Lahj, a coastal province that is the main gateway to the capital, Aden.”
Yemen has been witnessing fierce battles since the beginning of last September, following a large-scale, multi-pronged attack launched by the Houthis on areas of the western coast, Bab al-Mandab and Taiz, which resulted in thousands of deaths and injuries.
Houthis lay seige to Taiz
The Houthis are also laying siege to the city of Taiz in the mountains. Arab News says that the Houthis are also facing growing international criticism over their detention of United Nations personnel and the worsening humanitarian crisis in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
According to Arab News, the Houthis are holding 71 UN staff members, severely restricting the organization's ability to operate in areas under their control. “These actions render the delivery of humanitarian aid in areas under the control of the Houthis untenable at this time,” Shirin Yaseen, associate spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told Arab News.
The reports indicate that the humanitarian situation has deteriorated further around Taiz, where more than 800,000 people have been cut off from essential supplies. The Houthis intensified their siege in early October after seizing the road connecting Taiz with Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government. According to the World Food Programme, approximately three-quarters of the affected population depend on humanitarian assistance. Taiz has faced varying degrees of Houthi siege since 2015.

Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen. Now what?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:39:20 UTC
23:39:20 KST

What next as Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen?
Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset.
Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government.
The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53.
Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population.
"Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran."
The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect.
The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power.
Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister.
"No basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise"
The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear.
"An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement.
The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."
Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters.
Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians."
"An improper influence operation?"
While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins.
Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results.
"Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post.
Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on — Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.
Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically, will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

Emine Erdogan urges stronger cooperation on women, families across Turkic world

Türkiye’s First Lady Emine Erdogan has called for lasting cooperation on family and women’s issues across the Turkic world, highlighting women’s longstanding influence in Turkic societies.

The gathering aimed to turn a shared commitment to family and women’s issues into lasting cooperation.
Efforts to empower families and women
“We aim to make our council a lasting platform for cooperation. Today, together with you, we have taken the first steps toward establishing our council here in Ankara,” Erdogan said.
She expressed hope that the council’s first official meeting would take place during the 14th OTS summit in Uzbekistan next year, hosted by Uzbek first lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva.
In a subsequent post on NSosyal, Erdogan said the council would bring together efforts to empower families and women.
“We believe that keeping families, the unseen stronghold of our societies, strong is possible by supporting women in every sphere of life,” she said.
She stressed the importance of drawing on member countries’ experience and developing shared solutions, expressing hope that the council would deepen cooperation and strengthen ties across the Turkic world.

The Hummer's disappearance was first discovered Monday, after a similar vehicle was brought into an emergency equipment storage depot at the base. A request was also submitted to the military's Organization and Human Resources Branch to conduct a comprehensive inventory of all vehicle companies and emergency equipment storage depots.
The IDF Spokesperson's Unit said: "During routine inspections by a military unit in southern Israel, a military Hummer was reported missing. Following the report, the Military Police Criminal Investigation Division opened an investigation to determine the circumstances of the incident.
"The Military Police Criminal Investigation Division will continue to act decisively to combat the theft of military equipment and weapons and bring those involved to justice, should any be identified."

Poland Received New Batch of M1110 JAB Tank-Mounted Bridge-Laying Vehicles Based on Abrams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:33:28 UTC
23:33:28 KST

Another batch of American M1110 Joint Assault Bridge (JAB) tank bridge-layers has arrived in Poland.
This was reported by the Armaments Agency of the Polish Ministry of National Defence.
According to Defence24, the equipment will be received by the 18th Mechanized Division. The first batch arrived in the country in July.
The delivered units are designed to facilitate the crossing of heavy armored vehicles over various obstacles.
In particular, the assault bridges will operate in conjunction with units equipped with M1 Abrams main battle tanks.
The procurement of this specialized equipment is being carried out as part of large-scale contracts with the United States for the supply of this armored equipment.
In total, Poland has ordered 25 M1110 JAB bridge-layers: 8 units under the agreement from January 2023 for 116 M1A1 FEP units and 17 under the contract from April 2022 for 250 M1A2 SEPv3 versions.
The M1110 was developed by Leonardo DRS based on a modified M1A1 chassis with suspension components from the M1A2 variant.
This provides the engineering vehicle with a level of armor protection, cross-country capability, and speed comparable to that of tanks.
The vehicle is equipped with a hydraulic deployment system and a new release mechanism. It uses a standard 18.3-meter-long Heavy Assault Scissor Bridge (HASB).
The bridge-laying vehicle’s crew consists of two people—a driver-mechanic and a commander. The vehicle is capable of deploying a bridge across obstacles up to 11 meters wide in just 3–5 minutes.
The structure’s load-bearing capacity meets the MLC 115 class standard. This allows even the heaviest tracked platforms—including the M1A2 SEPv3, weighing over 65 metric tons, and the M88A2 Hercules armored recovery vehicles—to safely cross water and land obstacles.

Ukraine to co-found defense bank aimed at financing weapons production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:33:15 UTC
23:33:15 KST

Ukraine and eight partner countries plan to sign an agreement establishing a new international defense bank on Nov. 30, potentially opening another source of long-term financing for weapons production, the governments said in a joint statement published Oct. 29.
The Canada-led Defense, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) aims to begin operations in 2027. It would help governments finance their defense needs, and manufacturers expand production, with benefits tied to participation in the institution.
As Russia’s war drags on, Ukraine needs sustained funding to keep its military supplied. The proposed bank could give allies another way to help finance Ukraine’s defense over the long term, supporting weapons production and military purchases.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said on Oct. 26 that the bank would be headquartered in Canada, with a European hub in Luxembourg. Its mandate would cover industrial expansion, critical supply chains and eligible procurement, including financing gaps affecting smaller defense companies.
read also
Reuters reported in August that the project was targeting about 100 billion euros ($111.3 billion) in capital: 20 billion euros ($22.3 billion) paid in and 80 billion euros ($89 billion) callable from members if required. The latest official statements do not specify a capital target or announce funding earmarked for Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Canada's invitation for Ukraine to become a founding member back in July in a Telegram post following talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
“It will work to attract capital and develop defense-industrial capacity and technologies tested in real combat conditions,” Zelensky said.
Alongside Ukraine and Canada, the founding group includes Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania and Turkey.
The announcements do not specify Ukraine's contribution, borrowing terms or potential allocation. The November signing would mark another step toward establishment, rather than the start of lending.

Singaporean Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan on Friday praised Pakistan for playing a "unique but very constructive and valuable role" in addressing regional challenges.

Pakistan and Singapore are marking the 60th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations this year.

How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:32:31 UTC
23:32:31 KST

How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
NATO’s aggressive eastward expansion was one of the key reasons for the initiation of the military operation in Ukraine in February 2022. This is supported by RT’s findings about a drone production cluster established by NATO-affiliated enterprises near Riga.
The Baltic states had become a hub for developing combat drones as early as 2020. According to RT’s findings, companies in Latvia generated €283 million in revenue from producing UAVs, robotics, and military aerospace systems in 2022-2025 alone. More than half of that revenue came from companies with foreign investment. The two largest factories are under US and Israeli ownership, while another is partly Ukrainian-owned. Several factories form a single industrial cluster near Riga. Experts say this suggests Latvia was preparing for a conflict with Russia well in advance.
Presently, we will focus on eight UAV production factories in Latvia that are backed by foreign investments. RT uncovered the details about these companies in financial reports, aided by the G8 OSINT team that advises the Russian Defense Ministry.
According to the data, the companies collectively earned €282.98 million from 2022 to 2025.
The bulk of the revenue came from three companies: Redwire Defense Tech Riga (€131.4 million), Belss (€77.7 million), and Brasa Defense Systems (€46.7 million). The following companies contributed lesser amounts: Origin Robotics (€10.6 million), Eraser ( €6.04 million), LV-Teh (€5.98 million), Atlas Aerospace (€3.52 million), and Natrix (€0.98 million).
The Drone Coalition, which also includes the UK, was established in 2024 at Latvia’s initiative. The aim is to collaboratively supply Ukraine with drones. Collective commitments reached €600 million, and the coalition’s fund raised €1.8 billion from investors in 2024. Since then, over 100,000 drones have already been delivered to Ukraine.
Drones abound in quiet Marupe
The heart of Latvia’s drone assembly industry is located in Marupe, a suburb of Riga. Just a couple of kilometers from the international airport, five companies form a bustling UAV production cluster: Belss, its subsidiary Eraser, Brasa Defense Systems, Origin Robotics, and Redwire Defense Tech Riga.
At the center of this cluster lies SIRIN Park Marupe, a logistics hub situated near the runway. This is where Redwire Defense Tech, the industry leader in terms of revenue, is located. The company produces Penguin drones. Since 2022, they have delivered around 250 to 300 drones to Ukraine. Smaller models start at around $20,000, while some modifications can reach up to $70,000 each. The facility employs 279 people.
Nearby, at 26 Dzirnieku Street, there is Origin Robotics, which has around 60 employees. They specialize in building BEAK portable strike drones and BLAZE autonomous drone interceptors. Both models are used in Ukraine and are also part of Latvia’s military arsenal. By the end of November 2026, Origin Robotics aims to complete the development of a cargo drone system designed for precise automated delivery of cargo (i.e. explosives). In simple terms, the Latvians plan to equip quadcopters with guided mini-munitions.
Further on, in the direction of Riga, there is Brasa Defense, which occupies around 6,000 square meters of warehouse and office space at 16 Plienciema Street. They manufacture UNHUMAN ground robotic platforms designed to support infantry on the battlefield.
Located furthest from the airport, Belss operates in Ezisi Industrial Park. It is the largest defense communications integrator in Latvia (operating since 1994). The company formerly focused on secure military communications but pivoted in 2023 to develop its own line of UAVs. By 2024, they were supplying thousands of modular military drones to Ukraine. In June 2024, Belss spun off its drone division into a separate subsidiary named Eraser.
There are no doubts as to who is the primary consumer of Belss products: Latvian and Ukrainian flags are proudly displayed at the entrance. A satellite view reveals a private runway just 100 meters from the fence, used for testing equipment.
The other production facilities are located in Riga, but the difference isn’t critical since Marupe is very close to Riga. The area is home to the NATRIX, LV-Teh, and AeroVictory Baltic factories. The latter is a Baltic subsidiary of a Ukrainian company that has relocated UAV production to Latvia and has yet to submit financial reports.
Also registered in Riga is Atlas Aerospace – a company with Ukrainian roots and Israeli ownership – producing reconnaissance drones like the AtlasPRO, Atlas UAVs, and AtlasTETHER tethered systems. These devices are supplied to Ukraine and NATO countries. The company has 43 official employees.
The choice of location is strategic, according to specialists from the G8 group. In addition to proximity to the airport, a railway runs through Marupe that will soon connect with tracks leading to Ukraine via Moldova.
The father of ‘Penguins’ in the service of NATO
Latvia has its own key figure uniting several companies backed by American and European capital: Konstantins Popiks, a serial entrepreneur in the military industry. He was introduced to aeromodeling as a child and even represented Latvia in aeromodeling competitions. After enrolling at the University of Liverpool in 2005, he graduated in 2009 with a Master’s degree in aerospace engineering.
The Penguin reconnaissance drone and its combat versions, which are in service with the Latvian military and are being sold in large quantities to Ukraine, originated as Popiks’ student project. Upon returning to his homeland, he founded UAV Factory, which produces Penguin drones. Within ten years, the company reached the international level, and in 2021, it attracted an investor from the US: AE Industrial Partners. By 2022, Popiks departed, and the factory changed ownership and rebranded as Edge Autonomy.
In June 2025, the facility announced plans to double its production footprint, enabling it to produce up to ten heavy fixed-wing UAVs per month. According to documents, there were 270 employees at the time, and the company had contracts with the Latvian Defense Ministry.
In 2025, Edge Autonomy Holdings signed a merger agreement, becoming a subsidiary of American company Redwire Corp. By March 2026, it was rebranded as Redwire Defense Tech Riga, emerging as the leading company in the sector by revenue. Its reported income of €131.4 million accounts for nearly half of the total UAV sector earnings.
This defense contract not only brought Popiks fame but also significant wealth. As RT discovered, he resides in an upscale neighborhood of Jurmala (Kapu Street), where he owns a small castle. The property is surrounded by tall Baltic pines, with the Riga seashore and a beach just beyond the backyard. The property borders the Gulf of Riga.
After selling the factory, Popiks established another company – Origin Robotics. Funds from European investors began flowing in. In 2025, Belgium’s defense minister signed a €50 million contract with the company for the procurement of BLAZE drone interceptors. Currently, Origin is experiencing remarkable growth. Revenues soared from 2023 to 2025, reaching €10.6 million.
Under the wing of the IDF
Among the entrepreneurs in this cluster is Ivan Tolchinsky, an Israeli citizen of Ukrainian descent. Born in Gorlovka, Donetsk Region, he moved to Israel at the age of 10. As an adult, he served in the special forces and took part in combat operations in Lebanon. For around five years, he worked as an engineer in Israel’s aerospace industry and spent a year in China studying mass electronics production.
In 2015, Tolchinsky relocated to Latvia, where he co-founded Atlas Dynamics with Igor Zhidanov, a fellow native of Gorlovka. Zhidanov is a seasoned engineer with 35 years of experience and holds three world records in aeromodeling. He had his own club back in Gorlovka, which Tolchinsky was also a part of.
In interviews with Latvian and Ukrainian media, Tolchinsky revealed that his production facility produces over 300 Atlas drones per month – which, he says, is five times more than in previous years. He doesn’t conceal his collaboration with the Ukrainian Armed Forces. “We have a direct contract with the Ministry of Defense, which we’ve already fulfilled. Now we are working towards another contract,” he told Ukrainian journalists.
A few years before the conflict, in 2020, Tolchinsky established a subsidiary in Ireland called Atlas Dynamics UK. Originally registered at a residential address in Moreton-on-Lugg, Herefordshire, it soon changed its legal address.
The company had Israeli roots, as indicated by its founding documents drafted in Hebrew and English by a notary from Israel.
In the 2020s, Atlas Dynamics was rebranded as Atlas Aerospace SIA. In November 2025, Tolchinsky sold the company to Israel’s Xtend Reality Expansion Ltd – a company focused on creating FPV drones for entertainment and gaming prior to its collaboration with the IDF.
Russia is identified as the main adversary
Latvian UAV factories do not publicly mention contracts with Ukraine in their annual reports. Some only mention that Ukraine is among their clients, without disclosing what portion of their profits comes from supplying Kiev.
One thing is clear: Nearly all the above-mentioned companies receive investments from the Latvian Defense Ministry and EU agencies. This is part of measures to enhance defense capabilities, with Russia identified as the chief adversary.
According to EU Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, “Russia is outproducing Europe in key armaments.” This has been cited as a reason for increased defense spending, which is reflected in official documents.
According to reports reviewed by RT, one of the main sources of funding for SIA Belss is the European Defense Fund (EDF). In 2024-2025, the fund allocated €470,800 to the company under the European Extended Mine Countermeasures program, aimed at developing demining technologies. Earlier, RT reported on how the EU channels military expenditures through the guise of ‘humanitarian’ demining initiatives.
Even before 2022, Latvia’s drone sector was already experiencing rapid growth and consolidation. LV-Teh has been operating since 2020, while Brasa Defense Systems officially became a separate entity on September 13, 2021. Origin Robotics was registered on January 31, 2022 – just weeks before the start of the Ukraine conflict.
Belss has been in business since 1994, but significantly expanded its capabilities in 2022 and 2023. UAV Factory, known for its Penguin drones, was founded in 2009, and Atlas Aerospace emerged in 2015.
Only three new companies appeared after the start of hostilities: Natrix in February 2024, Eraser in June 2024, and AeroVictory Baltic (a company with direct Ukrainian roots) in February 2026.
In one of the reports, RT uncovered evidence of Latvia’s preparations for the conflict. In December 2021, just two months before the start of hostilities, the Latvian Defense Ministry allocated €88,000 to Belss for upgrading British infantry fighting vehicles in service with the Latvian army. This included installing automatic fire control systems on turrets, allowing operators to engage targets without exposing themselves, thereby enhancing crew survival on the modern battlefield, which is increasingly dominated by drones. This suggests that Latvians were gearing up for drone warfare well before the start of the conflict.
Long before the events of 2014 and 2022, a coalition of three countries with a firm anti-Russia stance formed in the Baltics, Vadim Avva, a Russian writer and political scientist born in Daugavpils, Latvia, says.
“The statehood of the Baltic nations led to the establishment of three sparsely-populated forts along [Russia’s] northwestern borders; their primary function is to support expanding NATO military bases and other infrastructure clearly being prepared for an operation to invade and occupy the territories of Russia and Belarus,” Avva says.
A launchpad for hatred
Avva recalled a viral video in which Estonian teenagers were asked which country should be erased from the world map, and many named Russia. He notes that during World War II, the national bourgeoisie of Latvia and Estonia “became a foundation for Latvian and Estonian SS legions,” and today, local schools are named after Lithuanian collaborators with Nazi Germany. He explains that the oppression of the Russian-speaking population in these regions began in the late 19th century and only intensified with the collapse of the Soviet Union.
“What has returned to the Baltics is not just bourgeois nationalism; it’s a blend of bourgeois Nazism and ‘brown’ [ultra-right] emigration,” Avva says. “What fate could befall this territory after the establishment of property monopoly and political monopoly and the welcoming back of the descendants of fascist collaborators? Obviously, it could only become a military launchpad.”
Latvian UAVs are occasionally identified and shot down by Russian drone interceptors. However, their share among the various models used by Ukraine remains small, according to a drone operator with the call sign ‘Baks’, who neutralizes enemy drones approaching Russian borders.
“Ukrainians definitely try out everything produced by the Balts and purchase a lot of their equipment, but it’s a question of scale and quantity. We don’t have much information on the BLAZE and BEAK models, but there is some info on ‘Penguins’ – our colleagues at Rubicon [Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies] managed to take down a few. The number of downed UAVs directly relates to their quantity. Compared to the Shark, Leleka, and other [Ukrainian drones], Latvian models represent a mere fraction [of the deployed drones].”
It’s not just Penguin drones that are being targeted, however, but their manufacturers as well. Redwire Defense Tech Riga, the company producing these drones, relocated to Sirin Park after their previous facility in Marupe unexpectedly burned down.
Similar incidents often occur at European companies that supply drones to Ukraine. In August 2026 alone, there were several incidents: A production facility belonging to Polish arms maker WB Electronics caught fire at the end of August; an explosion rocked the KNDS Ammo plant near Rome on August 13; and on August 15, unknown arsonists set fire to the building of Estonian military robotics manufacturer Milrem Robotics, which RT wrote about in the first part of its investigation.

Up to 100,000 people take part in protest against war economy in Rome — organizers

ROME, October 30. /TASS/. Some 100,000 people took to downtown Rome to march in protest against the war economy and rising prices, a TASS correspondent learned from the action organizers in the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) trade union, who were supported by other unions and associations, including youth and student groups.
Faculty and students are protesting against the reallocation of funds from social programs to military spending. "I came to the demonstration because I support its goals. And students have the same right to protest," a faculty member holding a banner reading "Money for schools, not for war" told TASS. Short speeches broadcast over loudspeakers criticized the government of Giorgia Meloni, "a Christian woman who, like a coward, sends young people into the maelstrom of war."
Despite the fact that most of the demonstrators were young people, the protest was held without incident. The entire central part of the city was deserted, with no cars, taxis, or public transport moving around. Only a few shops and restaurants closed while the rest were happy to welcome the hungry demonstrators. Some tourists emerging with their luggage from Termini Central Station, where the march began, looked quite surprised. The demonstrators then marched through the neighboring streets, including those near the Russian Embassy, and headed toward the Colosseum. Off the march’s route, particularly near the Colosseum, the atmosphere was completely the same as any other day: crowds of tourists and street vendors. The Colosseum museum is operating as usual. Despite the general strike called by the same trade union, the subway is operating as usual. Security measures have been stepped up, but police are keeping a good distance away from the protesters, blocking off only certain sections and guarding ministry buildings, in particular, the transport ministry, which the march passed by. According to s experts, such distance is maintained to avoid potential clashes. "But everyone has been placed on high alert," they told TASS.
Similar marches were held simultaneously in dozens of Italian cities. Thus, according to the organizers, demonstrations drew 50,000 participants in Turin, up to 20,000 - in Naples, and 10,000 - in Milan. Partial blockings of ports were reported from Naples, Livorno, and Genoa.

The Rutte way or the Carney method? Scaramucci says Europe’s Trump strategy is off the Mark
Unknown

14:32:19 UTC
23:32:19 KST

European leaders are using the wrong strategy to deal with U.S. President Donald Trump, according to Anthony Scaramucci, who briefly served as the White House’s communications director during Trump’s first term.
“You have to be firm with him. He doesn’t respect people that aren’t. I think you have got to wait him out,” Scaramucci told WELT AM SONNTAG, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.
Scaramucci described two ways of handling Trump: the Carney approach and the Rutte approach.
Advertisement
“There’s two models of behavior: one is [NATO Secretary-General] Mark Rutte and one is [Canadian Prime Minister] Mark Carney. I think Mark Carney is handling him better. The Canadian people are with him, even if it causes some level of economic hardship,” Scaramucci said.
“Rutte, on the other hand, is making a big mistake. Because when you equivocate or flatter him, when you act in the manner that Mark Rutte has acted, all you’re doing is losing his respect. You’re not gaining anything,” he added.
Rutte has often lauded the U.S. president: “I just like the man. I think what he is doing for NATO is great news,” the military alliance chief said in an interview with POLITICO this summer.
Europe has seemingly yielded to Trump’s wishes on numerous occasions. The EU-U.S. trade deal was criticized as playing in Washington’s favor, while European allies agreed to a 5% of GDP spending target by 2035 at last year’s NATO summit in The Hague, matching Trump’s headline demand.
Carney, by contrast, has been more unwilling to bow to Trump’s pressure. He walked away from U.S. trade talks, saying Ottawa could not accept the offer or the demands — and promised to match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.
In the interview, Scaramucci also lambasted members of Trump’s own Republican Party. “That is the other side of this story: the cowardice of the political servants that are supposed to check Donald Trump, the members of the Republican Senate caucus and the House caucus,” he said.
Advertisement
He added that lawmakers had failed to speak out against Trump’s decision to waive key provisions of the Russian sanctions law championed by the late South Carolina senator, Lindsey Graham.
“They’ve done nothing to speak out against that or to rebuke Trump, even though they could override him,” he said. “This is a case study in what you would call the strong arm tactics. People that believe in authoritarianism operate with levels of intimidation. That’s what Trump has done.”
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

The Ukrainian delegation, together with the evacuated residents of Oleshky, set off for Anapa. From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus and then get home by bus
