PSG to defend Intercontinental Cup title in December as Qatar hosts final stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:31:21 UTC
23:31:21 KST

Continental champions will compete in Qatar this December as PSG seek a second successive Intercontinental Cup title. The final stages return for a third year, following earlier matches in Saudi Arabia and South Africa.
Paris Saint-Germain will return to Qatar in December to defend their FIFA Intercontinental Cup title, after the country was confirmed as host of the tournament’s final three matches for a third consecutive year.
The French club will play in the final on 16 December at Ahmad bin Ali Stadium in Al Rayyan, returning to the venue where they lifted the trophy last year. The other two matches will take place on 9 and 12 December, organisers announced on Thursday.
PSG secured their place by retaining the UEFA Champions League title in the 2025-26 season. Under the competition’s format, Europe’s champions enter directly into the final, while clubs representing the other five continental confederations compete for the remaining place.
Last December, PSG beat Brazil’s Flamengo 2-1 on penalties after a 1-1 draw following extra time, winning their first Intercontinental Cup in front of 42,150 spectators.
Three clubs, one place in the final
Mexico’s Toluca, winners of the Concacaf Champions Cup, will face this year’s Copa Libertadores winners in the Derby of the Americas on 9 December at Jassim bin Hamad Stadium in Doha.
The winners will then meet South Africa’s Mamelodi Sundowns in the Challenger Cup at the same venue on 12 December, with a place against PSG in the final at stake.
Sundowns reached that stage by beating Saudi Arabia’s Al Ahli 2-1 in Pretoria on 19 September to win the African-Asian-Pacific Cup. Al Ahli had opened the tournament with a 1-0 victory over New Zealand’s Auckland FC in Jeddah on 26 August.
The South American representative will be decided in the Copa Libertadores final on 28 November.
The Intercontinental Cup is FIFA’s annual competition for the champions of its six continental confederations. It is separate from the expanded Club World Cup, which is held every four years.
Qatar hosted the final stages of the first two editions of the Intercontinental Cup in 2024 and 2025, having previously staged the 2019 and 2020 editions of the former annual Club World Cup.
This year’s December fixtures will overlap with the closing stages of the Under-17 World Cup, which Qatar is hosting from 19 November to 13 December.

In Germany, 70 rescuers removed a drunk man from a tree after he was unable to climb down following a party
Kyiv • UNN
A 25-year-old man became stuck in a treehouse six meters above the ground after a party. Rescuers brought him down with a blood alcohol level of 2.5 per mille.
In the German federal state of Saxony, around 70 emergency service workers took part in rescuing a 25-year-old man who was unable to descend from a treehouse on his own after a party. Bild reports, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred on the evening of October 29 near the settlement of Sehmatal in the Ore Mountains. A group of young people held a party in a treehouse about six meters above the ground. When one of the participants was unable to climb down because of severe alcohol intoxication, his friends called the firefighters.
Because of the treehouse’s hard-to-reach location near railway tracks, rescuers had to reach the site on a rail trolley. Height-rescue specialists climbed up to the man, secured him in a rescue stretcher, and carefully lowered him to the ground using ropes. The injured man was then transported by rail trolley to an ambulance and taken to hospital.
Before hospitalization, police checked the man’s blood alcohol level. The breathalyzer showed 2.5 parts per thousand, which corresponds to severe alcohol intoxication and may be accompanied by serious disruptions in the functioning of the body.
Firefighters, police officers, medical personnel, and height-rescue specialists took part in the rescue operation.

New Bulgarian Drone to Monitor Maritime Threats and Protect Shipping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

A Bulgarian company has developed an autonomous drone designed to protect shipping and support maritime security in the Black Sea, with controlled tests scheduled in the Bay of Burgas over the next two weeks.
The drone was presented at an International Forum on Security and Innovation in Burgas. It was developed by a 20-member team led by Dragomir Enchev, a software engineer, and can perform autonomous maritime missions while also allowing manual control by an operator. The device runs on batteries and solar panels.
Enchev said the project aims to offer a more affordable alternative to similar autonomous drones, which can cost millions. The plan is to deploy dozens of units along Bulgaria's coastline, where they would work in coordination with radar systems and provide continuous, real-time information to enable rapid responses.
The drone is still being tested, and its developers are open to discussions with interested parties. It is electrically powered and communicates with the shore through several channels. Its capabilities include jamming hostile devices and establishing "green corridors" for safe passage.
The device can also be deployed for environmental monitoring, collecting samples at regular intervals from areas affected by spills.
Burgas Mayor Dimitar Nikolov said he had checked whether rising tensions in the Black Sea could affect commercial shipping and the city's preparations to host the upcoming Eurovision contest. "I made inquiries yesterday regarding any restrictions on commercial traffic to or from the ports in Burgas. There have been no disruptions or interruptions," he said.
Nikolov also said he felt secure as mayor of a Black Sea city because Bulgaria is a member of the EU and NATO. While acknowledging the unease caused by instability in the region in recent days and months, he said the forum was focused on a different agenda.
"I hope this concerning situation ends soon, allowing us to shift our focus back toward development and the future - toward new transport corridors and the new technologies that will take root along our coastline," Nikolov said.
Atanaska Nikolova, chair of the association Prospecti M, which is organizing the forum together with the Municipality of Burgas, said this year's event focused on sustainability, security and innovation.
The forum brought together representatives of European and national institutions, businesses and the scientific community to discuss security challenges facing Black Sea countries and opportunities for joint solutions. Discussions covered the protection of marine resources, coastal development and the introduction of new technologies.
An exhibition area also presented technological developments intended to strengthen security in the Black Sea. The event took place against a backdrop of increasingly frequent drone attacks on commercial vessels and heightened regional tensions.
Enchev said the drone was produced using 3D printing, with manufacturing taking just 48 hours. He described it as one of the first devices of its kind worldwide and said it could be produced at a relatively low cost.
"When deployed in groups, especially given the current situation, these drones can rapidly generate comprehensive, interactive maps of high-risk areas, such as our Black Sea coast, and provide instant alerts whenever a danger arises," Enchev said.

7 candidates nominated to lead World Health Organization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:29:36 UTC
23:29:36 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Seven candidates have been nominated by member states to become the next director-general of the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN health agency announced Thursday.
The nominees include Qatar's Hanan Mohammed Al-Kuwari, a former health minister and current adviser to the prime minister on public health; Saudi Arabia's Hanan Balkhy, WHO regional director for the Eastern Mediterranean; and Belgium's Hans Henri P. Kluge, WHO regional director for Europe.
Also nominated are Spain's Maria P. Neira, a former director of WHO's environment and health department; Indonesian Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin; and China's Li Song, secretary of the All-China Women's Federation and former senior health official.
The seventh candidate is Armenian pediatric oncologist Gevorg Tamamyan, a professor and department chair at Yerevan State Medical University, who was nominated by Botswana.
They will participate in a public forum at the organization's headquarters in Geneva on Nov. 18-19, allowing member states to engage directly with them.
The WHO Executive Board will narrow the field to five candidates in early 2027 before conducting interviews and nominating up to three for consideration by the World Health Assembly.
A second public forum will be held March 15, 2027, for those shortlisted.
The assembly is scheduled to appoint the next director-general in May, with the successful candidate taking office Aug. 16, 2027.

Nvidia CEO sees Kazakhstan as potential AI hub for Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:29:33 UTC
23:29:33 KST

During his first visit to Kazakhstan, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the country's growing computing capacity could make it a major AI hub for Europe, as Kazakhstan expands its energy and digital infrastructure.
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang has visited Kazakhstan for the first time, saying the Central Asian country could emerge as a major AI computing hub for Europe.
Huang made the remarks during a fireside chat with Zhaslan Madiyev, Kazakhstan's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, at the Alem.ai International Artificial Intelligence Centre in Astana.
During the discussion, Madiyev said Kazakhstan plans to nearly double its installed power capacity to more than 40 gigawatts by 2035 as the country expands the infrastructure needed to support its growing AI sector.
One of its flagship projects is the Data Center Valley, a large-scale AI computing campus under development in Ekibastuz, one of Kazakhstan's main power-generating centres. Its first 50-megawatt phase is expected to begin operations in 2027, while the project's energy infrastructure could eventually scale up to one gigawatt.
Huang said Kazakhstan's energy resources and growing computing capacity could give the country a significant role in Europe's AI ecosystem.
“Kazakhstan has a lot of real estate. It also has a lot of energy,” Huang said. “You're going to have a lot of compute right here in Kazakhstan. It's going to be a hub, a computing hub, an AI factory hub for all of Europe.”
Huang described the country's abundant energy resources as a potential competitive advantage in the AI economy, arguing that electricity could increasingly be used to generate computing power and AI rather than simply being exported as energy.
“Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so much natural resource already. You have so much energy, and instead of just exporting energy in the future, you could transform the energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” Huang said.
Sovereign AI
But energy alone, Huang argued, will not be enough. Kazakhstan will also need to retain control over another resource — its data.
Madiyev said the country is already developing Kazakh-language large language models based on open-source foundation models and asked whether Kazakhstan should eventually build its own foundation model from scratch.
Huang said building a domestic foundation model “makes complete sense”, describing it as a national security concern.
He argued that countries should retain control over both their data and the AI infrastructure used to serve their citizens, comparing it to other essential national infrastructure.
“In the future, you will have your own electric grid, your own internet, your own telecommunications and your own intelligence grid,” Huang said.
The potential of Physical AI
Beyond computing infrastructure and sovereign AI, Kazakhstan is also looking to position itself in the emerging field of Physical AI — systems that can interact with and operate in the physical world.
Pointing to Kazakhstan's industrial base in mining, agriculture, transport and logistics, Madiyev asked whether the country could become a hub for developing and training Physical AI models and robots. Huang called the idea “fantastic”, saying these industries could be among the first to benefit.
“Physical AI is not just robotics,” Huang said. “It includes everything from seismic understanding to mapping mines and wells, to understanding geography and geology — where to mine, how best to mine — understanding material science, the processing of chemicals.”
With the technology still at an early stage, Huang said Kazakhstan has an opportunity to help shape the emerging industry.
Investing in AI startups
The discussion also turned to Higgsfield AI, a Kazakh-founded generative video startup in which Nvidia has invested.
Asked what attracted Nvidia to the company, Huang said the decision ultimately came down to its founders.
“The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” Huang said, describing Higgsfield's founders as “visionary” and capable of competing with leading AI companies globally.
Huang also pointed to the company's presence in both Kazakhstan and the United States, saying it could help bridge the two ecosystems.
Later that day, Huang met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who described the development of artificial intelligence and digitalisation as a national priority.
“This visit is very important for us in terms of giving a serious boost to cooperation with Nvidia,” Tokayev said.
Huang welcomed Kazakhstan's ambition to become an “AI nation” and said the country had the potential to become a global hub for Physical AI.
Huang's first visit to Kazakhstan came at the close of AI Month, a nationwide initiative launched in September as part of the country's Year of Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence.

Russia-Africa Summit: Four days of dealmaking the West wanted Africa to skip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:28:55 UTC
23:28:55 KST

Russia-Africa Summit by the numbers: What was achieved despite Western pressure
Delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 leaders, gathered in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit under the motto “For Peace, Security and Development.” The gathering concluded on Thursday with a final declaration and a new cooperation plan. Organizers reported 146 documents signed across the Summit and its accompanying economic, humanitarian and media forums, comprising 92 agreements and 54 memorandums.
More than 3,500 participants from 74 countries attended, including over 1,200 business representatives from around 630 companies.The forum hosted more than 40 sessions.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has already held at least nine bilateral meetings with African leaders, including the presidents of Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Mozambique, Namibia, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Kenya, as well as Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Libya’s Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed Al-Menfi.
Bilateral talks continued on Friday, with the day’s lineup including the leaders of Sudan, Madagascar, Ghana, Mali, South Sudan, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, and Eritrea, as well as Togo’s prime minister.
The October 28-29 summit capped four days of events, beginning with Monday’s media forum and including Tuesday’s separate gas exporters’ summit. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told RT that Western governments had tried to discourage African leaders from attending.
An overnight Ukrainian drone attack also prompted temporary restrictions at three Moscow airports before Thursday’s proceedings. Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported 231 drones destroyed on the approaches to the capital. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov questioned the timing during an international gathering and praised air defenses.
Here are the main outcomes and key moments.
A framework through 2029
Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the African Union chair, co-chaired Wednesday's and Thursday’s proceedings. Leaders addressed a plenary session in Kremlin before continuing over a working breakfast.
They adopted the Moscow Declaration, a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum action plan for 2027-2029 and a declaration on civilian applications of artificial intelligence.
The political declaration backed greater African representation in international institutions, opposed unlawful unilateral sanctions, and supported efforts to address colonial-era damage. It also called for South Africa’s full G20 participation to be restored, following its exclusion from meetings under the US presidency. Pretoria remains a member.
At their closing press conference, Putin emphasized the potential for further cooperation, while Ndayishimiye pressed for measurable benefits. Another summit will follow, with its date and location to be agreed.
Partnership: ‘Africa has not come to ask for aid’
Russia and Africa are “natural allies in building a multipolar, genuinely democratic world order,” Putin told the plenary. He backed stronger African representation in global decision-making and described Russian businesses as partners investing in host countries rather than pursuing colonial exploitation.
African leaders also stressed that cooperation should strengthen their ability to make independent decisions and develop their economies.
“Contrary to what malevolent forces might think, Africa has not come to ask for aid,” Ndayishimiye told the Kremlin plenary. He called for commitments to become concrete investment programs and for international cooperation to follow African priorities.
Democratic Republic of Congo President Felix Tshisekedi made a similar distinction. “Diversifying our partnerships is not about choosing sides: it is about strengthening our freedom of decision-making in the service of our populations,” he said.
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa highlighted the need to turn agreements into action while processing more minerals domestically. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi presented his country’s cooperation with Russia, including the El Dabaa nuclear plant and planned Suez Canal industrial zone, as a model for wider partnerships.
Russia also signed several documents to deepen cooperation with African regional organizations. These included memorandums with the East African Community, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, and the African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat, alongside an action plan with the African Union Commission.
Sergey Lavrov met counterparts from 41 African states.
Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said Lavrov pledged support for Accra’s application for BRICS partner status and would seek consensus among founding members.
Peskov said Putin presented country-specific cooperation roadmaps during bilateral meetings. Putin also highlighted expanding diplomatic representation: eight Russian embassies have opened in Africa since 2023, bringing the total to 48. Six trade missions cover 16 countries, while Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo plan embassies in Moscow.
Financing and nuclear cooperation
Signings included a Wednesday memorandum between Russia’s development institution VEB.RF and BCID-AES, the joint investment bank serving Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, to identify and assess development and integration projects.
Rosatom also signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation memorandum with Togo, establishing working groups to examine potential projects and training. Floating nuclear power units are among the possibilities.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed sought priority for nuclear cooperation, including financing, engineering training and medical isotopes. A roadmap for Ethiopia’s first nuclear plant was signed in March, Rosatom chief Aleksey Likhachev said in an interview published Friday. Site-selection preparations are underway. Burundi expressed interest in small modular reactors. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi highlighted El Dabaa and the planned Russian industrial zone near the Suez Canal as examples of bilateral cooperation.
Trade and technology at Gostiny Dvor
Wednesday’s Economic and Humanitarian Forum at Gostiny Dvor in the Russian capital set much of the practical agenda. Putin proposed at least doubling Russia-Africa trade to more than $50 billion. On Thursday, he reported that the ruble accounted for up to 85% of commercial transactions between the two sides.
Putin and African leaders toured the “Platform for Sovereign Development” exhibition, showcasing energy, healthcare, agricultural, and digital technologies.
Elsewhere, Kenyan President William Ruto visited Sberbank’s smart city development and highlighted potential AI cooperation in healthcare and education.
Gas diplomacy alongside the summit
Tuesday’s eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit adopted its own Moscow Declaration, separate from the Russia-Africa documents. It reaffirmed sovereign rights over gas resources and supported supply security, investment, and a balanced transition toward lower-carbon energy.
At Monday’s ministerial meeting, Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilev promoted a proposed gas bank for long-term infrastructure financing, including in Africa. The initiative remained under discussion.
Media cooperation and liberation legacies
The Russia-Africa Media Forum ran from Monday to Thursday, organized by RT alongside Sputnik and TASS. Organizers welcomed more than 200 participants from 46 African countries for discussions on reporting, professional cooperation, and media sovereignty.
The forum also produced several media partnerships. These included Ethiopia’s Fana renewing its agreement with RT and Libya’s national news agency signing with RT Arabic. Rossiya Segodnya concluded partnerships with outlets in Algeria, Chad, Morocco, Ghana, and Zimbabwe, as well as Ethiopia’s Debre Markos University and Niger’s Higher School of Journalism and Communication.
RT’s Thursday session, “Forging Independence: Lessons from the Founders of African Nations,” featured descendants of African liberation leaders. Samia Nkrumah, daughter of Ghana’s first president Kwame Nkrumah, credited Russian support during Africa’s independence struggles, saying, “We are all here in Russia for a reason.” Ndileka Mandela, granddaughter of South Africa’s Nelson Mandela, recalled first meeting him through a prison window on Robben Island in 1981, aged 16: “I touched the window on one side and he touched on the other.”
Education and healthcare commitments
Putin extended Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for Africa through 2029.
Eight countries have received 15 mobile laboratories, and around 450 African specialists have been trained under the program, he said.
Among the healthcare agreements was a five-year memorandum with DR Congo covering training, research, maternal and child health, nuclear medicine, and digital healthcare.
Nearly 40,000 Africans study at Russian universities, up 50% since 2020, according to Putin. Government-funded scholarship places have nearly tripled over that period, reaching 5,500 for 2026-2027. Announced initiatives include ten centers helping African applicants enter Russian universities and vocational training programs.
Andrey Maslov, director of HSE University’s Center for African Studies, told RT that extended visits by African leaders and their separate business programs showed political ties with Moscow are gaining practical substance.

Russia: Closure of Novaya Gazeta is a devastating loss for embattled media freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:27:13 UTC
23:27:13 KST

Responding to the announcement that Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s last independent newspapers, will cease operations on 9 November, Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Deputy Director, said:
“The closure of Novaya Gazeta is a devastating loss for everyone in Russia who turns to independent, investigative journalism to uncover the truth. This long-respected newspaper has withstood years of mounting state pressure, including criminal prosecutions, raids and attacks on staff members. Its journalists have been killed for doing their jobs. Its website has been blocked, its official registration cancelled and just last month, it was designated a “foreign agent.”
“The final blow has come with an eviction notice demanding that the newsroom vacate its premises, in addition to being cut off from online donations. While these measures were carried out by private actors, the authorities’ role is not in question. Their decades-long predatory campaign has resulted in the near complete annihilation of free media in Russia, and now, of its most celebrated and distinguished champion.
“Russian authorities must immediately end their persecution of independent media, including Novaya Gazeta, and abolish laws stifling freedom of expression and imposing censorship. Journalists must be able to work without fear of harassment, prosecution or violence.”
[The authorities’] decades-long predatory campaign has resulted in the near complete annihilation of free media in Russia, and now, of its most celebrated and distinguished champion
Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Deputy Direct
Background
On 30 October, Novaya Gazeta announced it would cease operations on 9 November, closing its Moscow office where staff had worked for 29 years, after the landlords told the newsroom to vacate the premises. The editorial statement said the newspaper had been deprived of the means to operate, including access to its donation system, due to financial organizations’ unwillingness to provide services to it following the 4 September 2026 designation of the newspaper’s entire editorial team as “foreign agents.”
In the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the authorities blocked Novaya Gazeta’s online resources and stripped it of its media registration. On 9 April 2026, Investigative Committee officers searched its newsroom for 13 hours in connection with a criminal case involving alleged “unlawful access to computer information” and “illegal use of personal data.” Investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested in connection with the case and later placed under house arrest. On 15 October, officers searched the home of editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov.

Meta, TikTok, X lose legal challenge against British watchdog over online safety data demands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:25:00 UTC
23:25:00 KST

Meta, TikTok, X lose legal challenge against British watchdog over online safety data demands
- Meta, TikTok and X lost a High Court challenge against Ofcom over data requests under the Online Safety Act. The case tested Britain’s new online safety rules.
- Ofcom asked for content moderation data in February, including removals, visibility limits and user exposure to harmful content. The firms said the demands were too broad and costly.
- The ruling strengthens Ofcom’s powers and could affect future cases, including Meta’s separate challenge over fees, fines and WhatsApp’s role in the regime.
AI generated
LONDON – Meta, TikTok and X lost a legal challenge against British regulator Ofcom on Oct 30 over information requests made under the Online Safety Act, in one of the first tests of Britain’s nascent online safety regime.
The case is one of several brought over parts of the 2023 act, which sets tougher standards for platforms such as TikTok, X and Meta’s Facebook and Instagram with the aim of protecting particularly children from harmful and illegal content.
The Oct 30 decision by London’s High Court is a boost for Ofcom, though a potentially more significant ruling on Meta’s separate case about how Ofcom calculates fees and potential fines is awaited.
Meta, which is also challenging Ofcom over the categorisation of WhatsApp in the new regime, was made the subject of Ofcom’s first formal investigation under the Online Safety Act earlier in October.
X did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
TikTok said it is considering the judgment, while a spokesperson for Meta said in a statement: “We’re disappointed with the court’s decision, but we and others across industry pursued this challenge because information-gathering of this scale goes beyond what is necessary or proportionate.”
Ofcom requested metric from Meta, TikTok, X
Ofcom has been gradually implementing the Online Safety Act regime, with its requirements backed up by the threat of fines of up to 10% of a company’s global turnover for the most serious breaches.
The regulator issued information notices to Meta, TikTok and X in February, requesting detailed content moderation metrics including data on how many posts were removed or had visibility restricted, and how many users were exposed to harmful content.
Meta, TikTok and X argued the notices create unprecedented regulatory burdens, with X claiming that what it described as “the most burdensome information request X has received from any regulator” would cost it millions of pounds.
But their case was dismissed by the High Court, which in its ruling rejected their arguments that the information requests were disproportionate.
An Ofcom spokesperson welcomed the ruling, saying that “gathering information from companies is fundamental to our ability to do our job”. REUTERS

Cambodia announces return of 18 looted Khmer antiquities from Britain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:23:49 CST
23:23:49 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia announced on Friday the return of 18 Khmer cultural objects recovered in London, following a successful repatriation effort spearheaded by the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts (MCFA).
The antiquities were recovered by the Art and Antiques Unit of London's Metropolitan Police Service, with support from the Heritage Crime Task Force led by the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said an MCFA's press release.
The collection was formally handed over to the Cambodian Embassy in London on Friday.
Dating from the 10th to the 13th centuries, the returned collection comprises stone sculptures, bronze ritual objects, and jewelry fragments. Notable pieces include stone heads sculpted in the 11th-century Baphuon style and the late 12th-century Bayon style.
The treasure trove also features a Buddhist bell with a handle bronze, dancing figures on a pedestal, decorative plaques with pendants, and a ceremonial bronze lamp.
"Together, these objects reflect the artistic achievements, religious traditions, and cultural life of Khmer civilization across several centuries," the press release said.
Authorities originally recovered the artifacts in November 2025, it said, adding that following authentication by experts who confirmed their Cambodian origin, the ministry submitted a formal claim for their return in September 2026.
For decades, countless cultural properties were plundered from Cambodia due to war, theft, and the illicit international antiquities trade.
"The return of these 18 cultural objects represents another important achievement in Cambodia's ongoing efforts to recover its displaced heritage," the press release said. "The kingdom remains committed to pursuing the return of cultural objects unlawfully removed from its territory." ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:23:48 CST

SYDNEY, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese market for Australia's tourism is showing strong growth, and the outlook for people-to-people exchanges between the two countries is highly optimistic, said the head of Australia's national tourism marketing agency.
"In terms of the connection between the countries and the importance of China, it continues to be one of our leading markets. We project it to be one of our leading markets in years ahead," Robin Mack, managing director of Tourism Australia (TA), told Xinhua at a briefing in Sydney on Friday.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, China was Australia's second-largest source of short-term visitor arrivals in the 2025-26 financial year, with 1,127,110 trips recorded, up 18.2 percent year-on-year.
China is leading the way with double-digit growth, and "that's something we've seen and continues for the last several months," said Mack, adding that the Chinese market is among "the ones that we focus our activity on."
According to the International Visitor Survey Results released by Tourism Research Australia, China continued to be the largest contributor to spend in Australia, making up 29 percent of the total spend in Australia in the year ending June 2026. During that period, holiday spend by Chinese visitors reached 369 million Australian dollars (about 259 million U.S. dollars), while visiting friends and relatives (VFR) spend stood at 121 million AUD.
Citing an L.E.K. Consulting forecast, Mack said Greater China is expected to deliver the largest potential incremental expenditure for Australia's tourism industry by 2028.
"I go to China at least twice a year with this role," the head of TA told Xinhua, "and I was there last July with the Prime Minister who was there. It was really an opportunity to put a spotlight on tourism because I think it's at the heart of people-to-people connections. Australians love going to China and the Chinese are coming to Australia. We just want that to grow both ways."
Mack also noted that more Chinese visitors are taking part in First Nations cultural experiences while in Australia, making China the third-largest market behind the United Kingdom and the United States.
Mack said TA has invested heavily in Chinese social media platforms such as Rednote, doing a lot of nuanced work and creating a series of spotlight activities to stay close to Chinese consumers.
"We've got the focus on 'the breadth drives choice'," Mack explained. "We want people in China and in all our markets to think, 'I know Australia for wildlife, I know it for welcoming people, safety and security.' But we want them to know Australia for food and drink and different elements that they might not think of immediately until they come. So we do a lot of activity, and we keep looking in and trying to tap into the trends of where the customers are." ■

====================================================================================================

Over 300,000 votes ‘wasted’ in Israel's election: Who lost out and who escaped the damage?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:23:45 UTC
23:23:45 KST

For weeks, much was made of the opposition bloc's successful efforts to consolidate its forces, while predictions suggested that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing and religious allies could lose several Knesset seats because of votes cast for small parties that would fail to cross the electoral threshold. The final results, however, tell a different story: The right-wing parties that failed to enter parliament received fewer votes combined than a single centrist party that might have joined Netanyahu's opponents.
A total of 306,172 votes were cast for parties that failed to cross Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold, leaving them without representation in the 120-seat Knesset. Another 25,983 ballots were declared invalid, including a handful cast for Benny Gantz's Blue and White party and the Achi movement associated with Rabbi Abergil, both of which withdrew from the race during the final week.
Although the number of votes that failed to translate into parliamentary seats was substantial, it was considerably lower than in the 2022 election. That year, Meretz and Balad failed to cross the threshold, leaving more than 417,000 votes effectively wasted and helping Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc secure 64 seats.
Of all the parties that failed to enter parliament this time, the joint Reservists-Economic Party, led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, came closest to the 3.25% threshold. It received 154,950 votes, or 2.72% of the total, falling approximately 30,000 votes short of securing representation.
The party performed better among special double-envelope ballots, which include votes cast by IDF soldiers, winning 3.87% of those votes. But even that stronger showing was not enough to push it over the threshold.
Among individual cities, Be'er Ya'akov emerged as Hendel and Zelekha's strongest base, with 5.5% of the vote. The party received 4.8% in Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut, 4.6% in both Kfar Yona and Rishon LeZion, and 4.4% in Hadera.
The second party whose hopes of entering the Knesset were dashed was Amcha Yisrael, led by former IDF general Ofer Winter. Like Hendel's party, it received more than 4% of the vote in Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut, where it won 4.1%.
Winter performed particularly well in Givat Shmuel, a stronghold of liberal religious Zionism, where 7.4% of voters backed his party. Apart from those two cities, the only other municipality where Amcha Yisrael exceeded the national electoral threshold was Yeruham, with 3.9%. The party also received 2.5% in both Petah Tikva and Yokneam Illit.
Following an aggressive campaign by Netanyahu against Winter, Amcha Yisrael finished with just 95,663 votes, representing 1.68% of the total, roughly half the support needed to enter the Knesset.
Two smaller ultra-Orthodox parties representing opposing positions on military conscription finished much further below the electoral threshold.
The Haredi Public, led by Moti Leitner, campaigned on addressing military enlistment issues and strengthening Israel's state-run ultra-Orthodox education system. At the opposite end of the spectrum was Black Color, a party strongly opposed to drafting Haredi men into the military and supportive of confrontational protests, including road blockades.
Neither managed to attract significant electoral support. Each received slightly more than 10,000 votes, representing approximately 0.2% of the total.
The far-right, anti-LGBTQ Noam party, led by Avi Maoz, who served as a deputy minister in the outgoing government, performed even worse, receiving just 9,923 votes.
Together, Amcha Yisrael, Black Color, The Haredi Public and Noam received approximately 125,000 votes, considerably fewer than the 154,950 won by Hendel and Zelekha's party, which also drew support from voters associated with the opposition's so-called change bloc.
At the bottom of the electoral results were several smaller parties whose performances were even more striking. Among them was Israel First, led by outgoing deputy minister Sharren Haskel, which received just 955 votes nationwide.
Several fringe parties managed to outperform her, including Sharshar for Love and Unity of the People, led by Eitan Shvili, who styles himself as a king and arrived at the Central Elections Committee wearing a crown when registering his party.
Shvili, known as "Sharshar," attracted 2,084 votes under the Hebrew ballot designation "Tzedek," meaning "justice," more than twice Haskel's total.
Even Israel's Pirate Party, which included prominent behavioral economist Prof. Dan Ariely in third place on its candidate list, finished ahead of the former deputy minister. The party, officially registered as The Pirates, Floating for Good, received 1,051 votes under the Hebrew ballot letters "Tzaf."
The final tally left Haskel behind both the self-proclaimed king and the pirates, underscoring how even candidates with experience in government struggled to attract support in an election dominated by the larger political parties.

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Closer cooperation between Russia and African countries could bring economic opportunities to Uganda and the whole continent, Ugandan educator and founder of the Chunga-Changa interactive Russian-language school Daniel Omara told TASS.
"Russian people and Africans have been tied in this sort of collaboration before. The Russian people, together with other peoples of the Soviet Union, helped Africans fight for and gain their independence," said Omara, who won the Grand Prize in the Art of Teaching category of the International Eurasia Award.
He said that Africa had continued to face economic dependence even after gaining independence, with some Western and European partners maintaining relationships that, in his view, benefited them at the expense of African countries.
"Unfortunately, after getting independence, we almost found ourselves in a new season called neocolonialism. These colonial powers did not actually let go of African peoples. They kept taking advantage of them, with deals that are almost parasitic in nature," he said.
Omara believes closer ties with Russia could help African countries build partnerships on different terms, with greater respect for their independence and sovereignty.
Speaking about the outcome of the Russia-Africa summit, which ended on Thursday, he said: "This forum is bringing us back to a new reality, where we respect ourselves, respect each country's sovereignty and are able to meet on equal terms. We are not taking advantage of anyone."
He also welcomed the growing trade between Russia and African countries and the expansion of Russian businesses on the continent.
Omara singled out plans for local manufacturing and pharmaceutical production, saying that producing vaccines and medicines in Africa could open up new possibilities for the continent.
"These kinds of economic collaborations that we are seeing announced at this forum this year are just the beginning of the future that Africa is contributing to create together with Russia and countries of BRICS," he said.
The third Russia-Africa Summit was held in Moscow on October 28-29, bringing together delegations from 48 African countries, including 22 represented by heads of state. Participants discussed expanding cooperation in trade, investment, education, healthcare, technology and other areas.

Norway awards 425 mln USD for floating offshore wind projects
China

22:22:57 CST
23:22:57 KST

OSLO, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Norway's state-owned enterprise Enova said Friday it has awarded 3.94 billion Norwegian kroner (about 425 million U.S. dollars) to two floating offshore wind demonstration projects aimed at reducing the technology's costs.
Fortius Offshore Wind will receive 2 billion Norwegian kroner (about 216 million U.S. dollars), while Fram Wind Solutions will receive 1.94 billion Norwegian kroner (about 209 million dollars). Disbursement is conditional on the projects being implemented, Enova said.
Each company plans to install two 18.5-megawatt floating wind turbines over the next five years at METCentre's demonstration site off Karmoy in southwestern Norway.
The four turbines are expected to generate a combined 300 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, equivalent to the annual consumption of around 15,000 households.
The projects will test floating foundations, mooring systems, and construction and operating methods. Enova has identified these as key areas for cutting costs and improving the commercial viability of floating offshore wind.
Enova Chief Executive Evy Glorstad said making the technology commercially viable could accelerate large-scale renewable energy development, help Norwegian industry, and reduce transport emissions.
The projects were selected through a competitive process assessing electricity output relative to funding, potential for wider technological adoption, environmental impacts and prospects for future cost reductions, Enova said. ■

Dockworkers strike in Europe and beyond against arms shipments, war deaths
ATHENS, Oct 30 - Dockworkers went on strike across Europe and beyond on Friday, disrupting shipping and ferries as they protested against the use of their ports for arms shipments and the number of seafarers killed in wars from the Gulf to the Black Sea.
Strikers across 113 ports in 22 countries also called for pay rises, better working conditions and the right to have doctors on board vessels crossing war zones.
"We will not work for their wars, and we will not become food for their cannons," Apostolos Kypraios, head of the Greek union of merchant marine engineers, told Reuters during a rally at the Greek port of Piraeus.
'SEAFARERS HAVE SUFFERED MANY CASUALTIES'
"We have felt it first hand, and our families have felt it too, living with the anxiety of whether a colleague will get back home," he added.
More than 25 unions have now backed the strike originally called in Italy, France, Greece, Spain's Basque Country, Turkey and Morocco.
On Friday, it covered major shipping hubs in Piraeus, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras and Genoa, as well as Morocco's Tangier Med and India's Nhava Sheva.
"Seafarers have suffered many casualties — numbering in the hundreds — including both the dead and the severely injured," the Greek seafarers' union PENEN said in a statement.
It said there had been 28 attacks on vessels in the Gulf in the first 21 days of October, a record since the start of the Iran war.
It said there had been 570 attacks confirmed in the Black Sea so far this year, leaving 40 seafarers dead and hundreds wounded.
A series of strikes in the western Black Sea has raised concerns about the widening scope of Russia's war in Ukraine.
Cargo operations were disrupted in Piraeus and ferry services to Greek islands were suspended, as about 3,000 dockworkers and seafarers joined the walkout.
Representatives of India's WTWFI union said about 15 Indian seafarers had died as a result of the Iran war, with many more stranded at sea as waterways were blocked.
A group of dockworkers and other activists, called 'No Harbour for Genocide' and campaigning to stop military cargo from reaching Israeli ports, said on Friday the protest would halt some 52,000 containers and snarl cargo worth $2.8 billion.
Reuters was not able to independently verify the impact.
In May 2026, dockworkers' unions from over 35 European countries published the so-called Istanbul Declaration demanding that port facilities not be used to transport weapons destined for war zones.
Dockworkers said they were also worried about the rising cost of essential goods and energy, stemming from the ongoing conflicts.
"We can't even afford to fill the car with fuel to get to the supermarket," George Gogos, head of the Piraeus port dockworkers' union, said. REUTERS

Israel’s next government must end Gaza’s catastrophe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:20:28 UTC
23:20:28 KST

Israel’s Arab voters have made themselves impossible to ignore. The question now is whether the country’s political leaders will accept their elected representatives as partners in shaping its future. The answer will shape both the next government and the prospects for peace.
By the morning of 29 October, reporting on the unfinished count converged on 53 seats for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp, 48 for the opposition grouping led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot and 19 for Arab-led parties. These are provisional figures, not a final allocation or a coalition agreement. Netanyahu remains in office, and neither principal camp has secured an absolute parliamentary majority.
Before the election, I wrote: “Netanyahu does not necessarily need his opponents to lose. He needs them to remain unable to govern together.” Former Israeli Foreign Minister Shlomo Ben-Ami had highlighted that dilemma at The Economist’s summit in Thessaloniki, where I was also a speaker. The emerging result strengthens the warning. It does not establish who will govern.
The arithmetic has changed since the early count. A 53-seat Netanyahu bloc would need eight additional supporters to reach 61, rather than the four implied by the earlier 57-seat projection. Eisenkot’s 48 and the Arab parties’ 19 would total 67. But adding seats cannot settle disagreements about policy, identity or participation. Representatives cannot be assigned to a coalition without their consent.
Democrats leader Yair Golan has urged cooperation with Arab parties. The Associated Press has reported conditional openness from Eisenkot’s camp, while other prospective partners remain resistant. Conditions concerning Israel’s identity, Hamas and military service obligations present substantial obstacles. The distinction matters: there is neither an agreed partnership nor a basis for assuming that negotiations are impossible.
The United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas, has sought a place in government. Joint List leaders have indicated willingness to help replace Netanyahu, including through support for a minority government, subject to their demands. These approaches should be negotiated seriously. Public safety, housing and fair public investment require enforceable commitments. Arab representatives must retain the freedom to disagree, including over the treatment of Palestinians beyond Israel’s borders.
Netanyahu’s route also remains uncertain. Leading the largest bloc does not automatically confer the first mandate to form a government. President Isaac Herzog must consult the parliamentary groups. The first nominee then has 28 days from assignment, with an extension of up to 14 days at the president’s discretion. The clock does not start on election night.
Sixty-one seats provide an absolute majority, but they are not an invariable requirement for winning an initial confidence vote: abstentions can allow a government to take office with fewer votes in favour. Outside support may therefore matter. The harder task is sustaining the cooperation needed to govern.
Coalition arithmetic must not obscure the Palestinian suffering inflicted by the genocide in Gaza prosecuted under Netanyahu’s leadership. UNICEF reported at least 21,700 children killed in Gaza between October 2023 and June 2026. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, citing Gaza Health Ministry data, reported that 11,301 women’s deaths had been recorded in hospitals by 7 October, 2026. These are human lives, not a footnote to an election. Innocent civilians cannot be made to pay for the crimes of Hamas, and no claim of security can excuse the abandonment of children’s protection.
The devastation extends to those who survive. In October, the UN’s International Organization for Migration reported 1.8 million people living in displacement sites and nearly two million in need of shelter assistance. UNICEF said 800,000 children remained displaced, most living in tents or dangerous bombed-out buildings. For families with no safe home to return to, this is a daily struggle for survival. Netanyahu and his government bear political responsibility for the conduct of the genocide and the restrictions that compound this suffering. Accountability, unrestricted humanitarian relief and safe homes must be central to any claim of a new beginning.
The first mission of any new government must be to end the catastrophe in Gaza: stop the killing of civilians, ensure unrestricted humanitarian access and enable safe shelter and reconstruction. Replacing Netanyahu alone would not deliver that change. Eisenkot’s stated opposition to Palestinian statehood is a substantial obstacle. Any incoming government should be judged by its protection of civilians, humanitarian access, response to settler violence and willingness to make Palestinian sovereignty achievable.
Netanyahu still faces pending corruption cases involving charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, all of which he denies. Coalition bargaining must not shield any leader from judicial scrutiny. Accountability for the failures surrounding 7 October and judicial independence must survive these negotiations.
Equal citizenship inside Israel and Palestinian self-determination are distinct obligations. Arab participation in an Israeli government cannot substitute for an independent, sovereign and viable Palestinian state. A two-state solution based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as Palestine’s capital, must be the explicit objective. Palestinians need a territorially contiguous state alongside Israel, with security and dignity for both peoples.
This cannot remain a promise deferred indefinitely: diplomacy must establish a credible timetable and resist the settlement expansion and annexation that undermine its fulfilment. Nor should Palestinian citizens of Israel have to abandon concern for Gaza and the West Bank to be accepted as political partners. Criticism of Israeli government policy must remain directed at those responsible, without collective blame against Jews or Israelis.
In my earlier articles, I argued that lasting security requires peace and that Europe’s peace project needs deeper cooperation with Türkiye. Those principles now demand practical diplomacy. Ankara, European capitals, Washington and Arab partners should connect Palestinian-led reconstruction with concrete steps towards a two-state solution and effective security guarantees for both states. They should support accountable Palestinian institutions and make clear what verified progress would unlock.
As a former EU minister and chief negotiator, I know that agreement requires sustained work across genuine differences. Governments must protect their citizens while recognising that their neighbours also need a future free from fear. Israeli security and Palestinian freedom must advance together. A Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders is essential to a durable regional peace.
The next government will be assembled through negotiations. Its legitimacy will also be tested by whose voices it recognises and what future it offers. Israel’s Arab voters have opened a possibility. Political leaders must now turn that possibility into meaningful inclusion and a credible path to peace.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Swiss climate adaptation plan criticised after record summer heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:19:46 UTC
23:19:46 KST

Swiss climate adaptation plan criticised after record summer heat
Following Switzerland’s hottest summer on record, the government has unveiled a new strategy to help the country cope with rising heat and drought in future. Environmental groups, city authorities and politicians say the plan falls short.
Summer 2026 will be remembered for successive heatwaves, record temperatures, melting glaciers, tropical nights, exceptionally low water levels and prolonged drought. The impacts were felt across agriculture, forestry, the economy and public health – around 600 people are thought to have died due to the heatwaves.
“It was extreme,” MeteoSwiss Director Stefan Uhlenbrook told a climate conference in Bern on Thursday. The summer offered a glimpse of a much warmer future, he warned. “We are probably moving towards a world that is 3°C warmer [above pre-industrial temperatures], and the climate scenarios will be even hotter.”
During the summer, Environment Minister Albert Rösti came under pressureExternal link over the government’s handling of the crisis.
On Wednesday, the government presented its updated climate adaptation strategyExternal link, a 92-page plan for the 2026-2031 period. It sets out 56 measures across 30 areas of action aimed at reducing climate risks and helping society, the economy and ecosystems adapt. It replaces a strategy adopted in 2012.
The plan focuses heavily on coordination and information-sharing. Measures include more precise early-warning systems, standardised heat maps for spatial planning, and support for cooling and greening projects in towns and cities.
The strategy is based on the Federal Office for the Environment’s 2025 climate risk analysisExternal link and climate scenarios developed by MeteoSwiss and the federal technology institute ETH Zurich. Its main priorities are protecting people from heat and improving drought management.
In August, the government announced a CHF70 million ($84.5 million) emergency package to help forests and farmers cope with climate change. Rösti highlighted the fact that a further assessment would be carried out by the end of October, with additional measures introduced if required.
More
Switzerland feels cost of record summer heat
Monitoring heat risks
Under the new strategy, the Federal Office of Public Health will establish a centre of expertise on heat- and climate-related health risks. This centre will coordinate stakeholders, develop a health monitoring system and improve the recording of heat-related deaths and hospital admissions.
The government also plans to seek agreement with employers and unions on minimum health and safety requirements for construction workers during heatwaves after earlier talks failed to produce a deal.
Additional funding will support research on animal health and food safety. Switzerland’s drought platform, launched in 2025, will be expanded to better monitor the economic impacts of water shortages. In addition, MeteoSwiss will develop new national heat maps and extreme weather scenarios.
The number of adaption measures has been reduced from 75 to 56 through the consolidation of existing programmes. Among them is Adapt+,External link a federal funding scheme launched in 2025 to support projects to reduce climate risks and strengthen resilience. The government says it intends to expand the programme following this year’s extreme summer.
Critics say plan lacks ambition
Environmental groups welcomed the strategy in principle but argued that it relies too heavily on existing initiatives and does not match the scale of the threat.
“The Federal Council’s plan contains hardly any measures that were not already mentioned in earlier strategies and/or are not already being implemented at local and cantonal level,” Nathan Solothurnmann, a climate expert with Greenpeace Switzerland, told Swissinfo.
He said the government remained too cautious on emissions reductions and relied excessively on voluntary measures. Greenpeace also argues the strategy lacks a long-term vision for agriculture, warning that future climate conditions may require more fundamental changes to food production and livestock farming.
Solothurnmann also criticised the government’s assessment of risks to the energy sector.
More
Why Switzerland is still not ready to face heatwaves
Patrick Hofstetter of WWF said this summer’s extreme weather showed Switzerland’s capacity to respond was already being stretched and that much of the burden of adaptation fell on cantons, municipalities, businesses and households.
“The adaptation strategy does not adequately address the challenges,” he told Swissinfo. “Without tackling the root causes – namely, reducing CO₂ concentrations in the atmosphere through massive emissions cuts in Switzerland and globally – the limits of adaptation are clear.”
WWF says drought remains an underappreciated risk and is calling for greater investment in river restoration and stricter implementation of water protection laws. The organisation argues that nature-based solutions can both strengthen climate resilience and absorb carbon dioxide.
More
What Switzerland needs to learn from earlier and longer heatwaves
The Swiss Cities Association also welcomed the strategy but said municipalities, which are on the frontline of heatwaves, must play a bigger role in implementation.
“It is now essential that the Federal Council swiftly makes available the human and financial resources required to implement the planned measures, and that cities are involved from the outset,” spokesperson Benjamin Fröhlich told Swissinfo.
Politicians voice reservations
Christian Wasserfallen of the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party insists that key problems exposed during the summer remain unresolved, particularly in the construction sector. He told the Tages-Anzeiger that practical measures such as earlier working hours during heatwaves and greater flexibility when projects are delayed by extreme weather were needed.
Gabriela Suter of the centre-left Social Democratic Party welcomed measures on heat and drought monitoring but criticised the lack of binding requirements. “The level of protection afforded to older people and others particularly at risk from extreme heat must not depend on where they live. That is why we need binding heat action plans in all cantons,” she told the Tages-Anzeiger. “The next heatwave won’t wait for the federal government’s findings.”
In a statement, the Green Party accused the government of offering “little that is new”. It urged it to accelerate the phase-out of fossil fuels, arguing that delays make climate adaptation more difficult and more expensive.

Germany, France, Italy and Spain: Where was inflation highest in October?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:19:16 UTC
23:19:16 KST

Inflation rose in Italy and France, held in Spain and fell in Germany in October. What is driving the gap between Europe's largest economies and will the European Central Bank hike again in December?
The eurozone’s four largest economies published fresh inflation data on Friday, offering an early read on what is shaping up to be another hot month for price pressures across Europe.
The October's inflation ranking was clear.
Italy came out on top, with prices rising 5.4% from a year earlier. Spain followed at 4.9%, France at 3.4% and Germany at 2.8%.
The more telling story, however, is the direction.
Inflation accelerated sharply in Italy and France, held steady in Spain and fell in Germany, even though all four major economies are dealing with the same surge in energy costs.
So, why are the same pressures producing such different bills, and what does it mean for the European Central Bank?
Italy: Why did prices jump the most?
Italian inflation rose to 5.4% in October from 4.2% in September, according to preliminary figures from national statistics office Istat.
That brings it back to its August 2023 level, and well above the 4.6% economists had expected.
Under the harmonised measure used to compare countries across the EU, Italian inflation reached 5.6%.
Energy did most of the damage. Istat said energy prices were 31.4% higher than a year earlier, up from 22.6%, still shaped by the international geopolitical backdrop.
Regulated energy, the tariffs that are not set freely by the market, rose 59.5% year on year, more than double the previous month’s rate. Prices in this category climbed 18.8% in October alone.
The pressure is also reaching supermarket shelves.
The so-called "shopping trolley," a basket of food, household and personal care products Italians buy most often, rose 2.5%, up from 1.5%. Unprocessed food prices accelerated to 7.5%, and transport services to 3.1%.
Core inflation, which strips out energy and fresh food to show underlying price trends, rose to 2% from 1.6%.
For Italian households, the timing is difficult. Istat also reported on Friday that the economy did not grow in the third quarter.
Melanie Debono, senior Europe economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, wrote in a note that the breakdown due next month is likely to show the energy shock weighed more heavily on consumer spending than monthly retail figures had suggested.
Spain: Why did inflation stop rising?
Spain’s inflation rate held at 4.9% in October, the same as September, according to a flash estimate from the National Statistics Institute (INE). That keeps it near its highest level since early 2023.
Prices still rose 0.6% compared with September. Annual inflation stayed flat largely because fuel was cheaper than last October, when petrol and diesel prices were climbing. Higher gas tariffs offset part of that relief.
Underlying inflation, which excludes energy and unprocessed food, held at 3.1%. The harmonised rate eased slightly to 4.9% from 5%.
Spain is also the bloc’s strongest big economy at the moment.
Joe Nellis, head of economic research at advisory firm MHA, noted in emailed comments that Spanish output grew 0.6% in the third quarter, supported by stronger domestic demand.
France: Is stagflation setting in?
In France, inflation rose to 3.4% from 3.1%, its highest since January 2024, statistics office Insee said. Economists had expected 3.2%.
Energy prices rose 24.1% year on year, accelerating for a fourth consecutive month, driven by gas and oil products. Services inflation, the largest part of the French basket, picked up to 2.7% as hotel and transport prices rose.
On the harmonised measure, French inflation reached 3.8%.
The figures came alongside data showing the French economy shrank 0.1% in the third quarter.
“France faces stagflation,” Claus Vistesen, chief eurozone economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said in a report.
The term describes rising prices combined with a stagnant economy.
He expects French harmonised inflation to rise above 4% by November.
Germany: Why did inflation fall?
Germany was the exception.
Inflation dropped to 2.8% from 3.3%, below the 3% economists had forecast, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) said.
The main reason was a cut in fuel taxes that took effect on 1 October and runs until the end of the year. Energy inflation slowed to 12.2% from 14.9%. Consumer prices fell 0.2% from September.
Core inflation, excluding food and energy, eased to 2.1% from 2.4%.
Economists warn that relief may be short-lived. Vistesen wrote that energy inflation is likely to stay subdued through the end of the year, but snap back in January and February if fuel duties rise again.
“The current German core inflation numbers look dovish, but this weakness won’t last long,” he said.
What does this mean for the eurozone as a whole?
Eurostat will publish its flash estimate for the entire currency bloc next week, and Friday’s figures point to another uncomfortable reading.
Before the Italian data, BofA Global Research expected eurozone inflation of 3.7% in October.
After the Italian surprise, Pantheon raised its own forecast to 4%, up from 3.8% in September and twice the ECB’s 2% target.
Paolo Grignani, senior economist at Oxford Economics, said the day’s data paint “a mixed picture for the Eurozone with stagflationary tendencies.”
Energy is still doing the heavy lifting, he said, but there are “worrying signs of the energy shock spreading rapidly to stickier components.”
With eurozone growth holding at 0.4% in the third quarter, Oxford Economics expects the ECB to raise rates twice more.
Will the ECB raise rates again?
On Thursday, the ECB kept its deposit rate at 2.5%, after a hike in September. Christine Lagarde said policymakers had discussed another increase but agreed unanimously to wait.
The meeting was overshadowed by her announcement that she will step down in February, nine months before her term ends.
Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at financial services firm Ebury, said in emailed comments that a December hike remains “very much ‘live’”.
He added that a drawn-out search for Lagarde’s successor “could inject volatility into markets at an already fragile moment.”
Nellis said the ECB is in a tough position. Years of sluggish growth argue for keeping borrowing costs supportive, but with price pressures mounting, the central bank “may be forced to raise interest rates further at its December meeting.”
Friday’s numbers show both sides of that dilemma.
In Germany, a targeted tax cut was enough to bring inflation down. In Italy, the energy shock is already showing up in what families pay for food and travel.
Which of those two stories spreads across the rest of the eurozone may decide how far the ECB has to go.

Defanging Laws and Bringing Home Billions: How Trump Has Rewritten the Corruption Rulebook At Home and Abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:19:00 UTC
23:19:00 KST

“When the President of the United States is accepting a gold bar as a gift, it is reasonable to ask whether similar gifts given to other foreign heads of state will be seen as grounds for investigations, much less prosecutions,” Nephew wrote in the law and policy journal Just Security. 
What about U.S. anti-corruption efforts abroad? 
Dating back to the 1960s, successive U.S. administrations have pioneered transparency, good governance, and programs to combat corruption around the world, even if their implementation was uneven and imperfect. But the Trump administration has actively retreated from efforts to curb graft abroad in ways both big and small. 
For instance, it quickly dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), one of the main instruments for funding anti-corruption efforts overseas, and froze the disbursement of foreign funding. 
(OCCRP formerly received grants from USAID, and became a plaintiff in a lawsuit against the Trump administration for illegally terminating funding that had been allocated by Congress.)
The State Department’s Office of the Coordinator on Global Anti-Corruption — a post created in 2021 to integrate anti-corruption efforts with Washington's foreign policy goals — was also eliminated soon after Trump took office, as was the Task Force KleptoCapture, a unit created by the Justice Department in 2022 to go after sanctions evaders, especially Russian oligarchs. The Justice Department said the latter was part of a policy realignment to focus on fighting cartels. 
The administration has also stepped away from smaller but symbolic efforts to stamp out corruption overseas, such as no longer including information about corruption in the State Department’s annual country reports on human rights. (The State Department did not respond to requests to comment). 
And then there’s the controversial use of the Magnitsky Act, which was passed in 2012 to allow the U.S. government to sanction foreigners who engage in corruption or human rights abuses.
The president shocked anti-corruption crusaders last year when he used the Magnitsky Act to sanction a Brazilian Supreme Court justice who oversaw the trial of  Brazil’s former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally later convicted of plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
(The conviction prevented Bolsonaro from running for office, leading his son Flavio to take up the family mantle and narrowly lose a presidential runoff election this past Sunday. Facing a money laundering investigation in Brazil, Flavio fled the country for the U.S.)
“Global Magnitsky was a huge win when it passed … and the human rights community and the anti-corruption community celebrated,” said Gary Kalman, director of Transparency International U.S. 
“Never in our wildest imagination would we have dreamed that a president of the United States would use the Global Magnitsky Act to go after a judge in another country for enforcing anti-corruption laws.”
What about Trump and his family? Have they engaged in corrupt behavior?
U.S. presidents have historically stepped away from their personal business interests to avoid conflicts of interest, or even the perception of a conflict. 
Yet Trump’s latest annual financial disclosure — which runs 927 pages long and covers his first year back in office — shows a significant increase in his income while president. Last month, Forbes estimated he was $2.7 billion richer than when he won the 2024 election.
The source of this wealth comes from cryptocurrency enterprises, Trump-owned resorts and real estate, his social media platform Truth Social, and a range of other business ventures, many of which are rife with potential conflicts of interest.
“I don't think that there's any president who has so brazenly used their office to create a web of foreign entanglements that enriches himself, his family, and some of his closest advisors and their families,” said Matthew Dallek, a historian specializing on presidential politics at George Washington University.
The examples to choose from are numerous. For instance, the collective Trump fortunes soared earlier this year when an investment firm reportedly connected to the United Arab Emirates’ ruling family bought nearly half of a Trump family-connected cryptocurrency company. 
A company backed by Trump’s sons has also sought to sell drone interceptors to Gulf countries while they were under attack by Iran following a war started by their father. 
Trump and other officials’ frequent visits to the president’s properties, meanwhile, generate advertising and revenue for those businesses — and open up avenues through which others can use their wallets to try to curry favor with the president.  
Taken together, experts have described it as an unprecedented level of political profiteering that raises the risk of the president putting his business interests ahead of those of the country. 
It’s also a problem that won’t be easy to fix. 
Trump’s second term has exposed just how much the U.S. presidential system depends on “an adherence to norms and a set of expectations and values…rather than strict rules and laws preventing a president from corrupt actions,” Dallek said. 
In previous comments to the press, a White House spokesperson has stated that “neither the president nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest.” When asked about his lucrative year following the release of his financial disclosures this June, Trump attributed the profits to the stock market “going up” and said he never spoke to the people who manage his money.
“We are experiencing what happens when you have an individual who dismisses ethical norms,” said Kalman of Transparency International. “People are now trying to figure out how you close these kinds of gaps in our ethics rules at the highest levels of our government.”
One avenue, he said, is to secure the roles of state actors that could provide a counterweight to the Justice Department, whose independence has been called into question as it has pursued investigations against the president’s opponents and dropped cases involving allies. 
“I think there's a lot of district attorneys and law enforcement officials that are concerned about what they're seeing as the weaponization of the Justice Department,” said Kalman. “If the U.S. Justice Department gets taken over by the executive, you have what we have now, which is a lack of accountability or unwillingness to enforce any of the violations that we've seen happen.”
The Justice Department did not respond to requests to comment.  
Democrats are trying to take back Congress. What is their plan if they succeed? 
Polls show voters cite corruption as a major concern, and Democrats have pledged to investigate corruption if they regain control of one or both chambers of Congress.
Should they win back at least the House of Representatives, they would be in a position to legislate and hold oversight hearings. They’ve already signaled plans to spotlight the business entanglements of the Trump family and friends, and say they won’t be shy about using their power to subpoena witnesses.
“We can bring in members of the Cabinet and ask them questions and perhaps see if there's any way we can get rid of some of them,” Rep. Dina Titus, a Nevada Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told OCCRP. Her panel will “look at some of this corruption that's going on around the rest of the world involving the administration and some of their buddies and relatives,” she added. 
Much of what Democrats will be able to do hinges on the size of their victory, and some of their plans have yet to be spelled out in detail. 
“Democrats are running on corruption, but they're not running on a specific platform of how they're going to reform or fix the system or address many of Trump's egregious acts,” said Dallek, the historian. 
In a recent interview with the TV outlet MS Now, New York Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, the current House minority leader, outlined plans for the first 100 days of the next Congress that included empowering two committees to look into corruption.  
He has said the Judiciary Committee and the House Oversight Committee would be tasked with accountability and looking into the Trump family business entanglements.
“We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and then let the chips fall where they may,” he said. 
Congressional Republicans, for their part, have prominently used their oversight powers to investigate people named in or associated with the Epstein files, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The committee has also investigated tax breaks given to politically opposed non-profit organizations, while their anti-corruption agenda has largely been focused on reversing the “Censorship Industrial Complex,” a term used to describe those they say are suppressing right-wing viewpoints online under the pretense of limiting disinformation. 
Hanichak, from the FACT Coalition, called on the next Congress — regardless of who holds the reins after Tuesday — to “strengthen guardrails to prevent public officials from profiting from power.”
“We are what we tolerate: in most cases, the recent reticence of both Republicans and Democrats to denounce corruption by colleagues in their own parties has bred public distrust about the sincerity of reform,” she said. 
“We need more transparency and accountability — in elections, in our financial system, in government contracts and services — to restore faith that democracy can deliver for ordinary people.”

Binance has suspended all transactions as it investigates a cyberattack, the crypto exchange stated on X, promising to cover all users’ losses. “It does look like a hack on Binance,” company founder and co-owner Changpeng Zhao wrote on X while assuring users that their funds are safe.
According to the latest data reported by Binance, the total damage amounts to approximately $6.3 billion. If the figure is confirmed, it will be the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The previous record for cryptocurrency theft was set in 2025, when hackers stole $1.5 billion from the crypto exchange Bybit. The FBI concluded that the North Korean group TraderTraitor was also behind that crime.

Dockworkers in 22 countries strike over arms shipments, Gaza war
