Paid to hire, paid to work: Inside India’s Rs 99,446 cr plan to reshape the formal workforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:44:26 UTC
21:44:26 KST

The government aims to create more than 3.5 crore jobs over two years, including 1.92 crore first-time employees.
The Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (PMVBRY) is a central government scheme designed to encourage formal employment by offering financial incentives to both employers and employees. It provides money to first-time workers entering jobs covered by the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), while also rewarding companies that expand their workforce and retain new hires.Approved by the Union Cabinet on July 1, 2025, the scheme has a total outlay of Rs 99,446 crore.PMVBRY has two components. Under Part A, eligible first-time employees receive a one-time incentive equivalent to one month’s EPF wage, capped at Rs 15,000.Part B provides incentives to employers who create additional jobs. Eligible employers can receive up to Rs 3,000 per month for each qualifying additional employee. The scheme covers eligible jobs created between August 1, 2025 and July 31, 2027. Manufacturing establishments receive support for four years, compared with two years for employers in other sectors.The government aims to incentivise more than 3.5 crore jobs over two years, including 1.92 crore first-time employees.
These are government targets, not independent estimates of jobs expected to be created.The scheme addresses a structural weakness in India's employment landscape: the limited availability of regular, salaried work.According to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation's Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for 2025, 56.2 per cent of India's workers are self-employed and another 20.2 per cent are engaged in casual labour. Regular wage or salaried employment accounts for just 23.6 per cent of the workforce.The challenge, therefore, extends beyond reducing unemployment. It is also about expanding access to stable, formal jobs that offer workers social security and a more predictable source of income. PMVBRY is the government's attempt to encourage that transition.
Where are India’s jobs?
The PLFS Annual Report 2025 estimated that India had 61.6 crore employed people aged 15 and above.
Distribution of India's workforce
Agriculture remained the largest employer, accounting for 43 per cent of workers. Manufacturing accounted for 12.1 per cent, construction 12 per cent, trade, hotels and restaurants 12.9 per cent, transport, storage and communications 5.8 per cent, and other services 13.1 per cent. Mining and quarrying accounted for 0.3 per cent, while electricity, water and related services made up 0.7 per cent.Grouped broadly, the figures put around 43.3 per cent of workers in the primary sector, including agriculture and mining. Another 24.8 per cent are in the secondary sector, including manufacturing, utilities and construction, and 31.8 per cent in the tertiary sector, including trade, transport and other services. These are employment shares, not shares of GDP or GVA.Employment status adds another dimension. In 2025, 56.2 per cent of workers were self-employed, 23.6 per cent were in regular wage or salaried employment and 20.2 per cent were casual labourers. The unemployment rate for people aged 15 and above was 3.1 per cent under the survey’s usual-status measure, while it was 9.9 per cent among people aged 15 to 29.Year-on-year comparisons need caution. The ministry revised the PLFS sampling design in January 2025 and shifted the annual reference period from July–June to January–December. It advises care when comparing the new series with earlier reports. The reported fall in agriculture’s share from 44.8 per cent in 2024 to 43 per cent in 2025, and the rise in manufacturing from 11.6 per cent to 12.1 per cent, are not conclusive evidence of a structural shift.PMVBRY targets a narrower problem: formal payroll employment recorded through EPFO. It is not an employment guarantee and does not directly address self-employment, casual work or agricultural underemployment.
Why manufacturing is central
PMVBRY covers eligible establishments across sectors but gives manufacturing employers a longer incentive period. Its official guidelines say the scheme is intended to complement the National Manufacturing Mission by promoting new industries and expanding existing ones, particularly in labour-intensive manufacturing.Under the revised national-accounts series with 2022–23 as the base year, manufacturing accounted for 14.7 per cent of GVA in 2022–23 and 2023–24, and 14.8 per cent in provisional estimates for 2025–26, according to the ministry of statistics and programme implementation. The figures are not directly comparable with estimates under the previous base year.The employment picture is distinct. PLFS 2025 put manufacturing’s share of workers at 12.1 per cent. Separately, the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) results for 2023–24 reported that employment in covered manufacturing establishments rose 5.92 per cent over the previous year, reaching nearly 1.96 crore persons engaged. The ASI covers registered manufacturing establishments within its survey scope, not every manufacturing worker in India.A working paper by Sangeeta Ghosh at the Institute for Studies in Industrial Development, Looking Through Employment Elasticities, found employment elasticities above 0.5 in many of the 55 organised manufacturing industries it studied for the period from the mid-2000s. Employment elasticity measures the relationship between output growth and employment growth. However, the paper also found that more than 40 per cent of new employment generated between 2008 and 2017–18 was contract employment. It focuses on organised manufacturing, so its findings cannot automatically be applied to the whole sector.The four-year incentive window signals the government’s view that manufacturing, particularly labour-intensive segments, can generate sustained employment. The National Manufacturing Mission, announced in the 2025–26 Union Budget, is part of the wider push.
What employers receive, and what startups need to know
Under Part B, employers can receive up to Rs 3,000 a month for each additional employee whose gross wages at joining are up to Rs 1 lakh, subject to the scheme’s conditions. The incentive covers eligible first-time employees and re-joiners. The amount depends on EPF wages:
Your eligibility, as an employer, for the scheme.
For employees earning below Rs 10,000, it is 10 per cent of wages, up to Rs 1,000.
For those earning more than Rs 10,000 and up to Rs 20,000, it is Rs 2,000.
For those earning above Rs 20,000, it is Rs 3,000, subject to the gross-wage ceiling.
The incentive is paid in six-monthly lump sums after the relevant six months of employment and electronic challan-cum-return filings. The employee must stay with the same employer for at least six months, with contributions received for that period. Employers must also maintain a minimum net additional-employment threshold. Those with a baseline below 50 employees must add at least two, while those with a baseline of 50 or more must add at least five. Incentives do not accrue for months when the applicable threshold is not met.The baseline is central to eligibility. For existing EPFO-registered employers, it is based on average employment during the relevant period before the scheme. For new establishments registered with EPFO between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2027, the baseline is fixed at 20 employees. Only qualifying additional jobs above that baseline and beyond the applicable hiring threshold can count towards the incentive.Startups and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) do not receive a separate incentive rate or automatic exemption from these rules. They can benefit if they are eligible establishments, comply with EPFO filing requirements and create qualifying additional employment. A new establishment with a baseline of 20, for instance, cannot claim the employer incentive merely by hiring a few people while remaining below the baseline and threshold.Consider an eligible employee with EPF wages of Rs 18,000, for whom the monthly incentive would be Rs 2,000. If the employer meets the hiring test and remains eligible for all 24 months, the notional incentive for that employee would be Rs 48,000. For a manufacturing establishment, the incentive can continue for 48 months, making the corresponding maximum Rs 96,000. These are illustrative calculations, not guaranteed payouts.
What first-time employees receive
Part A supports first-time employees earning up to Rs 1 lakh a month with an incentive equivalent to one month’s EPF wage, capped at Rs 15,000. The first instalment, capped at Rs 7,500, is payable after six completed months. The second follows 12 months of service and completion of a financial-literacy programme. A portion of it is placed in a savings instrument or deposit account.
Benefits for first-time employees.
Can the incentives create additional jobs?
The central question surrounding PMVBRY is whether lowering the cost of hiring will persuade companies to create jobs they would not otherwise have offered.Employment subsidies carry an inherent risk: governments may end up paying companies for recruitment that would have happened anyway. There is also the possibility that employers could replace existing workers with eligible employees to qualify for incentives. These are recognised risks in evaluating employment subsidies, not evidence that such practices have occurred under PMVBRY.The government's initial implementation figures offer an indication of the scheme's reach. In a backgrounder published on August 1, 2026, the Press Information Bureau said more than 72 lakh first-time employees had joined the formal workforce since August 2025. Nearly 30 per cent of the beneficiaries were women, while more than 15 lakh beneficiaries had received employment-linked incentives.
These are government-reported figures.PMVBRY is an attempt to use public money to make formal hiring more attractive, with manufacturing receiving a longer period of support. But the scale of enrolment and the amount of incentives disbursed will not, by themselves, establish whether the policy has succeeded.The real test will be whether the scheme creates additional jobs, whether those jobs offer stable employment and whether employers retain workers after government support runs out. For India, the challenge is not simply to move more people onto formal payrolls, but to ensure that the jobs they enter are productive, secure and sustainable.
Pranjal Pandey is a journalist with the editorial desk of The Times of India (Online). He looks at the implications of global events for India, with a particular interest in geopolitics and defence. You can sometimes find him looking at the world map, wondering what’s new.

Russians teach children to operate drones and fire assault rifles in occupied Crimea – Ukrainian intelligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:44:00 EET
21:44:00 KST

Russians teach children to operate drones and fire assault rifles in occupied Crimea – Ukrainian intelligence
The Russians in occupied Crimea are training children and young people to fly drones, fire assault rifles and take them apart. Ukrainian intelligence says the training uses drones and other equipment belonging to the Russian military.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) on Telegram
Details: In late October, around 50 schoolchildren aged between seven and 18 in Sevastopol qualified for the regional stage of competitions organised by the Russian Movement of the First and the so-called Drone Racing Federation.
The Russians are also teaching university students in the city to operate drones. They use simulators, actual drones and equipment used by Russian forces in the war.
Quote: "The aggressor state of Russia is creating an environment in Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories where military technology and participation in war are becoming a normal part of childhood."
Details: In schools across occupied Crimea, the Russians hold classes where children learn to shoot, strip down Kalashnikov assault rifles and march in formation on command. They also organise "military and patriotic" games and challenges involving participants in Russia's war against Ukraine and force students to learn songs by Russian pro-war propagandist singers.
The occupation authorities are also recruiting people into Russian security agencies and encouraging them to sign contracts to serve in the Unmanned Systems Forces. Those who have fought against Ukraine are being appointed to senior positions in the occupation administrations, and schools are putting up memorial plaques commemorating Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine.
DIU says the Russians are using these measures to justify their aggression and teach children to accept war as a normal part of life.
Quote: "Its goal is not only to maintain control over Crimea, but also to raise a generation for whom Russia's war, military training from the school desk and hatred of Ukraine will become the norm."
Background:
- In March, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) reported on Russian efforts to teach schoolchildren to operate combat drones. According to Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, the classes are conducted by Russian military personnel who have fought against Ukraine, and training drone operators is part of a federal course called Fundamentals of Security and Defence of the Motherland.
- The classes have been introduced in Kursk, Nizhny Novgorod and Vologda oblasts, among others. In Vladivostok, there were plans to include the subject of drones in school mathematics and physics courses.
- Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia previously also reported on the militarisation of education in Ukraine's occupied territories, where the Russians are introducing school subjects that focus on "patriotic" education and loyalty to Russia.

Zelensky Ready to Discuss Territory With Putin, Sybiha Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:43:06 UTC
21:43:06 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is ready to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and discuss territorial issues as part of efforts to end the war, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Speaking to Finnish newspaper Helsingin Sanomat in an interview published after his two-day visit to Finland, Sybiha said Kyiv had coordinated the decision to hold a call between Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Nordic leaders conveyed two main messages, he said: Ukraine’s demand for a ceasefire and its proposal for a face-to-face meeting between Zelensky and Putin.
“We want this meeting, and we are ready for it,” Sybiha said. “Probably only a meeting between Zelensky and Putin can bring a new quality to the negotiations. Zelensky is ready to discuss the most difficult and sensitive issues, including the territorial question.”
Sybiha said direct talks could lead to confidence-building measures, including prisoner exchanges and the return of Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.
The venue was not important to Kyiv, provided it was neither Moscow nor Belarus, Sybiha said, joking that North Korea could also be ruled out. He dismissed Russia’s invitation for Zelensky to visit Moscow as “not serious.”
Kyiv sees Nordic call as diplomatic opening
“Our assessment is that the call was a step forward in our peace efforts,” Sybiha said, adding that he hoped the channel of communication with Putin would remain open.
Putin Warns Europe War Will Not Produce Winners
The roughly 90-minute conversation also confirmed that trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, the US and Russia were expected to continue in Abu Dhabi in November, he said.
“Those talks will show whether Russia has serious intentions to end the war through diplomatic means,” Sybiha said, adding that Kyiv currently saw no signs of such intentions.
Asked whether Putin had made any important statements during the conversation, he replied: “At least it [the call] happened.”
The call drew criticism from some European officials. Stubb and Støre said they had acted in their national capacities, rather than on behalf of Europe.
Sybiha said the initiative reflected a shared decision with Kyiv to use every available diplomatic channel. He also urged Europe to establish a stronger role in negotiations and speak with one voice.
Stubb’s close relations with both US President Donald Trump and Zelensky already gave him an important role, Sybiha said. The Finnish president had now also heard Putin’s position directly.
Asked whether Stubb could represent Europe in the peace process, Sybiha said EU leaders would have to decide, adding: “Why not?”
Europe should reinforce US peace efforts, Sybiha says
Sybiha said greater European involvement was particularly important because he believed the Trump administration had moved further toward accommodating Russia’s demands.
He cited what he described as US pressure for a change in Ukraine’s leadership, sanctions relief and renewed US purchases of Russian diesel.
Despite those concerns, Sybiha said Ukraine had no alternative to keeping Washington involved.
“It is not realistic to end the war without them, or to obtain real security guarantees for the future without them,” he said.
Europe’s role should complement, rather than replace, US-led diplomacy, he added.
Sybiha said intensified Russian attacks were another reason Kyiv had sought additional diplomatic channels through Finland and Norway. Russia had launched 100 ballistic missiles at Ukraine over two weeks, he said.
He said he was returning from Finland more hopeful, praising the country’s support for Ukraine.
“We have hope that things will move forward after that call,” he said.
Moscow continues to insist on talks in Russia
Trump said on Oct. 28 that he hoped to hold a summit with Putin and Zelensky “very soon.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not rule out a meeting but said the timing was flexible and that talks would require “extensive, meticulous preparation.”
Zelensky had proposed meeting Putin on the sidelines of the G20 summit in the US in December. Peskov called that option “impossible,” saying Zelensky could accept Putin’s invitation to Moscow if he “truly desires” direct talks.
In early June, Zelensky proposed a summit in a neutral country in a rare open letter to Putin. He said the meeting should be backed by broader European and US security guarantees. The Kremlin dismissed the proposal and reiterated its invitation to Moscow.
Putin first issued that invitation in September 2025 while questioning Zelensky’s legitimacy and the value of a meeting. Zelensky rejected it and proposed Kyiv instead.
Putin did not respond to that proposal and has continued to insist that Moscow is the “best place” for talks, claiming Zelensky’s safety would be guaranteed.

BERLIN, October 30. /TASS/. Germany is growing more and more tired of Vladimir Zelensky’s non-stop requests for weapons and financing, Berliner Zeitung columnist Nicolas Butylin said.
"Plus a noticeable general weariness with Ukraine. We have been seeing one and the same scene for four and a half years now: Vladimir Zelensky, dressed in olive or black, either in parliament, at a conference, or via video link - and almost always asking for more weapons and money," he wrote in his column.
Since the outbreak of the Ukrainian conflict, Germany’s population has been "bearing the burden" of rising prices for electricity, gas, and food, as well as encountering its highest inflation rate in decades, while Kiev is demanding $27 billion more from the European Union," he noted, adding that whereas in 2022 such requests looked like a "cry for help," now they are perceived as an "endless cycle."
According to Butylin, the Germans have changed their opinion about sending Ukrainian citizens back to their homeland. "If, back in the spring of 2022, the Christian Social Union leader or the foreign minister had demanded that refugees from Ukraine be sent back to the frontlines, they would have been subjected to fierce political shaming," he noted, adding that now even officials often suggest this be done.
Germany is Ukraine’s largest donor, Since February 24, 2022, Berlin has provided Kiev with around 43.3-billion-euro worth of humanitarian and 57.6-billion-euro worth of military aid. In addition to official channels, various private and public German organizations regularly send humanitarian aid to Ukraine. Meanwhile, the Russian side has repeatedly stated that arms deliveries to the Kiev regime only protract the conflict.

On receipt thereof, let the Election Commission examine the factual aspects, thereafter take necessary corrective steps and file a compliance report," the bench said, according to PTI.The Supreme Court was hearing petitions filed by Congress MP Tanuj Punia and others challenging the SIR exercise in Uttar Pradesh. Senior advocate DS Naidu, appearing for the EC, acknowledged that bulk Form 7 applications had been filed but said no action had been taken on them."We found that bulk Form 7 applications had been submitted. Our officers checked and cross-checked them. They were false, and we have not acted upon them," Naidu told the court.Following the submissions, the CJI-led bench directed the EC to examine the matter.

Finland's unemployment rate remains worst in EU
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:40:56 EET
21:40:56 KST

The unemployment situation in Finland remains statistically the worst in the European Union, according to data released on Friday by Eurostat, the EU's number-crunching office.
The latest figures reveal that Finland's unemployment rate has now climbed to 11 percent, a 1.3 percentage point increase on the same period last year.
While Finland has taken the unwanted top spot in the unemployment rankings for much of this year, there was brief respite in August when a reading of 9.9 percent placed Finland in second place behind Spain (10.2).
However, modest signs that the Finnish economy is recovering from a period of sluggish growth have yet to make an impact on the country's grim unemployment stats.
Petri Malinen, Chief Economist of the Finnish Federation of Entrepreneurs, told Yle earlier this month that ongoing geopolitical uncertainties are clouding Finnish firms' outlooks and leading them to postpone recruitment.
"As long as economic growth doesn't seem to materialise concretely, consumers will remain cautious and consumption will recover slowly. In this situation, growth in demand for companies is modest, and they have no need to recruit," Malinen said.
Finland moving in opposite direction to rest of EU
The latest Eurostat rankings place Spain back in second place again, with 10.3 percent, while Finland's Nordic neighbour Sweden is in third, where the unemployment rate in September stood at 8.6 percent.
The EU countries' average unemployment rate — that is, the share of people without work counted as part of the total labour force — has stayed close to six percent throughout this year, coming in at 6.2 percent in September.
The lowest rates of unemployment in the EU last month were registered in the Czech Republic (2.8 percent) and Poland (3.4 percent).

Italian cured meat producers showcase their products in Budapest
Ambassador Giuseppe Scognamiglio also attended the event organized by Assica and the Italian Trade Agency

30 October 2026, 13:42
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
A B2B event dedicated to Italian cured meats was held in Budapest, organized by the Italian Trade Agency at the Matild Palace – Cova. Eleven Italian producers, members of the Association of Meat and Cured Meats Manufacturers (Assica), presented the excellence, quality, and tradition of Italian cured meats to Hungarian importers and industry professionals. Assica is the national trade association that, as part of Confindustria, represents companies engaged in the production of cured meats (both pork and beef), pork slaughtering, and the processing of other meat-based products. Since 1946, Assica has supported the growth of these companies, helping one of the historic sectors of the Italian food industry both in Italy and around the world. The Budapest event also celebrated two important anniversaries: the 100th anniversary of the Italian Trade Agency and Assica’s 80th anniversary. The Italian Ambassador to Hungary, Giuseppe Scognamiglio, also attended the event.

Binance says $6.3bn stolen in biggest crypto heist in history: What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:38:47 UTC
21:38:47 KST

Binance says $6.3bn stolen in biggest crypto heist in history: What we know
The world’s largest crypto exchange halts withdrawals as the theft is linked to North Korean hackers.
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, says hackers have stolen about $6.3bn in what appears to have been the biggest crypto heist on record.
The company, which was co-founded by the Chinese-born Canadian billionaire Changpeng Zhao, suspended deposits and withdrawals on Thursday and said it would cover all losses, telling Al Jazeera in a statement that user funds were “safe”.
Two United States blockchain analysis firms have claimed the attack originated in North Korea.
So how did it happen, and what does it mean for the crypto market? Here’s what you need to know:
What happened?
Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis say most of the theft unfolded over about 20 minutes, starting late on Thursday.
“An attacker moved approximately 6.36 billion USD out of Binance wallets on 10 blockchains,” TRM reported.
That dwarfs the previous record of $1.5bn, which was stolen from the exchange Bybit in February 2025.
Binance said about $3bn of that has since been frozen, including more than $2.3bn by stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle, according to the Reuters news agency.
Binance has not stated what has happened to the remaining $3.3bn.
It also warned on X that the $6.3bn figure “may continue to increase” as the company works to trace and freeze more assets.
Who carried out the heist and how?
North Korean hackers, according to the firms tracking the funds.
TRM said it had assessed with “high confidence” that the attack was carried out by TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit linked to the Lazarus Group.
According to the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), the Lazarus Group “targets and compromises entities primarily in South Korea and South Korean interests for espionage, disruption, and destruction”.
It also conducts cyberoperations for financial gain, including targeting cryptocurrency exchanges, the CFR says.
The US Department of the Treasury sanctioned the Lazarus Group in 2019, saying it was controlled by North Korea’s primary intelligence bureau. North Korea routinely denies involvement in hacking.
Chainalysis reached the same conclusion, however.
The FBI also blamed the Bybit hack in 2025 on the same unit.
TRM said the attackers ordered Binance’s wallets to empty into wallets they controlled, mirroring the Bybit hack.
Binance has been more cautious, however. “Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual,” co-CEO Richard Teng said on X.
The company initially said the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers. But on Friday, it said further investigation had uncovered “additional points of breach”.
Binance said it had found no evidence that any wallet’s private key, the digital password that controls a crypto wallet, had been leaked.
But Mark Karpeles, former head of the collapsed Tokyo exchange Mt Gox, told Reuters the attackers had probably accessed keys for at least two Binance wallets.
What was the purpose of the attack?
Money.
While North Korea denies involvement in crypto theft, it has become a much-needed source of foreign currency for Pyongyang, helping to prop up its economy and fund its nuclear programme, which is under United Nations sanctions, experts say.
In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency estimated that North Korean hackers had stolen about 1.5 trillion won ($1.1bn) in crypto and other virtual assets over five years.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity,” Ari Redbord, TRM’s global head of policy, told Al Jazeera, adding, “That makes this a global security issue, not just a crypto theft.”
What does this mean for the crypto market?
Prices have fallen, though markets steadied after the initial shock.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368, while Ether fell more than 3 percent to a two-month low of $2,178.
Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase, which said it was unaffected, fell 4.8 percent.
The hack comes as crypto had already been under pressure from higher US interest rates and weaker demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts told Reuters.
The stolen sum is more than six times Binance’s $1bn emergency fund, the Secure Asset Fund for Users, set up in 2018 and held entirely in Bitcoin to protect users in case of a breach.
Teng said company funds would also cover losses.
Is crypto an inherently unsafe investment?
The hack has exposed one particular weak point: Large, centralised exchanges, which hold users’ assets on their behalf.
“Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself, and the larger the exchange’s holdings, the larger a target it becomes,” Sean Foley, an expert in crypto markets at Macquarie University in Sydney, told Al Jazeera.
Insurance offers limited protection as most crime- and cyber-insurance policies do not cover stolen cryptocurrency, and crypto-specific cover remains a niche business offered largely by specialist insurers.
Thefts are frequent. Hackers stole $2.87bn in crypto in nearly 150 attacks in 2025, according to TRM’s 2026 Crypto Crime Report.
Binance itself has faced legal trouble. Founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
On Friday, Binance said it was coordinating with law enforcement and remained on track to resume withdrawals within 45 hours.

Olha Ivzhenko won silver and bronze at the World Weightlifting Championships
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian won silver in the snatch and bronze in the total in the up to 57 kg weight category. These are Ukraine’s first medals at the World Championships since 2023.
Ukrainian weightlifter Olha Ivzhenko won silver and bronze medals at the 2026 World Championships in Ningbo, China. The athlete finished second in the snatch and won bronze in the combined total of the two lifts in the up to 57 kg weight category. This was reported by the National Olympic Committee of Ukraine, UNN writes.
The World Weightlifting Championships are taking place in the Chinese city of Ningbo from October 27 to November 8. Ukraine is represented at the world championships by seven athletes in seven weight categories
It is noted that Olha Ivzhenko was the first Ukrainian to take the platform; she competes in the up to 57 kg weight category. Based on her performance, our weightlifter won two medals.
In the snatch, Olha lifted 96 kg, earning her a silver medal. In the clean and jerk, the Ukrainian lifted 118 kg and finished fourth. With a combined total of 214 kg in the two lifts, the athlete won a bronze medal in the overall competition — a major World Championships medal!
These medals were the first for Ukraine's national team at the World Weightlifting Championships since 2023. That year, Ukrainian athletes finished the world championships with four medals: two silver medals (one of them in the overall competition) and two bronze medals
For Olha, these are yet more significant achievements in 2026. In April, at the senior European Championships, she won silver in the clean and jerk with a result of 120 kg in the up to 58 kg weight category. And just two weeks ago, she became the absolute European champion among under-23 athletes in the up to 61 kg weight category, winning three gold medals.
It is worth noting that the 2026 World Championships mark the start of the qualification period for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. Therefore, the medals won by Olha are an important result on the path to an Olympic quota place.

Eurozone GDP growth slows to 0.4 pct in Q3: Eurostat
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:37:47 CST
21:37:47 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Gross domestic product (GDP) in the eurozone grew by 0.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the previous quarter, slowing from 0.6 percent in the second quarter, according to a preliminary flash estimate released by Eurostat on Friday.
GDP in the European Union (EU) increased by 0.5 percent quarter on quarter, down from 0.7 percent in the previous quarter, the EU's statistical office said.
On a year-on-year basis, GDP growth edged up to 1.3 percent in the eurozone and 1.5 percent in the EU, compared with 1.2 percent and 1.4 percent, respectively, in the second quarter.
The eurozone economy stagnated in the first quarter before rebounding in the second.
Economic performance weakened in several major eurozone economies. Germany's GDP increased by 0.2 percent quarter on quarter, down from 0.3 percent in the second quarter. France's economy contracted by 0.1 percent after remaining unchanged in the previous quarter, while Italy's GDP stagnated after growing by 0.2 percent. Spain recorded growth of 0.6 percent, compared with 0.7 percent in the second quarter.
Elsewhere in the EU, Ireland recorded quarterly GDP growth of 5.5 percent, the highest among member states with available data, while Lithuania posted the sharpest contraction, at 1.0 percent.
Eurostat cautioned that the preliminary estimates were based on incomplete data and remained subject to revision.
The European Central Bank (ECB) kept its three key interest rates unchanged on Thursday, warning that continued increases in energy prices posed upside risks to inflation and downside risks to economic growth.
Bert Colijn, chief economist at ING, said that persistently rising energy prices, including natural gas prices, would pose additional challenges to eurozone growth during the winter months.
The relatively high level of interest rates and weakening business demand for loans would also weigh on economic activity, he noted, citing the ECB's bank lending survey. ■

Thailand's economy improves in September on AI-driven exports
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:37:33 CST
21:37:33 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's economy improved overall in September on a monthly basis, as the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom lifted electronics exports and data-center investment, though tourism and consumer spending weakened, the central bank said on Friday.
According to the Bank of Thailand, merchandise exports excluding gold rose 3.7 percent in September from a month earlier on a seasonally adjusted basis, led by shipments of telecommunications equipment and computers.
The bank's private investment index surged 21.6 percent month-on-month in September, driven by increased imports of data-center equipment, which also boosted manufacturing output.
In contrast, foreign tourist arrivals fell 6.3 percent from the previous month as short-haul travel slowed after the summer school holidays amid flight constraints and higher travel costs following a rise in oil prices, said Pranee Sutthasri, senior director of the central bank's Macroeconomic Department.
Tourism receipts nonetheless rose 12.5 percent month-on-month as visitors stayed longer and the share of long-haul travelers increased, Pranee told a news conference.
Private consumption dropped 2.2 percent from the previous month, mainly due to weaker spending on services, particularly hotels and restaurants, as high living expenses made households more cautious, Pranee said.
She noted that government spending contracted 0.9 percent from a year earlier, reflecting lower disbursements from both the central government and state enterprises.
The central bank said the recovery remained uneven, with gains largely confined to businesses and workers in AI-related industries. Household consumption, however, is expected to recover gradually, supported by government measures and improving labor incomes. ■

China Focus: Global energy body proposes framework to protect biodiversity in clean energy transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:37:25 CST
21:37:25 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- A new framework could help energy transition projects protect biodiversity while advancing the shift to cleaner energy, according to a report released Thursday at a side event in Beijing during the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity.
The report, titled Energy Transition Empowers Biodiversity Conservation, was released by the Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization (GEIDCO), which organized the side event. It proposes a four-part framework for biodiversity protection and recommends typical practices.
Liu Zehong, executive vice chairman of GEIDCO, said at the side event that building an eco-friendly energy system not only provides energy security for economic and social development but also preserves living space for all living things.
He added that GEIDCO will study and formulate relevant standards to provide the energy and power industry with methods and tools for better biodiversity conservation practices.
According to the report, the framework includes four aspects: promote, avoid, reduce and offset.
"Promote" means actively creating positive ecological benefits. Energy transition projects are expected to go beyond the baseline goal of "do no harm," make full use of the unique advantages of clean energy, and proactively support ecosystem and biodiversity conservation.
Such practices include replacing fossil-fuel projects with clean energy projects, providing green energy support for endangered species conservation, and restoring damaged habitats through integrated development models.
The report cited the photovoltaic (PV) power base in China's Kubuqi Desert as an example of restoring damaged habitats. Kubuqi has carried out "PV desertification control," exploring a composite development model with power generation from the panels, planting beneath them, and livestock rearing between them.
"Avoid" means steering clear of highly sensitive areas. It aims to prevent irreversible ecological damage from the start. For example, site and route selection should avoid nature reserves, critical habitats, breeding grounds and migration corridors. Construction should be scheduled to avoid bird breeding seasons, fish spawning and migration periods, and animal migration seasons.
"Reduce" means on-site protection and lowering negative impacts. When impacts cannot be fully avoided, their scope, intensity and duration should be minimized through practices such as reducing pollution emissions, maintaining habitat connectivity and installing protective facilities to mitigate disturbance.
"Offset" means off-site compensation to achieve no net loss. It involves equivalent compensation outside the project impact area for residual impacts after reduction efforts. Offset practices include off-site reconstruction of damaged habitats, ex situ conservation of rare species, artificial breeding and preservation of genetic materials.
The report said the recommended practices cover the entire life cycle of energy projects, involving clean substitution, composite development, engineering mitigation, on-site restoration and off-site conservation. Different types of energy projects can choose one or more of these practices as appropriate to promote win-win outcomes between energy transition and biodiversity conservation.
GEIDCO also released the 2026 List of Energy Transition for Biodiversity and the Practical Cases of Energy Transition for Biodiversity 2026 at the side event.
GEIDCO is a non-profit international organization headquartered in Beijing and dedicated to promoting sustainable energy development worldwide. It has 1,450 members from 145 countries, covering fields such as energy, electricity, transportation, information, finance, science and technology, and meteorology. ■

Japan's central bank keeps interest rate unchanged, says inflation target generally achieved
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:37:25 CST
21:37:25 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Bank of Japan (BOJ) decided to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at around 1.25 percent after concluding its two-day monetary policy meeting on Friday.
The widely expected decision came after the central bank raised the key rate by 0.25 percentage points to a 31-year high of 1.25 percent at its previous policy meeting in September.
In its quarterly economic outlook report released after the meeting, the BOJ said that with the policy interest rate now higher than in the past, it is important to examine how financial conditions change under such circumstances.
The BOJ also said that Japan's underlying inflation has "generally" reached its 2 percent price stability target, nearly 14 years after the goal was set as part of efforts to end decades of deflation.
At a post-meeting press conference, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said the central bank's monetary policy will increasingly focus on keeping underlying inflation firmly anchored around 2 percent, signaling that the BOJ could raise rates further to prevent price increases from overshooting the target.
The BOJ cited higher prices of crude oil, semiconductors and other items, as well as the yen's depreciation, among the factors currently pushing up prices and likely to keep doing so for some time. It said it will closely monitor the impact of the situation in the Middle East, global demand related to artificial intelligence, and foreign exchange rate movements on Japan's economic activity and prices.
In the outlook report, the BOJ raised its core consumer price inflation forecast for fiscal 2027 to 2.6 percent from 2.4 percent, while lowering its real GDP growth projection to 0.7 percent from 0.8 percent.
The BOJ first adopted its 2 percent inflation target in January 2013, initially aiming to achieve it in about two years.
In April that year, under then-Governor Haruhiko Kuroda, the central bank launched an aggressive monetary easing program, but the target remained out of reach, with the BOJ repeatedly pushing back the timeline.
Japan's recent inflation has been fueled largely by external factors such as higher energy prices, and analysts said sustained wage growth would be key to creating a virtuous cycle of rising wages and prices.
The BOJ has one more policy meeting this year, scheduled for Dec. 17-18, at which markets increasingly expect another rate hike. ■

German unemployment rate falls to 6.3 pct in October
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:37:18 CST
21:37:18 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Germany's unemployment rate edged down to 6.3 percent in October from 6.4 percent in September, official data showed Friday, although weak hiring demand and a modest decline in joblessness pointed to continued pressure on the labor market.
The number of unemployed people fell by 40,000 from the previous month to 2.955 million, but remained 44,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Federal Employment Agency.
"Economic conditions remain insufficient for an improvement in the labor market," said Andrea Nahles, head of the agency, noting that the decline in unemployment in October was relatively modest.
Meanwhile, a business survey suggested that German companies were becoming more cautious about cutting jobs, following years of economic weakness and widespread plans to reduce staffing levels.
The Munich-based ifo Institute said Wednesday that its employment barometer rose to 95.5 points in October from 95.1 points in September, although the employment outlook in manufacturing remained weak, with further job cuts planned, particularly in the automotive industry.
"Companies are becoming somewhat more cautious about cutting jobs, but the economic upturn still lacks the strength for a broad expansion of the workforce," said Klaus Wohlrabe, head of surveys at ifo. ■

"The ceasefire remains in effect. Further details will follow," he said.

With about 2,000 people remaining at present, Oleshky lies on the left bank of the Dnieper River.
The town has been under Russian control since February 2022 and is facing a humanitarian crisis, with shortages of food, medicine and other essential supplies amid continued fighting, according to officials.
The humanitarian mission followed an agreement on a temporary ceasefire in the area to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
The ceasefire is scheduled to remain in effect until 10:59 p.m. Moscow time (1959 GMT) on Nov. 1, according to the Russian side. ■

German economic growth slows to 0.2 pct in Q3 as exports weaken
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:36:54 CST
21:36:54 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Germany's economy expanded by 0.2 percent in the third quarter of 2026, slowing from the first half of the year as exports weakened and investment declined, preliminary data from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed Friday.
The expansion, slightly above economists' expectations of 0.1 percent, marked the fourth consecutive quarter of growth in Europe's largest economy, following increases of 0.4 percent in the first quarter and 0.3 percent in the second.
Consumer spending edged up in the July-September period, while investment declined, according to Destatis. The strong export growth seen in the first half of the year also slowed noticeably in the third quarter, it said.
Germany's Economy Ministry warned earlier this month that the economic growth was likely to slow temporarily in the third quarter, citing disruptions to inland shipping caused by historically low water levels, weaker global demand for energy-intensive goods, and the erosion of purchasing power due to higher energy prices.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, said the German economy had continued its recent upswing, but cautioned that a short-term rebound did not necessarily signal a sustainable recovery.
He said the outlook remained heavily dependent on the impact of the government's fiscal stimulus, while longstanding structural problems remained unresolved and the German industry continued to undergo a difficult transition.
Reforms to restore international competitiveness were still urgently needed, Brzeski added.
Looking ahead, the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW) expected growth to pick up noticeably in the fourth quarter, supported by improving industrial activity.
"The German economy appears to be picking up pace towards the end of the year, driven largely by a recovery in industry after years of weakness," said Geraldine Dany-Knedlik, head of economic forecasting at DIW.
However, she warned that the recovery was not yet broad-based, with households spending held back by high prices and a weak labor market, while private investment remained subdued.
In its autumn forecast released earlier this month, the German government projected the economy would grow by 1.3 percent this year, before slowing to 1.1 percent in 2027 and 0.6 percent in 2028. ■

Official: Estonia should never even consider giving up its voice on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:36:00 UTC
21:36:00 KST

Official: Estonia should never even consider giving up its voice on Russia
Outgoing Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov said he is not aware of any request from U.S. officials for Estonia to change its message on the threat from Russia, following a report published by Reuters news agency on Friday.
The story, citing anonymous sources, said Pentagon officials had urged several NATO allies, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to tone down their public rhetoric on the threat posed by Russia.
"I am not aware of such official requests, but the fact that not everyone may like the content or style of Estonia's message is no kind of surprise to me," Vseviov told ERR Friday. "That anyone would have officially proposed that Estonia keep quiet — I am not aware of that. And perhaps also because a proposal like that would always and in any case get rejected."
"Estonia's voice is our most important trump card, the most important weapon for taking part in international politics. And while that voice must be used wisely and never belligerently, surrendering that voice is something we should never even consider," he added.
Vseviov declined to say whether such a request had been conveyed unofficially, but did not rule it out. "Unofficially, people talk all the time... I honestly can't find any news value in that in itself," he said.
He said he would not draw far-reaching conclusions from the Reuters article, as often only a fragment of what happened behind closed doors reaches the media. Asked whether Estonia should tone down its positions, he said everything said about Estonia internationally must be taken into account, but that Estonia must use its voice as well as it can.
"The time when going to Washington cap in hand, hoping to get the Americans to do our business for us, is over," Vseviov said, adding that Europe must stand on its own two feet and treat America as a pragmatic, balanced ally that "does not have to panic at every thought expressed there."
He said Estonia's official positions on the security situation have been accurate and have foreseen events. "It is no coincidence that after the start of the great war on February 24, 2022, a whole string of world leaders pointed out that Estonia and the other Baltic states should have been listened to earlier," he said.
On Friday, Reuters reported that one source said U.S. officials had taken issue with statements by European leaders suggesting Russia had been backed into a corner, and that Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby was one of those conveying the message. A Pentagon official said: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations."
Lithuania's Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said he too had no information about such a request. "What we speak is always based on facts. If a Russian drone flew in, we say that a Russian drone flew in," he said. "We state the facts and will continue to do so."
Vseviov announced last week that he was joining the Social Democratic Party and running in the Riigikogu elections, and is expected to be confirmed as the party's prime ministerial candidate. He steps down as secretary general next month.

Toblerone maker sues UK start-up over lookalike bar for vegans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:35:00 UTC
21:35:00 KST

Toblerone maker sues UK start-up over lookalike bar for vegans
- Mondelez is suing UK vegan chocolatier Catherine’s Originals over its O’bar shape, saying it is too similar to Toblerone’s famous triangular design.
- Catherine Dodd says the claim is worrying for her small business and argues her bars use more rounded peaks and an “O” theme.
- The case follows earlier trademark fights over Toblerone, including disputes with Poundland and Cocoa Luxury, as Mondelez says it must protect its brand.
AI generated
LONDON – Mondelez International is heading to the UK courts once again – over the triangular prism shape of its Toblerone chocolate bar.
Less than a decade after the US confectionery company won a trademark row with Poundland over the discount retailer’s Twin Peaks chocolate bar, Mondelez’s latest fight is with a small British vegan chocolatier.
Catherine’s Originals’ range of O’bar chocolates, which feature a row of rounded peaks on a thin slab, are too similar in shape to Toblerone’s triangles, according to a UK intellectual property infringement claim filed on Oct 15 by Kraft Foods Schweiz Holding, a company that is part of Mondelez.
“The iconic Toblerone shape is one of the most recognised and distinctive product designs in the UK and across the world,” a spokesperson for Mondelez said. “We have a responsibility to protect our trademarks and intellectual property, which we take seriously.”
Kraft Foods bought Toblerone in 1990 and successfully trademarked the shape of the chocolate bar in Europe that decade. Mondelez was created in the split of Kraft Foods in 2012.
Catherine Dodd, who was 18 when she launched her vegan brand in 2021, disagrees with Mondelez’s claims: the peaks on her chocolate bars are more rounded than those of Toblerone and are in line with the O theme used in other products like Catherine’s O tin and Milky O’s.
“Honestly, it’s fairly frightening for a small business we’ve put so much care and hard work into building,” Dodd wrote in an e-mailed statement. “But being a smaller business does not mean being afraid to stand up for what we’ve created.”
It is not unusual for consumer companies to sue rivals over similar versions of distinctive products. Nestle famously defeated Mondelez’s efforts to trademark the purple color used in the packaging of its Cadbury Dairy Milk bars. In turn, Mondelez blocked Nestle’s efforts to trademark the shape of its four-finger KitKat wafer.
Mondelez settled its claim against Poundland in 2017 before a full trial began. The two agreed that the budget retailer could release a limited number of its Twin Peaks bars as long as it changed the colour of its packaging and turned the mountains into asymmetrical hills.
Years later, Mondelez challenged Swiss-based company Cocoa Luxury over its Swissone bar. A local court in Switzerland initially ruled there was no likelihood of consumers being confused as the peaks on the smaller company’s bar were more rounded than Toblerone’s.
The two parties later reached a confidential agreement that meant Swissone changed its shape and packaging, a Mondelez spokesperson wrote.
Mondelez said several months of talks to find a resolution with Catherine’s, which makes its chocolate at a factory in West Sussex, have failed to yield results.
Previously Mondelez had to remove the Matterhorn peak from its packaging and change its label from “of Switzerland” to “established in Switzerland” after it moved some production to Slovakia.
Shares of Mondelez, which reports earnings later on Oct 30, are up more than 7% in the past 12 months. BLOOMBERG

Slovak Prosecutor General reopens case into transfer of MiG-29 fighter jets and Kub air defense systems to Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:34:47 EET
21:34:47 KST

Slovak Prosecutor General Maroš Žilinka has decided to reopen the case concerning the transfer of military equipment to Ukraine by the country’s previous government in 2023.
"After reviewing the case, I have concluded that the decision to close it was premature," Žilinka wrote on social media. He stated that the investigation must be resumed and that the relevant directive has been issued to the prosecutor in the city of Trenčín.
The case concerns the transfer to Ukraine of 13 MiG-29 fighter jets and Kub (SA-6 Gainful) surface-to-air missile systems that had been in service with the Slovak Armed Forces.
In February 2026, Bratislava prosecutor Rastislav Remeta, upon concluding a preliminary investigation, stated that the transferred fighter jets and air defense systems were obsolete and that their transfer to Ukraine did not constitute a criminal offense. Previously, on October 31, 2025, a police investigator had closed the criminal proceedings, and on January 26, 2026, a prosecutor rejected an appeal against that decision.
In September 2026, the Slovak Prosecutor General’s Office reported that it had reviewed the legality of the closure of the proceedings and concluded that the decisions made by the investigator and the prosecutor were lawful. Žilinka’s current decision means that the circumstances of the case are being re-examined; however, this does not, in itself, imply that a criminal offense has been established.

Evacuations begin in Russian-controlled Oleshky under US-brokered ceasefire

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

21:34:17 KST

The evacuation of residents from the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky began on Friday, with people gradually boarding buses to leave for both Russia and Kiev-controlled parts of Ukraine under a US-brokered ceasefire.
Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, said residents wishing to travel in either direction were gathering at the evacuation point and would be given the opportunity to leave.
“People who wish to travel to the Russian Federation are gathering here. There are also people here who wish to travel to Ukraine. Everyone will be given the opportunity to do so,” she said in a Telegram post.
Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia also confirmed that the operation was underway, saying evacuation and humanitarian aid distribution had begun.
Officials from both Moscow and Kyiv travelled to Oleshky to oversee the operation. Lantratova shared footage of residents waiting to board buses, while Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, posted videos showing emotional exchanges with residents, some of whom were seen crying and thanking him.
Months of shortages drive residents to seek safety
Oleshky, captured by Russian forces in 2022, has suffered extensive damage during the war. Residents have endured months of shortages of food, water and medicine, with some reportedly forced to hunt and eat pigeons, former residents told AFP.
The town's population has fallen from around 24,000 before the war to approximately 2,000, according to the supplied report.
Residents have been seen waiting outside their homes with bags of belongings, ready to leave. Officials from both countries have said some people will choose to remain in the town even if fighting resumes.
Ceasefire offers rare pause as attacks continue elsewhere
The temporary ceasefire, announced last week by US First Lady Melania Trump, is due to expire on Sunday evening. Now in its fourth day, it represents the longest pause in fighting along any part of the front line since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Previous limited ceasefires, including arrangements around Orthodox Easter, were accompanied by accusations of violations.
Despite the relative calm around Oleshky, attacks have continued elsewhere in Ukraine. Russian strikes overnight left around 200,000 households without electricity in the city of Dnipro.
A drone strike on a railway station there a day earlier killed at least 14 people, while an attack on the northern city of Chernihiv killed two teenage girls.

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated three communities in the Kharkov, Sumy and Zaporozhye Regions over the week of October 24-30 in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"During the week, Battlegroup North units liberated the settlements of Alisovka in the Kharkov Region and Barilovka in the Sumy Region through active offensive operations. <…> During the past week, Battlegroup East units continued advancing deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Obshcheye in the Zaporozhye Region through decisive operations," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian troops deliver 11 precision strikes on Ukrainian military sites over week
Russian troops delivered two massive and nine combined strikes by precision-guided weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises, energy and transport sites over the week, the ministry reported.
"On October 24-30, the Russian Armed Forces delivered two massive and nine combined strikes, hitting Ukraine’s military-industrial enterprises, logistics centers, energy and transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, workshops producing and sites storing ground robotic platforms, unmanned aerial vehicles and uncrewed boats, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
In addition, the strikes degraded Ukraine’s port infrastructure facilities used to receive, store and distribute military cargo, it said.
"During the week, 11 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of armament, military hardware and dual-use products for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 1,575 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 1,575 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed eight enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the week, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on formations of eight mechanized brigades, three motorized infantry brigades, two airmobile brigades, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and four territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,575 personnel, eight armored combat vehicles, 68 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and six electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 1,585 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 1,585 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed eight enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of four mechanized brigades, an airmobile brigade, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,585 personnel, eight armored combat vehicles, 108 motor vehicles, six field artillery guns and 12 electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 1,155 casualties on Ukrainian army in week

"During the past week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, an airmobile brigade, an air assault brigade, a mountain assault brigade, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,155 personnel, 24 armored combat vehicles, 217 motor vehicles, 12 field artillery guns and eight electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 2,400 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 2,400 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 38 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the week, Battlegroup Center units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of four mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an assault brigade, an airborne brigade, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army, three marine infantry brigades and five National Guard brigades," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 2,400 personnel, 38 armored combat vehicles, 67 motor vehicles, five field artillery guns and 13 electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 1,390 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,390 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 12 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.

North Korea warns South Korea with ballistic missiles as Seoul calls for talks to ease border tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:32:29 UTC
21:32:29 KST

Missile launches and a dispute over a landmine incident have heightened tensions between the two Koreas. Seoul is seeking military talks to prevent accidental clashes, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
North Korea fired around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea on Thursday, South Korea’s military said, a day after Seoul renewed its call for talks to prevent accidental clashes along their heavily fortified border.
The missiles were launched from the eastern coastal area of Wonsan at about 12.30pm local time and travelled around 250 kilometres, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff.
South Korea said it had stepped up surveillance for further launches and was sharing information with the United States and Japan.
Seoul proposed military talks on 23 October to jointly verify the location of the Military Demarcation Line, which separates the two Koreas, restore military communication lines and agree measures to prevent accidental clashes.
Unification Minister Chung Dong-young renewed the appeal on Wednesday in an address read on his behalf at a forum in Goyang, near Seoul.
“South and North Korea should align their positions on the MDL through dialogue,” Chung said, calling for communication channels to be restored so the area could be managed peacefully.
North Korea has not responded to the talks proposal.
Mine blasts deepen border tensions
The offer follows landmine explosions in the Demilitarised Zone on 21 September that injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul accused North Korean troops of planting the mines south of the demarcation line. North Korea denied responsibility and accused the South of fabricating the incident in a letter to the UN Security Council.
The US-led United Nations Command, which oversees the armistice, said a joint investigation with South Korea had identified an active North Korean mine south of the line and determined that an armistice violation had occurred.
North Korean troops have been reinforcing the border with roads, fences and landmines. South Korea says they have repeatedly crossed the demarcation line during the work, prompting warning broadcasts and warning shots.
Seoul says differing interpretations of the boundary could lead to accidental clashes. Many of the markers installed under the 1953 armistice have deteriorated or disappeared, with only about 200 of the original 1,292 still identifiable, according to Yonhap.
Direct military communication between the two Koreas remains suspended, although the command maintains a separate channel with the North Korean military.

Former Palestinian prisoners are being abused, taken by Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:31:42 UTC
21:31:42 KST

Breadcrumb
One year on since freedom, former Palestinian prisoners in the West Bank are being re-arrested and abused by Israel
Israa Nasrallah never imagined that the release of her husband, 35-year-old Bakr Khreiwesh, in the most recent prisoner exchange deal last October 2025 would be followed by continued harassment and his re-arrest.
21 August brought an unpleasant surprise to Isra and her husband; their home in the city of Tulkarm in the occupied West Bank was raided by the Israeli army. Once again, her husband was taken under "administrative detention", a practice that allows for indefinite imprisonment without charge or trial, repeatedly renewed.
The Palestinian Prisoners' Club has warned that Israel has been re-arresting, harassing, and interrogating at least 80 former Palestinian prisoners who have been released as part of previous exchange deals between Hamas and Israel.
In a statement, the organisation noted that these security and judicial measures prevent former detainees from resuming their normal lives and exacerbate the suffering of the families of those who were deported or exiled, leaving them unable to see their loved ones.
Bakr was one of 1,968 Palestinian prisoners released in the latest deal. He was among the small number of individuals whom Israel permitted to return to their homes in the occupied West Bank, rather than being deported elsewhere.
He had been serving a nine-year prison sentence, of which he had completed six years. During his time in prison, he and his wife had twins, conceived through sperm smuggled out of the Israeli prison.
Isra described to The New Arab how her husband’s release as part of the prisoner exchange deal was the end to the family's nightmare. Throughout the seven months since being free, Bakr spent with his family, Israeli intelligence repeatedly summoned him for questioning and interrogation.
"Israeli officers would constantly call to threaten him or summon him for interrogation, during Ramadan, during the Eid holidays, and at other times. They made sure he felt he was always being watched, signaling that his release under the deal didn’t guarantee he wouldn't be arrested again," she said.
At one point, Israeli intelligence threatened the landlord of the apartment the family was renting, warning that if he didn’t evict them, the Israeli army would take the landlord instead. Consequently, the family was forced to leave and move in temporarily with a relative.
"The pressure extended even to our housing; Israeli intelligence kept a close watch on our situation and threatened anyone who might rent a home to us. We felt as though we were constantly under their gaze," Isra explained.
Bakr is currently being held in the Naqab prison. His lawyer has been able to visit him only once since his arrest; afterward, Bakr asked his family not to send the lawyer again. When Isra inquired why, she learned that any prisoner is subjected to severe beatings immediately following such visits.
She is also deeply concerned about his health. He has begun to suffer from scabies due to a lack of hygiene. Furthermore, at the time of his release under the prisoner exchange deal, he had already lost a significant amount of weight and was suffering from chronic pain in his back and knees to the point where he could barely walk, as a result of the brutal beatings he endured prior to his initial release.
The New Arab contacted several former Palestinian prisoners; none were willing to comment, citing Israeli threats that they could be re-arrested.
Violation of international law
The Palestinian Prisoners' Club has linked these pursuits to an escalation in abuses including mistreatment, starvation, denial of medical care, and solitary confinement within Israeli prisons since the onset of the aggression on Gaza.
The organisation pointed to the severe physical and psychological toll observed among those released, particularly those from the Gaza Strip.
Approximately 3,985 Palestinian prisoners, men, women, and children, have been released through three separate exchange deals. These include a November 2023 agreement (240 prisoners), a deal spanning January and February 2025 (1,777 prisoners), and an October 2025 agreement (1,968 prisoners and detainees).
Helmi Al-Araj, director of the Hurriyat Center for Civil Rights, told TNA that Israel has never adhered to the terms of these agreements even those with clear and specific provisions.
He cited the "Shalit deal" as an example; in 2014, Israel re-arrested more than 50 prisoners who had been released under that agreement. Many remained in prison for long periods, and some were only released again during the more recent exchange deals.
Al-Araj explained that Israel is employing the same tactic regarding the latest agreement, re-arresting released prisoners, both men and women, in an apparent attempt to signal that it won’t bide by any conditions, and that anyone can be taken back into custody at any time.
He added that this serves as a message to the released prisoners; they remain under surveillance, subject to pursuit and arrest and even killing or assassination, as is currently the case in the Gaza Strip.
"The Israeli occupation’s underlying message is an attempt to terrorize the released prisoners, their families, and the Palestinian people at large, by asserting that everyone is being pursued and remains subject to arrest regardless of whether or not they are currently engaged in any activity," he added.
According to Al-Araj, Israel was compelled to release these prisoners but refuses to fully accept this reality; consequently, it pursues them more aggressively than others, under the pretext that they pose a threat to its security.
"As far as is known, none of these released prisoners are engaged in any activities in the West Bank. Yet, Israel is violating the terms of the prisoner exchange deal, as well as international law and international humanitarian law. It arrests these individuals without charge, subjects many of them to administrative detention, and fails to uphold the standards required for fair trials," he concluded.
As of 5 October 2026, the number of prisoners held in Israeli jails reached approximately 9,300, according to the Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association.
This figure includes 3,101 individuals held under administrative detention, as well as approximately 350 children and 91 women. The organisation also documented 1,419 detainees from the Gaza Strip whom Israel classifies as "unlawful combatants", though these figures don’t necessarily account for everyone held within Israeli military camps.

Woman jailed for mushroom poison murders given harsher sentence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:31:05 UTC
21:31:05 KST

Woman convicted of mushroom poison murders in Australia ordered to never be released from prison
An Australian appeals court on Friday ordered triple-murderer Erin Patterson to never be released from prison because of the "shocking criminality" involved in poisoning four of her estranged husband's relatives with death cap mushrooms.
 The three judges of the Victoria state Court of Appeal dismissed Patterson's appeal of her convictions and upheld prosecutors' challenge to the leniency of her 33-year nonparole sentence, meaning she will spend the rest of her life behind bars. Beforehand, she would have been 82 years old when she could be considered for release.
"Extraordinarily cold and calculated"
"This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms," Justice Stephen McLeish said on behalf of all three judges.
"In all the circumstances after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a nonparole period," McLeish added.
Patterson is only the second woman in Australia to be imprisoned for life without possibility of parole. The first is meatworker Katherine Knight, who was sentenced in New South Wales state in 2001 for the murder a year earlier of her partner John Price, whom she'd stabbed at least 37 times.
Patterson's convictions stemmed from a family meal she hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023.
She can apply to Australia's High Court to overturn the verdicts on her sentence and her convictions. The High Court is her last appeal option.
Patterson insisted she added death cap mushrooms to the beef Wellington pastry dishes accidentally.
Death caps are responsible for 90% of lethal mushroom poisoning globally, the BBC reported.
In 2022, doctors in Massachusetts were able to save a mother and son who nearly died from death cap mushroom poisoning. In 2020, a spate of poisonings in Victoria, Australia, killed one person and hospitalized seven others.
She was sentenced last year to three life sentences for murder and 25 years for attempted murder.
Murders attract global attention
The deaths of Patterson's parents-in-law Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, within days of having lunch immediately attracted an extraordinary level of global media attention.
The case has also inspired podcasts, books and screen adaptations.
Emmy-nominated actor Melanie Lynskey announced this week she will star as Erin Patterson in a six-episode series for the subscription video-on-demand streaming service Paramount+.
Lynskey is also executive producer of the series that dramatizes the 97 days from the fatal lunch until Patterson's arrest.
Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson survived the lunch after spending weeks in the hospital. Erin Patterson was convicted of his attempted murder.
Prosecutors argued at an appeal hearing in August that she should never become eligible for parole.
They argued the minimum period behind bars did not reflect the "calculated criminality" of the case.
McLeish said Patterson's intent to murder all four was sustained for almost three weeks from when she invited them to lunch.
Her crimes involved an "elaborate series of deceptions" including falsely claiming a cancer diagnosis to explain the absences of her two children from the lunch, the judge said.
The only survivor, Ian Wilkinson, testified that Erin Patterson had told her guests she wanted their advice about what to tell the children about her diagnosis. Wilkinson, a Baptist pastor, also testified about the grief after his wife died from the poisoning.
"I only feel half alive without her," Wilkinson said at the trial before weeping.
Patterson allegedly destroyed evidence
McLeish noted Erin Patterson had destroyed evidence, denied foraging for mushrooms and repeatedly made false claims about where the mushrooms had come from.
"The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust," McLeish said.
Patterson opted not to attend court and watched the verdicts by video link from prison.
Because of her notoriety, Patterson is held in the high-security Gordon Unit of Melbourne's Dame Phyllis Frost Centre women's prison. The unit is for prisoners assessed as being at high risk from other inmates.
In sentencing her in September 2025, trial judge Christopher Bale said there was a "substantial chance" that Patterson could be held in "solitary confinement for years to come."
Patterson's estranged husband, Simon Patterson, was invited to the lunch but declined the day before.
After her conviction, pretrial evidence was released that detailed the husband's suspicion that Erin Patterson had previously attempted to kill him.
Simon Patterson testified at a pretrial hearing that he had declined the lunch invitation out of fear.
