They rescued passengers during evacuation: five railway employees killed in strike on Dnipro train station
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:30:00 EET
21:30:00 KST

They rescued passengers during evacuation: five railway employees killed in strike on Dnipro train station
Railway workers Yevhenii Kryvko, Viktoriia Nosikova, Kateryna Borysova, Yana Shpakova and Ruslan Dil were killed in a Russian drone attack on the railway station in Dnipro on 29 October.
Source: Zalizna Rodyna (Iron Family) charity project; Ukrzaliznytsia
Details: Yevhenii Kryvko, 38, held the rank of first-category specialist and had spent the past four months working as one of the station's "angels" – the people who greet arriving passengers, accompany those who need a helping hand and make sure travellers can find their way around.
The Zalizna Rodyna team said: "Yevhenii was assisting passengers during the evacuation. In a moment of danger, when people needed support and help, he stayed by their side and did his job. His service to the people has taken on a special, tragic meaning: a man called to help others became a victim of the enemy's strike himself."
Yevhenii is remembered as a caring husband and father. He is survived by his wife and two sons, Illia, 9, and Danylo, 3.
Viktoriia Nosikova was also killed in the attack. She worked as a carriage attendant aboard a passenger train that was about to depart alongside the commuter train. She was injured as she made her way to a shelter.
Viktoriia came from Donetsk Oblast and had devoted more than 20 years of her life to working on the railway. Colleagues remember her as a dedicated, conscientious employee who always made sure her passengers were comfortable.
The Zalizna Rodyna team recounted: "She always performed her duties to a high standard and with an open heart, bringing warmth and care to passengers, and she was a reliable adviser and a good colleague for the depot team. In civilian life, she was the guardian of her family – a loving wife, a caring mother, and a grandmother whose heart always beat for her dearest ones."
The attack also claimed the life of carriage attendant Kateryna Borysova. She came under fire while walking to a shelter.
Originally from Kirovohrad Oblast, Kateryna had spent 24 years working as a carriage attendant on local trains.
Zalizna Rodyna noted: "At the depot, she was known as a person of extraordinary discipline and inner strength. Over nearly a quarter of a century of conscientious work, Kateryna Borysova earned the immense respect of her team and management.
But above all, she loved life and her family. She was a wonderful, caring mother and grandmother, for whom her sons and granddaughter were her main source of joy and the meaning of her existence."
In 2015, Kateryna was presented with a commemorative watch by the head of the railway, and this year she received a certificate of gratitude from Ukrzaliznytsia.
Yana Shpakova, 32, was also killed instantly. She ran the children's area at Dnipro railway station, had spent 13 years working for Ukrzaliznytsia and had long since become part of the railway family, the company said.
Yana began her career selling train tickets. She later went on to run the children's area, caring for the youngest passengers.
"When danger arose and there was a need to help passengers arriving in Dnipro, Yana joined other station staff. She and her colleagues helped people during the evacuation," Zalizna Rodyna added.
Yana is survived by her 15-year-old daughter Myroslava, whom she was raising as a single mother.
Ruslan Dil, 48, from Synelnykove, was also among those killed. After completing his training at Dnipropetrovsk Vocational School, he spent nearly three decades working on the railway.
He began as an assistant electric locomotive driver and worked his way up to driving locomotives himself.
"The period of his work in the Zaporizhzhia region since the beginning of the full-scale invasion was particularly important and difficult. Ruslan was involved in the operation of evacuation trains that took people out of dangerous areas, as well as the evacuation of equipment," the company noted.
On the day of the attack, Ruslan was on leave and making his way home. He was travelling by train from Zhmerynka and was due to change at Dnipro railway station for a commuter service to Zaporizhzhia.
He is survived by his two children, his son Rostyslav and daughter Polina, as well as his mother and sister.
The death toll from the strike on the train station in Dnipro has risen to 15. A further 14 people were injured. Six of them are currently in a serious condition, including a child.
Background: Yana Pieshkova and Mariia Mozhova, two 15-year-old classmates, were killed in a Russian attack with a Banderol drone-launched cruise missile on central Chernihiv on 29 October.

Italy inflation surges to 5.4% in October as energy costs bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:29:51 UTC
21:29:51 KST

Italian inflation rose 5.4% in October from a year earlier, a sharp rise from the 4.2% rate in September, Italy's statistics agency Istat said on Friday.
The increase, which was well above the European Central Bank's eurozone inflation target of 2%, was mainly due to rising energy, food and transport prices, the agency said.
It comes, however, as the eurozone economy grew more than expected in the third quarter, official data showed Friday, demonstrating resilience despite the impact of the Middle East war and surging energy costs.
Economists said the single currency area's growth held up well but warned of the potential for stagflation - a nightmare mix of stagnant growth and high inflation.
The EU's statistics agency said GDP across the 21-country euro area expanded by 0.4% in the third quarter, a slowdown from the 0.6% seen in the second quarter.
The figure was higher than the 0.2% predicted by economists surveyed by Bloomberg.
But Ireland's whopping 5.5% growth in the third quarter skewed the data, as economists said the euro area grew by 0.2% excluding Ireland.
"The eurozone economy seems to have shrugged off the Middle East crisis," ING chief economist Bert Colijn said in a note. "Despite a worsening energy shock, the economy continues to be resilient."
He pointed to European industry benefiting from higher spending on defence and infrastructure, as well as the tech boom.
Paolo Grignani, senior economist at Oxford Economics, said the data "paint a mixed picture for the eurozone with stagflationary tendencies: GDP growth held up well, but national inflation releases surprised to the upside".
Eurozone inflation hit a three-year high of 3.8% in September, as the US-Israel war on Iran fuelled a surge in energy prices.
With Europe heading for winter, experts warned there are challenges ahead.
Colijn said that "steadily" rising energy costs, including gas prices, means Europe "will see an additional growth challenge" in the winter.
Uneven' picture
The growth came despite France, the euro area's second-biggest economy, recording a quarterly GDP contraction of 0.1%, deepening concerns about its public finances and growing political tensions ahead of presidential elections next spring.
The figure means that France's economy has not grown at all in 2026.
There is already growing concern about France's problems since the country's bond yields - which affect the cost of government borrowing - surged to their highest levels since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year's budget.
Meanwhile, growth in Germany, Europe's largest economy, was higher than expected at 0.2% in the July to September period, after expanding by 0.3% in the second quarter.
Italy recorded no economic growth in the third quarter, while Spain maintained its rhythm at 0.6% GDP growth in the third quarter.
"Growth is becoming increasingly uneven across countries, with Germany and Spain gaining traction while France and Italy slow," Oxford Economics' Grignani said in a note.

Turkic states vow stronger ties in Ankara Declaration

21:29:36 KST

Leaders of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) adopted the Ankara Declaration at their 13th summit in the Turkish capital on Oct. 30, pledging to deepen cooperation as Türkiye assumed the organization’s rotating chairmanship.
The 163-point declaration stressed solidarity among Turkic states amid growing global uncertainty.
The leaders welcomed progress on a proposed treaty on strategic partnership, lasting friendship and brotherhood among member states. They also called for faster work to establish an OTS Cybersecurity Council and a Council for Combating Crime.
The declaration supported exploring the establishment of an OTS Defense Industry College in Türkiye to promote technology sharing and train qualified personnel.
On transport, the leaders backed efforts to develop the Trans-Caspian East-West Middle Corridor and integrate the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway line at full capacity.
The declaration also called for progress on regional green energy corridors and the mutual recognition of electronic signatures among member states. It supported efforts to promote a common Turkic alphabet comprising 34 letters.
On regional conflicts, the leaders reiterated calls for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza, the delivery of humanitarian aid and a lasting two-state solution. They also stressed the need for a sustainable settlement in Cyprus based on realities on the island and for safeguarding the rights of Turkish Cypriots.

‘Scared of crossing the border’: The Arizona farmers who rely on Mexican workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:28:44 UTC
21:28:44 KST

‘Scared of crossing the border’: The Arizona farmers who rely on Mexican workers
From our correspondent in Arizona – The vast produce farms of Yuma County, Arizona, rely heavily on foreign workers who cross the border every day from Mexico. John Boelts, a farmer and staunch supporter of US President Donald Trump, praises the administration’s strict border controls – though he says that competing Republican factions have complicated efforts to hire foreign labourers.
A melon in one hand and a machete in the other, John Boelts squints at the fruit, carves off a hunk and pops it in his mouth. Out in his sprawling fields in Yuma, Arizona, he knows how to spot a ripe cantaloupe. Even in early October, the temperature still reaches 43°C (109°F) in the region after having soared to a scorching 47°C at the start of September – well above the seasonal average. The harvest begins next week.
“The melons are starting to pull sugar, they are getting ready,” he said, dressed in jeans and a pristine checkered shirt.
“Once they're ready to harvest, you typically have about two days to get the melons harvested and off the vine.”
Last spring, this race against the clock took a heavy toll. Even as the produce stood ripe in the fields, the Mexican labourers he had hired to bring in the crop still hadn’t received their working visas. They finally arrived, six days late.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
They lost most of two or three fields, he said, adding that it could have cost him as much as $100,000.
“Those fields were the fields we probably could have made the most money off of during the spring season this year – we were super frustrated.”
Boelts, 49, is one of the main figures of this agricultural sector that depends so deeply on foreign labour. He sits at the head of Desert Premium Farms, an agricultural operation he set up with his wife Alicia and another couple. He also presides over the Arizona Farm Bureau.
North America's 'winter salad bowl'
To get to the Boelts’ farm, you first have to go through Wellton, a small town in the middle of the Sonora Desert. The roads cut straight between the fields, bordered by clay-coloured mountains. Here, there are no hedges or trees, just vast fields in brown and green, dotted with tractors and workers tending row after row of lettuce, covered head to toe to shield them from the sun.
Standing in the arid landscape, it’s hard to imagine that this region grows between 70 to 90 percent of all the leafy greens and vegetables consumed by the US and Canada during the long winter stretch between November and April.
Irrigation channels bring water from the Colorado River to nourish sweeping fields of lettuce, broccoli, cauliflower, spinach and melon – the fields of Yuma bring forth these greens on a massive scale, earning southwest Arizona its reputation as North America’s “winter salad bowl”.
These farms rely heavily on foreign workers – many of whom live on the other side of the border in San Luis Rio Colorado, in Mexico. In the high season, around 15,000 farm labourers cross the border every day to work in American fields, according to the Arizona Farm Bureau.
The hardline immigration policies put into place by US President Donald Trump, including the mass detention and deportation of suspected undocumented migrants by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, have only complicated the flow of workers.
Read moreWhy Trump wants H-1B skilled worker visas to cost employers more than $100,000
‘People are scared’
One man spoke to FRANCE 24 near an irrigation canal while helping his coworkers shift heavy pipes, explaining in Spanish that some labourers have become more reluctant to cross the border since Trump returned to power.
“They’re not comfortable with the laws, they think they won’t come anymore because of the problems linked to immigration,” said Alan, who has worked these fields for five years. “It’s not as easy as it was before – things have really become more complicated under Trump. People are scared of crossing the border, because they can get sent off to other places.”
In another field, Ana said that she now has to anticipate long lines at the border crossing. She said she regularly gets there at 1am to avoid missing the bus that brings workers from the border to the fields.
“Sometimes we wait one or two hours in line,” she said.
Ana said that she had, however, noticed a recent reduction in the wait time, which she attributes to the renovation and expansion of the border crossing. “It’s really modern, and a little bit faster,” she said.
Once in the fields, Ana works beneath the pounding sun, skin hidden behind long sleeves, gloves, and a black cap and mask. Around her, colleagues work to the sound of music. It’s tiring work, she said, but she appreciates the solidarity she feels with her fellow workers.
“We know each other really well,” she said. “We support each other, and we make a good team. And in any case it’s very pleasant to work in the fields, in the open air."
The work continues until midday.
No one comes around looking for work
To work his fields, Boelts directly employs between 30 to 50 workers and puts out calls for teams of between 30 to 100 temporary workers every day. Almost all of them are Mexican.
“We're short of workers in American agriculture,” he said. “Each year, for the last 20 years, we've been more in need of people. No one hardly ever comes around looking for work – it's pretty rare to have somebody come asking if they can work for us.”
Workers on his farm are paid above the minimum wage, and sometimes more than $20 an hour depending on the technical skills required for different tasks, he said.
Read moreThird-country removals: Trump’s deportation policy by the numbers
“We'd be glad to hire folks that are here in the country, a legal workforce here in the country,” he said. “But we don't have it.”
Of the more than 415,000 job listings in agriculture posted over the 2025 fiscal year, just 182 received domestic applications. For Boelts, the conclusions are simple enough to draw – there just aren’t enough willing US workers to meet the industry’s needs.
Farming is about more than just picking fruit, he said. Bringing in a harvest requires specific skills, and not every worker is suited to each position.
“The federal government wrongly thinks that people who work in agriculture are unskilled workers,” he said. “It’s absolutely not the case.”
Bringing in ‘guest workers’
To hire foreign workers legally, farmers can apply through the H-2A visa programme set up in 1986. It only allows employers to hire foreign workers temporarily if they are unable to find US citizens to fill the posts.
Employers are first required to establish that they have tried to recruit locally, as well as to respect basic obligations around salaries, accommodation and transport.
While Boelts considers the programme essential to his business, he complained that navigating the system often felt like running an obstacle course.
“If the programme was easier to work with, streamlined and simpler to use – if you didn't have to hire a professional HR team and lawyers to be able to work with the federal government, to have to work with four or five federal agencies, wait nine months, plan nine months in advance for the workers you need ... the whole idea is crazy, really,” he said.
The sight of melons wasting in their fields shows how costly this system can be. Boelts is calling for the scheme to be reformed, as called for by Republican Congressman Glenn “GT” Thompson, who has been arguing for the programme’s modernisation in Congress.
Boelts credits the Trump administration for trying to streamline the programme, while at the same time slamming the political obstacles that he said are holding up the reforms.
“It's getting derailed by folks that are telling all kinds of lies, that talk about the H-2A programme like it's an immigration programme,” he said. “It's not. It's a guest worker programme.”
For Boelts, the distinction is fundamental: bringing in foreign workers on a temporary basis to meet specific needs has nothing to do with opening up the US southern border.
‘Tired of being a political football’
He is not shy about his support for the current administration.
“I think President Trump and [Agriculture Secretary Brooke] Rollins are doing an amazing job,” he said, though he suggested that the president could sometimes let himself be steered in the wrong direction.
He called on Trump to publicly defend the H-2A visa programme reforms.
“Farmers are tired of being a political football,” he said. “We're tired of being left with certain administrations making things more difficult.” He added that he hoped the Republicans would be able to work together on agriculture after the upcoming midterm elections.
For Boelts, the priority is securing the border while still ensuring there are legal pathways for the foreign workers that the US economy needs.
He said that one of his employees was struck in the head by a “drug trafficker” while watering the fields at night in an apparent attempt to steal his vehicle. The attacker fled over the border to Mexico, he said, with his haul in tow.
“That's the sort of crap we have to put up with here,” he said. “Our border regions can be safe places of legal commerce, and they don't have to be places where there's contraband and human smuggling going on.”
Boelts said he doesn't see workers getting more worried about crossing the border – but not everyone agrees.
“We live in a community here where 15,000 people cross the border each morning from November until sometime in March, when the season starts to wind down,” he said. “Those people aren't afraid to come to work ... I have not seen them act in fear. People that have a legal right to work, they go to work. That's it.”
In the fields, the day’s work goes on. The labourers will soon be able to take a short lunch break before returning to the fields for a few more hours’ work. Later in the afternoon, once their work is done, they will get back in the buses that will take them across the border to San Luis.
Behind the difficulties of recruiting, another anxiety is weighing more and more heavily on the minds of Arizona’s farmers: the growing scarcity of water, a crucial issue in the midterms.
So far, priority water rights have spared Yuma’s farms from the restrictions imposed on the Colorado River by the Trump administration since August.
But Boelts worries that this protection may soon not be enough.
“The only reason the system hasn't run dry is agriculture typically isn't using its full allocation,” he said. “We're worried we're going to be up against it in the next year or two.”

Man who ran over cyclist and dragged him under car for a mile convicted of murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:28:21 UTC
21:28:21 KST

A motorist who drove through give-way markings, collided with a cyclist and then dragged him, trapped under his car, for more than a mile has been found guilty of murder.
Simon Richardson, 35, crashed into headteacher Michael Mullins, 56, who was cycling home from work at Stretford grammar school, Greater Manchester, on the evening of 20 April. Mullins hit the bonnet and windscreen of Richardson’s Volvo XC90 and then went under the car, becoming entangled in the suspension.
Richardson continued to drive for more than a mile, knowing that the trapped cyclist was just inches under his feet, a trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court heard.
Members of Mullins’ family were in tears after the guilty verdict was delivered on Friday. The trial judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, discharged jurors from taking jury service again for 10 years and told them: “This was, I know, an upsetting case and there was evidence which you may have found distressing.”
Richardson had denied knowing the father-of-two was under his car but the prosecutor Phil Barnes KC said the defendant knew “and he inevitably knew what the consequences of driving on would be, and he did it anyway”.
“For a split second after the collision, for a brief moment, he possibly thought about doing the right thing and getting out and taking ownership of what he had just done and help the man he had just run down.
“But Simon Richardson did not get out. He did not do the right thing. He chose to drive away. The obvious reason is because he wanted to escape the consequences of what he had just done.”
Richardson’s front-seat passenger, his cousin Gabrielle Debotte, told the trial they both heard “moaning” from outside as he drove away from the collision scene. Giving evidence for the prosecution, she said Richardson went on to say: “He’s under the car.”
The collision happened in the village of Warburton. The court heard Richardson drove to a secluded farm track in Lymm, 1.3 miles away, in an attempt to dislodge Mullins.
After he stopped, Richardson twice tried to pull Mullins out, before returning to the car and driving sharply and deliberately from side to side before mounting a grass verge, the court heard. Mullins was finally released but was then driven over again as Richardson reversed and drove away.
A motorcyclist followed a trail of blood from the collision spot and discovered Mullins alone and barely breathing on the grass verge, the court heard. Emergency services attended but were unable to save Mullins, from Northwich, Cheshire, who died from multiple injuries.
Richardson was arrested the next day after a police vehicle pursuit. He denied murder as he claimed he did not realise Mullins was underneath his car and said he did not get out of his vehicle to try to free him.
In a statement, the family of Mullins said: “He was devoted to his family and our lives will never be the same. A gap has been left in our hearts and within his role as a headteacher of Stretford grammar school.”
In his closing speech to jurors on Tuesday, Jaime Hamilton KC, defending, said: “You are likely to hold Simon Richardson in contempt. That contempt may well manifest itself in a loathing of Simon Richardson and, in fairness, you are probably right to. Because it is right that we acknowledge it was the actions of Simon Richardson that led to the death of Michael Mullins.
“Not only is he responsible for the death of Michael Mullins, he acted in the most selfish of ways with one thought in his mind – himself. But that does not make him guilty of the homicide offences on this indictment.”
Jurors went out to consider their verdict on Wednesday and returned to find Richardson guilty on Friday. The judge said she would sentence him on Monday.

Kazakhstan’s Current Priorities in a New Historical Cycle  - Kazakh President's Address to Nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
