DR Congo: Hunger deepens for millions amid conflict, Ebola and climate shocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

DR Congo: Hunger deepens for millions amid conflict, Ebola and climate shocks
More than 28 million people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) are not getting enough to eat and the number is expected to tick up in the coming months, according to the latest alert from the IPC global food security monitor.
The DRC continues to confront a severe food security crisis due to persistent conflict in the east, widespread displacement, an expanding Ebola outbreak, economic shocks and the potential impacts of the El Niño weather pattern.
The IPC is a UN-backed platform that uses a five-phase scale to classify the severity of food insecurity, with level 5 being famine.
Read our UN News explainer here
High levels of hunger
Roughly 28.8 million people, or 23 per cent of the population analysed, are forecast to experience high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) through December.
More than 3.6 million people, three per cent, are facing emergency conditions or IPC Phase 4.
The alert covers the period from September 2026 through next June and was published against the backdrop of the record Ebola outbreak that is about to enter a six month, with more than 10,000 cases as of this week.
The crisis first emerged in Ituri province in the volatile eastern region – where armed groups have terrorised the population for decades - and has now spread to eight provinces nationwide.
Deterioration in the east
“While the national proportion of the population in Phase 3 or above is only marginally higher than in the previous analysis, conditions have deteriorated more markedly in the northeastern and eastern provinces,” the alert said.
North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri remain the hardest-hit provinces, with 10.4 million people in Phase 3 or above, while four territories within them - Djugu, Fizi, Shabunda and Walungu - are classified in Phase 4.
Among those most affected are displaced persons, returnees, refugees and poor households.
“In eastern DRC, conflict and violence continue to drive displacement, disrupt livelihoods and restrict access to food and markets,” the alert said.
“A rapidly expanding Ebola outbreak, recurrent disease epidemics, rising food and fuel prices, and the impacts of floods and other climate shocks are compounding vulnerabilities,” leaving millions of people with only limited means to guard against hunger.
Conditions set to worsen
The IPC expects food security to worsen slightly from January to June. Some 30.3 million people are projected to face Phase 3 or above, including 4.2 million who are likely to face Phase 4.
The increase will be driven by continued conflict and displacement, the spread of Ebola, and the anticipated impacts of El Niño, including flooding that could disrupt agricultural production and market access.
Other factors include rising food, fuel and agricultural input prices, along with declining humanitarian assistance.

FACTBOX - From Binance to Bybit: The biggest cryptocurrency heists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:59:36 UTC
20:59:36 KST

- Binance breach involving estimated $6.3B in assets could become the largest cryptocurrency theft on record
- Bybit, Poly Network, Ronin Network and Coincheck among platforms previously targeted in major attacks
- Hackers have exploited weaknesses in digital wallets, transaction approval systems and blockchain networks
A cyberattack on Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, on Thursday has drawn fresh attention to cryptocurrency theft, with blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs estimating that about $6.36 billion was transferred out of its wallets across 10 blockchains.
Most transfers took place within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs attributed the operation, with high confidence, to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group.
Binance said its preliminary investigation pointed to a potentially compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. In a statement on Friday, it estimated the impact at around $6.3 billion and said about $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.
The exchange said user funds were safe, pledged to cover losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company funds, and reported no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. The investigation remains ongoing.
The incident ranks among the largest reported cryptocurrency thefts. Here are some of the biggest cases, based on the estimated value of assets at the time. 
Bybit, Feb. 2025 – $1.5 billion
Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange Bybit suffered one of the largest digital asset thefts on Feb. 21, 2025, when hackers stole approximately $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency from an Ethereum cold wallet.
The attackers compromised the transaction approval process, tricking authorized signers into approving a malicious transaction.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) attributed the attack to North Korea, identifying the operation as part of a hacking campaign known as TraderTraitor.
The FBI said the attackers rapidly converted some of the stolen assets into bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, distributing them across thousands of addresses on multiple blockchains. 
Ronin Network, March 2022 – $620 million
The Ronin Network, a blockchain platform associated with the online game Axie Infinity, lost cryptocurrency worth almost $620 million after attackers compromised its transaction-validation system.
Hackers gained control of private keys belonging to validators, enabling them to approve unauthorized withdrawals.
The US Treasury Department attributed the March 2022 attack to Lazarus Group, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking organization.
The department said the group had stolen almost $620 million from the blockchain project. 
Poly Network, Aug. 2021 – $611 million
A hacker exploited a vulnerability in Poly Network, a decentralized finance platform that enables transfers between different blockchains, stealing digital assets worth more than $610 million.
The platform said the attacker began returning the assets within days of the incident.
By Aug. 23, almost all the funds had been returned, apart from some stablecoins frozen by their issuer, media reported.
The hacker claimed the attack was intended to expose a security weakness in the platform. Poly Network offered a $500,000 reward for information about the vulnerability and the return of the funds. 
BNB Chain, Oct. 2022 – $586 million
An attacker exploited a vulnerability in the BSC Token Hub, a cross-chain bridge connecting two BNB blockchain networks, and withdrew around 2 million BNB tokens worth approximately $586 million.
BNB Chain said the attacker had exploited a flaw in the verification of cross-chain messages.
The network coordinated with validators to suspend operations and limit the movement of the affected assets.
Coinbase's threat intelligence team later published a technical analysis explaining how the attacker forged security proofs to exploit the bridge.
The initial amount involved did not translate into an equivalent financial loss, as much of the cryptocurrency remained on the network or was frozen. 
Coincheck, Jan. 2018 – $530 million
Japanese cryptocurrency exchange Coincheck suffered a major attack in January 2018, when hackers stole approximately 526.3 million NEM tokens from an internet-connected wallet.
The stolen assets were valued at around $530 million at the time, according to media reports.
The incident prompted Japan's Financial Services Agency to order improvements to Coincheck's operations and examine security arrangements at other cryptocurrency exchanges.
Coincheck later said it had compensated affected customers for the stolen funds, according to company filings. 
Mt. Gox, 2011–2014 – $480 million
Tokyo-based bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox collapsed in 2014 after disclosing that hundreds of thousands of bitcoins had gone missing through thefts spanning several years.
The missing cryptocurrency was valued at close to $500 million at the time, according to reports.
Mt. Gox, which once handled a large share of global bitcoin trading, filed for bankruptcy in 2014, leaving thousands of customers unable to access their funds. 
Wormhole, Feb. 2022 – $325 million
Wormhole, a platform connecting different blockchain networks, was exploited in February 2022, resulting in the theft of approximately $320 million in cryptocurrency.
Hackers exploited a vulnerability in the platform's verification process to create tokens without providing the required backing.
Media reported that Jump Crypto, whose parent company had acquired Wormhole's developer, replaced the stolen funds. 
Liquid Network, Sept. 2026 – $319 million
Attackers drained about $319 million in bitcoin from Liquid Network, a Bitcoin sidechain operated by Blockstream, on Sept. 6, 2026.
TRM Labs said the attackers exploited a software vulnerability to create unbacked synthetic bitcoin tokens and exchange them for real bitcoin.
About 85% of the funds, worth roughly $272 million, were later returned after Blockstream patched the vulnerability. Around $47 million remained with the attackers, according to the firm.

EU deforestation law faces enforcement test as palm oil giants risk violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:58:39 UTC
20:58:39 KST

After several setbacks, the EU's anti-deforestation rules are due to take force on 30 December 2026.
Some of the world's biggest consumer goods companies risk breaching the European Union's deforestation law through palm oil sourced from Indonesian plantations accused of illegal activities, according to investigations by Indonesian environmental organisations and government authorities.
The findings come as the EU's anti-deforestation rules are due to take force on 30 December 2026, following repeated delays and political pressure from EU governments and industry seeking to soften or delay the law.
The bloc's anti-deforestation law requires suppliers of cocoa, coffee, soy, palm oil, wood, rubber and beef to prove their goods are not linked to deforestation in exchange for access to the EU market.
The law has faced repeated political setbacks, with its implementation delayed amid concerns about administrative costs, traceability requirements and the burden on businesses and trading partners.
Several countries producing such goods, like Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Colombia, Ghana, and the United States, have also lobbied Brussels to reconsider the law.
US Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder has strongly criticised the bloc's law, labelling it as over-regulation, selective protectionism and an unnecessary non-tariff trade barrier.
Now the Indonesian investigation raises questions about whether the EU will enforce its environmental rules as planned, despite growing pressure to ease regulatory burdens on companies.
Environmental groups WALHI Kalteng, TuK Indonesia and Sawit Watch traced links between plantations in Indonesia's Central Kalimantan province and major international consumer brands.
Companies identified as recent buyers of palm oil from the plantation include PepsiCo, Unilever, Ferrero, Mondelez and Procter & Gamble, among others.
Their investigation identified signs of deforestation in 2024 at the palm oil plantation PT Karya Makmur Abadi, a subsidiary of the KLK Group, a rubber company, despite the law's cut-off date of 31 December 2020.
Under EU rules, if a forest was cut down after that date, products like coffee, beef, wood, or palm oil are completely banned from the EU market.
But the Indonesian findings indicate a risk that palm oil from land cleared after the cut-off date could enter the EU market. However, they didn't establish that every named company has violated the law.
Indonesia has been losing its forests at one of the fastest rates in the world because of illegal logging, mining, new oil palm plantations and slash-and-burn land clearing.
Devastating wildfires sweeping across Indonesia have also been linked to decades of deforestation and forest degradation. Environmental activists warned that clearing forests to make way for agricultural production, including oil palm plantations, leaves landscapes more vulnerable to fires.
Achmad Surambo, executive director of the NGO Sawit Watch, said Europe’s largest palm oil buyers have failed to self-police their involvement in deforestation and environmental destruction.
"Indonesian communities want immediate and strong enforcement of European supply chain sustainability regulations,” said Surambo.
Perrine Fournier, a trade and forest campaigner at global NGO Fern, said the Indonesian's findings reveal the country's palm oil industry "remains tainted by illegality," emboldened by the fact that major international corporations and European consumers are enmeshed in it.
"The investigation underlines why the EUDR (EU's anti-deforestation law) can be a crucial tool in halting the biggest cause of deforestation on earth: clearing land for agricultural commodities such as palm oil, as well as the pivotal role that NGOs can play in ensuring its success," said Fournier.
"It’s now incumbent on the Competent Authorities responsible for enforcing the EUDR (EU's anti-deforestation law) to act on these findings.”
The looming December date will be a litmus test for Brussels to prove it can pivot from negotiating environmental ambitions to actually enforcing them.

Kyiv Builds Backup Crossings as Russia Targets Bridges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:57:23 UTC
20:57:23 KST

Ukraine has begun building backup river crossings in Kyiv, with the first expected to open in early 2027 as Russia steps up attacks on bridges, Infrastructure Minister Mykola Kalashnyk told parliament on Friday, Oct. 30.
The construction forms part of a government program for 21 alternative crossings across Ukraine, including routes over the Dnipro River, Suspilne reported from the parliamentary session.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Work in Kyiv has already begun. The first bridges will start operating at the beginning of the year,” Kalashnyk said.
Kalashnyk said Russia had systematically attacked bridges over the past month to disrupt transport and logistics, citing strikes in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Kharkiv.
The central government is responsible for implementing the alternative crossings program, he added.
“Work in Kyiv has already begun. The first bridges will start operating at the beginning of the year,’’ said Kalashnyk.
South Bridge gradually reopens
Kyiv is also partially reopening its South Bridge after a Russian attack damaged the crossing on Oct. 27.
The Kyiv City State Administration said traffic would gradually resume from Oct. 30 on one lane from the left bank to the right bank. Vehicles weighing up to 10 metric tons (22,000 pounds), including passenger cars, are permitted.
Traffic in the opposite direction remains suspended while technical work continues. The partial reopening follows an inspection by the National Institute for Infrastructure Development.
Independent Russian Newspaper Novaya Gazeta Shuts Under Kremlin Pressure
Specialists are also drawing up repairs to damaged structures, including those supporting the metro line.
The Oct. 27 attack disrupted the Green Line, forcing trains to operate on separate sections on either side of the Dnipro. The crossing carries both road traffic and metro services.
Kyiv plans $22 million for backup crossings
Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced on Oct. 27 that Kyiv would allocate Hr. 1 billion ($22 million) for combined water crossings over the Dnipro and their access roads.
The proposal was discussed at a meeting of the Kyiv Defense Council. According to Klitschko, military commanders would determine the locations, subject to approval by the Kyiv City Military Administration.
Klitschko said the initiative followed a government resolution and was led by the state.
The defense council also discussed protecting existing bridges, with municipal specialists and military officials putting forward measures.
Strikes disrupt travel between Kyiv’s banks
Russian strikes have repeatedly disrupted movement between Kyiv’s two banks since the beginning of October.
On Oct. 2, bridge closures and restrictions caused major traffic jams, delayed buses and trolleybuses, and prompted some commuters to abandon vehicles and continue on foot.
The South Bridge was closed in both directions, while restrictions on the Paton and Metro bridges pushed more traffic onto alternative routes. Several bus services were diverted, and passengers faced long waits at stops.
Kyiv City Express continued running between the banks, providing an alternative as road transport struggled.
Engineers have warned that bridges can be disabled without collapsing. Repeated strikes can force temporary closures for inspections and repairs, while damage to vulnerable joints or other structural elements can create further risks.
Infrastructure specialists have also cautioned that pontoon crossings would carry far less traffic than permanent bridges. They require suitable access roads and ramps, and vehicles would generally travel more slowly.

Uzbek president calls for closer unity around ‘strategic goals’ at OTS leaders’ summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:57:20 UTC
20:57:20 KST

Burc Eruygur
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on Friday called for closer unity around their “strategic goals” as he addressed the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in the Turkish capital Ankara.
“We must unite even more firmly around our strategic goals and advance our interests together on the international stage,” Mirziyoyev told the 13th OTS leaders’ summit, expressing that they all share the same vision in this context and are “prepared to mobilize all our strength for the sake of Turkic solidarity.”
Describing the OTS as a partnership platform rooted in mutual trust and practical cooperation, Mirziyoyev said armed conflicts and disputes in the vicinity of the Turkic world are negatively affecting not only security but also other matters, including economic relations and transport links.
Mirziyoyev underlined the importance of holding regular political consultations within the OTS on current international and regional issues, noting that the organization’s global effectiveness and reputation depend on its ability to develop ties with external partners.
He proposed to commence cooperation with third countries under the “OTS+” format, saying discussions held should focus on concrete joint projects in areas such as trade, transport, and investment.
He further noted the need to deepen technological cooperation and develop industrial partnerships that would enable joint entry into the global market.
“As a concrete step, I propose the adoption of a program encompassing 100 strategic joint investment and industrial projects for the Turkic world. It is of particular importance that resources from the Turkic Investment Fund and international financial institutions be directed toward these projects,” Mirziyoyev added.
He also said that, in the current climate of shifting global supply chains, the geographical location and transit capabilities of the Turkic states are gaining increasing strategic significance.
"To expand our countries' participation in international freight transport and logistics, and to increase our economic gains, we must transform the Middle Corridor – along with other connecting transport corridors – into an integrated economic system," Mirziyoyev said.
Additionally, he proposed the establishment of a network of logistics complexes among Turkic states, which would be managed collectively, saying this initiative would strengthen regional cooperation in transport and trade.

Türkiye's 9-month tourism revenue reaches record $51.3B, tourism minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:56:37 UTC
20:56:37 KST

Özlem Limon
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Türkiye's tourism revenue climbed 2.4% year-on-year to reach a record $51.28 billion in the first nine months of 2026, Turkish Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said on Friday.
Speaking at a news conference at the Ataturk Cultural Center in Istanbul, Ersoy presented the sector's performance for the third quarter and the January-September period.
The country welcomed 49.13 million visitors during the first nine months of the year, including 23.37 million in the third quarter alone.
Russia topped the list of source markets with 5.7 million visitors, followed by Germany with 5.17 million and the UK with 3.2 million.
Average visitor stays stood at 10.34 nights in the first nine months and 10.69 nights in the third quarter.
Average spending per night rose 4.6% year-on-year to $107.70 across all visitors in the nine-month period, with foreign tourists spending an average of $119.90 per night and expatriate citizens spending $72.20.
Ersoy noted that regional conflicts, airspace restrictions and rising energy prices have driven up aviation costs and pressured international travel demand throughout the year.
"While all these negative developments are occurring in our region, Türkiye stands out as an island of stability through its strong state structure, diplomatic capacity and efforts for peace and stability led by our president," Ersoy said.
"When activity slows in one market, we can intensify our efforts in other markets and replan our promotional and marketing activities according to developments," he added.
Ersoy said promotional campaigns carried out by the Türkiye Tourism Promotion and Development Agency generated 7.1 billion digital impressions across 74 countries.
Additionally, 10 promotional miniseries highlighting destinations such as Cappadocia, Bodrum, Izmir, Ankara and the Black Sea reached 10.5 billion views globally during 2025 and 2026.
He said the ministry aims to expand tourism demand across all 81 provinces and throughout the year through initiatives such as the Heritage for the Future archaeological project and night museum access.
Looking ahead, Ersoy stated that Türkiye will intensify efforts in high-growth-potential markets, including the US, Canada, Asia, Africa and Australia, while expanding direct flight capacity in partnership with Turkish Airlines and tour operators.
He also emphasized that the ministry will make more effective use of data and artificial intelligence applications to monitor market demand, visitor preferences and campaign results.
Third-quarter tourism revenue rose 5% year-on-year to $25.53 billion, pushing both quarterly and nine-month revenues to the highest levels in the republic's history, Ersoy concluded.

UN Honors Forestami Project, Calling It a ‘Model for Ecosystem Restoration’
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:56:29 CET
20:56:29 KST

At COP17 on biodiversity, the United Nations awarded the Metropolitan City of Milan’s Forestami reforestation project the World Restoration Flagship designation, recognizing it as an international benchmark for ecosystem restoration. The announcement of the award took place, as explained by the Italian Embassy in Armenia, at the United Nations Conference on Biodiversity currently underway in Yerevan, and Italy was the only European country honored by the UN in 2026, 
along with other initiatives underway in China, Colombia, Ethiopia, and the United States.
                                    
Forestami was launched in 2019 as a scientific research project on the potential and benefits of urban reforestation in the Milan metropolitan area and involves citizens, citizens, local communities, institutions, associations, and companies in the shared responsibility of mitigating climate change by planting 3 million new trees by 2030. The Metropolitan City of Milan’s urban reforestation project is based on research conducted by the Polytechnic University of Milan and aims to bring nature back into the city by increasing the number of trees and restoring space for ecosystems in a densely urbanized area. Forestami aims to increase Milan’s tree cover by 5% through the planting of three million trees—roughly one for every resident of the area—and the subsequent redevelopment of 255 hectares of urban areas.
                                    
Nature in metropolitan areas can, in fact, help moderate temperatures, counteract the heat island effect, improve air quality, promote biodiversity, and serve as an ally in coping with the increasingly sudden and violent events linked to climate change.
                                    
“When we first began envisioning the project, we asked ourselves, above all, how much CO₂ three million new trees could absorb in our metropolitan area,” said architect Stefano Boeri, creator and founder of Forestami. “ We started on our own, then sought to involve everyone who could share this mission. Forestami was born from the idea of bringing nature back to the city. To do this, a territorial approach is needed, in which trees and vegetation become an integral part of urban infrastructure, helping to redesign streets, public spaces, and neighborhoods. However, a transformation of this magnitude can only be achieved through a shared vision and the collaboration of many different stakeholders.” “Forestami brings together institutions, municipalities, local communities, businesses, and multidisciplinary teams,” he added, “who work across various fields of expertise toward a common goal. The UN’s recognition as one of the World Restoration Flagships attests to the collective commitment to rethinking the relationship between cities and nature and to making ecosystem restoration an integral part of how we plan and transform the metropolitan landscape.”
   The award was accepted in Yerevan by Maria Chiara Pastore, scientific director of Forestami and professor at the Politecnico di Milano, alongside Italian Ambassador to Armenia Alessandro Ferranti, representing the Italian government. Ambassador Ferranti expressed his honor at receiving the award on behalf of Italy and congratulated the Politecnico di Milano, the City of Milan, the Metropolitan City of Milan, the Lombardy Region, and all the organizations, institutions, businesses, associations, and citizens who have contributed to Forestami. In thanking the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the ambassador reaffirmed Italy’s commitment to promoting ecosystem restoration as a fundamental pillar for the protection of biodiversity, climate action, and the building of a sustainable future for present and future generations.

Premier Giorgia Meloni has said her
government's staunch support for Kyiv as it battles the Russian
forces of invasion has cost her in political terms, while adding
that she does not intend to change stance.
                                    
"I am fully aware that our support for Ukraine may come at a
political cost, that there may even be a segment of our
electorate that disagrees, but I do not intend to change my
position," Meloni told veteran Italian TV journalist Bruno Vespa
in an interview for his new book, excerpts of which have been
released in advance ahead of publication.
                                    
"I do not support Ukraine simply for the sake of the Ukrainians.
                                    
"I do it for Italy. An international scenario in which law of
the militarily strongest is the only one that prevails is not in
our nation's interest.
                                    
"This is not a political opinion; it is a fact".
                                    
Deputy premier, Transport Minister and League leader Matteo
Salvini has repeatedly expressed scepticism about the policy of
supporting Kyiv and said he would seek to stop Italy's economic
and military support for Ukraine after being re-elected leader
of the right-wing League party on Sunday.

of aid for Ukraine was in the pipeline.

UP: Kravchenko stopped at border over NABU and SAPO flag, let through after call from Kyiv

UP: Kravchenko was stopped at border as flagged by anti-corruption agencies but let through after call from Kyiv
According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, then-prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko was prevented from crossing into Poland at the Shehyni crossing point due to a flag from the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), but was allowed through following a phone call from Kyiv.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda's investigation CarthageProsecutor: Why Ukrainska Pravda journalists were really detained in Vienna (English subtitles coming soon)
Details: UP's sources in law enforcement agencies said that Kravchenko's passport was taken away at Shehyni and not returned for a long time. The reason was reportedly a flag from NABU and SAPO in the border guards' database.
Quote from UP journalist Mykhailo Tkach: "Later, according to the same sources, the border guards received a phone call from Kyiv and let Kravchenko out to Vienna, where Vienna security services may have already been waiting for him."
Background:
- UP found out that Odesa businessman Volodymyr Halanternyk, a suspect in two NABU and SAPO cases, may have helped Kravchenko settle in Vienna. People who allegedly work for the businessman testified against UP journalists who were looking for the former prosecutor general at the building they believed to be his home.
- According to Austrian investigation files, during the interrogation of the journalists, law enforcement officers checked the residence register and confirmed that Kravchenko was registered at the specified address. UP also assumes that Kravchenko may have been guarded by Austrian intelligence services.
- Halanternyk ignored the editorial board's requests. Kravchenko, on the other hand, accused NABU and SAPO of plotting "violent acts" against him. The bureau rejected these accusations, calling them an attempt to secure protection abroad.
- Kravchenko left Ukraine on the night of 13-14 September. Under an order he had signed himself, he was due to spend five days in Paris, allegedly attending hearings on Ukrainian children under the auspices of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. However, his name did not appear on the list of participants in the discussion.
- His business trip ended on 18 September. According to Mariana Haivovska, spokesperson for the Prosecutor General's Office, Kravchenko had not returned to work by 21 September.

Finnish politician accuses Kiev of seeking to derail peace talks

STOCKHOLM, October 30. /TASS/. Ukraine is seeking to derail trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi by continuing large-scale drone attacks on Russian cities, said Armando Mema, a member of Finland’s national conservative Freedom Alliance party.
"If such attacks will continue in the coming week, especially during Russia's Unity Day, the trilateral talks with the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi are at risk of being cancelled," he wrote on X.
"The drone attack against Moscow during the Russia-Africa summit was truly difficult to understand as Ukraine is approaching peace talks with US mediation," Mema said.
"I do hope that Zelensky will not make vanish US efforts for Peace and Diplomacy with such actions," he added.
Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov earlier told reporters that President Vladimir Putin had informed US Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff during their meeting that Moscow was ready to resume trilateral talks around mid-November, focusing primarily on building a security framework for Russia and Ukraine. According to Ushakov, the next round of talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine could take place in Abu Dhabi.

‘Inner Need to Engage With Heritage’ – Ukrainian Singer Khrystyna Soloviy on Stories Through Music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:54:00 UTC
20:54:00 KST

Khrystyna Soloviy, Ukrainian singer-songwriter and musician, belongs to a generation of Ukrainian artists for whom music has become a way to explore national identity and give a voice to stories that have long remained on the margins of the cultural mainstream.
In this exclusive interview with Kyiv Post, Soloviy discusses how Ukrainian music – vibrant, contemporary, and full of surprises – can challenge stereotypes abroad. She also reflects on women’s independence, artists’ responsibility for the stories they choose to tell, and what it means to preserve one’s voice during wartime.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv Post: Russia’s war has profoundly changed Ukrainian culture. What messages are you most determined to convey through your work today?
Khrystyna Soloviy: Fundamentally, nothing has changed for me. My career began in 2014, when Russia launched its war against Ukraine. From the very beginning, I worked with the Ukrainian language, culture, and musical heritage. For me, this has never been a reaction to the political situation or an attempt to respond to public demand.
Of course, the full-scale invasion has changed how we perceive many things and heightened our sense of responsibility for what we do. Today, I feel particularly strongly about exploring our own culture, bringing attention to aspects that have been forgotten or undervalued, and showing just how diverse, bold, and contemporary it is.
Third Political Prisoner Dies in Russia This Month – Report
You frequently perform for Ukrainian service members. What resonates most with them?
I have performed extensively for the military since the first year of the full-scale invasion. I have made many trips, including to dangerous areas, but I have not spoken or posted much about them on social media. This is not something I want to turn into a public gesture.
Music cannot change the circumstances, but it can offer emotional support, provide a moment of escape, or remind people what they are fighting for. For me, these encounters are first and foremost an opportunity to thank the people who make it possible for us to continue doing our work.
What resonates most with Western audiences today?
This summer, I gave some very warm concerts in Poland and the United States. My performance in Warsaw was particularly memorable. When I sang “Liubyi Druh” (“Dear Friend”) and thanked the Polish people for their unwavering support for Ukraine since 2022, neither the audience nor I could hold back our tears. I felt just how powerfully music can bring people together.
I am also especially pleased that this fall, my album “Liubyi Druh” was finally released on vinyl.
This summer, you visited California and met Sestrichka Vika, who moved from Ukraine to the United States in 1993, the year you were born. Viktoriia Vradii was one of the most prominent Ukrainian rock performers of the late 1980s and early 1990s. She won the rock category at the first Chervona Ruta festival in 1989 before launching a solo career under the stage name Sestrichka Vika. What struck you most about meeting her?
Her sincerity impressed me most. She told me how important it is to preserve the child within yourself – to never lose the ability to be amazed by the world. Sestrichka Vika is not a manufactured image or a project. She is a genuine artist whose work is inseparable from who she is.
I encourage everyone to listen to our conversation. At one point, she chose to step away from public life, and I respect that decision. That is why it means so much to me that she allowed me to record my own versions of her songs and have this brief conversation with her.
I will remember for the rest of my life the moment I played her the demo of my version of “Proshchai” (“Farewell”), and she told me it gave her goosebumps.
                                                                                                                                                                         Khrystyna Soloviy with Sestrichka Vika. (Photo via Soloviy’s press office)                             
On Oct. 30, you will release your own version of Sestrichka Vika’s song “Proshchai.” What was most important to you when working on this track?
As a songwriter, it is very important to me to approach other people’s work with care and respect. When recording a cover, you need to find your own voice without losing what makes the original special.
“Proshchai” is an exceptionally precious song to me. Vika wrote it when she was 16, initially inventing words that sounded like English, even though she did not yet know the language. At one point, she performed it at a club where she had been brought to meet the band Arnika. Viktor Morozov was thrilled by the song, and the two later wrote its Ukrainian lyrics together.
I think some songs can only be created at a certain age, when you can experience the world with a particular kind of spontaneity, without trying to explain everything. My debut song, “Trymai” (“Hold On”), has something similar about it for me.
When working on “Proshchai,” I wanted to avoid overshadowing that sincerity with my own interpretation. Instead, I wanted to find a way to convey it through my own experience.
You are working on an album inspired by Ukrainian music of the 1990s, reinterpreting songs that became part of the country’s musical history. How should contemporary Ukrainian artists engage with the legacy of previous generations – not only to preserve it but also to introduce it to new audiences?
I started doing what has become mainstream today back in 2014. I began my career making Ukrainian-language music and exploring Ukrainian culture when our cultural space was still heavily Russified. Back then, I released an album of Lemko folk songs, when “reinterpretation” and “research” weren’t trends.
Today, this has become fashionable, part of popular culture, and sometimes even an expected stage in the career of every contemporary Ukrainian artist. I am genuinely happy about that. I think we are finally beginning to realize just how much we have – and how much we still do not know about our own culture.
At the same time, I would like there to be more behind this than fashion or commercial calculation. There is a risk that Ukrainian culture will become a convenient career-building tool: Today, you turn to it because it is relevant, and tomorrow, you move on to something else when the trend changes.
I would like artists to feel an inner need to engage with our heritage rather than simply feel that it is what they are supposed to do. For me, it is important to see more personal experience reflected in their work – their own traumas, mistakes, doubts, and genuine interests. I want to see a living dialogue.
Your new project dedicated to Ukrainian music of the 1990s will include reinterpretations, duets with iconic Ukrainian artists, and a concert film. What is your greatest creative challenge with this project?
One challenge is avoiding the temptation to make an album of covers. That would be too easy, and I do not think it would offer enough in terms of exploration. That is why the album consists primarily of my own original songs inspired by the lyrics and sound of Ukrainian music from the 1990s.
My sound producer and I are working extensively with instruments and sonic techniques characteristic of that era. The lyrics of my songs also contain a kind of dialogue with the artists who fascinated me back then.
Another important challenge is avoiding a stereotypical portrayal of the 1990s. My album is also about what was pushed aside, forgotten, or left out of the dominant cultural narrative. I am fascinated by how daring, experimental, and sometimes even eccentric Ukrainian music was during those years, while remaining deeply sincere. There will be plenty of unexpected choices on the album.
In a sense, this is a tribute to the artists I listened to as a little girl, watching music charts on television and imitating my idols in front of the screen. I want to return to that childhood sense of wonder, but look at it through the experience I have today – to understand what captivated me back then and how that music shaped the artist I became.
What messages about Ukraine and its culture should be communicated abroad today, and which stereotypes are we ready to leave behind?
We need to shed Soviet-imposed ideas about Ukrainian culture and stop being afraid to present it as modern and experimental.
For example, I am currently working on a song inspired by Komu Vnyz, an iconic Ukrainian band from the 1990s that combined Ukrainian martial lyrics with a heavy rock sound. I am fascinated by their boldness and how different musical languages can be combined without losing one’s identity.
I would like audiences abroad to see Ukrainian culture in precisely this way – as vibrant, contemporary, and capable of surprising them.
                                                                                                                                                                         Khrystyna Soloviy. (Photo via Soloviy’s press office)                             
You were born just a few years after Ukraine restored its independence. How do you think Ukrainian society’s attitudes toward women, their freedom, their choices, and their right to independence have evolved during this time?
I think we have changed a great deal, but genuine equality is still a long way off. Women continue to face numerous prejudices.
A man can express harsh opinions, criticize, and provoke, and this is often perceived as a sign of strength and boldness. When a woman does the same, she risks facing a wave of hate. Even if you write your own songs, you constantly have to prove that your talent as a songwriter is worth something.
A woman is allowed to be pleasant, but not too ambitious or outspoken. The moment she begins to belong to herself – to express her opinions openly, defend her decisions, or determine for herself who she wants to be – she is viewed negatively.
You have had relationships with charismatic, high-profile men. Looking beyond the public headlines and considering those relationships as experiences that shaped you, what did they give you — and what did they take away?
My mentor, Sviatoslav Vakarchuk, once gave me valuable advice: Do not comment on your private life; speak about it only through your songs. I broke that rule at one point, as everyone knows.
Eventually, there were more sensational headlines about me than discussions of my music. I realized that I did not want my private life to overshadow what I do as a songwriter and singer.
So now I have returned to his advice. If you want to know what I went through, what shaped me, or what I lost and found in relationships, look for the answers in my songs.
But I would be even happier if you found yourselves in them, too. Ultimately, that is what music means to me: a personal experience that, at some point, stops belonging exclusively to you and becomes something other people can relate to.
                                                                                                                                                                         Khrystyna Soloviy. (Photo via Soloviy’s press office)                             
Your studio, located on the grounds of the Dovzhenko Film Studios, was damaged in a Russian attack in the summer of 2026. How difficult is it to create music in a space that has been wounded by war?
It happened just as we were releasing the music video for “Druha Nochi” (“Two in the Morning”), a tribute to Ukrainian cinema that we created with support from the Dovzhenko Film Studios.
In the video, we revisit Ukrainian films that Russia has spent decades trying to appropriate or push out of the cultural space. What is happening now only proves that this struggle has never been limited to the informational or cultural sphere.
The studio holds many personal memories for me. It was where we recorded my debut album, “Zhyva Voda” (“Living Water”), and where we completed the recording of my new album about the 1990s. It is not simply a place where I work; it is a space that holds part of my creative history.
We are continuing to finish the album at other locations. I think it is especially important not to stop now. Culture is a way to preserve memory, defend our identity, and continue speaking about ourselves in our own voice.
How do you envision the next stage of your career?
I would love to bring this entire 1990s era to life – to release a full-length album, make a film, and go on tour. Unfortunately, it is very difficult to plan too far ahead right now, so I am trying to focus on what I can do here and now.
At the same time, working on this album has opened up many other creative directions. I can already see the outlines of my next albums.
I also have substantial material in development for a second album of Lemko songs. This is a very special project for me, one I approach with great love. So I do not feel that I will be facing a creative void after the 1990s album.
On the contrary, the deeper I dive into Ukrainian music, the more stories I discover that I want to tell.

Lithuania’s economy contracts 1% in third quarter, economists warn growth is slowing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:54:00 UTC
20:54:00 KST

Lithuania’s economy contracted by 1% in the third quarter compared with the previous three months, recording the sharpest quarterly decline among 15 European Union countries that have reported data, preliminary figures from the State Data Agency and Eurostat showed Friday.
Despite the quarterly decline, gross domestic product grew 2.3% year over year, after seasonal and working-day adjustments, reaching 24.4 billion euros at current prices. Without those adjustments, annual growth stood at 1.8%.
Economists said the figures suggest that a period of rapid economic expansion is coming to an end.
“The third quarter is the first swallow, the first warning that the days of rapid economic growth are over,” Swedbank economist Nerijus Mačiulis told BNS.
Lithuania’s quarterly contraction compared with an average growth rate of 0.5% across the other EU countries that had reported data. France also recorded a decline, of 0.1%. Year over year, Lithuania’s economy grew 2.3%, compared with the EU average of 1.5%.
Construction, information and communications, and transportation and storage were the sectors that made the largest negative contributions to GDP in the third quarter.
Mačiulis said the downturn was likely linked to the fading impact of a consumption surge in the second quarter, when residents spent about 1.5 billion euros withdrawn from second-pillar pension funds.
“That consumption factor has completely faded in the third quarter. Residents are consuming only from their current income – their salaries – and that has reduced GDP,” he said.
SEB economist Tadas Povilauskas noted that pension withdrawals continued to support household consumption in the third quarter, but their impact was weaker. About 745 million euros was transferred to residents in July, considerably less than during the first wave of withdrawals.
Luminor economist Žygimantas Mauricas said the preliminary figures were surprising because retail trade and industrial indicators had been relatively strong, while the housing market had also remained active.
Artea economist Indrė Genytė-Pikčienė said the slowdown was partly expected after the unusually strong second quarter, when the first major wave of pension withdrawals boosted consumption.
The State Data Agency said construction, transportation and information and communications had weighed most heavily on economic performance. Povilauskas said the negative contribution from transportation was unexpected, as there were no clear signs of a significant decline in freight volumes across the EU.
Mauricas suggested that stricter employment procedures for workers from third countries and the relocation of some transport companies’ operations abroad could have contributed to the sector’s weaker performance.
Looking ahead, economists expect slower growth next year. Swedbank forecasts that GDP growth will ease to around 2.8% in 2026, compared with its previous projection of more than 3%, while growth in 2027 is also expected to weaken.
The bank cited the gradual exhaustion of EU recovery funding, slower wage growth, a stagnating labour market, potentially higher European Central Bank interest rates and intensifying competition in export markets.
The Bank of Lithuania expects the economy to grow by about 3% this year and 2.5% in 2027, while SEB previously forecast growth of 3% in 2026 and 2.1% next year.

Finland will establish a military space operations center at the Finnish Air Force headquarters in Tikkakoski on Jan. 1, 2027, Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen announced Friday.
The facility will oversee the Finnish Defense Forces' space activities, including the development, planning and operation of military capabilities, according to the Defense Ministry.
It will also coordinate cooperation with NATO and partner countries.
The center will initially employ around 20 military and civilian personnel, with staffing expected to increase in the coming years.
Hakkanen said the initiative was part of broader efforts to strengthen Finland's defense capabilities as space becomes an increasingly important operational domain.
The country's military space capabilities are based partly on three synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites acquired from Finnish company ICEYE.
The military is expected to take operational control of the satellite system in April 2027.

Aboard the morning high-speed train from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv to Poltava, some 300 kilometres to the east, 24-year-old Daryna Styrchuk was nervous.
“I didn’t sleep well because I was worried about air raid alerts, delays and evacuations,” she told AFP on the journey.

Travelling by train is the only way for her to reach her family – but massive Russian attacks on trains, stations and railway infrastructure have turned simple journeys into dangerous, gruelling heavily delayed expeditions.
On Thursday, a week after AFP travelled with Styrchuk, a Russian drone smashed into a platform next to two waiting trains at Dnipro, killing at least 14 people.
Over Russia’s almost five-year invasion of Ukraine, the railway has become a critically important means of transportation.
With airspace closed to civilian aircraft, travel both within and to and from the country relies heavily on trains.
Since the beginning of 2026 alone, Russian attacks have damaged 4,856 railway facilities, including 380 locomotives and 146 carriages, according to Ukrainian Railways.
“The enemy has chosen our passenger services as a target,” Oleg Golovashchenko, head of the state operator’s passenger company, told AFP.
Amid an uptick in strikes, Ukraine started pausing and evacuating trains when there was the danger of an attack.
Now, every day sees between 100-200 evacuations, triggering widespread hours-long delays across the entire country.

- ‘Everything tightens’ -
The Kharkiv-Kyiv route, which AFP journalists travelled, connects Ukraine’s two largest cities.
Trains trundling to and from the northeastern terminus, some 30 kilometres from the Russian border, stop frequently due to the threat of attack.
As the overnight train departed Kharkiv, passengers preparing to sleep were warned that their rest could be interrupted by an emergency evacuation.
“We brought them aboard the train, we must get them to their destination alive,” train attendant Mykola Kryvenko, 50, told AFP.
Several hours into the journey, the quiet of the carriage was suddenly broken by the sound of hurried footsteps and knocks on compartment doors.
“Evacuation, evacuation,” the train attendant said, waking the slumbering travellers.
Russian drones were nearby.
Within minutes, a platform filled with anxious people listening intently to sounds in the sky, as the attendants urged passengers to move away from the carriages.
The sound of the approaching drone grew louder.
Some started running for cover, moments before the sky lit with an explosion in the near distance.
Unharmed, most of the passengers edged further and further away from the train.
Among them was marketing specialist Kateryna Kumratova, 35, and her four-year-old daughter, Nina.
Asked how she felt, she summed it up in a word: “fear”.
With the sound of drones still heard intermittently in the sky, Kumratova and her daughter headed towards a shelter.
“Everything tightens inside when you realise that the shelter is still far away and your child is beside you,” she said once inside the room.
Another explosion sounded, but within minutes, everyone began returning to the train.
The danger has passed, the crew announced, and the journey continued.
- ‘Ready for anything’ -

Authorities are warning of possible disruptions to electricity, water and heating as Russia’s attacks on energy infrastructure intensify.
And as temperatures drop below freezing, evacuation will become more challenging.
Ukrainian Railways plans to introduce preventative stops to allow passengers to remain on board.
Blankets and heating pads have also been prepared to keep people warm, Golovashchenko said.
Kumratova already carries an extra backpack with warm clothes and other essentials to make evacuations easier to bear for herself and her young daughter.
“It’s still better to travel by train with a child, even despite these evacuations,” she said.
While visibly anxious, Styrchuk said she believed relentless Russian attacks had made Ukrainians more resilient.
“I think we’re ready for anything now.”
