What’s the scariest object in the universe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:42:10 UTC
20:42:10 KST

Ah, autumn. Leaves are falling, days are shortening, and there’s a chill in the air.
But is that just a result of the approaching winter as Earth’s northern axis begins to tip away from the sun? Or is it caused by some other cosmic horror, a cold finger of dread running down your spine as you contemplate the legion of nightmares lurking in the universe all around us?
Space is a scary place. Certainly, many objects in it appear scary to our human brains, and we interpret their shapes as witches and skulls and fiery jack-o’-lanterns. These are in reality relatively harmless illusions whose specific structures only remind us of dreaded visions.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But there are actual terrifying objects in space, entities operating on a scale that crush our minds and reduce our human experience to a mote of dust floating in the dark.
I’m an astronomer, and I’ve studied and written about many of these objects for decades. What, you might wonder, in that vast cosmos, scares me?
There is, in fact, quite a list.
(But first, an aside: While cosmophobia—the dread of space—is not an officially recognized medical condition, I know some folks for whom this is a very real fear. I by no means am trying to enflame anyone’s actual terror, so let me state clearly: while real, the objects and events below are either so far away from us that even the most powerful has less effect on us than a whisper in a hurricane or are so rare that the odds of them occurring in a human lifetime—or even over eons—is so small as to be essentially zero. After all, how many people whom you know have been killed by a supermassive black hole merger?)
So here, let me show you what gives me a preternatural frisson down my back.
Wolf-Rayet Stars
Even the tiniest of stars is humbling on a human scale. TRAPPIST-1, an ultracool red dwarf barely massive enough to ignite nuclear fusion in its core, still releases the equivalent energy as the detonation of more than 50 million one-megaton nuclear bombs every second.
Now imagine the most luminous stars.
These are called Wolf-Rayet stars, and they’re so massive that the pressures and temperatures in their cores are almost beyond comprehension. They fuse hydrogen and helium into heavier elements at such fantastic rates that they blow out truly soul-searing amounts of energy.
R136a1 is just such a star, the most massive star known, at several hundred times the sun’s bulk. It is something like seven million times more luminous than the sun, a number that leaves me somewhat mentally paralyzed. Replace our sun with R136a1, and I fear Earth wouldn’t last long as a solid object. Happily, the star is actually in another galaxy, so distant it’s not even visible to the naked eye. And while there are many Wolf-Rayet stars in our own Milky Way galaxy, they are all still too far to damage us and in fact are fun to study, producing spectacular and gorgeous displays as they live—dangerously.
Magnetars
Neutron stars are boggling objects all by themselves. A neutron star is the leftover core of a massive star that exploded as a supernova, and its every property reads like a comic book headline. Containing the mass of a star squeezed down into a ball the size of a city, they are so dense a single cubic centimeter weighs several hundred million tons, equivalent to all the cars in the U.S. compressed down to the size of a sugar cube. The gravity on the surface can be several billion times Earth’s, and a typical neutron star’s magnetic field is billions of times stronger than Earth’s as well.
But there is a subclass of neutron stars that are more powerful yet: the aptly-named magnetars, with magnetic fields that can be more than a quadrillion times stronger than that of our own planet. Their magnetic field is tied to their crusts, the thin shell of “normal” matter surrounding the more exotic interior. If there is a starquake, a sudden shift in the neutron star crust, the magnetic field gets shaken violently. This creates a truly enormous explosion of energy that barrels into the galaxy at large like a tsunami.
In December 2004 such a wave swept over Earth, causing some havoc. It hit with such force that it compressed our planet’s magnetosphere, overloaded satellites and even partially ionized our atmosphere. While the damage was minor, this was all caused by the magnetar SGR 1806-20, which is 50,000 light-years away, halfway across our galaxy.
Happily, magnetars are rare, and only a few known are closer to us, all less powerful than SGR 1806-20. I’d hate to think there’s another one like it out there but nearer to us, just waiting to blow off some magnetic steam.
Short Gamma-ray Bursts
Speaking of neutron stars, if one can be a problem, what happens if there are two of them orbiting each other?
Nothing good.
Over time, the orbit of the pair can decay, the duo slowly approaching one another. Eventually the inevitability of gravity brings them close enough to suddenly merge, sending out a tremendous blast of matter and energy that can outshine the sun by a factor of many billions, though just for the briefest fraction of a second. Because of the high-energy photons they fling out and their milliseconds-long duration, these are called short gamma-ray bursts.
Such explosions are rare because binary neutron stars are rare. While no burst has ever been seen in our galaxy, a handful of local binary systems are known. The good news is they’re likely too far away to damage us in the eventuality of their merging. Those don’t concern me.
What does, however, is the possibility of a pair of neutron stars much closer to us, hidden from our view because of their extreme age, cooling over the eons until they are cold enough to be invisible to our telescopes. Massive, dark and in a mad whirl around each other, they will announce their demise in an eruption of energy powerful enough to dwarf the effects of a magnetar.
The odds of this are extremely low, so I don’t think there are any that close. I’m pretty sure. Probably.
Merging Supermassive Black Holes
But if I had to pick one thing out of the cosmic menagerie that gives me astronomical heebie-jeebies, it’s merging supermassive black holes.
These are black holes on a galactic scale, with millions or billions of times the mass of the sun. They can come in pairs, coupled after two galaxies collide, the monsters in their hearts brought together in the merger. Over billions of years, they slide ever closer together until finally they eat each other to form a single, even more Brobdingnagian beast.
But not all their mass gets glommed together to form the final black hole boss. Instead a significant fraction is converted into energy in the form of gravitational waves, a literal shaking of the fabric of the universe, sending out incomprehensibly powerful ripples like an angry god shaking the crumbs off an Olympian tablecloth.
How powerful? The merger’s gravitational roar in a fraction of second is equivalent to the amount of energy our sun emits in over a billion trillion years. It’s more powerful than the combined might of every single star in the observable universe.
Amazingly, the explosion is entirely dark; not a single photon of light is generated—all the energy goes into invisible gravitational waves. Also, these happen, on average, billions of light-years from us, so the energy is dissipated to far less than that of the beat of a bat’s wing on Earth. The gravitational burst is immense, but the vast distance between us wins.
Still, the very idea of such a thing freezes my brain, locking it into a mental feedback loop that’s the equivalent of running around in a tight circle flapping my arms wildly and screaming. Nothing should be that energetic. Nothing. Yet, as far as we know, the universe makes these all the time.
That’s what scares an astronomer.
So as you go trick-or-treating this holiday, be safe. Watch out for traffic and other costumed celebrants—but also keep a part of your attention on the sky. It’s pretty scary up there, too.

Father, two sons arrested on suspicion of trapping songbirds in near-invisible nets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:42:01 UTC
20:42:01 KST

A father and his two sons were recently apprehended in the West Bank between Halhul and Hebron last week on suspicion of hunting songbirds using nets, the Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA) announced.
The three men were questioned in preparation for further legal proceedings, and the Civil Administration, the IDF unit responsible for implementing Israel’s civilian policy in the West Bank, seized their vehicle during ongoing enforcement activity by the Nature Reserves Unit, according to the INPA.
In addition, two other suspects were arrested this week on suspicion of hunting, smuggling and trafficking in protected wildlife and natural resources, the INPA confirmed.
The arrests followed a covert investigation by the Erez Special Investigations Unit of the Northern Border Police and INPA, in coordination with the Civil Administration’s Nature Reserves Unit.
The two are alleged to have trafficked thousands of protected birds and sold them to customers across the country in violation of the law, INPA said. During searches and evidence collection, investigators seized hundreds of frozen black-capped babblers, a protected species.
The INPA notes that these recent cases of songbird hunting are "very common in Judea and Samaria throughout the year, but their scale increases significantly during migration periods" in the fall season. According to the INPA’s estimates, many groups are operating simultaneously throughout the region, and thousands of birds are being hunted using nets.
The West Bank region lies on one of the major bird migration routes between Europe, Asia, and Africa, and like other areas in the Mediterranean basin that serve as "bottlenecks" for migration - including Cyprus, Malta, Lebanon, the Sinai Peninsula, and North Africa - the concentration of large numbers of birds over a short period makes them particularly vulnerable to hunting.
Illegal bird hunting, which the INPA says also occurs in other regions of the Mediterranean Basin and the Middle East, threatens migratory bird populations and can cause significant harm.
Recent incidents are 'manifestation of a broader phenomenon'
The INPA announced that they are "working intensively to eradicate this phenomenon" in cooperation with law enforcement and security agencies, and has reportedly already begun the apprehension of numerous hunting rings.
"Despite the widespread nature of this phenomenon, public awareness of songbird hunting in the West Bank remains relatively low", the INPA explained. They emphasized that the incidents uncovered in recent weeks were not isolated cases, but rather a "manifestation of a broader phenomenon in which thousands of migratory birds are hunted each season."
One of the most common hunting methods is the use of "mist nets": thin, nearly invisible nets stretched between tall poles anchored to the ground, according to the INPA. This method means that hunters are not required to remain on site continuously; instead, they return to the nets every few hours to collect the birds that have been caught in them.
During the fall migration season, the mist nets are set up near trees that attract migratory birds, especially those whose fruits serve as a food source, among other places such as between rows of olive groves. This method does not distinguish between species, and many birds may become trapped.
A significant portion of the small songbirds caught during this period, including warblers and thrushes, are intended for consumption. The birds are fried and sold in trays as part of a widespread, large-scale hunting phenomenon during migration.
Up to 500 birds caught in single 'hunting shift'
During a single "hunting shift" of eight to nine hours, one can catch anywhere from 50 to 500 birds, according to an investigation of gangs apprehended in the past. In most cases, the investigation says that after being plucked, fried, and prepared for consumption, the birds weigh four to five grams and are sold for NIS 5 each. Each tray contains between 15 and 20 birds.
"Small songbirds play an important role in the ecosystem, in part due to their varied diet - throughout the year, they feed on insects and small invertebrates, thereby helping to regulate their populations, and during seasons when fruit is available, they also feed on fruit and help disperse seeds to new locations," the INPA explained. "In this way, they contribute to vegetation regeneration and the dispersal of plant species across the landscape."
Additionally, as a link in the food web, songbirds also serve as prey for birds of prey and other predators, thus forming part of the complex network of interdependencies that maintains the functioning of natural ecosystems."
The INPA urged the public not to approach or confront suspects if they encounter hunting nets or cages holding birds, but instead to withdraw and immediately report the incident to the INPA hotline.

AI is letting anyone reverse engineer anything. We talked to the developer at the center of it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:41:41 UTC
20:41:41 KST

Buy a new car, and you’re free to repaint the exterior or add new wheels. But you aren’t supposed to edit the code controlling the dash display and other electronics. Once software is packaged up and shipped, it’s meant to stay the way the manufacturer intended it.
Morluto, a software engineer who spoke with Scientific American on the condition that he remain pseudonymous, took that as a challenge. His tool, Reverse Engineer Anything, or REA, lets artificial intelligence agents pull apart programs and reconstitute them to their users’ liking.
His interest began with game decompilation, a corner of reverse engineering in which fans painstakingly rebuild the code of video games. Such work has taken years without AI assistance. Now Morluto—whose name comes from an old video gaming alias—sees much broader uses. REA’s Discord community includes examples of people modifying everything from printers to televisions. The project has more than 400,000 stars on GitHub, a rough gauge of its popularity.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“We’ve gotten used to the fact that software is all around us, but none of it is anything that we can influence,” he says. He hopes AI-enabled reverse engineering could fix this: “If code is magic, then we are all capable of it,” Morluto says.
For decades, software makers have enjoyed a sense of security through tedium: taking apart a compiled program was such a grind that few people bothered. But the packaging also kept us out of the guts of our own gadgets. If anyone with a ChatGPT subscription or an open-weight model can hand off that work, control over a device tilts toward whoever’s curious to look inside—no matter their intentions. “This is going to pose a crisis for trade secret and copyright law,” says James Grimmelmann, a law professor at Cornell Tech.
Morluto sees this as a natural progression in the relationship between people and the technology they use. Throughout our conversation, he kept invoking tech founders who shaped his work—Apple’s Steve Jobs, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Y Combinator’s Paul Graham. “A lot of the creators in the past,” he says, “were all hackers and tinkerers, experimenters growing up.” He believes REA can turn its users into that kind of creator. “You are capable not just of magic but of creating beautiful things,” Morluto says.
In his view, tech has become an industry full of walled gardens, and thanks to AI, “their walls were not as robust as they had thought.”
Those walls come from the way software is bundled into executable programs. Before a program can run, the code people write in a programming language such as Python has to be translated, or compiled, into binary, a sequence of 1’s and 0’s that actually tells the computer what to do. Reverse engineering software involves running that translation backward, turning binary back into code a person can read in the process of decompilation.
Reverse engineers have long done this with tools such as Ghidra, a program the U.S. National Security Agency developed as part of its cybersecurity efforts. REA provides the pipelines that let an AI agent orchestrate Ghidra and other programs on its own.
"Reverse engineering is a little bit like pattern matching," says Morluto. "AI has extremely strong reasoning and pattern matching skills."
Before 2026 decompilation was the domain of a select few experts, according to Zion Basque, an assistant professor at the University of Georgia, who studies reverse engineering. Now, he says, nearly anyone can play. His research group developed Kuna, one of the decompilers REA can equip AI agents with. The kinds of reverse engineering he sees people doing with REA could have been done before, just never at this scale. “I haven’t seen what the limits of this are yet,” he says.
Done by hand, that kind of work would take experts months, if they managed it at all, according to Grimmelmann. Now the limit, he says, is what you can afford. “If you have the tokens, you can set it loose on almost any piece of software,” he says.
For some corners of the software industry, that’s an existential problem that the law cannot easily patch. Copyright protects a program’s code, Grimmelmann says, but not the algorithms and ideas the code implements. “This opens up a whole world of mods and remixes and interoperable new clients that really reduce the lead time people get from deploying software,” he says.
REA isn’t the only thing eating into that head start. In early October Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 helped a developer build open-source clones of Adobe’s Creative Cloud programs, which are known for their tight controls and steep prices.
Joey Castillo, an open-source developer and technologist in residence at Cornell Tech, went after something smaller. He has reverse engineered various tools in the past, but his first brush with using AI to do it came when he tried to modify a smart ring he had bought in Shenzhen, China. He was impressed that the AI model could reverse engineer the ring and teach him at the same time. “I learned a lot just by watching Claude work,” he says.
The desire to tinker comes from wanting to take control of the things you buy, according to Castillo. “I bought this object, and it’s being gatekept from me,” he says. “Now I’m going to have the power to make it do what I want.”
Some of those gates serve an important purpose, though. Much as AI is proving adept at breaking into security systems, it is also very good at breaking things like digital rights management and the protected firmware baked into devices.
Projects like REA may also make it too easy for amateurs to gain a sort of synthetic expertise. Castillo and his open-source friends worry about people digging around in devices they don’t fully understand. “This is all going to be very fun and games until someone vibe codes firmware and it causes the battery to catch fire midflight,” Castillo says. He doubts AI models have the foresight that reverse engineering experts bring to deciding which modifications to make because AI “can only ‘yes, and.’ It can’t ‘no, but.’”
Since our first conversation with Morluto, some social media users have reported OpenAI and Anthropic banning or blocking their use of REA. In a reply on X, an OpenAI researcher called the block on reverse engineering “mostly accidental.”
Morluto isn’t worried. If anything, he says, the “fiasco” just brings more attention to the project and to the kind of discovery he was aiming for. “That’s the core of Reverse Engineer Anything,” he says. “It’s a road that leads you to question what it is that you want.”
Accidental or not, such obstacles are unlikely to stop people who really want to reverse engineer their devices. Castillo already has a fallback in GLM-5.3, an open-weight model from the Chinese company Z.ai. Once it’s downloaded, no one can take it away. “If Anthropic and OpenAI decide they’re going to ban my account for reverse engineering, I’m going to fire up GLM-5.3 and reverse engineer the smart ring,” he says, “because I think it’s really cool to make this thing do what I wanted.”

Humanist Gets Religious Exemption from Using AI at Work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:41:12 UTC
20:41:12 KST

A research administrator at the University of Kentucky objected on religious grounds to the pressure the university was putting on him and other employees to rely on AI in their work.
With the help of the American Humanist Association (AHA), he was able to secure a Title VII exemption from using the technology.
David Durman “felt he was being asked to offload his thinking to tools like Microsoft Teams Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT bots in his day-to-day work. That felt like a violation of his beliefs,” reports Religion News Service (RNS).
Durman is quoted in a press release from the AHA explaining his beliefs and how they relate to AI:
As a Humanist, promoting the wellbeing and flourishing of humanity is paramount to how I live my life, and I believe that our capacity to think and reason for ourselves is worth protecting… When it comes to AI technology — particularly generative AI and LLMs, it’s clear to me that the existence and use of these technologies run contrary to human wellbeing. AI is interfering with people’s ability to earn a living, the environmental costs spell disaster for humanity and our planet, and its supplanting and theft of human creativity threaten elements of our culture like art and literature that make society flourish. I sought out workplace accommodations because using AI violates my deeply held Humanist beliefs which demand I take personal responsibility for the morality of my actions. I cannot, in good conscience, partake in the use and proliferation of this technology.
Durman told RNS:
The process and work involved in thinking through situations, through my work, through my ethics, through the way I handle other people, is a key component in being able to develop myself as a moral person… Offloading that labor, regardless of whether it’s taxing or not, is undercutting my ability to be a moral actor.
RNS reported that Durman “worries AI could affect society in ways that are harmful. As a humanist, he believes in the importance of human flourishing. ‘At a societal level, I think that the use of AI technology runs counter to that,’ he said.”
Durman was inspired by a software engineer who received an exemption from using AI at work based on her beliefs as a Unitarian Universalist.
The AHA says:
Durman sent a letter to the University’s Office of Equal Opportunity (OEO) in late August requesting reasonable accommodations on the basis of his “sincerely held beliefs as a Humanist.” After meeting with the OEO in mid September, Durman’s request was approved on September 25, when the OEO determined it posed no undue burden on his department. Durman continues to perform all of his job duties without using AI.
The AHA notes that it helped craft the “Luxembourg Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Human Values.” The first of the ten principles of the declaration states:
AI systems have the potential to empower and assist individuals and societies to achieve more in all aspects of human life. But they must never displace human judgment, human reason, human ethics, or human responsibility for our actions. Decisions that deeply affect people’s lives must always remain in human hands.
As education administrators increasingly promote AI use, one might wonder whether Durman has blazed a trail that others at the university might also take.
UPDATE: In a September column at Psychology Today, Krista K. Thomason (Swarthmore) raises the question: “are employers asking workers to betray their values in using AI tools?”

He stressed the need to expand cooperation in the fields of transport and logistics, adding: “Connecting the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway to the 'Middle Corridor' via the Caspian Sea is of great importance for enhancing the transit potential of the Turkic states."
Japarov also highlighted that Kyrgyzstan possesses significant hydroelectric energy potential and extensive prospects for the development of renewable energy sources, adding that only 15% of the country’s hydroelectric potential is currently being utilized.

Political analyst's view: Why are potential ministers' names being leaked, and where do Zimbabwe's "fat catfish" really live?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:40:00 UTC
20:40:00 KST

The outlines of Latvia's future governing coalition have yet to become clear, but the public broadcaster is already naming potential ministers. Was this a signal to Kulbergs that "influential circles" are keeping a close eye on the government formation process, or was it simply political gossip? BNN asked Filips Rajevskis, political analyst and co-founder of the company Mediju tilts, for his assessment.
"I think gossip plays an enormous role in this," the political analyst said, pointing out that most of the politicians elected to the 15th Saeima from the United List have never been involved in forming a government.
"Let's be realistic, they are complete newcomers to politics, and that creates a very favorable environment in which even a name mentioned purely hypothetically can immediately spread. People involved in this process, and those listening to how everything is unfolding, do not seem to understand that you shouldn't leak the first thing you hear."
As an example, he cited the speculation surrounding a potential foreign minister. Latvian Television initially named one candidate before correcting the report to identify someone else. As a result, Kulbergs had to publicly call for an end to the rumors, explaining that he did not even know the person in question.
"This illustrates the situation very, very precisely. Various names are being leaked without those responsible fully understanding why they are doing it. In reality, the first names that emerge are very often nothing more than leaks and never translate into actual ministerial appointments," the political analyst said.
According to Rajevskis, greater attention should be paid to how Kulbergs describes the government formation process.
"A government declaration and a parliamentary declaration are being developed, which is actually unusual and has not been done before. But there is a certain logic to it, because a government cannot accomplish very much without parliament and agreements within the Saeima."
The political analyst also noted that an agreement on parliamentary priorities is necessary to ensure that members of the Saeima share responsibility for the government's actions and decisions.
Rajevskis also referred to "mission letters", which would establish specific tasks, priorities and measurable objectives for each minister, effectively serving as a written commitment.
"Kulbergs has borrowed this idea from the European Commission's practice, where commissioners are given fairly precise annual tasks and objectives. This model itself requires a somewhat different approach to selecting the people who will hold these positions."
The political analyst recalled that the traditional government formation process had been both straightforward and complicated at the same time.
"The president held consultations with political parties, the parties identified possible coalition models, and then they considered who could become prime minister. The president nominated a candidate for prime minister. By that stage, a coalition model was already envisaged, and the process of assembling the coalition and distributing ministerial portfolios began.
Only when the distribution of positions had reached a certain stage did they start thinking about what to include in the government's declaration. Let's be realistic, that is how things have worked. That was the standard approach."
According to Rajevskis, the situation has now changed completely, leaving the president with virtually no choice when it comes to nominating a prime minister.
"The United List has 41 seats and has achieved a historic victory. It would be strange for the president to start looking for coalition models that did not involve the United List taking the lead. At present, that is simply not possible.
As a result, all political forces are somewhat confused and are trying to understand how to behave in this situation. Meanwhile, those 41 seats give the United List an enormous mandate of trust, but they also place a tremendous responsibility on its shoulders.
When you have that level of trust and responsibility, you cannot first divide up the ministerial seats and only afterward start wondering what you are going to do. You have to begin by deciding what needs to be done and only then determine who will do it.
That is a simple change in the underlying approach, but one that is extremely difficult, especially for those who have been involved in politics for a long time. For newcomers, it is an especially painful part of the learning process."
Asked about the Foreign Ministry's decision to allocate EUR 76,000 to a non-governmental organization for a project developing African catfish farming in Zimbabwe, Rajevskis was sharply critical. "This is yet another example of how our Foreign Ministry, under Baiba Braže's leadership, is becoming a source of funding for all sorts of questionable initiatives.
The worst part is that this funding system and these questionable initiatives have, in one way or another, been linked to people considered useful in Latvian domestic politics – financing their projects and supporting them through the Foreign Ministry's budget.
It is disgraceful, and this situation must change. The next foreign minister will face the extremely difficult task of putting an end to this waste of money on utterly senseless initiatives."
Responding to BNN's reference to Braže's statement that "it is our duty to give to those who have less", given that Latvia itself once received extensive international assistance, Rajevskis said:
"I absolutely agree that solidarity and support are important, but there are well-fed intermediaries involved in all of this.
There is also the question of whether the money ever actually reaches any catfish farmers in Africa. Those Africans are right here. And the 'fat catfish' being raised are also right here in Latvia.
All these project justifications and objectives exist merely to pull the wool over people's eyes and conceal how the money is being redistributed and wasted."
Asked whether he believes Andris Kulbergs will succeed in preventing such waste of public funds and withstand the enormous pressure to preserve the existing system, Rajevskis said that Kulbergs has no other choice.
"With that number of seats and that level of public trust, he simply has no right to disappoint people.
Unity already let people down when voters entrusted it with 26 seats in the previous election, and we saw how significantly voter turnout declined this year.
The most important thing for Kulbergs is to ensure that people do not feel disappointed or deceived and that their hopes are not betrayed."

International Sports Court Overturns Ban on Russian Ice Hockey Teams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:39:24 UTC
20:39:24 KST

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday overturned the International Ice Hockey Federation’s (IIHF) decision to exclude Russian national teams from upcoming world championships, marking the latest step toward reintegrating Russia into global sporting events.
IIHF banned Russia and Belarus from its competitions in response to the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, after which the Ice Hockey Federation of Russia submitted an appeal to CAS.
The Switzerland-based court operates independently of any sports organization and handles significant sporting cases.
A three-person CAS panel “found that the IIHF arguments citing safety, security and other concerns were not supported by sufficient evidence,” the court said in a statement.
The ruling requires organizers to allow Russia to participate in the World Junior Championship, which kicks off in Canada later this year, as well as the Men’s World Championship, which Germany hosts in May.
The decision did not address whether Russian teams should be allowed to compete with their national flag and anthem or other issues that were not subject to the appeal, CAS said.
IIHF expressed disappointment with the ruling, saying the move would create a slew of additional challenges for tournament organizers, “including a review of competition formats, schedules, travel and accommodation arrangements, and safety and security measures.”
“While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments,” the world ice hockey governing body said.
Meanwhile, Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov welcomed the CAS ruling, saying it “puts an end to the issue, as it’s final and not subject to appeal.”
He acknowledged that “challenging work lies ahead” in returning Russian hockey players to IIHF competitions in line with the CAS decision.
The court ruling follows the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifting its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in July, a step seen as advancing Russia’s gradual return to international sport.
The ROC was suspended in October 2023 after recognizing regional Olympic councils in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories of Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia as its own.
The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine has appealed to CAS against the IOC's decision.

Estonia's land value up a third in four years to €44.1 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:39:00 UTC
20:39:00 KST

Estonia's land value up a third in four years to €44.1 billion
Estonia's total land value has grown 33 percent in four years, from €33.2 billion to €44.1 billion, according to the Land and Spatial Board's (Maa- ja Ruumiamet) regular valuation.
Harju County accounts for 57 percent of the total at €25.2 billion, far ahead of the next on the list, Tartu County at 11 percent, and Pärnu County at 7 percent. Values grew fastest in municipalities around Tallinn and Tartu.
The valuation gets carried out every four years and covers all of Estonia's roughly 780,000 cadastral units, using real estate transaction data and models based on location and land characteristics.
Commenting on the results, Marje Kolmar-Grüner, head of the land valuation department, said: "The biggest changes often appear in areas where previously unbuilt-on land has become a new living environment. For example, in Tartu near the former Raadi airfield, the assessed value of land has in some cases grown more than tenfold, and in Järveküla in Rae parish in Harju County, the assessed value has in some cases more than doubled."
Land value grew most rapidly among municipalities in the Tallinn and Tartu commuter belt, and of these it was Tartu Rural Municipality (as distinct from Tartu City Municipality to the south) which saw the most rapid growth, at an average of 59 percent.
Overall by county, growth was fastest in Rapla, Lääne and Võru counties, which were all above 40 percent, and was slowest in Ida-Viru County at 18 percent.
Nearly all cadastral units saw a land value rise — in 96 percent of cases, with the remaining 4 percent seeing unchanged or falling values.
While residential land is the most expensive in Harju County, it has not risen fastest there: values grew quickest at the other end of the country, in Võru County, at 55.9 percent, as well as in Järva County at 55.6 and Rapla County at 55.5. The slowest rise was seen in Ida-Viru County at 12.6 percent.
Forest land value rose across Estonia by between 46 percent in Harju County and 58.8 percent in Järva County, the fastest growth of any land type. The median price of unbuilt land roughly doubled in four years.
Residential land makes up about half of Estonia's total value at €22.2 billion, with commercial and industrial land coming to about 18 percent, at €8.1 billion.
Land values set in 2026 will be used to calculate land tax from 2028. Local governments decide the tax rate, for residential land between 0.1 and 1 percent. They also decide how much land tax may rise by in a year.

US court pauses order to reopen Green Card lottery

Unknown Publisher

US court pauses order to reopen Green Card lottery
A US appeals court has suspended an order requiring the State Department to reopen the 2027 Diversity Visa lottery while the government’s appeal proceeds, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent, citing the official court ruling.
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the government’s emergency request on October 29. The lower court had required officials to announce registration by October 29, open applications by November 1 and notify selected applicants by December 3.
The case was brought by immigration firm Red Eagle Law after the State Department failed to open registration for the fiscal year 2027 programme.
The appeals panel found that the government was likely to succeed because the firm’s financial interest in representing lottery winners fell outside the interests protected by the programme’s legislation.
“We do not endorse the Department’s failure to open the lottery registration period,” the judges wrote.
The ruling pauses the lower court’s deadlines pending appeal. It does not abolish the Diversity Visa programme or constitute a final decision on the appeal.
The programme provides up to 55,000 immigrant visas annually for people from countries with low immigration rates to the United States.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency explained who can apply for the Diversity Visa lottery and how the process works. The programme offers a pathway to obtaining a Green Card, which allows foreign nationals to live and work permanently in the United States.

Crypto platform Binance confirms 'complex' $6.3 billion hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:38:42 UTC
20:38:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Crypto platform Binance confirms 'complex' $6.3 billion hack
Cryptocurrency platform Binance said Friday it was working to resolve a "complex attack" that affected around $6.3 billion in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist.
The company—the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes—said investigations had "uncovered additional points of breach", contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.
"This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance wrote on X.
Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said it had "high confidence" that the attack was orchestrated by a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists," TRM said.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group -- which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview," a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Binance confirmed on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion."
That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform.
That heist was attributed at the time to North Korea-backed TraderTraitor.
Binance warned the $6.3 billion figure "may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets."
It said around $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.
Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses.
Fund freeze
At about 0900 GMT Friday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended".
"Deposits remain unaffected," it said.
The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer," allowing the unauthorized party to access a "service container" and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
"We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.
But it said later that "subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether -- a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT -- said his firm froze about $1.6 billion "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."
Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both "stablecoins," or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.
The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Crypto prices tumble
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.
Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly five percent and nearly six percent respectively on the news. BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 percent.
The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

Taiwan passes death penalty for repeat drugged-driving fatalities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:37:53 UTC
20:37:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The legislature on Friday passed amendments to the Criminal Code that increase penalties for driving under the influence of drugs, allowing the death penalty for repeat offenders who cause fatalities within 10 years.
Lawmakers passed the amendments to Article 185-3 after the KMT and TPP joined forces to approve their version of the bill, per FTV News. Under the revised law, drug-impaired driving carries a prison sentence of six months to five years and a fine of up to NT$500,000 (US$15,800).
If the offense causes death, the penalty increases to at least seven years in prison, with a possible fine of up to NT$7 million. Causing serious injury carries five to 12 years in prison and a fine of up to NT$5 million.
Those who reoffend within 10 years and cause a death face the death penalty, life imprisonment, or at least 10 years in prison, along with a possible fine of up to NT$10 million, according to FTV News. Repeat offenders who cause serious injuries face at least seven years in prison and a possible fine of up to NT$7 million.
The amendments follow several high-profile drugged-driving incidents that have fueled public calls for tougher penalties, per TVBS. In December 2025, a driver in Keelung who had allegedly used etomidate and amphetamines struck and killed a man in his 70s, injuring three other people.
Keelung District Court sentenced the driver to seven years and eight months in prison for drug-impaired driving resulting in death and other offenses. The victim's daughter questioned whether her father's life was worth just seven years and eight months in prison, prompting public debate over sentencing.
Another high-profile case involved Chen Chia-ying (陳嘉瑩), who killed New Taipei police station chief Liu Tsung-hsin (劉宗鑫) while fleeing a drug-related traffic stop on Sept. 30, 2024. Chen was sentenced to death for murder, obstruction of official duties, and drug-impaired driving in February this year, but appealed the verdict. The next hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, per TaiSounds.
The Cabinet approved its own proposed amendments to Article 185-3 on June 11, calling for a prison sentence of five to 12 years for drug-impaired driving resulting in death, per TVBS. Under its proposal, repeat offenders who cause a fatality within 10 years could face life imprisonment, but not the death penalty.
The Cabinet's version was rejected Friday by a vote of 57-41, with 98 lawmakers present. The KMT and TPP version subsequently passed 57-1, with one abstention, among 59 lawmakers present.
Most DPP lawmakers did not participate in the final vote, citing insufficient substantive discussion of the legislation, TVBS reported. DPP caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) was the only party member to vote against the measure.

Taiwan's Anxo broadens pharmaceutical portfolio

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Anxo Pharmaceutical Co. has expanded its drug portfolio, securing approval for a smoking cessation drug and exclusive distribution rights for a melatonin product in Taiwan, CTEE reported Friday.
The company received regulatory clearance to market a generic version of varenicline, a prescription drug used to help people quit smoking. Commercial sales in Taiwan are expected to begin next year.
Separately, subsidiary Taxo Pharmaceutical Technology Co. announced Friday that it had secured exclusive distribution rights in the country for a patented extended-release melatonin tablet developed by Israel's Neurim Pharmaceuticals Ltd. The deal adds another branded medicine to Taxo's portfolio.
Taxo has been shifting from distributing medicines manufactured by Anxo toward sourcing products from external suppliers. The agreement expands its portfolio of branded medicines and strengthens its position in the sleep medicine market.
Melatonin is a hormone that regulates the body's sleep-wake cycle. Although research suggests it may improve perceived sleep quality and help people fall asleep faster, evidence supporting its use as an insomnia treatment remains limited, particularly for long-term use, according to the Food and Drug Administration.
Anxo is responsible for developing, manufacturing, and marketing varenicline in Taiwan. The original branded drug faced recalls and supply suspensions in multiple markets beginning in 2021 over concerns about nitrosamine impurities.
Anxo worked with Handa Pharmaceuticals Inc. to develop the generic version, incorporating controls for these impurities into the development process. The product has received approval from the Food and Drug Administration, with launch preparations underway.

The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:36:52 UTC
20:36:52 KST

Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.
Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.
Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”
The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.
“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.
The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.
Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.
Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations—often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.
Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.
“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”
“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”
TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.
“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”
While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”
Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”

The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:34:16 UTC
20:34:16 KST

The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University College London
- Summary:
- Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.
- Share:
Why did crocodiles survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago? New research suggests that their preference for warm environments may have given them a crucial advantage during one of Earth's greatest mass extinctions.
Scientists led by UCL (University College London) found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives spent much of their 250 million years of evolutionary history following warm climates rather than adapting to dramatically different temperatures. When Earth grew hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes reaching as far as Antarctica. As temperatures fell, they moved back toward the tropics.
Published in Science Advances, the study analyzed more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. Researchers combined this evidence with computer models that reconstructed Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years.
The results suggest that tropical and subtropical regions remained suitable for crocodile relatives after the asteroid struck, even as the environments available to many dinosaurs deteriorated. Only the most extreme climate simulations eliminated these potential refuges.
Why Crocodiles Survived the Dinosaur Extinction
The researchers examined how conditions on Earth may have changed following the asteroid impact 66 million years ago. Their simulations indicated that areas near the equator could have remained warm enough to support crocodile relatives, providing places where surviving populations could persist and eventually recover.
Previous modeling by members of the same research team found that suitable habitats for non-avian dinosaurs (i.e., the ones that went extinct) contracted much more severely after the impact.
Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group.
"Crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out."
The discovery offers a possible explanation for how a group of animals that appeared around the same time as dinosaurs managed to endure two of Earth's five major mass extinctions.
Ancient Crocodiles Were Far More Diverse
Modern crocodiles and their close relatives share many recognizable features, but their evolutionary history reveals a much wider variety of body shapes, sizes, and lifestyles.
The broader crocodile lineage, known as pseudosuchians, once included heavily armored plant eaters, predators that hunted entirely on land, and enormous animals weighing more than a metric ton.
Among the most remarkable was Sarcosuchus, a giant predator nicknamed the "super croc" that could reach 12 meters in length. Another prehistoric relative, Postosuchus, was a land dwelling hunter capable of moving on either two legs or all four.
Dr. Chiarenza said: "Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex, to small, cute animals with the face of a pug.
"Our study shows that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate."
Fossils Reveal 245 Million Years of Climate History
To investigate that relationship, the scientists reconstructed the temperature and rainfall preferences of 400 crocodile species and their ancient relatives. They used fossil evidence, evolutionary family trees, and detailed maps of where living crocodile species are found today.
The team then compared these preferences with reconstructions of ancient geography and climate to identify where suitable habitats existed at different points in Earth's history.
A clear pattern emerged. Crocodile relatives generally followed warmer conditions as the planet's climate changed, expanding their ranges during hot periods and retreating when temperatures cooled.
About 50 million years ago, during the particularly warm early Eocene, global temperatures were approximately 10°C higher than today, and the polar regions had no permanent ice. Crocodile relatives lived at high latitudes across North America, Europe, and even Antarctica.
Over the following millions of years, global cooling gradually reduced the areas where they could thrive. Their geographic range contracted toward warmer tropical regions.
Two Surprising Exceptions
Although this preference for warm environments remained remarkably consistent, the researchers identified two important exceptions.
During the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, approximately 94 million years ago, global temperatures climbed as much as 14°C above modern levels. One branch of the crocodile family tree evolved the ability to tolerate hotter conditions than the broader lineage could withstand at other times.
A separate adaptation occurred around 34 million years ago in Australia. As a prolonged cooling period reduced rainfall and dried out the continent, an extinct group of crocodiles adapted to increasingly arid, desert-like environments.
These exceptions show that some crocodile relatives could evolve to handle different climates, even though most continued to follow their preferred warm conditions.
What Happened After the Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid?
The researchers also used climate simulations to investigate the decades and centuries immediately following the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered the extinction of most dinosaurs.
They explored several possible environmental consequences, including sunlight being blocked by dust and ash and rising carbon dioxide levels associated with volcanic eruptions.
When the simulations reduced sunlight by 5% or 10%, warm regions near the equator remained suitable for crocodile relatives. These areas could have provided critical refuges during the environmental disruption.
However, a more severe scenario involving a 15% reduction in sunlight left those regions unsuitable as well. The researchers noted that this extreme level of reduced sunlight is now considered unlikely.
Other simulated changes, including increased atmospheric carbon dioxide, did not alter the availability of suitable climates for crocodiles.
Together, the results suggest that crocodiles may have benefited from living in regions where temperatures remained within their preferred range, even as conditions became much less favorable for many dinosaurs.
The Survival Strategy That Could Now Become a Weakness
The researchers emphasized that favorable temperatures were probably only one reason crocodiles survived the mass extinction.
Other characteristics likely improved their chances, including relatively small body sizes, the ability to live partly in water, flexible diets, and modest energy requirements. As ectothermic ("cold-blooded") animals, crocodiles need less food to maintain their bodies than many animals that generate their own body heat.
The findings also raise important questions about how crocodiles will respond to modern climate change.
For millions of years, moving into regions with suitable temperatures appears to have been one of their main responses to a changing planet. Today, however, expanding cities, agricultural land, and roads increasingly limit where wildlife can move.
Professor Philip Mannion, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "These findings have implications for species today. If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today's species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder."
The research was funded by The Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust, and the National Environment Research Council (NERC).

Materials provided by University College London. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, Alexandra F. C. Howard, Grace L. Varnham, Alex Farnsworth, Paul J. Valdes, Philip D. Mannion. Climatic niche conservatism shapes the macroevolution, extinction, and survivorship of crocodile-line archosaurs. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (43) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg2217

Environmental rangers honored for protecting natural heritage

Environmental rangers honored for protecting natural heritage
TEHRAN – A ceremony was held on Thursday to mark National Environmental Ranger Day and honor the dedication, sacrifices, and vital role of environmental rangers in protecting the country’s environment and natural resources.
President Masoud Pezeshkian and Head of the Department of Environment (DOE) Shina Ansari addressed the event.
Emphasizing the need to reform environmental management approaches, Pezeshkian said protecting natural resources requires balancing available resources with consumption, preventing environmental degradation, strengthening continuous monitoring, revising regulations, and encouraging public participation. He added that the government is responsible for safeguarding the country’s natural assets and preventing their destruction.
The president described environmental rangers as being on the front lines of protecting the country’s natural heritage, stressing that they should receive greater attention and support in recognition of their responsibilities, challenging working conditions, and services.
Pezeshkian also warned that wars, misguided actions, and destructive decisions are damaging the planet and threatening human life. He described environmental protection as an intergenerational responsibility, emphasizing that education is the first step toward preserving natural resources for future generations. He cautioned that once the Earth’s natural resources are destroyed, restoring them to their original condition is far from easy.
Criticizing the benefits some developed countries derive from environmental degradation in developing nations, he said the consequences of such practices are increasingly threatening the planet.
For her part, Ansari said more than 13 protected areas across the country had been damaged during recent wars, with ranger stations, equipment, vehicles, and wildlife also suffering losses.
She noted that, alongside their conservation duties, environmental rangers had worked during the wartime period in coordination with military and provincial authorities to defend the country’s territorial integrity and continue protecting its natural assets.
Ansari also paid tribute to 154 environmental rangers who have lost their lives in the line of duty over the years, adding that 374 others had been injured or sustained disabilities while carrying out conservation missions.
In September, Pezeshkian described environmental protection as a key pillar of the country’s national and social security, stressing that the preservation of natural resources must be addressed within this framework.
Speaking at a meeting with environmental experts, Pezeshkian said the government was prepared to create the necessary conditions for using the plans, ideas and initiatives put forward by environmental activists and specialists.
He added that the government would support scientific and practical solutions for addressing the country’s real environmental challenges, IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian emphasized that tackling environmental problems requires close cooperation among the government, universities, the private sector, civil society organizations and the public.
“This shared capacity must be used to move toward sustainable governance, balanced development and the protection of the country’s resources for future generations,” he said.
The president also identified education and public awareness as key elements in reforming consumption patterns and protecting the environment.
“If we invest in properly educating the next generation, we are in fact investing in the future of the country,” Pezeshkian said.
He warned that without educating children and teenagers from an early age about environmental protection, efficient use of water and electricity, energy management and social responsibility toward natural resources, future generations could repeat patterns of environmental degradation, even if significant resources are spent on environmental protection today.
Pezeshkian stressed that environmental awareness should begin at school, saying that teaching students how to use water, electricity, gas, and other natural resources responsibly should be incorporated into the educational and developmental process.
The Department of Environment has taken different steps to promote public participation in environmental protection.
Encouraging eco-friendly students, teaching environmental awareness courses in universities, developing a plan titled “skilled ranger soldier”, and preparing guidelines for environmental protection are among the most important measures.
Over the past Iranian year, which ended on March 21, DOE mainly focused on enhancing formal and informal environmental education, developing public participation, utilizing the potential of new technologies, and promoting the culture of environmental protection, IRNA reported.
In the education sector, the DOE designed a ‘national environmental curriculum’, and the first scientific-educational event based on a book titled ‘Humans and the Environment’ was held for teachers and eleventh-grade students at the national level. During the event, the provincial and national winners were honored.
A national plan for environmental helpers has also been implemented. About 20 percent of the elementary students are health ambassadors. Some 25 percent of them will join the national plan over five years. Currently, there are 11,000 environmental helpers at schools across the country. The plan has also empowered 7,258 elementary school principals and 6,051 elementary school health care providers so far.
Another initiative of the DOE is to offer environmental courses in all universities in the country. It was previously implemented on a pilot basis in 10 selected universities. In addition, the Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) major for the MA degree has been revised.
The DOE has developed two other plans. The first, titled ‘skilled ranger soldier’, aims to employ students in environmental protection stations, and the second one intends to train and empower local communities with the participation of environmental protection students.
In an effort to strengthen the participation of local communities in conserving nature, the DOE has approved seven natural areas to be protected by the public.
The initiative showcases national determination to conserve the country’s environment and also opens a new prospect for people’s contribution and the development of participatory governance in protecting the country’s biodiversity.

King Charles' sorrow over slavery faces test as reparations movement gains ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:31:28 UTC
20:31:28 KST

King Charles' sorrow over slavery faces test as reparations movement gains ground
LONDON, Oct 30 - King Charles has since 2022 expressed sorrow for the suffering caused by slavery without crossing a line that Britain has long resisted: an apology.
That balancing act is likely to be tested at next week's Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, where Caribbean leaders who back a reparations campaign through the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) are expected to press their case.
Buckingham Palace has indicated Charles would not apologise on behalf of Britain, which has repeatedly ruled out financial reparations over its role in the transatlantic slave trade.
Speaking in the Bahamas on Tuesday ahead of a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting that begins on Sunday, Charles said it was "only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past," and said leaders from affected countries would discuss the issue at the summit.
But Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas' National Reparations Committee, said that did not go far enough. "We do not need more carefully crafted words about healing," she said in a statement. "We need action equal with the scale of the harm inflicted."
On Friday, about 15 people protested ahead of the king's arrival in Georgetown, Guyana. They gathered outside the Umana Yana, a conical palm-thatched hut originally built for the 1972 Non-Aligned Foreign Ministers Conference, where Charles later delivered a speech.
"It's an opportunity to try to impress upon him this historic responsibility for what took place here," said Terence Campbell, a member of parliament for the opposition APNU, who stood among the protesters holding a banner that read: "No apology will return what was stolen. Reparations now!"
ROYAL LINKS TO SLAVERY UNDER SCRUTINY
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations, according to the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database.
Alan Lester, a University of Sussex historian whose research spans the legacies of slavery and empire, said opponents of the reparations movement had "successfully weaponised" the idea that reparations simply meant writing a cheque, an idea that few Western governments will countenance.
Instead, Caribbean leaders often frame their demands in terms of debt relief, development finance, education, healthcare and climate resilience, measures they say would address inequalities rooted in slavery and colonialism.
"I think King Charles III is in a difficult position because you can express sorrow about something, but an apology goes much further," royal commentator Afua Hagan said.
Buckingham Palace said in 2023 that Charles had given his support to research that was examining the monarchy's links to slavery after the Guardian newspaper reported on a document showing a historical connection.
In a more recent finding, independent researcher Desiree Baptiste told Reuters her forthcoming book, "George IV, Empire, and Objects of Prestige," would cite House of Lords papers and other British government records showing that profits derived from enslaved labour helped fund furniture and decorative work commissioned by George IV at royal residences.
In a response, the Royal Collection Trust, a charity that maintains and displays artworks and historic objects held in trust by the king, said constant research helped it to keep its records "continually under review in order to improve the information presented on an object or subject". REUTERS

Greece and Türkiye clashed over the maritime agreement between Ankara and Libya during a United Nations Security Council debate on maritime security on Oct. 29, with both sides defending their positions on the legality of the 2019 memorandum.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis used a map during the open debate to criticize the Türkiye-Libya memorandum, arguing that it disregarded the sovereign rights of Greek islands and violated fundamental principles of international law.
Libya’s House of Representatives unanimously approved the maritime boundary agreement with Türkiye on Oct. 20, reversing its previous rejection of the deal and a decision to sever political ties with Ankara, according to a statement from the Libyan parliament.
The deal has long been a source of regional tensions, with Greece, Egypt and Greek Cyprus opposing it.
“The agreement completely disregards geography. It ignores the very existence of the Greek islands. It is as though these islands simply disappear from the way Türkiye and Libya view the region,” the Greek premier told the council.
Responding to Mitsotakis, Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the U.N. Ahmet Yıldız rejected Athens’ characterization of the agreement, arguing that the Security Council was not a judicial body mandated to delimit maritime zones.
He said maps could illustrate competing claims but could not establish their legal validity.
Yıldız defended the memorandum and pointed to its recent ratification by Libya’s House of Representatives as evidence of domestic support for the agreement.
He also rejected claims that the deal prejudged the maritime rights of third countries, stressing that it neither determined nor infringed upon the rights of states that were not parties to it.
Türkiye did not dispute the existence, population or sovereignty of Greek islands, Yıldız said, but argued that the legal issue was how much weight islands should be given when maritime zones are delimited in areas where claims overlap.

Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with "lantern-like" glass-block facade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with “lantern-like” glass-block facade
In the garden of a Melbourne family home, a facade of glass blocks set within recycled white brick and a concrete band beam tops this two-storey studio by Australian architecture practice Olaver.
Olaver designed Laneway Studio to appear as a “beautiful object” reflecting light into the garden in the day and glowing like a lantern at night. The multi-purpose building was designed in response to the growing needs of the family of five, offering a practical alternative to renovating the existing home.
It houses a study-cum-guest-room with an en-suite and terrace on the first floor and an open-plan living area below, fitted with concealed laundry facilities and a bar.
The new studio block was constructed behind the main house and its newly configured garden, designed by landscape architect Penny Starr to include a pool and areas of planted foliage.
Large glass-panelled sliding doors leading into the garden from both the house and studio create a seamless flow between the interior and exterior living spaces.
Another sliding door on the opposing wall of the studio, made from oak with a steel-clad exterior, connects the studio’s living space with the titular laneway behind the property.
“With large sliding doors on opposing walls, the ground floor can open right through, so it works as an extension of the garden and pool terrace to the laneway rather than a closed room”, Olaver director Emlyn Olaver told Dezeen.
“Open, the space feels far bigger than its footprint, and the family can spread across the house, the pool and the studio as one connected space when entertaining”, she continued.
Inside, the ground floor was designed to be minimal and open-plan to ensure its multi-functionality. It features neutral terrazzo flooring throughout. Oak cabinetry conceals storage, laundry facilities and a TV nook and frames a central bar area with a stainless-steel sink and surround.
“We wanted the studio to be calm, with joinery doing the heavy lifting so each space can change roles without feeling cluttered”, Olaver explained.
“Every space had to do more than one job; a laundry, a living room or a bar depending on the day. That flexibility also gives the building a longer life, because the family’s needs will keep changing as the kids grow up, move out and come back.”
On the first floor’s east-facing wall, overlooking the garden, a facade of glass blocks was installed above a concrete band beam to bypass planning restrictions on the use of conventional windows.
The glass-block facade brings in soft morning light while offering privacy to the first-floor interior and, viewed from the garden and house, transforms the studio into a “glowing lantern” at night, Olaver said.
The first-floor interiors were also designed to be multi-functional, comprising a combined study and guest bedroom with an en-suite and small roof terrace. Red wraparound tiling in the bathroom is echoed by red panelling in the nook of the foldable bed, itself concealed behind more oak joinery when not in use.
“The new studio’s interiors echo the existing home’s rich but calm textures,” Olaver said. “Natural materials and tactile elements exist in both spaces, but the studio is slightly more playful in its approach.”
The project tasked Olaver with extending the home of a family rapidly outgrowing their existing space.
“In Melbourne, the usual answer is yet another extension that eats into the backyard,” she said. “Laneway Studio goes the other way, keeping the garden at the centre of the site and showing how a well-designed studio can add flexibility and density to an existing lot.”
More studio developments recently featured on Dezeen include a Camber Sands studio made using waste materials and a green-tiled studio in a London garden.

Star’s Tech Starcrush (which until late 2026, was called Eco-St) promises to de-ice much more effectively than traditional road salt with almost none of the corrosive effect on steel. Its secret sauce? The porous bones of an invasive starfish breed that has devastated shellfish and seaweed farms, says Star’s Tech founder Seungchan Yang. In high school, Yang thought to combine the salt and calcium chloride used in traditional de-icers with crushed starfish bones, which he hypothesized would absorb excess chloride ions and make the final product less corrosive. Today, his company is the largest producer of de-icer in South Korea; it’s used by some airports and landscapers in North America, but is preparing for a U.S. retail launch.
