podcast: architecture that listens through nature and site intelligence
the room for utopias podcast debuts with indian architects and designers examining an architecture that begins by listening rather than imposing.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
DESIGNBOOM X INDX|GLOBAL: ROOM FOR UTOPIAS
Produced in collaboration with INDX|GLOBAL during designboom.paris, designboom presents Room for Utopias, a podcast series that gathers Indian architects and designers who are exploring architecture as a practical method for imagining and testing alternative ways of living. Across eleven conversations filmed in Paris, the series steps away from grand, speculative urban visions to examine grounded propositions embedded in contemporary practice: shifting relationships with natural ecosystems, adaptable living structures, regional material cultures, and altered dynamics between architects, clients, and users.
The first article – A World that Starts with Place – brings together two podcast conversations moderated by Iñaki Laguardia, designboom’s Managing Editor. Both episodes examine an architecture that begins by listening rather than imposing: one expanding how buildings coexist with natural elements, and the other uncovering spatial, cultural, and technological intelligence already present on site.
ARCHITECTURE COEXISTING WITH NATURE AND SENSORY LIVING
The first episode of the Room for Utopias podcast convenes four practitioners – Anushri Patel of HPAD, Shilpi Sonar of Creations & Urban Saints, Shiny Mariaselvam of Studio Sculpt, and Ridhima Sogani of Ankit Gupta & Ridhima Sogani Architects – to re-evaluate architecture’s relationship with its environment. Rather than treating green elements as decorative infill or post-construction additions, the panel positions natural systems as active participants in spatial design.
Anushri Patel of HPAD addresses how architecture interacts with raw site conditions in regions with high ambient temperatures. Rather than treating green elements as decorative additions, Patel describes using native vegetation as a functional building instrument for indoor microclimate regulation and thermal control. Patel points to an evolving client mindset, noting an increased willingness to preserve existing site topographies – such as building around natural rock formations – rather than clearing ground for maximum built area.
Shilpi Sonar of Creations & Urban Saints positions nature as a baseline that exists prior to construction. Sonar argues against viewing nature as an element added after building completion, asserting that true design begins by understanding site conditions that are already present. To balance built density, Sonar advocates for designing unprogrammed, reflective spaces that allow occupants room to pause. ‘Nature cannot be added second… it’s always prevalent. We have to understand how we take architecture to it,‘ Sonar explains.
Shiny Mariaselvam of Studio Sculpt focuses on how spatial layouts condition daily human habits and routines. Mariaselvam emphasizes the responsibility of architectural projects to engage surrounding production systems and support generational artisans through regional material sourcing rather than importing elements across long supply chains. ‘Give space for the local industries and local people to be able to produce what they’re good at for generations,‘ Mariaselvam states.
Ridhima Sogani of Ankit Gupta & Ridhima Sogani Architects addresses the sensory dimension of architecture, contrasting physiological experience with visual image-making. Drawing on references like Peter Zumthor, Sogani calls on architects to design for tactile climate harmony and daily rhythms rather than purely photographic appeal. ‘When I look at a site, I listen to it. I do not ask what I want to build; I ask what the place wants to become,‘ Sogani shares.
READING SITE CONTEXT, HUMAN USERS AND TECHNOLOGICAL INTELLIGENCE
The second conversation expands site reading beyond physical topography. Moderator Iñaki Laguardia sits down with Dinesh Panwar of Urbanscape Architects, Hiren Patel of HPAD, and Monika Choudhary of ZHCollective | Habitat Architects to discuss how existing site conditions, end-user requirements, and emerging digital tools shape architectural decision-making.
Hiren Patel of HPAD frames built intervention as a responsible footprint on the planet’s surface. ‘Will we be able to do something beautiful on the skin of mother planet that it is not a scar on her skin, but a beautiful tattoo?‘ Patel asks. Patel integrates digital testing with physical site visits, using artificial intelligence models to cross-reference design plans against Christopher Alexander’s spatial patterns. Patel’s studio is currently developing ‘HirenBhai’, a personalized AI model trained on his studio’s archive and design methodology.
Monika Choudhary of ZHCollective | Habitat Architects approaches site reading through regional history and collective identity, citing the principle of Ubuntu (‘I am because we are’). In an ongoing Haveli project in Punjab, Choudhary’s practice revives regional construction techniques and traditional Nanakshahi bricks to maintain historical memory in contemporary forms. ‘If we have to build, I would love to go backward and forward—learn from the tradition, but reinterpret it in a way that the nostalgia remains, but the intelligence is carried forward,’ Choudhary says.
Dinesh Panwar of Urbanscape Architects discusses site integration when surrounding conditions demand spatial restraint. Confronted with designing a project adjacent to a 21-meter (70-foot) structure, Panwar’s studio submerged a 2,787-square-meter (30,000-square-foot) building below ground, using the surrounding earth and planted landscape as the primary context rather than competing visually. Panwar adds that for specialized programs like schools or industrial facilities, the human end-user replaces physical terrain as the primary context shaping spatial decisions.
SMALL ARCHITECTURAL PROPOSITIONS FOR ALTERNATIVE FUTURES
Through microclimate planting, local artisan networks, subterranean layouts, heritage masonry, and AI pattern testing, both conversations outline an architecture rooted in careful site observation. These projects suggest that alternative futures emerge not from top-down urban schemes, but from precise, quiet adjustments in how architects listen to physical terrain, regional culture, and human behavior before construction begins.

Expecting entitlement, researchers asked young men about sex. What they found was fear, vigilance, and shame.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:00:41 UTC
20:00:41 KST

Many young heterosexual men interviewed for a new study described sex as a source of anxiety, vigilance, and shame rather than pleasure. The research, published in Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy, is based on in-depth interviews with 31 men who came of age amid heightened attention to sexual consent, and suggests that some have internalized a broad cultural suspicion of men, approaching intimacy as a hazard to manage rather than an experience to share. Their constant self-monitoring appeared to combine a sincere wish not to hurt a partner with a fear of social or legal ruin.
Sexual consent is the mutual agreement between partners to participate in sexual activity. Over the past decade, legal reforms, university policies, and public health campaigns have increasingly promoted a standard known as affirmative consent, which requires active, ongoing agreement rather than merely the absence of a “no.” Under many of these policies, that agreement can be expressed in words or through behavior, but silence or a lack of resistance does not count. These initiatives largely focus on educating young men to ask permission, pay attention to their partners, and verify willingness at every step, shifting the responsibility onto men to confirm that their partners want to participate.
Translating those formal standards into real-life bedroom encounters is often difficult for young people. Instead of pausing to ask direct verbal questions, young adults in a 2013 study of college students typically relied on body language and physical cues to gauge whether a partner was interested in sex. Interpreting those unspoken signals is rarely straightforward, as a 2016 review of research on consent among college students indicated that real-world intimacy is frequently complicated by alcohol use, casual dating norms, and traditional expectations that men should initiate physical contact.
Classroom lessons that present consent as a simple verbal checklist often clash with how young people actually interact, and a 2022 study of teenage boys indicated that this disconnect left many students feeling confused and anxious about how to approach dating in their own social circles. Public commentary and academic literature on male sexuality have largely focused on entitlement, aggression, or convicted offenders, leaving ordinary young men’s emotional experiences of consensual intimacy mostly unexamined.
“We wanted to understand the root causes of sexual violence in order to prevent it,” lead author Jossy Forrest, a PhD candidate at the Melbourne School of Public Health at the University of Melbourne, told PsyPost. “Early on, we noticed that almost all of the literature focused on the perspectives of female victims. There were very few studies of men, and those were mainly small, dated studies of incarcerated perpetrators, some decades old.”
Forrest answered PsyPost’s questions jointly with her co-authors, Jessie V. Ford of the Mailman School of Public Health at Columbia University and Jonathan Herring of Exeter College at the University of Oxford.
“That led us to a broader question: how this generation of young men navigates sex and consent, including the gray area between bad sex and non-consensual sex,” the researchers explained. “There was almost nothing on it. These men have grown up in a period of rapid cultural change. The past few decades have been described as the ‘age of consent’: young men have been the targets of education programs, public campaigns and a wider conversation about getting consent right.”
“We wanted to know how that messaging had been absorbed, how young men navigate consent in practice, and whether it shapes their emotional experience of sex,” Forrest and her colleagues added. “This generation has also lived through other changes that raised the stakes around sex: online pornography, app-based dating, #MeToo and the conversation about ‘toxic masculinity.’ We did not set out to study those influences. But they made it more important to hear from young men today rather than assume an earlier generation’s perspective still held.”
In an earlier paper drawing on the same interviews, Forrest and Ford found that the men tried to bridge the gap between formal consent rules and real encounters by piecing together multiple cues, such as trust, timing, setting, and physical reciprocity, to infer that a partner was willing.
“Much to our surprise, the young men we spoke to were not careless about consent,” the authors said. “They had absorbed consent education and had a fairly sophisticated understanding of what consent requires. Across the board, they wanted to get it right.”
While their earlier analysis showed how young men attempt to verify consent in practice, it did not address how that constant calculation feels from the inside. In the new study, Forrest and her colleagues sought to understand the emotions, sense of personal responsibility, and self-perceptions that shape how young heterosexual men experience sex today.
“Almost all of them applied a test for consent, which we called ‘multi-factor authentication,’ that sometimes went beyond what affirmative consent requires,” the researchers noted. “One indicator was not enough. They usually needed several to line up: reciprocated and escalating physical cues, contextual signals, and in some cases verbal check-ins before, during and after sex. This paper asked what navigating consent that way felt like.”
To explore these experiences, the researchers analyzed interviews with the 31 men, out of 35 interviewed for the larger project, who identified as heterosexual, all between the ages of 18 and 32. The participants were recruited through that project, called The Blurred Lines Project, at the University of Melbourne, using campus flyers and snowball sampling, a recruitment method in which initial volunteers refer acquaintances to the study.
To be eligible, participants needed to have had at least one sexual encounter with a known adult and could not have any history of being charged with or convicted of a sexual offense. At the time of the study, 24 of the men lived in Australia and 7 lived in the United States, and each received a $40 grocery voucher for participating.
Forrest conducted all 31 interviews in person or over video calls between September and November 2023, with 26 conversations held in English and 5 in Spanish. The sessions lasted an average of 92 minutes and followed a guide of seven open-ended questions. Participants were asked what sexual consent meant to them and to share stories about encounters in which they were sure both people consented, in which they themselves had not consented but had sex anyway, in which they were unsure whether their partner consented, and in which their partner had not consented. They were also asked why young men sometimes go ahead with sex when unsure of a partner’s consent.
Notably, the interview questions never directly asked the men about their emotions, their sense of moral burden, or their fears of being accused of wrongdoing. Those topics surfaced spontaneously as the men reflected on their dating lives. The researchers transcribed the recordings and used thematic analysis, a qualitative method for identifying recurring patterns of meaning across interviews. Through inductive coding, which builds themes directly from participants’ own words rather than sorting responses into pre-existing categories, the team identified three major overlapping patterns.
“This is qualitative research, so there are no effect sizes in the statistical sense,” Forrest, Ford, and Herring explained. “The study aimed for depth rather than breadth. To our knowledge it is one of the most in-depth interview studies of young men on this topic to date.”
Asked whether anything had surprised them, the researchers replied, “Almost everything. We asked these men how they navigate consent, and left room for them to say how they feel about sex. The fear, the vigilance and the shame came up unprompted, again and again.”
Across the entire group, the authors noticed that participants rarely talked about sex as fun, relaxing, or pleasurable. Instead, 29 of the 31 men (94 percent) described sexual encounters as spaces of high anxiety, fear, and constant vigilance. Several participants described feeling caught in a bind, facing social pressure to be sexually active while also feeling they could not afford to make a mistake.
One 28-year-old participant put it this way: “It’s like you’re trying to defuse a bomb, but you don’t know which wire to cut,” adding that it was “a very tense situation” in something “meant to be enjoyable and open and free.” Two of the younger participants reported that fear overpowered any happiness they might feel during intimacy. Many also described performance anxiety, worrying that they would fail to satisfy their partner or last long enough in bed, and for some, it was hard to separate from anxiety about consent. Rather than being present in the moment, the men described operating in a habitual state of self-monitoring, constantly scanning their partner’s reactions and filtering their own behavior.
A second major theme, also expressed by 29 of the 31 participants (94 percent), centered on a deep moral concern about causing harm. The men emphasized that they wanted to be decent, ethical partners and were petrified of accidentally scaring, pressuring, or hurting a woman. They were also acutely aware that, as they saw it, men are viewed with suspicion around sex, and the authors write that this healthy moral concern often tipped into an unhealthy extreme of people-pleasing and self-erasure.
To make sure their partners felt safe and never felt used, many participants prioritized the woman’s comfort to the point of ignoring their own desires. One man admitted he did not even know what he personally liked in bed because he was so focused on pleasing his partners, while another explained that he simply handed over full control of sexual encounters to the other person. The authors write that for many of these men, care for a partner seemed to become a kind of performance, of consent and of pleasure, rather than a shared desire.
“The interviews challenged a lot of our assumptions about young men,” the researchers told PsyPost. “These were not the confident, entitled men that society, and much of the literature, had led us to expect. They were thoughtful and articulate about consent. They were also acutely anxious and often overwhelmed.”
“Many had internalized a cultural suspicion of young men. One man told us young men feel like ‘ticking time bombs for sexual assault,'” the authors continued. “We did not expect that this was how young men might have come to see themselves. As we say in the paper, it suggests that well-intentioned efforts to make men more responsible for consent may be working, but with unintended side effects.”
Alongside empathy for their partners, 26 of the 31 men (84 percent) described an intense fear of shame and personal ruin. Specifically, 19 participants (61 percent) worried about formal accusations that could destroy their careers or lead to jail time, expressing fear that an encounter that seemed consensual in the moment might be reinterpreted as assault afterward.
One participant likened youth sexual culture to waking up at age 13 and being expected to pass a legal bar exam without a single lesson, where failing meant prison. Seventeen participants (55 percent) also feared the informal court of social gossip, noting that rumors of inappropriate behavior could trigger immediate and permanent banishment from friend groups and professional circles.
Participants described a social environment that left little room for seeking advice or talking honestly with male friends when they felt uncertain about a sexual interaction. One participant said that admitting to another man that he might have overstepped would be “the same as saying you’re a child molester,” and the authors observed that the men could talk to each other about sexual performance but not about doubt. Even more troubling to the researchers, 16 of the 31 men (52 percent) turned this harsh judgment inward. Rather than feeling guilt over a specific action, they expressed what the authors describe as a standing sense of shame about who they were, using phrases such as “I’m not a good person” and “I’m so bad.”
“The most concerning thing we learned was that these men had no one to speak to honestly about consent,” Forrest and her co-authors said. “They could not admit uncertainty to themselves. They could not raise doubts with friends, family or anyone else. They believed that admitting any imperfection would be taken as admitting they were sexual predators.”
“From that, there was no coming back,” the researchers added. “If no one can discuss consent, no one learns. And if no one learns, it is hard to see how we end up with better partners or less harm.”
The authors argue that the men’s experiences seemed to be shaped by two exaggerated fears: that they might commit sexual assault despite their best efforts, and that a partner might falsely accuse them. False accusations do occur, but the authors note that police and legal reviews consistently find them to be rare, far rarer than these men assumed. In the authors’ view, these fears made it hard for the men to trust either their partners or themselves, and several described pulling back from intimacy to protect themselves.
“The findings paint a rather gloomy picture of young men’s sexual experiences, seemingly colored more by anxiety, vigilant self-monitoring, and responsibility than by the pleasure, excitement, and sense of adventure one might expect from people exploring the relatively new terrain of sexuality,” Gurit E. Birnbaum, a professor of psychology at Reichman University, who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “Their relative inexperience, combined with the contemporary cultural climate surrounding sexual consent, may contribute to these feelings.”
“It would be interesting to investigate whether this pattern reflects a broader trend and whether growing anxiety surrounding sexual encounters might help explain the decline in sexual frequency among younger generations, beyond the factors already identified in previous research,” Birnbaum said. “After all, constant vigilance and self-monitoring may make it difficult to let go, a psychological state that is often essential for sexual enjoyment and functioning.”
In the wake of the study’s publication, the researchers addressed online reactions suggesting that the participants wanted to roll back consent standards or feel less responsible for their partners. In both phases of their interview project, the men emphasized that mutual trust and genuine connection were what they valued most in a sexual relationship.
“That is not what they told us,” Forrest, Ford, and Herring said. “They cared acutely about consent, but they wanted more than consent. They told us that trust and mutuality mattered as much as consent itself. What they were looking for was connection with a partner, not perfection.”
“Another misreading is that the study is a plea for sympathy for young men,” the researchers explained. “It isn’t. The aim was understanding. The only way to understand young men is to take their own accounts seriously, as we do for everyone else.”
The authors noted that research examining men’s perspectives on sex and consent often faces skepticism in public debates, where critics sometimes assume that studying men’s anxieties excuses harmful behavior. In their view, examining how public messaging affects young men is necessary for preventing sexual violence and improving relationships for both partners.
“If we want to protect women and men from non-consensual sex, we need to know how young men think and feel,” the authors continued. “The same is true if we want more than that: ethical, healthy sexual relationships. Knowing how young men think shows us which efforts are landing, which are not, and which are producing consequences nobody intended.”
“We have been surprised by the level of resistance to the idea of studying men and taking their accounts seriously,” Forrest, Ford, and Herring said. “This is a highly loaded space, and some responses assume, without engaging with the findings or the methods, that this must be research with a pro-male or anti-feminist agenda. That troubles us. If anything, we came to the study skeptical of young men.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these accounts. The findings come from a relatively small group of 31 young men, most of whom were recruited through a single Australian university and grew up in Judeo-Christian households, meaning their perspectives may not reflect young men from different cultural, religious, or educational backgrounds.
In addition, four of the seven interview questions focused on uncertain or non-consensual sexual encounters, which may have primed the men to focus on stressful memories rather than positive ones. The study also relied on single interviews with the men and did not include their sexual partners, whose accounts of the same interactions might differ.
“However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously,” Birnbaum noted. “This is a qualitative study based on a small, nonrepresentative sample, and its findings cannot be generalized to young men as a whole. More importantly, the interviews focused heavily on sexual consent, uncertainty, and potentially problematic encounters. Such questions may have directed participants’ attention toward anxiety and negative experiences rather than pleasure and enjoyment.”
“The absence of spontaneous descriptions of pleasure in these interviews should not be mistaken for evidence that pleasure is absent from these men’s sexual lives,” Birnbaum added. “Another important limitation is that the study cannot establish whether these anxieties are specific to the current generation or reflect concerns that have always accompanied sexual exploration. Nor can it establish that contemporary discourse about consent is responsible for them.”
The authors stress that their counts describe only these 31 men and are not estimates of how common these experiences are among young men in general. They also note that a woman conducted the interviews, which may have helped some men open up about vulnerability and shame, though the accounts might have come out differently with a male interviewer.
“As for caveats, the 31 men we interviewed were recruited mainly through one Australian university,” the researchers cautioned. “Their accounts cannot stand in for young heterosexual men more broadly, let alone men in other cultural settings. The study tells us what these men experience and how they make sense of it. It suggests lines of inquiry for others to test.”
“Participants came not only from Australia but from China, Singapore, Nepal, India, Sweden, Italy, Colombia, Argentina, Lebanon, Nigeria and New Zealand,” Forrest and her colleagues pointed out. “That such a mixed group described so similar a pattern suggests this way of relating to sex may be common among young men in Western, post-#MeToo societies. The study may usefully guide future research, including quantitative research.”
Despite these constraints, the findings point to important considerations for educators, therapists, and researchers. The authors suggest that consent education programs focusing exclusively on men’s duty to avoid harm and legal punishment may inadvertently teach young men to view sex as a technical problem to be solved without error.
In the authors’ reading, the men had taken on the duty side of consent, making sure a partner wants what is happening, without the matching right to ask for what they themselves want. Shifting educational messaging to emphasize mutual trust, shared communication, and the right of both partners to express what they enjoy could help young people build healthier connections, while future studies could track young men over time and incorporate partners’ perspectives.
As for their own next steps, the researchers told PsyPost, “We are now looking at how these same men understand and make sense of their own unwanted or ambivalent sexual experiences, a question almost never asked of men.”
“Perhaps the most important implication is that sexual consent and sexual pleasure should not be treated as competing concerns,” Birnbaum said. “Ideally, sex education should emphasize not only avoiding harm but also fostering mutual desire, responsiveness, communication, and enjoyment.”
For Forrest and her co-authors, fostering that mutual desire requires moving past the assumption that men’s and women’s interests in sexual relationships are inherently at odds. They hope the study encourages researchers and educators to engage directly with young men about their experiences.
“Its purpose was to learn how to better protect women,” the researchers explained. “And its premise is that men and women are not rivals. They complement one another. Understanding one helps the other.”
“We went into this research expecting to confirm what the literature says about young men,” the authors concluded. “The men themselves showed us a far more complex picture. Their honesty, thoughtfulness and vulnerability reminded us of their humanity. If readers take one thing from this study, let it be this: young men are worth listening to, and the way to find out what they think is to ask them.”
The study, “‘It’s Like You’re Trying to Defuse a Bomb’: Fear, Responsibility, and Shame in Young Men’s Sexual Lives,” was authored by Jossy Forrest, Jessie V. Ford, and Jonathan Herring.

Tech giants need legacy businesses to keep growing as they pour trillions into the AI buildout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

The tech megacaps are collectively placing a multitrillion-dollar bet that their infrastructure spending will result in many years of profitable growth. But that's all in the future.
For now, they're reliant on their legacy businesses — whether it's online advertising, business software or e-commerce — to fund their artificial intelligence ambitions.
Earnings this quarter revealed new levels of strain on those core businesses and offered an early test of whether these companies can sustain extended bouts of spending. Meta joined Alphabet and Amazon in reporting negative free cash flow, leaving Microsoft as the lone hyperscaler to remain positive in that realm.
Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, while Amazon's outflows swelled to $42.4 billion and Alphabet's reached $9.07 billion. Microsoft's cash generation declined dramatically for a second straight quarter, this time dropping 27% to $18.63 billion, and the company said it will now turn to the bond market as it continues to ramp up AI infrastructure spending.
Hyperscaler earnings over the past two weeks have coincided with intensifying concerns about the overall health and stability of the broader AI sector. Rising interest rates are making it costlier for companies to raise debt, putting pressure on cash-burning neoclouds that have become critical to the global buildout.
While the tech giants have a cushion not afforded to the neoclouds and other players, investors eventually need the historic rates of spending to convert into massive new revenue streams. Nerves are hitting the stocks this week, with Alphabet suffering its steepest drop ever on Thursday and Amazon sliding in extended trading after its report.
Amazon said growth slowed in both its retail and ad business. Online sales gained 2% year over year, decelerating from 10% a year ago and falling short of analysts' estimates. The midpoint of Amazon's revenue guidance came in lower than the $244.5 billion that analysts were expecting, a particularly disappointing figure for the quarter that includes the holiday shopping season.
Meanwhile, Amazon expects capital expenditures this year to reach $220 billion, and analysts project that number will top $280 billion next year, according to FactSet, as the company continues to produce negative free cash flow.
At Meta, investors have responded favorably to the company's early success with its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, which present potential new sources of revenue outside of advertising.
But it will take time for these efforts to significantly impact the company's overall business while it continues spending on data center and computing gear. Capex will reach as high as $145 billion this year, the company says, and analysts see it passing $210 billion in 2027, alongside a deepening cash flow hole.
Investors sent Meta shares down 7% after the earnings report last week even though the company beat on revenue. Meta followed its report by announcing on Monday that it's planning to raise a total of $95 billion in stock to support its AI investments.
'Borrowing from the for-now'
Alphabet's report concerned investors the most.
The company's core search business saw a third straight quarter of slowing growth and missed analysts' projections, underscoring the challenges it faces with the rise of ChatGPT, Claude and other AI-powered bots and agents. YouTube-related advertising revenue also came in light.
Mark Mahaney, an analyst at Evercore, told CNBC's "Closing Bell Overtime" on Wednesday that while Google's strong cloud revenue was "good news" for the company, its decelerating digital advertising business represented "the overwhelming bad news."
Forrester analyst Tracy Woo said in an email that "Alphabet's massive capex investment in infrastructure buildout has been tolerated for now," but the company "is walking a fine line," due to the online ad sales misses.
"Weakness in Search and YouTube revenue performance relative to expectations surfaces growing concern about AI displacement of the company's largest revenue generators," Woo said. "The issue is less the current earnings miss and more the possibility that future AI spending grows faster than the cash generation of the franchises expected to support it."
But not everyone is concerned. Bullish investors say that the tech leaders have long histories of operations, and legacy businesses that are dominant enough to prop them up for the foreseeable future.
Christopher Ballard, a managing director at Check Capital Management, noted that Alphabet's negative free cash flow of $9 billion is tiny relative to the company's overall business. Its operating income topped $40 billion for the quarter.
Unlike AI model companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which are still unprofitable and spending billions of dollars a quarter on infrastructure, Alphabet has a strong balance sheet, Ballard said.
"They're borrowing from the for-now in order to invest in the future," Ballard said. "I think it's OK, and they're doing it in a responsible manner."
Although the hyperscalers didn't provide specific capex projections for next year, they all implied their data center spending spree will continue to grow, even if it means reporting some uncomfortable metrics.
"Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years, and you can spread the capex over 25 years?" Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on Thursday's earnings call. "Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that's not the world that we live in, and that's not the opportunity."

"Lady in Blue is as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

“Lady in Blue is as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine”
Tschabalala Self’s sculpture is far from being out of place in Trafalgar Square, writes Priya Khanchandani.
Who belongs in public space? How should public art represent who we are? And who deserves to be celebrated, cast in bronze and placed on a pedestal? These are some of the questions that Tschabalala Self’s commission for the Fourth Plinth, Lady in Blue, has raised in recent months, since it was unveiled in September.
I was there that cloudy morning in Trafalgar Square – a space I’d always crossed, probably like most Londoners, without thinking much about what it symbolises. When the black cloth was pulled away, we saw the figure of a Black woman caught mid-stride, one leg pushing through the fabric of her bright blue dress.
Like most of the admirals and generals monumentalised around her, she is cast in bronze. But unlike them she isn’t posed in command, she’s on her way somewhere. Her head, hair piled high, looks straight out into the city towards Whitehall, her left arm and fingers outstretched, moving with intention.
My Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist
I couldn’t help but feel satisfaction that a sculpture of a Black woman was there, taking up space in the city, on what is probably the most visible public plinth in Britain, and assumed this sentiment would be widely shared. It turns out I was wrong; my Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist and often suggesting the sculpture doesn’t fit its context.
I feel the need, therefore, to address the notion of what and who belongs in public space, and particularly in a space like Trafalgar Square.
Before Trafalgar Square existed, the site was used for the royal stables that served Whitehall Palace. Designed in 1840 by Charles Barry, the square was conceived as a stage for Britain’s image of itself, articulated through the grandeur of neoclassicism, and statues were central to its story. If you linger, you’ll spot George IV in Roman robes, sitting valiantly astride his horse. The generals Henry Havelock and Charles James Napier, whose reputations were made in the violent consolidation of British rule in India (the latter for the conquest of Sindh, where all four of my grandparents happen to be from) stand on two further plinths.
Admiral Horatio Nelson himself, the Royal Navy officer whose victory at the Battle of Trafalgar gave the square its name, overlooks them from 50 metres high atop a granite Corinthian column, guarded by four bronze lions. This composition represents a particular vision of 19th-century imperial power, reflected in the monuments and civic spaces rolled out across the Empire.
The square might be beautiful, and a fitting monument to its time, but it is also a living, breathing entity formed not only through its monuments and buildings, but also through the way it has been used.
Its function and meaning as a civic space keep being shaped by the people who have held festivals, memorials, gatherings here – or even simply walked through it on their daily commute. After it was built, Trafalgar Square quickly became a place for public assembly. From Bloody Sunday to the suffragettes to Black Lives Matter and the Palestine Coalition, it has a long tradition as a space of protest.
The square has been redesigned over and over, most significantly by Foster + Partners and Atkins in a 2003 scheme that closed the road along its northern edge, adding a terrace and turning what was essentially a traffic island into a pedestrianised space.
For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual
Lady in Blue is in dialogue with this context. She echoes the other figures here through her medium, bronze. And yet while the other figures are rooted to their respective plinths, she looks frozen in motion, echoing the movement of the people in the square below rather than the stillness of statues. The vivid blue of the figure’s dress – evoking lapis lazuli, the stone that has been ground into pigment since antiquity – is far from an attack on the Western canon, but rather in conscious conversation with it.
Once intended for an equestrian statue of William IV, the Fourth Plinth stood empty for more than 150 years before it became a space for contemporary sculpture in 1998. Unoccupied, it was always suggestive of a history waiting to be told or – given that the sculptures around it were all commemorating a contemporary moment – a future moment waiting to be solidified in bronze.
The absence of a statue suggested the question of who belongs on a pedestal was always open. Its dedication to contemporary art has allowed for redefinition and offered a chance to bring a quite spectacular historic space, a space of democracy, protest and celebration, into sync with the present.
The Fourth Plinth has become a space where identities are made visible and histories challenged, from Marc Quinn’s powerful Alison Lapper Pregnant, to Yinka Shonibare’s sculpture of Nelson’s own ship in a bottle. Works like these have also, at times, provoked arguments about how the square should be used, and yet each of them has become a part of its changing meaning.
For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual – and yet, this year’s sculpture underscores why it exists and why it’s so necessary right now.
In 2026, when a Black woman crossing this space is one of the most ordinary sights imaginable, Self’s statue validates her as worthy of belonging, not just in the city but here, in a culturally and politically charged public space dominated by white men sculpted by other white men.
Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for
That elevating such a woman into the visual language of the monument should provoke rage is telling, especially when all the figure has done is walk. Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for.
Self has said her work is meant to speak to human experience beyond racial identity. She has described the sculpture as depicting “everywoman”, implying that an ordinary person merits acknowledgement.
In other words, she hasn’t put it into the world simply as a statement about race – though its reception shows how readily the presence of a Black woman in this setting becomes about who is allowed to stand for the universal.
It’s as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine. At such a fractured time, I can’t help but feel relieved she is there, elbowing her way through the noise, making room for all of us.
Priya Khanchandani is a writer and curator specialising in contemporary design and visual culture. She was formerly head of curatorial at the Design Museum, where she curated the exhibition The Offbeat Sari and an accompanying book. She was also previously editor-in-chief of Icon, while her writing has appeared in the Financial Times, Frieze, The Guardian and The World of Interiors, as well as numerous books.

This App Brutally Shames You by Tracking How Many Hours You’ve Lost to Scrolling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a healthier relationship with your device.
One of the newer ones, which takes a slightly different approach to the norm, is Oh My Hours for iOS. (There's no sign of an Android version yet.) Rather than giving you a mass of menus and options to wade through, it simply splits each day into blocks of hours that you can either waste or use productively, then puts a black mark next to the hours during which your phone has distracted you.
It's simple, it's effective, and it just might work. Rather than seeing how long you spent on X and Instagram, you see the hours you've lost to social media algorithms and the infinite scroll. Here's how Oh My Hours works on your iPhone, plus some other apps to check out if you’re looking to develop healthier phone habits.
Moments Lost
You can get started with Oh My Hours for free on iOS. But to really make the most of it, a $10-per-year or $20 lifetime payment is required. This lets you customize what counts as a “lost” hour or day, and it gives you access to month and year views, which provide the best insights into how you're spending time on your phone.
Here's how it works. First, you indicate which apps you consider distractions, either by category (social media apps and games, for example) or by selecting apps individually. If you use any distracting app for a certain amount of time—this can be customized in settings—then that hour of the day is marked as “lost.”
The main interface shows each day as a straightforward series of circles representing hours. Every circle that’s filled in black is an hour you’ve lost to an app that has pulled you away from something more worthwhile.
It’s quite a brutal and minimalist approach, but I like it. It really brings home how much time you can spend on apps that aren’t really all that good for you, especially when you start looking at your progress (or lack of it) over entire weeks or months. However, I did find that once I’d lost a particular hour, my brain wanted to cram in as much absent-minded scrolling as possible during the rest of that hour.
By default, an hour is marked as lost if only if you spend seconds inside a distracting app. It's quite a harsh approach, but it needs to be—otherwise I think there would be the temptation to use up any allotted free time after every hour resets. You can extend this threshold period through settings, if you pay for the app.
Another handy feature here is the ability to set designated quiet hours. These are times when you really, absolutely do not want to look at your phone unnecessarily: Any use of a distracting app here blackens the boxes for all the hours in the quiet zone, not just one. Again, this can be customized, whether or not you’re using the app for free.
There’s one more option here, which is to reset an hour if you think it’s been marked incorrectly. (Maybe your finger slipped and you really didn’t mean to launch Instagram.) It’s all very simple and easy to use, and there’s an export tool here that gives you a CSV file of your stats if you want to do more with them.
Other App Picks
As I’ve already mentioned, if you’re in the market for an app that’ll gently nudge your habits toward spending less time on your phone, there are abundant options that look at the problem from a variety of angles. These are in addition to the Digital Wellbeing (Android) and Screen Time (iOS) tools you’ll find on your phone, which can be accessed from the Settings screens.
One Sec for Android or iOS takes a simple approach to phone addiction. For the apps you specify, it will load up a breathing exercise for you to complete before giving you the choice to continue to the app or back out. It’s a small tweak, but it’s surprisingly effective, and it’s backed by science. You can get started for free, while $20 a year gets you more features, including full app blocking and more advanced time tracking.
Then there’s Forest, for Android or iOS, which I’ve found to be useful whenever I’ve wanted to try to encourage myself to spend less time on my phone. The longer you ignore your handset, the bigger your virtual forest grows, and the app developers invest in real tree planting to further incentivize you. The main focus timer can be used without paying, while upgrades like customizations and allowed lists will set you back at least $6 a month.
ScreenZen, available for Android or iOS, is comprehensive and completely free (though you can donate to the developer if you find it helpful, which I’d recommend). You can set up a variety of barriers between you and your distracting apps, depending on your preference, including customized pauses (with motivational messages) and math challenges. Conventional app and timer blocks are also included.
One of the most thorough options here is Roots, though it’s available only on iOS. You’re able to schedule phone-free periods, block specific apps, and set up phone detox challenges that you can take on with friends and family. Like Oh My Hours, the app is also really good at giving you a breakdown of how much time you’ve saved by staying out of certain apps. Basic blocks and limits are free, with more advanced customizations available for $10 a month.
Also worth considering is Brick, which combines the free Android or iOS app with a small physical device that’ll set you back $59. The Brick itself is an NFC transmitter (it works like tap-to-pay), and when you want some distraction-free time, just press your phone against it to block (or unblock) specific apps. The controls are all managed in the Brick app. It’s incredibly simple, and that’s what makes it effective.

The Key Congressional Races to Watch on Election Night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The fate of Congress hangs in the balance as the outcome of a few key races will determine which party controls the House and Senate for the remainder of Donald Trump's presidency.
Republicans currently control both chambers, with 53 seats in the 100-seat Senate and 218 seats in the 435-seat House.
History suggests that Democrats will gain seats, as the party in power usually cedes representation in the midterms. In 2022, Democrats under President Joe Biden lost nine seats in the House, and in 2018, during Trump’s first term, Republicans lost about 40 seats in the lower chamber.
Democrats are widely expected to gain enough House seats to take control of that chamber. The Senate remains a toss up amid several tightly contested races, many in red states Trump won in 2024. Between campaigns, super PACs and billionaire donors, hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on a handful of races.
Here are the Senate and House races to watch ahead of election day on Nov. 3.
Alaska Senate
Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for another term against Democrat Mary Peltola, who previously served as the first Alaska native elected to Congress. But there's also a Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, and his candidacy was part of a broader effort by Democrats to help Peltola’s bid, according to a recent New York Times report. Alaska’s Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into Peltola's campaign following the report.
Polling has indicated that Sullivan and Peltola are neck-in-neck, with Peltola occasionally gaining a slim lead. While Trump won Alaska in 2024 by 13 points, the race appears to be close enough that he travelled to Wasilla on Oct. 13 to campaign on Sullivan’s behalf.
Alaska uses rank-choice voting, which means that voters will rank their top candidates as opposed to selecting one. This month, the Justice Department filed a preemptive lawsuit seeking to block certification of the election results in Alaska’s Senate race if the election results suggest the incumbent lost due to “voter confusion” due to two Dan. Sullivans on the ballot.
Read more: The 7 Key Governor Races to Watch
Iowa Senate
This midwest contest to replace outgoing Republican Sen. Joni Ernst has emerged as among the tightest in the country, with Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former broadcast journalist, vying against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, a paralympic gold medalist.
This is another state that Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Yet the recent polling suggests a true toss-up. Hinson, who has represented Iowa in the House since 2021, has distanced herself from Trump, calling for an “immediate end” to the Iran war. Trump campaigned alongside Hinson last week.
Read More: Is Iowa the Senate Race No One Saw Coming?
Michigan Senate
Michigan’s open Senate rate has emerged as perhaps the most hostile of the midterms. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former public health director, has the chance to be the country’s first Muslim senator. He’s facing off against Mike Rogers, a former FBI agent who served in the House before losing a 2024 Senate bid. Both are vying to replace Sen. Gary Peters, the Democrat who has held the seat since 2015.
El-Sayed won his party’s nomination after a fierce primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, in which his criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza became a lightning rod issue. Since the primaries, prominent Democrats including Barack Obama, Kamala Harris, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York have all come to Michigan to stump alongside him.
Republicans have attacked El-Sayed for his Muslim identity and progressive politics. At a rally in Michigan last week, Vice President JD Vance accused El-Sayed of hating America.
Recent polls have shown El-Sayed leading Rogers, but usually within the margin of error.
Maine Senate
Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, is seeking a sixth term in Maine, a moderate blue state. She is facing off against Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger and former president of the Maine Senate, who became the party’s nominee after the winner of the primary, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race amid sexual assault allegations, which he denies.
Main is the only state Trump did not win in the 2024 election where an incumbent Republican is up for reelection. Collins has distanced herself from Trump across many policy issues and on the campaign trail. She voted to convict Trump following his impeachment after the January 6 riots on the Capitol. Yet she’s also drawn criticism for backing Trump’s previous picks for the Supreme Court, despite her longstanding support for Roe v. Wade, which the Court later overturned.
Collins is chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee and frequently boasts on the campaign trial of federal dollars she helped steer to the state. Recent polls show Jackson barely leading Collins, in a race that is widely viewed as a toss-up.
Ohio Senate
Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown faces off against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed by Republican Gov. Mike DeWine to replace Vance when he went to the White House in 2025.
More than $200 million has been contributed in outside spending on this race, making it one of the most expensive this midterm season. Yet the race is a special election to only finish the remainder of Vance’s term. The winner will need to run again in 2028 to secure a full six-year term.
While Ohio has mostly voted Republican in recent years, recent polls show Brown ahead. Brown served for over a decade in the Senate until losing re-election to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024.
Kansas Senate
Kansas has not elected a Democratic Senator since 1932. But that could all change if Adam Hamilton, who founded the largest Methodist congregation in the U.S., beats out the incumbent, Republican Roger Marshall.
Marshall, a physician and former military officer, has received the support of Trump, who called him “one of my favorite Senators.” Democrats have highlighted Marshall’s pursuit of unpaid medical bills from patients from a decade ago. State court records show that he filed more than 700 of these debt-collection lawsuits, which have been a source of controversy for his campaign.
Recent polls have shown Hamilton leading up to five points against Marshall, prompting a flurry of last-minute investments by both sides into the state. Republicans acknowledged the extent of their concerns about holding on to Kansas when they moved money there after pulling out of North Carolina’s Senate race.
Texas Senate
In perhaps the most closely-watched race of the midterms, James Talarico has a chance to become the first Democratic Senator in Texas since 1993. He faces off against Republican nominee Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated the incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, in a Republican runoff in May.
Talarico has had a slight edge in recent polling, but the race remains extremely tight, and one poll from last week had them tied.
The contentious race has topped $500 million in ad spending, which could make it the most expensive non-presidential faceoff in U.S. history.
New Hampshire Senate
A tight contest for Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s seat is taking place in New Hampshire, where four-term Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas is running against former Sen. John Sununu, who was beat out by Shaheen in 2008.
Sununu’s name is well known in his state. His brother served as governor until last year and his father was also governor.
Pappas has maintained a lead in recent polls against his Trump-endorsed opponent, but Republicans are hopeful that the power of the Sununu brand in New Hampshire will help turn out their voters.
Michigan-07
In one of the most expensive House races in the country, Republican Rep. Tom Barrett is facing off against progressive William Lawrence, a climate organizer who founded the climate advocacy organization the Sunrise Movement.
Michigan’s seventh district encompasses rural and suburban areas that turned Republican in 2024 after former Democratic Rep. Elissa Slotkin left to run for Senate. Lawrence, who beat out more moderate candidates in the Democratic primary, was polling near even with Barrett in August. More recent polls show Lawerence leading.
Texas-15
Deep in South Texas, Trump marked impressive gains with Hispanic voters in 2024. Now, Texas’ 15th district has emerged as a major test of whether Republicans can hold on to those voters. Roughly 75% of eligible voters in this House district are Hispanic.
Republican Monica De La Cruz, who flipped the district in 2022, is running for reelection against Democrat Bobby Pulido, a popular Latin Grammy-winning Tejano musician who is running as a moderate.
Some recent polls show Pulido in the lead, though election results in that region have at times defied expectations. Cook’s Political Report continues to rate the race as a toss-up.
Ohio-07
Republican Rep. Max Miller, a former Trump White House aide, is battling Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union worker and former councilman, in Ohio’s seventh district.
The House race has received outsized attention over domestic abuse allegations against Miller, which he has denied. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, who is Miller’s former father-in-law, said over the summer that Miller should “seek professional help.” Moreno was joined by Ohio’s other Senator, Republican John Husted, in publicly urging Miller to exit the race in a district that has traditionally voted Republican and which Trump carried in 2024 by 11 points. Cook’s Political Report rates the race a toss-up.

NATO supreme commander reveals what the Baltic states must prepare for amid Russian threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:59:23 UTC
19:59:23 KST

Russia poses a threat, but there is no need to dramatize the situation – resilience and preparedness are essential, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, told journalists during his visit to Latvia.
Speaking about the risk of war with Russia and what residents of the Baltic states should prepare for, the general noted that Russia's actions in Ukraine demonstrate its willingness to use violence and war to achieve its political objectives. He described the violence as unimaginable and, echoing US President Donald Trump, stressed that the war must end.
Grynkewich welcomed initiatives by various governments to strengthen societal resilience. He emphasized that Latvia and other countries on NATO's eastern flank have valuable experience from which allies can learn when it comes to strengthening the resilience of populations and institutions.
The general stressed that resilience must be built now, before it becomes necessary. Referring to Trump's principle of "peace through strength," he argued that being strong and preparing for conflict could help prevent it from happening in the first place.
Asked about NATO's most urgent needs in defending the Baltic states, Grynkewich first emphasized that the alliance is already prepared to confront existing threats. At the same time, he acknowledged that NATO is constantly seeking ways to improve its capabilities.
Given the rapid pace of innovation on the battlefield, the alliance must continuously introduce new solutions to stay ahead of developments emerging from the war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East, the general explained.
Grynkewich highlighted that his current focus is primarily on data and the algorithms used to interpret it. He stressed the need for a data architecture capable of integrating information collected by sensors and providing a comprehensive picture of the battlefield, airspace and ground maneuver areas along NATO's eastern flank, enabling a more effective response to potential threats.
According to the general, such capabilities would make military operations more effective and support the implementation of the "theory of victory" he outlined in Warsaw. For this reason, he would initially prioritize the development of data architecture.
According to information published on NATO's official website, the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) is responsible for the strategic-level command of all NATO military operations and leads Allied Command Operations.
SACEUR's responsibilities include planning military operations, identifying the forces required and requesting their deployment from member states in accordance with the authorization of the North Atlantic Council and the guidance of NATO's Military Committee.
In the event of aggression against a NATO member state, SACEUR is responsible for implementing all military measures within his capabilities and authority to preserve or restore the security of alliance territory. He also provides NATO's political and military bodies with advice on military matters that could affect his ability to fulfill his responsibilities.
Grynkewich has served as NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe since July 2025.

Gas in Europe jumped above €100 amid the risk of renewed war with Iran
Kyiv • UNN
European gas futures rose to €103.16 per MWh due to geopolitical risks and low inventories. Storage facilities are 75% full.
European natural gas prices resumed their rise above €100 per megawatt-hour amid concerns that the United States could resume hostilities against Iran, potentially prolonging supply disruptions in the region. UNN reports this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
Dutch gas futures for delivery in December, the most actively traded contract, jumped more than 5% on Friday, October 30, after briefly declining in the previous session. Benchmark contracts were up approximately 42% on a monthly basis, marking the biggest such increase since March, immediately after the start of the war with Iran.
A number of factors converged to drive a sharp rise in prices this month, including colder weather and growing heating demand, as traders began drawing on winter fuel stocks, which are already at a seasonal low.
Geopolitical risks added to upward pressure as concerns grow that the United States could resume strikes against Iran after next week's midterm elections.
On Thursday, October 29, a senior U.S. commander briefed U.S. President Donald Trump on military options, The Wall Street Journal reported. Following the report, oil prices also rose on Friday.
Oil prices rise for the fourth consecutive month amid the war with Iran30.10.26, 08:32 • 3974 views
Meanwhile, LNG exports from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz — which accounted for about one-fifth of global capacity before the conflict began — remain significantly below prewar levels despite a recent increase, leaving the market vulnerable to the risk of a complete halt in supplies from the region.
In addition, LNG supplies from another major exporter, Australia, declined over the past month, reducing global supply and supporting prices.
What analysts say about prices
Low gas stocks in Europe and geopolitical risks "are likely to continue pushing front-month prices to new highs as concerns grow about a potential escalation in the Middle East," according to an analytical note from Energy Aspects Ltd. They expect major supply disruptions during the first quarter of 2027.
European fuel storage facilities are only 75% full, well below the normal level for this time of year, while in the largest economy, Germany, the figure is below 62%. On Thursday, an Italian government official sharply criticized Germany for insufficiently replenishing its natural gas reserves this summer, arguing that the shortage is driving up prices across Europe.
"We, too, would like to see somewhat higher gas storage levels," Klaus Müller, president of Germany's Federal Network Agency, said in an interview with local radio on Friday morning, October 30. He added that the country had made progress in diversifying its energy supply sources.
Bloomberg expects higher LNG prices to reduce demand in some price-sensitive regions in November, such as South and Southeast Asia. Europe may still have to pay more for fuel supplies, especially when colder weather and periods of weak winds increase fuel demand.
By 11:40 a.m. Amsterdam time, Dutch December futures had risen 5.3% to €103.16 per megawatt-hour.

Estonia's judges may take pay dispute to European Commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:58:00 UTC
19:58:00 KST

Estonia's judges may take pay dispute to European Commission
Estonian judges may turn to the European Commission in the face of a four-year pay freeze, but Minister of Finance Jürgen Ligi (Reform) believes everyone must currently make savings.
Judges are concerned about a decision in the state budget strategy to curb salary growth for senior public officials over the next four years.
Judges have a special status under the Constitution, and their salaries are also linked to the obligation to hold office for life. As reduced indexation was initially supposed to end in 2028, the government decided to extend it until 2031.
Although judges are outraged, Ligi said he currently sees no reason to discuss judges' special status.
"The initial decision has been made, and it is not reasonable to discuss judges' special status. What is reasonable to discuss is whether those who currently fall outside this regulation should also have their regulations changed, primarily the Riigikogu," he said.
The minister added that indexing salaries and linking them to average wages or employment is a fairly safe approach.
"Nothing unfair or disproportionate is happening there. We are going through difficult times, and in a situation where the public sector is making cuts across the board, it is difficult to argue that anyone is exempt from the inevitability of cuts," he explained.
Ligi compared the current situation to the financial crisis, when there were also major political risks, but relief could then be expected from the introduction of the euro. Now the situation is more serious.
Anu Uritam, a Harju County Court judge who heads the Estonian Association of Judges, told ERR that this argument is understandable, but judges are unwilling to accept the situation.
"Which areas the state cuts and which it invests in is a political decision. We are going through difficult times, but that has not prevented the state from investing in major construction projects, from Süku to Rail Baltica. So ultimately, it is a political decision where the state chooses to allocate its resources and where to make cuts. As for the judicial system, the administration of justice is one of the state's core functions, and a state cannot function without it," she said.
Uritam explained that judges' workloads have increased, for example, due to the migration crisis, and that finding new judges is becoming increasingly difficult because the judicial system has undergone several budget cuts.
She added that by reducing indexation, the state has already broken its promise regarding judges' social guarantees.
Uritam therefore does not rule out raising the issue at the international level as well.
"One option we have not yet used is to approach the European Association of Judges through the Estonian Association of Judges and ask it to draw up a resolution supporting Estonian judges. This would be forwarded to the governments of European member states, and we could also inform the European Commission. In other words, we will try to draw attention to the problem internationally as well," she promised.

Report: Israel gives Gaza terrorists choice between dying alone or with family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:57:56 UTC
19:57:56 KST

Israeli intelligence officers have reportedly been calling Palestinian terrorists in the Gaza Strip and warning them that they must leave their families before being targeted in airstrikes or risk having their relatives killed alongside them, according to an investigation published Thursday by the London-based pan-Arab newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat.
The newspaper reported that at least five such incidents have occurred over the past three months, citing Palestinian field sources familiar with the cases. The accounts, which could not be independently verified, suggest Israeli forces have used advance telephone warnings to isolate suspected terrorists before carrying out targeted killings.
The latest reported incident occurred Wednesday afternoon in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip, where a Palestinian man identified as Muhammad al-Bayouk was killed in an Israeli drone strike after allegedly receiving a telephone call from an officer of the Shin Bet, Israel's domestic security agency.
According to Asharq Al-Awsat, the officer presented al-Bayouk with a choice: remain with his family and risk their deaths in an airstrike or go alone to the roof of a building at a shelter for displaced Palestinians, where he would be targeted.
Al-Bayouk reportedly chose to leave his relatives and climbed onto the roof of a room inside the shelter, where he was struck by a small missile fired from an Israeli drone.
Several members of the al-Bayouk family declined to comment when approached by the newspaper. Others confirmed the account, including a cousin who was present at the scene.
The relative said another family member, al-Bayouk's aunt, was seriously injured while attempting to stop him from leaving after receiving the alleged warning call.
The report did not establish al-Bayouk's organizational affiliation or describe the intelligence underlying Israel's decision to target him.
At least five reported cases in three months
Palestinian field sources told Asharq Al-Awsat that similar incidents have occurred repeatedly in recent months, although they cautioned that some claims circulating locally had exaggerated their frequency.
One source said initial rumors suggested the practice was widespread, but subsequent security reviews identified at least five cases over the preceding three months.
According to the source, individuals receiving such calls from Israeli intelligence officers felt compelled to comply with the instructions because they feared their families would otherwise be killed.
The source accused Israel of using the threat of harm to relatives to pressure targeted individuals into exposing themselves to military strikes.
He also drew parallels with allegations that Israeli interrogators had threatened Palestinian detainees with harm to their relatives if they refused to provide intelligence.
In some cases, the source alleged, detainees were shown photographs of dead family members as a means of psychological pressure.
Those allegations were not independently substantiated in the report.
The source said all the documented telephone-warning cases involved individuals with connections to terrorist activity.
By contrast, he claimed, Israel has continued to target senior commanders and prominent field operatives through larger strikes involving multiple missiles and attack drones, including attacks that have caused civilian casualties.
Palestinian sources reject suggestion of a more restrained approach
Sources interviewed by Asharq Al-Awsat rejected the suggestion that advance warnings reflected a broader effort by Israel to protect Palestinian civilians.
They argued that the practice should not be interpreted as evidence that Israeli forces had adopted a more humanitarian approach or were attempting to improve Israel's international image.
The sources pointed to continued Israeli strikes that they said had killed civilians, including women and children.
Nevertheless, the newspaper suggested that the reported use of smaller precision weapons and attempts to separate terrorists from their families could reflect an Israeli effort to reduce civilian casualties amid sustained international criticism.
The report also cited a September article in the Israeli newspaper Haaretz describing an understanding between Washington and Jerusalem over the use of force in Gaza.
According to that account, the Trump administration has generally refrained from intervening in Israeli military operations except in exceptional circumstances, while President Donald Trump has not demanded that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu broadly restrain Israeli forces in the territory.
The Haaretz report said American attention had focused particularly on civilian casualties, which had declined relatively as Israeli forces increasingly used drones armed with smaller bombs and missiles to target Hamas operatives.
A Palestinian field source disputed that assessment, telling Asharq Al-Awsat that civilians continued to be killed in strikes targeting terrorists and in what he described as indiscriminate shelling.
The source cited a strike Wednesday in southern Khan Younis that reportedly killed civilians, government employees and representatives of merchants.
According to the account, the strike hit a facility operated by government ministries responsible for monitoring the movement of goods entering the Gaza Strip.
The report did not provide an independently verified casualty toll for that incident.
Additional strikes reported across Gaza
The Asharq Al-Awsat report also described several Israeli military operations across the Gaza Strip amid continuing accusations of ceasefire violations.
Two Palestinians were reportedly killed in an Israeli strike targeting a vehicle in the Maghazi refugee camp in central Gaza.
Another Palestinian sustained moderate injuries in a separate strike in the Safatawi area, west of the Jabaliya refugee camp in northern Gaza.
The Palestinian Shehab News Agency reported that two bodies and several wounded people were brought to Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital following the Maghazi strike.
The agency characterized the attack as part of what it described as continuing Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement.
Elsewhere, several Palestinians were reportedly wounded by gunfire and artillery shelling in different parts of the territory.
In eastern Gaza City, a helicopter fired a missile early Wednesday at an unoccupied apartment on Yafa Street that had previously been struck, according to the report. No injuries were reported in that incident.
Shehab also reported additional Israeli military activity across the Gaza Strip, including gunfire directed toward tents housing displaced Palestinians, artillery strikes, a drone attack on a residential apartment, bulldozing operations and gunfire from naval vessels.
The casualty reports and circumstances of the individual incidents could not be independently verified.
The report did not include an IDF or Shin Bet response to the allegations.

Sports court orders Russia’s return to ice hockey world championships from 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:57:24 UTC
19:57:24 KST

The Court of Arbitration for Sport, known as CAS, has ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to ice hockey world championships from 2027, despite the international federation’s decision to maintain its exclusion.
The ruling covers several youth world championships and the men’s World Championship in Germany in May 2027, according to a statement on the court’s website.
The International Ice Hockey Federation, or IIHF, said it was disappointed by the decision but respected it. It warned, however, that Russia’s return would require changes to tournaments already organized.
The men’s championship has its 16 participating countries divided into two groups, and the match schedule has already been set.
“The change requires extensive coordination with the relevant national member associations, organizing committees, and host authorities.”
“This includes, among other things, a review of tournament formats, match schedules, travel and accommodation arrangements, as well as security measures,” the IIHF said.
The federation said the ruling did not account for practical changes that could not be implemented immediately.
Russia challenged exclusion
The IIHF decided earlier this year to maintain Russia’s exclusion on safety and security grounds. Russia appealed, but the federation’s appeals body upheld the decision.
Russia then took the case to CAS, which ruled in its favor following a hearing.
Russian national and club teams have been excluded from IIHF tournaments since February 28, 2022, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s ranking points have been frozen during its exclusion, leaving it with enough points to return at the top of the world rankings. Ukraine is the lowest-ranked participant in the upcoming men’s championship.
The women’s World Championship begins next week in Herning and Esbjerg, Denmark, without Russia. CAS said its ruling would apply to the women’s World Championship at the end of 2027.

Parcels arriving from outside the EU to Denmark and other EU countries will face a new fee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:57:13 UTC
19:57:13 KST

Cheap goods from Chinese online shops are arriving in EU in huge numbers, raising concerns about product safety.
In 2025 alone, Danish customs registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Therefore, the European Union will introduce a permanent handling fee of 2 euros per line item in parcels arriving from outside the bloc starting Sunday, November 1, the Danish Customs Agency said Friday.
The fee, equivalent to about 15 Danish kroner, will apply regardless of a parcel’s total value. It will be added to the temporary customs duty introduced this summer on parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Items with the same commodity code count as one line item. Three cotton T-shirts, for example, would incur a handling fee of 2 euros. A cotton T-shirt and a pair of denim jeans would count as two line items, bringing the fee to 4 euros.
The existing customs duty is 3 euros per line item in parcels with a total value below 150 euros.
Christian Lützen, director of the Danish Customs Agency, said the number of low-value parcels sent to consumers from outside the EU had fallen since the customs duty took effect.
“With the handling fee, we are stepping up efforts even further to, among other things, strengthen member states’ opportunities to inspect the contents of parcels,” he said in the press release.
“There are still problems with many of the goods in relation to consumer safety, and as an authority at the border, we must take that seriously.”
When the customs duty was introduced this summer, Lützen said the agency had previously seen a sharp increase in goods arriving from Chinese online shops. He called it “a major problem across EU countries” and said the duty should help make shopping with Danish businesses more attractive.
In 2025, the agency registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros. A count showed that more than 90% of parcels entering Denmark contained Chinese goods.
Shein and Temu were among the 10 online shops most used by Danish consumers in the latest survey by Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, a business organization.
The two platforms sell products ranging from clothing to kitchen equipment and have faced criticism over poor quality and illegal chemicals in their products.
