Seven governor races to watch as voters weigh Trump, economy
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:30:48 CET
19:30:48 KST

By Helen Coster
NEW YORK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Three dozen governors’ races will be decided in the November 3 elections, with President Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the cost of living at the top of voters’ minds, alongside local concerns ranging from water rights and data centers to cancer rates.
Some races have turned ugly, including an Ohio contest between Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton that features the Democrat’s estranged mother in an attack ad. Others could be history-making, such as Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms’ bid to become the country’s first Black woman elected governor.
Democrats now hold 24 governorships and Republicans 26. If Democrats can manage a net gain of at least two seats they will lead a majority of states for the first time since 2010.
Here are seven key governor races to watch:
ARIZONA
Water has become a key campaign issue in drought-hit Arizona, where Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs is seeking reelection against Republican US Representative Andy Biggs. Other top issues are cost of living and immigration, with Hobbs seeking to position herself as tougher on border security than many national Democrats.
Biggs is a former head of the right-wing US House Freedom Caucus, which has pushed for deep cuts in federal spending.
Abortion rights have featured prominently in the race, with Hobbs a supporter while Biggs has a long record as an opponent. Arizona voters approved a constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights in 2024.
MICHIGAN
Michigan’s race is one of the most competitive gubernatorial contests, pitting Democrat Jocelyn Benson, the state’s top election official, against Republican US Representative John James. The candidates are battling to succeed term-limited Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer, making it one of 19 open-seat races this cycle.
Michigan is a closely divided swing state that Trump won in 2016 and 2024, while Democrat Joe Biden carried it in 2020. Neither party has elected back-to-back governors in the state since the 1960s.
GEORGIA
Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, is running against Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, to succeed Republican Governor Brian Kemp. A Bottoms win would make her the first Black woman elected governor in the US and the first Democrat elected governor of Georgia in more than a quarter century.
Because Georgia will likely be a key presidential battleground in 2028, both parties view the gubernatorial race as an early test of voter sentiment.
Jackson, who has spent more than $100 million of his own money on the race, has generally aligned himself with Trump’s agenda, while Bottoms has sought to mobilize the diverse Democratic coalition that helped Biden win the state in 2020.
Bottoms rose to national prominence in 2020 as she guided Georgia’s largest city through protests, civil unrest and the COVID pandemic. Her base is in the Atlanta metro area, whose rapid growth has reshaped Georgia politics.
OHIO
The race between Republican entrepreneur Ramaswamy and Democrat Acton, a physician, drew national attention over an explosive attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother. In a video run by the Ramaswamy campaign, Donna Arthur disputes Acton’s account of a childhood marked by homelessness and sexual abuse and urges Ohioans not to vote for her.
Acton, a former director of the Ohio Department of Health who led the state’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, has said she was sexually abused by her stepfather. The stepfather, who died in 2004, fled the state after he was charged with raping his stepdaughter and never stood trial.
The state’s reputation as a perennial swing state faded after 2016 when Trump won it with strong support from working-class voters, who helped to turn it into a reliably Republican state. The race is being watched as a test of whether Democrats can turn economic dissatisfaction into votes. Democrats have won just one of the state’s last nine gubernatorial elections.
IOWA
Iowa is holding its first open governor’s race since 2006, after Republican Governor Kim Reynolds said she would not seek reelection. State Auditor Rob Sand, the only Iowa Democrat currently holding statewide elected office, faces Republican businessman Zach Lahn.
The state’s incidence of cancer, at the second-highest rate in the country behind Kentucky, has emerged as a major campaign topic alongside kitchen-table issues such as the cost of living. Interest has been fueled by worries that exposure to nitrates, pesticides and other environmental contaminants may be contributing to the high cancer rate.
The race has also focused on education and government accountability. Sand has campaigned as an independent watchdog critical of Republican fiscal management and the state’s private-school voucher program.
Lahn has embraced lower taxes, school choice and a more conservative approach to social issues.
NEVADA
In a contest centered on affordability, Republican Governor Joe Lombardo is in a neck-and-neck race with Democratic challenger Aaron Ford, the state’s attorney general.
Nevada residents have voiced concerns over tariffs, a tourism slowdown and high gas prices, giving Ford an opening to defeat Lombardo despite the incumbent’s 2-1 fundraising advantage.
Data centers have also emerged as a central campaign issue. Ford has proposed a halt to new data-center tax abatements and wants to require that developers shield residents from higher energy costs. He has also called for strong regulations to protect jobs from AI.
Lombardo, while imposing new restrictions on some of the tax incentives that lured the industry to the state, has generally championed data centers as an economic driver.
WISCONSIN
A central question in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race is whether voters, who backed Trump in 2024 and Biden in 2020, want a governor aligned with the Republican president. Republican Tom Tiffany, a three-term US Representative endorsed by Trump, has played down that connection. His Democratic opponent, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, has sought to link Tiffany to Trump’s agenda.
In Congress, Tiffany has supported conservative causes such as gun rights and lower taxes, and co-sponsored federal legislation that would have banned most abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy. Crowley supports abortion rights and has framed reproductive rights as a key campaign issue. Wisconsin bans abortion after 20 weeks and requires a 24-hour waiting period as well as parental consent for minors.
(Reporting by Helen Coster in New York; Editing by Paul Thomasch and Edmund Klamann)

By Steve Holland and Gram Slattery
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - The Trump administration does not plan to back Flavio Bolsonaro’s claim to be Brazil’s rightful leader, despite helping the defeated candidate reach the US after years of supporting him and his father, a US official and another person familiar with the matter said on Thursday.
President Donald Trump has said Brazil’s election on Sunday looked “rigged” but has pointed out that he offered no endorsement in the hotly contested race. Trump has also said he gets along well with incumbent leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the 81-year-old former union leader who beat the odds to clinch reelection by 3.5 percentage points.
The US official and the person familiar with the matter, who both spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Trump has no current plans to support Bolsonaro’s political ambitions even as the administration allowed him into the country, though they said the president could change his mind.
The Trump administration’s posture suggests the president may be reluctant to cause a fresh crisis in relations with Brazil, which have gone through ups and downs in recent months.
LAST-SECOND DEPARTURE AFTER COURT RULING ON PASSPORT
A third US official, also speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Bolsonaro’s political capital had fallen now that he is in self-exile. Many conservatives in Brazil who had expected him to lead the opposition in the coming years have criticized his flight.
The White House referred a request for comment to the State Department, which did not reply. The Brazilian government and a representative for Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.
Flavio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is imprisoned in Brazil for attempting a self-coup to stay in power after losing his reelection bid in 2022.
Some Brazilian officials, also speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters that Bolsonaro’s departure helps Lula by weakening the conservative opposition in Brazil’s Congress.
Bolsonaro’s flight was a last-second decision that came after a Brazilian Supreme Court justice ordered him to turn in his passport, granting a request by federal police who are investigating him over two alleged money-laundering schemes, US officials and others familiar with the matter said.
The police request came in just minutes after the election was called for Lula, according to Brazilian media reports, a timeline that some conservatives have pointed to as evidence of political motivation.
Supporters of Lula’s government point out that, days before the election, Flavio’s brother, Eduardo, suggested publicly that Flavio should leave Brazil if he lost. Eduardo, a former congressman who himself lives in the US, was convicted in Brazil in June of courting interference from the Trump administration in his father’s trial.
Argentine authorities said that Flavio Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters crossed a bridge into northern Argentina at 10:50 p.m. on Tuesday before boarding a chartered aircraft at 11:30 p.m. Bolsonaro and his family then flew to Miami via Ecuador.
It is unclear how Bolsonaro traveled from his home in Brasilia to the bridge crossing 750 miles (1,300 km) away or exited Brazil without the knowledge of Brazilian customs officials. But during that journey, Bolsonaro contacted multiple US officials regarding his departure, according to one of the US officials.
Jason Miller, a Trump adviser who is close to the Bolsonaro family, helped arrange the flight from Argentina, the person familiar with the matter said. During Bolsonaro’s journey, Secretary of State Marco Rubio recommended to Trump that Bolsonaro be admitted, a recommendation the president signed off on, according to the US official.
During Bolsonaro’s two-leg flight, State Department officials scrambled to determine the best legal route for admitting him and his family, discussing the matter with Department of Homeland Security personnel, the official said. Ultimately, US authorities granted them humanitarian parole at the border, a temporary status given to individuals when urgent humanitarian concerns or a significant public interest are at play, the official added.
In an open letter posted on X on Wednesday, Bolsonaro declared himself “the elected president.” He then deleted that version and updated it with another letter in which he said he was Brazil’s rightful “leader.”
BRAZILIAN POLITICS WORTHY OF A TELENOVELA
The Bolsonaro departure was the latest chapter in a tumultuous period in Brazilian politics and in US-Brazil relations.
Bolsonaro’s father was president from 2019 to 2023, then lost reelection to Lula and was jailed last year for his self-coup attempt. Lula himself spent 17 months in jail in 2018 and 2019 on corruption charges that were later annulled.
The US last year slapped sanctions on the judge overseeing the trial of the elder Bolsonaro and other Brazilian officials. Washington lifted the sanctions after Trump and Lula had a notably cordial interaction at the UN General Assembly.
During the campaign, Brazil objected to what it called attempts by some US officials to boost the Bolsonaro campaign, and the government has refused to seat the incoming US ambassador to Brazil, a close Rubio ally, in part due to those objections.
Reuters reported last week that two conservative State Department officials successfully pushed for the Brazil sanctions as well as terrorist designations of two Brazilian organized crime groups, measures aimed at tilting the election in Bolsonaro’s favor.
Still, even as Trump has attacked the way Brazil conducted the election, he has refrained from criticizing Lula.
“I like Lula, I get along with him very well,” Trump told reporters on Monday. “I just think it had a very bad look, the election.”

DUBLIN, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Ireland will set up a government body that would for the first time undertake research and preparations for the possibility of future unity with British-run Northern Ireland, Prime Minister Micheal Martin was quoted as saying on Friday.
Martin told the Irish Times that the new body would be tasked with scoping out the models and challenges for different potential outcomes, including Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom or maintaining its devolved entity but as part of a united Ireland.
He was fleshing out an idea first referenced in a speech this week, when he said a new approach was required to carefully address the need for an “independent and dispassionate base of knowledge on which you can have a credible discussion about constitutional futures.”
“What has concerned me about this push for a border poll since Brexit is that it’s partisan, it’s a one-sided advocacy approach,” Martin told the Irish Times.
“It’s sort of putting forward the idea that this would be easy and that it’s inevitable and our time has come. And it’s almost that this would be a victory for nationalism, as opposed to an approach which genuinely seeks to hear all voices.”
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement, the British government is obliged to call a referendum on Irish unity if it appears likely that a majority of Northern Irish voters would back it.
While opinion polls consistently show a majority in favour of remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed since the UK voted to leave the European Union a decade ago and Irish nationalist parties like Sinn Fein stepped up calls for a referendum.
Martin’s proposal, the first steps of which he said he would bring to cabinet before the end of the year, is the latest gradual move by the dominant government parties south of the border to consider what a united Ireland might look like.
His government partner Fine Gael will publish what it has described as a blueprint for a unified island at its annual conference next week.

Which vaccinations should you have this autumn and which are recommended in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:30:13 UTC
19:30:13 KST

In Germany new recommendations for coronavirus vaccinations now apply. Even last year far fewer people had themselves vaccinated against flu.
In the United Kingdom, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, 56, deliberately had his flu jab in front of the cameras. And in New York, the 35-year-old mayor Zohran Mamdani was already seen at the beginning of October laughing with a badge reading "I got my flu shot".
However, the flu jab hype is not felt in Germany, where fewer and fewer Germans are getting vaccinated.
As the German medical magazine Ärzteblatt reports, the share of people aged 60 and over who were vaccinated against flu in 2025 was 34%. According to the German federal government agency Koch Institute (RKI), this is the lowest level in 17 years.
Vaccination is recommended for people aged 60 and over; for everyone with chronic illnesses; for residents of care homes; for medical staff; for pregnant women; and for people who have contact with certain animals such as pigs or poultry, based on RKI recommendations.
Older people in particular should get vaccinated against flu before winter. In addition to the flu shot, immunisation against pneumococci is recommended for older people in Germany, as well as against herpes zoster, or shingles. Vaccination against the respiratory disease RSV should be discussed with a doctor as well.
Is another coronavirus vaccination needed?
Coronavirus vaccination is recommended for those over 75 or who belong to a risk group, such as patients with weakened immune systems or medical staff. Pregnant women with health risks should also be immunised.
Because of the reduced recommendation, however, not all patients with statutory health insurance now have the coronavirus vaccination fully reimbursed.
According to the RKI, as early as 2025, only 16% of people over 60 in Germany were still getting vaccinated against COVID-19.
Measles vaccination is compulsory for children in Germany
There is a special vaccination schedule (source in German) for babies and young children. Among other things, it provides for immunisation against the respiratory virus RSV, tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough, polio, hepatitis B, meningitis, measles, rubella and mumps.
In the United States, there have recently been waves of severe measles cases because of a lack of vaccination protection.
In Germany, the Measles Protection Act requires proof of vaccination or immunity for children before they start nursery or school and for people born after 1970 who work in childcare or healthcare facilities.
Vaccinations are good for health
Several studies indicate that vaccinations can have positive effects beyond the protection provided by immunisation against a specific disease. Research is being carried out into how far the flu jab protects against cardiovascular complications and which vaccinations can help prevent dementia.
The Deutsches Ärzteblatt reports evidence of so-called heterologous or non-specific effects, in which a vaccination influences the immune system in such a way that the immune response to other pathogens or diseases also changes.

Male Insecurity Over Penis Size Is a Booming Business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Bill Moore is what you might call a televangelist for big dicks.
At AdvancedYou, an anti-aging aesthetic clinic specializing in “biohacking and wellness treatments” that he runs out of a Dallas strip mall, Moore offers men a unique form of personal salvation through PhalloFill. It’s a penis enlargement procedure that, while not able to add inches in length, involves injecting hydrocyanic acid dermal filler for increased girth.
In Daniel Lombroso’s new documentary Manhood, in theaters this week, the director tracks this desperate quest for sexual adequacy among men who find themselves struggling with self-worth and the crisis of modern masculinity.
As headlines about the male loneliness epidemic were making the rounds a few years ago, which Lombroso felt were “sort of thin and maybe navel-gazy,” he decided he wanted to tell a more “propulsive story” about what was going on with men in America. Around that time, he also started hearing more about penile enhancement and began talking to some of the practitioners offering it as well as the men getting it, including Moore, who invited him to Texas.
Moore fancies himself something of a cosmetic revolutionary. He was among the first wellness professionals in Dallas to use platelet-rich-plasma for hair replacement. In Manhood, his goals remain unwavering: to make his patented penis enlargement technique as commonplace as Botox.
You could say Lombroso, a former editorial producer for The Atlantic and The New Yorker, has a metaphorical hard-on for subcultural deep dives. His first documentary, White Noise, followed white-nationalist groups for three years from Donald Trump’s 2016 win until the end of his first term.
With Manhood, Lombroso wanted to understand what was driving men to get on the operating table. During visits to Moore’s clinic, he met men with unique stories: a megachurch pastor; border patrol agents; a man suffering from brain cancer. David, a 24-year-old gay OnlyFans star shunned by his religious mother, who visits AdvancedYou following a botched procedure, and Ruben, an out-of-work father of five who moonlights as a stand-up comedian and listens to the Joe Rogan podcast, are cast as the central figures in the film, along with Moore.
“I was just like, this is fucking crazy that these guys are really eager to tell Bill, and were really eager to tell me, what was going on in their life,” Lombroso says. To his surprise, an overwhelming majority—he estimates around 75 percent—of the men undergoing the procedure were straight. “People for some reason make the assumption that it wouldn't be that division, but it's mostly straight men,” whom he notes were “conservative-leaning.”
Lombroso is careful not to reduce the men seeking penis enlargement to one type but says they all carried a similar trait: “this deep feeling of shame and social isolation.”
Penis size is an unusually intimate subject shaped by cultural ideas about masculinity and self-worth—though not everyone buys into the belief that the size of your penis determines your well-being. In one scene, Ruben talks with a bar patron about the documentary before his stand-up set, explaining that the film is about “mental health” and “normalizing” the procedure, only for the man to respond with gleeful skepticism. “Having a small dick makes you crazy?” he wonders jokingly.
“There’s a limit to what a scalpel and a syringe can provide,” Alex Tatem, a prosthetic urology specialist, says in the film. “I can fill your penis with filler, but I cannot fill the hole in your heart.”
There is a pressure on men to constantly improve, and Manhood suggests that perhaps Moore, despite his seemingly genuine intentions, has exploited that need. His “girth enhancement” procedure, which costs between $2,500 and $4,000 per visit, basically runs like a subscription model where he encourages men to visit three, four, even five times. The catch is that if they want to maintain their desired girth, they have to visit once a year for the rest of their life.
“You would think that this technique would have stayed in the hands of urologists, but now this is something that is in the hands of corporate marauders,” Paul Perito, a board-certified urologist explains in the film. PhalloFill has expanded to 32 clinics across the US.
More men are pushing their bodies to the limit for validation in ways they never did before. They have outpaced women as the fastest-growing demographic for plastic surgery in the US and are undergoing cosmetic procedures at a higher rate compared to years prior to 2020, according to the International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery. Among Gen Z and millennials, nonsurgical cosmetic treatments—everything from skin resurfacing to body sculpting—are growing more widespread.
Nowhere is this trend more pronounced than in the looksmaxxing movement, popular in manosphere and incel circles, where young men are encouraged to undergo extreme physical modifications in order to be more sexually desirable. One 21-year-old looksmaxxing YouTuber I interviewed last year likened the trend to a “looks inflation.”
“It is ridiculous how much it’s meant to be a sign of strength,” one client says, lying on the operating table as Moore pokes tiny needles into the shaft of his penis. “There are even allegations of, like, ‘Oh, a terrorist must have a small dick’ … And you’re a guy, so you’re just gonna take it.”
Morag Yule, president of the Society for Sex Therapy, puts it another way. “Insecurity is big business, and there is money to be made” off people who will “do almost anything to feel better about themselves.”
While Lombroso never paints Moore purely as a villain or savior, it is evident that PhalloFill is part of the larger wellness industry exploiting male insecurities. A 2026 study by researchers from the digital safety organization Reset Tech argued that the manosphere operates more like a pyramid scheme, preying on the vulnerabilities of men like Ruben, who, in the end, ends up pouring so much money into injections that he and his wife are forced to move out of their house and relocate to Phoenix with his “first baby momma.” “We weren’t making enough money to afford everything,” Ruben says.
What ultimately emerges in Manhood is a darker truth about exploitation and profit motives in the medical industry. Doctors and practitioners are recast as cash-thirsty business sharks. “When they see money, that excites them,” Lombroso says. “I think that’s a really unfortunate thing that we don’t talk enough about. A lot of the people in the movie are trained urologists who could be doing penile reconstructions or helping men with [erectile dysfunction]. Instead, they see a quick way to make a buck putting lip filler in people’s dicks.”

Italian inflation hit 5.4% in October says Istat
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:29:14 CET
19:29:14 KST

Italy's annual inflation rate climbed
even further this month, driven by soaring energy prices linked
to the Iran war, hitting 5.4%, the highest level since August
2023, according to a preliminary estimate for October released
by Istat on Friday.
                                    
The annual inflation rate was 4.2% in September.
                                    
The national statistics agency said energy prices had
accelerated, going from +22.6% to +31.4%.
                                    
"The acceleration of inflation was mainly due to the dynamics of
prices of non-regulated energy products (from +22.5% to +29.4%)
and of regulated energy products (from +25.8% to +59.5%), of
unprocessed food (from +5.5% to +7.5%), of services related to
transport (from +1.6% to +3.1%) and of processed food including
alcohol (from -0.6% to -0.2%)," Istat said.
                                    
The agency said its consumer price index was up 0.9% in
month-on-month terms.

China joins Germany in backing South Africa's G20 participation amid US' exclusion threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:26:56 UTC
19:26:56 KST

China on Friday voiced support for South Africa to continue participating in G20 meetings, as the United States prepares to host foreign ministers of the world’s 20 largest economies.
“The G20 plays an important role in strengthening multilateralism, promoting world economic growth and improving global governance,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
“It is a major platform for international economic cooperation, and South Africa is an important member of the G20. China supports South Africa in continuing its participation in G20-related activities,” Guo said.
He was responding to questions about the reported exclusion of South Africa from the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, which begins on Friday in Atlanta, Georgia.
Earlier, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had supported South Africa’s participation in the meeting.
US excludes South Africa from summit
In November 2025, US President Donald Trump said South Africa would not be invited to the G20 summit scheduled for November 2026 in Miami, Florida.
Trump had also skipped the leaders’ summit hosted by South Africa in Johannesburg in 2025.
At the time, the White House said South African President Cyril Ramaphosa had pushed to issue a G20 leaders' declaration addressing the climate crisis and other global challenges "despite consistent and robust US objections."
On Monday, South Africa’s ambassador to the US, Roelf Meyer, said the government “is no longer troubled” by its exclusion from the Miami summit.
South Africa had “moved on and was already talking” to next year’s G20 host, the UK, Meyer said, according to the Daily Maverick.
He added that South Africa would attend the B20 summit in Washington, DC, next month.

Iran names 16-man squad for 2026 AFC Beach Soccer Asian Cup
TEHRAN – Iran national beach soccer team head coach Ali Naderi has named a 16-man squad for the upcoming 2026 AFC Beach Soccer Asian Cup, scheduled to take place in Thailand from Nov. 18 to 28.
Naderi announced the squad following the conclusion of the final stage of Iran’s Premier Beach Soccer League, selecting 16 players to begin preparations for the continental tournament.
According to the Iranian Football Federation, the national team’s training camp will get underway on Oct. 30 at the National Football Center in Tehran, where the players will begin their preparations ahead of the competition.
Iran have been drawn alongside Afghanistan, Vietnam and Lebanon in the group stage of the tournament.
The Iranian side will be looking to deliver a strong performance in Thailand and maintain their reputation as one of Asia’s leading beach soccer nations.
Iran have enjoyed considerable success in international beach soccer in recent years, establishing themselves as a formidable force on the continental stage.
The upcoming tournament will provide another opportunity for Naderi’s men to demonstrate their quality and compete for Asian honors.
The 16 players called up to the national team are:
Mohammad Dastan, Reza Dayeri, Reza Amiri, Saeed Piramoon, Ali Nazem, Davoud Shokri, Ali Mirshekari, Movahed Mohammadpour, Mohammadali Mokhtari, Mohammadali Nazarzadeh, Mohammad Masoumizadeh, Abolfazl Sharifpour, Aydin Teshnehkam, Sobhan Faleh, Mehdi Shirmohammadi, Mehdi Mirjalili
The coaching staff will assess the players during the training camp as Iran step up preparations for their opening group-stage matches.
With a blend of experienced internationals and talented players, Iran will aim to make a strong start against Afghanistan, Vietnam and Lebanon and advance to the knockout stages of the competition.

FBI files reveal arms smuggling to early Israel, intelligence networks tied to US Zionist groups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:26:06 UTC
19:26:06 KST

Formerly classified FBI documents shed light on weapons smuggling networks, intelligence gathering, and political activities carried out in the United States on behalf of the Jewish community in Mandatory Palestine and the newly established State of Israel during the 1940s and 1950s.
The documents detail how US authorities investigated connections between Zionist organizations, intelligence officials, businesspeople, and political activists at a time when Washington supported the establishment of a Jewish state but restricted arms shipments to the region.
The documents were published on October 21 by the Institute for Research: Middle Eastern Policy (IRmep), following Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests the organization first submitted in 2014. They are part of an FBI counterintelligence investigation file known as ISINT, which focused on Israeli intelligence services.
According to the released archive, the FBI had been actively investigating the matter since at least July 1949, during the tenure of longtime FBI director J. Edgar Hoover. The materials include surveillance records, suspicions of arms export violations, contacts with Israeli representatives, and activities involving networks that had emerged before Israel declared independence.
According to reports from the period, one shipment was concealed in crates labeled "used machinery." While the crates were being loaded onto a ship, one fell and broke open, revealing containers bearing markings identifying their contents as explosives belonging to the US Army Corps of Engineers.
The discovery prompted an investigation by police and the FBI. On January 15, 1948, the bureau announced the arrests of four suspects: Philip Alper, Moses Wolfson, Jack Dorfman, and Joseph Sager. All four were accused of making false statements about the shipment's contents in export documents.
The incident occurred after President Harry Truman's administration imposed restrictions on arms exports to Mandatory Palestine and neighboring countries in December 1947, seeking to prevent an escalation of fighting in the region.
Although Washington supported the UN partition plan, its political backing for the establishment of a Jewish state did not authorize private individuals in the United States to circumvent export restrictions.
The man who smuggled aircraft and founded Israel Aerospace Industries
The documents also address the activities of Al Schwimmer, a central figure in the establishment of the Israeli Air Force who later founded Israel Aerospace Industries.
Schwimmer and his associates worked to acquire American aircraft for Jewish forces fighting in the War of Independence, before the establishment of the IDF, despite US restrictions on military equipment exports.
In 1950, Schwimmer was convicted in the United States of conspiracy to violate the Neutrality Act and export control laws and was fined $10,000. The conviction also resulted in the loss of certain civil rights.
He later moved to Israel, founded Israel Aerospace Industries, and became one of the most prominent figures in the history of Israel's defense industry.
In 2001, President Bill Clinton granted him a presidential pardon, approximately 50 years after his conviction.
The Anti-Defamation League and Arab League documents
Another section of the FBI files concerns activities linked to the Anti-Defamation League (ADL), the American Jewish organization that combats antisemitism.
According to FBI records, individuals associated with the organization obtained documents concerning Arab League activities in New York through a chain of intermediaries.
One memorandum describes how Herman Edelsberg, an ADL official, explained to investigators how the documents came into the organization's possession.
According to the account, a man named Wahid al-Dali, identified as the nephew of a senior Arab League official, passed documents to a journalist he believed was sympathetic to the Arab organization's positions.
The journalist then passed the materials to Sanford Griffith, who was described as working on behalf of the ADL. Subsequently, 76 pages of documents were transferred to American officials and ultimately reached the FBI.
The records demonstrate US intelligence authorities' interest in how information about the Arab League was obtained. However, they do not, in themselves, establish that the ADL committed espionage or that its activities were directed by the Israeli government.
The organization, which over the years became a leading force in combating antisemitism and monitoring extremist groups in the United States, also faced legal criticism in later decades over its information-gathering practices.
In 1999, the ADL reached a settlement in a lawsuit brought by Arab American and other groups.
The agreement included a commitment to delete certain information collected about the plaintiffs, as well as payments to cover legal expenses and contribute to a community fund.
The ADL denied engaging in illegal activities.
AIPAC founder also appears in FBI files
One of the notable names appearing in the FBI documents is Isaiah Leo Kenen, who later founded the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), the influential pro-Israel lobbying organization in Washington.
According to the investigation, FBI documents refer to Kenen's connections with the Israeli delegation to the UN and his activities on behalf of the newly established state.
Separate records indicate that Kenen previously worked within Israel's public diplomacy apparatus and registered as a representative of a foreign principal under the US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA).
A January 1951 memorandum documents a conversation in which Kenen discussed the possibility of leaving government employment and establishing a private public relations business, potentially with the Israeli government as its first client.
A US Justice Department representative informed him that such an arrangement would require a new registration under the law, and Kenen agreed.
However, Kenen's activities during that period must be distinguished from AIPAC's current legal status.
AIPAC describes itself as an American organization representing American citizens and emphasizes that it is neither funded nor directed by the Israeli government. It is not registered as a foreign agent.
The fact that its founder previously registered as a representative of a foreign principal does not establish that AIPAC itself operates under Israeli government instructions or is legally required to register as a foreign agent.
Disclosure comes as AIPAC changes its political activities
The release of the historical documents comes at a sensitive time for AIPAC, amid growing controversy in the United States over its influence on congressional elections and American assistance to Israel.
Last week, the organization announced that it would stop formally endorsing candidates in elections and making direct contributions to them through its political action committee.
However, AIPAC clarified that it intends to continue raising money from American citizens to support pro-Israel candidates.
According to figures published in the United States, AIPAC members have contributed more than $90 million to candidates during the current election cycle, and the organization plans to expand its fundraising activities in the future.
The newly released historical files do not establish a direct connection between weapons smuggling and intelligence gathering during Israel's founding years and AIPAC's operations today.
Nevertheless, they offer a glimpse into the period when some of the networks connecting the Zionist movement, the US government, and American Jewish organizations were being established.
Security cooperation and intelligence concerns
According to the investigation, the documents also include records of a shortwave radio receiver operating in a private home in Brooklyn between 1946 and 1947, as well as an individual described as an enthusiastic supporter of David Ben-Gurion.
Investigators attempted to trace the communications links, but substantial portions of the records remain redacted.
As a result, the publicly available documents do not establish what was communicated or whether operational instructions were transmitted.
The disclosure also comes amid discussions in the US Congress about expanding security and intelligence cooperation with Israel, including in defense technology and the sharing of classified information.
The newly released documents illustrate that even as the strategic relationship between the two countries developed, US authorities were examining the potential risks of foreign intelligence activities on American soil from the earliest years of Israel's existence.
However, these are historical investigative files, portions of which remain redacted. Not everyone named in the documents was suspected of wrongdoing, and not every allegation investigated by the FBI resulted in criminal charges or a conviction.
Their release provides additional documentation of the complex relationship between the United States, the Zionist movement, and the newly established State of Israel, but does not constitute evidence of illegal activity by organizations operating today.

Italian Language Week: The Embassy’s Initiatives in Baghdad
To strengthen and expand the teaching of Italian in Iraq
ROMA,
30 October 2026, 11:27
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
On the occasion of the 26th edition of the Week of the Italian Language in the World (SLIM), dedicated to the theme “Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, Creating with Italian,” the Italian Embassy in Baghdad promoted a series of initiatives aimed at strengthening and expanding the use of Italian in Iraq.
On October 27 and 28, at the Faculty of Languages of the University of Baghdad, language teaching training sessions for faculty members of the Department of Italian Studies, led by Giuseppe Maugeri, associate professor at the University of Urbino, and funded by the embassy. On October 28, at Al-Zahrawi University in the holy city of Karbala, cooperation agreements were presented between Al-Zahrawi University and the Italian universities of Catania and Urbino, which will further deepen cooperation between the Italian and Iraqi academic systems.

Russian bomb disposal specialist killed clearing way for US-backed aid mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:25:56 UTC
19:25:56 KST

Russian bomb disposal specialist killed clearing way for US-backed aid mission
A Russian bomb disposal specialist and another person have been killed while clearing the way for a US-backed Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian mission.
The fatalities in Russia’s Kherson Region were reported on Friday by Russian human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova, who briefed journalists on preparations to deliver essential supplies to the frontline town of Alyoshki and evacuate residents wishing to leave.
The Defense Ministry later named the military service member who was killed as Sgt. Andrey Vedernikov of the 98th Airborne Troops Division. He was fatally wounded while trying to defuse an explosive device deployed from a Ukrainian drone that was equipped with a proximity sensor, the statement said.
Lantratova held the press conference jointly with her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, in the town of Armyansk, approximately 90 km from Alyoshki, which Kiev claims as Ukrainian territory. The humanitarian operation was mediated by US first lady Melania Trump.
Organizers have assembled 25 buses capable of evacuating at least 750 people, along with specialized vehicles for up to 30 people with limited mobility, nine ambulances and more than 50 medical personnel, Lantratova said.
Lubinets said the ceasefire around Alyoshki had held without reported violations for more than 75 hours, making it the longest lull in fighting since the escalation of the conflict in 2022. He expressed hope that the arrangement could serve as a model for similar operations elsewhere.
Friday’s mission aims to deliver essential supplies requested by local residents, including food, fuel, medicines, and hygiene products. Evacuees will receive assistance relocating to either Russia or Ukraine, depending on their preference.
The joint briefing, held against the backdrop of a convoy of vehicles, was attended by dozens of journalists from Russia, Ukraine and the US, including RT’s Murad Gadziev. Organizers said they wanted to ensure maximum transparency throughout the humanitarian mission.

Crans-Montana New Year’s Eve to blend hope and contemplation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:25:52 UTC
19:25:52 KST

Crans-Montana New Year’s Eve to blend hope and contemplation
New Year’s celebrations at the Swiss town of Crans-Montana will be more muted than normal as it marks the first anniversary of a fatal bar fire that claimed 41 lives.
Thousands of locals and tourists will be celebrating New Year’s Eve in the canton Valais town, but the night is also likely to be marked by a sense of reflection.
“We are approaching this transition into 2027 with great sensitivity and respect,” Bruno Huggler, director of Crans-Montana Tourism, told the Keystone-SDA news agency. “Some will want to enjoy moments of conviviality, whilst others – particularly those directly affected by the tragedy – will experience this time with particularly painful memories.”
The municipality plans to set up two places of remembrance on New Year’s Eve and New Year’s Day, one of which will be in front of the bar where the tragedy occurred, Le Constellation. This marks the spot where 41 people – mostly young people – died in a fire, with 115 injured, on New Year’s Eve last year.
A few minutes’ walk away, near the Saint-Christophe Chapel, another memorial site is to be created. Relatives and visitors will be able to leave personal items and mementoes of the victims.
The memorial sites are intended as a temporary solution until a permanent memorial is erected.
Silent light installation
The official memorial service will take place on January 1 at 10am in Grône, Valais. The local council will broadcast the ceremony live to the Le Régent conference centre in Crans-Montana, so residents of the tourist resort can also take part in the memorial service.
The municipality is also marking the occasion at Lake Grenon, just a few minutes’ walk from the bar where the tragedy occurred. A light installation featuring star-shaped light effects is designed to invite people to pause and reflect in silence.
The municipality has deliberately chosen not to include music or sound effects. The installation will be on display on the nights of December 31 and January 1, from 9pm to 2am on both nights.
The coexistence of New Year’s Eve celebrations and the commemoration of the tragedy will not be easy in practice, said tourism director Huggler.
“Our approach is to create the conditions so that everyone can experience this time in their own way, whilst respecting the feelings and needs of others,” says Huggler.

Potentially the largest cryptocurrency theft in history – hackers breach world's biggest crypto exchange Binance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:25:18 UTC
19:25:18 KST

Hackers have targeted Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in an attack that could result in losses of up to $6.3 billion.
Analysts believe the incident could become the largest cryptocurrency theft in history.
Binance representatives stressed that the company is making efforts to freeze the stolen funds. So far, it has managed to trace approximately $3 billion.
Binance co-founder Yi He said the security breach may have been linked to the hacking of a software development and support engineer's laptop.
The breach allowed the attacker to gain access to a service container and initiate unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
She added that Binance would compensate customers for all losses. However, as a precautionary measure, all deposits and withdrawals will be suspended while security checks are carried out.
Meanwhile, US-based blockchain intelligence company TRM said the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor was most likely responsible for the theft.
"We make this assessment with high confidence," TRM stated.
"The attacker transferred approximately $6.36 billion from Binance wallets across ten blockchains, most of it within around 20 minutes," TRM explained.
In February last year, cryptocurrency exchange Bybit suffered losses of $1.5 billion in a cyberattack.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) attributed the attack to North Korea and the TraderTraitor hacking group.
"Several characteristics of this attack match previous thefts linked to North Korea, including the Bybit hack," TRM noted.
Blockchain analytics company Chainalysis also believes that TraderTraitor hackers were most likely behind the attack on Binance.
Experts explain that North Korea has increasingly targeted cryptocurrency exchanges and engaged in other illicit cyber activities to obtain much-needed funds to support its struggling economy and finance the country's nuclear programme.
In December 2022, South Korea's intelligence agency announced that North Korean hackers had stolen approximately 1.5 trillion won (around one billion euros) in cryptocurrencies and other virtual assets over the previous five years.
More than half of that amount was stolen in 2022 alone.
The agency stated that North Korea's capabilities in stealing digital assets were considered among the most advanced in the world.

EU countries pledge 20.5mn diesel barrels as winter supply fears grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:25:06 UTC
19:25:06 KST

The eleven countries also urged Brussels to ensure the bloc has functioning refineries capable of turning crude oil into the products its economy consumes, like diesel or jet fuel.
Eleven EU countries have pledged to release 20.5 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves by the end of January 2027, as persistent instability in the Middle East raises concerns over fuel supplies ahead of winter, according to a document seen by Euronews.
Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden agreed to release new diesel barrels following the G7 leaders' statement on energy security and an urgent call for action from the IEA.
"We, the undersigned EU members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), have taken and are taking decisive actions to increase the supply of crude and refined products in the short term through the release of significant volumes of strategic reserves, including diesel," reads the joint declaration.
The initiative was presented by French Energy Minister Roland Lescure on the sidelines of the gathering of energy ministers in Luxembourg on 29 October.
It unveiled the release of 42.6 million barrels of oil and refined products in March under a collective action coordinated by the Paris-based IEA.
Nearly half of the refined products are diesel, which the European Commission's oil monitoring group has described as "remaining tight".
While Brussels maintains that "physical shortages" are not foreseen, Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen argued that skyrocketing prices will end up depriving the most vulnerable.
Brent crude oil was trading at $112 on 20 October, up from the $40 pre-war levels.
The EU is exposed to diesel disruptions in refined fuel markets, which affect road transport, freight, agriculture and industry.
Releasing strategic stocks, under pressure from the United States administration, could help increase immediate supply and ease market pressures.
However, analysts see it as a temporary measure and not a solution to underlying vulnerabilities in the bloc's energy system.
Brussels urged to increase oversight of stock releases
The eleven governments urged the Commission to coordinate monitoring through the EU executive's oil monitoring group.
They want Brussels to collect monthly data on the volumes released, the types of products and the timing of deliveries.
The aim is to give global markets greater visibility over the additional supply and help governments coordinate further responses if conditions deteriorate.
The declaration also highlights the importance of Europe's refining industry.
The prolonged war in the Middle East, including attacks on Gulf refineries, and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have put further strain on an already tight global diesel market, driving up energy prices.
EU governments want the Commission-led oil group to monitor refinery output and encourage producers to increase capacity where possible.
The Commission has recently launched a strategic dialogue with European refineries and fuel producers to strengthen security of supply.
Given the scale of the disruption, Brussels recognised the bloc needs functioning refineries capable of turning crude into the products its economy consumes.
Strategic stock releases can bridge temporary shortages, but only for a short time.
Analysts argue emergency oil stocks can't compensate for disruptions to refining capacity or international supply chains.
FuelsEurope, the trade body representing the European refining industry, said the bloc needs an "approach that protects the competitiveness of its refining industry". It also asked Brussels to create the necessary investment conditions for its transformation.
Overall progress is due to be reviewed at the 10 December gathering of EU energy ministers, giving them an opportunity to assess implementation before the January deadline.

Pentagon urges Europeans to tone down rhetoric about the threat from Russia - Reuters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:23:53 EET
19:23:53 KST

Pentagon urges Europeans to tone down rhetoric about the threat from Russia - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
The United States asked Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia to soften public statements about the Russian threat. Washington is simultaneously reviewing its forces in Europe.
In recent weeks, Pentagon officials have approached a number of NATO countries asking them to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat from Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined the security of the continent. Reuters reported this, citing four people familiar with the situation, writes UNN.
Details
Among the countries that received messages urging them to restrain their public statements were Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, sources who spoke on condition of anonymity said. It was unclear whether the messages, conveyed during bilateral meetings, had been brought to the attention of other European governments.
The U.S. requests come as the Trump administration renews efforts to achieve a peaceful settlement to the full-scale war in Ukraine, which has been ongoing for a fifth year. The latest pressure campaign combines incentives for Russia, including sanctions relief, with pressure on Ukraine to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, the publication writes.
Private conversations between allies are just that—private conversations, so we will not comment on these claims
Among the comments that drew the attention of U.S. officials were suggestions by European leaders that Russia had been backed into a corner and was resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slowed, one of the sources said.
According to the sources, one of the U.S. officials who conveyed this message was Elbridge Colby, head of the Pentagon's policy office and a key figure in reviewing the size of U.S. forces in Europe. Reuters was unable to establish which other officials were involved in the process.
Pentagon has begun a review of the US military presence in Europe28.07.26, 16:45 • 4057 views
None of the sources, which included three European officials and one U.S. official, suggested that the recommendations had been delivered in a confrontational manner.
The U.S. messages reflect a debate within NATO over how to respond publicly to the threat from an assertive Russia, the publication notes.
Some Western officials argue that emphasizing the threat from Moscow could play into the Kremlin's hands, as they say it seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.
Others argue that European governments should be transparent in order to show their voters that deterring Moscow requires sacrifices and resources. This is particularly relevant as Russia appears to be accelerating a covert campaign of sabotage across the continent, the publication notes. Russia denies conducting such a campaign.
One source familiar with the situation told Reuters that Colby recently told a Baltic official that Russia should not be "provoked."
According to this person, Colby pointed to public statements by Europeans that Russia was "backed into a corner like a rat" as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.
It was unclear which specific statement Colby was referring to. However, in late September, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal called Putin a "rat in a corner," suggesting that the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage in Europe because Russia was becoming increasingly bogged down in the war in Ukraine.
"We are helping you. The Americans are there," another European official said, describing recent private messages from the Pentagon. "Just don't be loud. Don't make noise."
At a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be "restrained" in its messaging, according to a person briefed on the meeting, although that person did not say that Pentagon representatives had complained about any specific statement.
The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.
One European official said that although the Pentagon's recommendations were well-intentioned, they were surprising given that the intelligence services of the Baltic countries had consistently played down in recent months the likelihood that Russia would test the strength of NATO's mutual defense provisions.
Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia may sharply intensify its sabotage campaign in the near future.
The Pentagon's messages to NATO officials come at a tense time for European security.
According to Western intelligence officials, Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks against NATO countries.
On Wednesday, German prosecutors announced the arrest of two Belarusians on suspicion of planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area. In September, the German government accused Russia of attempting a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which Moscow denies.
Meanwhile, U.S. officials are discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration's efforts to achieve peace in Ukraine. These efforts have drawn a mixed reaction from European officials, many of whom insist on the Kremlin's continued economic isolation.
Meanwhile, Pentagon planners are reviewing Washington's military presence in Europe, which could lead to a sharp reduction in America's military presence on the continent.
U.S. officials said that European NATO members should take on more responsibility for their own defense, particularly as the United States focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America, and East Asia.

Five Ukrainians Evacuated From Temporarily Occupied Territories for Urgent Medical Care
Ukrainian authorities successfully evacuated five citizens from temporarily Russian-occupied territories to government-controlled area.
The individuals required urgent assistance due to severe health conditions and limited mobility, according to Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets on October 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The operation was carried out in joint efforts with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Ukraine.
Lubinets shared the harrowing account of an injured couple rescued during the mission. On September 11, their vehicle struck a landmine during a grocery trip in the temporarily occupied zone, leaving both individuals with critical blast injuries and shrapnel wounds.
A bystander helped the couple travel roughly 3 kilometers to reach home, but local emergency medical services failed to arrive due to severe security risks, leaving the couple stranded without professional care.
The husband lost his sight and suffered extensive shrapnel injuries, while his wife required urgent skin graft surgery. They were only able to reach a medical facility on September 23.
Their son eventually reached out to the Ombudsman's office, pleading for a safe return so his parents could receive vital medical treatment and proper care.
Lubinets emphasized that evacuating severely injured and low-mobility citizens requires detailed planning, personalized arrangements, and continuous medical supervision during transport.
“We are constantly working to bring back as many people as possible. And today we have another result. I am grateful to the ICRC in Ukraine for their joint efforts in this work,” Lubinets stated.
“After the explosion, a random passerby helped them get home, covering about three kilometers with them. Due to the difficult security situation, the ambulance crew they called did not arrive. Opportunities to receive help from other residents were virtually non-existent,” he wrote.
“Fortunately, the couple's son turned to me. He asked to save his parents—to safely return them to the territory controlled by the Government. To a place where parents could receive the necessary treatment and further care,” the ombudsman noted.
On June 23, 2026, fifteen children were evacuated from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine under the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA.
The returned youth included an eighteen-year-old who had been hiding to avoid forced mobilization into the Russian military, a seventeen-year-old whose family faced continuous threats from occupation authorities, and a thirteen-year-old whose parents were threatened with losing custody to an orphanage.
Following their return, the children began undergoing reintegration in dedicated centers, where they received psychological support, safe shelter, documentation assistance, and essential care to start their new lives.

On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:22:54 UTC
19:22:54 KST

On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote
Border issues helped propel Trump in the Rio Grande Valley in 2024; His deportation policies could bury Republicans.
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Leaning over plates of tamales, pan dulce, and sugar skulls, community organisers and local residents in the border city of Brownsville remembered the dead.
This year’s Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, vigil honoured victims of state violence, including those killed in immigration enforcement and detention. Just days before the US midterm election on November 3, the event reverberated in a region long subject to Washington, DC’s shifting political winds.
“The atmosphere here in the Rio Grande Valley when it comes to ICE detentions and the ICE raids, there’s just the overall feeling amongst folks that there’s no real due process to this,” said Mark Anthony Vasquez, a 52-year-old community organiser.
“What is it that we can do to move together and build together to try to make it past this, and make that change that we seek?”
Down the block, at a bookstore panel on border and immigration policy, 24-year-old Juliana Garcia raised her hand to ask advice on how to find a lawyer able to navigate the aggressively shifting policies of the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has used both an increase in physical enforcement, as well as a reinterpretation of administrative policies, to fuel its mass deportation campaign.
Garcia’s aunt, a well-known member of the community in the nearby border town of Progreso, was deported just weeks ago, after being called to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) hearing. There she learned she had missed a court date related to her immigration status.
In the stress of the moment, she signed a voluntary deportation form.
“Within 36 hours, she was deported,” Garcia told Al Jazeera, tucked between bookshelves. “People are waking up, and they’re remembering that politics, regardless of what branch you’re in, it’s going to impact you every day.”
Shifting dynamics
Views on immigration are complex in the Rio Grande Valley, a geographic and cultural region located in subtropical southeast Texas with about 1.5 million residents. That complexity has only increased in recent years as border policy and immigration enforcement have become increasingly partisan, leading, reformers say, to dramatic policy swings that prevent more sustainable solutions.
It is not difficult to find Latino – or Tejano, the local term for Texans of Latino descent – residents wary of the years preceding Trump’s return to office. After the restrictive policies of Trump’s first term, border crossings increased dramatically under US President Joe Biden, fuelled in part by the end of a COVID-era policy that made asylum seekers wait for their cases to be processed in Mexico.
Some felt the border region was left to deal with the fallout from the influx. That discontent has been credited, in part, with Trump’s success in the once-reliably Democratic region in the 2024 presidential election.
In Hidalgo County, home to the city of McAllen, Trump won 51 percent of the vote in 2024, a three-point margin over Kamala Harris. In 2020, Biden beat Trump in the county by 17 percentage points.
In neighbouring Cameron County, Trump won by about five percentage points in 2024, despite a 13-point loss in 2020.
Voter Jose Arizpe, a 40-year-old resident of Brownsville, assessed the two years since Trump took office as a “positive change”, with fewer asylum seekers waiting in the US for their cases to be processed.
Upon taking office, Trump declared a state of emergency at the border, staunching asylum claims in what rights groups say runs counter to US law. The US Supreme Court has since ruled that US border agents can physically block asylum seekers from reaching US soil to claim asylum.
“A lot of people claim that they support illegals and want to let them in,” said Arizpe, a regular Republican voter, “but then, I say ‘well let them in your house’. And they don’t want to do it, right?”
On border policy, “at first, I supported Trump,” said Martin Torres, a 55-year-old who cast his ballot for Democrats at a public library in Brownsville as part of the state’s early voting.
But domestic enforcement, and its impact on the local workforce, soured his views.
“Now he changes everything,” he said.
A report from the Caminos Institute has estimated the region has lost $180.6m in economic activity due to the Trump administration’s immigration policies, including in construction and restaurants.
Other voters saw Trump’s approach as fuelling bigotry. Last year, the US Supreme Court lifted a lower-court order barring immigration officials from considering “apparent race or ethnicity”, as well as language spoken, when on patrol. Rights groups say the decision effectively allows racial profiling.
In Texas, a state law also lets local officials stop individuals they suspect entered the country illegally.
“I just see a lot of discrimination going on,” said George Castorena, a 46-year-old department of education worker, who said he was voting for change.
To be sure, midterm elections can only offer incremental change on an issue as entrenched as immigration enforcement and border policy.
Democratic control of the House of Representatives would at best serve as a bulwark against the Trump administration legislating more immigration enforcement funding and policy, while opening the door to investigations into the administration’s approach.
Control of the Senate, which could be determined by the contest between Texas Republican Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico, could further increase the party’s leverage.
A change in the governor’s office, meanwhile, could end Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s myriad uses of state agencies to support federal immigration enforcement. But Democrat Gina Hinojosa, if she were to pull off an upset, would be largely constrained by a likely Republican-dominated state legislature and a mountain of pre-existing law.
A galvanising moment?
Although a more lasting transformation remains far off, evidence suggests the local dismay runs deep.
A poll conducted by the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas found that only 34 percent of respondents from the area felt that immigration enforcement by both local and state officials had made their communities safer. Fifty-three percent said it made their lives harder without improving safety.
Meanwhile, 64 percent felt ICE tactics have gone too far. The numbers broadly align with polls showing Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido leading Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz and Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez leading Republican challenger Eric Flores in two Rio Grande Valley congressional districts.
Republicans, eyeing Trump’s success in 2024, viewed the races as strong prospects early in the election season.
“What this survey conveys is: people along the border in the Rio Grande Valley are not in alignment with what they probably voted for back in 2024,” Osvaldo Grimaldo, a policy strategist at ACLU of Texas, told Al Jazeera.
Even prominent community figures who support Trump’s policies acknowledge a broader change in sentiment.
Eli Lara, the lead pastor at the non-denominational New Life Family Church in McAllen, Texas, said locals have been dismayed by the wide scope with which the administration has targeted undocumented individuals.
“The immigration issue is bigger because [the community] is seeing people being taken,” he told Al Jazeera. “I don’t like the separation of families, but here’s the thing: there are consequences for choices.”
That view held even for a congregant who had recently been deported in connection with a past drug possession conviction.
“He’s been faithful [to the church] for two, three years, but they picked him up,” Lara said. “Why? Because he had a bad criminal record in the past. God forgives, but the government doesn’t.”
Voter Garcia, who volunteers with the Hidalgo County Young Democrats, was among those who believed the current situation could galvanise the Rio Grande Valley.
She pointed to several instances that have recently shaken the region, including the assault of a 17-year-old by immigration agents in the town of Alamo in the Rio Grande Valley, and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July 2026 in the Texas city of Houston.
“I’ve had a lot of people tell me, ‘Why do I care about politics? Politics doesn’t affect me,'” she said. “And with all of these ICE raids, they realise politics does affect them, and it sucks that it took a lot of trauma to really bring that to people.”

Novaya Gazeta, Symbol of Independent Russian Journalism, Forced to Close
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:21:01 UTC
19:21:01 KST

Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it will shut down, with Editor-in-Chief Sergei Sokolov blaming pressure from Russian authorities, including the security services, following a search of his home and the arrest of one of the publication’s journalists.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” Sokolov said in a video statement posted on YouTube on Friday. He accused the authorities of forcing the editorial team to stop working, saying: “The Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
Sokolov said the newspaper would close its premises and shut down its servers on November 9, ending operations at the home where its staff had worked for 30 years. “Novaya Gazeta has been killed … On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave,” he said.
Earlier this month, Sokolov was questioned and police searched his home as part of a criminal investigation involving his colleague Oleg Roldugin, who was arrested in April.
Roldugin was charged with "unlawful access to computerised information," although authorities have not provided further details of the allegations. He denied the charges, according to the state RIA news agency.
Novaya Gazeta reported that Roldugin was awaiting trial under house arrest, which had been extended until November 10.
Russia has tightened its campaign against independent media since launching its offensive in Ukraine in February 2022, introducing censorship measures described as approaching Soviet-era levels and driving most independent journalists into exile.
Novaya Gazeta reduced its operations inside Russia after the offensive began, and authorities revoked its media license later in 2022. The newspaper has also been designated a "foreign agent" by the Russian authorities, a classification used to suppress dissent.
The publication was long regarded as one of Russia's leading independent news outlets. Its former editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” while leading the newspaper.

France's Economy, Finances and Industry Minister Roland Lescure leaves after attending the weekly cabinet meeting in Paris on Oct. 28, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — France’s economy shrunk by 0.1% in the third quarter of 2026, according to fresh estimates from national statistics agency Insee, pushing the country closer to recession and further complicating the government’s efforts to stave off a debt-driven financial crisis.
Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Friday that this summer’s extreme heat and spiking energy prices were responsible for the negative growth.
In an interview with Franceinfo, he said the new figures give added urgency for lawmakers to pass the 2027 budget proposed by the government, which aims to bring the deficit down to 5% of gross domestic product next year with €43 billion in savings.
Advertisement
“If we don’t have the budget adjustment we put in the budget, we will hit the wall,” Lescure said.
But France’s fragmented parliament failed to pass budgets before the new year in both 2024 and 2025, and the spring 2027 presidential election may further complicate efforts to seek compromise this time around. That could force Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to push through the budget using a constitutional backdoor that bypasses a parliamentary vote, but it would expose the minority government to potential motions of no confidence.
Lescure insisted that adopting a budget for next year was key to “reassure markets” and relaunch growth in the last quarter of the year. The French economy contracted by 0.1% in the first quarter of 2026 and recorded no growth in the three months that followed.
That anemic growth will likely complicate the government’s pledge to bring the deficit down to 5.4% of GDP this year, as the target was based on the assumption the economy would grow by 0.5% in 2026.
“The French economy is at a standstill,” Lescure said. “It has to restart.”

Independent Russian Newspaper Novaya Gazeta Shuts Under Kremlin Pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:18:46 UTC
19:18:46 KST

Russia’s flagship independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announced Friday it was closing, saying it had been “killed” by state pressure after years of repression targeting its journalists whose reporting was critical of the Kremlin and its Ukraine war.
The closure of Novaya Gazeta – one of the last outlets to openly criticise Russia’s offensive – marks a new low in Moscow’s campaign against dissenting voices that gained speed after the Kremlin sent troops into its neighbour in 2022.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Since then, the newspaper, long considered a bastion of independent journalism, has seen its media license revoked, journalists and editors questioned, detained, and their homes searched.
It was also branded a “foreign agent” -- a label reminiscent of Soviet-era repression used to stifle dissent.
“Novaya Gazeta has been killed. Novaya Gazeta is ending its existence,” editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a statement published on YouTube on Friday morning.
In the emotional video, Sokolov said that “the Russian authorities -- the Russian special services -- have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
Founded in 1993 after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Novaya Gazeta was one of Russia’s most reputable and renowned organisations reporting and documenting human rights abuses.
Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, donated some of his Nobel Peace Prize money to help set up the paper.
UN Refugee Agency Says 9 Million Need Extra Winter Help
-‘Finished off’ -
Several of its reporters have been murdered in killings widely seen as retribution for their work.
They include Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia’s military during its campaigns in Chechnya.
She was found dead in her apartment block on President Vladimir Putin’s birthday in October 2006.
Founder and former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his efforts to safeguard freedom of expression at the helm of the paper.
He had to formally step down from the post two years later after being declared a “foreign agent”.
“For nearly five years of war, we managed to operate while completely surrounded by intelligence services. But now, that’s it. We’ve ended up in a kill zone,” Sokolov said on Friday.
“This isn’t just our own private story -- it’s the story of a country and a society that are being finished off in exactly the same way.”
The paper, which used to be published several times a week, cut down production inside the country after the war began, but its online version was still available despite court orders.
In recent months, the Russian authorities searched the home of Sokolov and earlier this year arrested one of its journalists, Oleg Roldugin.
Charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”, he pleaded not guilty, according to state media, and is under house arrest pending trial.
International media rights groups have slammed Russia’s years of targeting Novaya Gazeta, with Reporters Without Borders calling on Moscow to “put an end to the judicial harassment” of its journalists.
“Human rights and freedoms have been abolished, and their defence has been equated with a crime,” Sokolov said in the video statement, adding: “Beliefs have become state treason.”
“The murder of Novaya Gazeta is yet another piece of evidence. All these years we wrote precisely about this, for as long as we could. Thank you to everyone who listened to us. And the final issue will come out.”
