What can a global strike of dockworkers achieve for Gaza?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:04:35 UTC
19:04:35 KST

What can a global strike of dockworkers achieve for Gaza?
More than 25 dockworkers’ trade unions in at least 110 ports in 22 countries are going on strike on October 30.
Dock and port workers have long had a tradition of solidarity with the oppressed, upheld by strong labour unions and workers’ rights.
In February 2025, nearly a year and a half into Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, dockworkers’ unions from Mediterranean countries came together to disrupt weapons shipments to Israel and Western countries’ military support of the onslaught.
“Weapons need transport, infrastructure, and workers’ hands to reach their destination,” Markos Bekris, leader of Greece’s dockworkers’ union, ENEDEP, at the Port of Piraeus in Athens, told Al Jazeera. “That is where our power lies.”
Now, dock and port workers in 22 countries across five continents are holding a strike on Friday, which workers and researchers told Al Jazeera is expected to be “historic” in scale. The International Day of Action of Dockworkers and Port Workers – also called “Dockworkers do not work for war” – involves 110 ports and 25 trade unions.
“Every union will do what they choose, but be connected to the same principles and struggle,” Francesco Staccioli, the national secretary of transport and ports in Italy’s USB trade union, told Al Jazeera.
The unions’ main demand is “an immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and all imperialist wars”.
Mohammed al-Attar, a dockworker who left Gaza in 2015 and is now based in Hamburg, Germany, said the workers “are the power”.
“We can save thousands of lives if we stop working just for two days,” he said.
Al-Attar feels hopeful about the global strike, but is “deeply disappointed” in his trade union Ver.di in Germany, which he accused of “incomprehensible silence” over Gaza.
What is the International Day of Action of Dockworkers and Port Workers?
In early 2025, dockworkers in the Mediterranean area came together to discuss how to concretely act “against privatisation, and against the genocide in Palestine”.
The original meeting included five unions organising in 20 ports across five countries, but continued to grow. The unions met several times, first in Athens, then in Genoa, and later in Istanbul. That was where unions from more than 35 ports published the Istanbul Declaration in May this year, and declared October 30 as their day of action.
In a statement, the unions called for the “recognition of an independent Palestinian state, recognised by the international community, within the 1967 borders and with East Jerusalem as its capital”, and “an end to the US-Israeli wars of aggression in the Middle East and against Iran, and full solidarity with the peoples of Cuba, Venezuela and Sudan”.
“Refusing the war is giving humanity a chance to live better. This is what I’m really convinced about,” the USB’s Staccioli told Al Jazeera.
How many ports and unions are taking part?
More than 25 dockworkers’ trade unions, representing more than 110 ports in 22 countries and regions across five continents, are taking part. Most of the strikes will happen at regular working hours, but in France, Italy, India, Greece and Turkiye, 24-hour strikes have been called.
Strikes of up to two hours have also been announced in Morocco, Cyprus and other ports.
Organisers told Al Jazeera that workers and trade unions from other sectors have been called on to join with port workers, notably in Greece, while in Italy the USB has called for a general strike.
“It’s bigger than we thought,” Staccioli said. “This has spread all over the world.”
No Harbour for Genocide (NHG), a campaigning collective that researches weapon supply chains, supports the action. A spokesperson told Al Jazeera that maritime infrastructure was important in “facilitating military trade within the context of the genocide in Palestine”.
Dockworker unions in India, Sweden, Denmark, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, Uruguay and the west coast of the United States have all pledged to take part, the spokesperson added.
The Palestinian labour movement endorsed the strike and called on more to join, urging unions to “escalate Boycott, Divest, Sanctions (BDS) pressure to end all state, corporate and institutional complicity in Israel’s illegal occupation, apartheid and genocide.”
How are these ports involved in wars?
Of the ports participating, Genoa, Livorno and Gioia Tauro in Italy, Marseille in France, Piraeus in Greece, and Tangier in Morocco all have proven links to weapons shipments to Israel, according to No Harbour for Genocide.
The group said that between August 2025 and September 2026 it tracked 315 shipments of components for Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer, moving through 56 commercial ports in 29 countries. All these 56 ports are expected to be on strike on October 30 , representing a major disruption, even if only for a day.
NHG said it expects that more than $2bn worth of cargo will sit idle on October 30 .
“Up to 95 percent of Israel’s imports and exports travel by sea, relying on port infrastructure across the Mediterranean,” the campaign’s spokesperson said. “Tangier, Piraeus, Gioia Tauro and Genoa, where the largest vessels unload containers onto smaller ships for the rest of the sea, are a few of the Mediterranean’s most frequently used transshipment hubs. All four are taking part on Friday.”
“The participating Mediterranean ports handle 63 percent of all container activity in the sea,” the spokesperson added, noting that “between southern France and Piraeus, the striking ports hold 74 percent of container activity. Worldwide, the ports taking part [in the strike] handle 13.5 percent of global shipping.”
Linda Maggiore, an Italian journalist and activist, said that she has discovered several examples of increasing weapons shipments from Italy’s major ports to Israel since the start of the war on Gaza.
“In Europe, a regulation on military mobility is about to be approved, which will make it even easier for arms to be transferred without scrutiny,” Maggiore told Al Jazeera. “Blockades are essential actions, because they make it clear that civil society does not wish to be complicit.”
From the Vietnam war to Iraq, the USB’s Staccioli said that “dockworkers have a long tradition of rallying against any imperialist war or aggression in the world.”
Are protest actions prosecuted?
In Greece, union leader Bekris is facing prosecution for a protest in which he and other workers blocked the loading of a container holding 21 tonnes of ammunition destined for Israel in October 2024.
“We carry forward the tradition of workers who refuse to load weapons against other people,” Bekris told Al Jazeera on the eve of the global strike. “Our hands get covered in grease and sweat every day. We refuse to let them be stained with the blood of other people.”

US pressures Lithuania to reopen port for Belarusian potash exports – Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:04:00 UTC
19:04:00 KST

The administration of US President Donald Trump is pressing Lithuania to allow Belarusian potash fertiliser exports through the port of Klaipeda despite European Union sanctions, Politico reported, citing European officials.
US special envoy to Belarus John Coale has in recent weeks asked Lithuanian diplomats about ways to ease restrictions on the shipment of goods from Belarus, according to four European officials familiar with the discussions.
The restrictions are part of EU sanctions against the government of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko. EU ports are prohibited from handling Belarusian goods, and the sanctions must be renewed annually.
Trump said last month that he was working on a “big deal” with Minsk to buy potash fertiliser at prices significantly lower than those currently paid by farmers to Canadian suppliers. Such an arrangement would require a route through Klaipėda, Lithuania’s main Baltic Sea port, or other regional ports.
“There has been intensified outreach to the Lithuanians by Donald Trump’s team in the last weeks,” a source familiar with the discussions told Politico.
The US State Department did not respond to a request for comment.
The administration’s interest in Belarusian potash, which accounts for about 20% of the global market, has grown following the collapse of US-Canadian trade negotiations in August and subsequent tariff increases, Politico reported.
The push is part of Trump’s broader efforts to ease sanctions on Russia and its allies in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war against Ukraine. However, the approach has faced strong opposition in Europe.
“They are pressing politely, but we say very clearly ‘fuck no’,” one Eastern European official told Politico.
Two Eastern European officials said Coale had been lobbying Lithuanian authorities at various levels for more than a year. Washington has also explored the possibility of shipping Belarusian potash through Latvia’s Riga port, which could offer a simpler route than transportation through Russia.
Lithuania has repeatedly rejected the possibility of resuming transit.
Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys has said EU sanctions prohibit not only imports of Belarusian potash but also its transit through EU territory, regardless of the ownership of the fertiliser or the country in which the exporting company is registered.
The Lithuanian president’s national security adviser Deividas Matulionis has also warned that violating the sanctions would carry legal, financial and moral consequences.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said in September that Lithuania had received no US request to allow Belarusian fertiliser transit. Former Prime Minister and opposition politician Ingrida Šimonytė has likewise argued that such shipments would be incompatible with EU sanctions and pose national security risks.

herzog & de meuron to convert former birkenstock warehouse into the eames institute museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:03:38 UTC
19:03:38 KST

herzog & de meuron to convert former birkenstock warehouse into the eames institute museum
beneath a sculptural concrete roof, a mid-century campus in novato, california, will house exhibitions, workshops, and public gardens, with a museum opening targeted for 2030.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
HERZOG & DE MEURON REVEALS EAMES INSTITUTE MUSEUM PLANS
A warehouse with a roof this expressive already has something to exhibit. In Novato, California, Herzog & de Meuron is reworking the former Birkenstock campus into the future museum of the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity, preserving its sculptural concrete silhouette while changing what happens beneath it. Newly released renderings show the proposal taking shape with San Francisco practice EHDD as executive architect and Field Operations designing the landscape. Across an approximately 88-acre site, the project brings exhibition spaces, workshops, a theater, and gardens into a cultural destination whose ambitions extend beyond the work of Charles and Ray Eames.
The existing campus was designed for publisher McGraw-Hill by Jan Lubicz-Nycz for the office of John Savage Bolles, before becoming associated with Birkenstock. Its most recognizable element is a roof assembled from repeated hyperbolic paraboloid shells, developed with structural engineer Raj Desai. These curved surfaces use geometry to span large distances with remarkably little material, producing a sequence of pointed edges that gives the industrial building its unexpected drama. Retaining this structure makes the museum itself an example of design ingenuity: visitors will encounter an experiment in construction before reaching the first exhibition.
A REFLECTIVE BRIDGE REFRAMES THE CONCRETE WAREHOUSE
Herzog & de Meuron organizes the interior around a generous central hall, keeping the roof’s geometry visible overhead. An entrance court cut into an existing earth berm establishes the approach, while a steel-clad bridge introduces an elevated route through the building. Its reflective finish will catch fragments of the surrounding space, setting a visually shifting surface against the weight of the concrete canopy. Below, circulation routes connect exhibitions with places to gather and work. Building services and lighting will be integrated into the ceiling to reduce the visual clutter beneath its peaks.
The museum’s program gives visitors opportunities to see how things are made alongside the finished works. Studios and workshops for wood and ceramics sit within an arrangement of flexible exhibition spaces, allowing creative activity to become part of the visit. This approach also informs the broader collecting strategy, which encompasses industrial design, painting, sculpture, and other disciplines. The Eames legacy provides a point of departure for a museum interested in experimentation across generations, with space for the practical, occasionally messy business that precedes an object’s arrival on a pedestal.
FIELD OPERATIONS BRINGS THE EAMES MUSEUM INTO THE LANDSCAPE
At the building’s northern and southern edges, recessed glass façades create deep covered areas between the interiors and gardens. These sheltered thresholds extend the possibilities for exhibitions and everyday use, while former loading zones become places to spend time outdoors. Field Operations connects ten gardens through paths, introducing native species including oak, manzanita, and California poppy. Planting draws on the region’s different habitats, from woodland to coastal prairie, giving the grounds a character rooted in Marin County rather than treating them as a uniform backdrop.
Outdoor sculpture, places to play, and areas for communal events will share this landscape with quieter spaces for sitting and walking. The proposal allows a museum visit to unfold across different settings and at different speeds, from a workshop or performance to an afternoon outside. Following the Institute’s acquisition of the property in 2025, the masterplan has been submitted to the City of Novato. Major construction is intended to begin in 2028, with 2030 set as the target opening year.
project info:
name: Eames Institute Museum | @eamesinstitute
architects: Herzog & de Meuron | @herzogdemeuron
Location: Novato, Marin County, California, USA

Naples Airport to close for the whole of November for €30m revamp – here’s what passengers need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:03:26 UTC
19:03:26 KST

The Italian airport will shut for the entire month of November for major runway upgrades, with flights diverted to nearby Salerno and extra bus and taxi services planned to limit disruption.
One of Italy’s busiest airports is set to close to air traffic for the entire month of November.
Naples Airport will shut its doors to allow for extensive renovation work on its runway and connecting taxiways, which will shore up the long-term safety, reliability and operational continuity of the existing infrastructure.
It will also include the replacement and modernisation of the airport’s visual aids lighting (AVL) systems, which include the runway and taxiway lighting and illuminated signalling systems, essential for guiding aircraft during take-off, landing and taxiing, especially in poor visibility.
The project, which will cost around €30 million, is being carried out at a time which typically sees fewer flights than in peak season. To minimise disruption further, the work will be done continuously, for 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
Workaround plans in place to avoid major disruption
For travellers needing to get to the region, some airlines plan to transfer their aircraft to – relatively – nearby Salerno Costa d’Amalfi and Cilento airports.
Flights here are operated by the likes of Ryanair, easyJet and Vueling, and fly to and from Bergamo, Milan Malpensa and Milan Linate, Genoa, Turin and Trieste in Italy.
Further afield, flights will run between the airports and Amsterdam, Barcelona, Casablanca, Dubai, Dusseldorf, Madrid, Paris, Sharm el-Sheikh and Stuttgart.
To handle the strain of Naples Airport’s closure, additional bus services between Naples Piazza Garibaldi and Salerno Airport will operate throughout November.
Services to Salerno railway station are also set to be increased, while existing routes to Potenza, Eboli, Battipaglia and the Amalfi Coast will continue to run as usual.
For those not keen to rely on public transport, a shared taxi service with fixed fares has also been introduced on a trial basis. It will cover two routes, one from Salerno Airport to Naples Central railway station, and the other from Salerno Airport to Salerno Central railway station.

What is known about 'security incident' at Binance cryptocurrency exchange
Unknown

19:02:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. The cryptocurrency exchange Binance could have lost $6.3 bln following a "security incident," the management of the platform announced on its X social media page.
TASS has gathered the key facts known at the moment.
'Security incident'
Former CEO of Binance Changpeng Zhao believes the platform could have been hacked.
The current management of the cryptocurrency exchange has said that its "teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating."
It was noted that no impact on user funds had been detected.
The management of the platform later reported on X that the cryptocurrency exchange Binance had suspended all deposit and withdrawal operations following a suspected hacker attack.
The team was conducting security checks, freezing funds, and working with law enforcement agencies, the report said.
The platform’s management said in a statement later that the "security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop."
This allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions, according to the statement.
Binance said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys were compromised.
The platform’s management later said that the incident was caused by several factors.
The crypto exchange’s security team is tracing the full path of the attack through a compromised computer, which may have served as the entry point for the incident.
A detailed report identifying the root cause will be published later, Binance added.
Loss
The cryptocurrency exchange Binance could have lost $6.3 bln following the "security incident," the management of the platform later announced on its X page.
The company also noted that a portion of the affected assets had been frozen in collaboration with partners in the blockchain industry, adding that around $3 bln had been blocked directly on the blockchain.
Binance will cover all losses, the management of the platform said.
It was noted that user funds were safe.
Resumption prospects
Binance expects withdrawals to resume within 48 hours, the trading platform stated on X.
Deposits remain unaffected and are operating normally, according to the statement.
Cryptocurrencies situation
The value of the top two cryptocurrencies by market capitalization, Bitcoin and Ethereum (ETH), has fallen sharply, according to Binance data.
As of 11:42 p.m. Moscow time (8:42 p.m. GMT) on October 29, the price of Bitcoin was down by 2.15% at $79,370.
The price of Ethereum was down by 3.71% at $2,265.
By 11:47 p.m. Moscow time (8:47 p.m. GMT) the Bitcoin price had widened its losses to 3.32%, reaching $78,341.
The price of Ethereum was down by 5.01% at $2,233.
According to Coinmarketcap data as of October 29, the total capitalization of the cryptocurrency market amounted to $2.67 trillion.
Bitcoin accounted for $1.6 trillion (60.2%), while Ethereum accounted for $276.6 bln (10.5%).
According to Coinglass data, global crypto exchanges liquidated over 158,000 traders' positions worth $923.54 mln in 24 hours.
Most of the liquidations involved Bitcoin.
Around $785.21 mln in liquidations were for long positions, and $146.7 mln were for short positions.
The largest liquidation order of the past 24 hours, valued at $11.09 mln, was submitted on the Binance exchange for the BTC/USDT pair.
Later Bitcoin and Ethereum recovered some of their losses.
They reduced their declines following a sharp drop of more than 5%, according to Binance data.
Specifically, the price of Bitcoin was down by 5.49% at $76,760, according to Binance data as of 3:29 a.m. Moscow time (00:29 a.m. GMT).

Human error or system failure? Spain probes deadly train crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:01:23 UTC
19:01:23 KST

Spain’s second major train collision this year has reignited questions over whether human error or systemic failures in its once-praised high-speed rail network are to blame.
The causes remain disputed.
Spain’s transport minister has pointed to a traffic controller’s alleged poor judgment as a key factor in Wednesday’s crash in Toledo province, which claimed 69 lives.
Railway unions, however, reject the focus on individual responsibility, arguing that worsening working conditions have left the network increasingly vulnerable. They cite a shortage of traffic controllers, heavier workloads and mounting pressure on staff responsible for the safety of some 45 million passengers each year.
A judge and a special government commission are conducting separate investigations into the deadly collision, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has pledged a thorough inquiry to establish what caused the disaster.
"This investigation must determine how and why this catastrophe happened," Spain’s King Felipe VI said Thursday after visiting injured passengers at a hospital in Toledo. "We will have to take measures so this never happens again."
The chain of events that led to the disaster began at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday, when the communication system essential to the line’s safety operations went down. Known as LZB, the system monitors train positions and can automatically activate a train’s brakes to prevent collisions.
The malfunction forced human controllers at a control center in Madrid to assume full responsibility for monitoring train movements and safety along a 63-kilometer (39-mile) stretch between Madrid and Seville. Authorities believe six trains were on the affected section at the time.
At 8:36 a.m., a controller told a train operated by state-owned RENFE that it could resume normal-speed operations. Another train, operated by privately owned IRYO and located 15.5 miles (25 kilometers) farther down the line, also attempted to restart, but its engineer was unable to override the automatic stop and notified the controller.
At 8:53 a.m., the trains collided, derailing carriages and leaving parts of the wreckage torn apart.
It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, farther south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente, who is facing calls to resign, described the controller’s decision to allow one train to resume at full speed while the other remained stopped as "inexplicable" and "erroneous."
Puente said the RENFE train should never have been authorized to move because a stop signal was still active on the line.
"An order is given for the train to restart, an erroneous decision," Puente told reporters. The decision "was taken in inexplicable circumstances given that a train was stopped and with a red light," he said.
Railway unions, however, argue that the circumstances surrounding the decision cannot be ignored.
Raquel Ayllon, a spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told The Associated Press that workloads regularly exceed what existing staff can safely manage. She said controllers have been calling for additional personnel for years while safety systems continue to fail.
"We believe (the minister) is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions," she said. "Human error isn't incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing."
SEMAF, Spain’s train engineers union, said the three-decade-old LZB safety system, which remains in use on the Madrid-Seville line as it is gradually phased out, has failed before, leaving human operators to manage train movements without its protection.
"The LZB system should have been replaced some time ago," said Diego Martin, a SEMAF spokesperson. "It failed us yesterday (Wednesday) and it has gone offline on repeated occasions in the past."
Railway workers went on strike Thursday in a previously planned action to demand that the government honor its commitments to improve safety conditions following the January crash.
Representatives of several unions also condemned what they described as the "irresponsible" leak of audio recordings of conversations between the control center and train engineers to Spanish media outlets.
Spain’s railways were exclusively operated by state-owned companies until the country opened its high-speed passenger network to private operators in 2021.
Both major crashes this year involved trains operated by RENFE and IRYO.
Rail traffic has increased since the market was opened to competition. Between Madrid and Barcelona, for example, the average number of daily services rose from 56 in 2019 to 89 in 2024, according to the SCF union.
Joan Rodriguez, a spokesperson for a Spanish railway workers union, said the increase in traffic following privatization had placed additional pressure on the network.
"We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," Rodriguez told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Wednesday. "I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind."

The world needs the United Nations more than ever. It needs a new lease on life | Alex Rondos and Mark Medish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:52 UTC
19:00:52 KST

To save the United Nations from the irrelevance in which it now wallows, the next secretary general will require the concerted backing of the few powers that govern the security council.
The paradox is that the great powers who created the institution in the 1940s and recently treat it with a cavalier cynicism are now the ones who need it most, as does the rest of the world.
This is not about nostalgia for what was created after the second world war. That world has changed. We are no longer in the cold war. But it is carelessness of high order to assume that some mystical process will create a world while, in the meantime, the most powerful give license to some dangerous pathologies that have brought us to ruin in the past.
The resort to war over dialogue and diplomacy has reared its head again. Restraint has given way to calculated recklessness. Changing facts on the ground before talking now creates leverage, and that is why we see an unprecedented multiplication of centers of violence. Militias and mercenaries abound.
Collective security to which all commit to be effective is now supplanted by a petulant isolationism. Revolutionary new technologies have spurred a rush to secure minerals and supply routes upending traditional notions of sovereignty. Drone warfare has made violence much more affordable. Frontiers are now up for grabs.
The permanent members of the security council, anachronistically still composed of the victors of the second world war, have a tall order. Quarrels that are as old as tribes, communities and nations now have new, more lethal weapons.
Civil wars, border wars and the return of imperial ambition are not relics. They drive the war in Ukraine, the drift toward conflict in the Horn of Africa, the instability around the Gulf and the Red Sea, and the standoff over Taiwan.
These conflicts are now multiplying at a scale and speed in a time when global regulatory arrangements over existential threats are denigrated. Proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, pandemics, climate change will either be fueled or managed by artificial intelligence.
As AI is woven into military planning, early warning and command systems, it compresses the time leaders have to think before they act, and it multiplies the tools of deception and destabilization. A world that learned, slowly and at great risk, to live with nuclear weapons must now learn to live with machines that may shape decisions about using them.
These dangers can only be contained if we dispense with some misplaced assumptions.
The first is that the UN is a club of the like-minded. It was never meant to be. The UN exists so that states that distrust or even detest one another have somewhere to meet – a place that offers hospitality to adversaries.
If the hard conversations about war and technology do not happen there, where else will they happen in a way that protects the rest of humanity? It is about co-existence, not convergence.
The second assumption is that power can be evenly distributed. It cannot. Pretending otherwise is idealism to the point of fault. A handful of states possess the disproportionate capacity to contain these dangers or to unleash them. In practice, today this means the United States, China and Russia.
But there is no reason to exclude India or a better-integrated European Union. Even if they do not trust one another, they need only recognize a shared interest in a world that remains manageable.
This harsh reality should temper the fashionable faith in “middle powers”. Their activism is understandable, even admirable: they see the great powers changing character and are trying to respond. But they are called middle powers for a reason. They cannot, on their own, end a major war or govern a technology developed mostly elsewhere.
This does not mean that might makes right. Neither does it mean that complicated times need simple answers which would be a repudiation of politics at the international level. Power checked by reasonable deliberation, negotiation and diplomacy is a core principle that inspired the charter of the United Nations. This moment calls for a rededication to principled pragmatism.
History has much to teach. When the plague swept Europe in the 14th century, the city states of Italy established the practice of quarantines and an early form of health certification. The science may have been wrong and the system imperfect. But it worked well enough, and it rested on self-interest, not virtue.
Since the mid-20th century, in a radically different technological era, nuclear proliferation and the risk of nuclear war have been contained, so far, through a lengthy process of negotiation and agreements.
Imagine a renewed UN that is a problem-solver rather than a bystander, a credible forum rather than a costly talking shop, and the prime instrument for collective action.
None of this happens unless the great powers want it to. Choosing a secretary general is one of the few moments when they must agree on a qualified person and a timely agenda. The superpowers, middle powers and emerging powers of the global south may each have reasons for skepticism. But they share a stronger reason to make this effort.
We need neither “peace in our time” nor “perpetual peace” – but enough peace to keep civilization.
- Alex Rondos is a former envoy of the European Union. Mark Medish is a former senior US national security and treasury official

Angela Rayner has said voters will begin to see a difference in their high street before the next general election as Labour prioritises investment in struggling local communities.

“There’s been a real sense of decline,” she said. “People see it as part of the identity of their town and area, and that’s why we’ve got our high streets strategy.”
Speaking after John Healey, the chancellor, earmarked more than £1bn in his debut budget on Wednesday to support retail, hospitality and leisure businesses, Rayner signalled that the government stood ready to take further action.
“The chancellor has shown he’s backing our high streets, backing our businesses that have been struggling and giving them the breathing space,” she said. “And he’s going to continue with that.”
In an interview for the Guardian’s series on the fortunes of Britain’s towns, Rayner insisted that the budget was “moving the needle” for the economy as she sought to defend Healey from criticism.
On Thursday the chancellor was warned by the Resolution Foundation and the Institute for Fiscal Studies that his measures were poorly targeted and had paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year.
Meanwhile, the owners of Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk in a blow for towns across the country where the discount chain is a high street fixture.
Speaking before that announcement, Rayner said the government was taking action to ease the pressure on businesses and households amid the damage to Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.
“All these businesses that people value, that make up a thriving high street, the chancellor is really giving them support,” she said.
Asked whether voters would be able to see a difference in their local shopping districts before the next general election, she said: “The money will start to come through. Already we’ve put the £5.8bn in.
“Next year, from April, business rates [cuts] will apply and you’ll see [other] money in more areas.”
On his way to becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged a new dawn for Britain’s high streets, placing the revival of overlooked town centres at the heart of his agenda for government.
In response to this agenda, Healey said he would cut business rates for retail, hospitality and leisure companies in a plan worth £1bn over two years, with the relief partly funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops.
Labour also launched a revamped “hope on the high street” strategy alongside the chancellor’s budget to coordinate investment and the transfer of power to local leaders. This includes the already announced £5.8bn “pride in place” programme to support regeneration projects and £210m fund to transform derelict buildings.
“There’s a lot of money and funding pots going into the high street, as well as work in the public realm to deliver services and housing,” Rayner said.
However, business leaders said more fundamental changes to the business rates system were needed, highlighting that Labour had promised to replace it entirely in its manifesto.
Before the budget Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, told the Guardian that changes to tax online sales at higher rates than in-store purchases were needed to help “level the playing field” for struggling bricks-and-mortar stores.
Hinting at further changes to come, budget documents show ministers are exploring “how the business rates system could better target online retailers in ways that minimise any indirect impacts for wider retail businesses” to fund support for the high street.

Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.
Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.
The plan forms a key part of the UK’s programme to clean up its heating networks and hit its overall emissions reduction targets. One government source said: “This is probably the most significant shift we have seen in energy policy since we came to office. The emphasis now is on cost, not just building to make sure there is enough capacity to hit our green targets.”
Paul Ovenden, a former adviser to Keir Starmer, said: “It is fascinating to see the energy capital budgets being raided to fund defence – this is the bones of Ed Miliband’s project being picked clean.

But allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.
They also said the government’s intention to change energy markets so electricity prices are no longer so attached to gas prices would help encourage consumers to move away from fossil fuels.
One source said: “Ed and Miatta have both made affordability their focus. It would be wrong to suggest that prioritising cost is in any way a shift away from the green agenda.”
A spokesperson for the energy department said: “Over the last two years, we have made considerable progress, thanks to the momentum of clean power 2030, seeing £110bn of private-sector investment announced and securing enough clean power for over 20m homes.
“We are committed to making the most of clean, homegrown power and meeting our heat pump target to protect consumers from volatile fossil fuel prices.”

Six future Trump officials wrote books before taking office. All six leaned hardest on the same metaphor.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:38 UTC
19:00:38 KST

Six books written by figures who went on to hold top posts in the second Trump administration lean heavily on metaphors of war, decline, disease, and betrayal, according to an analysis published in Frontiers in Psychology. Of the metaphors the researchers counted, about 90 percent described threats or damage while fewer than 1 in 10 described repair or renewal, and the books more often cast opponents as enemies inside the country than as foreign threats. The authors argue that this shared pattern suggests the movement’s rhetoric extends beyond Donald Trump’s own speaking style.
In everyday politics, speakers frequently use conceptual metaphors, which are figures of speech that explain abstract, complicated policy disputes in terms of concrete physical experiences like combat, illness, or building construction. Rather than serving merely as decorative language, these comparisons direct attention toward specific causes and make certain responses feel natural or necessary. For instance, a 2011 series of experiments found that changing even a single word to frame crime as either a wild beast or a virus subtly steered whether people favored police crackdowns or social reform, even though participants were unaware that the metaphor had influenced their reasoning.
The researchers pair this idea with a concept they call cognitive mobilization, which they define as a pattern within a text rather than an effect on readers: metaphors combine with emotional cues to define a crisis, assign blame, and point toward a course of action. A 2026 systematic review of 51 studies found that anger was the emotion most consistently tied to support for populist politics, followed by fear, resentment, and nostalgia, and that populist politicians routinely use emotionally charged stories and blame to rally supporters.
Much of the scholarship examining how these linguistic tools operate in the Make America Great Again movement has focused on Donald Trump himself. Earlier work, such as a 2018 discourse analysis of Trump’s campaign and inaugural speeches, indicated that he relied on familiar, everyday metaphors to frame issues such as immigration and the economy while casting himself as a warrior, builder, and repairman.
Similarly, a 2025 analysis of Trump’s speeches found that after the 2024 assassination attempt against him, his metaphorical language shifted from themes of action and success toward vulnerability and earlier patterns from his 2016 campaign. Focusing solely on one politician’s speeches and social media posts, however, leaves open the question of whether the wider circle of elites who joined his administration share a common way of framing politics.
To examine whether a common narrative blueprint exists across this broader coalition, Xuhai Chen, Zhiheng Zheng, and Jiaxuan Lv of the National University of Defense Technology, a Chinese military university in Nanjing, analyzed full-length books written by prominent figures before they entered the administration. Unlike short social media posts or campaign rally remarks, book-length texts allow authors to lay out complete arguments and stable value systems. Analyzing books published prior to the authors’ government appointments also allowed the researchers to observe how these officials framed political reality before being constrained by executive-branch roles.
The researchers assembled a digital collection of six widely circulated books published between 2016 and 2024 by individuals who later assumed top positions in the Trump governing coalition. The sample included Hillbilly Elegy (2016; 79,782 words) by Vice President J. D. Vance, Decades of Decadence (2023; 79,863 words) by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, For Love of Country (2024; 69,780 words) by Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, Battle for the American Mind (2022; 79,234 words; co-written with David Goodwin) by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Government Gangsters (2023; 74,171 words) by FBI Director Kash Patel, and The Real Anthony Fauci (2021; 190,132 words) by Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. After removing tables of contents, notes, and reference lists, the team divided the texts into individual paragraphs.
First, the authors used a machine-learning text-clustering method to map out the primary subjects discussed across all six books. Out of the entire collection, 914 paragraphs (11.57 percent) did not fit neatly into a consistent theme and were set aside as outliers. The remaining paragraphs clustered into 16 specific topics, which the researchers grouped into seven broad issue areas: public health and medical authority; education, religion, and the culture war; political and judicial institutions and the “deep state”; family, community, and class mobility; global order and national defense; economic decline and working-class anxiety; and immigration and borders.
Next, the team searched the paragraphs for candidate metaphorical words and manually checked each occurrence in context. A phrase was counted as a metaphor only when its contextual meaning differed from its basic, physical meaning and mapped a concrete experience onto an abstract political topic. For example, when Patel described political opposition to Trump as a “total war” or called the federal bureaucracy “rotten at the top,” those phrases were coded as metaphors of war and organic decay, whereas his reference to the actual armed conflict in Syria as a “civil war” was excluded as literal language. The keyword lists were built around six metaphor categories the researchers settled on after an initial open-ended reading, so other kinds of metaphors they noticed, such as those drawn from journeys, sports, or family life, were not part of the final counts.
From 3,660 candidate keyword hits, manual review confirmed 2,074 metaphorical expressions across six primary source categories: war and conflict, decline and fall, corruption and disease, invasion and infiltration, betrayal and abandonment, and revival and reconstruction. Because a single paragraph sometimes contained multiple metaphors from the same category, those 2,074 expressions corresponded to 1,704 paragraph-by-category pairings.
The researchers then coded those 1,704 pairings for how they positioned political groups (“us” versus internal or external “them”) and evaluated each pairing across 12 emotion categories, including anger, fear, disgust, nostalgia, humiliation, and hope. A second trained coder independently evaluated random subsets of the data, agreeing 80.0 percent of the time on whether a phrase was metaphorical, 99.5 percent of the time on which category confirmed metaphors belonged to, and 86.0 percent of the time on whether an out-group was present.
Across the 2,074 verified metaphors, the researchers found a pronounced imbalance between crisis and repair. Threat-oriented metaphors made up 90.55 percent of the total (1,878 instances), while metaphors of revival and reconstruction accounted for just 9.45 percent (196 instances). War and conflict was by far the most common category at 47.1 percent (976 instances), followed by decline and fall at 19.7 percent (408 instances), corruption and disease at 14.0 percent (290 instances), revival and reconstruction at 9.5 percent (196 instances), invasion and infiltration at 5.6 percent (117 instances), and betrayal and abandonment at 4.2 percent (87 instances).
Although the six authors wrote about very different subjects, the statistical difference in how they used the six metaphor categories was modest (showing a Cramér’s V of 0.178, where 0 would mean the authors used the categories in identical proportions and 1 would mean each used entirely different ones). The authors interpret this as evidence that the writers drew from a shared toolkit while emphasizing different elements.
War and conflict was the most common category in all six books, with Gabbard and Hegseth leaning on it heaviest at 71.38 percent and 54.47 percent of their metaphors, respectively. Patel (29.66 percent) and Kennedy (19.75 percent) stood out for their frequent use of corruption and disease imagery, with Kennedy also showing the highest rate of invasion and infiltration metaphors (9.39 percent). Rubio relied almost equally on war and conflict (37.25 percent) and decline and fall (36.47 percent), while Vance showed the highest proportions of revival and reconstruction (13.79 percent) and betrayal and abandonment (6.90 percent).
These metaphorical frames regularly crossed policy boundaries to turn domestic policy disputes into existential struggles. War and conflict metaphors were high in discussions of global order and defense (64.19 percent), but they also made up 57.00 percent of the metaphors in education and culture-war topics and 51.24 percent in discussions of political and judicial institutions. In Battle for the American Mind, for instance, Hegseth portrayed kindergarten-through-12th-grade schooling as a “16,000-hour war” and a “battlefield” for children’s minds where conservative parents confront “fortified machine-gun nests.” The authors argue that framing curriculum debates as military combat narrows the space for compromise or gradual policy reform.
Other metaphor categories performed specialized roles depending on the policy area. Decline and fall metaphors accounted for 60.49 percent of the metaphors in economic discussions, where authors like Rubio and Vance portrayed the loss of manufacturing jobs as the physical and moral collapse of working-class families and towns.
Meanwhile, corruption and disease metaphors linked political institutions (26.71 percent) with public health (19.81 percent), portraying federal agencies and medical authorities as sources of internal rot or contamination, framing that the authors argue makes forceful intervention seem justified. Invasion and infiltration metaphors appeared most frequently in public health (9.28 percent) and immigration (9.09 percent), using flood and breach imagery to depict both migrants and viruses as overwhelming forces pouring across vulnerable boundaries.
When the researchers examined how the 1,704 paragraph-metaphor pairings defined allies and enemies, they found that 82.4 percent (1,404 pairings) included collective group positioning. The single most common arrangement pitted “us” against an “internal them,” accounting for 31.7 percent of all pairings (541 instances), followed closely by passages focusing solely on an “internal them” at 25.4 percent (432 instances).
By contrast, passages pitting “us” against an “external them” made up only 4.6 percent (78 instances), and those mentioning an “external them” alone accounted for 1.3 percent (22 instances). Rather than focusing mainly on foreign nations, the books largely cast domestic figures, such as elites, government bureaucrats, institutional authorities, and ideological opponents, as insiders who had betrayed or infected the country from within.
The emotion analysis helped explain how these metaphors fit together as an argumentative structure within the texts, rather than a psychological sequence that readers necessarily move through. Expressions of fear and anxiety appeared in 95.54 percent of the 1,704 pairings, creating a near-constant backdrop of urgency across all six books. Against that anxious baseline, individual metaphor categories carried distinct emotional signatures above chance levels: war metaphors paired with anger and pride, corruption and disease metaphors clustered with disgust and humiliation, decline metaphors evoked nostalgia and loss, and betrayal metaphors combined humiliation, disgust, and anger.
Although revival and reconstruction metaphors represented less than a tenth of the total, they carried a strong concentration of hope, sacredness, pride, and appeals to justice, which the authors interpret as a focused promise of renewal that gives the anger and disgust of the crisis passages somewhere to go.
These patterns align with a 2025 analysis of Donald Trump’s speeches and social media posts, which found that Trump shifted his rhetoric from personal grievance to nationalized victimhood, using narratives of inflicted pain and retribution to morally justify retaliatory policies like sweeping trade tariffs. Even though the new study analyzed the metaphorical architecture of crisis and repair in book-length texts by coalition elites rather than Trump’s own speeches and social media posts on victimhood, both analyses point to threat- and conflict-centered narratives as a recurring feature of the movement’s rhetoric.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because the study examined published books rather than surveying readers or interviewing the writers, it maps out the structure of political arguments on the page rather than the private thoughts of the authors, and political books are often shaped by co-writers and editors.
The analysis also cannot determine whether reading these metaphors causes audiences to change their attitudes or take action. In addition, the six books were chosen because they were prominent bestsellers, and the study did not compare them with similar books by other politicians, so it cannot show whether this crisis-heavy pattern is unusual for Trump-aligned writers or typical of commercial political nonfiction, which often relies on dramatic, conflict-heavy storytelling.
The sample was also limited to six books of uneven length, with Kennedy’s 190,132-word volume more than twice as long as each of the other five books, which ranged from roughly 70,000 to 80,000 words. His book alone supplied about 35 percent of all the metaphors counted, giving public health debates outsized weight in the overall totals.
Determining where literal language ends and metaphor begins also involves subjective judgment: the 80.0 percent agreement rate between coders on whether a candidate word was metaphorical reflects only moderate reliability once chance agreement is accounted for (with a Cohen’s kappa of 0.556), the coders agreed 65.1 percent of the time on the exact seven-category group-positioning label, and the emotion labels were not checked by a second coder.
Future studies could normalize metaphor counts by book length, compare these works against books written by mainstream conservative or Democratic politicians, and examine whether these officials continued to use the same metaphorical framework in their official speeches after taking office.
The study, “From threat to repair: metaphorical architecture and cognitive mobilization in Trumpist governing-coalition texts,” was authored by Xuhai Chen, Zhiheng Zheng, and Jiaxuan Lv.

Press review: EU, NATO try to hinder Ukraine peace and Russia seeks constructive G20 talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Moscow suspects EU and NATO leaders are obstructing efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict; Russia and African nations called for closer economic and political cooperation at a major summit in Moscow; and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov travels to G20 talks in Atlanta against a backdrop of tensions with Western countries. These stories topped Friday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Russia says EU, NATO leadership is hindering efforts to resolve Ukraine conflict
Despite some European politicians expressing readiness to engage in dialogue with Russia, Moscow has noted attempts by the leadership of NATO and the EU to hamper efforts to resolve the Ukrainian conflict, the Russian Foreign Ministry told Izvestia. Vladimir Putin has said that Russia supports any steps toward rebuilding relations with both the European Union as a whole and individual European countries. At the same time, he warned that "there would be no winners" in a potential military conflict between Russia and Europe and urged caution against a repeat of the Strait of Hormuz scenario in the Baltic Sea.
Russia is ready for contacts with the EU and NATO, but it was not Moscow that cut off those ties, and "accordingly, the initiative for dialogue must come from the Europeans," Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Department of European Affairs at the Russian Foreign Ministry, told Izvestia.
"Some European politicians are beginning to acknowledge the need to restore contacts. At the same time, the leadership of both the European Union and the North Atlantic Alliance, along with many of their member states, has been striving for months to block any settlement of the Ukrainian conflict, hampering US negotiating efforts. Yet they publicly claim that it is Russia that is taking maximalist positions and displaying no willingness to negotiate," the diplomat added.
According to Maslennikov, the Europeans’ desire to "squeeze into" the negotiations and avoid being left on the sidelines is also plainly apparent. "Without the Europeans factoring in the realities on the ground, it would, frankly, be strange to engage in talks," he emphasized.
According to Andrey Kortunov, research director of the Russian International Affairs Council, the prolonged nature of the Ukrainian crisis is driven by the interests of a coalition of Western forces that can be classified into three main groups. First are economic and political circles linked to the military-industrial complex and the militarization of Europe. Second, the ongoing confrontation benefits the political leadership of European countries. Third, proponents of neoliberalism play an important role in hindering a settlement. For them, confrontation with Moscow is a matter of ideological dogma, he added.
Vedomosti: Russia, African nations discuss boosting cooperation at Moscow summit attended by 48 countries
The third Russia-Africa summit was held at the Kremlin on October 29, bringing together delegations from 48 of Africa’s 54 countries. The gathering featured more than 20 countries represented at the highest level in Moscow. At the conclusion of the event, participants adopted a final declaration and a declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of artificial intelligence technologies. According to experts interviewed by Vedomosti, Africa’s increasing role in global politics and the business contacts made at the Russia-Africa summit could assist Russian companies in strengthening their presence in African markets.
The summit comprised two sessions lasting more than eight hours in total. The first included speeches by heads of state, while the second was held behind closed doors in the format of a working breakfast. Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov had previously stated that this part of the summit would feature an exchange of views on its agenda. The opening session began with remarks by Vladimir Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, whose country currently chairs the African Union.
Several heads of delegation brought up the issue of conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, stressing the need for peace. Many heads of state also spoke about food security. Trade between Russia and African countries surpassed $27 bln in 2025, representing a 1.5-fold increase since the previous summit in 2023. Russia delivered 18 mln metric tons of grain in 2025 and 13 mln metric tons in the first nine months of 2026, while fertilizer shipments totaled 1.5 mln metric tons last year and surpassed 2.2 mln metric tons this year.
The need for an equitable partnership between Russia and Africa was another key issue at the summit. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called the model of cooperation between Russia and the African continent successful, pointing to the construction of Egypt’s El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant as an example.
Africa’s role in global politics has been increasing since the 2010s, as demonstrated by objective economic indicators, Ivan Kopyttsev, an expert at the Africa Center of the Russian Institute for Strategic Studies, told Vedomosti.
The expert also pointed out that dozens of business representatives were present at the event. "Undoubtedly, the personal contacts forged at the forum are of enormous importance for the further expansion of Russian businesses into African markets, since establishing that initial connection can sometimes prove decisive," he added.
Kommersant: Russia seeks constructive G20 dialogue as Lavrov gets ready for talks in Atlanta
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will participate in a Group of Twenty (G20) ministerial meeting in Atlanta, United States, on October 30-31. The trip is expected to be a difficult one: it remained uncertain until the last moment as US authorities held up the issuance of visas, while the Russian minister is expected to come under fire from his Western counterparts at the meeting, Kommersant writes. Nevertheless, the Russian Foreign Ministry voiced optimism that the gathering would "proceed in a constructive and unbiased manner."
It was not until October 28, just one day before his scheduled departure, that Lavrov’s trip to Atlanta was officially confirmed. According to Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, the Russian side "had the impression, particularly in light of the situation surrounding the issuance of US visas to Russian delegates by the US Embassy in Moscow, that not everyone in Washington was in favor of the Russian delegation’s planned visit." Most of the outstanding issues, she added, were settled literally at the last moment.
Apart from the difficulties surrounding the trip’s organization, the Russian delegation is expected to face criticism from Western countries at the G20 meeting. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, for example, has vowed to hold Iran and Russia responsible for increasing global energy prices and problems with international food security, arguing that the two countries are hampering the normal functioning of trade routes.
Nevertheless, before Lavrov’s departure for Atlanta, the Russian Foreign Ministry voiced confidence that the meeting would take place "in a constructive and unbiased manner." At the same time, the ministry indicated that Russia’s top diplomat also has concerns to raise with his Western counterparts.
According to the ministry, Lavrov’s remarks at the G20 will present "Russia’s perspective on the main factors behind international tensions, focusing on the refusal of certain powers to acknowledge the rise of new centers of power; the use of economic ‘weapons’ against opponents, including sanctions, trade wars, and supply chain disruptions; and the persistent North-South imbalances stemming from this destructive approach."
US authorities have also extended an invitation to Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami on December 14-15, but Moscow has yet to make a decision on whether he will attend. It appears that the decision will depend on several factors, including the outcome of Lavrov’s visit to Atlanta and how the Russian president’s trip to the APEC summit in China on November 18-19 develops, Kommersant writes. The latter event could serve as the venue for the first-ever trilateral summit between Russia, China, and the United States.
Izvestia: EU plans to request €20-25 bln from UK, Canada for Ukraine amid rising funding needs
The European Union plans to seek €20-25 bln from the United Kingdom and Canada to fund Ukraine in 2027. Brussels intends to raise the matter at upcoming summits with the two countries, a European source told Izvestia. The EU hopes to meet some of Kiev’s additional funding requirements of €70 bln, which persist despite an already agreed two-year loan of €90 bln. However, experts believe London and Ottawa are unlikely to consent to providing such a substantial amount.
"The EU will certainly request around €20-25 bln from the United Kingdom and Canada for Ukraine next year at the upcoming summits. Zelensky has asked for approximately €70 bln for next year. Japan and Australia may also contribute more modest sums of assistance. The outstanding funds could be provided by the European Union," a European source told Izvestia.
Financial assistance to Kiev also has political implications. According to the source, it is important for the EU to demonstrate to Vladimir Putin that Brussels "can outlast Russia."
If Kiev’s allies beyond the EU are unable to supply the necessary amount, the financial responsibility will fall on Brussels. The bloc is already considering the possibility of issuing debt instruments to finance Ukraine. Media reports indicate that some member states support providing a €45 bln loan. The funds could be secured through borrowing backed by guarantees from the EU budget.
The issue has already triggered heated discussions in the European Parliament. Slovak Member of the European Parliament Milan Uhrik is against increasing the EU’s debt obligations. "Brussels is seeking yet another decision to allocate €70 bln to Ukraine, but this uninterrupted flow of funds into a ‘black hole’ must come to an end. Officials are discussing irresponsible mechanisms, ranging from joint EU debt backed by European taxpayers’ money to the use of extraordinary returns from frozen assets," he told Izvestia.
The European Commission argues that the bloc has enough financial capacity to meet these expenditures. However, no concrete funding source has yet been identified. The situation is further complicated by the stance of Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Bulgaria, which, according to Politico, have already declined to contribute to interest payments on future loans to Ukraine.
Vedomosti: Gold prices forecast to stay above $4,000 through 2030 amid worldwide uncertainty
The average global gold price is projected to stay above $4,000 per troy ounce until at least 2030, according to a forecast featured in a report by consulting firm Kept, seen by Vedomosti. The report presents two scenarios. The first presumes that the current global geopolitical situation and elevated energy prices will continue, alongside further tightening of US monetary policy. The second anticipates progress toward resolving major geopolitical conflicts and a halt in interest rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve.
Under the first scenario, Kept analysts project that the average gold price will climb to $4,523 per ounce this year, representing a 31.5% increase from the previous year. Under the second scenario, the price is expected to average $4,560 per ounce, up 33%, according to the report. In 2025, the metal gained 44% in price to $3,439 per ounce.
Gold prices climbed sharply in January and February of 2026, hitting record highs and exceeding $5,000 per ounce. However, prices subsequently started falling despite the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, even though gold has traditionally functioned as a safe-haven asset during periods of increased global risk. Experts link the decline to gold sales by several countries seeking to replenish their energy stocks.
Andrey Smirnov, a stock market expert at BCS World of Investments, believes that deglobalization and the dedollarization of the global economy will fuel stronger demand for gold and drive prices upward. Elena Kozhukhova, an analyst at Veles Capital investment company, regards the geopolitical situation as the main factor determining price movements.
Gold could climb to $4,500-4,700 per ounce in 2027, Boris Krasnozhenov, head of the Investment and Industry Analysis Directorate at Alfa-Bank, told Vedomosti. Meanwhile, Nikolay Dudchenko, an analyst at Finam Financial Group, believes prices could reach $5,000 per ounce.

Samsung S95H OLED TV Review (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Another major difference has to do with the breakout box, called the Samsung One Connect. With the S95H, it’s no longer required or included in the box, so you have to connect all of your devices like a video game console or a streaming device directly to the television. That means the S95H is thicker at 1.04 inches compared to just 0.4 inches for the S95F. However, I actually preferred not using the One Connect. It meant less hassle with another device to plug in and set up. You can always buy the One Connect box later if you decide you want less clutter by your TV stand or on the wall.
The S95H has four HDMI ports on the right side (including one for gaming at 165 Hz and one for eARC passthrough audio for surround sound), an Ethernet jack, optical audio out, two USB ports for playing files off a storage drive, and a headphone jack. It supports Wi-Fi 6E for faster speeds and compatibility than older standards (like the Wi-Fi 5 used on the S95F). Both TVs mount flush to the wall, although I used the included pedestal stand, which attached easily.
For the UI, Tizen OS is not terrible, but as we noted in our previous S95F review, it’s still a bit of a maze. The setup process including adding apps and tweaking picture settings is far easier on a Google TV model like the Sony Bravia 7 II. I’m used to Tizen OS, since I test TVs often, but I still don’t love it. (At least I didn’t need to use the Samsung SmartThings app for setup.)
I really like the Samsung remote—It doesn’t overwhelm you with buttons. Hisense remotes tend to have way too many buttons, in my experience. Most of us need channel, mute, and volume, plus maybe a few shortcuts to apps like Netflix.
Samsung doesn’t officially list the color gamut specs like DCI-P3 or BT.2020 for the S95H. Equally so, there is no official mention of brightness rating in nits or contrast ratio, but I’m okay with that as well. Those specs can be misleading and really depend on the picture quality settings, the brightness of the room, and (mostly) the content you watch. Instead, I subjected the S95H to rigorous real-world testing to see how it measures up to recent models.
Competitive Color Quality
The S95H measures up to the competition quite nicely when it comes to color quality. It excels in many areas but is not always the de facto winner for every movie, show or game. Once again, there is so much competition that buying a flagship OLED like this one is no longer the obvious choice.
I started with the movie Awake because several scenes in that movie (about people who can no longer sleep) are extremely dark. Time and again, even top-end televisions can’t seem to show key scenes with enough color or clarity. The S95H performed surprisingly well, but it took some tweaks. On Filmmaker, Dynamic, and even Standard and Eco modes, scenes with the main character biking at night looked too dark. Enabling AI Optimized picture mode helped a lot, beating out what was possible on the Samsung Micro RGB R95H in the same scenes.

Crematoria Are Being Used to Heat Homes and Swimming Pools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

In 2011, Redditch Borough Council in England tried something that hardly anyone in the UK had heard of before. Staff announced they were going to warm the local swimming pool with heat from a nearby crematorium.
A public firestorm ensued. The plans were met with international headlines, and a labor union official branded them “sick and an insult to residents.” (A spokesman for the union, Unison, says this was not—and is not currently—the organization’s official position.)
“All you’re doing is basically heating a radiator and sending the heat down a tube,” says Guy Revans, of Redditch and Bromsgrove Councils, just south of Birmingham. “But death is always an emotive subject, isn’t it?”
Eventually, the relentless press coverage faded away. The project won a green award, and the crematorium has warmed Redditch’s swimming pool since 2013.
Although extremely rare in North America, European countries have been harvesting warmth from crematoria for years. The total volume of heat available from crematoria is modest, but as people search for ways of reducing the environmental impact of funeral rites, utilizing crematoria waste heat provides a way to lower their carbon intensity.
Roughly 1,200 cremations are carried out every year in Redditch. A heat exchanger captures heat from flue gases emitted by the facility’s two gas-fired ovens as part of a process to remove vaporized mercury from dental fillings, before venting the remaining gas into the atmosphere.
That’s a common process at many crematoria. In other words, excess heat is often captured by default, meaning the next question is, does it make sense to waste the heat—or use it? In Redditch, the heat exchanger connects to a water loop that travels 200 meters underground, eventually reaching another heat exchanger supplying the swimming pool.
Helpfully, such a sizable body of water “acts as a heat sink”, adds Revans. “You put heat into it during the day, it retains that heat for a considerable length of time.” The recreation center also has gas-fired boilers that can provide more heat when necessary. Overall, the system has saved the council tens of thousands of pounds per year in fuel costs.
Similar projects have emerged elsewhere recently. A school currently under construction in Aberdeen, Scotland, will receive excess heat from the city’s crematorium. The crematorium already relies on waste heat to warm its own premises.
“They were only utilizing a tiny amount of the heat available; the rest was going to the atmosphere,” says Ian Davidson, chief executive of Aberdeen Heat & Power, who says that the system now has full planning permission. The crematorium will provide just under 1 gigawatt-hour of heat annually, roughly half the school’s total requirement. A heat pump will cover the rest of the facility’s needs, and the entire system should be fully operational by February 2027.
Some crematoria are going even further in their pursuit of green credentials. The crematorium that will open in Kangasala, Finland, in 2028 will be connected to the town’s district heat network, a system of pipes that supplies more than 6,500 homes with hot water for heating. The crematorium will be fully electric, powered partly by solar panels on its roof.
“It’s a special thing,” says Timo Heikkilä, an energy and building systems consultant at Thenco Oy, who is working on the project. “I’m really glad I get to be a part of this.”
Winter temperatures in Kangasala can remain below 0 degrees Celsius for weeks on end. In Finland, there is a push to use less natural gas for heating, says Heikkilä. Although once cheaply available from neighbouring Russia, that country’s invasion of Ukraine and concerns over climate change have prompted Finland to seek alternatives. In some locations, this means utilizing waste heat from unusual sources, including crematoria.
“Finns,” says Heikkilä, “are quite practical.”
Ian Rudkin, who has managed multiple crematoria in the UK and is currently a board member of the Cremation Society of Great Britain, says many crematoria are becoming more eco-conscious. Today, software can schedule the firing of gas ovens to align with funeral services, ensuring they don’t waste energy and are only turned on when needed, for example. And some crematoria hold coffins for up to 72 hours, so that several may be cremated in a sequence, which is more efficient.
“When we first brought that in, [families] seemed a little bit shocked,” says Rudkin. Soon, however, people became more accepting. “They’d make comments like, ‘Dad always used to turn the light off at home to save energy.’”
But implementing heat recovery tech at crematoria in the US is more difficult, says Paul Seyler, director of strategy at Matthews Environmental Solutions. There, district heat networks are rare, and crematoria tend to be privately owned. That means the investment needed for heat exchangers and pipework necessary to link buildings together is higher.
“We’re studying this and watching it closely because, when the economics align, we’d like to be in a position to offer a solution,” says Seyler. Wasted heat is, after all, just a waste of resources, he adds. Besides a few small-scale experiments, Seyler says he isn’t aware of any fully operational systems in the US that utilize heat from crematoria.
The closest example is in Canada at a funeral complex in Sainte-Thérèse, Quebec. This 3,255-square-meter building houses family rooms, a large chapel, a crematorium, and a kitchen, among other facilities. Heat exchangers installed just over a decade ago soak up heat from cremation flue gases and distribute it around the complex, including the sidewalks to melt snow in the winter.
“The owner was not immediately on board as he thought it may have posed an ethical dilemma,” recall design engineers Martin Roy and Lianne Cockerton in an article about the project, published in the ASHRAE Journal.
Now, visitors pass an LED screen in the reception area that displays the energy performance of the building, based partly on the heat exchanger’s operation. While gas is still used for some of the building’s heating needs, as well as for cremations, the new system saves an estimated 29 metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually.
Recovering heat from cremations is one way of attempting to counter the “devastating impact” that humans have had on the environment, says Hannah Rumble, an associate at the University of Bath’s Centre for Death and Society. “I can see that would be a reason why people might choose to be cremated at a particular crematorium.”
Most crematoria contacted by WIRED say they do not emphasize the presence of heat recovery technology to families or mourners, though a spokeswoman for Aberdeen City Council adds that the council there will “undertake some public awareness-raising on the new system before it is operational to ensure transparency.”
Gaynor Doherty, an independent humanist funeral and wedding celebrant in the UK, says using waste heat from crematoria is “sensible,” though she suggests a natural burial, where bodies are simply shrouded or placed in biodegradable coffins and allowed to decompose in the environment, might be preferable to many eco-minded people. The carbon intensity of cremation varies from facility to facility, but could be around 250 kilograms of carbon per gas-fired cremation. Recovering heat from the process offsets some of those emissions (one company claims savings of 100 kilograms) but not all.
A study published in 2024 estimated that, if all crematoria in the UK were tapped for waste heat, they might only meet 1 percent of the county’s total heating needs. This sounds small, but decarbonizing heat is notoriously difficult, so any interventions to achieve that can be valuable. Plus, some people may feel that sharing the heat from their cremation could carry a lot of meaning.
In Finland, the all-electric crematorium in Kangasala will not produce as much heat as a gas-fired equivalent, though it will run 24/7 because it’s more efficient to operate by using electricity to gently top up heat retained in ceramic materials within the ovens. The connection to the district heat network means that, when mourners return home from funeral services at the new crematorium, it is conceivable that at least a small portion of that warmth they feel after stepping through their front doors will come from the cremation of the person they loved.
Heikkilä says working on the project has prompted some big questions for him. “I have thought about it, and once my time is up, I would like to be cremated, and I would like my waste heat to be recycled,” he says. “It’s the sensible thing. The last favor you can do for the world.”
