Iran, Turkey’s capacities pave way for expanding bilateral co-op: Iran’s minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:07:14 UTC
17:07:14 KST

Iran, Turkey’s capacities pave way for expanding bilateral co-op: Iran’s minister
TEHRAN- The Minister of Transport and Urban Development emphasized the necessity of expanding bilateral cooperation between Iran and Turkey in the political, economic, and transport/communications fields and said: Expanding economic and transport/communications relations between Iran and Turkey, in addition to securing mutual interests, can make an effective contribution to strengthening cooperation, prosperity, and sustainable development in the region.
According to an IRNA report from the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development, Farzaneh Sadegh, at a ceremony commemorating the anniversary of the founding of the Republic of Turkey, said: National days are an opportunity to honor the history and identity of nations and to respect their efforts to build their own future; this occasion is also a valuable opportunity to reflect on the importance of friendship and cooperation among countries and the role that nations can play in shaping a world enjoying peace, stability, and development.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, noting that Iran and Turkey, as two neighbors with a long history, have enjoyed deep cultural, civilizational, and human ties, added: The relations between the two nations have been formed beyond geographical borders on the basis of historical interactions, social relations, and rich cultural and religious heritage, and have continued and strengthened over time.
She stressed: These valuable ties are a lasting asset for strengthening friendship and expanding mutual cooperation between the two countries in today’s world.
Sadegh stated: Economic and trade cooperation between the two countries is one of the important pillars of these relations; Iran and Turkey, possessing diverse and complementary economic capacities, have considerable opportunities to expand relations and benefit from mutual capabilities.
Emphasizing that the geographical position of Iran and Turkey has given special status to transport and communications cooperation between the two countries, she said: The development of these connections can play a constructive and key role in linking the economies and markets of the region and strengthen the fraternal relations of the two countries in all fields.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development stressed: We believe that expanding economic and communications relations between Iran and Turkey, in addition to securing mutual interests, can make an effective contribution to strengthening cooperation, prosperity, and sustainable development in the region.
She added: The future of these relations, relying on existing capacities and the joint will of the two countries, creates a valuable opportunity for the growth and flourishing of the two nations.
Sadegh stated: The recent bitter developments and crises in the region have once again revealed the importance of peace, stability, and the shared responsibility of countries in maintaining security and calm; the experience of these developments shows that security and development are interconnected in nature, and achieving sustainable peace requires respect for the national sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries, adherence to the principles of international law, and prioritizing dialogue and peaceful solutions.
Iran and Turkey should strengthen trade ties by identifying competitive Iranian export products, assessing market demand and verifying potential buyers, Iran’s commercial attaché in Turkey said at a seminar on bilateral trade opportunities and challenges. on October 25.
Kamran Davari Niko, Iran’s commercial attaché in Istanbul, made the remarks at a seminar hosted by the Qazvin Chamber of Commerce and attended by its board members and business representatives, according to the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran (TPO).
Davari Niko said none of Turkey’s border crossings with Iran had been closed, expressing hope that trade between the two countries would continue. He stressed the need to monitor developments, identify suitable routes for maintaining trade flows and make better use of existing capacities to expand economic cooperation.
He also highlighted direct engagement and bilateral consultations as important tools for strengthening commercial relations, referring to a meeting between Qazvin Chamber of Commerce board members and Turkish counterparts in Istanbul.
The seminar examined Iranian goods with export potential in the Turkish market, as well as opportunities for imports from Turkey. Participants emphasized the importance of assessing market needs, evaluating products’ competitive advantages, calculating production costs and determining profitability before entering new business sectors.
Other topics included estimating operating costs, assessing mutual benefits, checking the commercial credibility of trading partners and understanding formal and customary contractual practices. Participants also discussed required regulations and permits, tariffs, transportation costs and payment methods as part of efforts to reduce trade risks.
Earlier in June, the representative of the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce Ibrahim Dogan Salman stated that in 2025, the trade between Iran and Turkey surpassed $5.6 billion.
During a meeting with members of the Board of Directors of the Yazd Chamber of Commerce, Doghan Salman added that the preferential trade agreement implemented between the two countries in 2015 has provided a solid foundation for the development of these cooperations.
Referring to the history of economic and cultural relations between Iran and Turkey, he said: "There are deep-rooted cooperations between the two countries, and we are interested in strengthening these relations more than ever."
Dogan Salman, stating that "we are not on two sides of the Silk Road, but rather walk side by side on this road," added: "Iran and Turkey have always been neighbors throughout history and have known and understood each other. What binds the two nations together is a shared history, culture, and civilization."
The Istanbul Chamber of Commerce representative, referring to the value of trade between the two countries, stated: "In 2025, the trade between Iran and Turkey exceeded $5.6 billion. Furthermore, the preferential trade agreement implemented between the two countries in 2015 has provided a solid foundation for the development of these cooperations."
He cited the active presence of entrepreneurs from both countries as the most tangible sign of this bond and said: "Currently, 7,288 companies with Iranian investment are operating in Turkey, and at the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce alone, the number of companies of Iranian origin has reached 2,040."
Dogan Salman also referred to the people-to-people ties between the two countries and added: "In 2025, more than three million Iranians visited Turkey, and this statistic shows that Iran and Turkey are not merely each other's markets, but are also true partners."
The Istanbul Chamber of Commerce representative emphasized: "To strengthen the bond between the chambers of commerce on both sides, we are prepared to hold joint meetings, bilateral talks, and specialized exhibitions."

Geneva Film Festival to honour lifetime work of Mira Nair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:07:06 UTC
17:07:06 KST

Geneva Film Festival to honour lifetime work of Mira Nair
Filmmaker Mira Nair, mother of the Mayor of New York and winner of many accolades for her movies, will be honoured for her life’s work at the Geneva Film Festival.
Long before Mira Nair’s son, Zohran Mamdani, took office as mayor of the largest city in the United States this year, she was already a leading figure in the world of film. Her very first feature film, Salaam Bombay!, won her the Golden Camera at Cannes in 1988.
This was followed the following year by an Oscar nomination. In 2001, she became the first Indian female director to win the Golden Lion at Venice for Monsoon Wedding.
In many of her films, Nair – who was born in India in 1957 – explores Indian society and the changes it is undergoing. However, her work also addresses conditions in the US.
Notable examples include The Reluctant Fundamentalist (2012), which deals with Islamophobia in the US following the September 11 attacks in 2001, or The Namesake (2006), which explores the consequences of uprooting and integration for Indian identity.
Nair initially studied sociology before moving behind the camera. She began by making documentaries until she made her feature film debut with Salaam Bombay!. The film is an unsentimental chronicle of the lives of street children in the Indian megacity.
Three years later came Mississippi Masala, starring Denzel Washington and Sarita Choudhury. The film tells the love story between a young woman of Indian origin and an African American man from Mississippi.
Set against the backdrop of a wedding, Monsoon Wedding explores sexual violence, class divisions and the contradictions of an India torn between tradition and globalisation.
Nair once said that her aim was for those who watch her films to view their own lives through different eyes, and for those who have long been regarded as “the others” to appear “just as human as anyone else”.
Famous politician son
Politically, she advocates for a cinema that no longer needs the West as an intermediary. “That era is over,” she said in 2023, referring to her perspective on India and the diaspora.
Her only son, Zohran Mamdani, was born in Kampala, Uganda, in 1991, at a time when she had already made her international breakthrough in the film world. His father is the academic Mahmood Mamdani. When Mamdani took office as New York’s first Muslim mayor, the family found itself in the spotlight.
The 32nd edition of Geneva Film Festival is now screening a selection of her works throughout the festival, which runs from October 30 to November 8. On October 31, Nair will participate in a moderated discussion.
In addition, the festival is putting Swiss cinema in the spotlight with over 110 films. Filmmaker Petra Volpe is expected to attend with her latest work, Frank & Louis, which has just been released in cinemas in German-speaking Switzerland.
The Geneva Film Festival has had a new director, Emilie Bujès, since August 2026. Bujès had previously headed the Visions du Réel documentary film festival in Nyon for several years. However, she will not take over as artistic director until the 2027 edition. Her predecessor, Anaïs Emery, is still in charge of the current edition.

BP profits jump as Middle East conflict drives up oil refining margins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:06:46 UTC
17:06:46 KST

BP’s quarterly profits have been labelled “obscene” after they hit an 18-year high of $8.46bn (£6.3bn), as the war in the Middle East drove up oil and gas prices.
The energy company hailed a “banner quarter” on Friday, with its underlying replacement cost profit – a key measure of its income – almost quadrupling in the three months to the end of September, from $2.2bn in the same period a year ago. The jump meant BP’s quarterly profits hit their highest level since the $8.9bn recorded in 2008.
BP’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill, told Bloomberg TV: “It really was a banner quarter for the refining business. We had very strong margins from the BP-operated refineries, we also had very strong underlying performance. We were able to capture the opportunity provided by the market.”
However, climate crisis campaigners said it was outrageous that BP was profiting so handsomely on commodities causing serious damage to the environment.
It is just over a week until diplomats will meet in Antalya, Turkey, for the Cop31 UN climate summit. Recent climate-linked disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal will be at the forefront of many delegates’ minds. There are likely to be tensions with fossil fuel producing countries, which have sought to stymie calls for a transition to clean energy.
BP’s strong results also come as motorists in the UK face high fuel prices, with diesel now at 198.79p a litre, according to estimates from the RAC. The cost of petrol has also risen, with an average price of 172.92p a litre, compared with 132.83p in late February, before the latest conflict in the Middle East began.
Jonathan Noronha-Gant, of the campaign group Global Witness, said it was “obscene that polluters are continuing to cash in on the fallout of the war in Iran, making more bumper profits from spiralling oil prices while innocent civilians suffer.
“These massive profits come as ordinary people across Europe are struggling with the rising cost of living, with many struggling to afford to heat their homes as winter arrives,” he said.
Danny Gross, of Friends of the Earth, said: “As millions of households brace themselves for a cold winter, huddling under blankets and clutching hot-water bottles as they struggle to pay their bills, BP is raking in huge profits while doubling down on gas and oil production and slashing investment in renewables.”
Although the link between fossil fuels and climate breakdown has been known for decades, scientists directly linked carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel companies to dozens of deadly heatwaves for the first time a year ago. Yet more heatwaves swept across Europe this summer, with separate research suggesting they led to a record 50,000 excess deaths.
As people in cities sweltered, infernos tore through forests and brush in parched rural areas. France experienced its largest area burned on record and fires blazed in usually cooler regions, such as the Cairngorms in Scotland.
In the Pacific, a supercharged El Niño is brewing, with water temperatures reaching more than 3C higher than usual. The weather phenomenon is likely to be the most extreme of its kind in at least 1,000 years, dumping vast amounts of extra heat into an atmosphere already warmed by climate breakdown.
“The climate crisis is not an abstract future threat,” said Clémence Dubois, head of global campaigns at 350.org. “People are facing deadly heat, destroyed livelihoods and growing insecurity now. Governments are being forced to find money to protect their populations, while fossil fuel companies are forecast to make extraordinary profits.”
Record oil company profits come as the UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is weighing up whether to allow drilling in the North Sea’s Rosebank oilfield, after approving a licence for the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield earlier in October.
BP’s quarterly earnings were bolstered by higher profits from the oil refining business as the difference between the cost of crude oil and the price of refined fuels such as diesel and gasoline soared, earning almost $47 for each barrel produced.
Although global oil prices have remained below the peaks recorded during the 2022 energy crisis, the pump prices for fuels, including diesel, have risen to all-time highs across the UK, Europe and the US in recent months because of severe disruptions to refineries in the Gulf region and across Russia.
BP’s earnings windfall announcement came after Shell and the French oil rival TotalEnergies reported their strongest profits since 2022, also thanks in large part to the profits made from refining crude into fuel products such as diesel.

EU directive forces 6-year renovation deadline on old non-residential buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:06:00 UTC
17:06:00 KST

EU directive forces 6-year renovation deadline on old non-residential buildings
Owners of old non-residential buildings must renovate them within six years under a Climate Ministry plan, a requirement the real estate sector says will cause problems in rural areas.
The plan will be codified in domestic legislation, which in turn transposes an EU directive.
Buildings in energy classes G and H are required to reach at least class F by 2030, and class E by 2033. Renovation costs are estimated at nearly €290 million, with a payback period of about six years.
Class H and G buildings are generally old and are not insulated. A 1970s brick apartment building in Lasnamäe for instance might be rated at F, while later 1990s buildings with individual improvements such as new windows might reach level E.
The Ministry of Climate plans to amend the Building Code and bring it into line with a European Union directive, which requires renovation of non-residential buildings in poor condition — commercial and public buildings, warehouses and office buildings among them.
The requirement covers buildings in the poorest energy classes. Those rated G or H must reach at least class F by 2030 and at least class E by 2033. Renovating them will cost nearly €290 million in total, with an average payback period of about six years, according to the draft legislation. Renovated buildings have lower heating costs and rise in value.
Ingvar Allekand, chairman of the EKFL, the national real estate association, told ERR the change would create a major problem, affecting not only property owners but the wider economy. He said it would impose unreasonable costs and that businesses, particularly in rural areas, would struggle to cope.
Allekand said: "We already have a problem today with agricultural businesses closing their doors. Regional businesses are also closing down, and jobs are being lost. With this amendment, we are simply adding fuel to the fire."
Allekand said Estonia should reconsider how it transposes the directive, arguing member states have considerable freedom in implementation, and that a more lenient form is the solution.
Lauri Suu, head of the construction department at the Ministry of Climate, told ERR the requirements for these buildings are part of a broader amendment covering all buildings in which people carry out activities, with requirements differing by building type. He said the draft will soon reach the Riigikogu, where amendments can be proposed.
Responding to the association's call for the most lenient possible implementation, Suu said that is already happening. "We have indeed implemented the absolute minimum package on our part, meaning we are not doing anything more than the directive requires as a minimum," he said.
The EU Directive requires renovation of non-residential buildings in poor condition, including commercial and public buildings, warehouses and offices. Member states decide how to transpose it. The draft legislation will soon reach the Riigikogu.

EXPLAINER - Why is India's proposed dam near Chinese border triggering protests?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:05:05 UTC
17:05:05 KST

- Local communities fear displacement and environmental damage from proposed 11,200-MW project
- Government say dam essential for storage amid China's plans for a major upstream dam
India has deployed paramilitary troops in parts of its northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh amid protests against a proposed mega hydropower project near the Chinese border.
The deployment follows a protest last week in the Siang Valley, which borders Tibet, during which four women were injured during a clash with police, according to reports.
The protesters were opposing the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP), a proposed 11,200-megawatt project, saying the dam would submerge ancestral villages, destroy farmlands, displace large populations and disrupt livelihoods
Police said protesters vandalized police vehicles and pelted stones at security personnel.
 
What is the project?
First proposed as a national project by the Congress-led government in 2008, the Siang River project has since emerged as one of Arunachal Pradesh’s most contentious infrastructure proposals. The Congress party is now the main opposition party.
The project is considered strategically significant for India, particularly in light of China's plans for a major hydropower project upstream on the same river.
India views the proposed dam as a major water storage facility to regulate river flows and strengthen the country's water and energy security.
In December 2024, China announced plans to construct the world's largest hydropower dam upstream, officially known as the Medog Hydropower Station.
The proposed Chinese project has raised concerns in Arunachal Pradesh, where the state government has described it as an "existential threat."
China and India both claim Arunachal Pradesh, which China refers to as Zangnan and considers part of southern Tibet.
The Siang River flows into Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet, where it is known as the Yarlung Zangbo.
Why the protests?
The proposed project, to be developed by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, is located in the Siang Valley, where opposition has largely come from local communities, particularly members of the Adi tribe.
Residents fear the proposed dam could submerge ancestral villages, displace communities and disrupt their way of life.
The Adi Bane Kebang Youth (ABKU), a local grassroots movement, has warned that the dam could submerge several villages and cause extensive losses.
This week, it demanded the immediate release of its workers detained or arrested in connection with the protests.
Former Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Gegong Apang has called for the immediate cancellation of the proposed dam.
In New Delhi, the Congress has linked the protests to a wider movement among young people to protect the "environment and local communities'" rights.
"Gen Z across the country is taking to the streets. In Delhi, it is for education. In Arunachal Pradesh, it is to protect the forests, rivers and ecosystems that the Adi people have depended on for centuries," Congress leader Pawan Khera wrote on X.
Government response
Apart from strengthening security to counter the protests, the Arunachal Pradesh government has attributed growing apprehensions about the project to what it described as "misinformation and misconceptions."
Chief Minister Pema Khandu this week held a meeting with various groups to discuss the project and strengthen efforts to spread awareness across the state.
"Our people deserve accurate information to understand the project, its strategic importance and the concerns associated with it," he said.
At a separate meeting with legislators from different political parties, Khandu said discussions covered national security, environmental concerns and the apprehensions of local residents.
"Our priority is to protect national interests while respecting the rights and aspirations of the people of Siang Valley," he said.
Arunachal Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Chowna Mein recently took to US social media platform X to explain how India's proposed dam could help address concerns arising from China's planned 60,000-MW hydropower project upstream.
"The answer lies in understanding that MW measures power, not water. The proposed Medog Dam in China is primarily designed for hydropower generation, with an estimated height of around 2,000 meters (2 km) and storage capacity of 5.5 billion cubic meters," he said.
Mein said India's proposed dam, with a height of around 280-300 meters and live storage capacity of approximately 9.2 billion cubic meters, was primarily intended to store, regulate and manage water, alongside generating electricity.
"In the event of sudden releases or extreme flows upstream, this storage can help regulate downstream discharge and reduce the risk of flooding in the Siang basin and downstream areas of Arunachal Pradesh and Assam," he said.

Construction of new renewable power plants with 6,000 MW capacity on agenda
TEHRAN- The Deputy Minister of Energy and Head of the Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency Organization (SATBA) announced the Ministry of Energy’s new plans to build 6,000 megawatts of new renewable power plants in the country and said: Alongside this process, creating a value chain and localizing the required equipment will also be pursued more vigorously.
According to an IRNA report citing SATBA, Mohsen Tarztalab, explaining the organization’s latest measures in the field of developing new energy, described attracting non-governmental investment and strengthening the domestic supply chain as the two main wings for realizing the major goals of this sector, and outlined the details of SATBA’s new plans in three areas.
Referring to planning for the construction of 10,000 megawatts of household solar power plants in the country, he announced the publication of a call for participation by non-governmental sector investors in the construction of small-scale distributed solar power plants.
Tarztalab stated: The financial model of these projects has been designed based on a combination of sources, including at least 40 percent investor equity, a maximum of 50 percent from National Development Fund resources, and at least 10 percent participation by electricity subscribers.
The Head of SATBA said: Investors who have a higher share in financing the project will be given priority in review, and the supply of equipment, installation, operation, and sale of generated electricity (with guaranteed repayment of principal and interest from the Green Energy Exchange) will be the responsibility of the investor.
Tarztalab, referring to the implementation of the national program for developing solar power systems and the production chain, noted: In order to enhance technological capabilities and reduce dependence on abroad, SATBA has long placed the localization of equipment and the establishment of production lines for equipment needed by solar power plants on its agenda, and now that the Iranian market has good attractiveness for investors, this matter is being pursued more seriously.
In this regard, he announced a call to identify and support capable applicants for the construction, development, and upgrading of solar panel production lines and reminded: Accordingly, entities meeting technical and financial requirements will benefit from SATBA’s facilities and legal support.
The Deputy Minister of Energy further announced the beginning of the maturity and payment of installments of National Development Fund facilities by investors and said: As projects progress, investors are obliged to settle the principal and interest of the allocated resources in accordance with the specified mechanisms.
He emphasized: After the end of the repayment period, ownership of solar power plants and other renewable power plants will be transferred to the investors.
Tarztalab continued: The National Development Fund’s participation in the construction of renewable power plants is the first successful example of national investment that, ultimately, in addition to building power plants and solar electricity generation facilities, has led to empowering the private sector and the return of spent resources to the National Development Fund.
The Deputy Minister of Energy added: This successful example can be expanded to other areas needed by the country while also preserving the resources of the National Development Fund.

Türkiye's Erdogan: Solidarity among Turkic states is a 'strategic necessity'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:02:01 UTC
17:02:01 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan described solidarity among Turkic states as a “strategic necessity” amid global conflicts, ahead of the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara.
“World politics is undergoing a profound transformation. At a time when the international system is struggling to establish justice and trust, and wars and crises are affecting vast geographical regions, solidarity among Turkic states has become a strategic necessity,” Erdogan said in an article published in media outlets across the organisation’s member and observer countries.
He said the unity of Turkic states was “the strongest expression” of their shared history and determination to shape a common future.
Stressing the importance of unity among the Turkic states, Erdogan said that “there is no room for division or discord in the Turkic world.”
The summit, to be held under the theme “The Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed,” will further strengthen that shared commitment, Erdogan said.
Türkiye will assume the organisation’s chairmanship from Azerbaijan, a move Erdogan described as a historic responsibility to advance common goals and strengthen the OTS’s institutional capacity.
Economic and security cooperation
Economic integration was among the organisation’s top priorities, Erdogan said, highlighting the Trans-Caspian East-West Middle Corridor as a major opportunity to expand trade and transport links between Asia and Europe.
“The Turkic geography has the potential to become one of the major hubs of global transportation and logistics networks,” he said.
He called for stronger railway, port, road and customs connections, as well as more effective use of the Turkic Investment Fund, energy resources and renewable energy potential.
He also urged member states to strengthen production, investment, technology and communications cooperation.
Erdogan said solidarity should also extend to security, with member states pooling resources to address terrorism, cross-border crime and cyber threats.
He highlighted cooperation in the defence industry, including sharing expertise, developing domestic technologies and expanding joint production.
Shared heritage
Erdogan described shared cultural heritage as the foundation of unity, citing figures including Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, Ali Shir Nava'i, Nizami Ganjavi, Magtymguly Pyragy, Yunus Emre and Chinghiz Aitmatov.
He said agreement on a common Turkic alphabet was a historic step towards cultural rapprochement and called for closer cooperation in education, science, publishing and digital technologies.
Regional issues and Turkish Cypriot rights
On the South Caucasus, Erdogan said a peaceful and stable South Caucasus will offer "significant opportunities" for regional countries and the entire Turkic world.
He urged Turkic states to "do more" to achieve a just solution to the Palestinian issue, calling for contributions to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza and launching reconstruction efforts as soon as possible.
The Turkish president also reaffirmed support for Turkish Cypriots, saying Türkiye would continue to defend their rights and interests and seek an end to their unjust isolation.
He called for expanding the opportunities provided by the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus’ observer status in the OTS and strengthening its relations with other Turkic states.
He also noted that Türkiye hopes that renewed Iran tensions will be resolved through diplomacy rather than arms.
Erdogan said the organisation could contribute to regional and global stability by turning shared political will into lasting achievements.
“I sincerely believe that the 21st century will be the ‘Century of the Turkic World’,” he said, adding that the Ankara summit would open new horizons for cooperation and strengthen solidarity among member states.

French economy 'headed for a wall' as GDP shrinks, finance minister warns
France's economy unexpectedly shrank in the third quarter while inflation rose more than anticipated, piling pressure on the government ahead of further nationwide protests this weekend that are making it more difficult to cut spending. Finance Minister Roland Lescure warned that the economy could be "headed for a wall" if parliament fails to approve a deficit-reducing budget soon.
The French economy contracted in the third quarter, data showed Friday, and could be "headed for a wall" if the government is unable to get a deficit-reducing budget passed soon, the finance minister warned.
Gross domestic product shrank by 0.1 percent in the three months to September, the national statistics office Insee said, amid deepening concerns about the state of public finances and growing political tensions ahead of presidential elections next spring.
The decline came as inflation accelerated to 3.4 percent on an annualised basis in October from 3.1 percent in September, the fastest rate since January 2024, Insee said.
The French economy had already stagnated in the second quarter after contracting by 0.2 percent in the first.
"For three quarters now, there has been no growth," Finance Minister Roland Lescure told France Info radio.
"The conclusion to be drawn from all this is that, as of 2026, the French economy is at a standstill," he said.
"France is not heading toward a crisis. But if we fail to achieve the turnaround outlined in the budget, we are headed straight for a wall."
Watch moreFrance unveils cost-cutting budget amid protests
Insee calculated that production of goods and services fell by 0.1 percent from July to September, while household consumption expanded by 0.4 percent.
Investment contracted by 0.6 percent, and foreign trade also made a negative contribution to growth, shaving 0.6 percentage points off GDP growth.
Analysts said the GDP data would indeed make it difficult for the government to reach its overall growth forecast of 0.5 percent for the current year or even the 0.4 percent anticipated by Insee and the Bank of France.
Worries about France's high debt and deficits have sent its government bond yields soaring in recent weeks.
An underwhelming 2027 budget plan last month fanned concerns that government spending would remain high ahead of next year's presidential elections in which the far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, seen as a fiscal populist, stands a chance of winning, according to opinion polls.
France has been rocked by widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, with nationwide demonstrations on October 17 degenerating into some of the country's worst rioting in years.

Pentagon urges Baltic states to tone down rhetoric on Russia – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:01:00 UTC
17:01:00 KST

Pentagon officials have urged several NATO allies in recent weeks to tone down their public rhetoric about the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials, including in the Baltics, have undermined the continent’s security, Reuters reported Friday.
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are among the countries that received the appeals for greater restraint in public statements, according to four sources who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
One source said US officials had taken issue with statements by European leaders suggesting that Russia had been backed into a corner and was resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine made little progress.
One of the US officials who conveyed the message was Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s top policy official, who is playing a key role in the ongoing review of the US military presence in Europe, the sources said. Reuters could not establish which other officials had been involved in delivering the appeals.
One source told Reuters that Colby recently told an official from one of the Baltic states that Russia should not be provoked. As an example of unhelpful rhetoric, Colby reportedly cited public statements by Europeans comparing Russia to a cornered rat.
Reuters said it was unclear which specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal described Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “rat in a corner” in late September, arguing that as Russia became increasingly bogged down in the war in Ukraine, its leader was resorting to sabotage across Europe.
A source familiar with another recent meeting said the Pentagon had urged an Estonian delegation to exercise restraint in public statements. The source did not indicate that US officials had expressed dissatisfaction with any particular remark.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there. Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise,” one European official described the message conveyed by the Pentagon during recent private discussions.
The defence ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. NATO declined to comment.
“Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations,” a Pentagon official said when asked about the report.
The US appeals come as President Donald Trump’s administration has renewed efforts to end Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine through negotiations.
Defence minister: we only say facts
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said he had no information about Pentagon officials asking Lithuanian leaders to tone down their rhetoric on Russia.
“What we speak is always based on facts. If a Russian drone flew in, we say that a Russian drone flew in. If a Ukrainian drone flew in, we say that it was a Ukrainian drone, in the context of the war caused by Russia,” Kaunas said on Friday.
“We do not try or wish to provoke in any other way. [...] We state the facts and will continue to do so,” he added.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda’s office said neither he nor his aides received any requests from allies regarding statements about Russia.
“The President’s Office has no comment on this publication. The president and his advisers have received no calls or requests from allies to soften their rhetoric regarding Russia,” it said on Friday.

Are Trump’s global actions, from Ukraine to Iran, going to hurt him in elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:00:49 UTC
17:00:49 KST

Outside the Ukrainian educational and cultural center in a quiet Pennsylvania suburb of Jenkintown, on the outskirts of Philadelphia, a banner expressed unqualified gratitude: “Thank you USA for supporting Ukraine.”
Inside, however, the sentiment was altogether different. Irene Skulsky, a retired teacher in her late 70s, voiced indignation at Donald Trump’s sudden turn against her ancestral homeland, which she believed had come close to killing her son, Darko, and a desire to punish his fellow Republicans at next week’s midterm elections.
“When we vote, we have to vote with Ukraine in our hearts,” she told her fellow retirees, gathered to hear a presentation by the Daughters of Knyahynya, a women’s group delivering military equipment to Ukrainian special forces on the frontline. “I know many people here are Republicans, but we can’t go according to party lines now. Ukraine needs us. They need our support. We need to shift the balance of power in Congress and in the Senate.”
Days earlier, Skulsky told fellow members at a meeting of the Ukrainian American Senior Citizens Association, Darko had been sitting in traffic en route to work in Kyiv when Russian drone missiles slammed into five cars immediately ahead of him.
There had been no prior alert, allegedly as a result of a decision by Washington to suspend its intelligence-sharing arrangement with Ukraine that has acted as an early warning system against missiles attacks since Russia invaded in February 2022.
In recent weeks, Trump – who pledged during his victorious 2024 presidential election campaign to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict within 24 hours of returning to office – appears to have abandoned Ukraine.
He struck a deal with the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, to buy nearly 5m tonnes of diesel, overriding US sanctions on Moscow. He called on Ukrainians to replace the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. His administration was accused of throttling the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service.
And while the Trump administration denied that it had stopped sharing intelligence this month, as relations with Ukraine nose-dived, Zelenskyy has said his country received no advance warning from US intelligence networks of two Russian missile attack waves.
Darko escaped injury, but several people in the vehicles in front were killed in the strikes, according to Skulsky. Her frustration spilled over to include Trump’s fellow Republicans, whom she said were “selling our souls” rather than standing up to the president.
“Republicans are afraid of Trump,” she said. “They’re afraid to lose their position. I think their heart is with Ukraine, but they’s sitting on their hands.”
Many American Ukrainians will express their outrage at the polls on 3 November, according to Eugene Luciw, a retired lawyer and local representative of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, an advocacy group.
“For [American] Ukrainians, I believe foreign policy is unquestionably the No 1 issue,” he said. “But I think even the average American without the added affinity of a homeland in Europe is going to see foreign policy as a very important issue.
“It’s beginning to reach people’s minds and hearts that something very important is brewing in Europe. If Ukraine loses this war, we have the beginnings of world war three.”
The most recent Ukraine development is the latest in a trio of Trump foreign policy decisions with the potential to hurt Republicans when Americans head to the polls next week.
More relevant to voters’ living costs – a key issue in this election, according to polls – has been Trump’s protracted war with Iran, and his determination to impose tariffs on imports from much of the world.
The Iran war, launched with Israel in February, shows no signs of ending despite Trump’s early claims that it would be a short-term “excursion” certain to end in the “unconditional surrender” of Tehran’s Islamic regime.
Instead, Trump has reportedly drawn up plans to launch renewed strikes against Iran after the midterms as he seeks to break Iran’s grip on the strait of Hormuz, an energy choke point that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s energy supplies before the Tehran regime closed it in response to being attacked.
The strait’s closure has resulted in soaring global oil prices, which have been passed on to US consumers in the form of higher prices for petrol and diesel, which is vital for supply chains and US farmers.
Polls have consistently shown voters’ disapproval of Trump’s handling of the war, and his management of the economy and inflation. Roughly 70% are now critical of both, according to a recent AP-Norc survey.
The war’s economic impact has compounded the inflationary effects of Trump’s tariffs, which has affected the prices of consumer goods and increased costs for manufacturers by increasing the costs of imported raw materials such as steel, copper and aluminum.
The tariff regime has also strained Washington’s relations with once-close allies – perhaps most visibly with Canada, the US’s second-biggest trading partner. Ties between the two neighbors plunged to a new low in August following the collapse of bilateral trade talks.
Following the collapse, the Trump administration imposed tariffs on $20bn of Canadian imports – including cars, forestry and dairy produce – triggering a retaliatory tit-for-tat response from Canada’s government, led by the prime minister, Mark Carney. In Michigan, which shares a border with Canada, even Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers released an ad calling on Trump to end the trade war and declared: “Canada is not our enemy.”
Trump has articulated his vision with characteristic bullishness. After January’s US attack on Venezuela, during which it ousted the country’s president, Nicolás Maduro, he dubbed his strategy the “Donroe doctrine” – a play on the Monroe doctrine, named after a 19th-century US president, which states that the western hemisphere should be Washington’s exclusive domain.
He bragged about extracting Venezuela’s oil resources and fantasized about making the country “the 51st state” in a speech this week in Corpus Christi, Texas, during which he showed off a tanker he claimed was carrying 1m barrels of oil and repeated a phrase – “to the victors belong the spoils” – that startled foreign leaders when he first uttered it at last month’s gathering of the United Nations general assembly.
There are fears that his neo-imperialist instincts could be applied after the midterms to Cuba, where he has repeatedly pledged to topple the communist regime that has ruled for the past 67 years.
Meanwhile, Trump’s fixation with autocratic leaders has been extended to China’s president, Xi Jinping. Having already met Xi at a summit in Beijing this year before hosting him at the White House, Trump will go to China again next month to meet the Chinese leader.
On a range of issues, he has shown disdain for diplomatic niceties – dispensing with seasoned diplomats to instead rely on Steve Witkoff, a real estate investor and attorney with no background in foreign policy, and Jared Kushner, his businessman son-in-law, as negotiators over matters as intricate as Iran, Gaza and Ukraine.
Yet Trump’s latest Ukraine turn carries special resonance, not least because it risks a dramatic rupture with Washington’s European Nato allies, who are heavily invested in Kyiv’s protection as a first line of defence.
It has highlighted once again Trump’s complex relationship with Putin, an autocratic leader for whom he has repeatedly voiced admiration. It is also a reminder of Trump’s failure to live up to his frequently expressed vow to swiftly end the Ukraine war during the 2024 presidential election campaign.
Trump has blown hot and cold towards Zelenskyy. At an explosive White House meeting in February 2025, he told the Ukrainian leader “you don’t have the cards” – but with a peace deal on terms acceptable to Russia seeming ever more distant, relations seemed to thaw, with Trump even publicly mooting giving Ukraine a license to build its own Patriot missiles.
In recent weeks, however, Trump appears to have definitively ditched the US’s putative ally and sided with Putin.
Economists argue that the volume of diesel covered by his deal with Moscow is too insignificant to reduce diesel prices, which have been inflated mainly by the effects of the Iran war, rather than by the actions of Ukraine.
Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, caused further consternation by praising Putin as a “humanitarian” after the Russian president agreed to release a 74-year-old US citizen, Stephen Hubbard, whom Russia had imprisoned for several years after falsely accusing him of fighting for Ukraine.
The Russia-friendly moves have stunned Ukrainian Americans, many of whom have pro-Republican sympathies dating back to the cold war, when staunchly anti-communist presidents like Ronald Reagan were seen as champions of self-determination for the constituent, so-called “captive nations” that comprised the Soviet Union, which included Ukraine.
“We are befuddled and upset by what’s going on,” said Andrij Chornodolsky, chair of the senior citizens association, who urged his fellow members to call the White House and leave comments criticizing the recent policy moves. “How can you be doing this to us?”
The US is “helping a country that wants to subjugate Ukraine back into a new empire, the Russian empire”, added Chornodolsky, who was equally angry with Republicans who have failed to criticize Trump over his abandonment of Ukraine.
“What are the comments coming out of Congress?” he said. “Silence speaks very loudly. If you do nothing, you agree with the person making the pronouncements.”
There are about 60,000 people of Ukrainian descent in Philadelphia’s metropolitan area, the second-largest such ethnic population in the US after New York. From 105,000 to 122,000 people are estimated to claim Ukrainian ancestry throughout Pennsylvania.
Peter and Orysia Hewuka, long-term Republicans who had both previously voted for Trump, said they were likely to vote for a local Democrat because of Ukraine, even though it represented a psychological hurdle.
“I am very hesitant to vote Democrat. I’m a lifelong Republican,” said Peter, 88, a retired nuclear physicist. “But I can’t vote for people who support what Trump is doing. The Republican party has left us, we haven’t left the Republican party.
“It’s very difficult for me and for a lot of Ukrainian Americans to vote for the Republican party based on what they’ve been doing in the past months.”
Luciw, of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, said even Trump’s diehard supporters in the Ukrainian community had been alienated by the diesel deal with Putin.
“From my interactions on social media and elsewhere, I would say more than 75% of those who supported him have now abandoned him because it’s now clear where this is headed,” said Luciw, 68, who described himself as a Reagan Republican, but now also intends to vote Democrat.
“Until the last few weeks, there was a hope that Trump’s swinging back-and-forth on Ukraine was a kind of negotiation … that maybe he would come to terms with things because it looked liked Ukraine was going to win and he would support a winner,” he said. “But the diesel deal reversed all that.”
Mykola Hryckowian, director of the Center for US-Ukrainian Relations, said he voted for Trump three times and been active in an ad hoc group called Ukrainian Americans for Trump – but has since severed his last vestiges of support.
“I went to the polling booth in the last election not knowing who to vote for, thinking I might write in Zelenskyy, but in the end voted for Trump, because I couldn’t vote for Kamala Harris,” he recalled. “Today, I could not vote for Trump.
“But a lot of my colleagues [on the committee] were very staunch, holding onto Trump until the very end. But in these last two weeks, they have turned around and said: ‘This is an abomination’.”
Not all Ukrainians are surprised by Trump’s actions. Mark Andryczyk, a Ukrainian studies scholar at Columbia University and board member of the Ukrainian League of Philadelphia – a cultural group that hosts performances by writers and musicians from the country – said the president’s actions were predictable.
“I never thought Trump would be a good idea for Ukraine,” he said. “You just have to look at how happy Russia was each time he was elected.”
“All his information on the war is basically Russian talking points,” added Andryczyk. “I can’t imagine why anybody would think he was pulling for Ukraine. Perhaps people somehow thought that he wouldn’t be doing this. I would think that their eyes are open now.”
A clear-eyed view of Trump’s foreign policy could reap an electoral whirlwind for Trump’s Republican allies on 3 November, with the pocket-book effects of his tariffs and the war on Iran looming large as voters head to the polls.
Yet such an outcome could be a double-edged sword. Should Trump become hemmed in at home by a Democrat-controlled Congress in the final two years of his presidency, where better to assert his power than the rest of the world?

The hill I will die on: Dumplings are the ultimate proof of our common humanity | Joseph de Weck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:00:49 UTC
17:00:49 KST

On a recent Saturday morning in Paris, I made a life-changing discovery. It came in the frozen aisle of an Asian supermarket: you can buy premade dumpling wrappers. Take a moment to think about the implications of this. Chinese shrimp wontons? Ukrainian potato varenyky? Italian veal ravioli? You’re halfway there before you’ve even chopped an onion (as long as you’re not precious about using exactly the right dough for each recipe).
Since then, I’ve fallen into a full-blown dumpling rabbit hole, my nights spent on YouTube, watching grandmothers sitting in circles, pinching dough. So many shapes. So many techniques. Team inward pleats or outward?
Columbia University Press has just published The Epic History of Macaroni and Cheese: From Ancient Rome to Modern America. But clearly someone should also write The Long Arc of Putting Things in Dough: A Transcultural History. Because what does it say about humanity that all around the globe, at various points in history, people have invented some version of a delicious thing wrapped in dough?
Perhaps we all secretly long to be dumplings; there is certainly something reassuring about being enclosed. The French philosopher Claire Marin calls this a nostalgia for our “lost envelopment” – a longing to return to that primordial experience of being fully embraced in the womb.
Indeed, how fortunate is a filling’s existence: held, knowing it is exactly where it belongs. Desired, yet protected. And entirely individual, but never alone; dumplings are herd beings. Plus, they’re cute. So much so that squishy mystery dumplings have become the latest trend toy. The Labubu is so 2025.
Perhaps we need to go back to the stone age to understand the worldwide dumpling craze.
In her 1986 essay The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction, the American novelist Ursula K Le Guin suggested that our narrative of human history may be badly skewed. We picture early humans as men chasing bison. Yet the first human tool may have been a basket, not a spear. Gathering probably provided most of the calories; hunting was more often a hobby to kill time. And the fact that we say “hunter-gatherers” rather than “gatherer-hunters” is probably another vestige of the patriarchy.
“It is a human thing to do,” Le Guin writes, “to put something you want, because it’s useful, edible or beautiful, into a bag … and then take it home with you.”
Dumplings, those lovely edible containers, take this human instinct and make it culinary.
Whatever the reasons for the dumpling’s global triumph, it fills me with hope. Every time I eat Afghan mantu, Argentinian empanadas or Austrian kasnudeln, I feel that these little envelopes are trying to teach me a small lesson in universalism.
Forget the clash of civilisations. Dumplings, whether you like them or not, are the ultimate proof of our common humanity.
- Joseph de Weck is an associate fellow with the German Council on Foreign Relations and writes for Guardian Europe from Zürich and Paris

Beach volleyball in Morecambe Bay? An Olympics of the north sounds like a winner | Emma John
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:00:49 UTC
17:00:49 KST

As someone who barely understands their own finances, let alone the country’s, I will admit that budget day doesn’t always register with me. Perhaps if there were outre outfits or horse-drawn carriages involved, like there are at the state opening of parliament, I’d get into it, but the only accessory of note is a briefcase and it doesn’t even glow mysteriously when you open it.
This week, however, the chancellor of the exchequer did manage to catch my attention. Somewhere amid the household energy payments and defence spending, he slipped in a cheeky £7m to assess a possible Olympic bid for the north of England. That’s only a preliminary step and a fraction of the cost of any actual bid – Tokyo and Paris spent more than £50m on theirs. Still, it’s enough to put thoughts in people’s heads of beach volleyball in Morecambe Bay or a British eight rowing to victory along the Tyne.
The idea has gained traction since February, when a group of mayors from the northern cities first wrote to the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, asking her to bring the Olympics to their neighbourhood. Three months later, Nandy had thrown her support behind the proposal – “It’s time the Olympics came north” – and announced an initial assessment. The new funds will support a more comprehensive one, with a view to hosting in the 2040s. And it surely doesn’t hurt to have a recently installed, sport-loving prime minister, who was previously mayor of Greater Manchester.
Andy Burnham is in the early, giving stages of his premiership and he can generate a lot of goodwill by spending a comparatively small sum exploring the option. The “detailed feasibility study” by UK Sport isn’t due until 2029, but you can still expect it to stoke a lot of excitement in the meantime. There has already been positive reaction to the news, not least from the former boxer Luke Campbell, the 2012 Olympic bantamweight champion who became Reform UK’s mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire last year.
Campbell has been a vocal supporter of the plan; he has also been on the ropes recently, with police investigating allegations – which he denies – that he showed naked pictures of himself to a female member of staff. Still, he came out of his corner to praise the funding. “I’m proud to be working with other northern mayors and leaders to get this idea taken seriously,” said Campbell, calling it “a legacy worth aiming for”.
London’s mayor, however, will be far less impressed. Sadiq Khan has been talking about bringing the Games back to the capital for the past five years. His office has been actively consulting the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and working up a plan to reuse 2012 venues to create “the greenest Games ever”. Khan has lobbied for it with Conservative and Labour governments. “The great thing to remember is the power of sport,” he said on the 10th anniversary of the London Games. “It’s above party politics, it’s above north versus south.”
Unfortunately, it seems he may be wrong about that. Perhaps Khan needs to remember that North v South has been a fundamental part of England’s sporting landscape since the Victorians first codified its favourite physical pursuits. Some of the earliest fixtures in England were literally played between North and South, be they in football, cricket, water polo or draughts. Even rugby union had North v South games, before the establishing of two separate codes would create a geographical divide of its own. It’s one more aspect of the divide baked in to the country’s social history.
And as John Healey’s £7m demonstrates, an Olympic bid is also, very much, politics. In this case, the politics of regional disparity – from the failure of levelling up to the devolution revolution, from No 10 North to Pride in Place. Whether the members of the IOC will vote for swimming in Sheffield, modern pentathlon in Manchester and table tennis in Teesside remains, for now, entirely moot. The government’s feasibility study answers the call of a more immediate voting base, who care as much about the promise of outside investment and regional infrastructure that an Olympics may provide as they do about the fortnight’s fiesta itself. And hey, how about that mythical high-speed rail line, while you’re at it?
It should be said that there’s nothing wrong with ambition or even just testing the waters. If an Olympics bid did come off, it would be a more than fitting way to celebrate the north’s prodigious athletic legacy. And that’s something to which Burnham, an Everton season-ticket holder and former president of the Rugby Football League, has shown a longstanding commitment. Indeed, he has a literal track record: last month, he became the first serving prime minister to complete the Great North Run (in a very respectable sub-two-hour time).
For now, however, the whole thing remains little more than a theoretical possibility and a politicians’ talking point. Perhaps we can find some other North v South contests to fixate on in the meantime. Unfortunately, the promised all-star footballing fixture at the Valley last year – with the North managed by Robbie Fowler and the South managed by Harry Redknapp – never materialised. But I see that England lacrosse has revived the fixture this year, after a hiatus of four decades.

Why Switzerland is missing from the debate over trust in government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Why Switzerland is missing from the debate over trust in government
How can governments regain the public’s trust? The OECD brought politicians, officials and civil society representatives together in Paris for a discussion. But Switzerland was absent, and the potential of direct democracy to rebuild that trust went unexplored. An analysis.
Hundreds of government and civil society representatives gathered at the heavily guarded Paris conference centre of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to confront a growing problem: public trust in government institutions is crumbling.
While participants debated among themselves inside the OECD headquarters, tens of thousands of school pupilsExternal link and university students were protesting on the streets of Paris. Later that week, over the weekend of October 17, there was looting and riots.
The scale of the problem is evident in the OECD’s Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions, published in summer 2026. It found that many people lack confidence in their governments’ ability to deal with major challenges such as global warming, migration and geopolitical tensions.
Across the 38 countries surveyed, an average of just 40% of people say they have at least a moderate level of trust in their government.
‘Growing expectations’ of a greater say in political decisions
According to the survey, fewer than one in three people feel that “people like them” have a say in government decisions, despite a large majority believing that elections can bring about change. This contradiction suggests voters want more ways to participate between elections. The report describes “growing and unmet citizens’ expectations about having a say in decision-making beyond elections”.
Switzerland is a clear outlier, where 62% of people trust the government, and 65% feel that those who have a say in political decisions are “people like them”.
For Switzerland, the findings could be seen as international validation of its political system. Regular nationwide votes help people feel heard, and a consensus government brings together almost all major political forces. This means nearly all voters have someone in the government who represents their part of the political spectrum.
On the face of it, Switzerland would seem an obvious case study for countries looking for ways out of the trust crisis. Yet the OECD report does not present it as an example, and its political model played no role in the conference discussions.
Participation models go largely unchallenged
Rather than endorsing a particular model, the study offers broader recommendations on what governments can do to build trust. These include giving citizens more opportunities to participate in decision-making and ensuring that the civil service is politically neutral.
Read our analysis of the OECD Trust Survey:
More
High Swiss trust in government sparks little interest abroad
Participation also featured prominently in discussions at the OECD conference. But speakers largely focused on what their countries were already doing. Costa Rica cited its social dialogue as a success story, and Andorra is making efforts to increase transparency in public administration.
Art O’Leary of Ireland’s Electoral Commission was particularly proud of his country’s citizens’ assemblies, where members are chosen by lottery. Their recommendations on same-sex marriage and abortion were put to referendums and approved by voters. The unexpectedly decisive results attracted considerable attention at the time.
O’Leary explained in detail how citizens’ assemblies work and how Ireland has used them. But he did not mention that Ireland’s last such assembly was three years ago, and that no more have been announced. No one pressed him on whether these assemblies, successful though they have been, are becoming a permanent feature of Irish democracy.
Read our article on the cancellation of a citizens’ assembly in Geneva and international developments in this field:
More
Are citizens’ assemblies on the decline in an era of eroding democracy?
When other politicians and civil servants at the OECD conference discussed what greater participation might look like, they often sounded as though their countries already had it largely under control. They showcased their petition systems, dialogues with citizens, and citizens’ assemblies. They seemed to suggest that others might follow their lead.
Yet these examples were rarely scrutinised. No one pointed out, for example, that the much-cited petition systems do not actually shift political power from politicians to citizens.
Plenty of concern, little talk of change
Calls are growing louder for participation that would genuinely shift political power to the people. The protests in Paris and elsewhere are only the latest sign of this, and speakers at the conference referred to them repeatedly.
“We have kids demonstrating right this morning in Paris,” Elsa Pilichowski, the OECD’s director for public governance, said as the conference opened. They have no say in decision-making, she added. Later, a Portuguese minister came close to shouting, as though he wanted to take to the streets himself: “People are angry, they are upset. They feel that governments are not solving their problems.”
No one denied the absurdity that inside, officials discussed public trust without the public, while outside, protesters encountered riot police and water cannons. Others saw the authorities failing to prevent the destruction of private property. Neither image does much to restore public trust.
Also, no one discussed what changes France might make to its political system in response to the protests. O’Leary presented Ireland’s experience with citizens’ assemblies but stopped short of suggesting that other countries adopt them. No one asked whether decisionmakers were genuinely prepared to surrender meaningful political power to citizens. In an international organisation, one does not interfere in another country’s affairs.
Still, many speakers seemed genuinely concerned. They appeared to recognise that technological and social change has fundamentally altered the relationship between citizens and the state. Governments and public institutions can no longer rely on the trust they once enjoyed. This is partly because people can now theoretically access vast amounts of information – and misinformation – on their own.
Those who ask must act
“All OECD countries are trying to improve trust. In a rapidly changing world, they are ready to take action. Hopefully, this will help stabilise public trust,” Pilichowski told Swissinfo. “In the past, people went to the polls every few years—and today, analysis shows that this isn’t enough.” That is why many countries are now developing forms of “participatory democracy”, she said.
Pilichowski said the data pointed to one clear conclusion: governments must react after consultations. “If you consult a representative group of citizens, decisions must follow,” she said.
Of course, it is unclear exactly how introducing more social dialogue would strengthen trust in society. Will angry citizens want to participate if they know they are only being listened to? The more consequential forms of “participatory democracy”, as Pilichowski calls it, require governments to relinquish some power. Under direct democracy, for example, the government must repeatedly win majority support from voters if it wants to get its proposals through.
During the two-day conference in Paris, direct democracy was largely absent from discussion. When referendums came up, Brexit was the main example, and was framed as a negative, populist exception.
Brexit is still a major issue in the UK:
More
Ten years after Brexit, the ‘Swiss model’ just keeps popping up
But the Brexit vote was fundamentally different from Switzerland’s instruments of direct democracy, which allow citizens to initiate nationwide votes from the bottom up. Brexit was initiated by the British government. Despite the slogan “take back control”, the UK had, and still has, no mechanism for citizens to bring their own proposals onto the nationwide ballot.
Can Switzerland be an example for others?
Pilichowski says the Swiss model received little attention because Switzerland is a special case. Its mechanisms of direct democracy are “so deeply rooted in society”. They are the “most direct and obvious means” of giving citizens greater power, she says, but countries do have other options. “There are different ways, and countries can choose different paths.”
For its approach to feature more prominently, Switzerland would probably need to take a more active role in the international debate over trust. But whether it wants to is another question. The country often likes to see itself as a special exception.
The next debate at the OECD will be about an issue that Switzerland has not yet solved: the gap in trust between people with and without an advanced education. While 80% of highly educated people in Switzerland trust the government, the figure is only 45% among those with lower levels of education.
How confident are you in the state and society? Tell us:
More

Over 75 hours of ceasefire: Ukraine's human rights commissioner arrives in Armiansk, 25 buses ready for evacuation from Oleshky
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:00 EET
17:00:00 KST

Over 75 hours of ceasefire: Ukraine's human rights commissioner arrives in Armiansk, 25 buses ready for evacuation from Oleshky
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets has reported that the ceasefire for the humanitarian mission to Oleshky has been holding for over 75 hours. The Ukrainian team is in Armiansk, where 25 buses with a total capacity of at least 750 passengers have been prepared to evacuate residents.
Source: Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Lubinets on X (Twitter); Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova
Quote from Lubinets: "We have now had a ceasefire between Ukraine and the Russian Federation for more than 75 hours. Special thanks to the people overseeing and monitoring the ceasefire process. Neither side has violated the ceasefire even once."
Details: The Ukrainian official noted that this is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established over such a large section of the front and has lasted this long.
Lubinets said the humanitarian mission was effectively launched on 23 October. Since then, he and Lantratova have been coordinating technical issues on a daily basis. Following his arrival the day before, the parties held another meeting and plan to travel together to Oleshky on 30 October.
The mission aims to deliver humanitarian aid to the city's residents and facilitate the departure of those who wish to leave. Lubinets noted that assistance will be provided both to people who want to leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory and to those who wish to go to the Russian Federation. Residents who decide to remain in Oleshky will receive humanitarian support.
Quote from Lantratova: "The humanitarian aid was put together according to the needs reported to us by the people. This includes food, hygiene products, everything essential, medical supplies, fuel – everything people need."
Details: According to the Russian representative, 25 buses with a total capacity of 750 passengers, special transport for about 30 bedridden individuals, and nine ambulances have been prepared for the evacuation. She stated that over 50 medical staff are working with the convoy.
Lantratova also reported that the buses are stocked with water and dry rations. A separate bus with cages has been allocated for transporting pets, and another bus has been designated for luggage.
Quote from Lantratova: "People who have made the decision to leave will have the opportunity to register and board the buses until 14:00. The distribution of humanitarian aid will take place after 14:00."
Details: She explained that boarding the buses and distributing aid were scheduled at different times to avoid crowding.
Lantratova also stated that two people had been killed whilst the mission was being prepared, including a bomb-disposal expert during demining operations. She did not specify the circumstances of the second person's death.
Journalists from Ukraine, the US and Russia have joined in covering the mission. Lubinets expressed hope that the experience of assisting Oleshky residents could be applied to humanitarian missions in other towns and villages.
Both officials thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her mediation. According to Lubinets, her team has been facilitating the mission since 20 October.
Background:
- Davyd Arakhamiia, the head of the Servant of the People faction who is involved in organising the operation, reported on 29 October that a delegation of representatives from Ukraine, the US and Russia had arrived at the location from which aid was to be delivered to temporarily occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast the following day.
- Under the agreements between the Russian and Ukrainian sides, the evacuation route for residents of Oleshky will run via Russia and Belarus to Ukraine.
- Earlier, US television channel Fox News published a document signed by Russian commissioner Yana Lantratova which stated that Oleshky residents who wish to evacuate to Ukraine will initially be taken to Anapa airport in Russia's Krasnodar Krai. From Anapa, the Ukrainian delegation and Oleshky residents will be taken to Homiel (Gomel) airport in Belarus on a Russian Defence Ministry military transport plane. This is likely to take place on Saturday 31 October.

Bulgaria's CEC Issues Extra Machine Voting Rules After First-Round Disruptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

The Central Election Commission (CEC) has issued additional instructions to municipalities and district election commissions ahead of the runoff to prevent disruptions during machine voting, CEC spokesperson Stoyanka Balova said on BNT.
The new guidelines follow problems during the first round, when some voting procedures were interrupted and ballots were not saved to the machines' flash memory despite voters receiving partial receipts. The CEC is urging voters to follow the operating instructions carefully, particularly by waiting for the audible signal before removing either the control receipt or the voting card.
Assoc. Prof. Dr. Stoyanka Balova said that removing the receipt too early could prevent the voting procedure from being completed and the ballot from being recorded. She also pointed to premature removal of the voting card, which was reported at several polling stations across the country on election day.
The commission has also issued guidance on how polling stations should proceed in the event of a power outage. Technical problems affected 31 voting machines during the first round, including two devices abroad and 29 in Bulgaria. Voting could continue in 27 polling stations where two machines had been provided.
Balova described the number of malfunctioning devices as very small, explaining that some problems occurred during transportation. One machine had a damaged display, while several others failed to start because their motherboards had burned out.
Under the agreement with the service provider, all affected machines must be repaired during the week before the runoff, the CEC said. The commission also confirmed that no payment would be made for machines that were not used.
The first round also exposed shortcomings in ensuring ballot secrecy during machine voting. Some polling stations lacked privacy screens because the clips needed to attach them had not been delivered. The clips will not be available for the runoff, but the CEC has provided alternative instructions for arranging the voting areas.
Balova said polling stations without the required screens must organize the space so that voters can cast their ballots privately without being placed inside fully enclosed, dark booths. At the same time, voters must remain visible to members of the sectional election commissions, she explained, adding that ballot secrecy must be guaranteed through these alternative arrangements.
The CEC also identified inadequate preparation among some sectional election commissions for handling technical problems with voting machines during the first round. It has therefore issued further guidance to commission members ahead of the runoff.
The commission says it is ready to handle a higher turnout, with Balova stressing that the organizational requirements remain unchanged regardless of how many people vote.
She also highlighted the processing of election documentation after the first round. All polling stations abroad had completed the processing of their materials by 6 a.m., while district election commissions submitted their reports as early as Monday.
The CEC spokesperson put the estimated budget for both rounds of the election at approximately 3 million euros. The amount covers the public information campaign, payments to members of district and polling station election commissions and support staff, as well as training activities for both rounds.

Greece arrests three over explosion that killed six people in Athens
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:59:26 CET
16:59:26 KST

ATHENS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Greece has arrested two Greek men and an Albanian national suspected of stealing copper gas pipes from a building, causing a leak that led to a deadly explosion in central Athens last month, authorities said.
Six people were killed during the September 25 blast in the tourist district of Plaka, four Americans among them.
Following an investigation, experts with the fire brigade’s crime investigation unit concluded that hours before the blast the suspects damaged the two-storey building’s main natural gas supply infrastructure as they removed the copper pipe parts, fire brigade officials said late on Thursday.
The explosion occurred early in the morning when one of the residents turned the light on.
The suspects are expected to appear before a prosecutor on Friday.
(Reporting by Yannis Souliotis and Angeliki Koutantou; Writing by Renee Maltezou; Editing by Alison Williams)
