Crypto platform Binance confirms major hack with more than $2.5bn frozen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:05:50 UTC
14:05:50 KST

Cryptocurrency platform Binance said on Thursday it had fallen victim to a major hack that hit around $6.3 billion (€5.5bn) in funds, with about half that amount frozen to prevent a massive theft.
The company - the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes - posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses".
Binance later said on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3bn (€5.5bn)".
"We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze the affected assets, with ~ $3bn (€2.6bn) frozen on-chain so far," it added.
That would be more than four times the amount involved in what had been the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5bn (€1.3bn) taken in February 2025 from the Bybit platform.
The Bybit heist was attributed at the time to a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.
Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said on Thursday it had "high confidence" that the Binance hack was also orchestrated by TraderTraitor, citing "robust on and off-chain intelligence".
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists," TRM said.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group - which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview", a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Fund freeze
At about 0030 GMT (0230 CEST) on Friday, Binance said all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement".
"This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company said.
The company's statement on X said an initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer", allowing the unauthorised party to access a "service container" and execute unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
"We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," Binance said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether - a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT - said his firm had frozen about $1.6bn (€1.4bn) "related to a potential Binance exchange hack".
Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800m (€696m) in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both "stablecoins", or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.
The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Crypto prices tumble
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, with the exception of stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.
At about 0400 GMT (0600 CEST), bitcoin and Ethereum were down 0.8%, recovering after plunges of nearly 5% and nearly 6%, respectively. BNB, Binance's native cryptocurrency, was up 2.7% after tumbling nearly 10%.
The attack on Binance comes as many observers express concerns that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

====================================================================================================

The White House Farm massacre phone calls: could a single disputed digit set Jeremy Bamber free?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

On 7 August 1985, five people were found dead at White House Farm in Essex, England: 28-year-old Sheila Caffell (known to her family as Bambi); her six-year-old twin sons, Daniel and Nicholas; and her 61-year-old adoptive parents, June and Nevill Bamber. All five had been shot with a rifle. Caffell’s 24-year-old brother, Jeremy Bamber, who was also adopted, had called to alert Essex police to a disturbance inside the farmhouse – he said his father had called to tell him – and had been outside with the police for four hours before the bodies were discovered. Caffell, who had recently been hospitalised with schizoaffective disorder and is said to have feared her children were going to be taken into foster care, was found with the rifle lying on her chest, pointing towards her neck. There were two gunshot wounds to her neck and chin and a bloodied Bible by her side.
The case was initially thought to be open and shut, a tragic murder-suicide committed by Caffell. But a month later, Bamber was arrested after relatives went to the police to voice their suspicions about him; his former girlfriend Julie Mugford then told police he had made a confession to her. The relatives went on to inherit from Nevill and June Bamber’s considerable estate after Bamber’s convictions. It was later discovered that Mugford had agreed to sell the story of their relationship to the News of the World for £25,000 if Bamber was convicted. Essex police and crown prosecutors had also agreed to drop charges against her for burglary, chequebook fraud and selling cannabis, because “prosecuting her could jeopardise her availability or credibility as a key witness” against Bamber.
Bamber was found guilty of the murders and has now been in prison for 41 years, but questions have always been asked about the safety of his conviction. These have grown recently. The proper body to examine these is the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), but it has already taken the CCRC four years to consider less than half the evidence that Bamber has submitted to them. In July 2025, it concluded that the first four of 10 points did not meet the high evidentiary threshold needed to refer the case back to the court of appeal.
In the third piece in our series considering discrete pieces of evidence, we analyse discrepancies in timelines recorded by Essex police that could prove Bamber’s innocence.
“Imagine how stupid I’d have to be to put myself in the frame for murdering my family by telling the police I’d received a phone call when I hadn’t,” Jeremy Bamber says. “Like most people, I assumed the police would have been able to trace the call. If it turned out Dad hadn’t called me, I’d have basically been handing myself in.”
Bamber is writing to me from Wakefield prison. For the past 41 years, he has been locked up for the murder of five members of his family, while always protesting his innocence.
In his letter, he is referring to a phone call he made to Essex police from his cottage in the middle of the night on 7 August 1985. Bamber, now 65, told the police his father, Nevill, had just called him to say Bamber’s sister, Sheila Caffell, had “gone crazy” at the family home, White House Farm, and got hold of one of Nevill’s guns. Bamber said the line had then gone dead. His call to Essex police has never been disputed. What has been disputed is his claim that Nevill called him.
At Bamber’s trial, the prosecution claimed he had made up the call to provide himself with a false alibi. They argued that he had killed the five members of his family at White House Farm between 12am and 3am, before cycling back to his cottage and calling the police himself.
This is a story about telephone calls, technology and timings. It is also a story about a single disputed digit in police logs, which could prove Bamber’s innocence. A digit that, at the time of the trial in 1986, neither the jury nor Bamber’s defence team could possibly have understood was so significant. It was only 25 years later, when 347,000 documents relating to the case were released, that its importance became clear.
The digit relates to the time Bamber called the police. At trial, there was confusion about whether it was 3.26am or 3.36am. The presiding judge, Sir Maurice Drake, told the jury to accept a timing of 3.26am. But a series of police logs and statements that were not disclosed at trial suggest Bamber made the call at 3.36am.
It appeared to be an obscure time-keeping argument in court, of little real significance. But it seems there is evidence that the jury was misled and that the differing times in fact refer to two different calls – the first made by Nevill and the second by Jeremy Bamber. And if Nevill did call the police to report his daughter had gone “berserk” with a gun, his son should not be in prison.
The trial
Chelmsford crown court, October 1986. PC Michael James West, who took Bamber’s call at Chelmsford police station in the early hours of 7 August 1985, takes the stand to give evidence for the prosecution. He explains that he works in the control room, a radio and telephone hub for the Chelmsford division, where the unit’s calls are received and officers are allocated their tasks. PC West says he filled out an event log, called a C1, as the conversation took place with Bamber, and that the practice is to log the time at the beginning of the conversation. Surprisingly, that C1 call log is not available to the jury. West tells Anthony Arlidge, the QC for the prosecution, that he recorded the time of 3.36am using the digital clock on the wall in the control room.
Arlidge doesn’t mention the time again. It is only when Geoffrey Rivlin, counsel for the defence, cross-examines West that he is challenged about the purported inconsistencies in his record-keeping.
In his first statement, made two days after the murder, West said he received the call from Jeremy Bamber at 3.26am. In a more detailed statement a month later, the time had changed to 3.36am. Rivlin suggested in court that West had got the time wrong when he changed it and that the call was made, as he had said in his first statement, at 3.26am.
Rivlin: I would like to ask you about times first, if I may. The time you have recorded was 03.36.
West: That is correct.
Rivlin: Is it right that you may have misread the clock and the time may have been 03.26?
West: I was informed I actually spoke to the information room at a time prior to the one that I have recorded so I can only assume that I have wrote – I actually recorded the wrong time, as it were.
But then West, it seems, becomes defensive. He is reluctant to say he made a mistake or that the clock was inaccurate.
Rivlin: The situation is, you looked at the clock and recorded 03.36. You were told subsequently that was almost certainly wrong and you said you may have misread the clock.
West: Well, there is a dispute over the times. I don’t know whose time is right and whose time is wrong.
Rivlin: Let me ask you this question. As regards the clock in the control room at the police station, is that accurate?
West:. Yes, it is.
Rivlin: Are you sure about that?
West: It has on occasion been inaccurate, but on very few occasions.
Rivlin: Would you agree with this, that the control room wall clock rarely shows an accurate time?
West: I would have to disagree with that.
Rivlin: You disagree?
West: Yes.
Rivlin: At all events, perhaps we need take it no further than this, that you did subsequently agree you may have misread the clock?
West: It is possible, although certainly there is a variance in times, yes.
This exchange must have been baffling for the jury. West appeared unwilling to concede that he got the time wrong. Rivlin seemed to suggest the difference between 3.26am and 3.36am was highly significant, but never explained why. He was determined that 3.26am should be recognised as the correct time, but the jury was given no explanation for his insistence.
The reason Rivlin was adamant that the call was made at 3.26am is simply because he thought it looked better for the man he was defending. Bamber had said he received the call from his father at about 3.15am, then rang his girlfriend, Julie Mugford, before calling the police. What kind of man waits 20 minutes and speaks to his girlfriend before contacting the police in such an emergency? Ten minutes, Rivlin thought, would seem more acceptable to a jury.
But Bamber says that is looking at it with the benefit of hindsight: “The last thing I thought when Dad called me was that this was going to end up with my whole family killed.” There had been previous incidents with Caffell, who had a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder and had been hospitalised after a psychotic episode five months before the murders. But none had ended in disaster.
The evening before the killings, Bamber had been at White House Farm and had taken out his father’s .22 rifle, to try to shoot rabbits. When he returned to the farmhouse, he had removed the magazine and the bullet in the breech of the rifle and left those items, and the gun itself, on a bench in the annexe of his parents’ kitchen.
He didn’t fear for the worst when he got the phone call from Nevill, he tells me, because he knew the gun was unloaded. “I assumed my dad, who was 6ft 4in and a strong man, would take the gun off Sheila and that she would calm down.”
As for waiting 20 minutes before calling the police, Bamber has always claimed his father was cut off in the middle of their conversation and that he tried a number of times to call him back, but kept getting the engaged tone. He says he then called Mugford at 3.30am and asked her what she thought he should do. Mugford – who told police a month after the murders, just after Bamber ended their relationship, that he had confessed the killings to her – advised him to “go back to bed”.
He ignored her and at 3.36am, he says, he called the police. “If I’d made up the call from Dad, why on earth would I have said I took 20 minutes to call the police? I would have said I called the police immediately.” Bamber is telling me this in letters sent a few months ago, before the prison banned him from discussing his case with journalists.
But the 3.26am timing of the call appeared to be supported by a rolling log made by a civilian phone operator, Malcolm Bonnett. He was situated at Essex police HQ, a building roughly a mile away from Chelmsford police station, where West was stationed.
Bonnett’s job was to log radio messages and send help from the police and other emergency services. Emergency 999 calls came in to Bonnett, but he also took phone calls from local police stations and officers such as West.
The Bonnett log was shown to the jury at the trial – exhibit 29. It was presented to the court as his record of a call West made to him about the phone call he had received from a Mr Bamber. The jury was told that the Mr Bamber in question was Jeremy. Bonnett’s rolling log starts with an entry at 3.26am. The subject line for this call is “Daughter gone berserk”. This is the only document the jury were shown in regard to the time of the call. It was never explained why West’s C1 log of the phone call was not included in the bundle given to the jury. They had no idea why West had logged the time as 3.36am or why the confusion in court when it was suggested he had got it wrong.
Something didn’t add up. At the trial, it was unclear whether West or Bonnett actually sent out the police cars. Both appear to claim to have done so. West said he radioed the officers asking them to attend the scene, but Bonnett also said that after receiving the call from West about the incident he sent the first police car, CA7, to White House Farm at 03.35am, followed by another car, CA5, at 03.36am. These timings only made sense if West had taken the call from Bamber at 3.26am.
After West and Bonnett’s evidence, the time of Bamber’s call played no part in the trial until the summing up, in which Drake stated that the clocks in the information room were later checked and found to be correct. He advised the jury to accept the true time of Bamber’s call as 3.26am. “You would, in effect, be giving the defence case the benefit of a doubt, and I will suggest that you may – although it is always a matter for you – work on the timing of 03.26 as the time when the phone call was made to Chelmsford police station, and accept that Police Constable West quite simply made a mistake when reading the clock, or writing down 03.36.”
In fact, though, insisting that the call was made at 3.26am gave Bamber anything but the benefit of the doubt. Instead, it put him in the time frame for the murder, because the chronology now made sense: Bamber called West at 3.26am, and West called local officers, who set off for White House Farm at 3.35am.
After a month-long trial, the jury came back with a 10-2 majority on 28 October 1986. Bamber was convicted of one of the most notorious crimes in British history and sentenced to life with a recommended minimum of 25 years. This was later extended to a whole-life tariff by the then home secretary Douglas Hurd in 1988, although Bamber was not made aware of this until 1994.
Fast-forward 25 years. It’s 2011 and Bamber now spends most of his life in prison searching for exculpatory evidence. There is also a campaign team working on his behalf to try to get his conviction overturned. He belatedly receives 347,000 pages of documents, initially withheld by Essex police, after public interest immunity laws are amended in favour of greater disclosure.
This is when Bamber’s team becomes convinced it has found the smoking gun. Amid the myriad documents is the C1 form that West filled in as he was speaking to Bamber on 7 August 1985. Astonishingly, this log wasn’t even included in the exhibit list, which includes every document that can potentially be shown to the jury. The time recorded on it is 3.36am, as he stated at trial. At the top, it clearly states who has made the call and from what address – Mr Bamber, 9 Head Street, Goldhanger. The subject is “Distress call”.
When West’s C1 log is compared with Bonnett’s log, important differences, apart from the times of the call, become obvious. In West’s C1 log of Bamber’s call, it says: “Father phoned (aged 62). Please come over your sister has gone crazy and has the gun. Phone went dead. Sister Sheila Bamber age 27 has history of mental illness.” This is clearly Bamber relating the call from his father – hence the reference to father and sister.
By contrast, the opening of Bonnett’s rolling log, which begins at 3.26am, is told from a wholly different perspective. For a start, it refers to Caffell as “daughter” rather than “sister”. The subject of the log is “Daughter gone berserk” and it says “Daughter Sheila Bamber aged 26 yrs has got hold of one of my guns”. The guns at White House Farm belonged to Nevill. In West’s C1 log it refers to the gun. Both logs get Caffell’s age wrong. Bonnett’s says she is 26, West’s 27. In fact, she had celebrated her 28th birthday a couple of weeks earlier. In West’s log, Bamber has mistakenly added an extra year to his father’s age. In Bonnett’s log, no age is given.
Then there is the different way in which the caller’s name and address is logged. The convention in police logs is to start with the informant’s name and address, because it immediately establishes who is providing the information, and it means they are traceable if contact is lost. Bonnett’s log of West’s call refers to “Mr Bamber, White House Farm, Tollshunt D’Arcy”. West’s log refers to “Mr Bamber, 9 Head Street, Goldhanger”. Next to the address for White House Farm is the phone number. Bonnett’s rolling log doesn’t have a number for the farm till 03.56am, when the police confirm that the phone is off the hook.
In addition, Bonnett’s 3.26am log makes no mention of Caffell’s history of mental health problems, a crucial fact that any officers dispatched to the scene should have been informed of. The differences in perspective and facts between Bonnett’s log and West’s log would surely have been spelled out by Rivlin for the defence if both had been available.
There is a line space in Bonnett’s log after the initial paragraph, and then it states: “Message passed on to CD [Control Chelmsford, the code used to refer to the central radio control room where West was stationed] by the son of Mr Bamber after the phone went dead”. The line space suggests it could be a new entry.
When Bamber’s team came across West’s C1 form, they were convinced that this explained the confusion between 3.26am and 3.36am and why the first police car had been dispatched before Bamber’s call: there had been two distinct calls. They believed that the first section of Bonnett’s log referred to a call from Bamber’s father, Nevill, and that this was the information the police appeared to have responded to. This would finally explain how a car had been sent to White House Farm before West said he took Bamber’s call. And, crucially, it would prove Bamber’s innocence.
“At the trial, I had no idea why they were making such a fuss about whether I’d made my call at 03.26am or 03.36am,” Bamber writes. “It was only when we finally saw the log from West 25 years after I was first jailed that it became obvious there must have been two calls. The language is different, the perspective’s different, the information provided is different. It can only be two different people reporting the same incident as they see it.”
In 2016, a documents expert, Dr Chris Davies, studied the new evidence and concluded that the most likely reason for the inconsistencies was that there were two phone calls. “I consider that this would be my preferred explanation for them,” he said. If Nevill called the police at 3.26am to say his daughter had “gone berserk” and had the gun, it puts Bamber in the clear.
If there was an earlier call from Nevill Bamber, there are various theories about who may have taken it, including Malcolm Bonnett (who died in 2023) and officers who were in the control room with PC West (there were at least two others).
Bamber’s team felt that the 3.26am and 3.36am logs finally enabled them to make sense of a mystery from the original investigation: why had the police devoted so much energy to trying to prove that Bamber could have cycled from White House Farm back home to Goldhanger in 10 minutes, before finally concluding that it was impossible? This early police theory appears to have allowed for two calls – one from White House Farm at 3.26am and the other from Goldhanger at 3.36am, both made by Bamber.
Fifteen years on from the disclosure of West’s C1 log, Bamber’s team are still scouring the 347,000 documents that were released to them. In 2020, they came across “pocket book no.49”, belonging to DC Stephen Myall, one of the three officers originally radioed, alongside PS Bews and PC Saxby, asking them to attend the incident at 3.30am, six minutes before West stated on his C1 log that he received the call from Bamber. At the time, they were on an undercover foot patrol of an industrial estate after a spate of burglaries.
In his pocketbook, Myall wrote that he, Bews and Saxby immediately returned to Witham police station when, at “03.37am approx”, they received a phone call from West about the incident at White House Farm. “The Officer (PC West) at CD Control was on the phone and told us that he was relating information to us and still had the informant (Jeremy Bamber) on the other telephone.” Myall wrote that Bamber had told West that his father had said “words to the effect of ‘Come quick, your sister’s gone berserk. She’s got a gun’. The telephone had then gone dead.”
Bamber’s team believes it is now clear that Bews, Saxby and Myall were contacted by radio at 03.30am, as a result of a call from Nevill at 03.26am. The police officers were not at Witham police station at that point, but immediately returned from the nearby industrial estate to collect the police car, which they hadn’t taken with them on the undercover job. West then contacted Witham police station, by telephone, at 3.37am, having spoken to Bamber for a minute, from 03.36am.
The CCRC, the body that investigates alleged miscarriages of justice, has examined Bamber’s convictions three times. In 2002, it sent the case back to the court of appeal, but the judges concluded: “The more we examined the detail of the case, the more likely we thought it to be that the jury were right.”
In 2011, the CCRC refused to refer the case, stating that the evidence did not raise a real possibility that the court would find Bamber’s convictions unsafe. In 2021, his legal team made a new submission, consisting of 10 points. The CCRC has been widely criticised in recent years for its tardiness and its poor referral rate. In 2024/25, only 2% of cases – 31 out of 1,541 applications – were referred back to the court of appeal. (This rate has improved considerably since Dame Vera Baird became interim chair in June 2025.) By July 2025, the CCRC had examined four of the 10 points in Bamber’s submission and declared that, on the basis of these four points, it would not be referring the case back, although it would continue to explore the remaining six points.
One of the four points that was dismissed was the discrepancy between 3.26am and 3.36am being recorded as the time of Bamber’s call to the police. The CCRC remains adamant that the different timings are a result of police error and that there was only one call, from Bamber, at 3.26am. This is despite the C1 log from West stating it was at 3.36am and despite Myall’s record stating that West had Bamber on the phone at 3.37am.
The CCRC also claims that the issue of the call timings “had been dealt with at trial”. This is plain wrong. At trial, and at his 2002 appeal, Bamber’s team had no idea that there were two logs suggesting two calls to police about the same incident.
Since the 2021 submission to the CCRC, more valuable evidence has been uncovered. After the trial, Drake ordered the Dickinson review, an internal inquiry by Essex police into what the Times called the “blunders, omissions and ineptitude” of the force’s early investigation into the murders. The review would examine, for example, why the crime scene was grossly contaminated; the destruction and mismanagement of vital evidence; and the timeline and call-log inconsistencies.
The findings of the inquiry have never been made fully public. However, some documents from the review were released to Bamber’s lawyers in 2011 after a legal challenge. His defence team only recently discovered that the Dickinson review supports the 3.36am timing of Bamber’s call in its timeline of events on the day. It states that Bamber called West at 3.36am and, at 3.37am, “PS Bews, PC Myall & Saxby [were] at Witham. Receive telephone message from PC West. Despatched to White House Farm.” All these references are consistent with the first call to the police having been made by Nevill at 3.26am, officers being asked to attend White House Farm, then West taking a second call from Bamber at 3.36am.
Today, West works for the Masons. I contact him to suggest that his original log, which stated that Bamber called the police at 3.36am, was in fact accurate and consistent with the statements provided by other officers. He tells me he cannot recall the details, 41 years on, without seeing the specific documents and suggests that we meet face to face.
After this conversation, West does not respond to my calls. I text him with an explanation of why I believe his initial record of 3.36am was correct and suggest that a separate call may have been made at 3.26am. But he is having none of it: “Simon, I have nothing to add to anything that has been said and absolutely no comment on any of your rather ridiculous postulations. Jeremy Bamber was found guilty and remains a convicted felon. No one seems to ask: ‘What if that was the correct decision?’”
Meanwhile, Bamber’s team continue to try to piece together the missing pieces of the jigsaw. A few months ago, they re-examined PC West’s trial transcript and came across an astonishing exchange between him and defence council Geoffrey Rivlin.
Rivlin: You made it clear to him [Bamber] that police officers would be sent to the house.
West: Police officers had already been sent when I spoke to him, yes.
Here, PC West states that police officers had already been sent when he was speaking to Bamber. But if the police only received one call alerting them to the incident and the time of it was 3.26am, as the CCRC and Essex Police now insist, that would mean the first car had left before then. Yet the earliest mention of a radio call to officers is 03.30am and officers leaving is 03.35am. On the other hand if we stick with the 03.36am timing on West’s log, it only makes sense if there had been an earlier call because of the radio call to local officers at 03.30am and the leaving time of 03.35am.
This was the closest the jury ever came to hearing that the police appeared to have received two different calls about the incident. Unfortunately, neither the defence nor the jury picked up on West’s answer that officers had already been sent to White House Farm when he spoke to Jeremy Bamber.
When asked to comment about the failure to disclose evidence and inconsistencies in officers’ logs, a spokesperson for Essex Police said: “In August 1985, the lives of five people, including two children, were needlessly, tragically and callously cut short when they were murdered in their own home by Jeremy Bamber. In the years that followed, this case has been the subject of several appeals and reviews by the court of appeal and the Criminal Cases Review Commission – all of these processes have never found anything other than Bamber is the person responsible for killing his adoptive parents Nevill and June, sister Sheila Caffell and her two sons Nicholas and Daniel.”
A CCRC spokesperson said: “Mr Bamber has made three applications to the CCRC. The first application led to a referral to the Court of Appeal in 2001. His conviction was subsequently upheld. The second application to the CCRC in 2004 did not result in a referral. A third application received in 2021 is currently under review. A provisional decision on part of this latest application was issued to his legal representatives, and they responded to us in January this year. Work now continues to consider additional matters which were raised in Mr Bamber’s application. It would be inappropriate for us to discuss the case or make any further comment while the application is being reviewed.”
Those convinced of Bamber’s guilt maintain that Nevill Bamber’s calls to his son and the police never happened. Which takes us back to the first statements Bamber made when he was arrested. At the end of an aggressive 11-hour interrogation by Essex Police on 10 September 1985, Bamber is getting frustrated with all the questioning about the phone call he claims to have received from his father. He suggests there is one easy way of settling the issue. Get hold of British Telecom’s records. Bamber is apparently convinced this will provide him with an alibi and prove that he is telling the truth. If his father never called him, this is a kamikaze defence. All Essex Police need do is check BT’s records, and if there isn’t a call from White House Farm, he has implicated himself.
Bamber: Telecom must be able to tell you the times of phone calls on my parents’ phone.
Officer: What d’you mean by that?
Bamber: It would be proof that I received a phone call from my father.
Officer: If I tell you that Telecom can’t give such details then your theory can’t be checked.
Bamber: I thought Telecom could.
But it couldn’t. Or at least that’s what he was told. Despite an extensive advertising campaign in Essex stating that phone records were being digitised at the time, Essex Police said that calls in the area could not yet be itemised and bills still relied on an anonymised meter system. Years later, documents emerged showing that Telecom did indeed have itemised bills of earlier calls made from Bamber’s home phone number, though these were long-distance calls.
One aspect of the Bamber case that must have shocked the judge was how much evidence was destroyed on the day of the murders. At the time, the police believed it to be an open-and-shut murder-suicide. But that can never excuse the destruction of bloodied mattresses and bed linen.
However, in 1996, 11 years after the murders, an even more shocking obliteration of evidence took place. Although it was known that Bamber was preparing an appeal for the Home Office (which was subsequently inherited by the newly formed CCRC, in 1997), Essex police unilaterally destroyed vital evidence. Among the list of exhibits that were destroyed are bullets, blood samples and swabs, all of which may have provided exculpatory evidence for Bamber as DNA testing became ever more sophisticated. It was particularly alarming that Essex Police destroyed Sheila Caffell’s heavily bloodstained night dress, which may have shown her to have been in contact with the other victims, who were also very bloodied.
As so often in Bamber’s case, the document listing the evidentiary material and whether it was to be filed or destroyed is incomplete. Here it starts at number 167 and finishes at 661. At numbers 598 and 599, it says “British Telecom extract of calls”, citing the telephone numbers for Bamber’s home and White House Farm. By the side of both entries, it says “Destroy”.

Could 2026 be the year that democracy fought back? | David Van Reybrouck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

It is undoubtedly too early to declare victory, but the recent electoral defeats of Viktor Orbán, Aleksandar Vučić and Flávio Bolsonaro make me wonder: is 2026 turning out to be the year democracy slowly, but surely, fought back?
Even in Israel, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reigning bloc lost its parliamentary majority and saw the spectacular rise of Arab parties. Though the opposition may not be able to form a government yet, it does have the larger parliamentary bloc.
The shift began with an astonishing election result in Hungary in April. Against all odds, Orbán, the EU’s most deeply entrenched autocrat, was unseated by challenger Péter Magyar. Over his long years in office, Orbán had done everything possible to consolidate and perpetuate his authoritarian grip on power. The media were in his pocket, the judiciary ate from his hand and academic freedom was systematically curtailed. Yet a broad civic movement coalesced around Magyar’s party and succeeded in ousting him. The banks of the Danube witnessed their most exuberant night of celebration this century.
Joy was equally palpable last Sunday night, 300km down the river in Belgrade. There in Serbia, the Student List, a bottom-up alliance of students, academics and angry citizens, unexpectedly sent Vučić packing. Vučić had held a tight grip on power since 2014, first as prime minister, then president, relying on a familiar cocktail of far-right bravado, financial scandals and contempt for the rule of law: the winning formula of recent years. But there seems to be a limit to what citizens are ready to accept. Vučić’s fate was sealed after the newly constructed roof canopy of the Novi Sad train station collapsed in 2024, killing 16 people and triggering widespread public fury against systemic corruption.
Then came the biggest news of all on Monday morning, when Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defied expectations to emerge victorious in Brazil’s presidential election. In the first round, Flávio Bolsonaro had been in the lead, and almost every poll predicted he would win the run-off. Many Brazilians braced themselves for an administration at least as radical-right as his father’s. Instead, Lula, the son of poor, illiterate farmers and a former factory worker himself, surprised friend and foe alike by winning the presidency of Latin America’s largest economy for the fourth time.
Commentators were quick to point out that Lula’s victory halted a winning streak for rightwing populists across Latin America. That is certainly true, but zooming out reveals a broader pattern. This is not primarily a story of left v right, but rather of democrats v post-democrats. Hungary’s Magyar is by no means a leftist; he is a centre-right leader who was once a member of Orbán’s own party. In Serbia, the Student List was headed by Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist and university professor with no pronounced ideological profile. While he champions liberal values such as press freedom and the rule of law, his stance on Kosovo aligns with traditional Serbian nationalism: it should not be independent.
What Magyar, Srdanović and Lula share – despite significant political differences – is a fundamental belief that the rules of the democratic game must be respected. Elections must be fair, judges and journalists must work independently, and checks and balances exist for a reason.
Post-democrats, by contrast, treat laws and international agreements as mere suggestions, a convenient menu of policy options from which they can cherrypick. They use elections to gain power, only to hollow out democratic institutions once they are in office and maximise their private business profits. As corruption is key, they have to remain in power to stay out of jail. Opposing voices must be muzzled and critical media prosecuted. Post-democrats only keep the outer shell of democracy. Bolsonaro Jr took a page from Donald Trump’s playbook: election results are declared unimpeachable when he wins, and rigged when he loses. Similarly, Netanyahu is now attempting to discredit the Israeli election outcome, by suggesting Qatar interfered on behalf of the Palestinian parties.
Post-democrats have been on the rise for years, and it is terrifying. Since 2000, we have witnessed a steady, deliberate dismantling of democratic achievements across every continent. Anyone reading the latest international Democracy Report, produced by the V-Dem Institute, could easily despair. In terms of overall democratic health, it finds that we have effectively regressed to the levels of 1978. Only 7% of the world’s population live in liberal democracies.
Yet after years of alarming headlines about global democratic backsliding, the news from Budapest, Belgrade and Brasília offers rays of hope in dark times. So does the massive wave of Gen Z protests this year, from India and the Philippines to Albania, Argentina and Chile. Huge crowds of young people have taken to the streets to challenge autocratic power and corruption in their countries.
Could liberal democracy be finding its second wind? Is it actually possible to defeat autocrats and authoritarian regimes after all? Could this mark the beginning of a democratic revival that might extend to the US next week? Most polls suggest that the Democrats stand a strong chance of reclaiming at least the House of Representatives in the upcoming US midterms.
Meanwhile, the delegitimisation of Arab voters in Israel this week reminds us of the limitations of change via the ballot box. Elections can help us get rid of post-democrats, but in deeply divided societies they are not enough to heal. The individual, silent act of voting must be complemented with collective processes of deliberation.
Nonetheless, globally, 2026 may come to rank as the best year for democracy in more than a quarter of a century. Could this be the turning point?
What this tells us ahead of critical elections in some of the EU’s largest member states in the year ahead – France, Spain, Germany and Poland – remains anyone’s guess. Looking at the momentum of the AfD in Germany, rightwing populist parties with post-democratic tendencies remain very much alive in Europe. And Vox could be part of a People’s party-led government in Spain in a matter of weeks. But Hungary, Serbia and Brazil have delivered a vital reminder: the rise of autocrats and their permanence in power are not immutable laws of nature. Soon enough, post-democracies may start to feel passé.
- David Van Reybrouck is a Belgian author and philosopher laureate for the Low Countries. He is the author of Against Elections: The Case for Democracy, and the initiator of Democracy27

Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Sandu* checked his watch. He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vast Google datacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. People have been fired after saying no.”
The task was one Sandu had done many times before and involved a series of tests measuring the safety and integrity of the electrical wiring. A protective suit was locked away in an equipment room. The round trip would have added another 15 minutes to the job, he says, and people were waiting, so he decided not to retrieve the suit.
Once in the voltage room, Sandu says the managers confirmed the lines had been de-energised. In the first round, everything went as planned. Then, on the second test, while holding insulated tongs, he linked the cables. But this time, the lines were live.
The blast was immediate and catastrophic. In milliseconds, 400 volts and 12,000 amps hit Sandu’s face and across the right side of his body. “I went completely blind,” he says. When doctors received him in the Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, he says he was placed in an induced coma for five days.
Hospital records seen by the Guardian and Investigate Europe show that the arc flash electrocution had burned 12% of Sandu’s body, with second-degree burns to the face and neck, as well as third-degree burns across his right shoulder and fingers.
When Sandu woke from surgery in the intensive care unit a week later, his wife was at his bedside. He says his entire body felt like a “white-hot blister … It was so much pain. The human heart cannot comprehend it.”
Sandu says the regional director of Google, along with a representative from Dornan Engineering, an Irish company that oversaw his contractor, and his recruiter, came to visit. While he lay bandaged in the hospital bed, he says the Google director told him he was lucky to be alive.
To date, no company or contractor appears to have been found liable for the accident. The local labour inspectorate closed its investigation in late October and found no wrongdoing.
A spokesperson for Dornan Engineering said it was “committed to maintaining safe working conditions, complying with applicable labour laws and continually learning to help prevent incidents like this from happening again”.
Sandu’s electrocution appears brutal and harrowing, but far from unique, according to a five-month investigation by Investigate Europe and the Guardian into conditions for migrant workers on datacentre sites across Sweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands.
Europe is in the midst of a datacentre boom, the largest infrastructure surge the continent has seen in decades, with more than 2,300 datacentres rapidly altering the physical and energy landscape of Europe (at least 500 of them in the UK) and hundreds more under construction.
 
But unions say the push for tech sovereignty in Europe is becoming increasingly reliant on the exploitation of migrant workers.
In dozens of interviews we found evidence of debilitating injuries, squalid living conditions, an unreported infectious outbreak, unpaid wages and exploitative employment practices.
In the UK, a general contractor died while working on a datacentre site last year, while another fatality was reported in 2024 at an electrical substation being built for a Microsoft datacentre. Serious accidents have also been recorded this year at projects in Italy, Sweden, Norway and Belgium, and exploitative labour practices have been found at projects around the world, including in Brazil.
On the outskirts of Gävle, a city two hours north of Stockholm, past timber-framed cottages and dense pine forests, lies a smooth road leading to one such site. The remote clearing is part of a 130-hectare, €3bn expansion plan begun in June 2024 to scale up Microsoft’s AI datacentre infrastructure.
One subcontractor at the site is the Irish-owned construction company BenBau. It is among 148 firms working under Collen Construction at the Gävle site, including 28 direct subcontractors.
For months, there has been a growing sense of outrage among Adrian*, 45, and his colleagues working for BenBau on the Microsoft site. They showed evidence of crowded living quarters – 24 people to a kitchen, 14 men to a single bathroom – and say they have reported vermin infestations, broken ventilation systems and lack of heating during the sub-zero Swedish winters, but the problems remain.
Such conditions can make the transmission of disease more likely. In February this year, one Romanian worker tested positive for active tuberculosis, medical records show. Shortly after, others living in the same shared housing showed similar symptoms. BenBau initially informed only a few men who shared close quarters with the infected worker and then told the men that testing was optional, according to workers. After the first worker who contracted the disease had left for hospital, Benbau moved another worker into his bedroom.
Freedom of information requests made to Sweden’s national work authorities and its Public Health Agency say no outbreak had been reported.
The living and working conditions form only part of the story. More than 30 workers have shown hundreds of payslips to the Guardian and Investigate Europe that appear to show some of them working up to 50 or 60 hours a week with no overtime pay and missed holiday pay. With many foreign workers unfamiliar with the laws, unions say inequity can arise quickly.
Days before publication of this investigation, the union Solidariska Byggare, representing the 70 Romanian workers at Microsoft’s site in Gävle, brokered a settlement with BenBau, which it says will give workers back pay and allow unions access to sites.
A spokesperson for BenBau said the company “takes all concerns regarding the welfare, health and safety of our people extremely seriously” and has “stringent procedures for reporting, investigating and addressing workplace concerns”.
Since 2021, Sweden’s Work Environment Authority (AV) has opened 50 cases into working conditions at datacentre sites involving Microsoft and a number of Irish firms, according to a freedom of information request.
Earlier this month, a contractor fell through a roof hatch while carrying out maintenance work on a ventilation system at the Microsoft site in Gävle, according to freedom of information request to AV.
In October 2021, a forklift allegedly ran over the foot of a supervisor working for Collen at the site. The worker subsequently needed surgery. An incident report submitted by Collen to work authorities says that the wrong machine had been used, the driver had no formal certificate for it and the lift plan was incomplete. Still, it had been signed off. The Work Environment Authority saw no grounds to report the employer to prosecutors.
A spokesperson for Collen said: “We are committed to ensuring that every Collen site is a safe, healthy and respectful place to work, where everyone is treated with dignity and their fundamental human rights are protected. We expect the same throughout our supply chain and have zero tolerance for any conduct inconsistent with these principles.
“Our projects are subject to rigorous compliance with our own mandatory policies and procedures, our clients’ requirements, all applicable laws and regulations, and recognised industry standards in every jurisdiction in which we operate.”
A similar pattern is found throughout Europe, says James McCabe from Unite the Union, an Irish-UK group representing more than 1.2 million workers. “Everywhere we’ve encountered Irish datacentre contractors at tech-giant datacentre sites we’ve learned of lack of normal and meaningful union access … as well as serious concerns of labour crimes and exploitation of workers,” he says.
Johan Danielsson, a European parliament rapporteur in charge of regulating subcontracting chains, says: “If people let these big American multinationals come here and import their anti-union business models, then it becomes a problem. Because behind the fence they are abusing workers, and they don’t want anyone to know it.”
A spokesperson for Google said: “Our supplier code of conduct and contracts require all suppliers to comply with local labour laws and uphold safe, healthy working conditions. We maintain active dialogue with union leaders and trade groups, and are committed to providing transparent information about our workplace.”
A spokesperson for Microsoft said: “In our datacentre construction, we work with contractors and suppliers, with whom we set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining. To ensure our contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies, we have robust processes in place, including audits.”
* Names have been changed
This investigation is led by Investigate Europe, a cross-border team of investigative journalists: Lorenzo Buzzoni, Jan Daalder, Pascal Hansens, Ella Joyner, Chris Matthews, Nico Schmidt and Astri Thunold.

Ministers should explore writing off a crippling £197m loan to the British Council by converting as much of it as possible into “a grant or similar”, MPs have said.
The Commons public accounts committee said the government lacked a “positive vision” for the council, whose soft power value to the UK is put at £1bn a year. The MPs called on the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to set out what more it could do to support the council and its work.
Despite slashing a third of its headcount and selling off historical assets, the council’s future remains precarious because a £60m Covid-era FCDO loan on commercial terms has grown to £197m.
The loan was agreed by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government when the pandemic shuttered the council’s English teaching and exams business overseas. The loan was due to have been repaid this year but was restructured to be cleared over the next 15 years.
Even with a turnaround plan to reduce staffing by a further 25% as well as dispose of more assets and close operations in nine countries, the council forecasts it will not generate an operating surplus until 2029–30, according to the committee.
The report said: “The FCDO should write to us on what steps could be taken to offset the loan against the soft power value provided by the British Council and convert as much of the loan as possible into a grant or similar.”
British Council staff across Europe have staged widespread strikes and protests against the cuts. The planned further job losses will mean numbers will have almost halved since 2020, with more than 2,000 full-time equivalent posts lost since 2021.
The report called on the FCDO and the council “to work together to set out a positive vision for the future of the British Council that will build on its soft power value to the UK”.
“It seems to the public accounts committee that the future of the British Council is still precarious and both it and the FCDO need to carefully monitor the situation as partners so that the British Council can confidently demonstrate to the world that the UK values its work in providing soft power,” it said.
The committee said it recognised the council’s “inestimable value” and called for a “more collaborative tone” in relations between the FCDO and council, where there has been “a lack of trust”.
Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the committee, said: “With the council seeking a leaner operation at a time of continuing precarity and obvious vulnerability for its finances, it needs the government’s help to continue its vital work, not to be simply pursued as a debtor. The FCDO says the British Council must adapt to survive. That may be true – but it will fail to do so without the government’s full-throated support.”
The council is an arm’s-length body of the FCDO as well as an established charity and a commercial organisation. It operates in just under 100 countries and claims a reach of more than 700 million people a year.
The majority of its income is from its teaching and exams business, while grant-in-aid from the FCDO accounts for about 15% of its annual revenue. The funding is used to support the council’s three charitable objectives: cultural relationships, the English language and education.

Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.
In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).
Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.
“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.
Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.
However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.
Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.
Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.
South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.
In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.
The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.
Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.
Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.
For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.
The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.
However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.
Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.
“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.
“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”
Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.
“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”
In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.
While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.
Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.
“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”
Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Wildlife Trusts hit £30m target to buy and rewild huge Northumberland estate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:00:44 UTC
14:00:44 KST

One of the most ambitious nature recovery projects ever undertaken in England can go ahead after campaigners announced they had raised £30m to buy an estate in Northumberland.
The Wildlife Trusts’ bid to buy the Rothbury estate, an area the size of Athens, had been championed by David Attenborough who on Friday thanked the public for their help.
“The Wildlife Trusts called for your support and you answered in your thousands,” he said. “The opportunity to bring the vision of a landscape where nature and people thrive side by side can become a reality. This will be a place where nature, community, farming and heritage can combine to create something very special for generations to come.”
The fundraising campaign was launched two years ago after the estate was put up for sale by the Duke of Northumberland’s youngest son, Max Percy.
At more than 3,800 hectares (nearly 15 sq miles), the Rothbury estate is the largest piece of land in single ownership to have come up for sale in England for more than 30 years. Campaigners said buying it was “a once-in-a-generation opportunity”.
Mike Pratt, the chief executive of Northumberland Wildlife Trust, said he felt “elated” at the success of the campaign and “humbled” by the public support.
“We are absolutely elated, it has been a long haul and it hasn’t all been easy,” he said. “The other word is humbled. There was £17m from the public to make this happen and that is at the forefront of my mind – we’ve got to honour that support and make sure that people come here and really enjoy getting close to wildlife.”
The estate is a thrilling, spirit-lifting mosaic of different habitats, including the looming Simonside hills, sweeping wild moorland, valley woodlands and farm fields.
Pratt was talking to the Guardian at Lordenshaws, the site of an iron-age hill fort and one of the largest clusters of strange, ancient cup and ring marked rocks in England. He thinks people rallied to the campaign because it “represents hope … a positive view of what the future can be”.
The trust has big plans and hopes that by making interventions, restoring and extending habitats, it can increase numbers of species which are already there, whether mountain bumblebees or red squirrels.
“We should have water voles in this landscape,” said Pratt. “Maybe we can help bring them back. Pine martens are making their own way back, maybe we can encourage them. Hopefully we’ll see more curlew.”
The eventual hope is that the Rothbury estate will be the “beating heart” of a 40-mile nature corridor from the coast at Druridge Bay to the Scottish-English border at the Kielderhead and Whitelee Moor national nature reserves.
The trust also believes that more nature tourism will bring benefits to the town of Rothbury itself.
Sophie Bulgin, the Rothbury project manager, said the enthusiasm of volunteers in the various projects that had been running had taken her aback. “It has overwhelmed me,” she said. “I didn’t imagine that much interest and enthusiasm. People are taking ownership.”
One of the projects is eco-acoustic monitoring, with “people walking for miles across the estate in bracken as high as their shoulder” to install and retrieve monitors which record the sound of small mammals, bats or anything else that might be close by. In a fortnight, there will be earthworm counts which might reveal more about the health of the soil.
As well as gifts from 25,000 members of the public, the National Lottery Heritage Fund gave a gamechanging £5m. Large donations also came from charitable foundations and philanthropists, and the government this week pledged £1.94m.
Not everyone supported the campaign, however, with some farmers calling it a “folly”.
Guy Renner-Thompson, a councillor and the chair of Northumberland Conservatives, this week questioned the government’s priorities after its decision to give money.
“Farmers on the estate have already raised concerns about food production, changes to traditional land management and whether their businesses can remain profitable,” he said. “Those concerns deserve answers before ministers reach for the chequebook.”
Pratt said the trust had been working closely with farmers. “We want to demonstrate that you can have lots of wildlife and still have a productive business model.”

How to prepare your garden for the heat this summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:00:29 UTC
14:00:29 KST

Seven ways to prepare your garden for the heat this summer
With spring off to a warm start and weather experts tipping another hot summer, it's a good time to start preparing your garden for the heat.
Rather than waiting until summer hits, a little work now — and knowing a few things to avoid — can help stop your plants getting crispy.
Perfecting your mowing technique and laying mulch are just some of the easy jobs that experts recommend tackling.
Don't squash your soil
A simple thing you can do in the months ahead of summer is avoid compacting the soil on wet days, says Naarm/Melbourne-based horticulturalist and Sustainable Gardening Australia community training manager Liz Rowe.
"If we can reduce how much we're compacting, that's going to leave those air pockets available for water to fill it in [in the future]," she says.
"Stick to paths or … if you have to step into your veggie beds or your garden beds, put a board down."
Ms Rowe says the aim is to capitalise on any rain your garden is getting before the heat hits.
"If we compact our soils, the water's not going in there — it's just going to flow away. So … reducing compaction is going to be one of the first big steps."
Avoid digging and top-dress
Top-dressing your garden can also aid soil health and water retention, Ms Rowe says.
"You could do a compost or manure layer," she says.
"We don't want to dig it in because … the microbes and bugs will do a lot of that work for us.
"They're burrowing or creating air pockets as well, which is going to help our water-holding capacity and infiltration in the long term.
"The more we till or turn our soils, we're actually killing off a lot of the beneficial life … that is going to help drought-proof it as well."
If your soil needs aeration, Ms Rowe says a broad fork will do the job with no turning.
Get mulching
A good layer of mulch on top of the soil also helps conserve water and prevent evaporation, says Australian National Botanic Gardens director Matthew Parker, from Canberra/Ngunnawal and Ngambri land.
Choosing the right mulch depends on what your garden looks like, according to Ms Rowe, who says outdoor plantings generally fall into three categories: perennial beds, annual beds and pots.
"In our perennial beds (with plants you don't need to replace every year, such as trees and shrubs), we often advise leaning towards wood-based mulches [such as woodchip]," Ms Rowe says.
"And straw [or hay-based] mulches, which are a lighter organic option … we prioritise those on our annual beds (with plants that need swapping out every year, such as vegetables or cut flowers)."
Pots can be mulched with "almost anything", she says, adding the most important thing is its capacity to reduce evaporation without cutting off the soil's access to water and air.
Dr Parker says the depth of your mulch is also important, and 70–100 millimetres is ideal for a garden bed.
"It needs to be a decent thickness that will effectively create a mat or a barrier to limit evaporation," he says.
However, Dr Parker warns wood-based mulches may not be a good choice for areas with high bushfire risk.
Cut your grass longer and avoid pruning plants
Dr Parker also recommends increasing your turf height by adjusting your mower to help protect the lower parts of the grass from the sun.
"If people are cutting the grass really low, then that's going to increase the stress on the plant," he says.
Similarly, he says you should avoid hard-pruning your plants in the lead-up to a heatwave.
"Often people think that the plant's going to be losing water, so it's better to prune it and reduce the size of the crowns," he says.
"But … pruning and removing branches can create additional stress."
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
Create shade
If your gardening budget is a little bigger, you could also consider creating some shade.
"If you have a veggie plot, you might be able to put a shade cloth over the top to reduce the intensity of the UV," Dr Parker says.
"The leafy [vegetables] over summer need a lot of water. But installing some shade … would be useful, particularly during those peaks of the heat waves."
Set yourself up for watering
Setting up irrigation lines with timers ahead of summer is also an option.
"The gold star that's often recommended is your drip-line irrigation, but these things cost money," Ms Rowe says.
"But you could also look at a [cheaper] trickle hose on a timer."
Once the heat hits, both experts say early in the morning is the best time to water the garden, before the sun is at its hottest.
Protect your pots
Potted gardens tend to be more vulnerable to the heat, but Ms Rowe says grouping them together can help protect them.
"If we can group our plants together based on their water needs, it makes it easier for maintenance, but … they can also insulate one another and help cool each other down," she says.
If your plants are in plastic pots or containers, she suggests using a ceramic pot as a "sleeve", but says other vessels — for example, a Styrofoam cooler box — can be just as effective.
"Putting them inside something else that's going to insulate around the root system can help," Ms Rowe says.
Dr Parker says shifting your potted plants to a shaded area ahead of a heatwave can also help.
Choose the right plants
And although it requires some forward thinking (sometimes years in advance), planting heat-tolerant species appropriate to your area, such as local natives, is the ultimate way to help your garden survive hot weather.
"Consider the types of plants that you're growing and check that they're suitable for the environment," Dr Parker says.

Lighting design a “strategic economic investment” says Signify’s Sameer Sodhi
According to business leader of entertainment and Colour Kinetics at lighting brand Signify, Sameer Sodhi, lit-up architecture and public installations can encourage interaction, strengthen local identity and support overall wellbeing.
Sodhi explained that for decades, the value of a building has been measured by appearance, energy performance, return on investment and construction costs. A building’s lighting design is one of the most influential factors but is often overlooked and seen as a “finishing touch”.
He added that well-designed lighting can shape the experience of places, support local economies and strengthen communities.
“The question is no longer whether lighting matters,” Sodhi said. “But whether we can accurately measure the (overlooked) value it creates.”
Sodhi points to a recent study by lighting brand Colour Kinetics that examined four illuminated spaces across the United States and found that lighting generated social, economic, and cultural benefits “well beyond the initial investment”.
“The report assesses lighting through a broader framework that includes community engagement, tourism, economic development, media visibility, partnerships, sustainability and health and wellbeing,” Sodhi explained.
“Rather than viewing lighting as an isolated building system, it recognised it as infrastructure capable of influencing how cities function and how communities connect,” he added.
Sodhi cites the lighting of Daniel Hoan Memorial Bridge in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, as an example, which has transformed the infrastructure into a “dynamic visual icon” that reflects the city’s identity and connects residents and visitors to the waterfront.
“The bridge now hosts community and civic events, causes and initiatives and annual festivals, while serving as a canvas for civic celebrations throughout the year,” he said.
According to Sodhi, architectural lighting also creates economic value. For example, the thoughtful lighting design of West Sacramento’s Barns in California has supported the area’s placemaking.
Although the venue was originally conceived as an event and dining venue, the strategic lighting design has helped establish it as the focal point for the surrounding mixed-use district, which includes spaces for hosting concerts, festivals, community activities and sporting events.
Sodhi explained that, because of the building’s lit-up impact, approximately ten residential developments have since been built or are under construction nearby, highlighting the role “quality public spaces” can play in wider regeneration.
“Importantly, the value created extends beyond construction economics,” added Sodhi. “Visitors stay longer, businesses benefit from increased footfall, and the location develops an identity that encourages repeat visits and investment.”
According to Sodhi, lighting can also serve as a form of public communication. For example, Philadelphia City Hall’s lighting is programmed to respond to national celebrations, charitable campaigns and civic events, “transforming a historic landmark into a dynamic expression of the city’s identity”.
“Whether celebrating sporting victories or marking important social causes, the building becomes an active participant in public life rather than simply a backdrop,” added Sodhi.
This also applies to Nashville’s illuminated installation, Loqui, Sodhi explained. The artwork includes words and stories from more than 400 local residents and demonstrates how illuminated public art can amplify local voices and bring a community together.
“Rather than lighting serving the artwork, the lighting becomes integral to the experience itself,” he added.
“These projects suggest that good lighting is no longer simply about visibility. It is about participation.”
Sodhi added that buildings are also assessed by how efficiently they operate, but also how effectively they create meaningful experiences.
“Architectural lighting is uniquely positioned to support that ambition,” he explained. “It can extend the usability of spaces after dark, strengthen local identity, encourage social interaction and help transform ordinary infrastructure into memorable landmarks.”
“When thoughtfully integrated from the earliest stages of design, lighting becomes a strategic investment rather than an aesthetic upgrade,” he added. “Perhaps this is the real measure of good design.”
