Israel’s coalition politics: How can you win an election and still lose power? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:12:26 UTC
13:12:26 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party appears to have won more votes than any other party in Israel’s October 27 election. Yet Netanyahu could still be out of office, replaced by someone whose party received far fewer votes. And the next government, whoever leads it, might include ministers from parties with very different political philosophies, perhaps even from opposite ends of the political spectrum.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
For Americans, accustomed to seeing the winner of a presidential election take office and appoint a Cabinet, this may seem strange. But the explanation is easier to grasp when we consider how American political parties operate.
The Republican Party, for example, encompasses religious conservatives, libertarians, populists, fiscal conservatives, and moderates. These groups disagree over taxes, government spending, foreign policy, immigration, and the role of religion in public life. Some disagreements are so fierce that, in another political system, they might be separate parties.
The same is true of the Democrats. Progressives, democratic socialists, labor-oriented politicians, environmentalists, and business-friendly centrists coexist within the party, frequently fighting over its platform and direction.
In the United States, these factions generally compete for influence within two large parties. The parties themselves are broad coalitions, assembled before voters go to the polls. Their members may have little in common beyond preferring their own party over the other.
Israel approaches the problem differently. Rather than forcing so many political tendencies into two dominant parties, its electoral system lets many of those tendencies be represented by separate parties, each seeking its own share of parliamentary seats.
Imagine the Republican Party splitting into four or five parties, with religious conservatives, libertarians, moderates, and populists running separately. Now imagine the Democrats doing something similar, with progressive, centrist, environmentalist, and labor parties competing for votes.
After the election, these groups would have to negotiate which ones could work together, which policies they could agree on, and who would lead the resulting government.
That is roughly how Israeli politics work.
Winning seats not the same as winning power
Israelis vote for party lists rather than individual parliamentary candidates. The 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, are distributed roughly according to each list’s share of the national vote, provided it receives at least 3.25% of valid ballots.
In the 2026 election, 38 candidate lists were approved, although one withdrew before voting. Preliminary results indicated that 11 would enter the Knesset.
The parties represent a broad range of political, religious, and social interests. Some are secular, others religious. Some favor territorial compromise with the Palestinians, while others oppose it. Some represent the ultra-Orthodox community, some draw much of their support from Arab citizens, and others focus on economic and security policies.
With the votes still being counted Wednesday, Likud was projected to receive approximately 26 seats, or 21.7% of the Knesset. That would make it the largest party, but it would leave the other 94 seats in the hands of its rivals and potential partners.
For an American comparison, imagine Republicans holding 26 seats in a 120-member House of Representatives, Democrats holding 21, and nine smaller parties dividing the rest. Republicans would have the largest delegation but would be unable to govern without making deals.
Israel’s prime minister is not elected separately by the public, as an American president is. The prime minister heads a government that must command sufficient support in the Knesset to take office and remain in power. Usually, that means assembling a coalition with at least 61 of the 120 seats, although minority governments can sometimes survive with support from parties outside the coalition.
A party holding just six seats might determine whether a prospective government commands a majority. Its leader can demand substantial concessions to join the coalition, even if the party represents only a small fraction of the electorate.
Those concessions might involve religious education, military conscription, housing, economic policy, or the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. They can also involve Cabinet appointments.
In the United States, the president generally chooses Cabinet secretaries from among political allies, although presidents occasionally appoint members of the opposing party. In Israel, prospective coalition partners negotiate over which ministries their parties will control.
A small party might demand the Education Ministry or Finance Ministry as part of a coalition agreement. Another might insist on the Foreign Ministry, even if its foreign policy views differ considerably from the prime minister's.
A right-wing prime minister could therefore serve alongside a center-left foreign minister or a left-wing health minister. The coalition agreement sets out the broad compromises that let these parties govern together, though they may still disagree on key issues.
The prime minister whose party won seven seats
Israel provided a striking example of this system in 2021, when Netanyahu’s Likud won 30 seats, considerably more than any other party.
Yair Lapid’s centrist Yesh Atid party finished second with 17 seats. Yet neither Netanyahu nor Lapid became prime minister initially.
Instead, Naftali Bennett, whose right-wing Yamina party won just seven seats, took the job.
Bennett and Lapid reached an agreement that brought together eight parties spanning much of the Israeli political spectrum. Their coalition included right-wing parties, centrists, the left-wing Labor and Meretz parties, and Ra’am, an Islamist Arab party.
Few of these parties would ordinarily have chosen to govern together. Their common objective was to replace Netanyahu, who had dominated Israeli politics for years.
Under their agreement, Bennett became prime minister, while Lapid became foreign minister and alternate prime minister, with an arrangement for the two men eventually to exchange positions. Nitzan Horowitz, the leader of Meretz, became health minister.
Ra’am did not receive Cabinet posts, but it negotiated policy commitments and funding for Arab communities in exchange for participating in the coalition.
Despite leading the party that won the most votes, Netanyahu became leader of the opposition.
The outcome was entirely consistent with Israel’s electoral system. Bennett and Lapid had assembled enough parliamentary support to establish a government, something Netanyahu had been unable to do.
Their coalition lasted only about a year before collapsing under the weight of its internal disagreements. Netanyahu returned to power following another election in November 2022.
Bennett’s premiership remains a particularly instructive example for Americans: A politician whose party finished far behind the election's leading party became prime minister because he reached an agreement with other parties that together commanded enough parliamentary support.
When political rivals need each other
Personal relationships and political rivalries can matter as much in coalition negotiations as ideological differences.
Two parties might agree on nearly every major policy issue but refuse to govern together because their leaders distrust one another. Parties with substantially different views, meanwhile, might find common ground in their determination to remove an incumbent prime minister.
That helps explain the deadlock following this week’s election.
As of Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu’s traditional right-wing and religious allies were projected to hold 53 seats, eight short of a majority. The four-party opposition bloc was projected to win 48, while two Arab-led lists were expected to win 19 combined.
On paper, the opposition and Arab parties would have enough seats to replace Netanyahu. In practice, some opposition leaders have firmly rejected governing with Arab parties or relying on their parliamentary support. The arithmetic allows for a government that the politicians involved may be unwilling to create.
American politicians are familiar with this problem, even if they encounter it in a different form. A president trying to pass legislation must often negotiate with members of the president’s own party whose views differ sharply. Congressional leaders spend considerable time keeping their party’s competing factions together, sometimes finding that a handful of members can frustrate the wishes of a much larger group.
Israeli coalition bargaining makes those tensions more visible because many of the competing factions have their own parties, leaders, and electoral mandates. Their negotiations over Cabinet positions, policy commitments, and the leadership of the government take place between separate political organizations.
Israel’s system gives voters a wider choice of parties and allows smaller religious, ideological, and minority groups to gain parliamentary representation. But those parties can exercise considerable leverage, and the compromises required to accommodate them may produce unstable governments.
America’s two-party system offers a different bargain. Its parties generally present voters with two broad alternatives, but the ideological divisions within them do not disappear after an election. Much of the political bargaining Israelis do between parties happens within the Republican and Democratic parties themselves.
Of course, there are limits to the comparison. America's president is elected independently of Congress through the Electoral College, while Israel's prime minister depends on parliamentary support. Even if American political factions broke away to form separate parties, they would not be choosing a president through congressional coalition negotiations.
Still, the comparison helps explain why the results of an Israeli election are often only the beginning of the struggle over who will govern.
Netanyahu's Likud appears to have finished first, but neither he nor his allies or opponents currently has a clear route to forming a government. The next stage will involve negotiations among parties that have spent months campaigning against one another, with decisions about the premiership, Cabinet appointments, and government policies all potentially on the table.
For Netanyahu, the question is whether he can attract enough partners to remain in power. For his opponents, the question is whether they can overcome their differences and agree on an alternative.
The 2021 election reminds us how surprising the outcome can be. Netanyahu's party won 30 seats, Bennett's won seven, and Bennett became prime minister. The party that finishes first on Election Day has an advantage, but the alliances formed afterward determine who governs Israel.

Without political renewal, Israel will remain stuck - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:11:50 UTC
13:11:50 KST

Three days removed from Israel’s pivotal election, many of the questions Israelis had going into the election remain unanswered.
The country is still caught in a political deadlock, with neither side able to secure a clear path forward. For many, the results look remarkably similar to those of Israel’s deadlocked elections in 2019 and 2020.
Unfortunately, so do many of the politicians.
Disappointing takeaways
After the October 7 massacre, years of upheaval, and an endless war that has reshaped Israeli society, one might have expected a greater appetite for political renewal. Instead, Israelis are once again left looking at familiar faces, familiar arguments, and a familiar stalemate.
Perhaps the most disappointing takeaway from this election is that, with the exception of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, new political forces have struggled to break into the conversation. Whether one agrees with their platforms or not, the failure of these parties to gain meaningful traction should concern anyone who wants to see Israel’s political system evolve.
The Haredi Public party, for example, offered haredi voters a genuine alternative to the established ultra-Orthodox parties. Yet, as of Thursday afternoon, it had received just 10,145 votes, leaving it far from parliamentary representation.
People of Israel leader Ofer Winter, who ran with an impressive list of fresh candidates, also fell short of the Knesset, attracting fewer than 100,000 votes before the double-envelope ballots were counted. His party’s performance was further undermined by Likud’s targeted campaign, although it appears he remained well short of the 3.25% electoral threshold regardless.
Yoaz Hendel’s attempt to appeal to reservists exhausted by years of service failed to cross the electoral threshold. His running mate, Yaron Zelekha, built his campaign around economic issues that other parties largely pushed aside. They, too, failed to translate their messages into parliamentary representation, according to the results counted so far.
These parties differed in their ideologies, constituencies, and priorities. Some offered a challenge to established political structures, while others sought to put neglected issues back on the agenda. Their failure does not necessarily mean their ideas lacked merit, or that their potential voters were wrong to seek alternatives.
It does, however, highlight how difficult it has become for new voices to establish themselves in Israeli politics.
There are some important caveats. Yashar is, after all, a new party, and its success in entering the political conversation demonstrates that renewal is still possible. The incoming Knesset will also include many new MKs within established parties. Political change does not always require the creation of an entirely new political movement.
Still, the broader picture is difficult to ignore. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who was absent from the previous Knesset, is back in the political arena. Yair Golan, another familiar figure from past Knessets, has returned to the forefront.
The other side
On the other side of the political spectrum, Moshe Feiglin may be presented as a fresh alternative, but he is hardly a newcomer, having already served in the Knesset a decade ago.
There is nothing inherently wrong with experienced politicians returning to public life. Experience matters, and voters are entitled to choose familiar leaders if they believe those leaders can deliver. Nor should novelty, by itself, be mistaken for competence.
New parties can disappoint, and new politicians can bring the same old habits into the Knesset. But the Israeli people, who have undergone such profound trauma since October 7, should be able to expect more from their political system than another contest between deeply entrenched camps.
Israel’s political deadlock will not be resolved by fresh faces alone. At the moment, divisions between the country’s political camps remain too deep, and any government that emerges from the current negotiations will have to find answers to the difficult issues that have divided Israelis for years.
But if one lesson can be learned from the election results, it is that without new voices and new ideas, the country risks remaining trapped in the same cycle of political instability that produced five elections between 2019 and 2022 and repeatedly prevented Israeli leaders from establishing a stable government.
After everything Israel has been through, that would be a missed opportunity at best, and a catastrophe at worst.
The country needs political renewal – not because every new party deserves a seat, but because a democracy that cannot make room for alternatives risks becoming stagnant.
Until Israel finds a way to break that pattern, the deadlock will remain – and the country will continue to struggle to find a way forward.

Editor's Notes: Any unity deal must start with the leaders who are here, including Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:11:41 UTC
13:11:41 KST

By 2:15 a.m., when we began interviewing Benjamin Netanyahu at Likud’s campaign headquarters in Petah Tikva, some of the people around him were taking naps on couches and chairs. We finished at a quarter to three. He was alert, focused, and still had things to do after we left.
There is something almost hassidic about the way people around Netanyahu speak about him. Everyone seems to have a story about the rebbe. That night, in a studio in an industrial area, the man at the center of it all appeared to need less sleep than the people waiting for him.
I keep thinking about that scene when I hear suggestions that Likud should simply choose someone else. Many of its voters chose Netanyahu personally. Their attachment to him cannot be transferred to another Likud MK by a clever coalition agreement. His opponents understand that attachment, even when it drives them mad.
A serious unity proposal has to begin with the people who are actually here, including leaders their opponents hoped the election would remove.
So, here is the offer I would put on the table: Netanyahu remains prime minister. Gadi Eisenkot becomes defense minister. The Bennett-Lapid partnership takes responsibility for finance and foreign affairs. Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu joins the same negotiation over military service and the budget. They agree on the policies and funding before entering together.
I know what the first objection will be. Netanyahu stays. For people who hold him responsible for the October 7 massacre, that may be enough to reject the proposal. They deserve an answer about what Israel would gain from the arrangement. Telling them to put their feelings aside will not do.
Eisenkot’s Yashar would have authority over defense and a negotiated role in security decisions. Together, the party led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid would nominate the finance and foreign ministers. Its leaders could shape the budget and conduct diplomacy, and they would have to answer for the results. Liberman would need a military-service agreement his voters could recognize as an achievement.
Subject to parliamentary arithmetic, this partnership would allow Netanyahu to form a government without his current haredi and far-right partners (although we should differentiate between Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, since the former can potentially be part of this type of coalition). He would have to explain why he was leaving them out. That conversation would presumably be less pleasant than announcing another ministry.
Netanyahu would keep the office he wants most, while conceding control over important decisions to people with their own voters and ambitions. His rivals would give up the immediate removal of Netanyahu in exchange for authority and policies they could not deliver from the opposition. They would have to judge whether the gains justified that concession. So would their voters.
I would want to see the contents of the military-service agreement before taking any of this seriously: recruitment obligations, financial consequences for avoidance, a funded implementation plan, and tangible relief for reservists and their families. The Finance Ministry would have to budget it, and the Defense Ministry would have to show how it could work. Another committee would not impress the people being called up again.
An independent October 7 inquiry would also have to be agreed upon before entry, with the freedom to examine political and security failures wherever the evidence leads. Its findings could not become grounds for renegotiating the coalition’s commitment to its independence.
The parties would also need to agree on which changes to the balance among the government, the Knesset, and the courts require their joint consent. Lawyers would have to examine how to make those commitments enforceable.
A coalition document cannot simply award ministers powers the law does not give them. Israelis have already had enough experience with assurances that looked better at the signing ceremony.
South Africa provides a useful comparison. When the African National Congress lost its parliamentary majority in 2024, Cyril Ramaphosa retained the presidency, while the Democratic Alliance and other parties gained executive responsibilities under an agreed-upon minimum program. The arrangement ran into a serious budget dispute in 2025. The disputes were part of the difficulty of sharing authority.
Our opposition parties should negotiate together, with entry conditional on the same agreement. Sending one leader across first leaves him defending the handshake while everyone else explains why they would never have been so foolish. Their authorized party institutions should approve the deal before they enter, sharing responsibility for the concessions as well as the achievements.
Another Likud prime minister could, in principle, make the same broad partnership easier. I consider that very unlikely. Netanyahu’s personal mandate among his voters, his ongoing trial, and his own calculations about leaving office all weigh against assuming he will step aside. His consent or a genuine internal change in Likud would be needed. Neither is something a columnist can supply.
There may be an additional reason for these leaders to work together: a regional diplomatic initiative, explored with Washington and willing Arab partners alongside the coalition negotiations.
First, find out what is available. What security cooperation, diplomatic steps, and investment could be offered? What would Israel have to commit to, including on the Palestinian question? Netanyahu could pursue an achievement he values while his partners helped write the conditions Israel would accept.
I am not reporting an offer or ongoing negotiations. If no credible opportunity emerges, it should be dropped from the coalition calculation. We cannot ask people to accept a painful domestic compromise in exchange for a regional promise nobody has made.
Italy’s broad government under Mario Draghi had a substantial European recovery program, backed by grants and loans, to administer in 2021. Even with that concrete purpose, it collapsed in July 2022 when political support fractured. The money was real. Political loyalty remained more complicated.
Netanyahu may believe another election would improve his position. His rivals may believe joining him would finish their careers. An offer has to change those calculations to have a chance.
The man I interviewed in the middle of the night did not look ready to go home. I would rather test what he is prepared to give up to keep governing, and what his opponents could deliver in return, than wait for exhaustion to settle Israeli politics.

Brazil's President Lula won, but its people elected ‘a divided government’ - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:11:39 UTC
13:11:39 KST

Flávio Bolsonaro was already in the United States by Tuesday, two days after losing Brazil’s presidential election. Back home, his own party's leaders had accepted President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory. Bolsonaro had not, and Brazilian markets were still digesting a result many investors had not prepared for.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Voters gave Lula 51.79% of valid ballots, a margin of more than 4.4 million votes. That was enough to keep the left in the presidential palace, but not to give it control across Brasília. Lula will begin his fourth term facing a stronger conservative presence in Congress, strained public finances and fresh trouble with US President Donald Trump’s administration. The vote also made a rapid repair in relations with Israel less likely, despite Bolsonaro’s campaign promise to deliver one.
The final count was 64,256,232 for Lula and 59,826,041 for Bolsonaro. Lula trailed in the first round, making the runoff result both a comeback and a reelection. The congressional vote told a different story. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party won 121 seats in the lower chamber and 28 in the Senate. Gilson Schwartz of the University of São Paulo estimates that the broader right now holds about 59% of the Chamber of Deputies.
“Brazil has therefore elected not a left-wing political regime, but a divided government,” Schwartz told The Media Line in written responses. He said the split reflected an electorate less ideologically consistent than the country’s polarization suggests. Voters backed Lula for social protection, institutional stability, and his personal political standing, while supporting conservative congressional candidates on crime, taxes, regulation, and cultural issues, Schwartz explained.
That division will likely hinder the president’s domestic agenda. Congress can block large spending packages and sweeping institutional changes, but it can also demand money for lawmakers’ districts and favored projects. Igor Barenboim, a former Brazilian secretary of economic policy and a Harvard University doctorate holder, rejected the notion that a conservative legislature would automatically impose fiscal discipline.
“Congress likes to spend. That’s what they do,” Barenboim told The Media Line. Lawmakers have strong incentives to send money to their constituencies, he said, regardless of whether they sit on the right or the left. Even so, he expects Lula’s long experience with coalition politics to produce a workable arrangement with the center and moderate right.
Economic effects of Brazilian election results
Monday’s selloff was severe. The Ibovespa closed 13.88% lower after trading was temporarily halted, and the dollar gained more than 8% against the real. Barenboim’s reading of the move was less dramatic than the closing numbers. He said money had flowed into Brazilian assets after Bolsonaro led the first round, and traders who had bet on a change of government rushed to unwind those positions once Lula won.
For Barenboim, the harder numbers are in the public accounts. He estimated that government debt rose from about 72% to 83% of gross domestic product during Lula’s third term. Brazil’s potential growth is still around 2% a year, while the primary deficit is close to half a percentage point of GDP. Once high real interest rates are included, he puts the nominal deficit at roughly 9%. The government’s demand for credit then makes money scarcer and more expensive for private companies, he said, leaving fewer investments worth undertaking.
Lula campaigned on expanded public programs, leaving investors waiting to see which promises survive the election. Naming a market-friendly finance minister would help calm sentiment, Barenboim said, but the president's decisions will matter more than personnel. “What matters is what the president wants to do. And we don’t know,” he said.
Barenboim expects Lula to pursue limited consolidation, probably by withdrawing tax breaks that the government classifies as tax expenditures rather than through dramatic spending cuts. His central scenario is one of “muddling through,” with Lula doing enough to prevent fiscal disorganization but stopping well short of the adjustment sought by many investors.
The political pressure is not confined to the budget. Bolsonaro refused to concede Sunday and initially said he would seek to annul the election because voting was extended at some polling locations following transportation problems and severe weather. His campaign had also requested additional voting time in affected areas. Only about 34,300 ballots were cast after the original closing time, far below Lula’s winning margin, and Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party later recognized the result announced by the Superior Electoral Court.
Bolsonaro subsequently shifted his argument, saying he would seek to disqualify the Lula ticket over alleged abuse of political and economic power. By Tuesday, he had traveled to the United States after failing to surrender his passports as ordered in a separate money-laundering investigation. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing in that case. A senior US official said he and his family would be granted visas, although Washington did not announce that he had received asylum.
Schwartz said the legal challenge appeared weak but warned that questioning the election could still keep Bolsonaro’s supporters mobilized through Congress, social media and allies abroad. His departure may reduce his ability to manage the opposition day to day while strengthening his symbolic position among its most radical members.
“The danger is the emergence of a kind of transnational opposition operating simultaneously through Brazil’s powerful conservative congressional bloc and political networks in the United States,” Schwartz said. Whether Bolsonaro can lead it from abroad, he added, will depend on whether governors, senators, and party officials continue to accept his family’s leadership after another presidential defeat.
Trump questions results of Brazilian election
Trump has questioned the Brazilian result without presenting evidence of fraud. His administration’s willingness to admit Bolsonaro and his family has added another point of friction to a relationship already strained by trade disputes and Washington’s interest in Brazil’s critical minerals. Schwartz said Brasília should distinguish between legitimate US economic interests and interference in Brazilian institutions. “Sovereignty is the red line,” he said.
Neither Schwartz nor Barenboim expects the argument with Washington to end in a diplomatic or commercial break. Barenboim described Brazil as a relatively closed economy whose exports are concentrated in products such as soybeans, corn and coffee. Washington has an interest in Brazilian rare earths, he said, but little incentive to confront Brazil on a scale that would seriously damage both countries. His principal caveat was the banking system: US financial sanctions would be far more consequential than a political quarrel or another round of tariffs.
Messages from the region offered Lula an early measure of room to maneuver. Presidents José Antonio Kast of Chile, Keiko Fujimori of Peru, Daniel Noboa of Ecuador and Abelardo de la Espriella of Colombia all acknowledged his victory, although each governs from the right or center-right. Their governments still need Brazil on border security, energy, infrastructure, migration and the Amazon. Schwartz said those interests make practical cooperation more likely than an effort to divide South America into rival ideological camps.
A Bolsonaro administration would have changed Brasília’s posture toward Israel almost immediately. He had pledged to move the Brazilian Embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, receive a new Israeli ambassador and expand defense cooperation. Lula offers no such opening. He has accused Israel of genocide in Gaza, supported Palestinian statehood and intervened in South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice. Neither country currently has an ambassador posted in the other’s capital.
The diplomatic chill has not stopped cargo from moving. According to Schwartz, Brazil sold about $569 million in goods to Israel in 2025 and bought roughly $1.3 billion. Food, fertilizer, machinery, technology and medical equipment remained part of that exchange. Brazilian agricultural sales to Israel from January through September 2026 had already passed the figure for all of 2025.
Brazil and Israel may enter 2027 without ambassadors, but they won't be without business to conduct. Fertilizer, food, machinery and medical equipment continue to move even as official channels remain diminished. For Lula, the more revealing test will be whether he can turn that stubborn commercial connection into political access, defending Palestinian statehood without allowing Brazil’s criticism of the Israeli government to become a refusal to engage with Israel itself.

5 things Westminster doesn’t know about the UK economy (but probably should)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

5 things Westminster doesn’t know about the UK economy (but probably should)
From immigration to the number of rough sleepers on Britain’s streets, experts tell POLITICO’s Westminster Insider that the data used in government is notoriously patchy.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey attend the Labour Conference in Liverpool, England on Sept. 28, 2026. | Ian Forsyth/Getty Images
LONDON — Britain’s government runs on numbers — but what if they’re a shot in the dark?
From tepid economic growth to squeezed household incomes, this week’s budget from Chancellor John Healey was packed with grim figures about the state of play in the U.K. — and a host of costly measures to try and turn things around.
Yet it’s almost certain that the budget forecasts Healey relied upon Wednesday will be revised by the time the next fiscal event rolls around.
Advertisement
In this week’s episode of the Westminster Insider podcast, POLITICO unpacked the numbers that govern the U.K. — and found out just how many doubts there are about the information the country relies on.
1. True levels of immigration
Few issues divide Brits like immigration — but grappling with hard data on the issue has proven to be a repeated challenge to governments of all stripes.
For decades, immigration into the U.K. was calculated by the International Passenger Survey (IPS) — essentially people with clipboards at airports, train stations and ports asking people about their intention to stay in the U.K.
The Eurostar platform is pictured at St. Pancras station in London on Nov. 14, 2007. | Cate Gillon/Getty Images
But between 2012 and 2020, the number of European Union nationals coming into the country was off by 76% — or 93,000 people a year. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) only discovered this error after trialing a new approach to counting immigration that focused less heavily on the IPS, which was dropped altogether in 2025.
The ONS now uses this new measurement — relying on a combination of Home Office data, information from the Department for Work and Pensions and tax receipts.
But this was again wrong in the year to June 2023 — by 234,000 people.
Advertisement
The original numbers published by the ONS in November 2023 said net migration to the U.K. was 672,000. A year later, the ONS admitted there had been a mistake and said it was in fact 906,000.
Laura Gilbert, who ran data science in No. 10 Downing Street until last year, told POLITICO that net migration numbers are often incredibly misleading — and even the way we calculate those numbers is “highly spurious.”
Gilbert says the quality of the numbers on immigration normally improves months later, sometimes by “quite a lot.” But she warned, “if politicians are making a decision based on exact numbers, often they are using the first number that comes out, which is the worst one.”
2. The scale of unemployment
Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have vowed to get welfare spending down “but in a Labour way.” Much of this will rest on getting young people into work, the subject of a 217-page report by Tony Blair-era minister Alan Milburn.
But Britain’s workforce — and the number of young people out of work — is counted by the Labour Force Survey (LFS), an ONS measurement beset with issues.
For example, between 2019 and 2024, the LFS missed 1 million workers because people with full-time jobs are less likely to answer the phone to surveyors during the week, according to the Resolution Foundation think tank.
Advertisement
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) admitted just this week that the survey is too unreliable to measure productivity. “In recent years, falling response rates have significantly affected the quality of the LFS, making it more difficult to estimate reliably the number of workers and the hours they work,” the watchdog said.
Gilbert says Healey’s claim that there are “1 million young people out of work” is unlikely to be accurate.
The number of NEETs — people not in education, employment or training — is also based on figures from a subset of the LFS, which is particularly susceptible to inaccuracies.
Healey leaves No. 11 Downing St. in London to present the budget to Parliament on Oct. 28, 2026. | Peter Nicholls/Getty Images
“I think being within 50,000 on either side of that number is very unlikely to be the sort of level of accuracy that you’re at,” Gilbert said. “It’s entirely spurious, if I’m completely honest, but it’s a big number, you write it down, and everyone reads the papers.”
Ben Warner, who set up 10DS, Downing Street’s data science unit, says the LFS can’t accurately measure the number of entrepreneurs arriving in the country, either, making it difficult for ministers to know if decisions — such as a much-hyped tax relief for founders — are actually encouraging people to come to the U.K.
“I’m willing to bet you a hundred quid [we don’t have accurate numbers] at the level that you would need to make thoughtful policy around this,” Warner said. “I am sure there are people who have very, very good knowledge of the economic statistics. But if you’re a minister, you don’t necessarily have access.”
Advertisement
3. Where inflation and GDP sit
These are hugely important measures for a government: Are costs rising for households — and is the British economy growing?
But buried inside this week’s budget assessment by the OBR was a startling admission: There is a one in five chance inflation in 2027 will come in at over 4.5% … and the same chance it will be under 2.5%. They are profoundly different outcomes for the cost of living, a top political issue.
Warner told POLITICO, “The whole thing is mental. We are discussing the uncertainty of the numbers and pretending that these are real.”
Gilbert says there are knock-on effects at play: problems with net migration numbers and workforce data bleed into inflation and GDP projections.
“Understanding migration tells us about the demographics of the country, and when we look at how many people are in work, and that is wildly undercounted, it looks like there are more people who are unemployed, which has a knock-on effect on GDP and inflation,” she explained.
4. The number of kids on free school meals
The number of pupils in England on free school meals is just over 2.2 million, according to government statistics from the start of this year. That’s more than a quarter of all children in the country.
Advertisement
But Gilbert warns that these numbers are likely to be overestimated because schools “game the system” when census data is collected. “So for anyone who has children in school they may have received a text message that says don’t send them to school with a packed lunch — because the schools get funding based on how many children are on school meals,” she said.
5. The number of rough sleepers on the streets
One of Burnham’s flagship promises when he became prime minister was to end homelessness in the U.K., and Wednesday’s budget put £432 million towards precisely that promise.
Yet the way rough sleepers are counted in the U.K. varies according to each council, with some areas relying on an estimate and others on a street count — sending workers out to physically count the number of people on the streets on a particular day in autumn.
Tents line the side of Euston Road in London on Nov. 13, 2025. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Some councils have swapped between methods — which can make it look as though they have dramatically reduced their rough sleepers from one year to the next.
For example, in 2017 Brighton and Hove Council used an estimate of rough sleepers which put that number at 176. The following year, the council used a street count — but this took place on a snowy night, so the number fell to 68.
This made it appear as though the number of people experiencing homelessness had been more than halved.

Modern Architecture in Bahia: Climate and Culture in the Work of Assis Reis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Last October 24th marked the centenary of the birth of Brazilian architect Francisco de Assis Couto Reis (1926–2011), who lived and built most of his work in the city of Salvador, Bahia. Assis Reis, as he was better known, had a career shaped not only by the buildings he designed but also by his urban renewal proposals, his design for the Brazilian Pavilion at the World Expo in Osaka, Japan (unbuilt), and the Scale Model of the City of Salvador, landmarked in 2020. His vast and diverse body of work belongs to a specific moment of modern expression in Brazil, when architects of this "second generation" were particularly concerned with adapting to local climatic, geographical, and cultural conditions.
Born in Aracaju, Sergipe, on October 24, 1926, and raised in Parnaíba, Piauí, Assis Reis moved to Salvador in 1942. In 1957, he graduated with a degree in architecture from the Faculty of Architecture of the Federal University of Bahia (UFBA), an institution where he began teaching in 1968, contributing to the development of contemporary architectural thought in Bahia.

How Ireland plans to beat the data center backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Cables link servers in carefully controlled environments inside Servecentric Data Centre on the outskirts of Dublin on December 10, 2018. | Paul Faith/AFP via Getty Images
TALLAGHT, Ireland — In a suburban industrial park south of Dublin, a sprawling mass of tubes, vents and steel stretches as far as the eye can see, forming a dense web of gray monoliths that encircle the city.
As the EU’s tech capital, where most of the world’s technology giants have their European headquarters, Ireland was ground zero for the backlash against the energy-guzzling data centers needed to power the promised revolution of artificial intelligence.
Dublin is now leading an experiment within Europe to force tech firms to invest in renewable energy. As pushback spreads across Europe and data centers prove a hot-button issue for the U.S. midterm elections, that puts Ireland at the vanguard of countries globally that are trying to quell voter anger over financial and environmental disruptions caused by data centers.
Advertisement
Back in 2021, Ireland was far ahead of the curve in slamming the brakes on data centers as its utilities regulator almost entirely halted new facilities connecting to the creaking electricity grid around Dublin. Authorities warned that the exploding data center industry posed a “significant” risk to the security of the country’s electricity supply.
Last year when the effective moratorium was lifted, Ireland imposed a checklist for tech firms that want to connect new data centers to the grid. That includes requirements to fund new renewable energy projects in Ireland to meet at least 80% of their energy demands.
As countries from the Netherlands to Denmark and U.S. states from New York to Oregon consider their own moratoriums, Ireland’s approach is a test as to whether strict clean-energy rules can be part of the solution — or whether they will gradually drive investment away from the region while sucking up local renewable energy supplies and continuing to alienate locals.
“The mood music coming out of Europe now is Ireland’s the canary in the coal mine,” said Ronan Kelly, chief executive of data center lobby Digital Infrastructure Ireland. “We’re leading the charge to say we need to take a responsible approach to building new data center infrastructure and new capacity. We can’t just turn up diesel generators and run them 24 hours a day.”
Leading the charge
Ireland is at the top of the EU’s rankings on data-center capacity, with 31 megawatts per 100,000 people — more than triple the capacity of the Netherlands in second place.
That still trails well behind data center hotspots in the U.S. like Virginia, Texas and California, where more than one in three Americans live within five miles of a center that’s already operating.
Advertisement
Data centers accounted for almost a quarter of all electricity use in Ireland last year, a surge from 5% a decade ago, and close to the same amount of electricity used by all of the country’s households combined. A UN report in June described Ireland’s dense data center web as a “cautionary” tale of how not to let AI infrastructure growth outpace local power grids.
Brussels is looking to get out in front of the issue, with the European Commission's green transition and competition chief Teresa Ribera telling POLITICO that the EU should force tech firms to invest in clean energy to power their data centers.
As the EU works on upcoming energy efficiency standards for data centers, Kelly said the “worrying” part for Ireland’s data center sector, and the 875,000 jobs it underpins, is whether other countries in Europe will follow suit with similar rules — or if Ireland’s requirements will be an “anomaly” that drives data investment elsewhere.
Countries like Spain and Germany have introduced rules for data centers to show that a certain portion of their electricity consumption is covered by renewables. But Ireland has gone one step further in asking data center developers to fund new renewable energy projects.
For Microsoft, one of the biggest data center investors and operators in Ireland, the clarity around renewables is a “critical” green light to keep investing in Irish projects. The U.S. tech giant has said it already matches 100% of its global energy consumption with renewables, mainly through power purchase agreements with renewable energy providers.
James O’Connor, site lead for Microsoft Ireland, said the company is now moving to the design stage for a “significant” new data center development at Jiggenstown outside Naas, although the project is already facing local opposition.
Advertisement
“We understand the public concerns that are out there, clearly, when you have this sort of demand on electricity,” O’Connor said. “[But] I think we have a huge opportunity to tap into huge amounts of renewable energy, because we can invest in that, we can provide consistent demand, and we know that's going to be critical.”
The largest share of Ireland’s electricity last year at 40% came from burning gas, but the share of electricity generated by wind reached 32%. The island nation still has massive untapped potential to produce renewables from offshore wind.
Cannibalizing renewables
Ireland’s new data center policy requires companies to immediately provide their own power, and they have six years to get new renewable projects up and running to bring that power up to 80% renewable energy.
Environmental activists have warned that in the first six years, new data centers could still be mostly powered by fossil fuels like gas generators, driving up emissions and electricity prices.
“On paper it looks good, but in practice it's actually quite dangerous,” said Rosi Leonard, from environmental NGO Friends of the Earth Ireland. “It doesn't seem to hold up against Ireland’s climate commitments, because it’s creating the conditions for a massive build out [of new data centers]. But companies have a six-year glide path to build out the renewables.”
Friends of the Earth Ireland is part of a group of environmental organizations lodging a case against Ireland’s utilities regulator over the new rules, and is campaigning for a complete moratorium on new data centers, as well as limits on the expansion of existing facilities.
Advertisement
When 80% of data center power eventually comes from renewables, Leonard said, that’s a lot of renewable energy going towards fueling AI. Ireland's Climate Change Advisory Council has warned that data centers are “cannibalising any increase in Irish renewable capacity.”
“What happens in terms of the existing industries and sectors that need to decarbonize?” Leonard asked. “You're giving one industry permission to expand at a very significant rate, saying it’s no problem because you need to build renewables, but that actually will reduce the share of renewables on the system as a whole.”
Economic trade offs
A recent report commissioned by the Irish government says data centers are “fundamental to Ireland’s position as a leading global hub for digital and technology-driven enterprise,” noting that jobs dependent on data centers bring in about €14.6 billion in annual employment-related taxes.
The report was criticized by Irish MEP Lynn Boylan from the left-wing Sinn Féin party for omitting findings on how data center expansion could drive up people's electricity bills.
Standing outside the Amazon data center in Tallaght, David McManus, a local councilor in South Dublin from Fine Gael, the center-right party currently in coalition government, said data centers are part of the deal that comes with Big Tech.
“This is part and parcel of what Amazon, Google, Microsoft see as being essential to their operations,” he said. "You can't just turn around to these high-tech companies and say, yes, we want the high-paid engineers, and lots of people employed, but we don't want the data centers that back it all up."
Advertisement
McManus points out that heat from the data center is piped into nearby social housing, the library, and other council buildings. South Dublin County Council also brought in more than €30 million in commercial rates from data centers last year.
“They are consuming a lot of [energy] on the national grid, but that also generates revenue for us to invest in the national grid,” he said. “Ultimately, when it comes to AI and data centers, it’s tempting to put up the fortress fence and say ‘no, we won't have any of this.’ If that's the case, we should be going back to where the economy was probably 10 years ago where we had less employment, less high paying jobs, less income tax, and less corporation tax."
But Leonard said voters perceive that Big Tech firms have too much power: “A lot of these companies have lobbied quite heavily at EU level, not to have to disclose certain energy and water metrics ... people just feel like this is just a joke at this stage, how much power these companies have.”

New York state police will take over future sexual assault investigations at Cornell University, Governor Kathy Hochul said on Thursday, in the latest fallout over the university's handling of an alleged gang-rape on campus.
The announcement follows widespread criticism of the university's conduct in the case and questions about why no criminal charges were filed after a woman identified only as Jane Doe said she was raped by members of a Cornell fraternity.
New York state police and Cornell University signed an agreement that sexual offense complaints, which normally fall under the jurisdiction of campus police, will be referred to state police for criminal investigation unless otherwise requested by the accuser, Hochul said in a statement.
"When someone reports sexual assault, they deserve to be heard, treated with compassion, and know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated," Hochul said in her announcement.
Referring to the Jane Doe allegations as "horrifying," Hochul said: "Survivors should be able to trust the institutions responsible for protecting them. We cannot afford to let them down."
Hochul previously named Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to reopen the criminal investigation into Jane Doe's complaint, and a committee of Cornell's board of trustees appointed former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct a review of the university's response to sexual assault claims.
No confidence vote underway
Jane Doe said she was drugged and gang-raped during a visit to the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, according to a civil lawsuit filed this year.
Fraternity members pressured her to take ketamine and sexually assaulted her over several hours while she was too intoxicated to consent, the suit alleges, naming seven former students.
Attorneys for the fraternity members have denied the allegations. Some of the attorneys have said the sexual activity was consensual, while others have disputed their clients' participation in the events described in the lawsuit.
Although Cornell expelled or disciplined several of the students involved in the incident, no criminal charges were filed.
The lawsuit triggered widespread criticism of the university in Ithaca, New York, with students, alumni and advocates calling for greater transparency about how the school handles sexual assault claims.
Cornell's Faculty Senate is currently moving forward with a vote of no confidence against the university administration. About 135 members of the governing body can vote on the non-binding resolution from Friday until November 6, the Cornell Daily Sun reported.
"The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University," the resolution reads.

Addressing a Security Council meeting on maritime security, Gholamhossein Darzi rejected attempts by Western powers to blame Tehran for disruptions in the vital waterway, emphasizing that Iran has consistently upheld freedom of navigation as a responsible coastal state for decades, the Tehran-based Press TV reported.
“Regrettably, at today's meeting, some speakers have once again ignored the root causes of the current situation,” the envoy stated. “The responsibility for any disruption, obstruction, or other interference with maritime navigation in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz lies directly with the aggressors and those who facilitate or assist their act of aggression against Iran.”
He added, “Attempts to shift this responsibility onto Iran are unfounded and lack credibility.”
The Iranian diplomat clarified that the Strait of Hormuz—a crucial global maritime trade route—remained entirely open and secure until February 28, 2026. Since that date, he noted, the US and the Israeli regime launched a "brutal war of aggression" against Iran, deliberately targeting the country's civilian and maritime infrastructure, ports, and vessels.
To illustrate the gravity of the US military campaign, the envoy detailed a series of specific, unlawful attacks on Iranian assets.
He noted that on April 19, 2026, US military forces attacked the Iranian commercial vessel Tuska. Less than two months later, on May 23, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) reported redirecting 100 commercial vessels in a move to enforce its illegal naval blockade against Iran.
The envoy further said that on July 23, US forces attacked two Iranian search and rescue vessels, Naji 15 and Naji 16, inside Iran's territorial waters while they were actively engaged in humanitarian operations.

‘Flagrant violation’

Beyond the military implications, the diplomat highlighted the severe humanitarian toll of the siege.
“The US blockade threatens civilian access to food, medicine, fuel, and other essential supplies, imposes collective punishment, and deprives them of essential needs indispensable to their survival,” he warned.
Reaffirming Tehran's position, the envoy stressed that any restrictions or security measures implemented by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz are entirely defensive and lawful.
“As a coastal state, Iran has the legitimate right under international law to take all necessary and appropriate measures to protect its sovereign rights, its territorial integrity, its people, and its vital national interests against the US ongoing threat or aggression,” he declared.
The Iranian representative demanded full accountability for the severe violations of international law and the damages inflicted upon Iranian civilians.
He called upon the Security Council to abandon its silence and explicitly demand that the United States immediately cease its unlawful acts.
“Iran will pursue all available legal avenues to ensure that those responsible are held to account,” the envoy concluded.

Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:50:51 UTC
12:50:51 KST

Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK)
- Summary:
- Earth is warming faster than ever recorded, with scientists detecting a major acceleration in global temperatures since around 2015. A new study reveals that the warming rate has surged to approximately 0.35°C per decade, nearly double the average pace observed from 1970 to 2015. After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence.
- Share:
Global warming has accelerated sharply over the past decade, with Earth heating up faster than at any point since modern temperature records began in 1880. A new study from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) provides the first statistically significant evidence that the pace of global warming has increased since around 2015, even after accounting for natural factors that temporarily raise or lower global temperatures.
Researchers found that the planet has warmed at a rate of approximately 0.35°C per decade over the past 10 years, although the exact figure varies depending on the temperature dataset used. That is nearly twice the average rate of just under 0.2°C per decade recorded between 1970 and 2015. The findings suggest that global temperatures are not simply continuing to rise. The rate at which they are increasing has also become substantially faster.
"We can now demonstrate a strong and statistically significant acceleration of global warming since around 2015," says Grant Foster, a US statistics expert and co-author of the study, published in the scientific journal Geophysical Research Letters.
Scientists Uncover a Hidden Acceleration in Global Warming
Detecting changes in the underlying pace of global warming is more complicated than simply comparing temperatures from one year to the next. Natural climate patterns can temporarily make the planet warmer or cooler, potentially obscuring longer trends.
For example, El Niño can temporarily increase global temperatures by releasing heat from the tropical Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere. Volcanic eruptions can have the opposite effect when particles released into the atmosphere reflect sunlight back into space. Changes in solar activity can also influence how much energy Earth receives from the Sun.
These natural variations create fluctuations in temperature records that can make it difficult to determine whether the underlying warming trend is accelerating.
To address this problem, the researchers mathematically adjusted the temperature observations to account for these known influences. This allowed them to examine the longer warming trend more clearly, without the temporary fluctuations that can disguise changes in its pace.
"We filter out known natural influences in the observational data, so that the 'noise' is reduced, making the underlying long-term warming signal more clearly visible," Foster added.
The team analyzed five major global temperature datasets (NASA, NOAA, HadCRUT, Berkeley Earth, ERA5). These widely used records combine observations and, in some cases, additional atmospheric data to track how Earth's temperature has changed over time.
The results were remarkably consistent. Regardless of which dataset or statistical method the researchers used, they found strong evidence that global warming has accelerated.
"The adjusted data show an acceleration of global warming since 2015 with a statistical certainty of over 98 percent, consistent across all data sets examined and independent of the analysis method chosen," explains Stefan Rahmstorf, PIK researcher and lead author of the study.
In statistical terms, this means the evidence for a change in the warming trend is strong enough that the researchers could distinguish it from ordinary fluctuations in the temperature record with a confidence level exceeding 98 percent.
Even After Adjustments, 2023 and 2024 Remain the Hottest Years
One important question was whether the extraordinary global temperatures recorded in 2023 and 2024 were making the recent warming trend appear steeper than it actually was.
Both years were exceptionally hot, partly because of natural influences such as El Niño and a period of heightened solar activity known as the solar maximum. During a solar maximum, the Sun reaches the most active phase of its approximately 11-year cycle.
After accounting for these effects, the researchers found that the adjusted temperatures for 2023 and 2024 were somewhat lower than the original observations. Nevertheless, both years remained the warmest since instrumental temperature records began.
The analysis also revealed that signs of accelerating warming were already emerging in 2013 or 2014 across all five temperature datasets, indicating that the finding was not simply the result of unusually high temperatures during the most recent years.
To determine whether the warming rate had changed since the 1970s, the researchers used two different statistical techniques. The first, called quadratic trend analysis, looks for a curved pattern in temperature records that would indicate warming is speeding up rather than continuing at a constant rate.
The second, a piecewise linear model, compares warming trends across different periods and identifies when the rate of temperature increase appears to have changed. Unlike an approach that assumes the acceleration began in a particular year, this method allows the data to determine the most likely timing of the shift.
Both approaches supported the conclusion that global warming has accelerated significantly.
What Is Causing Global Warming to Accelerate?
Although the findings provide strong statistical evidence that global warming is speeding up, the study was not designed to determine exactly why the acceleration has occurred.
The researchers emphasize this distinction because detecting a change in the warming rate is different from identifying the physical processes responsible for it.
However, the observed acceleration is consistent with what current climate models can produce. These models use established physical principles to simulate how Earth's atmosphere, oceans, ice, and land respond to changes in the climate system.
The findings therefore do not suggest that climate models are fundamentally incapable of representing the recent increase in warming. Instead, they provide additional observational evidence that the pace of climate change can vary significantly over time.
Could Earth Exceed the Paris Agreement Limit Before 2030?
The acceleration has important implications for international efforts to limit global warming.
Under the Paris Agreement, countries agreed to pursue efforts to limit the long-term rise in global temperatures to 1.5°C above preindustrial levels. This threshold refers to sustained global warming rather than a single unusually hot year.
If the warming rate measured over the past decade continues, researchers warn that the planet could cross that threshold on a long-term basis sooner than previously anticipated.
"If the warming rate of the past 10 years continues, it would lead to a long-term exceedance of the 1.5°C limit of the Paris Agreement before 2030," says Stefan Rahmstorf. "How quickly the Earth continues to warm ultimately depends on how rapidly we reduce global CO2 emissions from fossil fuels to zero."
The study highlights an increasingly important concern: Earth's temperature is not only rising, but has been rising considerably faster in recent years than during the preceding decades. Whether that rapid pace continues will have major consequences for how quickly the world reaches critical climate thresholds.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- G. Foster, S. Rahmstorf. Global Warming Has Accelerated Significantly. Geophysical Research Letters, 2026; 53 (5) DOI: 10.1029/2025GL118804

Binance hit by $6.3 billion security breach in potential record crypto heist
Binance said on Thursday that a security breach had affected an estimated $6.3 billion in assets, potentially making it the biggest cryptocurrency heist on record. The world's largest crypto exchange said it had recovered or frozen about $3 billion, while analysts have pinned the blame for the hack on North Korea.
Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record theft that analysts pinned on North Korea and said could shake faith in digital assets.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would cover the losses. About half the stolen assets were quickly frozen by stablecoin issuers such as Tether, Circle and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial.
The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order wallets that Binance uses to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the US Federal Bureau of Investigation had attributed to Pyongyang.

"TRM attributes the attack to ... North Korea’s elite hacking unit," the firm said in an analysis of the hack posted to its website. Both TRM and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible.
'Biggest hack in history'
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
Binance said user funds were safe and that it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It expects to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours.
It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion.
"Your money is safe and we're covering every loss," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. "Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual."
"It's the biggest hack in history," Aravind Srinivasan at market maker GSR said as crypto prices fell broadly.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilised.
BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to CoinGecko, while shaky confidence hit listed crypto exchange shares.
Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global, which said it was unaffected, slid 4.8%, while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading.

Compromised labtop
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance's engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.
"Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident," Binance said.
Mark Karpeles, former chief of defunct Tokyo-based bitcoin exchange Mt Gox, which collapsed a dozen years ago after $500 million in bitcoin was stolen, said attackers probably accessed private keys for at least two Binance wallets.
"Binance appears to have split its assets across multiple systems, ensuring a hack can only affect a part of the assets, but even so a single hack is a large loss," he said.
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.

Hack size tops Binance secure asset fund
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2025 annual report.
The crypto exchange runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a $1 billion reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website.
Co-CEO Teng said that "and company funds" will cover losses.
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
World Liberty Financial said it worked with custodian BitGo to freeze funds, and Binance co-founder Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen. Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's vulnerability to hackers.

Asia-focused investment firm PAG will acquire a 51 percent stake in Evergrande Property Services Group, a unit of debt-laden developer China Evergrande Group, for HK$4.03 billion, the two said in a joint announcement on Friday.
The acquisition marks a major step in liquidators' efforts to sell assets and recover funds for creditors of China Evergrande, which received a combined US$46 billion in creditor claims.
The sale follows a competitive auction run by the liquidators, according to the filed announcement.
PAG said in the filing that Evergrande Property's business generated stable, recurring revenue from a diversified portfolio of managed properties across China.
PAG said taking control of the listed services unit would remove uncertainty tied to the liquidation of China Evergrande and CEG Holdings, and could strengthen market confidence.
PAG will fund the acquisition and the offer, if fully accepted, with acquisition financing and equity committed by PAG Fund IV, the filing said.
The offer values the 5.52 billion shares at HK$0.8359 each, a 29 percent discount to Evergrande Property's last closing price on Wednesday. 
The stock was suspended on Thursday pending the announcement and dropped 13.5 percent after trading resumed on Friday.
The offer values Evergrande Property Services at about HK$9.04 billion, compared to a market capitalisation of roughly HK$11.08 billion after the shares dropped to HK$1.025.
PAG will also pay 500 million yuan at completion for certain taxes, transaction fees and other liabilities of CEG Holdings, according to the filing.
Following completion of the deal, PAG will be required to make an unconditional offer for the remaining 5.3 billion shares in the company.
Goldman Sachs is advising PAG on the acquisition and potential mandatory offer, while UBS and Citic Securities are joint financial advisers to China Evergrande and CEG Holdings.
The deal remains subject to Chinese antitrust approval, among other conditions. 
The parties can terminate the agreement if these conditions are not met or waived by February 12, 2027, according to the filing.
China Evergrande, once China's premier property developer, defaulted on most of its US$300 billion in liabilities following Beijing's sweeping crackdown on the property sector six years ago.
The liquidators of China Evergrande and CEG Holdings informed Evergrande Property a year ago that they were seeking  to sell the 51.016 percent stake, according to the filing.
PAG intends to keep Evergrande Property listed in Hong Kong and does not plan major changes to its operations or workforce, apart from nominating new directors at the earliest time permitted under takeover.

It might have turned some heads when Luis Carlos Rúa attended the 2026 TIME100 Next gala in a full white elephant suit. But for the newly elected Colombian senator, the outfit wasn’t a fashion statement; it’s central to his mission as an advocate and political influencer against corruption.
Rúa had been making videos on Instagram and TikTok for five years anonymously under the name Elefante blanco, or the White Elephant, a reference to the unfinished and wasteful infrastructure projects that Rúa exposes.
Earlier this year, he was elected to the Senate of Colombia after revealing his identity just three days before the vote. Rúa told TIME on the red carpet before the gala, which took place on Oct. 29 in Manhattan, that his work exposing government mismanagement is more important than ever.
“I have been traveling for five years in my country, denouncing massive public projects called white elephants, and in this moment in my country, we are facing the biggest one, the biggest white elephant in our history,” Rúa said.
Rúa was referring to what he calls insufficient rebuilding after a 7.4 magnitude earthquake hit Colombia in August, killing over 200 people and injuring 4,000 more. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the earthquake also left more than 45,000 homes damaged, 9,000 destroyed, and 140 buildings collapsed.
“I want to call the attention of the world, and to raise my voice, to say that the reconstruction of my country still doesn't begin,” Rúa said on the carpet. “I say to the Colombian President, begin the reconstruction of a country, because two months ago a big earthquake destroyed some cities…we need the reconstruction to begin from here.”
He directly addressed Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative backed by U.S. President Donald Trump before he was elected in a presidential runoff in June this year.
“There's people without home, people that lost their job, that lost families,” Rúa said. “We need the reconstruction to begin, President. It's your work. You have to do that.”
When asked about the best way for people to advocate for Colombians, Rúa recommended people follow in his footsteps, using social media as a way to call for government action.
“Go to the internet and you can explore the situation my country is facing in this moment, and make a video saying to the President: ‘We need the reconstruction to begin,’” he said. “That's the way the people can help from any space, from no matter what country.”

TOKYO, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Japan's industrial output climbed 2.2 percent in September from a month earlier, marking the first increase in three months, driven by a rebound in automobile production, government data showed Friday.
The expansion came after output shrank 2.4 percent in August.
According to a preliminary report released by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, the seasonally adjusted index of production at factories and mines stood at 104.1 against the 2020 base of 100.
Output grew in eight sectors, with motor vehicles, production machinery, and general-purpose and business-oriented machinery leading the gains. Seven sectors, including iron, steel and nonferrous metals, posted declines.
Based on a survey of manufacturers, the ministry projects output to increase 5.1 percent in October and 0.8 percent in November.
Meanwhile, the index of industrial shipments edged up 0.6 percent from the previous month to 101.0 in September, while that of inventories rose 2.5 percent to 99.9. ■
