Burnham tries to avoid a slavery reparations ‘disaster’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Prime Minister Andy Burnham will have an unofficial goal when he meets members of Britain’s former empire next week: Avoid a fight about slavery reparations.
Good luck, as they say, with that.
His predecessor Keir Starmer’s trip to the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, at a beach resort on the Pacific island of Samoa in 2024, is still the stuff of rueful mutters in parts of Whitehall.
Advertisement
Lined up in a semi-circle of armchairs — “like an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting,” as one person briefed on the gathering put it — leaders from many of the 56 Commonwealth nations negotiated live over a 16-page communique on laptops and tablets. Starmer, a barrister, found himself personally redrafting a key paragraph about reparations on a screen surrounded by other leaders, said two further people briefed on the meeting.
The unusually intimate format of the leaders’ retreat meant they had no officials with them on the veranda, and Starmer had just one civil servant — No. 10’s private secretary for foreign affairs — stationed in a tent close by. His chief of staff Morgan McSweeney was woken at 4 a.m. London time by a phone call to talk about the strategy for reparations.
That, however, was never clearly resolved. The retreat dragged on hours late; some leaders left before it was even over. Starmer was frustrated and felt he had been “ambushed,” said one U.K. official involved in the 2024 trip. A second said they had blocked the incident from their memory. A third said Starmer was left “furious,” adding: “He went in blind and it was terrible for him.” A fourth said simply: “It was a disaster.” All were granted anonymity to speak frankly.
The eventual communique agreed on a “conversation towards forging a common future based on equity.” This fudge kicked the issue of reparations down the road — where it now lands in Burnham’s lap.
Britain’s new prime minister will touch down at the biennial summit in Antigua and Barbuda next week to find the issue still firmly on some Caribbean and African leaders’ minds.
At the United Nations in May, 123 countries passed a motion calling for “inclusive, good-faith dialogue on reparatory justice.” The U.K. abstained. Barbados PM Mia Mottley announced a manifesto from Caribbean leaders on the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations in June. Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey said last week that an apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade “wouldn’t hurt.”
Advertisement
The visit will be a test of how Burnham — who has a reputation for speaking off the cuff, especially on issues of moral justice — maintains a delicate U.K. government line that reparations are not “the answer,” as Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told POLITICO last month. And Burnham will face that challenge in a unique spotlight: It will be his first overseas visit with King Charles III, who is the head of the Commonwealth.
POLITICO spoke to a dozen U.K. officials or politicians who were involved in the 2024 summit or the planning for Burnham’s upcoming visit. They painted a picture of acute anxiety in the British state over how to deal with calls for reparations from its former colonies; tensions between Downing Street and the Foreign Office over the handling of 2024; and serious questions in Whitehall about whether the summit is even useful for No. 10 — despite the king’s role leaving U.K. prime ministers little choice but to attend.
Burnham will not have to deal with the extreme jetlag and communications hurdles that dogged Starmer’s trip, which involved a 28-hour flight in each direction. But like Starmer, he will fly out at a time when his in-tray is crowded by other issues — not least the U.S. midterms happening at the same time and the domestic aftermath of his first budget, just unveiled this past Wednesday.
Keir Starmer attends a a state banquet during the CHOGM summit in Samoa, on Oct. 24, 2024. | Pool photo by Fiona Goodall via Getty Images
The first U.K. official quoted earlier in this story said: “There’s a sense that there can’t be a repeat of [2024] this time around.” The third U.K. official quoted above said: “I don’t understand why they’re making the same mistake. Does the prime minister really have to go?”
A No. 10 official, however, said Burnham made clear soon after taking power on July 20 that he was “very keen” to attend the summit. Miliband has “laid the groundwork so that things hopefully won’t be as tricky as they were in 2024,” this person added.
“Andy’s style is that he is an honest broker with people, and he will give an instinctive response to things,” the official said. “But the government’s position is clear that reparations are not seen as the right route. It’s a careful balancing act, but one that we’re well prepared for.”
Advertisement
Climate resilience fund in the works
One tactic for the current No. 10 will be to try to avoid talking about it public.
Downing Street has broken with recent precedent by deciding not to bring the usual “pack” of political journalists, taking a smaller media “pool” instead. This will limit the scope of questions that Burnham faces. (Political editors from news outlets, including POLITICO, have written to No. 10 to object to the arrangement.)
Timing could also allow the visit to slip under the radar. Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will be there alongside counterparts including Anthony Albanese of Australia and Mark Carney of Canada, creating a rare opportunity for them to discuss the implications of the U.S. midterm results in private. The symbolism, as “middle power” nations deal with a drift in U.S. relations under Donald Trump, would be obvious.
British PM Andy Burnham, center, leaves the stage at the end of the Labour Conference in Liverpool on Sept. 30, 2026. | Ian Forsyth/Getty Images
Officially, the agenda is to build an alliance that can boost these middle powers, along with the developing states that global summits usually overlook.
The Commonwealth Secretariat — the London-based body that co-ordinates the summit — said the aim of next week’s gathering is “partnerships and investment,” including in climate and youth employment, and removing trade barriers.
Likewise, the U.K. Foreign Office has been working on a climate resilience fund for developing nations, two people with knowledge of the talks said. A third said conversations in the U.K. government had focused on mobilizing public and private finance, and improving access to finance for climate-vulnerable countries.
Advertisement
Three people with knowledge of the planning emphasized that this summit would be an opportunity to build on relations with countries that could discuss bilateral trade, though they did not name specific nations and no U.K. trade ministers are due at the event.
“There will obviously be trade and investment discussions with a range of partners,” said one of the three people, a U.K. government official, who also noted that the U.K. will raise the impacts of El Niño. “The bigger picture is that we want to use the Commonwealth network to deepen trade and investment links across its 56 members — that Commonwealth advantage is one of the reasons the grouping matters to the UK.”
‘Playing Scrabble with words’
But leaders at these events, known by the awkward acronym CHOGM, can raise whatever topics they wish — reparations included.
Denis O’Brien, the Irish telecoms billionaire who founded the Repair Campaign calling for financial reparations to the Caribbean in 2022, said: “The conversation has moved radically forward.” He urged Britain and other European nations to “start off with an apology and then have an engagement,” adding: “The Foreign Office and the prime minister’s office are playing Scrabble with words — and unfortunately they’re leaving King Charles, who is so highly respected in the Caribbean, in a very difficult position.”
Paul Boateng, the Labour peer who was Britain’s first Black Cabinet minister and now campaigns on the issue, said Caribbean nations “are going to be pressing it. This issue is not going to go away.” The recent UN resolution reinforced Caribbean and African nations’ argument, argued Boateng: “We can’t be seen to simply ignore it … We cannot hold the Foreign Office line that it changes nothing.”
That position cast a long shadow two years ago.
Advertisement
No. 10 flew to Samoa in 2024 insisting reparations were “not on the agenda,” even though the summit’s free-wheeling format meant the choice was effectively out of Downing Street’s hands.
This message “went down like a bag of sick” with Caribbean nations who saw it as “colonial” and “arrogant,” recalled one person involved in conversations at the time.
The handling created tension between Downing Street and the Foreign Office, then led by David Lammy, who also attended, according to six other people with knowledge of the 2024 trip.
King Charles and Queen Camilla attend the bestowing and farewell ceremony on Oct. 26, 2024. | Pool photo by Manaui Faulalo via Getty Images
One of the six people said No. 10 figures had expected the Foreign Office to better manage expectations among Commonwealth nations ahead of Starmer’s arrival. The person said: “No. 10 did not feel like they were well enough informed, and felt some of this could and should have been handled in advance. There was the feeling that both Lammy and the Foreign Office were institutionally pre-disposed to this sort of stuff and not shutting it down. The PM didn’t know what he was going into.”
A second person said: “The FCDO world does forget, sometimes, the politics of what’s going on in the U.K. It’s very institutionalized.”
A third person stressed that senior aides in No. 10 had blamed Foreign Office officials, not Lammy personally. Before Starmer left office this year, No. 10 had been drawing up plans for Starmer to skip this year’s CHOGM — and send Lammy as his representative. By then Lammy had been moved from the foreign office and was Starmer’s deputy prime minister.
Advertisement
Another of the six people countered that it was No. 10 that persisted, ahead of the 2024 summit, with a line that was too binary — reparatory justice, as campaigners prefer to call it, has a wide definition that includes support for climate adaptation and education — and failed to listen to Foreign Office warnings ahead of time about the strength of feeling among Commonwealth nations.
“The audit trail would completely exonerate David and the Foreign Office,” this person said. They argued No. 10 officials — who were keen to hold on to the mantle of fiscal responsibility ahead of Starmer’s first budget — had viewed the row too much through how it would be perceived by the right-wing Daily Mail newspaper.
Two other people with knowledge of the 2024 trip insisted they did not remember any significant friction between No. 10 and the Foreign Office. Lammy’s office did not immediately respond to an invitation to comment.
UK review mooted a scaled-back summit
More significantly, the 2024 summit also led to discussions in Whitehall about the set-up of CHOGM itself.
Lammy commissioned an internal review by Foreign Office officials on the Commonwealth in the wake of the 2024 summit, his former Special Adviser Ben Judah told POLITICO.
Judah said the review suggested reducing the frequency of CHOGMs to “every four or five years,” potentially aligned with the hosting of the Commonwealth Games, and seeking to remove the final communique and leaders’ retreat.
Advertisement
It suggested an investment conference in alternate years modeled on the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which could keep the Commonwealth branding but with no organizational role for the Secretariat, said Judah.
Judah suggested this would improve attendance at CHOGM, which is often patchy; India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi does not plan to attend next week’s summit, for example, though there will be a delegation led by External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar. “The Indians think this thing is ridiculous and self-harming and just totally bizarre,” said Judah. “They’d be interested in a real investment conference, not this farce.”
A second former U.K. government official said they knew about the report, which has not been made public, adding that No. 10 figures under Starmer discussed similar concerns about the format of the Commonwealth summit after the Samoa visit.
Starmer sits with other leaders during the opening ceremony of CHOGM 2024 in Apia, Samoa. | Fiona Goodall/Getty Images
The Foreign Office declined to respond to questions about the report when contacted by POLITICO, including when it was finalized or whether any of its recommendations were pursued. One Foreign Office official, however, stressed that it was not the U.K. government’s position and that any decisions about future CHOGM arrangements would be for Commonwealth members collectively.
The U.K. government official quoted on trade and investment earlier in this piece said: “The Commonwealth is more important to our geostrategic position now than at any time throughout its 80-year history. In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful, values-based force for good in the world.
“This gives us a huge opportunity to drive U.K. interests and priorities — Commonwealth relationships have helped to drive global support for Ukraine, and it is hugely important for our work on climate.”
Advertisement
Funding pulled from reserves
Judah, however, argued that the Commonwealth Secretariat is a “broken institution” and Britain should wind down its involvement to focus on an investment summit instead.
CHOGM has ended up as a “platform for the reparations campaign,” argued Judah: “There’s nothing else on the agenda because it’s not a real international organization, and it’s not a real summit with deliverables.” The Commonwealth and Secretariat, he said, has “essentially been taken over by the only countries that are still really invested in them, which are the Caribbean countries supported by a few African countries, to push the reparations agenda.”
For some, that extends to questions about the way the Secretariat spends its money.
Two people with knowledge of the situation said part of this year’s CHOGM summit is being paid for out of the Secretariat’s reserves. “There is a real sense of concern about the malaise and drift of the organization,” argued one of the two people. “Financially it’s in a dire, dire state.”
A Commonwealth spokesperson responded: “The Commonwealth Secretariat accesses reserve funds for the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and always with member country approval.”
Back in 2024, Starmer’s most senior aides privately raised the question about whether he should attend the Samoa summit at all. “We were overruled,” said another person who worked under him.
Advertisement
Whitehall officials initially assumed that Burnham would not go either, until he said otherwise. “To a lot of the Caribbean countries, the word [from officials] was that he wasn’t going to show,” said O’Brien. “I think people were taken aback by that.”
But despite Starmer’s experience in 2024, Burnham will attend.
Among all other reasons, there is one very obvious one. “It’s very difficult for a prime minister not to go because the king goes,” said one person who worked under Starmer. “It’s important to him.”
Burnham’s ‘surer touch’
Once Burnham is in the room, campaigners hope he will at least be a listening ear.
Outside the prime minister’s Manchester office No. 10 North is a statue of Abraham Lincoln, commemorating the mill workers who refused to touch raw cotton picked by slaves.
Burnham referred to it in his first speech to the United Nations last month. “In 1862, people with little power used it to help those with none on the other side of the world,” he said. “The best change is change like that, bottom-up change led by people.”
Advertisement
The new prime minister “understands the importance of Manchester as the second great city of empire, and he has a surer touch than his predecessors,” argued Boateng. “We’ve got an opportunity to reset the relationship.”
What reparatory justice would look like is another matter.
Previous estimates have suggested Britain should owe as much as £18 trillion, but the conversation is far more nuanced than talking about a single big number.
Burnham departs Downing Street for prime minister’s questions on Oct. 21, 2026. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
While Boateng argues that no measures should be taken off the table, he would begin with reforming the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to give more Commonwealth countries a meaningful seat at the table, and returning historic artefacts such as the Benin bronzes that are displayed in London’s British Museum. “The British Museum holds loot, literally loot. These are stolen goods,” he said.
Britain is working on debt relief too. Chancellor John Healey plans to make international finance for developing countries a key theme when Britain hosts G20 finance ministers next year.
NGOs have urged Healey to make debt relief more generous by changing the G20’s common framework and UK domestic law, which sets the terms for 90% of debt that low-income countries owe to private lenders.
Advertisement
Maria Finnerty of Bond, the membership body for NGOs, said Britain “continues to play a role in enabling illicit financial flows through loopholes linked to the City of London and its overseas territories, amounting to the loss of billions from some Commonwealth countries.”
Miliband reflected all this in his POLITICO interview last month at the Labour Party Conference. While condemning the slave trade as “terrible,” he said his focus was on addressing current issues in countries “on the front line of the climate crisis, of the debt burden, of trying to reduce poverty in those countries.”
O’Brien is calling for monetary payments, however. Through the Repair Campaign, he wants to see the EU and U.K. make money available to the 15 Caribbean Community (CARICOM) countries — with a special case for Haiti — “each year for the next 75 years” for issues such as education, green energy and storm defenses to deal with climate change.
O’Brien would not be drawn on a single figure, but suggested payments should supplement the national budget of each affected country by around 10% a year.
Asked if he had had conversations with the Foreign Office, O’Brien replied: “What do you think?
“I mean, we would like to. We’re approaching this in a very friendly way, taking a very, very sensitive period of history and trying to get results. We have the highest respect for the British government, and particularly the King. But it can’t go on forever.”

Actually, Israel's election polls didn't get everything wrong. But reality is still gloomy | Analysis
When the results of the country's most historic election are dizzying, disappointing, exhilarating and inconclusive all at once, there's only one thing you can do to calm your nerves: Analyze the polls.
There's still too much we don't know about who will form the next government. What we do know is confusing. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud sort-of won the election by coming in as the top party, but his governing coalition definitely lost, with just 53 seats out of 120. That's an 11-seat decline from the 64 that these parties won in the last election.
(The coalition today holds 68 seats because Gideon Sa'ar, the current foreign minister, joined the government after running in 2022 as one of the leaders of an opposition party. He brought four seats into the coalition.)
On Tuesday, a majority of Israeli voters rejected Netanyahu, giving parties outside his coalition a decisive 67 seats. But the bloc of Zionist opposition parties led by Gadi Eisenkot fell far short of Netanyahu's bloc, and this was a major miss for nearly all of the final surveys and exit polls, which had put Eisenkot's bloc – without Arab parties – ahead of Netanyahu. What's going on and which polls were correct? Did anyone get it right?
If Netanyahu stays, even his voters will feel it in their pockets | Analysis
Tuesday's election cost Netanyahu's coalition its majority, yet the opposition may still be unable to replace him. The frustration of its voters does not augur the demise of the state. But there is a real danger that the decline will continue, even accelerate, a process that began with Netanyahu and Likud's relatively surprising victory in 2015 (then too, contrary to the polls and even the exit polls).
In retrospect, this was the moment the prime minister's self-confidence swelled and when he became more immersed in the three criminal affairs in which he was charged in 2019. His investigation and subsequent prosecution brought on a holy war against the judiciary, a series of closely spaced general elections amid political instability, his close alliance with the far-right parties and, finally, his absolute shirking of responsibility for the failures that made possible the October 7 massacre.
In recent years, Netanyahu resembled a driver who was determined to smash the Zionist project into a wall, indifferent to the outcries of the passengers who were stuck behind him and had no way of extricating themselves.
For many in the change bloc, the hope for an exceptional showing by Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party on Tuesday represented the last off-ramp from the expressway to hell. So far, that hasn't happened. The power of tribal-religious identity politics and fanning the fear of the Arabs played into Netanyahu's hands, even though his bloc is 11 Knesset seats smaller than after the 2022 election. In that one, too, a year before the massacre, he played on the same sentiments.
Netanyahu is making Arab Israelis' right to vote a crime | Opinion
On Thursday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanayhu's plan to undermine the legitimacy of the election results by vilifying Israel's Arab citizens reached its culmination.
He laid the groundwork for the plan on the eve of the election, when the prime minister and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir held a baffling meeting with police chief Danny Levy to discuss election integrity on Sunday. This was despite an explicit order barring such a meeting from Justice Noam Sohlberg, the Central Elections Committee chairman.
That meeting was then followed by a racist campaign targeting Arab citizens on Election Day: The public was bombarded with dozens of phone calls and text messages demanding a redo of the election, a salvo that has continued into Thursday.
And then, an unexpected player entered the fray. Sohlberg sent a rare letter to Shin Bet security service chief David Zini, instructing him to investigate suspicions of what he described as election bribery and foreign interference by Qatar.
The Democrats doubled their Knesset seats, but alienated Arab voters along the way
The Democrats ultimately won eight seats: short of expectations, but double the representation of Labor in the outgoing Knesset. In the 2022 election, Labor and Meretz – the two parties that later merged to form the Democrats – ran separately. Labor won only four seats, while Meretz failed to cross the electoral threshold.
Still, the party appears to have fallen short in reaching voters it had neglected, particularly Arab citizens. During the Knesset term, Democrats lawmakers Naama Lazimi, Efrat Rayten and Gilad Kariv stood out for their parliamentary work, while during the campaign the party's candidates traveled extensively around the country. Kariv was particularly active in reaching Arab communities, and the party recruited a large volunteer network.
But Soumaya Bashir, the party's representative from the Arab community, finished only 10th in the primary, and the Democrats won only small shares of the vote in many of Israel's larger Arab localities.
Issawi Frej, a former Meretz minister and lawmaker, does not consider the Democrats' result a significant achievement. "The Democrats were never genuinely interested in partnership with Arab society. It was a pretense," he charged.
At Shin Bet's request, Mossad to assist in probe into suspected foreign election interference
Mossad has agreed to a request from the Shin Bet security service to assist in its investigation into suspected foreign interference in Israel's elections.
The move comes after Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg instructed Shin Bet chief David Zini to investigate what he described as "serious suspicions" of improper foreign influence on the election through foreign funding. Sohlberg clarified in the letter that he could not "attest to the nature of the suspicions."
According to a source on the committee, claims were raised, among others, that Qatar had invested money to increase voter turnout in the Arab community. The Shin Bet said it was conducting an investigation but declined to provide further details.
Qatar, for its part, denies interfering in Israel's elections.
PM's son says Israeli Arabs are Israel's 'greatest threat' after nuclear Iran
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's son Yair said Friday that Israeli Arabs are the "greatest threat to the survival of the State of Israel, apart from the Iranian nuclear threat."
The prime minister's son wrote in a post on X that Arab citizens of Israel pose a greater threat than "their Palestinian brethren in the West Bank and Gaza, more than Turkey, and more than the surging antisemitism in the West." He added that Israel cannot survive "when 20 percent of its population identifies with its enemies and wants to see its destruction."
United Arab List Chairman Mansour Abbas calls Joint List leaders, urges cooperation and coordination
United Arab List Chairman Mansour Abbas talked with Joint List leaders Yousef Jabareen, Ahmad Tibi and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh on Friday, congratulating them on their election results.
Abbas stressed the responsibility facing all Arab lawmakers in the coming period and called for strengthening cooperation and coordination between the two parties, against the backdrop of high voter turnout in the Arab community.
The conversations also addressed the election results, the political landscape in the next Knesset and the prospects for forming a new government.
Eisenkot appoints Roy Folkman chair of Yashar's Knesset faction
Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot appointed incoming MK Roy Folkman to chair the party's faction in the Knesset.
In the role, Folkman will lead the faction's parliamentary work, coordinate between its lawmakers and oversee its legislative activity, including advancing Yashar-sponsored bills.
Folkman previously served as chairman of the Kulanu faction in the Knesset, where he coordinated the party's parliamentary work and helped advance economic and social legislation and reforms.
The party said the appointment is part of its preparations for its work in the next Knesset and for advancing its political agenda.
Bennett appoints Eitan Ginzburg chair of Together’s Knesset faction
Former Prime Minister and Together chairman Naftali Bennett announced that he has appointed MK Eitan Ginzburg to chair the party's faction in the 26th Knesset.
Ginzburg previously served as communications minister, deputy Knesset speaker, chairman of the Knesset House Committee and mayor of Ra'anana.

China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:56:46 UTC
11:56:46 KST

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Since returning to the White House in early 2025, Trump has sought to crack down on government leaks, accusing news outlets of conducting a smear campaign against him.

In April 2025, Hegseth fired three senior Pentagon aides – Dan Caldwell, Darin Selnick, and Colin Carroll – amid an investigation into alleged leaks of sensitive information to the media. ====================================================================================================

Kim Jong Un urges drone dominance as North Korea fires missiles, rockets
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:44:05 CET
11:44:05 KST

By Joyce Lee and Heejin Kim
SEOUL, Oct 30 (Reuters) - North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for his country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology as he attended an exhibition and demonstration of unmanned aeronautical technology, state media KCNA reported on Friday.
The firepower demonstration featured tactical suicide attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and 600mm multiple rocket launchers, KCNA said.
The display highlighted Kim’s push to modernise North Korea’s armed forces by using drones and artificial intelligence as Pyongyang draws lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine and other global conflicts.
It came amid heightened tensions between the two Koreas, with Seoul vowing to respond firmly to what it called North Korean breaches, and Pyongyang denouncing joint South Korea-US air defence drills.
KCNA photographs showed unmanned aerial vehicles bearing the North Korean Air Force’s emblem at the exhibition, attended by Kim.
Other images showed what appeared to be an unmanned aerial vehicle crashing into a military vehicle and exploding in a ball of flame during a weapons demonstration.
South Korea’s military said on Thursday that North Korea had fired around 10 projectiles, including short-range ballistic missiles.
Kim said that pursuing superiority in drone technology was “an indispensable option” given the changing nature of modern warfare, according to KCNA.
He also said using high-level AI in unmanned weapons systems should be a top priority for North Korea, KCNA reported.
Kim has repeatedly called for the development of drones and military AI. State media said Kim ordered mass production of suicide attack drones in November 2024, oversaw tests of AI-equipped versions in March 2025 and in September 2025 called AI a top priority in weapons modernisation.
DRAWING LESSONS FROM UKRAINE WAR
Since October 2024, North Korea has sent more than 16,000 personnel to Russia to aid Moscow in its war against Ukraine, and gained battlefield experience in drone, electronic and combined-arms warfare, according to South Korean intelligence.
North Korea is transforming its military with drones and AI, drawing lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University.
By showing a comprehensive display of weapons, North Korea is trying to “shut off the possibility of dialogue or negotiations” with South Korea, Lim said.
North Korean state media also displayed for the first time what analysts described as a tailless, flying-wing stealth drone.
Photographs showed racks of small suicide drones and loitering munitions similar to the US Switchblade 600, suggesting an emphasis on cheap, mass-produced weapons, potentially drawing on lessons from the Ukraine war, analysts said.
Mock targets resembling South Korean K9 howitzers, M1 Abrams-type tanks and radar vehicles suggested the weapons were intended for use against South Korean and US forces, they said.
BORDER TENSIONS
South Korea will respond firmly to protect the military border despite Pyongyang’s assertion that it is conducting operations within its territory, Seoul’s national security adviser Wi Sung-lac said on Friday.
Separately, North Korea’s Defence Ministry said US and South Korean air defence drills were raising tensions on the peninsula and that there was “no limit” to its option for maintaining a strong deterrent posture, KCNA reported.
Tensions have escalated since a landmine blast inside the Demilitarised Zone seriously wounded several South Korean soldiers last month. Seoul said the blast was caused by a North Korean mine, which Pyongyang has denied.
Kim’s powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, said earlier this month that North Korea would activate anti-South Korean propaganda loudspeakers along its entire border by the end of October.

John Turturro Gives a Career-Best Performance in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:44:04 UTC
11:44:04 KST

To paraphrase the old-school comedian Rodney Dangerfield, a pickpocket in 2020s New York gets no respect. Almost no one carries much cash anymore, and credit cards are useless unless you’re willing to commit fraud. What’s a poor guy with crackerjack observational skills and exceedingly dexterous fingers supposed to do when he can’t even pay for his diner breakfast with his morning’s earnings?
That’s where John Turturro’s Harry Lehman finds himself in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, writer-director Noah Segan’s charming, nimble, and affecting drama about a guy who has seen his city, and his world, change drastically during his lifetime. For Harry, a typical workday involves boarding the subway and identifying the easy targets. In his soft, elegant tweed coat—a garment he might have bought 20 or 30 years ago, maybe at Barneys, when the dough was really flowing—he swirls through New York, his vision attuned to checked-out, earbud-wearing Wall Street dudes, or women who allow their purses to dangle precariously. He sees what others miss, though he’s living in a world where no one pays any attention to their environment. It’s a lonely life.
But there’s a bright spot in Harry’s world: Though his wife, Rosie (Karina Arroyave), has been stricken with an unnamed ailment and can neither move nor speak, his days revolve around her. He cares for her tenderly, as best he can, talking to her, laughing with her. At one point he puts Odyssey’s 1977 sequins-and-stardust disco hit “Native New Yorker” on the stereo and dances for both of them, in a kind of disco-salsa shuffle, his arms whirling as if the breeze itself were his dance partner.
Rosie’s care costs money, which means Harry needs to hustle harder than ever. Watches can still bring in the bucks, as long as they’re not fake. And to unload those, Harry has a close pal and longtime co-conspirator, the wily, wisecracking pawnshop owner Ben (Steve Buscemi). Ben will also take stolen phones, though they’re troublesome: they need to go to a guy in Chinatown, Kelvin Han Yee’s Frank, who knows how to scrub them, after which they’re packed into a container and shipped off to god knows where. When Harry boosts a USB crypto wallet from a brazen young criminal and spoiled rich kid, Dylan (Will Price), Ben has no idea what to do with it—plugging it into his circa-1995 desktop personal computer sends the machine into a tailspin. So he sends Harry downtown to see Frank—whose front is a herb shop, though it seems less like a front than a side hustle—and that’s where Harry’s troubles really begin.
The Only Living Pickpocket is part drama, part comedy, part thriller. It’s also a movie about a man reckoning with his past: We may warm to the sight of Harry caring so lovingly for Rosie, but there’s much more to his story, as we learn. And you can’t always tell where the movie is headed; its beats are wriggly, unpredictable. Until recently, writer-director Segan has worked mostly as an actor, often with director Rian Johnson (he appeared in Brick, Looper, and the Knives Out movies), and he has directed one previous feature, the 2022 horror movie Blood Relatives. The pickpocketty lightness of touch he shows is remarkable for a fledgling director.
It doesn’t hurt that he’s got Turturro as a star. In the early part of his career, as a favorite of Spike Lee and the Coen Brothers, Turturro, with his tightly coiled, jack-in-the-box energy, always looked like he might blow at any moment. But he’s become much subtler, and sexier, over the years. in the underappreciated 2013 comedy Fading Gigolo, which he also wrote and directed, he played a foxy florist who becomes a classy male escort, servicing sultry hotties (Sharon Stone, Sofia Vergara) before falling for a lonely Hasidic widow (Vanessa Paradis). Suddenly, he was a leading man, and a hot one.
Turturro still has some of his old combustibility; you occasionally catch an air of menace behind that snaggle-tooth smile. But he now has more softness, more range, and the performance he gives in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is one of his finest, as well as one of the best of the year. In the first section of the film, you believe Harry is just a guy whose glory days have passed: He belongs to a dream New York, that of the 1970s and ‘80s, of strobe-lit dance clubs and independent cinemas seemingly on every block. (Cinematographer Sam Levy, who also shot Frances Ha and Lady Bird, is in tune with the old New York nestled within the current one; he captures the city, from the Bronx to Chinatown, in all its shabby-shiny glory.) At one point, Harry suggests to Rosie that the two hunker down for the evening and watch an old movie, maybe something with Barbara Stanwyck; he comes from a generation that was used to looking toward its past as well as its future.
The city wasn’t a safe place in Harry’s younger days—but we’re talking about something other than physical safety, a kind of creative vitality that, if you were attuned to it, could rub off on you like glitter. Harry still has some of that sparkle, but it’s tempered by melancholy, the aftermath of little mistakes and big ones he’s made along the way. Turturro captures all of it—and shows how Harry intends to do right by those he’s harmed—with the kind of lived-in ease you earn, if you’re lucky, over the course of a career. Whirling through the city in that tweed coat, he’s like Fred Astaire breezing through an obviously fake white-cardboard Venice or descending a staircase from nowhere. The grit of the city is his glamour, its noise his music. It’s all his for a song, or a watch deftly separated from its owner’s wrist. His city is a tough place and, as Odyssey sang, he should know the score by now. But at least he knows the dance steps, because as much as New York may change, those never do.

Vessel reported on fire in Strait of Hormuz: UK maritime agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:43:14 UTC
11:43:14 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center said late Thursday that a vessel was on fire in the Strait of Hormuz.
"UKMTO has received a report of an incident 25NM Northeast of Khasab, Oman in the Strait of Hormuz. A third party has reported that a vessel transiting outbound is on fire, the cause is unknown at time of report," the agency said in a statement.
It later reaffirmed having received a verified report confirming that the crew were safe and there was no environmental impact.
"The report indicates that the tanker was approached on the port side by a small boat which attached two explosive devices to the hull above the waterline. The subsequent blasts resulted in a fire in the engine room which temporarily disabled the vessel," it noted.
UKMTO said the fire had been extinguished and the vessel continued to its next port of call. It further advised vessels to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity as authorities investigated the incident.
The incident comes amid rising tensions between Iran and the US about navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy and commodity supplies.
In February, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran. Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the strait, but its implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway as tensions continued to escalate.

Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:40:00 UTC
11:40:00 KST

Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
October 30, 2026
The German pharmaceutical giant Bayer won a trial on Thursday over claims the Roundup weedkiller, manufactured by subsidiary Monsanto, caused cancer in three women.
The Missouri jury sided unanimously with Bayer. It's the first trial since a US Supreme Court ruling that limits complaints over the product.
Bayer is waiting for a separate court ruling where the company is seeking a $7.25 billion (€6.5 billion) settlement in relation to tens of thousands of other Roundup cases.
What is the complaint against Roundup?
Thursday's court ruling follows a case brought to a St. Louis court by Theresa Aretino, Cynthia Fernandez and Betty Larkin in 2020.
The three women had said they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma after regularly using the weedkiller.
Their attorneys argued that Roundup was defectively designed and unreasonably dangerous, and that Bayer was negligent in selling it.
The three were not participating in the Bayer settlement. Some 65,000 other cases have been filed against the company, claiming Roundup gave them cancer.
What did the Supreme Court rule in regards to Roundup?
The US Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that plaintiffs could not argue that the Roundup label failed to warn users about the risk of cancer since the US Environmental Protection Agency had concluded the label does not require a cancer warning.
"We are pleased with the jury's favorable verdict for Monsanto validating our belief that there is no evidence to prove design defect, fraud or negligence claims in the Roundup litigation," Bill Dodero, the company's US general counsel and global head of litigation, said in a statement.
"This verdict should send a strong signal that plaintiffs who wish to pursue claims in the court system following the Durnell ruling will face significant challenges both in demonstrating they have viable claims and putting forth the necessary evidence to prove them in court," he added, using the name of the Supreme Court case.
The company has repeatedly defended the use of glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, as safe, calling it "one of the most studied agricultural tools in history."
The EPA has previously concluded that glyphosate is probably not carcinogenic, but it is in the middle of a new review of its safety. The International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2015 that the chemical was "probably carcinogenic" to humans, but Bayer has rejected the study's findings, calling it an outlier.

Salvadoran ex-president Saca released after 10-year sentence for corruption

Unknown Publisher

Salvadoran ex-president Saca released after 10-year sentence for corruption
Elias Antonio Saca confessed to diverting over $300m in public funds during his presidency and took a plea bargain.
Elias Antonio Saca, the former president of El Salvador, has been released after serving a 10-year prison term for corruption.
Saca, 61, arrived at court to formally report his release on Thursday after fulfilling the terms of a plea deal in which he confessed to diverting and laundering more than $300m from public funds during his 2004 to 2009 administration.
His lawyer, Mario Machado, said the former president had served his sentence in full without receiving early-release benefits.
Arrested at son’s wedding
Saca was first arrested during his son’s wedding in 2016 and was sentenced to five years for embezzlement and another five years for money laundering in September 2018.
A plea bargain allowed Saca to avoid a potential 30-year prison sentence.
In 2019, the former president was found guilty of offering $10,000 to a court employee to obtain information about a case against him, though a judge determined the second sentence to be part of his existing 10-year term.
Saca, a businessman and radio broadcaster, served as president as part of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance (ARENA).
During the initial trial, prosecutors said Saca appropriated funds from the state budget for himself and others, including taking more than $7m for his former party.
Saca was also ordered to repay $260m to the state. He is one of four Salvadoran presidents who have faced corruption charges, including his successor Mauricio Funes, who escaped to Nicaragua in September 2016 and died there in 2025.

11:37:21 KST

US President Donald Trump pledged to secure a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon if Beirut agrees to join the Abraham Accords, a senior Gulf diplomatic source told the Lebanese newspaper Ad-Diyar.
The claim was published in an article by Nour Naameh amid ongoing diplomatic efforts and concerns in Lebanon over the potential consequences of another military confrontation between the US and Iran.
According to the report, the source described the American promises as official commitments. However, the newspaper provided no documents supporting the claims, did not identify the diplomat or the country he represents, and offered no confirmation from the White House.
The report also did not specify when the commitments were made, who they were communicated to, or whether a timetable had been set for their implementation.
Senior Israeli officials responded to the report by insisting that Israel would not withdraw its forces before Hezbollah was disarmed.
"No withdrawal before Hezbollah is disarmed," the officials said.
The officials stressed that any redeployment of IDF forces would depend on Hezbollah's disarmament throughout Lebanon, rather than solely in areas near the Israeli border.
However, Israel has not ruled out the possibility of reaching a peace agreement with Lebanon once the security threat posed by Hezbollah has been removed.
"A peace agreement after resolving the security issue and removing the threat to residents of the north, that is excellent and consistent with our objectives," the officials said.
US-Iran negotiations could shape future of Israeli withdrawal
The Lebanese newspaper reported that progress toward such an arrangement would depend on a broader agreement or strategic understanding between Washington and Tehran.
According to the report, any such understanding could have immediate implications for Lebanon's domestic political and security situation, particularly for Hezbollah, which is backed by Iran.
The report also claimed that Iranian leaders had explicitly instructed Hezbollah not to enter another war in support of Tehran, fearing that its involvement could trigger a broader escalation in Lebanon.
Sources familiar with the matter separately told the newspaper that Israel continues to condition its withdrawal from southern Lebanon on Hezbollah's disarmament.
They assessed that Israel's continued military strikes and threats reflect its determination to address Hezbollah's weapons before proceeding with any withdrawal.
The newspaper attributed this assessment to its sources, rather than presenting it as an official Israeli response to the reported American proposal.
Lebanese leaders push for diplomatic solution
The article also highlighted the Lebanese leadership's preference for resolving the situation through diplomatic means.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun emphasized that his country wants the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), the UN peacekeeping mission stationed in southern Lebanon, to maintain its presence in the area.
Alternatively, Aoun proposed deploying European forces in place of UNIFIL, potentially forming the basis for a broader international force made up of personnel from countries friendly to Lebanon.
Aoun argued that wars lead to destruction, displacement, and loss of life without resolving the underlying conflicts.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, meanwhile, emphasized that the Lebanese government must exercise authority over the country's entire territory exclusively through its own security forces.
He described this as essential to restoring the state's authority and made clear that his government would continue pursuing that objective despite the challenges and opposition it faces.
Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem, whose remarks were also cited in the article, expressed interest in a potential agreement between Iran and the US.
Qassem described such an agreement as a source of strength for Hezbollah, alongside the continued support and steadfastness of its followers.
At the same time, he defended the continuation of what he called "resistance" activities and rejected the legitimacy of the framework agreement.
The report linked the future of Israel's military presence in southern Lebanon to Hezbollah's disarmament and the outcome of negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
However, the newspaper provided no indication that an agreement had been reached or that Lebanon's leadership had agreed to join the Abraham Accords.

Final vote results in Israel set up weeks of uncertainty about who will govern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:35:00 UTC
11:35:00 KST

Final vote results in Israel set up weeks of uncertainty about who will govern
Leo Sands, Johnatan Reiss and Ephrat Livni
- Israel’s final election count left Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc on 53 seats and the main opposition on 48, so neither can form a government alone.
- President Isaac Herzog will choose who gets first chance to build a coalition, likely Gadi Eisenkot, as parties face weeks of talks, complaints, and possible legal challenges.
- The vote followed the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack and exposed deep division over Netanyahu, Arab parties, and the risk of another long political deadlock.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – The final vote count in Israel’s election, released early on Oct 30, confirmed that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hard-right coalition nor the main opposition alliance won enough votes to form a government.
The result sets the stage for weeks of jockeying and political uncertainty.
Netanyahu’s Likud party and its hard-right allies won 53 seats in Parliament, not enough to meet the 61-seat threshold for an outright majority.
The final count, from Israel’s Central Elections Committee, showed Netanyahu’s alliance was down from the 64 seats it won in the last election, in 2022.
The main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who had led in opinion polls for months, won 48.
Two Arab parties secured 19 seats, their highest-ever number of seats.
The results are subject to potential “minor corrections” in coming days before they are submitted to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Nov 4, the committee said just after midnight.
Herzog will decide who he thinks has the best shot at assembling a majority and ask that person to try to form a government.
Herzog has said he will consult party leaders after formally receiving the vote count next week.
The final seat tally will be formalised on Nov 4, and the political parties will be able to file complaints and legal challenges until Nov 18.
Herzog is likely to offer Eisenkot the first chance to form a government, said Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, a non-partisan research group.
Based on Israeli law, and past elections, the party leader who receives the most recommendations from the other leaders who consult the President is generally given priority, he said.
The election was widely considered a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, and his government, the most hard-right in Israeli history.
It was also the first vote since the Hamas-led attack on Oct 7, 2023, the deadliest day in Israeli history, that ignited the devastating war in the Gaza Strip.
Voter turnout was the highest since 1999, but despite widespread public anger over Netanyahu’s refusal to take responsibility for preventing the Oct 7 attacks, the Jewish-led opposition parties failed to secure enough seats to immediately oust him.
Netanyahu outperformed expectations, playing on voters’ fears of Arab political power and potential security threats to win the most votes.
Eisenkot had presented himself as a foil to Netanyahu throughout the campaign, arguing that the Prime Minister was pushing the country toward authoritarianism and destroying its international standing.
Netanyahu’s edge in Parliament presents Eisenkot and his ideologically diverse bloc with a difficult choice: Seek an alliance with Arab parties to topple him or join forces with Netanyahu in a potential unity government.
The process to form a government could be bitter and drawn out, lasting weeks if not months.
Once Herzog selects a candidate, that person has 28 days to negotiate with other factions to try to assemble a governing majority.
A 14-day extension to the deadline can also be requested.
If the first candidate fails, the President can task up to two others to try to form a government.
If they also fall short, new elections will be held.
Herzog, however, said on Oct 28 that everything possible must be done to avoid another election.
Historically, it has typically taken between 20 and 100 days to form a government, according to the Israel Democracy Institute.
A number of scenarios have been floated, in addition to a national unity government.
Another is that the opposition bloc reaches out to the Arab parties, whose strong showing could make them major players in the negotiations for the next government.
But most Jewish parties, including those in the opposition bloc, are not keen on that approach.
Many Israeli Jews have long objected to including Arab parties – especially those that are unwilling to back Zionist positions – in any governing coalition.
Both leaders could also try to get parties or individual lawmakers to defect from the rival bloc.
Since the Oct 7 attack, views towards Arab parties have hardened.
Netanyahu repeatedly invoked the spectre of Arab voters throughout his campaign, accusing them of “trying to steal the elections” and galvanising his right-wing base with racially charged language.
For his part, Eisenkot has largely declined to say whether he would partner Arab parties, but he has said that none of them meet his conditions for joining forces as potential coalition allies.
A deadlock in political negotiations would suit Netanyahu, analysts say, as he would remain caretaker prime minister until the next government is formed.
For many voters, the election result threatens an uncomfortable prospect: A return to the political deadlock that paralysed Israel between 2019 and 2022, when voters headed to the polls five times.
While many supporters of Netanyahu are relieved that he still has a chance to retain power, others who had hoped for his decisive defeat have felt crushed by the possibility of a political stalemate. NYTIMES

Drone attack reportedly kills worker at Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
A drone attack on Oct. 29 reportedly killed an employee of the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on X.
The victim was reportedly a welder working at the plant's centralized repair workshop, according to the United Nations nuclear watchdog.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said that attacks on nuclear plant personnel are unacceptable and violate the agency's Seven Indispensable Pillars for Nuclear Safety and Security during armed conflict.
Grossi renewed his call for maximum military restraint around nuclear facilities to prevent the risk of a nuclear accident.
The IAEA did not specify whether the attack was carried out by Russian or Ukrainian forces, or provide further details.
The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, located in the city of Enerhodar in southern Ukraine, is Europe's largest nuclear power plant. It has been under Russian occupation since the start of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The plant has repeatedly faced threats to nuclear safety, including drone attacks, disruptions to external power supplies, and incidents affecting plant workers.
On Oct. 3, the IAEA reported a series of drone attacks that damaged transformers at the nearby Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant, threatening the nuclear facility's external electricity supply.
In August, a drone explosion at a bus stop used by plant personnel killed one person and injured 15 others, according to the IAEA.
The agency has maintained a permanent monitoring presence at the Russian-occupied facility since September 2022 over concerns of the risk of a nuclear accident.
The reported death at the nuclear plant came on the same day Russian forces launched multiple missile and drone attacks against the Ukrainian-controlled city of Zaporizhzhia, injuring at least 14 people, including a child, according to Ukraine's National Police.

Teen rallies take to the streets across Italy

- Officials fear violence after clashes in Milan on 17 and 18 October, when cars were burned and shops looted. Security forces are preparing as students plan to “block and empty schools”.
- The protests reflect wider anger over a social and economic crisis. Experts say young people feel ignored, while the government has promised aid and future plans for under-30 workers.
AI generated
ROME – School and university students are to rally in several Italian cities on Oct 30 to call for more funding for schools and support for housing, with security forces preparing for possible clashes.
Students have been protesting for weeks, setting up tent camps and occupying schools to make their demands heard, matching similar movements across the border in France.
The Italian protests have taken place alongside those of truck drivers and farmers over the spike in fuel prices and the cost of living, as well as rising defence spending.
“On Friday, we expect a massive mobilisation of students, who will block and empty schools,” Laura Teresi, 18, from Rome’s Cavour high school, a spokesperson for the OSA student movement, told AFP.
“We will take to the streets to denounce the rearmament policies of (Prime Minister Giorgia) Meloni’s government and the rising cost of living, which is weighing ever more heavily on families, workers and students,” she added.
The students will also protest against the “endless budget cuts to teaching”, Teresi said.
Officials are worried about a repeat of the violence on Oct 17 and 18 in Milan, the country’s economic capital, where groups of young people set cars on fire and looted shops.
‘Malaise’
On Oct 30, the radical left USB union has called for a general strike.
“The broader Italian and European context is marked by a crisis and a social, economic and cultural malaise affecting different segments of society and different regions,” said Rosario Forlenza, professor of contemporary history and political anthropology at Rome’s Luiss University.
“The younger generation (is)... a generation that is under-represented politically, that sees political leaders’ attention focused elsewhere and therefore lives in a situation of precarity, social distress and even a lack of a future,” Forlenza said.
In response to the youth protests, Meloni’s hard-right government has eased rules on detaining minors and toughened laws on public gatherings.
The government also last week agreed on a €175.2-million (S$250-million) aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.
Measures in favour of young people and families are also planned in the draft 2027 budget currently being discussed among the various governing parties, such as an annual bonus of €2,500 for workers under 30.
“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general... who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Meloni said at a press conference on Oct 28, stressing that these measures were “not for those who smash windows”.
Psychologist and psychotherapist Matteo Lancini said part of the problem was schools themselves because they were “totally disconnected” from young people’s needs.
“What we need are schools that change radically, schools that are not designed around adults’ pension systems,” Lancini said at a meeting with the foreign press in Rome.
Instead, “everyone eases their conscience by saying it’s social media’s fault”, he said. AFP

How Trump could interfere in US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:30:00 UTC
11:30:00 KST

How Trump could interfere in US midterm elections
- Trump’s team may try to affect the US midterms by challenging voter lists, pressuring officials, and sending more federal monitors. Critics fear this could scare voters and disrupt voting.
- Officials also fear federal agents could seize ballots or records during the count, which may slow results and fuel fraud claims. Courts have mostly blocked such legal moves so far.
- After voting, Trump could try to block certification or challenge Democratic wins, but experts say federal law limits this power. Legal teams are ready to fight any interference.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – State officials who run US elections are bracing for further intervention by US President Donald Trump’s administration in next week’s midterms – fearing federal authorities could disrupt voting, challenge ballot counts or try to block unfavourable results.
Trump, whose Republicans face an uphill battle to keep control of Congress, has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections and urged his party to “nationalise” voting in at least 15 places.
The White House says it is protecting election security, and many of the feared scenarios remain hypothetical. The US Constitution gives the president no direct role in running elections, and federal courts have so far rebuffed the administration’s main legal challenges.
Here are the key potential flashpoints:
Before election day
1. Voter eligibility
The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to obtain their voter registration lists, saying it needs them to find non-citizens. It has lost more than two dozen of those cases.
It has also demanded that ballots be set aside from about 20,000 people in California and more than 400 in Washington state whom it suspects are non-citizens.
A federal judge rejected the California request on Oct 28, saying it would wreak havoc on an election already underway. Washington state has also refused the demand.
Studies have repeatedly found non-citizen voting to be exceptionally rare.
2. Pressure on officials
The Justice Department has warned election officials in every state that they could face prosecution if they knowingly allow non-citizens to vote.
And Trump on Oct 27 offered US$1 million (S$1.3 million) for information leading to a voter fraud conviction, without giving details.
At polling stations
1. Federal monitors
The Justice Department plans to send around 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states – its largest deployment ever.
Monitoring is a decades-old practice, but Democrats and voting rights groups fear monitors could intimidate voters.
The department says they will be unarmed, barred from interfering with voting and drawn from neither the FBI nor Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
2. Immigration agents and troops
Advocates fear ICE operations near polling stations could deter voters in immigrant communities.
The administration says it is not planning operations targeting polling places, although Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said ICE agents could serve warrants there.
Trump has declined to rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act, which allows the president to deploy troops at home.
A Civil War-era law bars troops and armed federal agents from polling places, and legal experts say an emergency declaration would not give the president power over elections.
Counting the votes
1. Seizing election materials
Federal agents could seek warrants or subpoenas for ballots, voting machines or records – potentially disrupting the count.
In January, the FBI seized ballots and other 2020 election records in Fulton County, Georgia, a focus of Trump’s false claims that he won that year.
Election officials warn that similar action during an active count could undermine safeguards tracking how ballots are handled.
2. Challenging the count
Trump could allege fraud involving mail-in ballots, voting machines or votes counted after election night, fuelling demands for recounts or attempts to halt counting.
But the US Supreme Court ruled in June that states may count mail ballots postmarked by election day that arrive afterward, and courts can intervene against unlawful disruption.
After election day
1. Blocking certification
The Justice Department has sued Alaska to delay certification of its Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, citing a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who it says is trying to confuse voters, which he denies.
Trump said he ordered the lawsuit.
Experts say federal law does not allow the department to block certification, which courts can compel officials to carry out.
2. Challenging Democratic victories
Trump could pressure state officials to dispute results, as he did after losing the 2020 election.
Experts warn unresolved disputes could also delay the seating of newly elected lawmakers in January. But courts have repeatedly upheld states’ authority over elections, and Democrats and voting rights groups have assembled legal teams to fight any interference. AFP

Intelligence data: How many Su-34 fighter-bombers has Russia lost, and how many remain in service?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:29:00 UTC
11:29:00 KST

Intelligence data: How many Su-34 fighter-bombers has Russia lost, and how many remain in service?
This was reported by the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, according to Ukrinform.
As the agency notes, such losses are quite significant for the aggressor country’s aircraft fleet, as its restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation. By way of comparison: the number of Su-34s destroyed is equivalent to approximately 2.5–3 years of their production, based on an estimated production capacity of 14–18 aircraft per year.
As of October 22, according to intelligence data, the Russian Federation’s Aerospace Forces had approximately 140 Su-34s of various modifications in service, including the upgraded Su-34M (Su-34NVO).
It is emphasized that the sheer numbers of the Russian Su-34 fleet do not fully reflect its actual combat capability. Such an assessment must take into account a range of factors: the technical condition of the aircraft, the number of trained crews, the intensity of operation, maintenance capabilities, and the ability to replace losses.
According to the Main Intelligence Directorate (GUR), the Su-34s deployed in the war against Ukraine are one of the key components of the enemy’s strike aviation. The use of these aircraft as carriers of guided aerial bombs has enabled the aggressor country to expand its capabilities for striking ground targets, particularly in areas of active combat operations and in settlements near the front lines.
Despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernize the Su-34, seeking to maintain the size of its air fleet and sustain the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes. The potential for further expansion of this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components, and the ability of the aggressor country’s military-industrial complex to compensate for losses.
Serial production of the Su-34 is concentrated at the V.P. Chkalov Novosibirsk Aviation Plant, which is part of the United Aircraft Corporation of the Russian Federation. The production capacity of this facility allows for the manufacture of approximately 14–18 aircraft of this type per year.
The priority is the production of modernized Su-34Ms, which feature improved onboard equipment and expanded capabilities for the use of airborne weapons. The modernization is intended to enhance the aircraft’s effectiveness, taking into account combat experience gained during the war against Ukraine.
At the same time, production resources are divided between the needs of the Russian military and export orders. In particular, part of the production capacity is dedicated to fulfilling a contract to supply Su-34ME aircraft to Algeria. This places an additional strain on the production system, forcing Russia to balance replenishing its own air fleet with fulfilling international contractual obligations.
“However, between October 22, 2025, and October 22, 2026, 22 new Su-34s were delivered to the Russian Aerospace Forces. This figure exceeds the estimated annual production volume by 14–18 aircraft,” the Main Intelligence Directorate reports.
Intelligence data indicates that during the initial phase of the full-scale invasion, the Russians used the Su-34 primarily to bomb ground targets with unguided aerial bombs, including the FAB-250, FAB-500 M-62, and the concrete-piercing BetAB-500. The use of such weapons required the aircraft to fly close to their targets, which increased their vulnerability to Ukraine’s air defense systems.
At the same time, the enemy began using the Su-34 as a platform for the Kh-31 and Kh-59 guided air-to-air missiles, as well as, in some cases, the Kh-35U anti-ship missiles to strike ground targets.
As noted by the Main Intelligence Directorate, fundamental changes in Russian aviation tactics occurred with the widespread introduction of aerial bombs equipped with a standardized guidance and correction module. The combination of the Su-34 with relatively inexpensive UMPC kits became one of the key factors in the aggressor country’s buildup of its strike aviation capabilities.
These guidance and correction modules enable Russian invaders to convert significant stockpiles of conventional aerial bombs into guided munitions suitable for use from a distance, thereby reducing risks to the carrier aircraft, as the Su-34s can remain outside the engagement ranges of certain Ukrainian air defense systems.
The use of Su-34s in Russia’s “scorched earth” tactics leads to large-scale destruction of infrastructure, civilian casualties, and the forced displacement of survivors from frontline communities.
According to intelligence data, the Russian aircraft manufacturing industry remains dependent on a complex supply chain for electronic components, high-tech equipment, and specialized materials. Of particular importance are components for avionics, navigation systems, communications equipment, and electronic warfare systems, as well as industrial and measuring equipment necessary for the manufacture of modern aircraft.
International sanctions are hindering Russian manufacturers’ access to certain critically important technologies. Under these conditions, the aggressor country continues to use schemes involving intermediary entities, third countries, and alternative import channels to meet the needs of its military-industrial complex.
“In this regard, intensifying sanctions pressure on Russia remains a pressing issue. Specifically, this involves the ability to block mechanisms for circumventing sanctions, strengthen export controls, and restrict Russian companies’ access to critical production technologies for the Russian aircraft manufacturing industry—technologies that allow Moscow to continue its genocidal war against Ukraine,” the Main Intelligence Directorate states.
As reported by Ukrinform, in October, the Russian army suffered record casualties on the front lines.

Dream cruise derailed as fuel crisis puts pressure on global operators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:23:23 UTC
11:23:23 KST

Australian passengers in financial limbo after Odyssey cruise ship runs out of money
In short:
Australian retirees are among passengers caught up in a luxury cruise ship's financial crisis.
Soaring fuel costs have been blamed after the vessel became stranded in Cambodia.
What's next?
Anxious passengers are waiting for answers about the ship's future and whether they will get their money back.
A Queensland woman has handed over $63,500 from her superannuation for a dream retirement at sea — only to watch it unravel before she even stepped onboard.
Lisa McKay was weeks away from joining the luxury residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey when she discovered passengers had been forced off the vessel in Cambodia after it ran out of money.
The former teacher said she feared she would never see her money again after paying for a voyage she hoped would transform her retirement.
"This was going to be my trip of a lifetime," Ms McKay said.
"I don't have that money to waste and lose. It's just been devastating, absolutely devastating."
On Tuesday, more than 200 passengers were told to pack their bags during a scheduled stop in the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville, with the company no longer able to cover the costs of operating the cruise.
The US ship set sail from Belfast in 2024 on a three-and-a-half year round-the-world voyage, promising residents visits to 425 destinations across 147 countries.
"Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement.
Brisbane passenger Rina Cavazza is among those left scrambling to find accommodation and make arrangements to leave Cambodia after being forced off the ship.
Ms Cavazza, who paid $170,000 to live aboard the Odyssey, still had 18 months remaining on her voyage when passengers were told to disembark.
She is now staying in a local hotel and is making arrangements to return to Brisbane.
"It's been a sad time for many," Ms Cavazza said.
"We have had no word and no idea what is happening. I just know that this is our last day of access to the ship and I'll have one opportunity to go back and collect my belongings."
Questions about finances
The bulk of passengers onboard the Florida-based ship were from the US and Canada, according to the Cambodian government.
Some had sold their homes to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars for the years-long cruise, marketed as an alternative to retirement options.
Ms Cavazza said passengers were asked for funds to help pay for fuel, as far back as February and again, just before docking in Cambodia.
"Some people paid hundreds of thousands of dollars extra to help out with fuel," Ms Cavazza said.
Ms McKay, a former Brisbane school teacher, said she used her superannuation to pay for the trip via a direct bank transfer, and was due to board in Kuala Lumpur on November 15.
She said she had concerns about the company's finances after reading negative comments online and raised them with a booking agent, before paying.
In messages seen by the ABC, the booking agent said she "wouldn't be working for them if [she] thought they were in trouble" and that if the ship could no longer operate, the "company would arrange another ship".
"My chances of getting my money back [are] very, very slim," Ms McKay said.
"Travel insurance doesn't cover boutique ships."
Sign of things to come
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences said monthly fuel costs per cabin had averaged about $US1,800 but were now $US6,000 to $US8,000 in parts of Asia, due to the ongoing war in Iran.
"The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents, and the resulting shortfall has placed its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure," it said.
It is not the only cruise company feeling the fuel crunch.
The world's largest cruise operator, Carnival Corporation, said higher fuel prices had added about $US150 million to its 2026 outlook.
The company recently announced it was halving its fleet in Australia next year.
Other major cruise operators such as Disney and Royal Caribbean no longer operate full-time in Australia.
Royal Caribbean said its fuel costs rose 27 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, from $US279 million to $US355 million.
