NEW DELHI: How much time do teaching doctors spend away from hospitals, and what happens to patient care and classes when they do? The Centre is seeking detailed records from three Delhi medical institutions as an expert panel reviews summer and winter vacations for govt medical colleges faculty.An expert committee constituted by Union health ministry to examine vacation and academic/on-duty leave arrangements for Central Health Service (CHS) teaching doctors had held its first meeting on Aug 31, according to official documents.
The ministry sought information from Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, ABVIMS and Dr Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, and Lady Hardinge Medical College and its associated hospitals. A reminder issued on Sept 28 said the required information had not been received. On Oct 28, RML Hospital directed heads of clinical departments to submit verified data within two days.The prescribed format seeks details of faculty strength, the duration and actual dates of summer and winter vacations, the number of doctors allowed to take leave at a time, and the deployment of non-teaching doctors and residents during vacation periods.
Institutions must also provide monthly data on outpatient attendance, admissions, ICU occupancy and surgeries for 2024-25 and 2025-26.The committee will assess whether the existing 50% faculty roster ensures uninterrupted patient care and whether vacations affect undergraduate and postgraduate teaching, examinations, research and academic administration.Sources alleged that some doctors combine vacations with academic leave and child care leave (CCL), extending their absence from work. One doctor was alleged to have taken academic leave nearly 100 times over the past 10 years, often for foreign visits. These allegations could not be established from the official documents and require documentary verification and a response from those concerned.
Sources also questioned whether faculty in certain central govt medical colleges face vacation and administrative rules that are not applied in the same way at institutions such as AIIMS, PGI and UCMS. The extent of any differences in the applicable rules remains to be established.The ministry is also seeking details of outcomes from academic/on-duty leave, including research publications, grants, new projects, teaching initiatives and clinical skills acquired. Institutions have been asked whether doctors must submit reports after availing such leave and whether the outcomes are monitored.The documents do not announce any decision to reduce or cancel vacations. The committee is gathering data to assess the existing arrangements.

Ukraine Pauses Strikes on Russian Refineries Under US Pressure Ahead of Midterms – WSJ

11:10:57 KST

Ukraine has suspended strikes on Russian oil refineries following weeks of pressure from US President Donald Trump, as Washington seeks to contain rising fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to a new report by The Wall Street Journal (WSJ).
The unofficial pause began in mid-October and could continue beyond the US elections into November, the newspaper reported Thursday, Oct. 29, citing people familiar with Ukrainian military operations.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukrainian units conducting long-range strikes were instructed to suspend new missions against Russian refineries after completing operations already underway.
The decision came amid mounting tensions between Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky, with Washington increasingly frustrated by Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s energy sector as diesel prices reached record highs.
The reported suspension has not been independently confirmed.
30-day halt to refinery strikes
According to the WSJ, Trump’s adviser Jared Kushner pressed Ukrainian officials to halt refinery attacks for 30 days as a gesture of appreciation for Washington’s diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war.
Kyiv sought assurances that Russia would reciprocate by suspending its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure or that Washington would provide additional Patriot air defense missiles.
Neither proposal produced a breakthrough, the report said.
European allies also encouraged Ukraine to exercise restraint, amid concerns about rising fuel costs and further deterioration in relations between Kyiv and the White House.
Russia Launches Overnight Attacks Across Ukraine, Leaving Over 350,000 Without Power in Dnipro
The pressure intensified after Trump publicly criticized Zelensky earlier this month, calling for Ukraine to replace its president and demanding an end to strikes on Russian oil facilities.
“He better damn well stop,” Trump said on Oct. 10, referring to Ukraine’s refinery attacks, according to an earlier WSJ report.
The remarks came as Trump announced an arrangement to increase purchases of Russian diesel and ease sanctions affecting Moscow.
The developments raised concerns in Kyiv that Washington was reducing economic pressure on Russia while demanding restraint from Ukraine.
Russia continues striking Ukraine
The reported pause comes as Moscow continues its campaign of missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s civilian and energy infrastructure, raising fears of widespread power and heating disruptions ahead of winter.
Russian forces launched another wave of attacks on Thursday, Oct. 29, killing civilians and damaging infrastructure across several Ukrainian cities.
In Dnipro, a Russian drone struck a crowded railway platform, killing at least 14 people. Additional attacks struck Chernihiv and Kremenchuk, while a late-night ballistic missile strike on Kyiv killed at least one person.
The continued bombardment highlights the absence of a reciprocal arrangement under which Russia would halt attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in exchange for Kyiv suspending strikes on Russian refineries.
Ukraine has repeatedly defended its long-range drone campaign as a means of disrupting Russia’s war economy and responding to Moscow’s attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine’s domestically developed long-range drones have enabled strikes deep inside Russian territory, targeting refineries and other energy facilities far from the front lines.
The campaign has become an important tool for Kyiv to impose economic and logistical costs on Russia despite its smaller military and limited access to Western long-range weapons.
Ukraine’s dependence on US support
The Journal reported that Ukraine’s reliance on American military assistance, intelligence-sharing, and communications technology has made Kyiv vulnerable to pressure from Washington.
The deterioration in relations coincided with restrictions on Ukraine’s use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service, which temporarily disrupted some Ukrainian drone operations and air defense capabilities before service was restored.
Ukraine also depends on US-supplied Patriot air defense systems and interceptors to protect cities and critical infrastructure against Russian ballistic missiles.
According to the Journal, the dispute has further weakened Ukrainian confidence in Washington’s commitment to supporting Kyiv.
Midterm elections and US peace efforts
The timing of the reported suspension coincides with the final days before the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, when high fuel prices have become a sensitive domestic political issue for the Trump administration.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising diesel prices, although energy analysts point to the war in Iran and broader disruptions to global oil markets as the main drivers of the surge.
The WSJ reported that the suspension could last beyond the elections.
The reported pause raises questions about why Ukraine is being pressed to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities while Moscow faces no comparable pressure to stop its relentless attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.

WELLINGTON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Nearly 3.8 million people have enrolled to vote in New Zealand's 2026 general election scheduled for Nov. 7, with the provisional enrolment rate at 93.6 percent, below the final rates recorded in the previous two elections.
The Electoral Commission said on Friday that the enrolment rates were 94.7 percent in 2023 and 94.1 percent in 2020. The final rate for this year's election will not be confirmed until after voting ends.
The provisional enrolment rate for people aged 18 to 24 was 74.2 percent, up from 53.9 percent at the end of July and close to the 76.7 percent recorded in 2023, the commission said in a statement.
Among voters of Maori descent, the provisional enrolment rate was 85.9 percent, with 603,968 Maori voters enrolled, up from 567,012 in 2023, according to the commission.
Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne said the figures showed awareness of the new requirement to enroll before voting began. He said the commission would review its efforts to increase enrolment and report back to parliament after the election.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's center-right National Party is seeking a second term after taking office in 2023, while Labor, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins, is campaigning to return to power amid public concerns over the cost of living, economic growth, jobs and public services.
Meanwhile, 309,876 people cast advance votes in the first three days of voting, which started on Monday, up from 235,515 in the same period in 2023, the commission said.
More than 2,300 voting places are expected to operate nationwide on election day. Official election results are scheduled to be declared on Nov. 27.
New Zealand citizens or permanent residents aged 18 or above, who have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more at some time in their life, are eligible to vote in the election, according to the commission. ■

Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:07:19 UTC
11:07:19 KST

Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that three bizarre deep-sea fish that look exactly like seahorses actually belong to a separate evolutionary group, proving that nature created the same unusual body shape more than once. Nicknamed "sea muppets," these elusive creatures are known from just seven specimens, and no one has ever seen one alive.
- Share:
At first glance it looks exactly like a seahorse. It has the same horse-shaped head tilted down from the body, the same curled and grasping tail, and in the males a fully enclosed pouch for brooding the young.
But this little fish, no longer than your thumb, is not a seahorse, as we report in our new study published in the Journal of Lost Species. This is Australyichthys aegis, a newly described fish from the deep reefs off southern Australia. We have given it the common name helmethead sea muppet, after the domed, helmet-like crest on its head.
Its scientific name follows the same idea: in Greek mythology the aegis was a protective shield. Together with its two relatives, the bullneck sea muppet (A. minotaur) and the paradoxical sea muppet (A. paradoxus), it makes up a small group we nickname the sea muppets.
All three, we have now shown, belong on their own branch of the family tree. The seahorse look has arisen more than once, and these fish are a case of it evolving well away from the true seahorses. That evidence had been sitting in museum drawers, misfiled, for decades.
Bycatch from the deep
You will not find these fish while scuba diving.
Every known specimen was brought up by accident, caught in trawl nets or dredges working the seafloor between about 50 and 125 meters down. The single specimen of A. aegis came up in 2006 near the Gambier Islands, at the mouth of South Australia’s Spencer Gulf.
The dredge that caught it was sampling for small shelled animals known as brachiopods during a natural history expedition. Because that expedition was after invertebrates, the fish was mistakenly catalogued into the invertebrate collection of the South Australian Museum, where it sat unrecognized for years.
After each chance capture the fish were preserved, then largely forgotten. The rest are held in Australian museum collections, among them the Australian Museum, Museums Victoria and CSIRO.
The whole genus is known from just seven specimens gathered over about 65 years, scattered across more than 2,500 kilometers of coastline, and nothing has been collected in nearly two decades.
Irreplaceable specimens
The specimens are irreplaceable, so we could not dissect them. Instead we used micro-CT scanning, the same X-ray technology used in hospitals but fine enough to resolve tiny bones.
That let us build three-dimensional models of each fish’s skeleton and compare them bone by bone with true seahorses (Hippocampus).
Every earlier assessment had rested on external appearance, and the skeletons did not support it. Seahorses have a particular internal architecture, including a rigid cage of fused bony plates supporting the belly and a bony crown, called a coronet, on the head.
Our scans showed that Australyichthys has neither. In their place is a different arrangement of bones supporting the belly, one that appears in no seahorse.
Only one specimen could give us DNA.
A. aegis had been fixed in ethanol rather than formalin, the only member of the genus stored that way, and ethanol leaves genetic material intact. Sequencing it placed the fish well outside the seahorses, on the branch that is their closest relative. The genes said what the bones had already said.
All three species had been placed in the seahorse genus on the strength of how they look, and on that evidence they were seahorses. They are not, and they needed a genus of their own. We named it Australyichthys, from the Latin for southern and the Greek for fish.
A shared way of life
When separate lineages evolve to look alike, biologists call it convergent evolution, and it usually reflects a shared way of life rather than shared ancestry.
The whole seahorse body, with its bent head, gripping tail and brood pouch, has been built at least twice within a single fish family, the Syngnathidae, which includes seahorses, pipefishes, pipehorses and seadragons.
Working out how that happened may reveal why evolution keeps arriving at the same solution.
All this happened along the Great Southern Reef, the connected system of kelp forests and rocky reefs that rings southern Australia. Many of its species are found nowhere else, and its deeper zones are barely explored.
In fact, an entire genus of vertebrate hid there, misidentified, until a CT scanner settled the question.
No one has ever seen one of these fish alive; they have turned up only by chance in a passing net or dredge. On that record they now qualify as lost species, known from a handful of preserved animals and never from a living one.
Calling them lost is not a prediction of extinction. It marks them as a priority for targeted surveys that go looking rather than waiting for the next accidental catch. They are most likely still down there, in a part of the sea we hardly ever visit.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Graham Short and David Harasti. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Hackers exploit PHP flaws to seize servers in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:06:26 UTC
11:06:26 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan was among the targets of a recent hacking campaign that exploited PHP flaws to seize servers, according to a new report that says the operation bears signs of a nation-state effort.
Israeli AI firm Dream released a report Monday detailing how an AI-assisted campaign in October identified and took full control of 25 Palo Alto Networks firewall and management servers across Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and the US. The report said the selection of targets indicated “potential nation-state adversary efforts,” adding that the four countries are China’s primary geopolitical rivals.
The campaign exploited PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP that prompted Taiwan’s Administration for Cyber Security (ACS) to call for software updates across government agencies and businesses last week. The vulnerabilities in the programming language allow attackers to execute code remotely without authentication.
In the latest campaign, 22 compromised firewalls across the four countries were left with hidden backdoors that allow return access and are “ready for exploitation at any time.” Three servers in a US government-affiliated environment were singled out for deeper intrusion.
Taiwan’s ACS said Friday that companies have been fixing their systems and updating PHP in light of the critical flaws.
Dream did not attribute the activity to a specific actor but pointed out that the operation ran on China Standard Time and that the attackers used FOFA, a Chinese search engine, to find targets.
The report also found signs that hackers used AI tools while developing code, including an installation of Claude Code and settings configured for the Chinese language models DeepSeek and Kimi.
The findings follow what experts said may have been the first known end-to-end autonomous cyberattack against Taiwan’s government systems using AI. Dream, which exposed that operation in August, said at the time that evidence “points to a Chinese-language operator.”

====================================================================================================

Loving someone with dementia is hilarious and heartbreaking in new show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Before I Forget celebrates humour, aging and Blak matriachy on the main stage
As Kamarra Bell-Wykes's mother's dementia worsened, the playwright began developing what would eventually become Melbourne Theatre Company's latest play, Before I Forget.
The Yagera/Badtjala/Butchulla theatre-maker's mother was Jeanie Bell, a prominent Aboriginal linguist and academic who played a critical role in language reclamation. She has since passed, but her presence looms large in the play.
"Sometimes I could just hear mum talking to me as I was writing," Bell-Wykes tells ABC News.
The story centres on three women: Faith (Roxanne McDonald), based on her mother; Faith's daughter Karma (Melodie Reynolds-Diarra); and her granddaughter, Hope (Tyallah Bullock).
The names poetically hint at their character arcs and mirror the intergenerational connection between Bell-Wykes, her mother and her daughter.
Translating personal truth into fiction
Bell-Wykes brought together a trusted team of creatives on stage and behind the scenes to add a familial feel to the production. McDonald, who plays Faith, knew Dr Jeanie Bell and translated some of her mannerisms into the character.
"When you're an actor, you study people, whether you do it in a conscious or unconscious way," says McDonald.
"Jeanie just embodied the community and took everyone in. I just remember her laugh. It brings back all these beautiful fond memories back for me."
Bell-Wykes also has long-standing friendships with Reynolds-Diarra and frequent creative collaborator Carly Shepherd, who is the assistant director.
She candidly admits directing was a "black-mirror experience"; she had to be well past her grieving process to enter that metaphorical and physical space.
Despite the play grappling with death, Bell-Wykes found ways to inject humour into the dialogue; her mother's larger-than-life personality provided ample material for laughs.
"Particularly for Blackfullas, humour is a natural part of our communities, our lives. We use it as a survival mechanism; we are naturally funny people," Bell-Wykes remarks.
"Dementia is a hilarious, heartbreaking disease."
The challenge was to navigate how much of her own personal truth to embed into the characters and stories, and what aspects to dramatise, while still making it feel authentic.
"How do you protect the people that are passed and are still alive, while also telling a good story? It's been a very slow, careful process," Bell-Wykes says.
Matriarchy, motherhood and preserving legacy for future generations
Jeanie Bell's significant legacy in preserving Aboriginal language is imbued through integrating Butchulla and Gubbi Gubbi dialogue in the play.
Reynolds-Diarra describes the impact of Dr Bell's work on future generations with admiration, ensuring the community could proudly speak their language on Country again.
"She was more than just the typical matriarch of the family; she was also preparing her community with tools that could help them in the whiter societies," says Reynolds-Diarra.
"My mum's legacy does exist in a written form, and I have been reconnecting with my matriarchal knowledge through the process of this play," Bell-Wykes shares.
Since colonisation, Aboriginal women have been essential to keeping families together and on Country, which can also be a source of intergenerational trauma.
When mothers pass away, families can drift apart. Grandmothers also play a pivotal role in raising children, with Bullock, McDonald and Reynolds-Diarra noting the influence this had on their upbringing.
"I think within that direct lineage from the grandmother to the grandchild, there's something that's passed down specifically through that; I suppose it's the strength," says Reynolds-Diarra.
"Even with my mum being passed away, she is now teaching me language and teaching my daughter," says Bell-Wykes.
Bullock notes the role that Elders play in communities, particularly in relation to younger generations — represented in the character of Hope.
"It's taking authority of your culture and actually embodying it, finding ways that you've grown up knowing about it, but then taking courage and steps to actually go beyond that, follow your ancestors," says Bullock.
An Indigenous play with a universal story
Caring is a core part of the story, and the cyclical nature of it. How do you care for the ones that once cared for us? Despite the play focusing on an Aboriginal family, the universal themes of mothers and daughters, as well as loss, will connect to audiences from all walks of life.
"This play is about our daughters becoming our mothers and our mothers becoming our daughters. But that's also part of our kinship systems. Our grandmothers come back as our grandchildren … even though our little ones are there to learn from us, they are also there to teach us," says Bell-Wykes.
Loading...
"This is a universal story about love and acceptance and forgiveness; of death, and celebrating the lives that we have and always taking that knowledge with us."
Bell-Wykes responds directly when asked how her play will take audiences on an unforgettable emotional journey.
"Get 'em laughing, punch 'em in the guts."
Before I Forget is at Melbourne Theatre Company until November 28.

Kyiv • UNN

Another information operation aimed at inciting anti-Ukrainian sentiment and worsening relations between Ukraine and Poland has been detected in the Polish segment of social media. The Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD) reports, UNN informs.
Details

They point out that the presentation style and use of AI to manipulate public opinion are consistent with Russian information operations previously detected in the Polish information space. The Russian trail is also indicated by calques from the Russian language in the voiceovers of the videos.

US Democrats push anti-corruption message in midterm homestretch
- Democrats are using anti-corruption attacks to win midterm votes, with Barack Obama saying Trump is focused on “enriching himself and his family and his cronies”.
- A Gallup poll found 89% of Americans think government corruption is widespread, the highest level in 20 years, and Democrats hope to link this anger to high prices.
- Trump faces scrutiny over business ties, stock trades and gifts, but none has caused a backlash like Watergate, raising questions about public tolerance and media attention.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Nearly nine in 10 Americans believe government corruption is widespread – a consensus Democrats hope to capitalise on as voters make up their minds on whether to keep billionaire Donald Trump’s Republicans in power.
Former president Barack Obama has hammered the message home in recent days as he stumps for Democratic candidates in must-win states, hoping to flip control of Congress.
Trump “is very much focused on enriching himself and his family and his cronies”, Obama told a rally on Oct 28 in Georgia.
“The guy has made billions of dollars while in office.”
“We have never seen a president so intent on selling favours like this,” Obama added, echoing a speech he made days earlier in Michigan, another swing state.
Ray La Raja, a political science professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, said Democrats’ goal with such anti-corruption rhetoric is partly about “energising the base” of steadfast Democrats to make sure they vote.
But it also aims to create a “narrative to get those swing voters, those persuadable independents” who are generally upset about the economy, to “come out” on Nov 3.
Some Republican voters also “might be so demoralised, they won’t show up”, La Raja added.
Who’s to blame?
Democrats head into the midterm elections with high expectations, as the party of a sitting president historically loses seats – Trump’s approval ratings are at record lows – and there is broad discontent over high prices.
Meanwhile, a Gallup poll released in September showed 89% of Americans believe there is widespread government corruption in the United States – 10 percentage points higher than in 2025 and the highest level in 20 years.
The spikes in perceptions of corruption were most elevated among Democrats, according to the poll.
La Raja said that the most important issue for voters, always, is economics, and most people now believe those conditions are not good.
“And they’re looking for why. Who’s to blame for this? And corruption is one of those narratives that works,” he said.
Democratic leaders hope to funnel that anger at soaring petrol and grocery costs toward Trump, while highlighting, like Obama did, that the President’s net worth has risen by billions of dollars since he began his second term.
“There’s a direct link between the unbelievable levels of corruption and the continued rise in the cost of living,” Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat, said in September.
Trump has also repeatedly accused his political opponents of wrongdoing, though his attacks primarily focus on alleged election fraud.
He has denied any conflicts of interest or that he has been involved in his family’s business deals since taking office.
Watergate?
Nonetheless, he openly blurs the lines between government and personal business – a prime example being the choice of his own golf resort to host an upcoming Group of 20 summit.
He has also faced scrutiny over his historically high number of stock trades, contracts being inked by his family around the world, and the peculiar gift of a free luxury jet by Qatar to be used as Air Force One.
But none of the scandals with whiffs of corruption have so far triggered sensational backlash comparable to the Watergate saga, which led to Richard Nixon’s resignation in 1974.
Could Trump be getting a pass due to his businessman background, or are there deeper shifts in how the public and media perceive alleged corruption?
Trump’s vice-president, J.D. Vance, remarked that had such a scandal as Watergate occurred nowadays “it would be like a 12-hour news story”.
“The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy,” the likely 2028 presidential contender added. AFP

Canada and Europe share challenge of diversifying without antagonizing US and China
Unknown

European Council President António Costa speaks alongside Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney during a roundtable with business leaders at the EU-Canada Summit in Montreal on Oct. 29, 2026. | Christopher Katsarov/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
MONTREAL — There’s one thing the European Union and Canada want to avoid with their new alliance: stoking new fury from Washington and Beijing.
Officials have been under pressure to check off everything they said they would do at the last summit and on Friday will unveil the areas they plan to focus on over the next year, as they intensify their transatlantic cooperation. But don’t expect a parade of new deals.
“Canada has objectives where they need our technology — so you can build a beautiful relationship if you focus on it,” one senior EU official told POLITICO about shared challenges in diversifying away from the U.S. and China. The official was granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive diplomatic negotiations between Brussels and Ottawa.
Advertisement
One of the core EU interests in Canada, the official explained, is a chance for the bloc to diversify its supply of critical raw materials and sources of energy to further reduce its dependence on China and Russia, respectively.
“They have most of what we need,” the official said about Canadian minerals. “There’s also a huge opportunity to bring Canadian fossil fuels and gas to the EU.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the controversy over whether the EU should label the relationship with Canada as an “associate membership,” saying on Thursday it was a sideshow to what’s been billed as a landmark summit.
Earlier this week, Germany, France, Greece and other countries opposed the definition in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal. That came after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put forward the “associate membership” label in September.
But Carney told reporters on Thursday that the new alliance wasn’t “a marketing exercise” and that the name doesn’t matter. “What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthen Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects — AI,” he said.
A tricky political road lies ahead as Carney and von der Leyen make moves to draw the EU and Canada closer in a partnership that doesn’t include its southern neighbor. They’ll need to tiptoe forward with an “association without accession” work plan in the last years of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s time in office.
Advertisement
Diplomatic balance
Montreal’s historic Fairmont The Queen Elizabeth hotel was a hub of summit activity on Thursday, beginning with a morning spectacle of von der Leyen heading out of the hotel in runners, taking staff out for a walking meeting. EU commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers sailed in and out of the hotel’s perfumed lobby, greeting colleagues.
Jet-lagged Europeans, along with Canadian officials and lobbyists, commiserated over what they saw as poor summit organization, spread across multiple locations.
The debate over membership semantics became a luncheon laugh line when European Council President António Costa endorsed Von der Leyen’s offer to Canada before joking the final designation is “subject to revision”
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas signs the EU-Canada Host Country Agreement with Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand in Montreal on Oct. 29, 2026. | Christinne Muschi/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
Then, between servings of frisée salad and roast salmon, Costa struck a diplomatic balance.
“Tomorrow, the European Union and Canada will launch an alliance for the future of Europe,” he said, invoking German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s preferred label and a term Carney has also used to describe the relationship. But Costa also backed von der Leyen’s “ambition” of Canada as an “associate member” of the EU, admitting the term might not matter in the end.
By mid-afternoon, Carney seemed to come around to the term, recognizing the work underway to deepen relations as “an alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member, between Canada and the European Union.”
Advertisement
The two sides are expected to announce a wrap on talks on a new digital trade agreement on Friday, ending negotiations that were launched in the spring. Other anticipated outcomes include an agreement between the European Investment Bank and Canada, geared to allow the bloc to fund Canadian critical minerals projects.
Eleven EU commissioners in town to “further an agenda” is no small accomplishment, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told reporters. “It’s a historic moment that we need to seize.”
AI and energy companies are expected to be major beneficiaries of an enhanced EU–Canada relationship, making the absences of European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and Canadian Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson noteworthy.
Zoya Sheftalovich contributed to this report from Montreal.

New York state police to take over sexual assault complaints at Cornell
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:50:32 CET
10:50:32 KST

By Daniel Trotta
Oct 29 (Reuters) - New York state police will take over future sexual assault investigations at Cornell University, Governor Kathy Hochul said on Thursday, in the latest fallout over the university’s handling of an alleged gang-rape on campus.
The announcement follows widespread criticism of the university’s conduct in the case and questions about why no criminal charges were filed after a woman identified only as Jane Doe said she was raped by members of a Cornell fraternity.
New York state police and Cornell University signed an agreement that sexual offense complaints, which normally fall under the jurisdiction of campus police, will be referred to state police for criminal investigation unless otherwise requested by the accuser, Hochul said in a statement.
“When someone reports sexual assault, they deserve to be heard, treated with compassion, and know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated,” Hochul said in her announcement.
Referring to the Jane Doe allegations as “horrifying,” Hochul said: “Survivors should be able to trust the institutions responsible for protecting them. We cannot afford to let them down.”
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said the agreement would “improve campus safety, restore confidence, and better support survivors of sexual assault,” noting that survivors would retain the option to have campus police, local police or sheriff’s deputies conduct the investigation.
“Cornell Police will assist state law enforcement partners with these investigations as requested,” Kotlikoff said in a statement.
Hochul previously named Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to reopen the criminal investigation into Jane Doe’s complaint, and a committee of Cornell’s board of trustees appointed former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct a review of the university’s response to sexual assault claims.
NO CONFIDENCE VOTE UNDERWAY
Jane Doe said she was drugged and gang-raped during a visit to the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, according to a civil lawsuit filed this year.
Fraternity members pressured her to take ketamine and sexually assaulted her over several hours while she was too intoxicated to consent, the suit alleges, naming seven former students.
Attorneys for the fraternity members have denied the allegations. Some of the attorneys have said the sexual activity was consensual, while others have disputed their clients’ participation in the events described in the lawsuit.
Although Cornell expelled or disciplined several of the students involved in the incident, no criminal charges were filed.
The lawsuit triggered widespread criticism of the university in Ithaca, New York, with students, alumni and advocates calling for greater transparency about how the school handles sexual assault claims.
Cornell’s Faculty Senate is currently moving forward with a vote of no confidence against the university administration. About 135 members of the governing body can vote on the non-binding resolution from Friday until November 6, the Cornell Daily Sun reported.
“The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” the resolution reads.
Kotlikoff called the faculty discussion and debate “an important component of Cornell’s shared governance” and said the university had taken measures including adding staff to its civil rights office, expanding sexual assault prevention education, and hiring staff focused on victim advocacy.
“We remain committed to listening, learning, and partnering with the Cornell community to create real cultural change and build a safer Cornell,” Kotlikoff said in a statement.
(Reporting by Daniel Trotta in Carlsbad, California; Editing by Tom Hogue and Sanjeev Miglani)

Trump DOJ issues subpoenas in California noncitizen voting probe, escalating pressure campaign
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:50:28 CET
10:50:28 KST

By Andrew Goudsward
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration has demanded records from California as part of a criminal investigation into alleged voting by noncitizens – escalating its battle with the largest US state ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election.
The Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received federal grand jury subpoenas last week seeking information about the agency’s methods for detecting “unlawful voting by aliens” and preventing such ballots from being counted, according to copies of the subpoenas seen by Reuters on Thursday.
The Trump Justice Department has heaped pressure on California over alleged noncitizen voting, filing a civil lawsuit against the state and sending a series of letters this month warning election officials that they risk criminal exposure if they do not verify voters’ citizenship status.
The subpoenas also seek records related to Los Angeles County’s response to those letters, according to the documents.
The demands are part of a nationwide effort by the Trump administration to identify cases of voter fraud, raising concerns among Democrats and other critics that Trump could use the issue to sow doubt about the results of the election, which will determine control of Congress.
“At every step, the US Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach,” Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement on Thursday. “Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law.”
It was not immediately clear if Logan’s office was the focus of the investigation.
LEGAL BATTLE
Though studies have repeatedly shown that voting by noncitizens is rare and has no impact on election results, the Trump administration has intensely focused on the issue.
The Justice Department has charged 156 immigrants with voting or registering to vote unlawfully in a pre-midterm push, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told reporters on Thursday. The agency has used subpoenas to state and local election officials to build such cases.
A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment on the latest subpoenas but said that California and the federal government “agree that noncitizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law.”
On Wednesday, a federal judge rejected a Justice Department request to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from a list of 20,000 voters the administration alleges are likely noncitizens. The DOJ has appealed the ruling.
Lawyers for California have questioned the reliability of the Trump administration’s immigration data and argued that the federal government does not have the authority to intervene in its elections.
Under the US Constitution, states administer elections and not the federal government.
Before ruling against the DOJ, US District Judge David Carter told agency lawyers at a hearing on Tuesday that the “court believes that it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately.”
(Reporting by Andrew Goudsward; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage and Stephen Coates)

El Niño-driven drought in Papua New Guinea a ‘national crisis’ as rivers dry up and local farms fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:45:56 UTC
10:45:56 KST

Extreme drought driven by an historic El Niño is affecting as many as 8 million people in Papua New Guinea, causing a cascade of issues from shortages of food and water, to electricity scarcity and schooling disruption.
An influential coalition that includes churches, trade unions and business groups has said the Pacific nation is in the midst of a “national crisis”, but there appears to be “no coordinated plan to protect vulnerable communities from the worsening impacts of El Niño.”
Residents and community leaders have told the Guardian that rivers and creeks have dried up and family food gardens – a vital source of food and income for many – have shrivelled. Schools and health facilities are being forced to close early because they lack sufficient water to provide basic services.
Emilly Meren, humanitarian projects manager at CARE International in PNG, said in rural highland areas families were rationing food to one meal a day – while food insecurity was leading to localised disputes between families.
“For women and girls, they are expected to do more to support their families,” she said, yet they were “the last to eat because they have to serve others first”.
“They have to travel three to four hours to source water and food and are exposed to a heightened risk of harassment. We are hearing stories of transactional sex happening in the community – exchanging sex for money or for food.”
The El Niño climate pattern is gaining strength in the tropical Pacific with forecasts suggesting it will be the strongest ever recorded with its impacts worsened by global heating.
Some parts of PNG have had less than a quarter of their usual rainfall since August.
The PNG National Weather Service declared the onset of El Niño in June but Kasis Inape, the service’s assistant director, said at that point, much of the country was already in drought and about 8 million people had been affected.
Inape said PNG was one of the wettest places in the world with rain fed by warm tropical waters, but the El Niño had seen those waters shift east “and we’re starved of rain”.
“Because we’re a rain-fed country, a lot of our people are subsistence farmers and they depend just on rainfall to survive and to feed themselves,” he said.
PNG’s wet season is between November and April and Inape said while some short term relief was forecasted, there were concerns El Niño would shorten the season.
“The place is so dry – just two months of rain is not enough to allow crops to grow and water levels to be comfortable,” Inape said.
In Morobe province’s Bulolo district, smaller rivers have dried up leaving families without access to water for drinking, cooking and washing.
Resident Theophil Zarack said many schools and health centres were operating for only half a day, with some clinics no longer accepting inpatients due to a lack of available water.
Martha Zureno, a resident in Leklu village, said: “All our rivers have dried up, including the one behind my house. Now, my children and I have to walk for miles every afternoon to fetch water for cooking and drinking from the other side.
“We have a well that we dug ourselves, but we only use that water for washing. All the crops in our gardens have dried up and died, and we cannot grow anything now.”
Zureno said that most of the local residents depend on panning for gold to earn an income, but without water, “even that has become increasingly difficult”.
Meanwhile, a destructive hailstorm in parts of Enga province earlier this month – not blamed directly on El Niño – buried sweet potatoes under ice, exacerbating the food scarcity issue, according to George Iki, president of the Sambe Unity Development Association.
In the capital Port Moresby, PNG Power has begun planned electricity blackouts after falling dam levels cut hydropower generation and said disruptions could continue for up to 10 months. The company was working to manage dam releases to protect the city’s water supply.
Peter Aitsi, a prominent PNG business figure and co-chair of the Community Coalition Against Corruption, said the government needed to carry out “proper assessments” of the unfurling impacts, particularly on rural communities.
Last month the group called the drought situation a “national crisis”, but according to Aitsi, urban centres have been mostly shielded from the impacts. That could change, however, with electricity blackouts and a shortage of fresh food from drought-stricken areas, he said.
Aitsi said the capital had been covered in a smoke haze in the past week from fires elsewhere on the island, and in Indonesia to the west, that scientists say have been fuelled by El Niño.
Prime minister James Marape has directed provincial and district authorities to prepare for a prolonged dry season, saying his government was examining financial arrangements to support disaster responses.
“Cabinet is looking at tailoring provisions of our financial instructions to make sure that districts and provinces are assisted to respond to disasters as they happen where appropriate,” Marape said.

Kazakhstan to train renewable energy specialists with AI skills
Kazakhstan has prepared five draft professional standards for specialists in solar and wind energy and green hydrogen production, with the documents expected to be released for public consultation soon, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Ministry of Energy.
On October 29, the Sectoral Council for Professional Qualifications in Renewable Energy met to discuss workforce training and development in the sector.
According to the Ministry, Kazakhstan is developing professional standards for the renewable energy industry for the first time. Based on an analysis of technological processes and labor market demands, five draft standards have been prepared covering key occupations in the sector.
The proposed standards outline qualification requirements for specialists involved in designing, building, commissioning, operating, and maintaining solar and wind power plants, as well as producing green hydrogen.
A key focus is on digital competencies, with the draft standards covering skills in digital monitoring, automated control systems, production data analysis, and the use of artificial intelligence tools.
The initiative is being carried out in line with Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov's directive to develop and approve 100 professional standards that incorporate artificial intelligence and digital skills.
During the meeting, participants also reviewed the 2027–2029 Sectoral Plan for Qualifications and Skills Development in Renewable Energy, which aims to prepare specialists for the industry's future workforce needs.
The five draft professional standards will soon be published on Kazakhstan's Open Legal Acts Portal for public consultation.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan had approved a comprehensive plan for the development of unmanned systems for 2026–2029.

New Analysis: Air Force Should Buy 250 Blended-Wing Tankers, as 2027 Demo Looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:41:16 UTC
10:41:16 KST

A new think tank analysis finds a hypothetical blended-wing body tanker could offer twice as much refueling performance as the KC-46A Pegasus and recommends the Air Force buy scores of them, as the service prepares to evaluate a BWB demonstrator next year and must juggle its future tanker plans with a host of other modernization priorities like fighters and bombers.
The report, released by the Hudson Institute on Oct. 27, makes the case that the Air Force needs a fleet of 250 advanced new tankers to meet the challenge of refueling operations in a potential conflict with China.
Traditionally during conflicts, the Air Force has launched tankers from uncontested airfields relatively close to bomber and fighter strike objectives. But the vast distances of the Western Pacific and the long reach of China’s missiles make that untenable, report authors Timothy A. Walton and Shane Dennin write.
By 2035, they note, Chinese forces will likely be capable of suppressing large-scale tanker operations from “the forward and many of the intermediate airfields that tankers normally rely on,” a capability that “could collapse U.S. air operations and heavily contribute to U.S. defeat in a war against the People’s Republic of China,”
The solution, they conclude, are tankers that can launch from farther afield and carry more fuel to the fight.
Blended-wing body aircraft blur the line between wings and fuselage for a design that is considered more aerodynamically efficient and has a large cabin/cargo space. The combination, the Hudson report concludes, means a “medium BWB can refuel more than twice as many force packages or refuel force packages more than twice as far as the KC-46A,” the report states. “At longer-ranges and higher offloads, the medium BWB can deliver up to five times as many operationally relevant increments of fuel as the KC-46A.”
Since 2023, the Air Force has been developing a BWB demonstrator/prototype program with startup JetZero, which is partnering with Northrop Grumman. That aircraft, dubbed Z4, is expected to make its first flight in 2027.
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed that the “blended-wing body project is currently active, on schedule, and meeting assembly milestones; the demonstrator’s first flight is scheduled for late 2027.”
JetZero has proposed a tanker variant, dubbed KC-Z4, though the demonstrator will not be a refueler.
The Air Force’s future tanker plans are not settled—the Eisenhower-era KC-135 fleet is showing its age, and officials have stressed the need for refuelers that can survive in contested airspace. At one point, they were exploring concepts through the Next-Generation Aerial Refueling System program, but they shifted gears in the 2027 budget request, saying they would focus on protection systems over a new aircraft.
Meanwhile, the service is still planning on buying up to 75 additional KC-46 Pegasus refuelers on top of the current program of record for 188. In May, the Air Force signed an agreement with Boeing to fix critical issues with the Pegasus, such as fielding an improved remote vision system that boom operators use to refuel other aircraft—a requirement that senior leaders have said must be resolved before the Air Force will sign the new contract extension to buy an extra 75 tankers.
The Hudson paper recommends the Air Force move forward with the KC-46 production extension contract. Then, assuming the BWB demonstrator evaluation goes well in 2027 and 2028, the service should direct fiscal 2027 research, development, test and evaluation funding to “mature medium-sized, long-range, high-offload capacity tanker designs, such as medium BWB,” the report states.
“Our proposed plan’s yearly tanker costs would require additional RDTE outlays in the late 2020s and early 2030s, but its total RDTE, procurement, and operations and support costs over 30 years could amount to $15.5 billion less than a plan that solely procured KC-46A,” according to the report, which compared acquiring and operating 250 Medium BWB tankers to the same number of KC-46s.
Retired Air Force Gen. Mike Minihan, who led Air Mobility Command between 2021 and 2024, said he saw the potential of the BWB demonstrator effort when it was conceived as a way to reverse the service’s neglect of tanker fleet modernization when compared to efforts to develop fifth- and sixth-generation bombers and fighters.
“One of my biggest concerns was the equilibrium of the strike force with the enabling force; I love B-21, I love F-15 EX, I love F-35, I love the [Collaborative Combat Aircraft], … but if we don’t invest in the enablers to make those things successful, we’re going to look silly on the modern battlefield,” said Minihan, who retired in 2024.
Minihan said his continued belief in the BWB design convinced him to become an advisor to JetZero earlier this year.
“It’s almost two times everything—two times fuel the efficiency, two times the amount of receiver service, two times quicker, two times the distance—I mean, it’s quite remarkable,” he said.
Douglas Birkey, Executive Director for AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, also noted the potential benefits of the BWB design.
“There is no question the Air Force needs new refueling capacity, and it needs to ensure that it can maximize offload range—you want to haul as much fuel as possible, not burn a whole lot on your way to the refueling track, offload as much as possible and then get back home,” Birkey said. “And the blended-wing body has definite, distinct aerodynamic advantages, being highly efficient to maximize that off-loader range.”
But Birkey said he is skeptical whether the Air Force can commit to a long-term funding plan for a next-generation BWB tanker in the current budget environment. The service’s $267.7 billion budget request in fiscal 2027 is $53 billion more than it 2026 budget, but even then, competing modernization priorities such as the sixth-generation B-21 bomber and F-47 fighter limited any investment in tanker fleet modernization. Buying a new fleet of BWB tankers would require even larger toplines of reliable funding over the next decade for the service.
“There’s got to be sustained long-term investment; this isn’t a one-year plus-up kind of investment. They need a decade’s worth of solid investment,” Birkey said. “They’re making up for so much underinvestment.”
For its report, Hudson evaluated the KC-46A, the Airbus A330 MRTT+, a medium-sized BWB design, a medium-sized reduced signature design, and a collaborative tanker aircraft—the latter two to theoretically shuttle tank from parent tankers such as the KC-46A at short-to-moderate distances. The KC-46A and A330 MRTT+ are medium-range, multirole designs while the Medium BWB is a long-range, high offload dedicated tanker. The medium BWB tanker is being designed to carry 300,000 pounds of fuel compared to the KC-46’s max capacity of 212,000 pounds of fuel. The A330 MRTT+ can carry 245,000 pounds of fuel.
Hudson concluded that the Air Force should take a holistic approach that includes:
- Prioritizing military construction and other funding to enhance capacity and resilience of its most important tanker airfields.
- Continuing to increase funding for command, control, and communications; self-defense; fuel transfer; and automation and autonomy mission systems for current and future tankers.
- Developing and procuring 250 medium-sized, long-range, high-offload tankers, such as the medium BWB, which could prove capable of standing in a moderate distance from threats.
The Air Force could begin fielding the new fleet of medium BWBs by the mid-2030s “for reasonable RDTE and procurement costs that align with projected budgets, and it could cost considerably less than simply buying more KC-46As,” the report states.
The report estimates that a mixed fleet with roughly 260 KC-46s and 250 medium BWB tankers would run $398 billion in totals costs over 30 years, while fielding an additional 250 KC-46s for a total fleet of 510 would cost $413 billion.
Both aircraft in the mixed fleet would complement each other, the report states: “Together, the force could succeed in its most stressing scenarios, as well as sustainably execute other operations across the world.”
Minihan said he agrees that the Air Force needs “bombers and fighters of fifth and sixth generation, but we generally don’t pay attention to the enabling force until it fails. … To think that we can take a four-generation gap between our strike force and our enabling force into combat with a near-peer adversary is a fool’s errand.”
Minihan said he was “on the record from my time in uniform as supporting” the medium BWB demonstrator effort. “It fits perfectly into the NGAS concept,” Minihan said. “Every pound of gas I save getting to the fight is a pound of gas I can give away to a fighter or a bomber.”

Apple’s main assembly partner Hon Hai Precision Industry expects its expansive global manufacturing presence will help it fulfil growing demand for the US company’s marquee foldable device.
The US company launched the US$2,000 (S$2,600) iPhone Duo earlier in October.
The limited in-store stock was sold out quickly, while some online orders were offered delivery at the end of January, marking some of the lengthiest delays for a new Apple product in the company’s modern era.
The Duo is now primarily assembled by Hon Hai, also known as Foxconn, in the Taiwanese company’s “iPhone City” campus in central China. The company also makes components for Apple in other facilities in China and beyond.
“We have over 240 sites in 24 countries all over the world, which enable us to have a timely supply to our customers’ demand whenever they need. So I’m quite confident that we can fulfil the demand,” Hon Hai’s rotating chief executive officer Michael Chiang told Bloomberg TV, when asked about meeting holiday season orders for the Duo.
Chiang added that he thinks AI will boost demand for consumer gadgets.
While Chiang did not refer to Apple or iPhone Duo by name, he plays a critical role in coordinating business between Foxconn and the US company.
When Apple chief operating officer Sabih Khan visited Foxconn’s facility in central China in October, Chiang accompanied him on a tour of the iPhone Duo production line.
Hon Hai chairman Young Liu has been fostering his potential successors through the rotating CEO programme. Chiang, seen as a rising star within Foxconn, assumed his new role in April.
Like many of its hardware peers in Taiwan, Hon Hai’s business has undergone a transformation in the AI era.
Apple used to account for more than 50% of its revenue, but that is no longer the case. Hon Hai’s cloud and networking unit contributed to 51% of its total sales in the second quarter, a sign that AI-related hardware is what is driving the company’s growth now.
Hon Hai is scheduled to showcase the latest Nvidia-powered server offerings on Oct 30 at its annual flagship event, and it is also expected to unveil its new electric vehicle line-up. BLOOMBERG

Player prepares for World Cup after career reshaped by injury
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:31:39 UTC
10:31:39 KST

The Physical Disability Rugby League World Cup is being staged alongside the men's, women's, and wheelchair tournaments.
It will be contested by Australia, England and New Zealand, with all games in Sydney.
What's next?
Australia faces England in the opening game tonight at Cabramatta Rugby Leagues Club.
There are many things to prepare for when playing a game of rugby league. How to break a line, gain an edge or pick a way through a defence.
You don't prepare for one unfortunate tackle to alter the course of your life forever.
In 2020, at the age of 18, while playing for the Narellan Jets in south-west Sydney, Bryce Crane was on the wrong end of a tackle and suffered permanent nerve damage and paralysis of his right arm.
Yet, there was only one thing on his mind.
"You don't really quite understand how much something means to you until it is ripped away," Crane said.
"It's weird to think about but I didn't think about my life, I just thought that I lost the game that I loved growing up playing."
For the love of the game
Crane was told not to worry about the sport. Now, he is preparing for a home World Cup as Australia's Physical Disability Rugby League (PDRL) star fullback.
Australia will host New Zealand and England in the three-team round-robin tournament which runs from October 30 to November 8 in Sydney.
"It's really exciting to get into the World Cup; we have had a few camps with the squad, so we are getting around knowing each other," Crane said.
It will be his second PDRL World Cup after he starred for Australia in the inaugural edition in 2022.
Despite Australia failing to win a game, Crane's performances earned him a spot in the Rugby League World Cup Dream Team, which also contained players from the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.
He was the only PDRL player in the team, and was named alongside fellow Australian internationals Josh Addo-Carr, Cameron Murray and Tarryn Aiken.
In the eyes of his teammates though, he does not just contribute to the team through his talismanic play.
Luke Vella, who is also an NRL assistant coach at the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, knows the hallmarks of a top-quality player.
"He is obviously very skilful and has a great ability to play the game, but he is very humble," Vella said.
"He is also very encouraging, there is times I know Bryce can make a break or make a tackle, but he puts others before himself quite often and encourages them and supports them along with their game."
Full circle moment
The final of the tournament will be held at the Sydney Football Stadium before one of the men's semifinals, the biggest stage the game has been played on so far.
Vella was injured at the ground while playing for the Bulldogs' under-20 side in 2014, and should Australia qualify for the decider, he will step onto that field for the first time in a playing role since then.
"It's funny, I haven't really thought about it too much to be honest," Vella said.
"Obviously the stadium got knocked down and rebuilt, it is a little bit different.
"I can't really describe what the emotions would be if we get there and I get the opportunity to play on the field again."
Vella's passion for the game quickly returned after his career-ending injury, and in 2019, he was named head coach of the Bulldogs' under-20s team, giving him a chance to push players to achieve dreams of making the NRL.
After coaching the team to the Jersey Flegg Cup in 2023, he earned his promotion to the first grade coaching ranks for the 2024 season, while balancing his return to playing.
He made his international debut for Australia against New Zealand in November 2024 in Auckland.
"When I got injured at 20, I fell back in love with it because it got taken away from me," Vella said.
"I love it because my thing for coaching is to develop players and help them achieve their goals, but then the competitive side, running around, throwing the ball around, a bit of contact too.
"All things rugby league, all come back to love."
For Crane and Vella, the pride in representing their country is palpable.
"At the end of the day, I'm not just representing myself, my family, my country, but I'm also representing people with all different types of disabilities," Crane said.
"I feel like that is a pretty cool thing to do."

SC said it is not inclined to completely ban firecrackers but warned authorities that orders are meaningless without ground-level enforcement
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday said it was not inclined to completely ban firecrackers, but there was no point in passing orders and directions every year unless authorities implement them on the ground.“It concerns every living being,” a bench of Justices M M Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale observed while hearing a matter on the bursting of firecrackers in Delhi-NCR.Additional solicitor-general Aishwarya Bhati told the bench about the measures taken by Delhi govt and Commission for Air Quality Management to deal with air pollution.“There is no point in passing orders and directions unless you give effect to them on the ground, otherwise, it becomes a mockery,” the bench observed, while stressing enforcement.While saying that it was not an adversarial matter, the bench observed that authorities have to take up the issue seriously and take action. “You have to really regulate it. Every year we are trying to balance it out but unless there is cooperation from everyone, it can’t be done,” it said.“We also understand the sentiments of the public. We are not inclined to completely ban, but don’t push us to take a very harsh stand,” the bench told Bhati.

Bhati requested the bench to grant three weeks to complete the consultation.The top court was hearing two petitions, including a suo motu case concerning air pollution in NCR covering issues like firecrackers, stubble burning and solid waste management. The other plea relates to a ban on manufacturing firecrackers.

Flagging the issue of enforcement, the amicus said there was no proper mechanism to assess whether the firecrackers which are being sold are actually green crackers.The bench had said that a middle ground would have to be found by specifying hours during which firecrackers could be used.

Trump administration renews bid to block Alaska election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:30:30 UTC
10:30:30 KST

Trump administration renews bid to block Alaska election results
The updated lawsuit cites a new report that Democratic operatives recruited a competitor to confuse voters and unseat a Republican incumbent.
The United States Department of Justice has filed a revised lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of a Senate race in the state of Alaska if Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan loses narrowly.
The updated lawsuit on Thursday comes just days before the November 3 midterm election, which will determine control of Congress.
The complaint accuses Democrats of trying to confuse voters by placing a candidate with the same name as Sullivan on the ballot.
Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-ups that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in Congress’s upper chamber.
Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is seeking to unseat Sullivan, a Republican ally of US President Donald Trump.
But a New York Times report on Wednesday alleged that members of Peltola’s campaign helped recruit a retired teacher, Dan J Sullivan Jr, to run for the Senate seat as a spoiler candidate, designed to draw votes away from the incumbent.
The Times report prompted a renewed legal push under the Trump administration to bar Alaska from certifying its election results, should Senator Sullivan lose.
The Department of Justice issued 40 subpoenas and document preservation requests as part of the revised complaint, the Reuters news agency reported.
Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy also ordered a criminal investigation into the allegations. Peltola’s campaign has denied involvement in Dan J Sullivan Jr’s bid for the Senate.
Prosecutors, however, have accused the Democrat and her allies of playing partisan tricks – and undermining voters as a result.
“They orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected,” Justice Department lawyers wrote in their amended complaint.
But the Justice Department’s lawsuit has raised concerns about election integrity and federal meddling.
Under the US Constitution, election administration falls to the states, not the presidency.
In June, Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled that Dan J Sullivan Jr could compete in the midterms, and the state’s election office has already taken steps to reduce confusion between the two Sullivans.
Recruiting candidates to split an opponent’s vote – a practice known as ballot stacking – is also generally considered to be legal and has been used by both parties in Alaska.
Critics have been sceptical of the Justice Department’s bid to pause the certification of Alaska’s Senate results if Senator Sullivan does not win re-election, noting it would be impossible to divine voter intent based on the final tally alone.
Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under President Joe Biden, also questioned what legal authority the federal government had to get involved in the case.
“I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DOJ would have jurisdiction over,” Levitt told the Associated Press news agency.
“Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”
Democrats and Republicans are locked in tight races nationwide that will determine which party holds a majority in the US Senate for the remainder of Trump’s second term in office.
Republicans currently hold a slim majority in the legislature’s upper chamber, with 53 out of 100 seats.
Democratic candidates are hoping to win seats by capitalising on Trump’s deep unpopularity and frustration over the cost-of-living crisis.
Trump has suggested he may not accept the midterm results if his party loses its majorities in Congress, and he has pushed false claims of widespread voter fraud.
The Justice Department has also attempted to challenge the voting process in several states, including California.

It called for international pressure to reopen roads and ensure that humanitarian assistance reaches civilians without obstruction.
The ministry warned that those responsible for attacks against civilians and their commanders would not escape accountability.
Taiz has been one of the main flashpoints in Yemen’s civil war, with government forces and Houthi fighters battling for control of the strategically located province for more than a decade.
The Houthi group has maintained positions around parts of Taiz since 2015, with restrictions on major access routes contributing to a prolonged humanitarian crisis.
Fighting has intensified in recent weeks as government-aligned forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition have carried out military operations against Houthi positions in Taiz and other provinces.
The escalation comes amid renewed hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with both sides reporting attacks and military operations across Yemen and the wider region.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) -- The U.S. economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment more than offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its advance estimate of third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.
Estimates ranged from a 1.0% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.
The strength in growth is in stark contrast to households' downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump's record-low approval ratings and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment. The report was published less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.
The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%. The U.S. central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."
Economists expected the Fed to raise rates in December. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters "economic activity is expanding at a strong pace," noting that "while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient."
Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation.
But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran drags on, economists anticipated a slowdown in consumer spending.

The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) launched an emergency appeal for at least $50 million to assist nine million people across Ukraine, Syria, Lebanon, and Afghanistan, where rising energy costs, shortages of heating fuel, and shrinking humanitarian funding are worsening conditions ahead of winter.
