====================================================================================================

Why the US economy looks strong but feels bad to many
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:20:00 UTC
10:20:00 KST

Why the US economy looks strong but feels bad to many
The US economic expansion is in its seventh year, and there is no recession in sight.
Unemployment and layoffs are historically low. Consumer spending data suggests that Americans are splurging on things like live entertainment, travel and eating out. The economy is growing at its fastest pace in a year.
However, by many measures, people are miserable.
A significant portion of Americans say it feels like the economy is stacked against them.
Polls indicate that they are stressed out about the cost of living, anxious about job security and pessimistic about their economic future. And do not even get them started on petrol prices.
Economic issues keep showing up as voters’ top concerns ahead of the US midterm elections on Nov 3. 
But are things as shaky as many say?
How much have prices gone up?
Americans confronted the hottest inflation in more than four decades in the years immediately following the Covid-19 pandemic.
They are still struggling with sticker shock. Prices continue to go up, though at a slower pace than a few years ago.
The basket of goods and services measured by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics’ consumer price index was 3.7% higher in September than a year earlier. That is less than half the 9.1% pace of inflation reached as the US emerged from the pandemic.
But it is still high enough for people to notice.
The steady rise in prices comes on top of the post-pandemic spike. 
Since the end of 2019, overall consumer prices are up by about 30%.
Groceries are 32% more expensive. Eating out is close to 40% more. Rents are up by more than a third. Electricity costs are up by 43%. Auto maintenance jumped by more than half and car insurance by about 48%.
How unusual are the price increases?
Prices are almost always rising, but usually not this fast. In the decade before the pandemic, annual inflation averaged around 1.8%. Now it is roughly double that.
That is in part because the economy faced a series of shocks that accelerated price gains.
Supply chains stretched and broke in 2021 after the global economy reopened.
Then Russia’s invasion of Ukraine choked off fertiliser, wheat and oil shipments, sending food and fuel prices higher.
The Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs spooked markets, and subsequent levies raised prices on many goods.
The buildout in artificial intelligence technology fuelled business investment and construction hiring but also sent prices for computer software and components higher.
And most recently the Iran war has led to higher energy prices and rising borrowing costs.
“Supply shocks have come more frequently, hit harder and lasted longer,” Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee said in a speech in London in September.
In an effort to tamp down inflation, the Fed in September raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, but left them unchanged at a subsequent rate-setting meeting in October.
How are Americans getting by?
Americans’ hourly earnings are, on average, up about one-third since the end of 2019.
But adjusted for inflation, pay has barely kept up with rising prices. And even the marginal gains Americans have made are beginning to evaporate.
Inflation-adjusted pay was down from a year earlier for six straight months as at September.
Even so, workers continue to spend – tapping a range of resources to do so.
Regular pay cheques are not the only source of income or wealth.
Some people work in the gig economy.
The stock market hit a series of records in 2026, lifting investor portfolios.
Home values have grown substantially over the past few years, and big tax refunds in 2026 boosted household budgets.
But wages are the main contributor to income for most Americans up until retirement.
Sluggish wage growth alongside rising prices has forced many to save less – or not save at all.
What is happening in the job market?
On the good-news front, plenty of people are earning a pay cheque.
The US economy is by many measures operating at or near full employment. The unemployment rate is historically low, though it edged higher, to 4.2%, in September.
Healthcare, construction and manufacturing have all been adding jobs in recent months.
And the labour force participation rate also rose in September, typically a positive sign that more people are looking for work.
But sector-specific strength and the low unemployment rate mask a sluggish job market.
Employers are not laying off many workers, but overall they are not hiring many workers, either.
That has left some people feeling stuck in place.
Glassdoor’s employee confidence index, which measures how optimistic workers are about the business outlook of their employer over the next six months, fell in September to the lowest level in the survey’s 10-year history.
Others are simply locked out. Entry-level college graduates have had an especially tough time cracking the job market, and the ranks of the long-term unemployed are growing.
So while there are pockets of strong demand, the overall job market is not hot enough to broadly lift real wages or create wide-ranging opportunities.
Who is feeling stuck?
A person who has a job is likely to keep it – layoffs are historically low.
US home owners who bought before the pandemic have watched property values soar.
And investors have done well. An index fund tied to the S&P 500 has more than doubled in value since the end of 2019, even if the gains have not been reinvested.
But when these milestones do not apply, it might be a sign of falling further behind.
Home ownership is one area of frustration.
The median sales price of an existing home is up by about half since the end of 2019, and rates on 30-year fixed mortgages have climbed to more than 7%, from less than 4%.
Excluding taxes and insurance, that equates to a payment that is roughly double what it was before the pandemic.
What role is AI playing?
Investment in artificial intelligence is one of the economy’s bright spots.
But that has been cold comfort for many Americans who worry that the technology will eliminate their jobs while its data centres swallow up land in their communities.
Capital spending on data centres could total US$5.5 trillion (S$7 trillion) cumulatively by 2030, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co.
Some 54% of Democrats and 37% of Republicans said they oppose construction of new data centres in the US, according to a June survey by Reuters/Ipsos.
“People are very concerned, either directly or indirectly, around what this is going to mean for their jobs,” said John Leer, chief economist at Morning Consult.
“It’s another way in which the rules and the structure of the economy seem to be changing.”
What actually is shaping consumers’ outlook?
Americans’ views about their economic standing tend to be shaped by more than just their personal finances.
Indeed, surveys show that individuals generally feel more optimistic about the economy when their party holds the White House. 
When their party is out of power, they become more pessimistic, even when their own situation is stable.
After Donald Trump was re-elected president in 2024, for example, consumer sentiment surged among Republicans and dropped among Democrats, even before his inauguration.
But since the start of 2026, measures of sentiment have slumped across political affiliation, geography and income, suggesting a wide swath of Americans harbour concerns about the economy. BLOOMBERG

WELLINGTON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand household living costs rose 3 percent in the year to the September quarter, easing from a 3.2-percent increase in the year to the June quarter, as higher petrol prices drove inflation, official data showed on Friday.
The increase was mainly driven by a 19.1-percent rise in petrol prices, which accounted for almost one quarter of the increase in average annual household living costs, according to Stats NZ, the national statistics agency.
Electricity prices rose 9.3 percent over the year, while local authority rates increased 6.2 percent, also contributing to higher living costs, Stats NZ said.
Superannuitant households, or households receiving New Zealand's government retirement pension, recorded the highest annual inflation rate at 4 percent, while higher-spending households experienced the lowest annual inflation rate at 2.5 percent among all household groups, it said.
By comparison, consumer price index (CPI) inflation, which measures overall price changes, was 3.7 percent in the year to the September quarter, down from 4.1 percent in the year to the previous quarter, Stats NZ said, adding that falling interest payments helped keep household living-cost inflation below the CPI rate, with interest payments for the average household declining around 10 percent over the year.
Meanwhile, international airfares rose 12.5 percent during the period, mainly due to higher fares to Europe and Asia, the agency said. ■

Polish president meets Supreme Court chief amid Constitutional Tribunal standoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:12:16 UTC
10:12:16 KST

Jo Harper
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Polish President Karol Nawrocki returned to Warsaw late Friday after cutting short a trip to Senegal and met Supreme Court First President Zbigniew Kapinski amid an escalating standoff over control of the Constitutional Tribunal.
Nawrocki landed shortly before 10 pm local time (2100GMT) after turning his plane around above Spain, saying the president had to be in Poland because of events at the court.
Kapinski earlier condemned the events at the tribunal and said disputes over constitutional institutions could not justify actions that paralyzed them or stripped them of authority.
He said the constitution and law set the limits of state power, “not political decisions or demonstrations of force.”
The confrontation remained tense late Friday as opposition politicians and demonstrators gathered outside the tribunal.
Law and Justice (PiS) leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski accused the government of preparing to use force against opponents and urged them to “win the battle for Poland.”
Piotr Duda, head of the Solidarity trade union, also sharply escalated the rhetoric, addressing Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski and Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek. “Do you want a war? Then you shall have one,” he said, calling on Solidarity members to gather outside the tribunal.
US Ambassador Tom Rose described the situation as “very serious” and said the two sides were presenting “diametrically different versions” of events.
“We may be witnessing an unprecedented confrontation concerning the government’s use of state power and the independence and authority of a constitutional institution,” Rose said.
He urged state officials, police and demonstrators to avoid actions that could provoke violence or further escalation, adding that Washington would not judge or interfere in Poland’s internal dispute.
The crisis also drew comment from Moscow, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova mocking Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski over the confrontation.
Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who said she had assumed control of the tribunal, indicated late Friday that Nawrocki could come to the court for talks, but only without accompanying officials.
She said conditions had been prepared for a meeting with the president, while rejecting the possibility of other officials entering with him because of security concerns.
Police remained deployed around the tribunal but said officers had not entered the building.
The standoff began after orders appeared to suspend Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and Vice President Bartlomiej Sochanski. The tribunal’s account on US social media platform X rejected the move as illegal and accused those involved of a “coup d’état.”

Family of real estate CEO wounded in Toronto home invasion, officials say

Family of real estate CEO wounded in violent Toronto home invasion, officials say; 3 suspects at large
A search is underway for three armed men who broke into a mansion in Toronto, Canada, belonging to a real estate CEO in the early morning hours Thursday and attacked and injured the family inside, authorities said.
The suspects, who were masked, forced their way through a back entrance of the five-bedroom home in the Bridle Path neighborhood at around 3:40 a.m. local time, wielding guns and a hammer, Toronto police said.
Once inside, police said they went to the second floor of the home and confronted 75-year-old David Morton, his wife, 64-year-old Doriana Morton, and their two adult daughters, Maggie and Cristina.
"There was a demand made for valuables from within the home," Toronto Police Service Inspector Kristy Smith told reporters. "Whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain at this point."
Police said David Morton, CEO of the MAC Group, and his daughters, ages 28 and 26, tried to fight off the intruders when shots were fired.
All three sustained gunshot wounds, Smith disclosed. And in a separate statement Friday, David Morton said that all four family members were also attacked by the suspects with the hammer.
David Morton said that he and his two daughters were still hospitalized Friday with gunshot wounds, but he did not provide details on their conditions.
"What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience," David Morton said in his statement. "... It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home."
The three male suspects, all believed to be in their 20s and wearing dark clothing, fled the scene in an SUV, police said.
"All these houses have good security," Cecil Hawkins, a former resident of Bridle Path, said. "So I'm kind of surprised. Shooting people in the house, it just seems mind-boggling."
According to Toronto police, there have been 119 home invasions so far in 2026, up 32.2% over this time last year.
Thursday's home invasion happened in the same neighborhood where a mansion belonging to rapper Drake was targeted in multiple break-in attempts in May 2024. A security guard for Drake was also wounded in a shooting outside the home at that time.
